15827-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
William Beverley Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, this number dated July 1, 1897. Sold at five cents, it gave young readers the week's news in words they could follow, plus science and serial stories. Premiums lure new subscribers: four new names earn a pocket Kodak, small enough to fit a coat. The paper's mix of news and prizes marks its age well.

News, nature notes, and tales fill the pages, with the world outside America kept in plain view. Editors explain treaties, wars, and inventions without talking down to children. A serial thread and picture notes keep the pace lively. Reading it now shows a hopeful American childhood: curious, busy, and told that the world could be known week by week.
16346-preface-to-the-works-of-shakespear:
Lewis Theobald's 1734 preface to his edition of Shakespeare's works gets a modern reprint here, with an introduction by Hugh G. Dick. Theobald, a pioneer editor, argued for careful collation of old texts and for fixing corrupt lines by reason and evidence rather than guess. His preface states the case for scholarly editing.

Issued in 1949 by the Clark Memorial Library as part of the Augustan Reprint Society series, the booklet serves students of Shakespeare's text. Short as it is, it marks a turning point: the editor as detective, hunting true readings through quartos and folios. Modern textual work still owes much to Theobald's lead.
24626-a-journey-to-america-in-1834:
Robert Heywood of the Pike, Bolton, kept this journal of a journey to America in 1834, privately printed at Cambridge in 1919 in one hundred copies. His route ran from Bolton to Liverpool, then by the packet Britannia to New York from 1 May to 8 June, and on by steamer and stage to Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington.

Heywood notes towns, people, prices, and manners as a Lancashire traveller saw them. His journal is plain, observant, and personal, the record of one man's America in the age of Jackson. Readers of travel history will enjoy its detail, and its picture of a young republic through English eyes.
5937-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Ducal business and Sancho's road fill chapters fifty-four through fifty-seven of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter fifty-four deals with matters relating to this history and no other. Duke and duchess resolve that Quixote's challenge to their vassal should proceed. The young man, however, has fled to Flanders to escape it. Chapter fifty-five follows Sancho on the road, chapter fifty-six a prodigious and unparalleled battle, and chapter fifty-seven Quixote taking leave of the duke.

Readers see the great household episodes winding down, as challenges, battles, and farewells replace daily pranks. The part favors closure and movement, letting knight and squire leave luxury for the road again. It suits readers following volume two toward Barcelona, since its leave-taking frees Quixote for his final adventures.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Martin Van Buren of Kinderhook, law student at fourteen, fills this third volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Born in 1782 to a small farmer, Van Buren read law for seven years before entering politics. The volume prints his messages and papers down to March 1841. Richardson's series keeps the official record of Van Buren's presidency in print.
a-popular-history-of-ireland-from-the-ea:
Thomas D'Arcy McGee's popular history appears here in its complete form, both volumes in one file, from the earliest period to the Emancipation of the Catholics. The publishers' preface frames the whole: a nation degraded and scorned, flashing at times with its old spirit. Book one runs from the first inhabitants and Christianity at Tara through the Danish wars to Brian at Clontarf.

Later books carry the English invasion, the Geraldine leagues, the Ulster confederacy, the Williamite war, the penal century, the rebellion of 1798, the Union, and O'Connell's long campaign ending in Emancipation. McGee, an Irish nationalist who became a Canadian statesman, writes narrative meant for the people's shelves. The complete edition lets a reader take the whole arc in one sweep.
act-of-supremacy-1534:
Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, during the reign of Henry VIII. The law declared the king to be the supreme head of the Church of England. With that step, England broke in law from the authority of the pope in Rome.

The act grew out of Henry's fight with Rome over ending his first marriage. It gave the crown power over church courts, appointments, and doctrine in England. Later monarchs kept, lost, and regained this title as religion shifted. The statute marks the legal start of the English Reformation, a change that remade English life for generations.
antony-and-cleopatra-pg1534:
William Shakespeare's tragedy is given here with a detailed contents table tracing its many scenes from Alexandria to Rome, Messina, Athens, and Actium. The scale is vast: palaces, camps, streets, and a galley at sea. Antony divides his time between Cleopatra's Egypt and the hard politics of the Roman triumvirate.

The five acts track Antony's drift from Rome, his marriage of policy to Octavia, his return to Egypt, and the sea fight at Actium. Defeat, shame, and pride bring both lovers to staged, splendid deaths. The scene list alone shows Shakespeare's method: short, swift scenes cutting between empires, until private love and public power destroy each other.
arxiv-2509-00134:
Cody E. FitzGerald and James P. Keener model whether predators can curb Chronic Wasting Disease in deer in 2025. The disease harms deer, elk, and moose and is caused by a prion, a misfolded protein that spreads harm. Prions persist in soil and other carriers for more than a decade, which makes the disease hard to control.

A bifurcation analysis, which maps where a model's behavior shifts, charts a simple spread model. A modified Gillespie algorithm, a random-step sim method, then tests predator use as an ecological control in varied scenarios. Further math shows that lowering the susceptible herd also helps curb outbreaks. A richer model with predators extends the check. Natural predation could join other tools against a stubborn wildlife disease.
arxiv-2509-00234:
Eojin Kim and Brian F. Farrell study Langmuir turbulence in the ocean surface layer in 2025 through statistical state dynamics. The ocean mixed layer governs fluxes of momentum, heat, gases, and particles between sea and air. Langmuir circulations are ordered rolls and streaks in that layer, aligned with the wind, and they shape those fluxes.

Their long-range order hints at a modal instability, yet surface wind stress alone supports no such instability in the mean flow. With velocity fluctuations present, from surface waves or background turbulence, two instabilities of the needed roll form do arise. The statistical method tracks how those patterns grow and persist. Clearer physics of surface rolls improves models of air-sea exchange.
arxiv-2509-00634:
Chaoyu Zhang leads a team of seven authors on trust in federated learning. In federated learning, many devices train one shared model. The server must trust each device's local training. Yet client data varies in natural ways. So bad updates are hard to tell from benign ones. Malicious clients can exploit this gap with Byzantine attacks.

The team proposes Sentinel to restore trust. Sentinel rests on remote attestation. That is a signed proof of what code ran on a device. Tracking code follows control flow and key variables during training. A trusted recorder sits in a protected hardware area. It signs a report that the server can verify. Only verified updates then join the global model. Tests on Internet of Things devices show low extra cost.
arxiv-2509-01934:
Nikolay Yegovtsev builds a solvable toy model of a heavy impurity inside a trapped gas of fermions. Fermions are matter particles that avoid sharing states, and a polaron is an impurity dressed by the gas around it. His impurity is infinitely heavy and touches the gas only on contact. Both sit in a harmonic trap, a bowl shaped hold that pulls particles toward its center.

Exact energy levels come from a single equation whose weak and strong coupling limits he solves step by step. He also gives wave shapes and overlaps between states with and without the impurity. From those results he finds the polaron energy and a contact style relation for the center density. A quasiparticle residue, which gauges how much bare impurity character survives, completes the picture.
arxiv-2509-02134:
Andrea Eirale, Matteo Leonetti, and Marcello Chiaberge teach robots social heuristics for human aware path planning. Social navigation research mostly targets obstacle free paths, polite distances, and motion prediction. True social acceptance needs norms that plain navigation cannot supply. Their method learns a value function that encodes the cost of social behavior.

That learned value acts as an extra heuristic inside a search based planner. Heuristic planning thus weighs social cost alongside distance and safety. The test scenario is joining a queue of people, a common social task. Early results support the methodology in that setting. The team intends to generalize the approach to further human activities.
arxiv-2509-02334:
Ryan DeWolfe wrote a 2025 solo paper on finding communities in network data without forcing every node into exactly one group. Real networks contain odd nodes that belong nowhere, and many standard tools ignore that fact.

DeWolfe borrows the first stage of HDBSCAN, a clustering tool for points in space that allows outliers. That stage redefines distances so simple single-linkage clustering, which joins nearest neighbours step by step, works well. He pairs it with several node and edge similarity scores and tests them on synthetic and real graphs. No pairing won everywhere. Still, results were strong enough to show the approach is a viable new direction for graph clustering with overlaps and outliers.
arxiv-2509-02534:
Tianjian Li and seven co-authors present a 2025 machine learning paper on a trade-off in language model training: polishing answer quality often narrows the range of ideas a model produces. That narrowing hurts brainstorming, storytelling, and open problem solving.

Their DARLING framework trains for quality and semantic diversity together. A learned partition function measures diversity by meaning rather than surface wording. During online reinforcement learning, that diversity signal is added to the reward for quality, so both goals shape each update. Tests span instruction following, creative writing, and competition maths across model families. Diversity-aware training beat quality-only rivals on quality and novelty at once. In maths, both first-try accuracy and variety across tries improved. The authors argue that chasing diversity actively fuels exploration.
arxiv-2509-02634:
J. T. Korley wrote a 2025 solo biostatistics paper on survival analysis under interval censoring, which arises when the moment of an event is pinned down only between scheduled check-ups. Standard tools for right-censored data do not apply directly and can bias results.

Korley compares three tiers of method. An expectation-maximization version of the Turnbull estimator recovers the survival curve with few assumptions. Accelerated failure time models, in Weibull and log-normal forms, add smooth covariate effects. Bayesian versions of those models supply full uncertainty and principled model choice. Simulations show the first method best for curve recovery, the second best for prediction when correctly specified, and the third best calibrated. An ovarian cancer example demonstrates the combined workflow.
arxiv-2509-03334:
Roshan S. Trivedi and 11 co-authors recreated lunar soil rims in the laboratory in 2025 using a synthetic solar wind. Space weathering darkens and alters the outer few nanometers of Moon minerals, and those rims let scientists estimate how long a surface has been exposed. How much of the rim comes from solar wind versus micrometeorite hits has stayed debated, especially for tiny metallic iron clusters inside the rims.

The team bombarded ilmenite, a common lunar mineral, with deuterium ions and low-energy electrons standing in for solar wind plasma. Microscopy and spectroscopy showed the artificial rims matched lunar samples in all main traits. They conclusively identified the nanophase iron and mapped it by depth and dose. From that map they estimated the solar wind exposure of a specific Apollo soil sample.
arxiv-2509-03434:
Elias Zikkos studied systems of power functions in weighted function spaces in a 2025 analysis paper. The system consists of powers x raised to an increasing sequence of exponents with gaps bounded below and reciprocals summing finitely. Such systems generalize the setting of Müntz's theorem, a classic result about when powers can approximate arbitrary functions.

Working on sets of positive measure in the non-negative half-line, Zikkos proves that every function in the closed span of the system has a Fourier-type series expansion in those powers. The coefficients come from a unique biorthogonal family, a partner system that picks out one power at a time. That makes the system a Markushevich basis for its closed span. Under extra boundedness conditions on the weight and shape of the set, the system is also hereditarily complete, and a moment problem is treated.
arxiv-2509-03734:
A 2025 computer science paper by Anders Aamand and three co-authors asks how fast a good statistical hypothesis can be found. In hypothesis selection, an algorithm sees samples from an unknown distribution and a menu of candidate distributions. It must output one whose distance to the truth rivals the best candidate on the menu, without wasting samples or time.

Known results fix how accurate proper algorithms, which must pick from the menu, can be. Improper ones may blend candidates instead. The best improper method reaches an accuracy factor but runs in time growing with the domain size, failing for continuous data. Blending candidates into a mixture gives a compact output that might restore speed. The authors prove no mixture-output algorithm beats a certain factor unless sample counts grow with the domain. They then give an algorithm running in polynomial time in the menu size, with that same factor.
arxiv-2509-03834:
Lucas Lopes Felipe and two co-authors view community detection through game theory, using the Constant Potts Model, in a 2025 research paper. Community detection splits network nodes into disjoint groups with dense internal links. The Constant Potts Model scores a partition with one global energy-like objective, and the Leiden algorithm optimises it.

The authors decompose that global objective into local utility functions, one per node, making the model a potential hedonic game. In such a game, each agent's gain from moving matches the global gain. Better-response dynamics, where nodes keep moving to better communities, then provably converge to an equilibrium partition in pseudo-polynomial time. Two stability criteria follow: a strict robustness notion, asking nodes to maximise internal neighbours and minimise external ones, and a relaxed weighted version steered by a resolution parameter. In tracking experiments, robust partitions seed the Leiden algorithm better than ordinary ones.
arxiv-2509-04034:
Antonín Knížek and two co-authors published a 2025 research paper that models the whole atmosphere of Jupiter in one system. Their single-column calculation joins deep layers, the cloud region, and the thin upper air. It tracks how gases react under sunlight and heat, and it adds sulfur reactions across that full span for the first time.

Checked against telescope data and earlier models, the system matches the planet's main observed chemical patterns. It correctly forms a mixed cloud layer where ammonia meets a sulfur compound. It also predicts where hydrogen cyanide, a carbon and nitrogen gas, should peak high above the clouds. That forecast can be tested by future observations.
arxiv-2509-04234:
Sanjaye Ramgoolam and one co-author, Michał Studziński, open a systematic study of walled Brauer algebras in their harder regime in a 2025 mathematics paper. These algebras organize mixed tensor representations, mathematical objects that mix a group action with its mirror version. They appear in string-theory-related models and in quantum teleportation calculations. When the size parameter N is large, the algebras behave tamely and formulas for their building blocks are known.

The authors move into the wilder regime where N falls short by a gap called l. Restricted diagrams carry known large-N data across into this territory. Inside a stable region, those diagrams depend only on the gap. Their counting is governed by an endless tower of simple harmonic oscillators, echoing a classic field theory.
arxiv-2509-04434:
Hyunsoo Cha and two co-authors animate portraits that borrow traits from other faces in a 2025 research paper. Their system, Durian, moves a target portrait while drawing attributes, such as hairstyle or accessories, from reference images of different people. Training such transfer normally needs paired examples of the same person with and without the trait, which rarely exist at scale. Their self-reconstruction trick splits ordinary portrait videos into pseudo pairs: one frame supplies the attribute, another supplies identity.

A dual reference network reads both frames separately, then fuses them through spatial attention inside a diffusion model. Complementary masking keeps each stream specialized. Mask expansion and augmentation bridge the gap to true cross-identity use. Multi-trait blending and smooth interpolation come free.
arxiv-2509-04634:
On the three-dimensional torus, a special kind of smooth map is built in a 2025 mathematics paper by Hangyue Zhang. The construction is a DA, a derived-from-Anosov diffeomorphism, meaning a smooth invertible map with expanding and contracting directions. Zhang's example has partial volume expansion, with a two-dimensional centre-stable direction.

The construction complements earlier work by Gan, Li, Viana, and Yang, who gave a non-invertible embedding in the same dimension case. Zhang notes the inverse map has a mostly expanding centre. Using a similar approach, he can also build a nontrivial mixed centre example, extending the known picture.
arxiv-2509-04734:
Many representation learning methods turn out to share one hidden loss function. Jasmine Shone, lead author with four co-authors, build on that finding in a 2025 paper extending the Information Contrastive framework. That framework showed many methods in effect minimise KL divergence, a measure of difference between distributions, whose one-sided shape and lack of a cap can make training hard.

The new framework, Beyond I-Con, lets researchers swap in other statistical measures and search in a planned way for better losses. Swaps improve clustering with no labels, contrastive learning with labels, and squeezing data down in their tests. The authors argue the choice of measure deserves direct care in representation learning.
arxiv-2509-05034:
Labelling defective pixels on industrial products is slow, and that bottleneck limits anomaly detection training. Jingqi Wu, lead author with five co-authors, propose ADClick in a 2025 computer vision paper. Their interactive segmentation algorithm creates pixel-wise anomaly annotations from just a few clicks by the user, plus a short text description.

Those annotations improve anomaly model performance sharply on a standard benchmark in their tests. A companion framework, ADClick-Seg, aligns visual features with text prompts through prototypes. It reaches leading results on the hard multi-class anomaly task in the authors' evaluation, combining pixel priors with language guidance.
arxiv-2509-05134:
Quantum key distribution receivers could shrink onto chips if single-photon detectors integrate well with waveguides. Joseph A. Dolphin, lead author with nine co-authors, build such hybrid receivers in a 2025 quantum communications paper. Superconducting detectors need cryogenic cooling, so the team use gated avalanche diode arrays that work without it.

They overcome array gating, inter-pixel crosstalk, and waveguide coupling challenges. Combined with low-loss silica waveguide chips, the arrays form compact receivers. Protocol experiments achieve secure key rates of megabits per second at short range and useful rates over a hundred kilometres of fibre in their tests, showing a scalable integration route.
arxiv-2509-05234:
Hot plasma that appears just before a solar flare could give earlier warnings, argue Anant Telikicherla and two co-authors in a 2025 space physics paper. These hot onset precursor events show up in soft X-ray light shortly before the main flare erupts on the Sun.

The team studies two flare samples, one from a solar X-ray spectrometer and one from a weather satellite sensor. Before the flare peak, temperatures rise and the amount of hot plasma grows sharply, while element patterns shift. A detection method built on these signs flags flares minutes before their peak. Earlier alerts could help radio operators and teams planning flare observations.
arxiv-2509-05334:
Measuring a badminton smash with an ordinary phone camera is the goal of Diwen Huang in a solo 2025 sports technology paper. Shot speed and angle give players useful feedback, but the gear that captures them has been costly and complex, shutting out amateurs.

Huang trains a compact object detector to find the shuttlecock in video and pairs it with a Kalman filter, a tracker that smooths noisy positions over time. A video-based method with space and time scaling then converts the tracked path into speed automatically. Everything is packaged in a simple mobile app. Affordable analysis of this kind could help recreational players train with the feedback once reserved for professionals.
arxiv-2509-05434:
Little Red Dots, a puzzling population of red active galaxies found by the Webb telescope, are far less luminous than first thought, Jenny E. Greene and twenty-nine co-authors report in a 2025 astronomy paper. Their odd energy output across wavelengths has resisted easy explanation.

Using X-ray through far-infrared data on two of the brightest known examples, the team measures total luminosity directly. More than half of it appears to emerge in visible light, while the X-ray, ultraviolet, and reprocessed infrared parts are all minor. Their new correction factors cut inferred luminosities roughly tenfold compared with published values. That lower scale implies much smaller black holes and eases several tensions about the early universe.
arxiv-2509-05534:
An enlarged version of the Standard Model of particle physics has its vacuum checked for stability by Apriadi Salim Adam, Yunita Kristanti Andriani, and Bayu Dirgantara in a 2025 theory paper. Their extension adds an extra global symmetry and a scalar sector with two doublets plus two singlet fields.

A richer scalar sector means many possible vacua, states of lowest energy, to sort through. The authors test whether the energy stays bounded below, whether a global minimum exists, and whether the theory stays well-behaved up to the Planck scale. Limits from invisible Higgs decay add an experimental check. A small region of parameter space passes every test with a stable vacuum.
arxiv-2509-05734:
A single trapped ion becomes a many-part cat state under non-linear control, in a 2025 quantum physics experiment by Matteo Simoni and nine co-authors. Schrödinger cat states superpose a system in several distinct states at once, and strong non-linearities make them hard to steer deliberately.

Working deep in the non-linear regime of the atom-light interaction, the team uses a new form of non-linear reservoir engineering. It generates localised cat manifolds with two, three, four, and five components. They then select Hamiltonians that allow measurements on those manifolds. The authors describe the work as a first experimental use of such high-order processes for oscillator control, with uses in error correction, computing, and sensing.
arxiv-2509-06134:
Tests of whether random vectors spread uniformly over a cube are built from a Brownian sheet in a 2025 paper by A. Cabaña and E. M. Cabaña. The Brownian sheet is a multiparameter Gaussian process, a random surface over the hypercube. The authors construct it as a sum of independent Gaussian processes closely related to Brownian pillows, one per corner pattern.

With the construction in hand, they compute the probability laws of the squared L2 norms of those pieces. Those laws power new consistent tests of uniformity for samples of independent random vectors on the cube. A power comparison against established uniformity tests favors the newcomers, especially at detecting copula alternatives, dependence structures hiding inside otherwise uniform margins.
arxiv-2509-06834:
Reading the early universe's history from a faint hydrogen signal is made easier to enter by Bisweswar Sen in a solo 2025 cosmology paper. The twenty-one-centimeter line of neutral hydrogen can probe cosmic dawn, but pulling astrophysical parameters from its power spectrum is hard. Sen presents a beginner-friendly pipeline built in PyTorch.

The method is marginal neural ratio estimation, a simulation-based inference method that avoids writing down an explicit likelihood. Runs from the 21cmFAST code supply training data. From power spectra alone, the pipeline recovers key parameters such as how well gas was ionized and the X-ray brightness of early sources. Openness and ease of use are the stated aims, offering newcomers a hands-on entry point into twenty-one-centimeter cosmology rather than a black box. The work is a teaching tool as much as a measuring method.
arxiv-2509-07034:
A large language model system built for chemical engineering is presented by Heng Zhang and eight co-authors in a 2025 paper. Developing chemical engineering technology runs from lab research through scale-up to industrial deployment. It demands work across many fields, plus heavy time and money costs. The system is based on a model called ChemELLM.

Users can interact freely with the model through a public website the authors provide. The team presents the system as a new paradigm for AI-driven innovation in the chemical sector, meant to speed up new technology. The abstract gives few technical details about training or testing. As described, the contribution is the deployed interactive system itself, plus the claim that a domain-tuned model can serve engineers across the development pipeline.
arxiv-2509-07134:
Satellites circling the Moon shift each other's radio signals as they move. Baris Donmez, with 2 co-authors, models that shift in a 2025 research paper. The team studies links between satellites near the Lunar South Pole. They measure the Doppler shift in parts per million, so results do not depend on the carrier frequency. The shift is the change in signal frequency caused by motion.

Simulations show the shift grows as one orbit tilts farther from a reference orbit, reaching its largest values near an eighty-degree tilt. A Gaussian mixture model, which blends several bell-shaped curves, fits the spread of shifts best. The authors check the fit with two error measures. Their model gives mission planners a practical way to predict signal changes for future lunar satellite networks.
arxiv-2509-07434:
Ali Ghalavand, writing alone in 2025, attacks a twenty-year-old conjecture about graph measurements called Zagreb indices. The Zagreb indices summarize a graph, a network of points and links, by adding powers of node degrees, the counts of links at each point. The conjecture compares the two indices after averaging, one by node count and one by link count. It was disproved for general graphs but proved for chemical graphs, whose nodes have low degree.

Ghalavand studies graphs whose minimum and maximum degrees differ by at most three. Any counterexample in that class, he proves, must have minimum degree two and maximum degree five. He then exhibits infinitely many connected counterexamples meeting exactly those bounds, each with at least 218 nodes. The result narrows where believers in the conjecture can still hope it holds, at least for near-regular graphs.
arxiv-2509-07934:
Richard Montgomery and 2 co-authors pin down the Ramsey numbers of many trees in a 2025 maths paper. Colour each edge of a full graph red or blue. A tree's Ramsey number is the smallest graph that forces a red copy of the tree or a blue copy. Burr guessed a simple formula in 1974. The guess failed for some star-like trees.

For trees where no vertex has too many edges, the pair prove Burr's formula is exact. The size limit is a small fixed share of the whole tree. Only the sizes of the tree's two sides enter the formula. Exact Ramsey numbers are rare. Each solved family sharpens the map of patterns that colour alone cannot avoid.
arxiv-2509-08034:
Mixing a thick, slow blob into thinner fluid inside porous rock is simulated by Mijanur Rahaman and 2 co-authors in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. The blob is miscible, meaning it dissolves into the surrounding fluid rather than staying separate, and the porous medium has realistic no-flux boundaries that nothing crosses. How the blob stretches and deforms controls how fast mixing finishes.

High-accuracy numerical methods, a compact finite difference scheme in space and Crank-Nicolson stepping in time, solve the governing nonlinear equations. Simulations span flow strengths and viscosity contrasts, measured by the Péclet number and log-mobility ratio. Better mixing predictions matter underground, from cleaning contaminated groundwater to sweeping oil or stored carbon dioxide through reservoirs.
arxiv-2509-08234:
Grayscale chest X-rays must be reshaped before vision transformers can read them, and Faisal Ahmed proposes a simple fix in a solo 2025 medical imaging paper. Transformers pretrained on colour photographs expect three input channels, while X-rays have one. His RepViT-CXR strategy replicates the single channel to fill the format, adding no invented information and losing none.

Chest imaging is a frontline tool against tuberculosis and pneumonia, and automated classification could speed triage where radiologists are scarce. The replicated-channel adapter is evaluated on tuberculosis and pneumonia classification. Trivial-sounding adapters matter in practice: they let hospitals reuse powerful pretrained models on scans as they are, instead of redesigning networks for every imaging format.
arxiv-2509-08734:
Andreas Burger and 3 co-authors speed up molecular simulations with deep equilibrium models in a 2025 paper. Machine learning force fields predict forces between atoms for molecular dynamics. Successive states in a simulation are very alike, a fact earlier models largely ignored.

By recasting a strong symmetry aware model as a deep equilibrium model, the team reuses features from prior time steps. Accuracy and speed both rise by about ten to twenty percent on three datasets. Training also uses far less memory. That saving lets researchers train larger models for bigger molecular systems.
arxiv-2509-09034:
The Hubble tension may signal new physics, or it may be an artifact of how measurements get compressed. Nathalia M. N. da Rocha, Andre L. B. Ribeiro, and Francisco B. S. Oliveira decompose the discrepancy in a 2025 research paper. Their Bayesian hierarchical framework splits the observed tension into three parts. The parts are ordinary measurement error, information lost when parameters are projected down, and genuine physical tension.

Fisher matrix analysis with estimated loss coefficients drives the split. Most of the tension's variance landed on the real component. Measurement error and information loss together explained only about a fifth. The implied real discrepancy remains highly significant. The authors conclude the tension is robust and probably points beyond the standard cosmological model. Their decomposition method also gives other precision disputes a way to ask how much of a disagreement is real.
arxiv-2509-09134:
Chirantan Mukherjee proposes a new algorithm for computing integer hulls of two-dimensional polyhedral sets in a 2025 paper. The integer hull is the smallest convex polyhedron containing all integer points of a set. Maple's existing function computes it by moving facet planes inward.

The old method can become costly when integer points already lie on facet planes, enlarging the brute force region. The new method moves each plane inward from the opposite vertex until it meets an integer point. Smaller regions then follow the old procedure or a recursive technique. The paper focuses on the two-dimensional case in Maple's PolyhedralSets library.
arxiv-2509-09234:
Answering questions over real tables means translating plain English into database queries across messy, varied schemas. Rishit Tyagi, Mohit Gupta, and Rahul Bouri report a system for that task in a 2025 research paper. Their entry targeted a shared benchmark of large, domain-diverse tables. The approach generates SQL queries dynamically with large language models.

The pipeline selects examples, generates the query, extracts the answer, verifies it, and refines it in a loop. Several leading models were tried as the query writer. Accuracy landed far above the benchmark's baseline scores on both the full and lite versions. The authors also document alternative approaches they explored and where the method strains. For organizations sitting on spreadsheets, a reliable question-answering layer turns archives into something staff can simply ask.
arxiv-2509-09434:
Tom-Christian Riemer and 1 co-author address a memory problem in adaptive isogeometric analysis in a 2025 numerical paper. Their method works with truncated hierarchical B-splines, which refine a mesh only where detail is needed. Once that local refinement breaks the neat global grid, assembling matrices turns slow and heavy, and that step becomes the main bottleneck.

Their low-rank framework recasts the geometry weights and source terms inside spline spaces that separate by direction, then stores everything as tensor trains. The active basis is cut into a few box-shaped regions, each adding a simple factor, and operators are built level by level. A MATLAB prototype cut memory use and assembly time on model problems while keeping accuracy.
arxiv-2509-09534:
Sena Ergisi and 2 co-authors propose ProDiGy in 2025, a federated learning method designed to survive dishonest participants. Federated training lets many clients improve a shared model without pooling their data. Attackers inside the group can still poison updates, and defences often fail when client data differ strongly from one another, the non-identical case.

ProDiGy grades each incoming gradient twice, once for closeness to others and once for difference from them. Honest clients tend to resemble each other naturally, while copycat attackers look suspiciously uniform. Wide numerical tests show the dual score holding accuracy and defence where rival methods collapse, especially under uneven data. That balance is the method's main selling point.
arxiv-2509-09734:
Zikang Guo and 5 co-authors release a benchmark in 2025 for judging language agents that work through the Model Context Protocol. That open standard is quickly becoming the common plug between agents and outside tools. Older tests, the authors argue, miss how agents behave under it, flattering some systems and blurring real differences in skill.

Their testbed runs thirty-three live servers offering one hundred eighty-eight tools. Six hundred questions span six categories of rising interaction difficulty, and a scoring method called MCP-Eval grades real task success over surface polish. Running leading agents through the suite gives a first grounded picture of who handles protocol-mediated tools well, and where the common failures sit.
arxiv-2509-09834:
Yuzhe Qin and 3 co-authors simulate electrically driven droplets whose surfaces actively pump ions in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Their phase-field model weds ion transport and electrostatics to a two-fluid flow description, with the pumps entering as prescribed fluxes across the droplet skin. Without pumping, an applied field only polarises a droplet and barely bends it, a quiet baseline for contrast.

Switch the pumps on and positive ions pile up inside, raising the inner voltage and warping the field unevenly. The resulting stresses stretch the droplet, pinch a neck until it snaps, and the daughters later merge again, often after touching a wall. Crowded droplets repel sideways and bend into crescents or stars under confinement, hinting at sorting tricks.
arxiv-2509-10034:
Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar's 2025 paper proves that a certain kind of neural network can copy a probabilistic finite automaton exactly, step for step. Such automata hop between states with set odds, the basic grammar of random sequences. His symbolic feedforward design stores the state distribution as a vector and each transition as a stochastic matrix, so one matrix multiplication advances the whole distribution without any recurrence in the network.

Subset construction and epsilon-closure, the classic tools for taming these automata, are rebuilt inside the layered computation, and equivalence with the automata is proved. The stronger claim is learnability: ordinary gradient training on labelled sequences recovers the true automaton's behaviour exactly. Symbolic rigour and gradient learning, often treated as rivals, meet here on paper.
arxiv-2509-10134:
Rini Smita Thakur and 2 co-authors adapt an eye-scan segmentation model to a new clinic's images without ever seeing the original training set in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Outlining the optic disc and cup guides glaucoma care, yet a model trained elsewhere fades when cameras and protocols change. Source-free adaptation must repair that fade using only the pretrained model and fresh, unlabelled target pictures.

Grad-CL first uses gradient signals to pull out class-specific features, sharpen uncertainty estimates, and clean the noisy guessed labels on target scans. A contrastive stage then pushes cup and disc features apart by their angle, firming the boundary between them. Across difficult cross-domain fundus collections, the method beat the standing state of the art the authors compared against.
arxiv-2509-10234:
Can Cui and three co-authors present a training-free way to clean up sound for speech recognition in this 2025 paper. Their setting is hard for computers: several people talking over each other in a noisy, echoing room, recorded on many microphones. Their idea is to aim beamforming, which favors sound from chosen directions, at set angular sectors before recognition begins.

The method needs no training data and does not depend on a learned model of the room. On the AMI meeting recordings, feeding the recognizer beamformed signals instead of raw microphone feeds cut the word error rate by up to eleven percent. Speaker counting also improved, by up to twenty-seven percent relative, showing that fixed directional processing makes multichannel recordings easier to use.
arxiv-2509-10334:
Jordan Sassoon, Michal Szczepanski, and Martyna Poreba squeeze vision transformers onto small devices in this 2025 paper. They introduce I-Segmenter for semantic segmentation. That task labels an image pixel by pixel. Transformers segment well, but they demand heavy memory and compute. Simply quantizing them to low precision usually breaks accuracy. Errors pile up through the network.

I-Segmenter is, by the authors' account, the first fully integer-only framework of its kind. It swaps every floating-point operation for an integer counterpart. It adds a new activation function. That function tames long-tailed value distributions, a known weak point of uniform quantization. Two decoder steps get integer-friendly replacements as well. The result stays within a modest margin of the full-precision baseline. It shrinks the model up to about fourfold, and it runs faster. It even holds up when calibrated with a single image.
arxiv-2509-10534:
Anand Gopalakrishnan and three co-authors separate what a token says from where it sits in this 2025 deep learning paper. Transformer attention matches queries to keys using both content and position, and the popular RoPE embedding braids those two signals together. When a decision needs content alone or position alone, that braid can hurt.

Their replacement, PoPE, encodes position in polar coordinates and removes the confound entirely. On a diagnostic task built around indexing by one factor at a time, PoPE wins decisively. Across music, genomic, and language modeling, transformers with PoPE beat RoPE baselines on loss and downstream scores, with gains holding from small to larger models. PoPE also stretches to longer sequences than it trained on, outperforming even a method designed for that trick.
arxiv-2509-10634:
Quantum networks need traffic control, and Guo Xian Yau with five co-authors bring reinforcement learning to the job in this 2025 quantum networking paper. Future quantum applications, like distributing secret keys, impose strict demands, and near-term hardware is scarce. Network dynamics fit a Markov decision process, so learning methods should apply, but key performance measures are nonlinear tangles of state quality and generation rate that standard reward designs cannot express.

Their gradient-based framework optimizes such nonlinear, differentiable objectives directly, while accounting for delays in the classical messages that coordinate the network. They test it on entanglement distillation between two multiplexed nodes, a purification step for quantum links. In the right parameter ranges it beat heuristic baselines by about twenty percent, a first step toward learning-based control of real quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-11134:
Jiaang Duan and nineteen co-authors present GFS in this 2025 computer systems paper. It concerns GPU clusters in the age of large language models. Cloud providers rent spare capacity cheaply as spot instances. Low-priority jobs on them get evicted often. They also wait long in queues.

GFS forecasts each tenant's GPU needs. It adjusts the spot quota for low-priority work. Minimum durations are guaranteed. It also preempts carefully. Urgent jobs go first. As few other jobs as possible are displaced. Tests ran on a production cluster. The cluster held more than ten thousand GPUs. Evictions fell by about a third. Queuing delays dropped sharply. Savings reached hundreds of thousands of dollars per month.
arxiv-2509-11334:
A thermal camera cannot tell heat glow from reflected warmth, and Sriram Narayanan, Mani Ramanagopal, and Srinivasa G. Narasimhan attack that ambiguity in this 2025 computer vision paper. Near room temperature the two signals are similar in size, which makes separating them especially hard.

Their dual-band video method combines two clues at every pixel. Spectrally, the ratio of an object's emissivity between the two infrared bands is unknown but fixed. Temporally, the object's own radiation drifts smoothly while the reflected background changes fast. From these cues the authors build an image formation model and an algorithm that jointly recovers emissivity in both bands plus the changing temperatures of object and background. Everyday scenes, from a heating coffee pot to a palm print fading on a mirror, came apart cleanly in their tests.
arxiv-2509-11634:
Saketh Vishnubhatla and 6 co-authors study how online data can speed up disaster impact assessment in a 2025 paper. Ground surveys by volunteers and responders estimate losses and casualties, but they arrive late and carry their own biases.

The authors curated a county-level dataset for several billion-dollar disasters, drawing on social media, news reports, aerial imagery, and satellite data. They analyzed how estimates from these online sources compare with traditional offline assessments. Different sources proved to provide complementary information rather than duplicating each other. The findings show which online streams help estimate which aspects of impact at a given administrative unit. That guidance can help response planners combine fast online signals with slower ground truth.
arxiv-2509-11834:
Alexander Pigazzini and Magdalena Toda prove a lower bound for geometric structures on product manifolds in a 2025 geometry paper. Their setting joins two compact surfaces. The objects are metric connections whose torsion, a gauge of twisting, has a special form that respects the product split.

For a calibrated connection whose harmonic part stands for a nontrivial mixed cohomology class, they bound the size of part of its holonomy from below. The bound does not change under deformations that keep certain strata of parallel forms. It blocks reducing the holonomy along the product split. A counter case shows the assumptions are optimal. A special case with a circle factor forces torsion to survive reduction to fewer dimensions.
arxiv-2509-12134:
Thomas Fernique models scrambling a Rubik's cube in a 2025 mathematics paper. He treats random scrambling as a Markov chain, a process where each step depends only on the current state. Inside that model he defines a stopping time, a rule for when to stop, that looks like a natural candidate for a strong uniform time.

A strong uniform time would help estimate how many moves are needed to scramble a cube thoroughly. Fernique shows, however, that his candidate does not have that property. The result is negative but useful: it closes one plausible route and clarifies what a successful approach would need. The paper's title states the lesson plainly, warning how not to approach the scrambling problem.
arxiv-2509-12434:
Jiahao Yu and 3 co-authors propose EntroPO in a 2025 paper on building coding agents. Software tasks require reasoning over large code bases and coordinated tool use across many steps. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench show that current language models still struggle to resolve real-world issues.

Test-time scaling, generating many attempts, can help, but only if the model's outputs are diverse. Standard preference optimization methods can reduce that diversity while aligning outputs with human preferences, and they are usually designed for single-turn tasks. EntroPO adds an entropy focus, preserving variety, and adapts preference optimization to multi-turn, tool-using settings. The goal is a coding agent that both follows preferences and keeps enough diverse attempts for scaling to work.
arxiv-2509-12534:
Jia-Hong Huang's 2025 thesis, DeepEyeNet, addresses automated medical reports for retinal images. Retinal diseases are becoming more common, and demand for ophthalmologists exceeds the available workforce. That imbalance creates a bottleneck that can delay diagnosis and treatment for patients who need timely care.

Traditional report writing relies on manual interpretation of images, which is time-consuming and error-prone. The thesis investigates artificial intelligence that analyzes large volumes of image data and identifies subtle patterns needed for accurate diagnosis. A multi-modal deep learning approach captures interactions between textual keywords and retinal images, among other proposed methods for key challenges in automated reporting. Automating the process could reduce doctors' workloads and let them focus on more complex cases.
arxiv-2509-12934:
Jeremias Ferrao, Matthijs van der Lende and two co-authors open up in 2025 how preference training changes a language model, step by step. Standard training shifts many weights at once, so what the model truly learns stays hidden.

Their frame trains a small adapter that steers clear sparse traits of the model. They show the steer can match the shifts of normal training, then use it for preference choice. A cause check finds the model learned to reward style and format as a stand-in for quality, more than honesty-linked traits. The frame gives a clear dial and a test for training strain.
arxiv-2509-13134:
Talaya Farasat and Joachim Posegga search in 2025 for the best pairing of code vectors and learners to flag Python flaws. Hand checks no longer scale as code grows. Learned checks hinge on how code is turned into numbers and which learner reads them.

Three vector ways and two deep learners are crossed. A graph-aware vector with a folded net scores well. Yet a sequence learner with classic word vectors wins overall by a steady edge. Newer code models do not always beat older vectors. Pair choice matters as much as model size for sound flaw hunts in Python.
arxiv-2509-13234:
Nadim Barakat and William Lotter model clinical AI assistance for diabetic retinopathy screening in a 2025 paper. Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness, and AI systems can expand access to screening from fundus photographs of the eye. Current cleared systems primarily give binary referral outputs, which may limit clinical trust and utility.

The authors evaluated multimodal large language models for detecting the disease and their ability to model assistance across varied output types. Two models, a general-purpose model and an open-source medical model, were tested on two data sets. Tests covered benchmark evaluation, modeled assistance with synthetic predictions, and actual AI-to-AI collaboration where one model incorporated the other's outputs. The medical model outperformed the general model at benchmark on sensitivity and related measures.
arxiv-2509-13334:
Anand Swaroop, Maheep Chaudhary and three co-authors train in 2025 for faithful chain thought with LIFT, no human labels needed. Chains can read well yet not drive the answer. Faith scores must catch that gap in a cheap, sound way.

Each step is swapped for a matched irrelevant fact. The drop in answer log score gauges causal weight. Training keeps high-weight traces and tunes for faith plus accuracy. Three models and three benchmarks show faith gains. Accuracy matches accuracy-only tuning. Automatic causal scoring replaces costly human marks for this task and scales to new domains.
arxiv-2509-13634:
Md Bokhtiar Al Zami, Md Raihan Uddin, and Dinh C. Nguyen combine drones with federated learning in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, scattered devices train a shared model locally and upload only updates, keeping raw data private. Drones acting as mobile base stations can run such systems, but energy use, weak links, and security threats hold them back.

Their framework adds digital twins, live virtual copies of the drones that support monitoring and predictive maintenance, and zero-knowledge proofs, which let updates be verified without exposing the data behind them. A dynamic strategy adjusts flight paths, transmit power, and processing rates, cutting system energy use by up to about thirty percent in simulations while improving learning performance and scalability.
arxiv-2509-13834:
Nguyen Lan Vi Vu and six co-authors present Semi-MoE in a 2025 medical imaging paper, the first mixture-of-experts framework for semi-supervised segmentation of histopathology images. Labeling tissue slides is slow expert work, so semi-supervised methods learn partly from unlabeled images, but ambiguous gland boundaries make their guessed labels noisy and misleading.

Three expert networks split the job: one segments, one regresses a signed distance field describing shape, and one predicts boundaries. A multi-gating module fuses their features into refined pseudo-labels, while an adaptive loss balances the several training goals without hand tuning. On the GlaS and CRAG benchmarks the method beat leading approaches precisely where labels were scarcest.
arxiv-2509-14134:
Ola Mæhlen characterizes a singular limit of the Benjamin-Ono equation in a solo 2025 analysis paper. That equation models internal waves in deep water. Its zero-dispersion limit asks what solutions look like when the smoothing dispersion term is sent to zero. In that regime the wave can break into rapid oscillations. He works on the circle, with periodic waves, for general bounded starting data.

Using an explicit formula due to Gérard, Mæhlen shows the limit has a clean form. It is an alternating sum of the branches of the multivalued solution of Burgers' equation, the classic breaking-wave model. The result extends earlier work that covered only bell-shaped periodic data. It matches the picture known on the whole line. From the characterization he extracts regularity properties of the limit, including maximum principles and an Oleinik estimate.
arxiv-2509-14234:
Dulhan Jayalath and seven co-authors ask in 2025 where a model can learn from when training has no checked answers. Their answer is to use the model itself at run time. Many attempts at a task are gathered and merged into one stand in answer, which then guides further learning.

The method, called Compute as Teacher, turns that merged answer into rewards for reinforcement learning, meaning training driven by scores rather than fixed labels. For health guidance, where no program can check an answer, the team builds scoring rules from the stand in answer and has a judge model apply them. On a health test set, models trained this way matched or beat plain merging while using far less computing at test time.
arxiv-2509-14434:
Farnaz Jahanbakhsh and six co-authors propose value aligned ranking for social media feeds in 2025. Feeds today follow engagement signals, clicks and dwell time, not any stated values. The outcome is not neutral: engagement tends to favour individualistic content.

Their method uses Schwartz theory of basic human values, a cross cultural map of values that support or oppose each other. Posts are scored for which values they express. Users then set weights for values they want more or less of. Ranking blends post scores with those weights, respecting stated trade offs. Controlled tests with over a hundred participants check the controls. Giving users value dials shifts feed design from hidden engagement maximisation toward explicit choice.
arxiv-2509-14534:
Shao-Feng Ge, Jie Sheng and Chuan-Yang Xing rebuild in 2025 the theory of dark matter scattering off electrons bound in atoms. Such scattering is a main route to hunt light dark matter below a gigaelectronvolt. Standard treatments factor atomic effects into one form factor times a free electron result.

That factorisation is not necessarily valid, the authors argue. Bound electrons are off shell, so free electron kinematics and phase space do not apply consistently. Starting from quantum field theory first principles, they set up a consistent formalism for atomic effects. A scalar interaction example quantifies how relativistic and nonrelativistic calculations differ. Detector predictions for direct dark matter searches depend on getting these atomic corrections right.
arxiv-2509-14834:
Jinhee Jang and four co-authors introduce a roundtable of language model agents for scoring essays in a 2025 education technology paper. Automated essay scoring is a long-running use of language processing, but matching human judgment from several viewpoints at once is hard. Their framework, called Roundtable Essay Scoring, works with no task-specific training examples.

Each agent is built for a specific prompt and topic, writes its own trait-based rubric, and scores the essay independently. The agents then hold a simulated roundtable discussion and reason through their differences to reach one final score. Tests on the ASAP dataset with two leading chat models show large gains over simple prompting. The design shows how structured debate among agents can bring machine scores closer to human ones.
arxiv-2509-14934:
Francisco Messina and four co-authors fight data copying in text-to-audio generation in a 2025 audio AI paper. Generative models sometimes reproduce chunks of their training data, a problem called data replication or memorization. For audio models trained on music and sound libraries, that raises legal and creative concerns.

The team applies Anti-Memorization Guidance, which steers the sampling process of a pre-trained diffusion model away from memorized content. Three guidance variants are explored, each aiming to cut replication while keeping sound quality and prompt alignment. Experiments use Stable Audio Open, chosen because both the model and its training set are fully open. Results suggest the guidance sharply reduces memorization without hurting fidelity, offering a practical safeguard for open audio generation.
arxiv-2509-15034:
Suat Dengiz and İzzet Sakallı map out exotic phases of nuclear matter inside a holographic model in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Holographic quantum chromodynamics uses string-theory constructions, here the Sakai-Sugimoto model, to mimic the strong nuclear force. Earlier work found chiral soliton lattices, regular arrays of solitons, inside strong magnetic fields.

Dengiz and Sakallı study skyrmions sitting on the domain walls of those lattices. The skyrmions, realized as undissolved branes inside other branes, carry baryon number two. Magnetic field strength, pion mass, and baryon chemical potential together decide whether the configuration is stable. Energy analysis shows a mixed lattice-skyrmion phase becomes favorable once a product of chemical potential and field strength passes a threshold. The resulting phase diagram has three regions with distinct matter organization.
arxiv-2509-15234:
Hanbin Ko and seven co-authors adapt language model encoders to chest X-ray reports for image-text retrieval in a 2025 medical informatics paper. Pairing radiology images with reports is powerful but messy: reports mix abbreviations, impression-only notes, and house styles that differ by institution. Naively pooling such noisy text can stall or even degrade cross-modal learning.

The team trains a bidirectional language model encoder with masked token prediction and supervised contrastive learning on clinically equivalent report variants written in different styles. The encoder learns embeddings that ignore style and keep clinical meaning. Plugged into a dual-tower contrastive system with the image encoder, it supports retrieval of films from text and text from films. Style robustness is the central contribution for hospital-scale archives.
arxiv-2509-15334:
Zhen Guo and a large team of co-authors investigate an eruptive young star with an unusually cool spectrum in a 2025 astronomy paper. The source was caught by a decade-long infrared variability survey of the Milky Way and nicknamed within the survey's What Is This series for its puzzling behavior. It brightened enormously in the near-infrared, held a plateau for years, then faded rapidly back to its earlier level.

Photometric monitoring in near- and mid-infrared bands traces the whole outburst arc. Spectra taken during outburst and decay with instruments on large telescopes show cool molecular features, unusual for an eruptive star. Follow-up observations combined with theoretical models aim to identify what kind of young star erupts this way and what powers the long plateau. The event stretches standard categories of stellar eruptions.
arxiv-2509-15434:
Travis Lloyd leads a team that studies crowd written notes on social media posts. The best known case is Community Notes on X, where users add context to posts. Other platforms are adding like systems as a swap for paid fact checks. The team call these crowdsourced context systems and ask how they are built and what they change.

They review past studies of such systems and look at real cases in use. From that base they build a two part frame. One part defines what these systems are, and the other maps six design choices, from who takes part to how open the process is. They also flag the values at stake in each choice. The work sets terms for future study.
arxiv-2509-15834:
Shardul Chiplunkar and Clément Pit-Claudel automate the drawing of railroad diagrams. These diagrams draw a grammar as tracks with branches and loops, and readers find them intuitive. Yet they are mostly drawn by hand, since tools are scarce and layout had no formal treatment. The pair give that treatment and build a working system.

They split the task into two languages: one says what parts a diagram has and how they join, the other fixes shapes, sizes, and spots. Their compiler wraps lines to a target width and aligns parts by user policy. Wrapping is cast as an optimization with principled goals. Common forms like regular expressions compile cleanly into their language.
arxiv-2509-16434:
Teaching a robot hand to grasp from camera views alone is attractive, since the hand can learn to look as it reaches, but vision training is memory hungry. Ritvik Singh and five co-authors split their simulator and learner across separate graphics chips, which doubles the number of training worlds on the same hardware. Larger batches follow, and with them better policies.

They train depth and state policies, then distill them into stereo camera policies for real use. Depth-based distillation worked best, in both simulation and the real world. Their end-to-end policies beat the prior best vision-based grasping results when deployed.
arxiv-2509-17134:
Mohammad Ali Abam and four co-authors study fairness in two-stage voting in a 2025 arXiv paper. Voters are split into groups, each group picks a local winner, and the final winner comes from those winners. The setup mirrors systems like United States presidential elections, where state results decide the national outcome. The cost of a result is measured by how far voters sit from the winner.

The authors tighten the known bounds on distortion, the gap between the chosen winner and the best possible one. They cover fixed and random methods, and four ways of adding up voter costs. In several cases their new bounds are exact, and in others they close most of the gap. The upshot is a near-complete picture of how much two-stage voting can distort the will of the full electorate.
arxiv-2509-17334:
Jiawen Wei, Elena Verona, Andrea Bertolini, and Gianmarco Mengaldo ask whether AI systems in healthcare must explain themselves. Their 2025 arXiv perspective paper tests the claim that explainability is essential in critical fields such as medicine. To probe it, they set two extremes side by side: an opaque oracle and an AI colleague that can explain its output.

The authors trace how automation level and explainability shift who bears liability when harm occurs. The choice among the doctor, the facility, and the maker of the system turns on how much the system can show its reasoning. They argue that explainability plays a central role in a fair responsibility framework under the law. It shapes how each party behaves and can cut the risk of defensive medicine, where care is given to dodge lawsuits rather than to heal.
arxiv-2509-17534:
Changzhen Sun and Erik Wahlén study when periodic water waves keep their shape. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats two-dimensional gravity-capillary waves, where both gravity and surface tension shape the motion. The question is spectral stability: whether small disturbances of a traveling periodic wave grow or fade.

The pair derive a criterion built on an index function whose sign decides stability. The criterion matches earlier formal work by Djordjević and Redekopp and by Ablowitz and Segur, who used a nonlinear Schrödinger approximation. Near spectral crossings away from the origin, instability is ruled out when surface tension is positive and a flow parameter sits in a stated range, since the Krein signatures agree. For a further sub-range, they draw a curve above which small waves are stable. Surface tension emerges as the stabilizing hero.
arxiv-2509-17834:
Duygu Kabakci-Zorlu and 4 co-authors show a tool that turns plant papers into a structured risk file. Their 2025 demo deals with Failure Mode and Effects Analyses for work gear. Such files list how gear can fail and what harm may follow, but they take long to write by hand.

The tool uses large language models and papers the user gives it. It pulls facts from more than one paper, drafts the risk file, and stores it in a database. The team says draft time falls well below hand work. The demo points to a way firms can build such files fast.
arxiv-2509-17934:
T Petersen leads a large team that built a coated cavity to speed up ions. Their 2025 paper reports on a niobium-tin coated radio cavity for the ATLAS facility at Argonne. ATLAS fires ion beams for nuclear physics at low speed.

The coat cuts radio loss into cold helium by about tenfold next to a plain niobium cavity. Field strengths reached rank among the best yet for such coats. Tuning was a hard part, since the coat is brittle. The team found a set of steps to tune the cooled cavity to the ATLAS clock while keeping its strong run.
arxiv-2509-18234:
Yu Gu leads a large team that stress-tests top AI models on medical tasks and finds them brittle. Their 2025 paper deals with a gap between bench wins and real clinic readiness. Models score high on medical tests, yet weak spots hide in multi-step and multi-mode thought.

Trick variants of test items expose those spots. Top systems can guess right with key inputs stripped out. Small prompt tweaks can also throw them off, while their stated reasons sound smooth but flawed. Doctor-led rubrics show that known benches vary a lot in what they truly measure. The team calls for tougher checks.
arxiv-2509-18834:
A quantum internet needs devices that turn microwave photons into optical ones on demand. Hai-Tao Tu and nine co-authors demonstrate such a transducer with a Rydberg atom ensemble in this 2025 paper. Quantum memories and transducers have each advanced, but joining them in one device is hard. Their system stores first, then converts at retrieval.

Cascaded transparency effects let the ensemble hold microwave photons in a highly excited shared state. At readout, those photons emerge as optical photons. A huge optical depth for the microwave side and low dephasing drive the performance. The device reached about ninety percent area-normalized storage efficiency. Its bandwidth sits in the megahertz range and its noise level is modest, all without a cavity. The design also suits cryogenic setups. The authors see a path to practical quantum interfaces.
arxiv-2509-19634:
Under crushing pressure, some metals quietly rearrange their electrons, and nuclear magnetic resonance can catch the shift. Y. -H. Nian and seven co-authors squeezed the compound CeRhIn5 while watching two indium sites inside it. A measure called the Knight shift tracks how local fields at each site respond. Along one crystal direction, the shift barely moved with pressure, a telling asymmetry.

The team read the pattern through a tight-binding model of the electron structure. Changes in the crystal's electric environment could not explain the data. Instead, more of one electron type reached the active surface as pressure rose. That growth points toward a nearby quantum critical point where the electron system reorganizes. The result sharpens the map of how heavy-electron materials behave near such tipping points.
arxiv-2509-19734:
Robot paths must thread through clutter without contact, and corridor methods box the free space into safe chunks. Akshay Jaitly, Jon Arrizabalaga, and Guanrui Li reshape that idea with ellipsoidal corridors. Their parameterization writes a path as living inside a product of balls, one per segment. Problem size then decouples from how complex the scene geometry is.

No fixed time windows need to be assigned to segments, since motion evolves smoothly inside the corridors. The authors pose a trust-region problem with separable blocks and build a solver that exploits that split. Parallel subproblems keep the solver fast. Safe corridors matter for drones, arms, and warehouse robots alike. A cleaner parameterization can turn a brittle planner into a routine tool.
arxiv-2509-20034:
Tracking an epidemic's reproduction number is hard enough in one place; doing it across territories with bad case counts is harder. Etienne Lasalle and Barbara Pascal estimate the number and the map of spread together. Regions lend each other statistical strength when the connectivity between them is known. That connectivity is usually the missing piece.

Their joint estimator uses a sparsity-promoting penalty to learn a lean spatial structure alongside the reproduction curve. COVID-19 surveillance exposed how poor counts can mislead single-region tools. Borrowing strength across borders improves both accuracy and robustness, provided the borders are drawn right. The method learns those borders from the data. Decision makers get an intensity gauge plus the routes that drive it.
arxiv-2509-20534:
Symbolic algebra systems drown in copies of the same subexpression. Bowen Zhu and five co-authors cure that swell with hash consing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their integration brings the technique into JuliaSymbolics, a fast symbolic toolkit in the Julia language. A global table with weak references canonicalizes every expression, so identical pieces are stored once.

Benchmarks across several domains show broad gains. Symbolic operations ran up to about three times faster, and memory use fell by up to half. Code generation sped up fivefold, compilation tenfold, and numerical evaluation up to a hundredfold on larger models. Workloads with few repeated pieces gained less and sometimes paid slight overhead early. Downstream stages benefited almost everywhere. The authors point toward combining hash consing with e-graphs for equivalence-aware sharing in AI-driven mathematics pipelines.
arxiv-2509-20934:
Inside atomic nuclei, gluons crowd together at small momentum fractions and start to recombine. F Abdi and B Rezaei compute the effect in a 2025 nuclear physics paper set to appear in Physical Review C. They study nonlinear corrections to heavy flavor structure functions.

The authors solve a nonlinear evolution equation, the GLR-MQ-ZRS equation, at next-to-leading order for the nuclear gluon distribution. Gluon recombination tames the growth of the distribution at small x. Their results compare well with an existing distribution set and a global parametrization. They then feed the gluon solutions into charm structure functions, contrasting linear and nonlinear behavior. The work matters for predicting what future electron-ion colliders will see inside heavy nuclei.
arxiv-2509-21134:
Strategic choices depend on what rivals will do, and language models are increasingly asked to make them. Yiwen Zhang and four co-authors present ToMPO in a 2025 paper on training strategic decision making. Earlier work focused on social conversation games or ignored how decision types interlock.

The authors first define a strategic decision problem with two decision types and their temporal dependencies. Their algorithm, Theory of Mind Policy Optimization, trains the model to perceive other agents' strategies while optimizing its own. Standard reinforcement learning struggles to represent opponents during training. ToMPO builds that opponent modeling into the update. The goal is models that reason about a game's situation as a whole, rather than reacting move by move.
arxiv-2509-21234:
Abi Aryan and 2 co-authors wrote a short 2025 paper on reinforcement learning tests. Agents learn by trial and error in a small world. Most test worlds stay fixed, so agents can learn brittle tricks. Those tricks fail when the world shifts a bit. The paper offers a way to make tests adapt.

The authors present AbideGym, an add on for the MiniGrid world. It adds changes that react to the agent during a single run. It can also raise the level of difficulty in a scaled way. By showing weak spots in fixed policies, it pushes agents to adapt on the fly. The tool is built to be modular and easy to repeat.
arxiv-2509-21334:
Global temperature change looks different at long trends and at short cycles, and wavelets can separate the two. Credit goes to Luis Aguiar-Conraria and 3 co-authors. Wavelet tools track how links between variables change over time and by cycle length. The authors study global mean temperature anomalies and climate forcings. Forcings are factors that push the climate, such as greenhouse gases and natural drivers. Data span from 1850 to 2022.

They find that greenhouse gases drive the very low frequency trend in temperatures. Carbon dioxide plays a central role in that trend. The link holds even after natural forcings are controlled for. At shorter frequencies, the effect of forcings switches on and off. The authors link that pattern to complex feedback mechanisms in the Earth climate system. The work separates long trends from short cycles.
arxiv-2509-21534:
In context learning lets language models use provided context to predict what comes next. Tankred Saanum and 3 co-authors ask which circuit supports learning of hierarchical patterns in a 2025 paper. Induction heads are known to copy successors of repeated tokens. Natural language patterns are often hierarchical, not flat repeats. The word the, for instance, prefaces many different nouns in one text.

Predicting the right noun after the requires integrating wider contextual cues. Naive induction heads would attend to all past successors at once. The authors investigate whether the same mechanism can support structured patterns. Their study probes a circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in context. The work refines accounts of how transformer attention implements in context learning.
arxiv-2509-21634:
Open radio networks in 6G widen the attack surface while legacy defences stay reactive and manual. Prakhar Sharma and 5 co-authors present an agentic security framework in a 2025 paper. MobiLLM orchestrates threat mitigation as a closed loop in Open RAN environments. A modular multi agent system, powered by large language models, runs the workflows. Detection alone is not enough; automated response is the goal.

Current Open RAN applications focus on optimization or passive detection. Closed loop, end to end mitigation is largely missing. MobiLLM targets that gap for public telecom and private enterprise networks. Resilient, low cost, autonomous security is the design brief. The framework coordinates agents across the mitigation cycle, from detection through response, inside the open architecture.
arxiv-2509-21934:
Buildings produce long streams of energy data, and turning those streams into useful advice is hard because the patterns are nonlinear and span many time scales. Amine Bechar and four co-authors propose a visual route in this 2025 paper, presented at an IEEE data mining conference. Their framework fine-tunes vision-language models on three-dimensional pictures built from the raw data.

Two transforms make the pictures: wavelet analysis, which shows how patterns change across frequencies over time, and recurrence plots, which show when states repeat. The pictured data lets the models read consumption patterns, spot anomalies, and suggest efficiency steps in words. On real data from a university in Sharjah, the fine-tuned models monitored building states and flagged recurring faults. They also beat models fine-tuned directly on the raw number streams, on the loss measure used for anomaly detection.
arxiv-2509-22034:
Reasoning models think longer and answer better, but long thinking costs more to run. Xiaochong Lan, Yu Zheng, Shiteng Cao, and Yong Li study a training-free dial for that trade-off in this 2025 paper. The dial is model merging: blend the weights of a general model with those of a reasoning specialist. By varying the blend strength, one can in principle slide between cheap, shallow answers and deep, costly ones.

The team tested many merging methods across several reasoning benchmarks, mapping accuracy against token use at each blend level. Merging gave smooth, controllable control of the trade-off, even when the two parent models sat far apart in weight space. In some cases a merged model beat one parent on both measures at once: higher accuracy with fewer tokens. The authors offer the study as practical guidance for building models with a chosen reasoning profile for a given job.
arxiv-2509-22234:
Sebastián Flores-Sepúlveda, Gabrielle Nornberg, and Alexander Quaas study a population that can only thrive inside a moving patch of good habitat. Outside the patch, conditions kill at a steady rate. The habitat drifts at a prescribed speed, and the population spreads by fractional diffusion, a nonlocal kind of dispersal with long jumps. Their 2025 paper models this as a reaction-diffusion equation of KPP type, the classic family for invasion and growth.

The authors first settle when traveling wave solutions exist, through the first eigenvalue of a linearized operator with drift. That criterion then decides the long-time fate of the population for any reasonable starting state: survival or extinction. Two critical patch speeds emerge. If the patch moves slowly enough, the population persists by keeping up. If it moves too fast, the population is left behind and dies out.
arxiv-2509-22434:
Margherita Martorana and 3 co-authors build a shared map of what service robots know and can do. Home robots must make sense of a changing room, grasp the task, and pick the right action. Past knowledge models tend to cover one domain and miss links between setting, action, and robot skill. Their ontology, OntoBOT, extends prior models to join tasks, actions, settings, and skills in one frame.

The team tested the model with questions posed across four robots: TIAGo, HSR, UR3, and Stretch. The same frame fit all four platforms. That fit shows the model can support context-aware reasoning and let robots share knowledge across platforms.
arxiv-2509-22634:
Christopher Candelora and Ilija Zeljkovic argue that a reported magnetic effect in a kagome superconductor is a flaw of the tool, not the sample. This family of materials shows a charge density wave and signs of broken time symmetry, with no spin magnetism. Past microscope work had hinted that a magnetic field changes the wave's twist and even the lattice spacing. That was read as a rare effect called piezomagnetism.

Candelora and Zeljkovic trace both signs to the probe itself. Atoms shifting at the tip change how strong the wave looks. Creep, lag, and heat drift in the scanner warp the images. They find no sign the field changes the sample, which undercuts the piezomagnetism claim.
arxiv-2509-22834:
Anis Bekri and 3 co-authors turn plain-language goals into verified optical network designs. Intent-based networking lets users state high-level goals instead of hand-configuring gear. Translating loose language into a formally correct optical topology is hard, because language models are ambiguous and lax. Their hybrid pipeline parses intent with a language model, then checks the design with formal methods. Optical retrieval-augmented generation enriches choices with domain standards.

Symbolic reasoning and verification run through the pipeline, so each design comes out explainable and checkable. The authors argue reliability and correctness are essential for mission-critical networks. Their approach aims to make intent-driven design trustworthy enough for such use.
arxiv-2509-23134:
Black holes in vector Horndeski gravity with nonlinear electrodynamics face a stability gauntlet here. Che-Yu Chen and 3 co-authors test which charged solutions can exist and stay stable.
