The setting is static and spherically symmetric, with electric and magnetic charges. Nonsingular black holes, they show, need zero magnetic charge. Purely electric ones then get a perturbation check.

Nonsingular electric holes fail through a Laplacian instability near the center. Singular holes fare differently across theories. Power-law models can pass all linear checks without the coupling. With the coupling on, instabilities appear inside the horizon unless it is tiny. Rebuilt models keep one clean branch but suffer ghost and strong coupling issues.
arxiv-2509-23234:
Sampling settings can quietly wreck a language model's output quality, and each task wants its own tune. Runyan Tan, Shuang Wu, and Phillip Howard propose p-less sampling, which sets its own threshold. At each step, the full token distribution fixes the truncation point. No hyperparameters remain to tune. Information theory grounds the rule.

Math, logic, and creative writing tasks test the method. Quality beat rival samplers and held up as temperature rose. Generation ran faster too, with shorter outputs and quicker token picks. Accuracy did not suffer for that speed. Case studies and diversity checks round out the evidence.
arxiv-2509-23434:
Autistic and neurotypical people often misread each other's styles, yet the burden of adapting falls one way. Rukhshan Haroon and 5 co-authors built NeuroBridge to rebalance that effort. The online platform simulates an AI character who speaks directly and literally, a common autistic style. Four scenarios let a user chat with that character. Feedback after each round guides reflection.

Twelve users, all neurotypical, tested the platform. All left describing autism as a social difference needing understanding from others. Users praised the personal format and the non-judgmental feedback. Most also found the portrayal accurate, which raises care questions about AI disability images.
arxiv-2509-23634:
Joining two ultracold molecules into a four-atom molecule is a step toward chemistry at the quantum limit. Zhengyu Gu and 7 co-authors work with sodium-potassium molecules dressed by a microwave field. When the field mixes the two lowest rotational states, weakly bound tetramer states appear in the entrance channel. A second microwave field probes their spectrum by driving transitions from the populated dressed state.

Reading the crowded hyperfine pattern of a dark excited level against the dressed-state spectrum let the team measure the tetramers' binding energy. The work adds to few-body physics in microwave-dressed systems. It also points toward making and controlling ultracold polyatomic molecules more broadly.
arxiv-2509-23834:
Differential privacy promises safety only if the software adding the noise is honest. Haochen Sun and Xi He show how it could cheat: their Gaussian pancake mechanism mimics the standard Gaussian mechanism so closely that the two are computationally indistinguishable. Yet its true privacy guarantees can be arbitrarily weaker. That gap turns ordinary implementation defects into an active, covert backdoor attack on data privacy.

The authors prove the covertness, characterize the leakage, and show a distinguishing attack reaching near-perfect success under suitable settings, in theory and in experiments. They close by urging transparent, open-source privacy libraries and formal verification of implementations.
arxiv-2509-24134:
Starlight that rises and falls in uneven steps still carries clues about the star. Antony Tan and 5 co-authors built AstroCo, an encoder for such irregular light curves. Its design mixes attention with local convolutions and gating, in the conformer style, so it can catch both broad trends and fine local shapes.

On a standard survey data set, AstroCo cut prediction error well below two prior Astromer models. Its scores on a broad classification measure also rose. The learned embeddings carried over to few-shot tasks, where only a handful of labeled cases are given. The team offers AstroCo as a label-efficient base for time-domain astronomy.
arxiv-2509-24334:
Ocean temperature maps from satellites are too coarse for many climate uses, and sharpening them is a super-resolution task. Wankun Chen and 5 co-authors built WMSR, a wavelet-assisted Mamba framework for sea surface temperature data. Mamba models track long-range links at linear cost, but they had seen little use for this task.

WMSR splits the signal by frequency. A low-frequency module uses a two-dimensional state-space block to keep the broad temperature pattern intact. A high-frequency module uses a pixel-difference convolution to repair fine texture. On three temperature data sets, WMSR beat leading methods, and the team plans to release code and data.
arxiv-2509-24434:
Fernanda M Baêta extends classic results on approximating convex bodies with polytopes to the world of functions. She derives asymptotic formulas for the weighted approximation of smooth convex functions by piecewise affine convex functions. The setting lets the number of flat facets grow without bound, and the error settles into a pattern.

Those formulas are stated through a functional that extends affine surface area, a classic measure of curved boundary, to functions. Weighted approximation matters where some regions of a function count more than others. Exact asymptotic forms tell how fine the affine pieces must be as accuracy demands rise.
arxiv-2510-00334:
Kieran Drury, Martine Barons, and Jim Smith published this 2025 review on filling in Bayesian network models when data runs short. Such networks link variables through conditional probability tables, which can hold huge numbers of entries. Experts often must supply those numbers by judgment, and asking for all of them is hopeless. A family of structural refinement methods shrinks the burden by simplifying the tables themselves.

The review explains each method's inner logic, its requirements, and its weak points. A worked example runs all of them on a cardiovascular risk assessment network. Seeing the same model treated every way makes trade-offs concrete for the reader. The authors close with practical guidance for choosing a method in real projects. Their aim is to help practitioners parameterize defensible models when direct elicitation is infeasible. The paper doubles as a field guide to an underused corner of applied Bayesian practice.
arxiv-2510-00534:
Jaehak Lee and six colleagues published this 2025 review of hybrid quantum computing with light. Photons make appealing information carriers: fast, quiet, and free of bulky cryogenics. Their weakness is feeble photon-photon interaction, which throttles scalable machines. Hybrid schemes mix several photonic encodings to borrow each one's strengths.

The review walks through discrete-variable, continuous-variable, and bosonic encoding paradigms in turn. Recent theory and experiments get surveyed, with the hybrid route in the spotlight. Highlights include efficient resource-state generation and operations that need almost no active feedforward. The authors tabulate error thresholds and resource overheads for fault-tolerant designs explicitly. That side-by-side accounting clarifies what each architecture must still achieve. Their verdict: hybrid photonics offers a credible, compatible path toward machines that correct their own errors.
arxiv-2510-01034:
Scholtz and forty-four co-authors present the data reduction and emission-line products of JADES Data Release 4 in this 2025 arXiv paper, the companion to the release's Paper I. JADES is the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey, observing the two GOODS fields with the NIRSpec spectrograph. This paper documents how the complete spectroscopic sample was reduced and analysed. The spectra cover 5,190 targets at medium, deep, and ultradeep exposures, using the low-dispersion prism and all three medium-resolution gratings.

The team measured 3,297 robust redshifts reaching out to redshift 14.2, with 974 galaxies beyond redshift four. Released products include one- and two-dimensional reduced spectra with slit-loss corrections and background subtraction tuned for point sources. Emission-line flux catalogues with signal-to-noise above five accompany both prism and grating spectra. The authors also document remaining calibration mismatches between dispersers and launch a JADES online database for browsing the release.
arxiv-2510-01234:
Agrawal and Gupta route each incoming prompt to the language model most likely to handle it well for its cost. Models differ wildly in skill, speed, and price, so one-size deployment wastes money or quality. Their router, LLMRank, reads human-visible features of the prompt instead of opaque embeddings.

Task type, reasoning patterns, complexity cues, and a small proxy solver's behavior all feed a ranking model. Training covered tens of thousands of prompts across eleven benchmarks and eleven models. The router captured most of the perfect oracle's value in balanced tests. Feature attributions explain each routing choice, which black-box routers cannot offer. Interpretable features let operators audit why a prompt went cheap or premium. A hybrid ranking objective balances the competing pressures during training. Small models win their share of easy prompts under the policy. Efficiency stops being guesswork.
arxiv-2510-01634:
Lin, Ojha, and Bai let each token in a transformer choose its own geometry, routing among flat, hyperbolic, and spherical attention branches. Standard attention assumes Euclidean space, which fits hierarchical or cyclical data poorly. Earlier fixes commit the whole model to one curved geometry in advance.

A light gating network learns the routing per token, end to end. Each branch runs operations native to its manifold, and the gates reveal interpretable preferences. Knowledge-graph benchmarks improved by roughly a tenth over fixed-geometry baselines. The overhead stayed small in parameters and inference time alike. Euclidean attention remains the default backbone for most tokens. Hyperbolic branches wake selectively for hierarchical structure. Spherical attention activates sparsely where cycles dominate. Five percent more parameters buy the geometric freedom. Mixed geometry in real data motivates the whole design. One geometry per model was the constraint.
arxiv-2510-01734:
Pawel and Held tackle a weakness of adaptive clinical trials in this 2025 statistics paper. Response-adaptive randomization shifts patients toward treatments that look better as data arrive. Thompson sampling is the popular version of that idea. Early in a trial, though, its allocation chances swing wildly, and patients may land on weaker treatments.

The authors add a point null hypothesis stating that all treatments work equally well. Belief in that null pulls the allocation chances toward equal randomization. One prior weight controls how strong the pull is, with the two extremes recovering equal randomization and plain Thompson sampling. Simulations showed the method tames the wild early swings of Thompson sampling. Its statistical behavior matched common quick fixes like probability capping. The team also released the method in an open-source R package called brar.
arxiv-2510-01934:
Zhai and five co-authors turn foundation vision models into few-shot anomaly detectors in this 2025 paper. Factories need inspectors that spot defects from only a handful of normal examples. Learning that boundary from so few samples is hard, especially across many product categories. Foundation encoders, trained on huge image collections, already know what normal images look like.

Their detector, FoundAD, exploits a simple empirical pattern in those embeddings. The more anomalous an image is, the farther its embedding sits from normal ones. A lightweight nonlinear projector maps features onto the manifold of natural images. Regions that project poorly are flagged as out-of-distribution defects. The method handles multi-class detection with far fewer parameters than prior systems. Tests across several encoders, including the fresh DINOv3, beat existing few-shot detectors. The authors argue foundation features hide more anomaly signal than the field had assumed.
arxiv-2510-02434:
Lopes, Milagre, and Silva map every unitarity bound for theories with extra scalar particles. Their 2025 particle physics paper covers models beyond the Standard Model. Extra scalars often appear as doublets and singlets under the weak force. Some carry electric charge, and others stay neutral. Such additions are nearly universal in dark matter models. Unitarity limits how strong particle scattering can grow. Breaking those limits signals an inconsistent theory. The authors give a complete description of the bounds. A minimal set of scattering matrices carries all the needed information.

They also built a Mathematica tool called BounDS. The tool applies the bounds to user chosen models automatically. Several simple cases were worked fully and matched older literature. A public code repository hosts the notebook. Model builders can now screen theories quickly. Dark matter candidates face these consistency checks first.
arxiv-2510-02534:
Iranmanesh and co-authors use language models to filter false alarms from security scanners. Their 2025 software security paper presents a framework called ZeroFalse. Static testing tools flag many harmless code patterns as flaws. Developers drown in triage and stop trusting the tools. ZeroFalse treats each scanner alert as a structured contract. Flow sensitive traces and context enrich every alert. Knowledge tied to the weakness class joins the packet. A language model then judges the alert with that evidence. Ten leading models were tested across benchmarks and real projects.

Reasoning focused models judged alerts best in their tests. Weakness specific prompting beat general prompting clearly. False positives fell while real coverage stayed intact. The paper also guides model choice by cost and speed. Security teams can pick a tier that fits their budget. Trustworthy automation may finally stick in development pipelines. Noisy alerts become signals worth reading.
arxiv-2510-02834:
Dobrotka, Magdolen, and Melicherčík hunt for a faint rhythm in flickering star systems. The systems are nova-like cataclysmic variables. In each one, a white dwarf pulls gas from a companion star. The gas forms a bright disc that flickers at random. Buried in the flicker is a break frequency. Past work placed it near one millihertz. The team mined data from the TESS and XMM-Newton space telescopes.

They found a fresh optical break in three systems. The values again clustered near one millihertz. Two systems showed matching X-ray breaks, which points to the disc's inner edge. Long records showed the break can shift or vanish as brightness changes. A guessed link to white dwarf mass did not survive the new data. A link to viewing angle held up instead. Face-on systems show the break, while edge-on ones hide it.
arxiv-2510-02934:
Vu and co-authors check AI-written code by reading the writer's mind. Language models now draft much new software. Their code can fail to compile, misbehave, or open security holes. Prior studies found clues inside the models' own signals. Those studies, though, fixed one layer and token spot in advance. A fixed choice may not suit every model or task. Their system, AutoProbe, picks the best signals on the fly.

An attention step learns a score for each hidden state. Strong states are pooled and fed to a small classifier. The classifier judges compile success, function, and safety. Tests covered many benchmarks and many code models. AutoProbe beat black-box and white-box rivals throughout. Its security scores passed the best white-box method by a wide edge. It also held up best as code grew complex. Function scores showed the largest gains of all.
arxiv-2510-03034:
Hitzelhammer and co-authors set hard limits on how well microscopes can locate tiny particles. Coherent scattering microscopes find particles by their scattered light. Interferometric versions mix that light with a reference beam. Tilting the light off-axis has been said to help. A rotating variant claims sharper images that way. The authors ask what the true precision limits are. They use Cramér-Rao bounds, the floor set by photon noise.

Their math covers slanted light in the interferometric setup. Off-axis light does add information about the particle. Three-dimensional precision can thus improve over the straight-on case. The rotating method, though, scored worse on location precision. That holds despite its finer spatial resolution. Resolution and precision, the paper stresses, are different virtues. Judging a microscope by one number misleads buyers and builders. The bounds give designers a firm target per photon.
arxiv-2510-03134:
Giorgi and co-authors turn counterfactual explanations into stories small models can tell. A counterfactual shows the smallest change that flips a prediction. Such examples are sharp but hard for lay readers to parse. Small models are cheaper to run but narrate poorly alone. Their pipeline teaches small models through knowledge distillation. A teacher model drafts several narrative versions first.

A refining stage then merges those drafts into one. It fixes clashes and errors that single drafts carry. A simple checker grades each story against ground truth. It tests fit with both the factual and the flipped case. Distillation proved essential, not merely helpful. Undistilled small models failed the task outright. Distilled ones gained strong fidelity and coherence scores. Refinement lifted quality further in test after test. The result points to deployable, low-cost explanation tools. Clinics and banks could explain decisions without giant models.
arxiv-2510-03234:
Berger and Conus compute the optimal betting strategy for the television game show Lucky 13. Contestants answer thirteen trivia questions first. They then bet by naming a range for their own correct count. Picking the range well matters as much as knowing trivia. The authors model correct answers with binomial random variables. Question categories carry different success chances in the fuller model. Two utility functions frame the player's goal. One maximizes the chance of winning any money. The other maximizes expected winnings outright.

Tables lay out the optimal range for each situation. The two goals often recommend different ranges, they show. Case studies examine decisions made by actual contestants. Monte Carlo simulation estimates how a typical player scores. Category mixes from the sampled shows feed those simulations. The model extends to per-question success probabilities if desired. Modeling the producers' buyout offers needs richer records.
arxiv-2510-03434:
Jiang and colleagues at Bagel Labs present a 2025 arXiv report on Paris, a text to image diffusion model trained without any central cluster. Big image models normally train on thousands of linked graphics cards that swap updates constantly. Paris instead trains eight expert models in complete isolation, each on its own cluster of related image data. No gradients or weights move between the experts during training. A small transformer router then picks which expert should answer each prompt.

The team reports image quality comparable to centrally trained baselines. Paris used fourteen times less training data and sixteen times less compute than the prior decentralized baseline in their comparison. Open weights serve both research and commercial users. Removing the need for special interconnects lets odd, scattered hardware join large training runs. The work sketches a path toward community scale model building outside the biggest labs.
arxiv-2510-03534:
Dal Fabbro and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on mapping a river plume with a fleet of underwater robots over days. The Douro river spills fresh water into the Atlantic off Portugal, and its plume shifts with tides and weather. Fixed sensors and crewed surveys cannot track such a changing feature. Their approach sends autonomous underwater vehicles out under a central coordinator that checks in now and then. That sparse contact saves energy and bandwidth on long missions.

A Gaussian process model stitches the scattered samples into a map. A multi head learning controller steers each vehicle by direction and speed. In ocean model simulations, the fleet beat single and multi agent benchmarks on mapping error. Doubling the fleet sometimes more than doubled endurance while accuracy held or improved. Learned policies also carried across seasons and years. Coastal teams could watch pollution and fisheries habitat with less ship time.
arxiv-2510-04234:
Huang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on legged robot control that can improvise new behaviors at test time. Reinforcement learning produces fixed policies that resist later adjustment, while classical model predictive control needs accurate dynamics models that legged robots defy. The authors replace the hand-built model with a learned diffusion model acting as a dynamics prior. The planner jointly predicts future states and actions by denoising whole trajectories.

At each denoising step, reward guidance steers the trajectory toward the current task objective. Constraint projection keeps it inside physical and safety limits. An training loop runs this planner in the environment, then filters and reweights collected trajectories by realized return before updating the model. On a real robot, the system showed strong locomotion and adaptation to new reward specifications without retraining. Diffusion priors may offer a general route to adaptable embodied control.
arxiv-2510-04934:
Satvik Dixit, Soham Deshmukh, and Bhiksha Raj of Carnegie Mellon University study how to grade AI answers about sound in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their field is audio question answering, where a model listens to a clip and replies in free text. Old grading metrics compare wording, not meaning. They miss context, reasoning, and answers that are partly right.

The team first built AQEval, a benchmark of ten thousand model replies scored by human judges. Testing old metrics on it showed weak agreement with human ratings, above all for longer answers. Their new metric, AURA, uses language-based reasoning plus an audio entailment check. AURA's correlation with human judgment was 2.2 times higher than the best older metric. The authors release both tools for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-05234:
Alex Friedlan and Hae-Young Kee explain a symmetry-breaking phase in kagome metals in this 2025 arXiv paper. These layered vanadium compounds host charge order, magnetism, and superconductivity. Experiments recently found nematic order that cuts the lattice's sixfold symmetry down to twofold. The nematic state also breaks time-reversal symmetry, which needs explaining.

Starting from a nine-band model with nearest-neighbor interactions, the authors find nematic order in a narrow window. The state mixes charge-bond order on one kagome bond with loop currents on the other two. One mirror plane survives the mixing. A patch model shows the phase coupling between the three bond orders stabilizes this arrangement. The nematic phase also reshapes the Fermi surface into a distinctive elongated form.
arxiv-2510-05334:
N. Nishu Karna and Tatiana Niembro trace a geomagnetic storm from the Sun to Earth in this 2025 arXiv paper. The storm struck on May 28, 2011, and registered a moderate minus 80 nanotesla on the disturbance index. Its source active regions sat beside a large coronal hole. Two filament eruptions left the Sun eight hours apart.

The authors built three-dimensional magnetic models that matched the telescope images. The nearby coronal hole lowered the eruptions' stability threshold sharply. Flux ropes broke free with about three times less axial flux than comparable cases without coronal holes. Data from STEREO and near-Earth monitors showed two distinct ejections and no early collision between them. Hydrodynamic simulations then tracked each structure out to Earth's orbit with good agreement.
arxiv-2510-05434:
Gangam and colleagues study fair rent division, a classic problem in economics and computer science. A group must assign rooms to housemates and split a fixed total rent between them. A split counts as fair when no one envies another person's room and price. The 2025 paper adds two real-world limits that older models ignored. Rent bounds reflect contracts and shared caps that real landlords and campuses impose.

One limit puts lower and upper bounds on what each room can cost. The other gives each person a separate budget cap for each room. The authors build fast methods that find a fair split or prove that none exists. They also pick the fairest splits by goals such as raising the worst-off person's outcome. Both limits fit inside one shared method, which suits tools like the Spliddit housing platform.
arxiv-2510-05634:
Liu and colleagues explain the heaviest black hole merger yet observed. GW231123 joined black holes of about 137 and 103 solar masses. Both components sit inside or above the pair-instability mass gap, defying standard stellar evolution. Their 2025 study tests Population III star clusters as the birthplace.

Using N-body simulations of first-generation star clusters, they find three production channels. Stellar mergers, black hole mergers, and mixed mergers all build suitable progenitors. One to three repeated mergers assemble the candidate systems. Stellar mergers dominate in low-mass clusters and dodge recoil ejection. Their mass distribution covers both component masses of the event. A top-heavy initial mass function helps by making more massive stars. Predicted merger rates span a range that includes the observed rate. Future detectors like LISA and the Einstein Telescope could catch similar systems.
arxiv-2510-05734:
Veyron and colleagues design an all-optical bubble trap for ultracold atoms in microgravity. Shell-shaped traps hold atoms on a hollow sphere's surface, enabling curved two-dimensional physics. Magnetic schemes exist, but an optical route promises cleaner control. Their 2025 scheme builds the shell purely from light-atom interaction.

Optical double dressing of the ground state creates a strong short-range repulsive barrier. A long-range attractive potential combines with it to form the shell. Two crossed beams with parabolic profiles can make a fully spherical bubble. Trap traits depend on polarizability ratios and the excited state's lifetime. The design reaches the quasi-two-dimensional regime for standard atom numbers. A rubidium benchmark gives 250 hertz transverse confinement on a 35 micron bubble. Residual scattering stays below ten events per second. Switching one laser's detuning tunes radius and stiffness toward the thin-shell limit.
arxiv-2510-06134:
Sike and six co-authors run the first galaxy simulations forming whole star cluster ensembles with live cosmic ray physics in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Star clusters host the massive stars whose feedback reshapes the gas around them. Capturing that loop requires parsec-scale resolution plus a multiphase interstellar medium.

The team used the CRISP feedback model inside the moving-mesh code AREPO, running tall-box patches of a galaxy. Cosmic rays were dynamically coupled, with several transport variants under self-confinement theory. Cosmic rays lowered the star formation rate, flattened the cluster mass function, and cut formation efficiency. Cluster radii and velocity dispersions changed only modestly, but virial parameters shifted significantly. With fewer supernovae stirring the gas, the new clusters ended up more tightly bound by their own gravity. Every run matched observations, and cosmic ray feedback moved results along known cluster relations.
arxiv-2510-06334:
Shoji and Trailović present a stable numerical method for Lefschetz thimble intersection numbers in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Oscillatory integrals like real-time path integrals decompose over thimbles attached to saddle points. Knowing which thimbles contribute, and with which signs, was numerically fragile in several variables.

Their approach applies multiple shooting to the upward flow equations. The flows run from each saddle point to the original integration cycle. Solving them yields the intersection numbers together with their signs. Tests show stable performance up to twenty variables. Quadruple-precision arithmetic can extend it further. The authors determine intersection numbers for complex saddle points in a discretized path integral. Those results illuminate real-time path integrals, a long-standing computational obstacle. The method should apply broadly to oscillatory integrals in physics and mathematics.
arxiv-2510-06534:
Jiahe Jin, Abhijay Paladugu, and Chenyan Xiong study how language models search the web to answer hard questions. Their 2025 paper examines agentic search, where a model plans, searches, and then combines what it finds. Good results depend on how the model reasons during that process. The team built a pipeline to study the reasoning inside successful searches.

From those successful runs, they identify four helpful reasoning behaviors. The behaviors are checking information, judging source authority, adapting the search, and recovering from errors. Models that show these behaviors more often also perform better on search tasks. The authors then train models to copy the behaviors, using fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. They call that training method Behavior Priming. Tests on three benchmarks, named GAIA, WebWalker, and HLE, show the approach works well.
arxiv-2510-06634:
Shiye Su, Yuhui Zhang, Linqi Zhou, Rajesh Ranganath, and Serena Yeung-Levy study generative models that turn one kind of data into another. Their 2025 paper concerns tasks like drug discovery and simulating how species evolve. A method called flow matching can learn such transformations. It has mostly been used to turn noise into data, though.

When the starting point is also real data, learned from few samples, standard flow matching fails. The supervision becomes too sparse to guide the transformation. The authors fix that by injecting randomness at three points during training. They perturb the source samples and the in-between steps of the flow. Across five imaging tasks in biology, radiology, and astronomy, quality improved sharply. Their method beat existing baselines by an average of nine FID points, a standard quality score. It also lowered the transport cost between inputs and outputs.
arxiv-2510-06934:
Ricardo Campos and Bruno Vallette build the machinery that turns local symmetries into ones for a class of algebras. Their 2025 paper develops integration theory for Lie-graph algebras. These algebras carry a product enriched with operations drawn as graphs. Classical Lie theory integrates a Lie algebra into a group through an exponential map.

Doing the same for graph-enriched algebras was the open task. The authors produce formulas for the exponential map of these structures. They also pin down the gauge group and how it acts on Maurer-Cartan elements. Those elements encode changes, so the formulas serve deformation theory. The work extends the pre-Lie algebra case, which governs changes to operadic algebras. A sequel article applies this to bialgebra deformation theories. Abstract as it sounds, this machinery decides when two deformed structures are the same. That question sits underneath much of algebra.
arxiv-2510-07134:
Liu and co-authors present TrackVLA++, a robot model that follows a moving target named in words. Their 2025 paper tackles embodied visual tracking. A companion or service robot must keep its target in view through clutter. Older models lost the target when it hid behind objects. Look-alike bystanders also lured them off course.

Two new parts address those failures. A reasoning step works out where the target sits relative to the robot, using polar terms for direction and distance. A memory unit guards the target's identity over long stretches. It updates with care so brief hidden moments do not erase the trail. Tests on public benchmarks set new best scores in both single-camera and multi-camera setups. On a hard tracking split, the model beat the prior best. Reliable following is basic for robots that guide or assist people.
arxiv-2510-07334:
Deshpande and Szefer define a young field: the security of quantum computers themselves. Their 2025 article extends a short newsletter piece of the same name. Most readers know post-quantum cryptography, which shields classical data from quantum attack. The authors flip the question. Cloud platforms now rent access to real quantum processors, and those machines have their own attack surfaces. The article maps the components of a typical cloud quantum system and marks where attackers could strike.

Quantum systems do gain one natural shield: unknown quantum states cannot be copied perfectly. The authors sort attacks into classes, ending with targeted attacks that use deep system knowledge for precise harm. Their call is for defenses built in from the start, across hardware design, software toolchains, and algorithms. As quantum machines handle more sensitive work, that agenda grows more urgent.
arxiv-2510-07534:
Krause and a large team review the evidence that supermassive black holes sometimes come in pairs. Their article surveys a prediction of hierarchical galaxy growth. When two galaxies merge, their central black holes should sink to the new center and form a binary. Direct evidence exists in dual active nuclei, separated from kiloparsec scales down to parsec scales. Jets from some active galaxies carry signatures that may betray even closer pairs.

The hardening physics dominates uncertainty in the expected gravitational wave signal. The space antenna LISA should eventually hear actual mergers of these giants. Before launch, pulsar timing arrays hold the best hope for detection, listening for a background hum from countless inspiraling pairs.
arxiv-2510-07734:
He and twelve coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a newly studied Algol-type binary star system. In such systems, one star spills material onto its companion. The authors identified this pair as a spectroscopic binary in LAMOST survey spectra. TESS space photometry then charted its regular eclipses. They give the system a full photometric and spectroscopic analysis in this report.

The orbit takes about two and a half days and looks circular. The primary is an A-type star of roughly one point eight solar masses. Its companion is far lighter yet bloated, filling its Roche lobe and feeding the primary. A double-peaked hydrogen emission line points to a swirling accretion disc. Their disc model matches the size inferred from that emission. Drifting system velocity hints at a third companion star. The light secondary may one day shrink into a helium white dwarf.
arxiv-2510-08034:
Ji and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper improving how LoRA adapters are initialized when fine-tuning language models. LoRA adds small trainable matrices instead of updating the full model. The usual setup treats the query and value projections of attention alike. The authors show the two play different roles. Query parameters carry task-sensitive knowledge. Value parameters encode token features that stay comparatively stable.

Their method, AILoRA, initializes the two adapters asymmetrically. It injects the principal components of the query matrix to preserve task-adaptive capacity. It injects the minor components of the value matrix to preserve generalizable features. Across three model families, the approach beat existing parameter-efficient methods. Gains covered understanding and generation benchmarks, with faster convergence. The work argues initialization should respect what each part of attention does.
arxiv-2510-08134:
Sahu, Macca, and Samala wrote this 2025 numerical analysis paper on simulating hyperbolic balance laws whose source terms are stiff. Stiffness forces explicit schemes into tiny time steps, while fully implicit schemes are costly. The authors extend the classic Nessyahu-Tadmor central scheme with a semi-implicit treatment of the source, blending a midpoint rule in space, a trapezoidal rule in time, and a backward Taylor expansion.

The method keeps second-order accuracy as the relaxation parameter vanishes. Its stability region is significantly larger than conventional central schemes, allowing bigger time steps. The team validated it on five benchmarks, including a relaxation model, shallow water flow, the Broadwell model, and Euler equations with stiff heat transfer and friction. Convergence tables confirmed the predicted order. The scheme preserves the simplicity that made central schemes popular.
arxiv-2510-08334:
Weixin Li and co-authors propose a new surface wave for magnetic computing in a 2025 arXiv paper on hematite. Hematite is a classic insulating antiferromagnet, a material whose atomic magnets point in opposing patterns. Its spin waves, called magnons, can carry signals without moving electric charge. Coupling magnons strongly to photons, particles of light, is a goal for coherent spintronics.

The team shows a surface magnon-polariton, a mixed magnon-photon wave, can live at the surface of canted hematite. Canting means the opposing magnets tilt slightly, which helps on-chip electrical layouts couple the modes. The surface mode sits inside a gap of the bulk magnon-photon bands. Its existence traces to the nontrivial topology of those bulk bands. Magnon-photon coupling boosts Berry curvature near band crossings, giving a topological Chern band behind the surface mode.
arxiv-2510-08434:
Laura Cui and co-authors ask when physical quantum dynamics can pass as truly random in a 2025 arXiv paper. Random unitaries underpin quantum algorithms, cryptography, and chaos studies. Local random circuits converge to fully random Haar unitaries over time, but they follow no fixed physical Hamiltonian. Real systems evolve under one time-independent energy operator instead.

On the negative side, they prove constant-local Hamiltonians never look fully random. For any such ensemble and any evolution times, the dynamics can be efficiently told apart from Haar-random. It forms neither a unitary 2-design nor a pseudorandom unitary, both standard randomness benchmarks. On the positive side, slightly richer Hamiltonians in one dimension succeed. Random polylog-local Hamiltonians, acting on modest neighborhoods, become indistinguishable from Haar-random in constant time. They form k-designs and pseudorandom unitaries, and can be simulated efficiently under cryptographic assumptions.
arxiv-2510-08534:
Arianna Rizzieri, Clément Leloup, Josquin Errard, and Davide Poletti study how to clean Milky Way foregrounds from cosmic microwave background maps in a 2025 arXiv paper. The hunt for primordial B-modes, a fingerprint of early-universe gravitational waves, needs precise foreground removal. Galactic dust and synchrotron emission vary across the sky in both strength and spectral behavior. Their tool, fgbuster, performs parametric component separation by maximum likelihood.

Using simulations and analytic arguments, they test fitting different spectral parameters in distinct pixel subsets. Allowing parameters to vary across sky regions proved essential for competitive signal-to-noise after cleaning. It also keeps residual foreground bias under control, they show. Satisfactory configurations exist where statistical and systematic residuals become negligible for next-generation missions. The statistical uncertainty depends only weakly on foreground properties, and they propose a semi-analytic way to estimate it.
arxiv-2510-08934:
Rosko presents a geometric scheme for checking logical proofs with arithmetic on Fibonacci numbers, in this 2025 arXiv paper on logic and computation. The Fibonacci sequence, where each term adds the two before it, can encode any whole number uniquely as a sum of chosen terms. Rosko maps the witnesses of simple logical claims onto such encodings. Under the mapping, the basic inference step of logic becomes an equation to solve in whole numbers.

Because the mapping chains across steps, checking a tautology becomes arithmetic on Fibonacci indices rather than a search through meanings. Rosko states the check runs in time tied to fast integer multiplication, independent of what the propositions say. He frames the system as proof by alignment: a claim holds when its encodings line up. The construction consciously echoes Ada Lovelace's early vision of symbolic computation, while respecting the known limits that incompleteness places on any such system.
arxiv-2510-09234:
Shi shows that quantum fluctuations can turn a smooth change between two superconducting states into a sudden jump, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Some superconductors host two rival pairing channels. Combined with a phase offset, they break time-reversal symmetry, an exotic state prized for topological quantum computing. Existing theory treated this transition at mean-field level, ignoring the wild phase fluctuations the state should suffer.

Working with the hole-doped square-lattice t-J model, a standard cuprate stand-in, Shi computes a fluctuation-corrected free energy. The correction reshapes the phase diagram. The time-reversal-breaking s-plus-id region splits off a dome whose border with the d-wave phase is first order, meaning abrupt. That signals possible separation into coexisting symmetric and asymmetric regions. Fluctuations also shrink the exotic phase's territory considerably. Shi links the findings to disorder-driven breakdown experiments and twisted cuprate junctions.
arxiv-2510-09334:
Peteris Daugulis, the sole author, offers a data-driven way to redraw local government boundaries in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fair access to town services depends on where borders fall and where offices sit. Populations, roads, and local economies keep changing, so old divisions can leave some residents with far longer trips than others.

Daugulis builds the divisions from a road network where each road carries a travel weight. The method partitions the network in a Voronoi style, assigning each place to its nearest centre, and then places centres by solving a vertex k-center problem. That problem asks for spots that keep the worst travel burden as low as possible. He shows the approach at work in Latvia, a country with varied terrain and uneven settlement, aiming for smaller gaps in travel time.
arxiv-2510-09434:
Xixi Wang and five co-authors, among them Francisco Camara Pereira and Robert Thomson, study crash reports in a 2025 arXiv paper. Police and investigators write free-text narratives after real crashes, and these stories hold clues that structured fields miss. Yet the writing is unstandardised and varies by author, so no documented tool can yet process the narratives in bulk.

The team asks whether compact open language models can extract facts that require inference, not just explicit statements. They predict two things for each crash: its manner of collision, and the crash type for each vehicle involved, the second drawn from nearly one hundred categories. They adapt models to the domain with fine-tuning, including low-rank adaptation for large models and a tuned BERT model. Experiments use the Crash Investigation Sampling System, an authoritative real-world crash dataset, chosen partly to keep sensitive data away from closed external services.
arxiv-2510-09934:
Jain and Elie Alhajjar propose a denoising diffusion framework for underwater images in this 2025 arXiv paper on image processing. Underwater photos support ocean research and checks on marine ecosystems. Yet water degrades them with noise, color distortion, blurry textures, and low visibility.

Diffusion models clean an image by reversing a gradual noising process, removing corruption step by step. The authors adapt that idea as a fresh framework for the underwater setting, where the damage differs from ordinary photo noise. Their approach treats the murk and color shift of submerged scenes as the corruption to undo. The goal is clearer images for scientists who read reefs, seabeds, and marine life from camera footage.
arxiv-2510-10234:
Blot proves that two quantizations of one hierarchy coincide in this 2025 arXiv note in mathematical physics. The dispersionless Korteweg-de Vries hierarchy is a tower of equations from soliton theory. Quantizing it means building a quantum version whose structures mirror the classical one.

Wang built such a quantization using the Heisenberg vertex algebra. Independently, Blot and Rossi obtained one from meromorphic differential hierarchies, in the simplest cohomological field theory case. This note proves the two constructions are the same. Agreement between unrelated routes is strong evidence that the quantization is the natural one. It also lets results proved in either language transfer to the other.
arxiv-2510-10434:
Kangjian Zhu and five co-authors present a new way to find a robot's pose from a single camera image in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pose means the robot's position and orientation in space. Their method needs no markers attached to the robot. It treats pose estimation as a diffusion process, a method that starts from noisy guesses and cleans them up step by step.

Their framework has two parts. A diffusion stage creates varied training poses while keeping the robot inside the camera's field of view. A reverse stage then refines a pose estimate step by step, moving from coarse to fine, with each step's scale guiding the network. On the DREAM and RoboKeyGen benchmarks, the method beat prior approaches. On the hardest dataset it reached an AUC score of 66.75 points, a gain of 32.3 percent over the previous best result reported there.
arxiv-2510-10634:
Shaoning Li and seven co-authors compress protein structures into a smooth latent space, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Good encodings of protein shape are key for protein science, above all for generating new structures. Existing approaches wrestle with rotation symmetry, chop structures into discrete tokens, or juggle several training goals, all of which hinder training. Their system, ProteinAE, is a diffusion autoencoder that maps backbone positions directly into a compact latent space.

It uses a Diffusion Transformer with a bottleneck design for tight packing. Training is end to end with a single flow matching objective, which simplifies the pipeline. ProteinAE achieved state of the art rebuilding quality, beating existing encoders. Its latent space then supports a second model that generates structures without explicit symmetry handling. The output quality rivals leading structure based methods and clearly beats earlier latent based approaches, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-10834:
Jeffrey Shallit proves two impossibility results about automatic sequences tied to the Tribonacci constant, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Tribonacci constant, about 1.839, generalizes the golden ratio: it comes from a recurrence where each term sums the previous three. Numbers can be written in a Tribonacci representation system, and a natural question is which relations between numbers a finite automaton can check by reading two representations in parallel.

Shallit shows that no automaton accepts the Tribonacci representations of n and of the integer part of n times the Tribonacci constant, read in parallel. In other words, that simple looking multiplication relation is beyond finite state recognition in this numeration system. He also shows that no Tribonacci automaton generates the Sturmian characteristic word with slope one less than the constant. Such negative results map the limits of automatic theorem proving for Tribonacci combinatorics.
arxiv-2510-11334:
Agents in a network, from sensors to opinion holders, reach consensus when their states converge to one common value, but real networks drop connections from time to time. Fabio Ancona, Mohamed Bentaibi, and Francesco Rossi strengthen the known theory for that setting in this 2025 arXiv control theory paper. Conditions found by Moreau guarantee consensus under intermittent connections; what was missing was the speed of the convergence.

The authors prove that Moreau's conditions in fact ensure exponential convergence to consensus, and they give an explicit rate. The key quantity behind the rate is the length of the graph, meaning the number of connections needed to reach a common agent: the larger that length, the slower the convergence. The general result also supplies convergence conditions for second-order cooperative systems with missing connections, covering agents whose states include both position-like and velocity-like components.
arxiv-2510-11634:
Auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo is among the most accurate methods for simulating molecules, but its cost grows with the fourth power of system size, walling off systems and cavity-coupled chemistry. Yu Zhang cuts that cost in this 2025 arXiv computational chemistry paper. The setting is polariton chemistry, where molecules coupled to an optical cavity form hybrid light-matter states whose properties standard electronic structure methods struggle to reach at scale.

The savings come from structure in the Cholesky decomposition of the electron repulsion integrals: in molecular ensembles the tensors are naturally block-sparse. Zhang keeps high-rank blocks in sparse form and compresses low-rank blocks with tensor hypercontraction, a mixed representation that drops exchange-energy evaluation from quartic to cubic scaling and memory from cubic toward quadratic. Benchmarks up to about twelve hundred orbitals confirmed linear growth of nonzero counts and sublinear rank growth, with accuracy preserved.
arxiv-2510-11834:
Sarah Ball and Andreas Haupt tackle a subtle failure of safety tuning for generative AI. Such models often pair with a classifier that filters harmful outputs. A common fix fine-tunes the generator to dodge the filter, but that pushes outputs toward the classifier's decision boundary. Near that line, harmless outputs get blocked and harmful ones slip through more often. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes Boundary Guidance instead.

Boundary Guidance is a reinforcement learning fine-tuning method that steers generation away from the classifier's margin on purpose. On a benchmark of jailbreak attempts and ambiguous prompts, the steered models scored better on both safety and usefulness. The scores came from evaluations that used a language model as judge. Extensive ablation studies covered different model sizes and reward designs. The approach held up across all of them.
arxiv-2510-12034:
Thomas Lehéricy studies how far the fastest wanderer strays in a branching random walk. In this model, each particle reproduces, dies, and leaves offspring scattered near its own position. The walk is critical when each particle averages exactly one child, and centered when the average step is zero. His 2025 arXiv paper works under minimal assumptions: only finite variance for offspring counts and step sizes.

The main theorem pins down the tail of the maximum displacement. The chance that the rightmost particle passes a large distance r falls off like an explicit constant times one over r squared. That sharpens an earlier result of Lalley and Shao, extending its reach. Conditioning on the maximum being large, Lehéricy also finds the limiting family tree of the whole process. The machinery then transfers to multitype branching random walks, where particles come in several kinds.
arxiv-2510-12134:
Hongbo Cai, Pengjie Zhang, and Yilun Guan hunt for crashes between universes in the sky's most indirect mirrors. Eternal inflation predicts bubble universes crashing, leaving round symmetric scars on superhorizon scales. The remote dipole and quadrupole fields rebuild how the cosmos looks from distant vantage points, dodging the cosmic variance that limits the usual microwave background. Their 2025 arXiv paper computes the crash's imprint in closed form.

Theirs is the first closed-form expression for the remote quadrupole signal from a bubble collision, checked against a new public code, RemoteField, with strong agreement. Joining it with earlier dipole math, they project detection power for CMB-S4-like and LSST-like surveys. The dipole rebuild alone rivals the primary microwave background's grip. The quadrupole rebuild improves constraints by about tenfold. More modes and tomography could sharpen things further. The approach extends to other beyond-horizon physics, cosmic topology and domain walls too.
arxiv-2510-12434:
Zai and co-authors answer multi hop questions by planning on the fly over knowledge hypergraphs, in a 2025 arXiv paper on retrieval augmented generation. Knowledge hypergraphs represent relations among several entities at once. Earlier systems using them planned retrieval once up front, ran it without adapting, and used the hypergraph structure only on the surface.

Their framework, PRoH, adds three pieces. A context aware planning module sketches the local hypergraph neighborhood to ground the plan. Question splitting organizes subquestions as a directed acyclic graph that evolves during the search, enabling exploration along several paths. A retrieval algorithm scores reasoning paths by entity weighted overlap, favoring coherent hyperedge traversals. Across domains the system reached state of the art results, beating the prior best model by clear margins in both F1 and a generation score. It also stayed robust on long multi hop questions, where static planners break down.
arxiv-2510-12534:
Nareti and colleagues build a text classifier whose explanations are example passages a human can inspect, tuned for reviews carrying several labels at once, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Prototype based models explain decisions by similarity to learned example texts, but earlier versions worked at coarse sentence or document level and ignored multi label data. User reviews, their target, routinely express several aspects in one sentence.

ProtoSiTex alternates two training phases: an unsupervised phase that discovers semantically coherent, diverse prototypes, and a supervised phase mapping prototypes to labels. A hierarchical loss enforces consistency across sentence, sub sentence, and document levels. Adaptive prototypes with multi head attention capture overlapping and conflicting meanings. The authors also release a hotel review dataset annotated at sub sentence level with multiple labels. On that dataset and two public benchmarks, ProtoSiTex reached state of the art performance while giving faithful, human aligned explanations.
arxiv-2510-12634:
De Rújula defends the Cannonball model of gamma ray bursts against the challenge of recently observed extremely energetic photons, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Gamma ray bursts are the most violent explosions known, and a few intrinsically bright ones have emitted gamma rays reaching tera electron volt energies. Any successful model must explain both those photons and the near absence of accompanying neutrinos.

Writing in the first person, De Rújula argues the Cannonball model, which pictures bursts as jets of dense plasmoids ejected by a supernova like event, has no difficulty accounting for either fact. The model describes the origin and approximate properties of the high energy gamma rays naturally. At the same time it makes the accompanying neutrinos extremely hard to observe, matching the null detections. The paper is a position piece marshaling the model's long record of predictions, rather than a report of new observations.
arxiv-2510-12834:
Guichoux and collaborators introduce Gelina in this 2025 arXiv paper, a system that generates speech and gestures together from text. Human communication couples voice and movement tightly, yet most generators produce speech first and gestures afterward, which weakens their timing match and rhythm alignment.

Gelina instead interleaves speech and gesture tokens, the discrete units each mode is built from, inside one prediction sequence, then decodes each mode with its own decoder. The design supports cloning multiple speakers and styles, and it can also produce gestures alone when given speech as input. In subjective and objective evaluations, speech quality stayed competitive with specialized systems while gesture generation improved over single-mode baselines. The authors present Gelina as a step toward avatars whose voice and body stay in sync.
arxiv-2510-13134:
Álvarez-López and Hernández analyze dropout through random batch methods in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Dropout, randomly silencing neurons during training, regularizes neural networks, and in continuous-time models it resembles random batch schemes invented to cheapen particle simulations. The authors build that analogy into rigorous theory.

They construct an unbiased estimator that mimics dropout by drawing neuron batches over time intervals. Trajectory-wise convergence holds at a linear rate in the interval length, and at the distribution level the continuity equation is stable with a slower, square-root order error. An adjoint analysis based on Pontryagin's principle bounds deviations in cost, control, and gradient iterates. On the design side they compare sampling schemes and recover Bernoulli dropout as a special case. They derive a closed-form optimal interval from a cost-accuracy trade-off. They validate it all on a neural ordinary differential equation.
arxiv-2510-13234:
Yan and co-authors unify vector extraction from images in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in Nuclear Physics B. Vector extraction recovers structured geometry, polygons, polylines, and line segments, from raster images for maps and engineering drawings. Existing methods are usually built for one vector type, forcing separate models per structure, because they treat instance attributes and geometric attributes independently.

Their framework, UniVector, encodes each vector as a structured query carrying both instance-level and geometry-level information. It then iteratively updates the queries through an interaction module that exchanges context across the two levels. This echoes how human perception mixes semantic and spatial cues. A dynamic shape constraint refines global structure and key points. The team also built a Multi-Vector benchmark dataset mixing all three structure types. UniVector set new state-of-the-art results on both single-structure and multi-structure extraction tasks.
arxiv-2510-13334:
Feng and co-authors defend language model cache eviction against its own fragile assumption in this 2025 arXiv paper. Long generation fills the transformer's key-value cache, so methods evict entries judged unimportant by a scoring and aggregation scheme. Nearly all of them average scores, trusting a stability assumption that one fixed subset of entries stays important throughout generation.

The authors argue that assumption is inherently fragile, making mean aggregation vulnerable in extreme cases where importance shifts suddenly. Their countermeasure is defensive aggregation: a simple two-step, linear-time strategy that controls worst-case risk with negligible overhead. Built on it, DefensiveKV and its layer-wise budget extension cut generation quality loss by large multiples against the strongest baseline. That held when the cache is shrunk to a fifth of its size, across seven task domains and eighteen datasets.
arxiv-2510-13434:
Wang and co-authors at Alibaba introduce M2PO, a preference optimization method for machine translation. Their 2025 arXiv paper improves on Direct Preference Optimization, which trains models on better-versus-worse output pairs. Two flaws limit current methods, the authors argue. Reward signals from quality estimation models can miss errors such as hallucinated content. The goal is translations that people judge faithful as well as fluent.

Standard practice also keeps only one winning and losing pair, discarding other useful comparisons. M2PO builds a richer reward by combining two perspectives on quality. One is a new penalty for hallucination, which punishes invented content. The other is a dynamic score that blends outside grades with the model's own evolving judgement. A multi-pair strategy then builds preference pairs from the whole pool of candidate translations. On WMT21-22 benchmarks, M2PO clearly beat existing preference methods and rivalled leading commercial models.
arxiv-2510-13934:
Jaume de Haro and Emilio Elizalde revisit the geometric foundations of general relativity in this 2025 arXiv paper. General relativity describes gravity through the shape of spacetime, often pictured as a flexible fabric. The authors argue that this image misleads, and that curvature is better understood through the dynamic interplay of matter and interacting fields, a view Einstein and Weyl themselves stressed.

Working from gauge invariance, the freedom to describe the same physics in different coordinate choices, they rebuild a Newtonian framework, meaning a classical gravity picture, that still captures essential features of cosmology. The shift they propose is from substance to relationships: gravity emerges from how matter and fields relate, not from a material spacetime. They note striking similarities between this classical approach and recent, more ambitious work at the quantum level.
arxiv-2510-14134:
Oluwashina Adegoke and a large collaboration dissect the 'failed outburst' of the black hole system IGR J17091-3624, in this 2025 arXiv paper. This black hole binary is famous for exotic variability rivaled by one other system. In a failed outburst, the source brightens in its hard state but never transitions to the soft state before fading back within weeks.

The team analyzes six observations by the NuSTAR X-ray telescope from the outburst. None showed the soft-state variability classes, but one epoch revealed dips in count rate lasting about four thousand seconds, a first for this source. Across epochs, the hot corona's properties evolved with luminosity. Signatures of relativistic reflection off the accretion disk stayed largely unchanged. A stable quasi-periodic oscillation persisted through the first five epochs. The dips match obscuration by ionized gas, and the authors discuss its origin and constrain the system's orbit and distance.
arxiv-2510-14234:
Ning Han and co-authors develop a controller that reshapes soft, deformable objects with a robot while guaranteeing the deformation stays within preset bounds, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Manipulating three-dimensional deformable objects is hard because their state is infinite-dimensional and their dynamics are complex; most methods simplify the object into abstract features and lose spatial detail.

Their model-free approach instead uses the coordinates of key points, extracted from the object's point cloud by deep learning, as the feature vector, preserving spatial information while shrinking the control problem. Shape dynamics are described through a deformation Jacobian matrix, turning manipulation into a visual servoing task. A prescribed performance controller built on barrier Lyapunov functions, which grow steeply near forbidden limits, enforces constraints on the key points throughout the motion. The authors prove closed-loop stability with Lyapunov analysis and show the method's power and robustness in experiments.
arxiv-2510-14334:
Sung-Soo Byun and Peter J. Forrester review how classical electrostatics, the physics of still electric charges, keeps solving modern problems in statistical mechanics and random matrix theory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Random matrices model systems from nuclear energy levels to wireless signals, and their eigenvalue statistics often mirror how charged particles behave, repelling each other, which is where electrostatics enters.

The review collects results chosen to illustrate general principles. The topics include electrostatic potentials and energies of balls and hyperellipsoids in any dimension, and equilibrium charges on their surfaces. They also include conformal mappings in two dimensions, and the balayage measure, which sweeps charge onto a boundary without changing the outside field. Examples show these tools giving the leading values of the integrals and particle density in such systems. They also give formulas for spread and gap probabilities, the chances that no particle falls in a given interval.
arxiv-2510-14534:
Salehi, in a short 2025 arXiv note, returns to Cantor's theorem, the classic result that no set can be matched onto the set of all its subsets. Cantor's own proof, from 1891, uses his diagonal argument to build a subset that any proposed matching must miss. Later writers found other proofs, some constructive and some not, and Salehi adds a new one to that list.

His proof is deliberately non-constructive, meaning it shows a matching cannot exist without exhibiting a missed subset directly. For finite sets he relies on the pigeonhole principle, showing by induction that a set with n elements has a powerset with more elements than the set itself. For infinite sets he splits the set into finite pieces and extends the counting argument across them. The note also reviews earlier non-constructive arguments and explains where they quietly depend on the axiom of choice.
arxiv-2510-14834:
Russell, Hamilton, Almassalkhi, and Ossareh design, in a 2025 arXiv paper, safer automatic voltage control for power grids filling with solar panels and batteries. Grid-connected inverters can run decentralized Volt-VAr control, adjusting reactive power as local voltage changes. Designed badly, the feedback between many inverters and the grid can go unstable. Good design needs a trustworthy model of that closed loop.

The authors build one from a linearized power flow fitted to historical data, improving on the standard LinDistFlow model. They then choose each inverter's control slope to minimize steady-state voltage deviation. The choice is subject to a stability constraint on the spectral radius of the loop, a non-convex condition not previously used in this setting. Comparisons with existing convex restrictions favor their constraint. On a realistic simulated feeder, the spectral radius design regulated voltage more effectively, suggesting a practical path to stable, autonomous voltage management.
arxiv-2510-15034:
Brito and Marston ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, what spin Hamiltonian, if any, has two quantum liquid states as its ground state. Gutzwiller-projected wavefunctions, a Fermi sea and a pi-flux state with correlations projected in, are leading pictures of spin liquids, magnetic states with no standard order. Whether a simple local energy function has them as ground states is a basic question for the theory.

The authors use a correlation matrix technique that rebuilds candidate Hamiltonians from a wavefunction's correlations. They work in two dimensions on finite square and triangular lattices. The answer is negative: no spin Hamiltonian with simple, local interactions stabilizes either state at finite sizes. The paper goes further, measuring how much each local term matters. It weighs the arguments for where such terms could come from. The result disciplines spin liquid theory: these states are superb trial answers in search of a question.
arxiv-2510-15134:
Mohammad Heydari Rad, Rezvan Afari, and Saeedeh Momtazi present a system that writes Persian multiple-choice exam questions automatically. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a real gap, since question generation tools are scarce for lower-resource languages like Persian. Good multiple-choice items need plausible wrong answers, called distractors, that challenge students without tricking them unfairly.

Their framework, FarsiMCQGen, generates candidate questions, filters them, and ranks the results, leaning on transformer models and knowledge graphs alongside rule-based checks to craft convincing distractors. The source material comes from Wikipedia's general knowledge content. Alongside the system, the team releases a new Persian dataset of 10,289 questions and tests it with several leading large language models. Their results support both the quality of the generated questions and the dataset's value for future research on Persian testing.
arxiv-2510-15234:
Xinrui Fang and five colleagues in human-computer interaction test whether AI companions can sharpen how young researchers read papers critically. Their 2025 paper starts from a gap: swapping views with peers builds critical thinking, but junior researchers often lack peers with varied viewpoints. The team designed an interface that exchanges thoughts with the reader right inside the paper, shaped by a small formative study.

Over two weeks, forty-six junior researchers read under three setups: no agent, one agent, or several agents. Agent-supported reading significantly improved critical thinking scores compared with reading alone. With one agent, readers wrote more reflective notes on the paper's content; with several, they engaged more with the agents and compared competing viewpoints. Fang and colleagues draw design lessons for AI reading support, cautioning that the style of exchange, not just its presence, shapes how readers think.
arxiv-2510-15434:
Huan Chen and five colleagues use street-level photos to find which features of a street make crashes more or less likely. Their 2025 workshop paper, Semantic4Safety, starts from about thirty thousand accident records in Austin, Texas. Street view imagery shows the roadside in fine detail, but turning pictures into trustworthy causal claims is the hard part.

Zero-shot segmentation, which labels image regions without task-specific training, converts the photos into eleven readable streetscape indicators. A gradient-boosted classifier then predicts crash types, and explanation tools rank which indicators drive the predictions. Propensity score weighting strips out confounding so the team can estimate causal effects per accident type. They found that scene complexity, exposure, and road geometry dominate prediction. More drivable area and emergency space lowered risk, while excessive visual openness raised it. The authors offer the framework for diagnosing high-risk corridors and targeting fixes.
arxiv-2510-15634:
Galaxy clusters should glow faintly in gamma rays where cosmic rays strike gas between galaxies. Ludwig Böss leads the sixth SLOW simulation paper, posted to arXiv in 2025, to size up that glow. The team ran the first cosmological MHD simulation with a live spectral cosmic ray model. Cosmic ray protons are injected at shocks, advected, and their gamma-ray output computed directly. Constrained initial conditions make the virtual universe resemble our actual local neighborhood.

The simulation finds protons gaining energy at structure and accretion shocks across clusters and filaments. Yet the predicted diffuse emission sits orders of magnitude below current Fermi-LAT upper limits. Detecting the Coma cluster's emission would need sensitivity beyond present instruments.
arxiv-2510-16234:
Hanane Nour Moussa and nine co-authors build ScholarEval, a tool that grades research ideas against the published record. AI now drafts research ideas freely, but weak ideas waste time if no one vets them. ScholarEval scores each idea on two axes: soundness, whether its methods hold up, and contribution, how far it moves past prior work.

To test it, the team built ScholarIdeas, the first expert-marked set of research ideas and reviews. It holds one hundred seventeen ideas across four fields. ScholarEval covers far more of the points human experts raised than rival tools. Judges also preferred its reviews over a top deep-research system for depth, evidence, and usefulness. A user study found it helps users engage with sources and refine ideas. The code, data, and tool are released for others to build on.
arxiv-2510-16334:
Eden Shaveet and three co-authors test whether Yelp complaints can flag dirty restaurants before inspectors do. Foodborne illness is badly underreported through official channels, while diners narrate symptoms in reviews, so a classifier's illness signals across reviews might track real hygiene failures.

The team feeds reviews through a hierarchical attention classifier and compares its signals with New York City health inspection outcomes from 2023, aggregating at the census tract level and mapping spatial patterns. The honest answer is mostly negative: correlations with inspection scores are minimal, and tracts heavy in C-graded restaurants show no significant signal difference. The authors discuss why tract-level aggregation may dilute the effect and outline finer address-level analyses as the next step.
arxiv-2510-16634:
Abeer Al Ghamdi, Gin Jose, and Almut Beige rethink atom-light models in a 2025 paper. The Jaynes-Cummings model treats light in a cavity as one lone mode. A cavity is a small box with mirror walls that trap light. As such boxes grow more fine, that lone-mode view shows strain. Their take tracks the full field in the box, mode by mode.

They find the decay rate of a source in a tiny metal-walled box first. That rate can far top the free-space rate, thanks to waves that add in step. Yet in most cases the two rates match to a close degree. That match may explain why strong coupling has eluded past tests. Strong coupling is the state where atom and light swap energy fast.
arxiv-2510-16734:
Siddharth Kasthurirangan and three co-authors classify active galactic nuclei and trace host galaxy growth using optical spectra from the ESO-GOODS-S field. Active nuclei are bright galaxy centers powered by growing black holes. The team sorts more than six hundred candidates with classic emission-line diagrams and two newer variants.

Their own fitting code reads the spectra and, with a standard stellar population model, returns host galaxy ages and metal content. Adding published redshifts gives each galaxy a lookback time. Combining lookback time with galaxy age lets the authors probe early cosmic epochs, reaching back about thirteen billion years, even though the survey itself stays at modest redshift.
arxiv-2510-17134:
R. Bucik and five co-authors trace extra light helium in slow solar storms in this 2025 paper. Light helium marks fast, brief solar bursts, yet it also shows in slow, wide storms. The team asks where that extra helium comes from in the slow kind. They match high-energy proton storms with low-energy helium-rich spells over two decades.

Some cases mix leftovers from past brief bursts into the slow storm. In most of the rest, thin jets burst from the source zones. The top helium shares came with jets, not with old leftovers. Helium and iron shares rose in step for jet cases. The pattern points to jets as a fresh seed source for slow storms.
arxiv-2510-17634:
Landon Johnson, with Walter Malone and five co-authors, speeds up defect forecasts for irradiated materials in a 2025 arXiv paper. Radiation creates structural defects, which are flaws in a material's crystal pattern, that grow and change how it performs. A standard method called cluster dynamics tracks each defect type with rate equations. That method grows costly when many temperatures and pressures must be explored.

The team trained a machine learning model to predict defect amounts directly. Their model skips the slow step by step tracking yet stays highly accurate. They demonstrate it on uranium nitride, a nuclear fuel material. The model captures complex links among material traits, temperature, radiation level, and defect amounts. It should transfer to other materials too.
arxiv-2510-17934:
Haoyu Huang, with five co-authors, packs a billion-scale knowledge graph into a language model using very little graphics memory. Retrieval systems must search outside the model and paste in long context, which slows answers at large scale. AtlasKV instead turns graph facts into key and value form inside the model's own attention.

Two new parts handle the conversion and keep time and memory growth below linear. The authors report strong grounding and general results with no outside search at run time. Readers who need models with vast built-in facts get a design that fits on a single modest graphics card.
arxiv-2510-18134:
Soheil Abbasloo, writing alone, argues that grading model reasoning by final answers misses most of what reasoning is. A real reasoning process, on this view, is a moving path where ideas clash and merge into new insight. The paper borrows the old dialectic pattern of claim, counterclaim, and synthesis to judge that path.

The SIEV frame scores how well a model holds up under challenge, adapts in conflict, and joins rival views. On math and general benchmarks, top models showed wide gaps on these measures. Evaluation researchers get a lens on reasoning quality that a right answer alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2510-18234:
Haoran Wei, with Yaofeng Sun and Yukun Li, presents DeepSeek-OCR in a 2025 paper on reading documents. OCR, meaning optical character recognition, turns pictures of pages into machine-readable text. The team asks whether long text can instead be squeezed into far fewer vision tokens by rendering it as an image.

DeepSeek-OCR pairs an encoder, called DeepEncoder, with a language model decoder. At compression below ten to one, decoding precision reached ninety-seven percent in their tests. Even at twenty to one, accuracy stayed near sixty percent. On a document benchmark it beat rival systems while using far fewer tokens per page.
arxiv-2510-18434:
Qingqing Gu and her seven co-authors propose a prompting method that helps large language models handle everyday conversation. Step-by-step reasoning prompts work well for math and coding, where clear logical steps exist. Open conversation has no such fixed steps, so the same prompts lose their power. The new method, Chain of Conceptual Thoughts, asks the model to first name the concepts behind a reply, then write the full reply following those concepts.

Concepts in their setup cover emotions, strategies, and topics, giving the reply a simple plan before any words are produced. The team tested the method on daily chat and emotional support tasks, including topics the model had not been guided on before. Human judges, automatic checks, and model-based judges all favored the new method over several rival prompting styles, suggesting concept-first planning could help across many open-ended tasks.
arxiv-2510-18534:
Uraz Odyurt works with Richard Loendersloot and Tiedo Tinga. They tackle a planning flaw in research projects. Teams rarely define what a demonstrator must prove, and they define it far too late. Vague plans breed confusion, and loose readiness labels make things worse. Projects then promise demos they cannot deliver. The authors offer a framework to fix this. It spells out demo requirements before work starts. Feasibility can then be judged early, and targets adjusted in time.

The framework sets five levels of demonstration. Each level ties to clear expectations, to how work packages interact, and to the project's use cases. The scope is software-heavy systems and industrial cyber-physical systems, where software and machines act as one. A full test would take years. Still, use on two real projects showed its worth. It exposed gaps between targeted and feasible demos.
arxiv-2510-18834:
Jia Zhou and Chang-Xing Ma develop statistical tests for clinical studies of paired organs, such as eyes or ears, where outcomes from the two sides of one patient are correlated.
