Some patients contribute both organs and others only one, mixing unilateral and bilateral data, and the question is whether two proportions, say success rates under two treatments, truly differ.

Working under a model with constant within-patient correlation, the authors build three likelihood-based tests: a likelihood ratio test, a Wald-type test, and a score test. Simulations showed all three kept false-positive rates under control with comparable power, the score test being slightly more stable. The methods are illustrated on ear and eye study data, and an online calculator supports power analysis and testing. The authors recommend the score test for practical work with such mixed paired data.
arxiv-2510-18934:
Shuofeng Zhang and Ard Louis argue that many measures of generalization in deep learning are fragile. Such measures are computed after training to explain why a network should work well on new data, yet small changes in training can shift their values a great deal.

Minor changes in learning rate or optimizer can flip the slope of a learning curve for common measures such as path norm. Even a trusted PAC-Bayes measure misses differences in data complexity, the authors note. Their position warns researchers not to trust these scores without checking how steady they are.
arxiv-2510-19334:
Cuize Han and Sesh Jalagam describe a system for legal contracts. It uses large language models to extract metadata. Contract review is core to contract management. Finding key clauses by hand is slow work. Labeling them is repetitive too. Careful automation fits the task well.

Tests use a public contract dataset and private contracts. The system rests on three elements. First, solid conversion of documents to text. Second, smart selection of text chunks. Third, model techniques such as step-by-step prompting. The authors name what makes extraction reliable. Legal technology teams get a concrete recipe.
arxiv-2510-19634:
Hrittik Roy, Søren Hauberg, and Nicholas Krämer argue that least squares, the workhorse of fitting, is underused in modern machine learning. The trick is to make a matrix-free least squares solver differentiable, so it can sit inside a learning pipeline like a neural network layer. The authors derive custom gradients that flow through the solver without forming large matrices explicitly.

Three demonstrations show the range: enforcing sparse weights on a fifty-million-parameter model, imposing conservativeness constraints inside a score-based generative model, and tuning a Gaussian process's hyperparameters by predictive performance. The paper positions differentiable least squares as a general tool that machine learning practitioners can reach for far beyond simple curve fitting.
arxiv-2510-19734:
Bhavya Agrawalla, Krishnakumar Balasubramanian, and Promit Ghosal build the first fully online framework for confidence intervals around stochastic gradient descent estimates in high dimensions. High-stakes uses of SGD need honest measures of uncertainty. But past theory demands far more steps, relative to the size of the problem. It also needs large covariance matrices inverted, which is costly.

The authors prove non-asymptotic Berry-Esseen bounds for linear functionals of online least-squares SGD iterates. That gives a Gaussian limit under a much weaker growth condition on steps versus problem size. Their procedure runs in time linear in the size per step and stores only a vector. They add an online estimator for the asymptotic variance, with high-probability error bounds. The package makes data-driven uncertainty checks for SGD practical.
arxiv-2510-19934:
Xiang Li and four co-authors tighten the privacy accounting for decentralized federated learning, where users train a shared model without a central server. Adding differential privacy to such systems is complicated by peer-to-peer communication, local updates, and shared randomness. Working within the f-differential privacy framework, the authors develop two accounting methods tailored to this setting.

One method tracks privacy leakage between pairs of users under random-walk communication; the other exploits shared secrets to structure the injected noise. Both capture the privacy amplification that sparse communication, local iterations, and correlated noise provide, using Markov chain concentration tools. Experiments on synthetic and real data gave consistently tighter privacy bounds and better utility than the standard Rényi-based accounting.
arxiv-2510-20034:
Yuxiao Hang and three co-authors use a quantum computer to follow how Majorana fermions move and interact in real time. Studying quasiparticle motion matters for understanding systems driven out of balance, but circuit depth and noise have limited such work on present hardware. A recently developed constant-depth circuit algorithm helps them get around those limits.

The team tracks site-by-site magnetization in a transverse-field Ising chain, writing each spin as a pair of Majorana fermions. They identify two distinct regimes set by the strength of the spin interaction. Local impurities can also act as barriers and probes of Majorana modes, showing a practical route to study these effects on current processors.
arxiv-2510-20134:
Jiachen Liang and five co-authors improve out-of-distribution detection, the task of flagging inputs that differ from what a model was trained on. Post-hoc methods are popular because they are cheap to deploy, yet they often waste the rich information held in a model output logits. Their method, LogitGap, scores an input by the relation between its largest logit and the remaining logits.

A training-free strategy then picks the most informative subset of logits, making the score more compact and sharper. The authors support the design with theory and experiments on both vision-language and vision-only models. Across diverse benchmarks and scenarios, LogitGap reaches leading performance, helping keep deep learning systems reliable in open-world use.
arxiv-2510-20234: Van Huynh, Hieu Trinh, and Riley Bain present a collection of observer-based differentiators, which are observation systems designed to estimate the derivatives of a signal. The central difficulty they address is noise: the input signal is prone to noise, yet a usable estimate of its rate of change is still required. Different types of observation systems are gathered and presented together as alternative ways to perform that estimation task.
arxiv-2510-20434:
Rosella Giacometti and three co-authors construct market-implied sustainability scores for firms from the portfolio holdings of investment funds. The central idea is that a stock being over- or under-represented in sustainability-oriented funds reveals a market-based judgment of its sustainability profile. Their implementation uses European regulation, treating the darkest green Article 9 funds as the sustainability segment and comparing their holdings with other funds.

Scores are computed for a large cross-section of European companies over the years twenty ten to twenty twenty-five and compared with conventional ESG ratings from LSEG. The market-implied scores capture dimensions that differ systematically from those ratings. In portfolio tests, tilting toward high-scoring firms improves risk-adjusted performance, while rating-based tilts do not deliver comparable gains.
arxiv-2510-20934: Felipe Gonçalves and João Paulo Ferreira prove a sharp Fourier extension inequality. An inequality is a statement that one amount bounds another. Their proof concerns the circle and an exponent named Tomas-Stein. It applies to functions whose spectrum is lacunary, meaning values spread out fast. More precisely, each next value is more than three times the last. A sharp result means the bound cannot be improved in general. The work sits in Fourier restriction theory, a branch of harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2510-21034:
Barkavi Sundararajan leads two co-authors on how input structure changes factual errors in language model summaries of NBA play by play data. Sports reporting is accuracy critical, and generated recaps that invent plays erode trust fast.

Over thirty three hundred factual errors were hand annotated across one hundred eighty summaries from two large models, fed the same games as rows, as JSON, or as unstructured text. Structured JSON input cut error rates by roughly two thirds against unstructured input for both models, and row format also helped substantially. Input formatting, often an afterthought, emerges as a major lever on factual reliability.
arxiv-2510-21334:
Richard D. Canary surveys a meeting point between two areas of geometry. He writes for researchers who know real hyperbolic manifolds well. His aim is to draw those readers toward discrete subgroups of higher rank Lie groups. That richer setting gives many familiar questions new forms. Answers there can differ sharply from the classic ones.

The survey uses a deliberately breezy style. It walks through selected uses of ideas from Kleinian group theory. That theory studies discrete groups acting on hyperbolic space. Canary shows where the old intuition carries into the higher rank world. He also points to examples already built there. The survey proves no new results. It maps an entry route into a field that extends the reader's own tools.
arxiv-2510-21734:
Giovanni Battista Regazzo and five co-authors give a surgical robot a sense of touch for sealing off a heart pouch that can spawn stroke-causing clots. In atrial fibrillation, the left atrial appendage collects clots, and closing it with an expandable plug lowers stroke risk. But today's deployment leans on manual catheter work plus radiation imaging with limited placement precision.

A delivery sheath lined with fiber Bragg grating sensors feels the forces where catheter meets plug, while electromagnetic tracking follows the tip's position inside a lifelike anatomical phantom. Their force-displacement profiling method reads the deployment's unfolding dynamics from those signals and identifies the procedure's key steps with no ionizing radiation at all. The measured forces stay low, hinting at gentle stress on nearby tissue, and richer feedback for the clinician follows.
arxiv-2510-22434:
Prajyot Pyati and four co-authors study separation for a new kind of robot that cannot see its own colour. Each robot carries a colour others can see, and the robots are anonymous, forgetful, and silent as they move in the plane. Unlike earlier work, these robots are opaque, so one robot can block the view of two others behind it.

Same colour robots must part from the rest and settle into clear shapes. The team gives a collision free method that sorts the robots into concentric semicircles under a semi synchronous timing rule. The method finishes in a number of rounds that grows in direct proportion to the robot count.
arxiv-2510-22734:
Database tuning tools often rely on a Gaussian process model. That model makes strong shape assumptions. Yuanhao Lai leads a team with seven co-authors. In 2025 they argue those assumptions often fail in practice. Tree based models can avoid many of those pitfalls.

Still, tree models have their own limits. They give point estimates with weak uncertainty claims. New boosting methods also stay unused. The team proposes Centrum to fix these gaps. It aims for better surrogate modeling of database speed. Better modeling should guide tuning choices more soundly. The goal is faster, more effective auto tuning.
arxiv-2510-23434:
Aristotelis Epanomeritakis and Davide Viviano ask a planning question faced by researchers who run field experiments. Experiments give trustworthy effect estimates, but cost limits them to few sites, small groups, or narrow questions. Teams often merge experimental results with observational evidence to answer bigger policy questions, yet that outside evidence may carry unknown bias.

The authors build one framework for choosing which experiments to run and how to split the sample under any budget. They judge each design with a robust regret rule that compares it against an ideal planner who knows the bias limit. The result is a clear trade-off between bias and variance that needs only the inputs of a standard power calculation. They show the method at work on cash transfer programs, where economy-wide effects matter.
arxiv-2510-23634:
Soutrik Sarangi and three co-authors ask when sets can be turned into vectors without scrambling their containment order. For set containment problems, a useful embedding would keep smaller sets below bigger ones exactly: one set contains another precisely when its vector sits below the other's in every coordinate. Functions with that property, called monotone and separating, are the subject here.

The authors bound the vector dimension such functions need, based on the sizes of the multisets and the ground set. With an infinite ground set, exact versions cannot exist at all. They therefore build a neural model with a relaxed version of the property, plus smooth stability in the Hölder sense. Such functions also yield universal models that are monotone by construction and can mimic any monotone set function. Experiments on containment tasks favor their model over standard set networks that ignore containment as a built-in bias.
arxiv-2510-23834:
Boyan Sirakov and a co-author settle questions about nonlinear elliptic equations whose coefficients are allowed to be unbounded. The central result is a Keller-Osserman theorem, which gives conditions under which an equation of the form L of u equals f of u has solutions. Earlier versions needed the operator's ingredients to be locally bounded; the new proof works in the regime where they are only locally integrable.

The authors answer a question left open in earlier work about the strong maximum principle for supersolutions of the same equation. Their condition is the optimal one suggested by Vázquez. They prove a Harnack inequality for positive solutions, extending a result of Julin. Harnack inequalities bound how much a solution can vary across a region, making them workhorses of the theory. Together the results widen the class of equations on which these classic tools can be used.
arxiv-2510-24034:
Yufan Liu and six co-authors red-team text-to-image models with adversarial prompts that read like ordinary English. Safety filters catch many attacks because optimizer-generated prompts are gibberish, and most attack methods need white-box access. Their framework, AutoPrompt, works black-box: a large language model writes human-readable adversarial suffixes for benign prompts.

Training alternates between optimizing suffixes and fine-tuning the language model on the winners. Two tricks defeat defenses. An auxiliary model's perplexity score keeps the suffixes fluent, slipping past perplexity filters. Penalties on banned tokens keep blacklisted words out of the text entirely. The resulting prompts transfer zero-shot to unseen prompts and exposed weaknesses in a commercial service, Leonardo.Ai. The authors frame the work as proactive auditing: readable, filter-resistant attacks reveal where image generators actually break, so builders can fix the holes before someone less friendly finds them.
arxiv-2510-24434:
Julian Valline and three co-authors introduce LuxIT, a large instruction tuning dataset for Luxembourgish, a low resource language. Instruction tuned models perform poorly where high quality training data is scarce. The team synthesized the dataset from native Luxembourgish texts using DeepSeek-R1, chosen for its strength in the language, then applied quality checks with a model as judge.

The process kept 227,507 high quality instruction and answer pairs. To test its value, the authors fine tuned fourteen smaller language models on LuxIT and evaluated them on Luxembourgish tasks. The dataset aims to bring capable instruction following to a language that commercial models often underserve.
arxiv-2510-24734:
Qirui Hou, Wenzhang Sun, Chang Zeng, Chunfeng Wang, Hao Li, and Jianxun Cui rebuild moving street scenes in three dimensions as a drive goes on. Past tools faced a trade off between sharp views and speed, with few side shots to work from. Their tool, DrivingScene, works from just two frames of wide view shots at a time.

A small flow net in the tool gauges how moving things shift, on top of a learned base scene. Training moves from rough to fine steps to dodge the wobbles of end to end training. On a known drive set, the tool gave depth, flow, and point clouds at once and beat past tools.
arxiv-2510-25234:
Yuxiang Mao, Zhijie Zhang, Zhiheng Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Chen Zeng, and Shihong Xia are the six authors. They split the face moves of a talk head into two parts. One part is speech, the other is feel, so each can be driven on its own. Speech led lip sync has grown fast, but full feel in a talk face is less worked. Real feel face data in three dimensions are dear to catch, which blocks the work.

They treat the face as a plain sum of two shape sets, learned as one from two sets: a calm talk set and a feel forms set. A sparse rule keeps the two sets apart, while cross bleed from real data is let in. The sets can then map to pose marks for use.
arxiv-2510-25434:
Shakib Yazdani leads four co-authors on sign language testing. Yasser Hamidullah, Cristina Espana-Bonet, and Eleftherios Avramidis helped. Josef van Genabith closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper critically studies automatic testing metrics. Sign language translation needs reliable automatic quality measures. Current metrics like BLEU and ROUGE are text-based only.

It remains unclear how reliably text metrics capture quality. They study six metrics under controlled settings. Metrics include BLEU, chrF, ROUGE, and BLEURT. Language model evaluators like G-Eval were also tested. Settings covered paraphrasing, hallucinations, and sentence length variation. Lexical overlap metrics showed clear limitations in study. Language model evaluators captured semantic equivalence better often. Yet they showed bias toward model-paraphrased translations. All metrics detected hallucinations in outputs to some degree. BLEU was overly sensitive to subtle cases. Other evaluators were comparatively lenient there. Multimodal testing approaches are needed, they argue.
arxiv-2510-25534:
Rita P Santos, Krinio Marouda, and David Hilditch study critical gravitational collapse. Their 2025 paper evolves a Yang-Mills field characteristically. Answers near black hole formation threshold show critical phenomena. That allows extraction of global quantities at null infinity. Bondi mass and news function are such quantities.

Their numeric method is fourth-order accurate. The collapsing field exhibits local discrete self-similar actions. An echoing period characterizes that self-similar pattern. It agrees with previous works to two decimals. Global quantities display the same self-similar actions. Bondi mass and news function both echo similarly. Black hole mass scales with distance to criticality. A critical exponent near zero point two governs scaling. Findings indicate universality irrespective of initial data. Near-threshold evolutions produce that same scaling law. Gravitational collapse criticality connects to phase transition analogies. Their method extracts radiation information at infinity cleanly.
arxiv-2510-25734: Emily Heath, Grace McCourt, Alex Parker, Coy Schwieder, and Shira Zerbib define Kneser Ramsey numbers. Their 2025 paper seeks the smallest n forcing a red or blue clique. Every red-blue coloring of the Kneser graph is considered. They obtain general bounds on these numbers. They also advance two related Ramsey-type problems. One was raised by Holmsen, Hrusak, and Roldan-Pensado. Another was posted by Palvogyi.
arxiv-2510-25934:
Jipeng Li and Yannning Shen propose a watermark for graph neural networks that does not rely on a planted trigger. Graph neural networks learn from linked data, and they are valuable property that owners need to protect. Trigger based marks can break under common edits and can create doubt about who owns the model.

Their method, InvGNN-WM, ties ownership to how the model senses a graph invariant, a property that stays fixed under relabeling. A small head predicts algebraic connectivity on a private carrier set, and a decoder turns the output into bits. The mark kept clean accuracy, beat trigger and compression baselines, and survived pruning, fine tuning, and quantization, though plain distillation weakened it.
arxiv-2510-26134:
Max Aires and Jeff Kahn work on a conjecture about balanced pairs in partially ordered sets. A poset is a set with a partial order, where some pairs are incomparable. A linear extension lists all elements in an order that respects the poset. Kahn and Saks conjectured that a wide poset always has two elements whose order in a random extension is close to a coin flip.

Aires and Kahn show that the conjecture follows under a weaker assumption: that some element is incomparable with many others. Their route has two steps. Large incomparability forces large variance in the position of some element, and large variance plus bounded width yields the balanced pair. The same ideas give an easier proof of a known result on sorting probabilities for Young diagrams.
arxiv-2510-26234:
Mathis Engelbart, Mike Kosek, Lars Eggert, and Jorg Ott explore a publish subscribe version of the Domain Name System, the directory that maps host names to addresses. Classic DNS works by request and caching: a resolver asks for a record and keeps it until it expires. Some uses, such as load balancing and service discovery, would benefit if updates were pushed at once to every resolver that had shown interest in a record.

The authors design a strawman system and protocol based on the Media over QUIC transport architecture, which supports publish subscribe delivery over modern web transport. A prototype implementation shows that pushing updates can limit update traffic and considerably shorten the time until a resolver holds the latest record version. That supports fast changing content distribution uses.
arxiv-2510-26834:
Samuel W Remedios, Aaron Carass, Jerry L Prince, and Blake E Dewey introduce MedForj, a family of generative models for brain MRI. A foundational prior learns what real brain scans look like, so it can later help solve imaging tasks. Their models are diffusion models trained on over seventy-two thousand one-millimetre brain volumes. The volumes came from more than thirty-eight thousand subjects across thirty-eight public data sets, hand-checked for quality.

Remedios and his three co-authors train six variants that differ in how the diffusion is set up. They compare the samples against real data on segmentation, quality scores, five inverse problems, and blind human judgement. Flow matching was strongest overall, topping the inverse problems and fooling raters most often. Rectified flow made the most convincing fresh samples. All weights and code are public, with flow matching as the recommended default.
arxiv-2510-27034:
Sricharan Raghavan-Chitra, Arghadip Koner, and Joel Yuen-Zhou report a subtle light effect that challenges a textbook assumption. At low intensity, light passing through clear materials is usually governed only by their linear response. In high-Q microresonators, meaning tiny cavities that trap light for long times, photons linger long enough for rare quantum events to leave a mark.

Those events, mediated by the quantum vacuum, stamp Raman fingerprints, meaning molecular vibration signatures, of a substance in the cavity onto the normal transmission spectrum. Adding more of the substance lifts the signal well above typical noise. The authors argue the effect is reachable with current photonic hardware. It could open new routes to chemical and biological sensing with very small samples.
arxiv-2510-27334:
Ali Raza Jafree, Konark Jain, and Nick Firoozye study how high-frequency market makers learn to profit from slower traders large orders. Medium-frequency traders executing a meta-order, meaning one big order split over time, suffer adverse selection as opportunistic fast traders exploit the price drift the order creates. The team models the limit order book with a Hawkes process, which captures self-exciting order flow and endogenous price impact.

A reinforcement learning market maker, trained with policy optimization and self-imitation under an impulse control framing, learns to capitalize on meta-order drift when trained against such a trader. Empirical motivation notes slippage costs for medium-frequency traders likely rise as fast trading proliferates. Interestingly, higher market maker profits do not necessarily cause significantly larger slippage for the slower trader in their simulations.
arxiv-2510-27534:
Yue-Yang Fei, Zhenhuan Liu, and eight other co-authors clean noisy quantum channels in a working experiment, reported in 2025. Quantum networks link quantum computers so they can share tasks. The channels between them pick up noise that garbles the signals. Channel purification suppresses that noise without heavy encoding and decoding steps.

Their setup uses photons, playing on their position and polarization. Two Fredkin gates, controlled swap gates, make independent noisy channels interfere with each other. The interference cancels much of the noise across a wide range of levels and types. Applied to entanglement distribution, sharing linked photon pairs, the method preserved the link better than standard entanglement purification. That suits it for long-distance optical links, where simplicity counts.
arxiv-2511-00034:
Aditya Akella probes a failure mode of decentralized learnable reward shaping in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Reward shaping that learns its own feedback signals works in single-agent settings, but each agent shaping rewards independently may undermine the team. His fully decentralized system, where every agent learns individual shaping, is tested on cooperative navigation tasks.

Despite sophisticated reward learning, the decentralized system scored far below a centralized-training MAPPO baseline on the standard spread task. Readers in multi-agent learning get a documented limitation with numbers. Locally learned incentives can conflict with global cooperation, and the gap quantifies how badly.
arxiv-2511-00134:
Angana Borah, Adrija Datta, and Ashish Kumar quantify how city greening can backfire in humid climates by raising how hot air feels. Vegetation cools surfaces, but physiologically active plants also release moisture, and humid heat is a growing urban hazard. They study the heat index, which combines temperature and humidity, across one hundred thirty-eight Indian cities in three climate zones.

Vegetation structure and function are linked to whether cooling or moisture accumulation wins. Urban climate readers get evidence that the same planting can cool dry cities and worsen humid ones. Planting policy needs physiology and climate zone, not just canopy area, to avoid reversing its purpose.
arxiv-2511-00234:
Pamud Akalanka Bethmage, Ryker Fish, Brennan Sprinkle, and Michelle Driscoll study tiny spinning particles suspended in fluid, a clean test bed for how order forms far from equilibrium. In open settings the particles interact mainly through the flow they create. The team asks what changes when walls close in and the chamber is tightly confined.

Experiments and large simulations agree: confinement creates density patches far larger than one particle. The patches grow or shrink with the degree of confinement. The cause is a broad swirling flow that the spinning particles drive inside the sealed chamber. Distant walls, it turns out, can reshape structure at mid-range scales.
arxiv-2511-00334: César Bautista-Ramos answers a question posed by D Galvin about independence polynomials of trees. An independence polynomial counts the sets of vertices in a graph with no two joined by an edge, grouped by set size. Log-concavity, a smoothness property of those counts, was once hoped to hold broadly. Bautista-Ramos builds endless families of trees whose polynomials break log-concavity at any chosen number of positions, as many as desired.
arxiv-2511-00534:
Xiao Nan Chen, Sining Zhang, Zhengxuan Wang, Minping Zhang, and Guangtao Wang compute the magnetism of two silver fluoride compounds from first principles. Divalent silver ions distort their surroundings strongly and order their orbitals, and that orbital order steers magnetic coupling. The two compounds, with different potassium content, choose contrasting ground states in the calculations.

The first compound settles into an A-type antiferromagnetic pattern with C-type orbital order and shows altermagnetism, a newer magnetic class with unusual transport. Its signatures include anomalous Hall, Nernst, and thermal Hall effects, plus strong Kerr and Faraday optical responses. The second compound behaves as a conventional antiferromagnet that preserves combined symmetry, which forbids an anomalous Hall response. The contrast makes the pair a clean test case for altermagnetic ideas.
arxiv-2511-00634:
Mark Kocherovsky, Illya Bakurov, and Wolfgang Banzhaf revisit a dogma of Cartesian genetic programming, a method that evolves programs laid out on a grid of nodes. Crossover, the mixing of two parents' material, is prized in other genetic programming families, yet in this one it is widely said to harm search, so mutation-only strategies became canonical. A general fix has been missing.

The authors compare basic one-point and uniform crossover against variants with node preservation, where crossover may not tear instructions apart, including a published subgraph crossover. They also test a node mutation that swaps whole nodes against traditional point mutation. On symbolic regression benchmarks, node preservation improved search in both crossover and mutation. Respecting the building blocks of a program, it seems, lets crossover finally pull its weight.
arxiv-2511-01034:
Nicolas Bedaride, Julien Cassaigne, Pascal Hubert, and Renaud Leplaideur prove a freezing phase transition for a potential built from the Thue-Morse sequence, a classic self similar pattern in symbolic dynamics. The potential of a word depends on how long its prefix agrees with a word from the Thue-Morse subshift.

They study the pressure function, which balances entropy against the potential at inverse temperature beta. For beta large enough, the pressure equals zero, the frozen regime. Earlier published proofs of similar results by Bruin and Leplaideur contained significant gaps needing substantial clarification, and this version, which replaces an older one containing mistakes, supplies a corrected proof.
arxiv-2511-01734:
Soufiane Hayou proves a claim practitioners of deep learning rely on but had not seen justified. Under the maximal update parameterization, known as muP, the best learning rate for a neural network stays put as the network gets wider. MuP is a way of scaling weights and learning rates with width designed to keep feature learning alive in the infinite-width limit.

For a linear multi-layer perceptron, Hayou shows the optimal learning rate converges to a nonzero constant as width grows. That is exactly the transfer property trainers exploit. They tune on small models and deploy on large ones. The property fails under standard parameterization and under the neural tangent parameterization, both analyzed for contrast. Intuitive proofs are backed by extensive experiments.
arxiv-2511-02034:
Shashank Motepalli, Naman Garg, Gengrui Zhang, and Hans-Arno Jacobsen study a hidden weakness in major blockchains: their validators cluster in a few places. The team checked five large proof of stake chains: Aptos, Avalanche, Ethereum, Solana, and Sui. In each, a small set of regions held most of the voting power in consensus. That clustering, they argue, cuts against resilience, fairness, and safety from local rules.

Their fix is GPoS, short for geospatially aware proof of stake. It folds geographic diversity into stake-based voting power, so spread out validators count for more. In experiments, GPoS raised geographic decentralization by about 45 percent on average, measured with a Gini coefficient of eigenvector centrality. The cost was small: tests with the HotStuff and CometBFT protocols showed minimal extra overhead. The authors argue where validators sit should be treated as part of a chain's security.
arxiv-2511-02234:
Jiawei Liu and six co-authors test whether weaving audio directly into a language model's prompt teaches it to reason about sound more deeply. Standard multimodal training simply glues non-text tokens onto the front of a text prompt, which may never force real integration with the language model's reasoning. The team worked with an audio model called LTU, short for Listen, Think, and Understand.

They built a benchmark, SHARD, that probes semantic reasoning about audio through synonym and hypernym recognition. Simply prompting with interleaved audio helped even with no training. A small amount of fine-tuning with interleaved prompts improved the reasoning scores further, though at the cost of the model's audio labelling ability. The study weighs that trade-off for designers of audio-language systems.
arxiv-2511-02634:
Fast radio bursts are brief flashes of radio energy from space, and their cause is still unknown. Rohan Arni, Carlos Blanco, and Anirudh Prabhu used deep learning to sort these bursts in a 2025 study. They worked from the first catalog of the CHIME telescope, which recorded many bursts, some repeating and some seen only once.

Their model joins a variational autoencoder with a supervised sorting task, so it learns both labels and patterns. It sorted repeaters with high accuracy and showed clear gaps between the two groups. Three traits drove the split most: extra dispersion, spectral index, and spectral running. The team also flagged four bursts seen once as likely repeaters, two of them already suspected by others.
arxiv-2511-02834:
Huawei Lin and five colleagues present Agent-Omni, a system that reasons across text, images, audio, and video by coordinating existing models rather than training one giant model. Single multimodal models usually handle fixed pairs of inputs and need costly fine-tuning on aligned data. A fully omni-capable model is still out of reach, as their 2025 paper notes.

Agent-Omni uses a master agent that reads the user's intent, hands subtasks to agents built for each modality, and merges their outputs into one answer. On benchmarks spanning all four input types, the system matched or beat state-of-the-art scores, with the clearest gains on hard cross-modal tasks. Because parts can be swapped as better models appear, the design stays current without retraining.
arxiv-2511-02934:
Theophile Dolmaire and Alessia Nota derive a classic kinetic equation from the motion of a single light particle bouncing through a random field of scatterers. The particle loses energy at each hit, following a fixed restitution rule, and the scatterers sit at Poisson-random spots. Their 2025 paper, the first of a series, works in the Boltzmann-Grad limit and in any dimension from two up.

They prove that weak solutions of the inelastic linear Boltzmann equation exist and are unique, within a class of measure-valued solutions with a finite exponential moment. The particle system's solution converges to that equation with an explicit rate. They also build strong solutions through a series representation. The result puts a widely used model of dissipative gases on firm ground.
arxiv-2511-03134:
Juan Manuel Sanchez-Cerritos and Mayte Torres-Hernandez find choreographies for the N-body problem, paths where masses chase each other along one curve. The jewel is the figure-eight orbit of three equal masses. Their 2025 paper takes a variational route. Instead of fixing the size of the path, they optimize the spatial scale inside the action itself. The result is a functional that mixes kinetic and potential terms with tuned powers.

They prove this functional has critical points whose curves cross themselves exactly once. Every such critical curve, after reparametrization, obeys Newton's equations and never collides. The method recovers the famous Chenciner-Montgomery eight for the classic force law and extends to a whole range of power-law attractions, widening the family of provable choreographies.
arxiv-2511-03534:
Zhaoxin Chang and colleagues propose PnPSelect, a way to pick a smart-home device simply by pointing at it. Crowded homes make scrolling through device lists slow and error prone. PnPSelect uses ultra-wideband radio on ordinary commercial gear, with no extra hardware bolted onto each device, keeping deployment cheap and truly plug-and-play.

Pointing direction is inferred from readings at a single anchor, a trick that avoids a full anchor array. A light localization step lets users register where devices sit with little effort. Together, those pieces turn selection into a natural gesture. The authors test the design on real hardware and argue it can scale from a few lamps to a house full of connected gear.
arxiv-2511-03634:
Alexander Pfefferle, Johannes Hog, Lennart Purucker, and Frank Hutter rebuild a leading tabular foundation model in miniature for teaching and tinkering. TabPFN changed how small data tables get predicted, yet its codebase runs past ten thousand lines with thin documentation. nanoTabPFN reimplements the core design and training loop in a lean, readable form that loads pregenerated training data.

In a small-data setting, the miniature matches classic methods while staying easy to follow line by line. Students can trace how prior-fitted learning turns a table into predictions without a long pipeline. Researchers gain a cheap test bed for new ideas before scaling them. The authors trade full power for clarity on purpose, betting understanding compounds faster than features.
arxiv-2511-04034:
Nilanjan Chaudhuri, Sourav Duari, Pradip Roy, and Sourav Sarkar evaluate how thermal photons are emitted from a chirally asymmetric quark-gluon plasma, using the Hard Thermal Loop approximation. At finite temperature, quasiparticle and plasmino modes split into left and right modes when chiral imbalance is present.

Those split modes disperse differently and carry different thermal masses. The soft part of the emission rate, obtained from the retarded self-energy, gains extra terms tied to the squares of the quark and chiral chemical potentials. Those terms enhance thermal photon emission when chiral imbalance is present. Photon yields could therefore carry information about chirality in hot QCD matter.
arxiv-2511-04234:
Alex Fang, Thomas Voice, Ruoming Pang, Ludwig Schmidt, and Tom Gunter measure how much value pretraining leaves unused in its own data, by retrieving from training corpora at test time. Language models learn from vast datasets, yet little work asks how efficiently pretraining extracted the knowledge those datasets contain.

Retrieval plus test-time compute produced large accuracy gains on knowledge, mathematics, and question benchmarks, surviving contamination checks. On one benchmark retrieval acted like a fivefold compute multiplier over pretraining alone. Spending more compute to parse retrieved context lifted a public eight-billion-parameter model by ten percentage points on that benchmark. Pretraining, the authors conclude, underuses its data badly.
arxiv-2511-04334:
Saul Alonso-Monsalve, Leigh H Whitehead, Adam Aurisano, and Lorena Escudero Sanchez segment kidneys and kidney tumours in computed tomography scans with submanifold sparse convolutional networks. Precise tumour outlines feed quantitative analysis and precision oncology, but manual tracing is slow specialist work, and full-resolution three-dimensional scans punish dense networks computationally.

Voxel sparsification drives a two-stage design. A low-resolution sparse network finds the region of interest, then a high-resolution sparse network refines the outline inside that crop, cutting memory and inference time. On a public renal cancer dataset with cross-validation, overlap scores for kidneys, masses, tumours, and cysts were competitive with leading challenge entries.
arxiv-2511-04434:
Cristian Tabares leads six authors with a protocol for reading ground-state energies on quantum simulators. Finding those energies is a central hard task in quantum simulation. Their method needs only global time evolution, with no controlled operations.

Energy gaps come from measurements of the Loschmidt echo, taken from a rough ground-state guess. Combined with direct energy readings, the values feed a set of equations that yields each eigenenergy. Tests on free-fermion systems show precision gains of orders of magnitude over direct readings. Because analog simulators can run it, the protocol widens where phase estimation ideas apply.
arxiv-2511-04534:
Jonas E. Katona and two colleagues add uncertainty estimates to reduced-order surrogate models. Such models simulate big physical systems cheaply, but users rarely know how much to trust them. Older uncertainty tools often tie to one architecture or training scheme.

Their framework works after training, on any latent-space model, with no changes inside. Conformal prediction supplies intervals for the latent motion, the reconstruction, and the full forecast. Tests use a cloud microphysics model that tracks droplet-size distributions. Accurate intervals there show the method can flag when a fast surrogate is guessing beyond its evidence.
arxiv-2511-04634:
Koki Okada and his co-author build quantum LDPC codes by controlled random reshaping. These error-correcting codes rest on pairs of sparse orthogonal matrices. Row and column weights in those matrices drive how well belief-propagation decoding works.

Their local tweak swaps entries in small two-by-two blocks, then repairs orthogonality by integer programming. Repeating the swap at random yields whole ensembles of fresh codes. Each repair's cost depends only on the largest weights, not on the full matrix size. That keeps the method scalable, a key need as quantum codes grow toward practical sizes.
arxiv-2511-04834:
Jiwoo Shin leads five authors showing that prompt-based safety guidance fails on unlearned image models. Two defenses against harmful generations are usually combined for safety. One fine-tunes the model to unlearn bad concepts, the other steers sampling with negative prompts.

Joined together, the defenses often add nothing or even defend worse, they find. That incompatibility blocks the obvious belt-and-suspenders approach to safety. Their fix swaps the negative prompts for implicit guidance matched to the unlearned model. Tests show the simple replacement restores robust defense, a practical lesson for guarding text-to-image systems.
arxiv-2511-04934:
Hadi Reisizadeh and co-authors test whether methods that make large language models forget still work when text is sampled in the normal random way, not just greedy choice. They study removal of private, toxic, or banned content that rules and ethics require.

The team adds a new score, leak at k, which checks how often removed facts return across k samples. On three known test sets, they find that nearly all current methods leak. Facts that look gone under greedy checks come back under normal sampling, so past tests gave a false sense of safety.
arxiv-2511-05134:
Hendrik Paul Lopuhaa gives a unified route to MM-estimation with an added scale estimate, for balanced linear models whose covariance has a set structure. MM-estimators are prized for standing up to outliers while staying sharp on clean, normal data.

The unified view covers regression values and scale-free forms of the variance parts. Its main case is linear mixed effects models, but it also spans other standard multi-part models. Lopuhaa states terms under which the strong traits hold for all of them. That breadth lets users apply one proof to many model types.
arxiv-2511-05234:
Philipp Dahlinger and co-authors teach mesh-based simulators to use context from a whole path, not just one step. Learned graph simulators can rival classic physics codes for bent and stretched objects, with more speed and smooth gradients for design work.

Past learned models look at a single step, which wastes past clues about material and load. Their trajectory-level meta-learning lets a model adapt fast to a new case from its recent history. The aim is sharper forecasts for robot handling and factory tuning, where each object bends in its own way.
arxiv-2511-05334:
Giovanni Fiaschi and co-authors set out a formal model for scoring sets of paths in a network, not just single paths. Path choice drives telecom and transport systems, and each choice needs a score to rank it against rivals.

Past work scored single paths in depth, but sets of paths lacked the same care. Fiaschi stresses that a set's traits rest on which properties one picks, more so than for lone paths. His model gives a shared tongue for those scores, so backup route sets can be judged on firm ground.
arxiv-2511-05534:
Kunxi Li and colleagues introduce FlowMM, a way to cut memory use when multimodal AI models work with long inputs. These models store past tokens in a cache, and dropping the wrong ones can cause lost context or made-up answers. Merging tokens works better, but image and text tokens behave in unlike ways.

FlowMM uses the flow of information between modes to pick a merge plan for each layer. A matching step weighs how alike two tokens are and how risky each one is to lose. In tests, the method cut cache memory by a large share and sped up replies while keeping task scores close to full-cache runs.
arxiv-2511-05734:
Joshua Arroyo works on a formula in algebraic combinatorics tied to the geometry of the Lagrangian Grassmannian. The objects are GQ functions, symmetric functions indexed by strict partitions that encode certain geometric classes. A Pieri rule tells how to expand a product of two such functions back into single ones.

Buch and Ravikumar proved such a rule using a family of shifted tableaux, small diagrams filled with numbers. Arroyo identifies a different family of tableaux that counts the same expansion. His result partly settles a conjecture from earlier work, which predicted these tableaux would count a broader product with a trapezoid-shaped index. The paper is a focused contribution to the combinatorics of Schubert calculus.
arxiv-2511-05934:
Ayantika Das and co-authors model how Alzheimer's disease progresses in brain scans, without needing paired scans of the same patient over time. Generative models can learn what brain images look like, but steering them to show one person's future scan usually needs that person's follow-up data as a guide.

Their diffusion auto-encoder squeezes each scan into a compact code holding high-level meaning. The code can be split into disease progression and personal identity parts. Shifting the progression part, steered by progression attributes and disease-relevant regions, generates a plausible follow-up image from a single earlier scan. They checked the results with image quality scores, volume-change analysis, and downstream tasks. The approach aims at progression forecasts that clinics could actually use.
arxiv-2511-06034:
Ali Ghalavand and co-authors study how deleting edges from a target graph changes its anti-Ramsey number. That number counts the most colors an edge-colored complete graph can use while avoiding a rainbow copy of the target, fully multicolored. The target here is a disjoint union of short paths.

For a chosen set of edges whose endpoints all have degree two, the authors ask whether removal changes the number. In several parameter regimes they prove it does not: the anti-Ramsey number stays the same after deletion. One regime breaks the pattern, where deletion does matter. They then compute the anti-Ramsey number itself across four regimes. The work extends a line begun by Erdős and co-authors in the nineteen-seventies.
arxiv-2511-06134:
Wei Yang and co-authors orchestrate teams of language models so that wild idea generation and careful synthesis stop interfering. Multi-agent systems can beat lone models on hard problems, but they tend to agree too early, spread errors, and misassign credit between real reasoning and plausible fluff. Their framework, Maestro, splits the two modes structurally.

Parallel execution agents explore widely, while one central agent evaluates and converges on an answer. A new training objective, CLPO, tunes that synthesis step. It separates the signal for strategic choices from the signal for written rationales, ranking justifications against each other for cleaner credit assignment. On math and general problem-solving benchmarks, Maestro with CLPO improved results consistently, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-06534:
Sinnou David, Noriko Hirata-Kohno, and Makoto Kawashima prove that values of hypergeometric functions at several algebraic points cannot all be tied together by one linear relation. Results of this kind measure how independent special function values are, with uses across number theory. Earlier work often handled a single point or narrower families of parameters.

A uniform construction of type II Padé approximants does the heavy lifting, joined by a new argument that certain Hermite-style Wronskian determinants never vanish. The method covers every parameter regime at once, in both ordinary complex and p-adic settings. Multi-point results over general number fields extend the single-point theory, and the divergent regime is handled through arithmetic Gevrey series.
arxiv-2511-06634:
Kaiyuan Zhai and co-authors predict heating and cooling energy for buildings the model has never seen. Every new building lacks the labeled history that energy forecasting craves, and climate differences tempt models into shortcuts based on spurious correlations. CaberNet learns causal features instead, aiming for predictions that travel across buildings and seasons.

A global feature gate, trained with self-supervised Bernoulli regularization, sorts strong causal inputs from weak ones without any prior knowledge. A domain-wise training scheme balances each building's contribution and keeps latent factors independent. On real data from three buildings in three climates, CaberNet beat every baseline, cutting normalized squared error by about twenty-three percent against the best rival.
arxiv-2511-06934:
Dennis Thumm asks whether classic game theory can be extended to capture the causal reasoning of AI agents, and reports a largely negative answer. He builds Sequential Causal Multi-Agent Systems, which add Pearl's causal hierarchy to leader-follower games. The system is theoretically rich: he proves PSPACE-completeness, develops equilibrium refinements, and connects it to signaling theory.

Yet across more than fifty Monte Carlo simulations and hand-crafted examples, the causal equilibrium gives zero welfare improvement over the classic Stackelberg equilibrium. Backward induction with rational best responses erases any advantage from causal distinctions, and even relaxed rationality for followers does not rescue a benefit when good instincts match optimal play. Thumm argues truly new systems beyond standard Nash equilibrium are needed for agentic AI.
arxiv-2511-07434:
Selling a large bitcoin holding quickly can push the price down against the seller. Enzo Duflot and Stanislas Robineau study that liquidation problem on historical bitcoin order books. They train a reinforcement learning agent, RL-Exec, to sell under a fixed deadline while limiting market impact.

The agent watches twenty levels of book depth plus microstructure signals, under fees, delays, and partial fills. Training used January 2020 replays and testing used February 2020, with repeated daily runs to avoid false precision. Against time-weighted and liquidity-weighted baselines on identical conditions, the learned policy performed better. Careful statistics back the comparison.
arxiv-2511-07534:
Sarbani Basu and Sylvain Korzennik measure the shape of the solar tachocline, the thin shear layer between the Sun radiative core and its churning outer zone. Sound-wave data from years of solar watching let them probe that hidden boundary. Earlier fits forced the layer to be simply stretched or flattened.

Long records spanning thousands of days now allow freer shapes. The tachocline still deviates from a simple prolate form and bulges outward at mid latitudes. Its center sits in the radiative zone near the equator, rises into the convection zone at middle latitudes, then returns. The refined shape constrains how solar rotation and magnetism couple.
arxiv-2511-07634:
Chadani Acharya audits whether course syllabi actually serve blind and low-vision students. A syllabus is often the only structured guide to deadlines, grading, safety, and how to request accommodations. Screen reader users can use it independently only when the file is machine readable and easy to navigate.

Syllabi from five United States institutions, from an elite private university to a technical college, were coded on five dimensions. Checks covered logistics readability, safety information, and the burden placed on students seeking accommodation. Gaps force extra emails and dependence on staff goodwill. The audit gives concrete fixes so access starts with the document itself.
arxiv-2511-07734:
Shu Hong, Yongsheng Mei, and Mahdi Imani optimize costly functions defined on graphs. Bayesian search shines for costly black-box problems, but graphs are discrete and huge, and often only partly observed. Full-topology methods break at scale, while local wandering converges slowly.

Spectral forms compress graph structure into low-rank features learned from sparse observations. Process models built on those features support global search. The fitted model captures the seen links well enough to guide sampling. Applications from molecules to networks need global graph optimization without listing all structures, making such models a practical unlock.
arxiv-2511-08134:
Mustafa Alfarhan, Fuqiang Chen, George Turkiyyah, and David Keyes replace a costly time shift calculation inside full waveform inversion. That inversion method builds underground velocity maps by matching modeled and observed seismic traces. Waveforms oscillate, so simple mismatch measures skip cycles when the starting model is poor, and classic dynamic time warping is expensive here.

A neural network learns, in supervised fashion, the shifts that align two time series. Inside inversion it compares traces smoothly and cheaply, with gradients available through backpropagation. On the Marmousi model and a Chevron blind test, convergence matched a soft warping method while adjoint source computation became much faster.
arxiv-2511-08534:
Panagiotis Gavriilidis, Kyriakos Stylianopoulos, and George Alexandropoulos analyze multiple input multiple output communication assisted by a one bit reconfigurable intelligent surface under Ricean fading. These surfaces tune reflections with the coarsest possible settings, just two phase choices per element. Using random matrix theory, the authors show that in the large system limit the dominant channel directions settle onto their line of sight components, almost regardless of fading strength.

That stability yields a closed form sign alignment rule for setting the surface using line of sight information only. With a very large surface, the end to end channel becomes nearly diagonal, removing interference between streams without transmitter channel knowledge. A waterfilling inspired allocation algorithm matches far costlier optimization at a fraction of the runtime.
arxiv-2511-09034:
Christian Canete and Archil Kobakhidze entertain a heretical possibility: dark matter might not be a new particle at all, but an emergent state of fields already in the theory. Their vehicle is a three-form gauge field coupled to the cosmic fluid of ordinary matter and radiation.

Left alone, the three-form theory carries only a global, non-propagating state, which the authors associate with dark energy. Couple it to the fluid and an emergent dynamical state appears inside the medium, and that state is identified with dark matter. One framework then covers the whole dark sector. The authors further speculate that the three-form field could have a gravitational origin, possibly supported by the lepton-number asymmetry of the primordial plasma. If the picture is right, they note, conventional dark matter searches would likely be futile.
arxiv-2511-09134:
Zexu Wang and nine co-authors hunt a smart contract flaw that lets one signature pay out again and again. Contracts verify digital signatures to check authority. But when nothing records that a signature was already spent, attackers can replay it and drain assets. That failure mode is what the authors name the signature replay vulnerability.

From fourteen hundred audit reports by thirty-seven security firms, the team distills one hundred eight detailed cases and sorts the flaw into five types. Their detector, LASiR, pairs a language model's semantic reading of code with static taint analysis of signature state, then confirms reachability by symbolic execution. Screening over fifteen thousand signature-using contracts drawn from nearly a million across four blockchains finds the flaw widespread. Affected contracts hold about four point seven six million dollars. Nearly a fifth of Ethereum's signature contracts are vulnerable.
arxiv-2511-09234:
Thrassos K. Oikonomou and five co-authors design detection schemes for wireless receivers whose hardware distorts both signal amplitude and phase. Real transceivers add residual noise to both components, and standard schemes handle them poorly. Their approach performs maximum-likelihood detection while handling the distortions jointly.

Their detector, PAD-D, works in the polar domain and weights signals according to the distortion. It beats the conventional Euclidean scheme and a Gaussian phase-noise scheme. In simulated runs it cuts the error floor by up to an order of magnitude. The authors derive a closed-form high-signal formula for symbol error probability that fits arbitrary constellations. They also optimize constellation layouts for the new detector. Extensive simulation confirms the gains.
arxiv-2511-09534:
Adam Gargasson and four co-authors measure how E. coli bacteria swim toward food chemicals, both in open fluid and near surfaces. Chemotaxis lets bacteria drift up concentration gradients, but the response does not scale in a straight line with concentration or its local slope. Their team tuned a three-channel microfluidic device to hold a stable, linear chemical gradient.

Tracking single bacteria responding to casamino acids or a model attractant, they measured the group's drift more quickly and precisely than before. In fluid, the chemotactic speed follows a susceptibility law that peaks at middling concentrations. Between set limits it simplifies to drift proportional to the gradient of the logarithm of concentration. On a surface, by contrast, the chemotactic flux is inhibited, they find.
arxiv-2511-09934:
David X. Lin, Giannis Fikioris, Siddhartha Banerjee, and Éva Tardos design an auction-like mechanism for handing out one item per round to competing agents without money. Each agent's benchmark is the value of her favorite equal share of rounds. A mechanism is robust if every agent is guaranteed a fixed fraction of that ideal no matter how others behave. Earlier artificial-credit auctions topped out below a clear barrier.

Their simple mechanism asks bidders each round whether they want the item, then allocates uniformly among those who ask. The twist is competitive subsidies: the winner pays in artificial credits an amount that shrinks when fewer agents compete. This breaks the old barrier with a robustness factor of five eighths, nearly matching the best possible non-strategic bound, and they argue it is optimal within a wide class of auction mechanisms.
arxiv-2511-10534:
Giordano Viviani and Richard I. Anderson present the third paper of the VELOCE project, a framework for reconstructing the radial velocity curves of classical Cepheids from sparse observations. Cepheids are pulsating stars used as cosmic distance markers, but large spectroscopic surveys will catch each one only a few times.

Built from high-precision VELOCE measurements, the framework supplies prior templates for the curves' principal components. With full data it recovers average velocities within 20 to 30 meters per second; even three randomly timed observations give useful accuracy. Applied to Cepheids in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, it found nine single-lined spectroscopic binaries, three of them new, and measured binary fractions close to the Milky Way value.
arxiv-2511-10634:
Kyle Miller, Surhud More, and Bhuvnesh Jain quantify how galaxy formation blurs the cosmic matter distribution that upcoming weak-lensing surveys hope to measure at percent precision. Gas cooling, star formation, and black hole feedback push matter around inside halos, suppressing the matter power spectrum on small scales.

Using the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical simulations, they swap matter around halo centers between the full-physics run and its collisionless counterpart, radius by radius and mass by mass. Group-scale halos turn out to dominate the suppression, and reproducing the full effect requires tracking matter redistribution beyond each halo's virial radius while conserving mass. The same halos produce the strongest lensing deviations around foreground groups, offering an observational test of feedback models.
arxiv-2511-10734:
Madyson G. Barber leads a 20-author team validating a young giant planet, TOI-6448 b, as part of a survey of exoplanet demographics in their infancy. Planets younger than 50 million years on close orbits are vital clues to how the mature planet population discovered by Kepler came to be, but the sample is still small.

The planet has about 8.8 times Earth's radius and a 14.8-day orbit around a Sun-like star in the Vela association. Combining isochrones, variability, and gyrochronology, the team pins the star's age at 34 million years, give or take three. Like other young planets, this one sits in a size range where older planets are scarce, adding support to earlier findings of an excess of mid-sized planets around young stars.
arxiv-2511-11034:
Pooja Singh, Siddhant Ujjain, and their colleagues introduce CrossMed, a test set for whether medical image models can mix known parts in new ways. A model may know a scan type, a body part, and a task, yet still fail when those three appear in a fresh mix. CrossMed checks that skill in a strict, structured way.

The set rebuilds four public collections, covering X-ray, MRI, and CT, into over twenty thousand choice questions. Two open models were tested on mixes close to their training and on mixes with no overlap at all. Scores fell sharply on the fresh mixes, which shows how hard this kind of broad skill still is.
arxiv-2511-11234:
Jader Martins Camboim de Sá, Jooyoung Lee, and their colleagues propose LANE, an adversarial training strategy that sharpens how neural language models pin down a word's sense in context. Such models often lean on the whole sentence's gist and miss local cues, so fine-grained meaning slips away. LANE deliberately shifts the learning focus onto the target word itself.

The method crafts hard negative examples by marking alternate words in training sentences, forcing the model to separate like sentences that differ only in the marked word. On sense disambiguation and semantic change benchmarks, it beat standard contrastive baselines. Checks show the learned forms capture subtle meaning gaps, and the method fits existing frameworks.
arxiv-2511-11434:
Wei Chow, Jiachun Pan, and their colleagues present WEAVE, a suite for testing unified multimodal models on interleaved understanding and generation across many turns. Current data sets focus on single exchanges, which miss how real image creation and editing depend on history. Their suite pairs a large training set with a human-scored benchmark to cover both learning and grading.

The training set holds one hundred thousand interleaved samples spanning hundreds of thousands of dialogue turns and half a million images. The benchmark sets one hundred tasks over hundreds of images, judged by a hybrid method that weighs reference and edited images. Training on the set built skills in comprehension, editing, and their interplay.
arxiv-2511-11734:
Kamalpreet Singh Kainth and four co-authors introduce PI-NODE-SR, a physics-informed neural differential equation method built for stiff biological systems, where some variables change vastly faster than others. Standard neural ODEs often need huge numbers of iterations on such systems and still settle on solutions with the wrong rhythm or amplitude.

Scale-aware residuals normalize the physics loss so fast and slow variables contribute fairly, and a low-order explicit solver, Heun's method, keeps training stable without costly implicit solvers. Tests center on the Hodgkin-Huxley equations, the classic model of nerve cell firing. Reliable learning of stiff dynamics would help model hearts, neurons, and chemical networks alike.
arxiv-2511-11834:
Vahid Hemmati and five co-authors test a signal called Volatility in Certainty. It aims to spot attacks on image classifiers while they run. A deployed model has no ground truth to check against. So a detector has to sense trouble from the model's own output pattern.

The signal measures how unevenly the sorted confidence scores fluctuate. It uses averaged squared log-ratios between neighboring values. Tests use small neural networks and convolutional networks trained on MNIST. A regularized VGG-style model is also tested. The signal is checked as a proxy for accuracy. It is also checked as an alarm for adversarial drift. A cheap internal gauge would suit real-time systems well.
arxiv-2511-12134:
A. Zahra and six co-authors study how dense, self-gravitating matter evolves in a modified theory of gravity. They use the Starobinsky model, which adds a squared curvature term to Einstein gravity, to describe nonlinear behavior. Their focus is spherical systems where pressure differs by direction, and how dark matter changes them.

Applied to the compact object Her X-1, the model gives physical quantities that stay free of singularities. Dark matter shifts the radial and sideways pressure in clear ways. Changing a key metric parameter also reshapes the object strongly. Checks for energy, balance, stability and causality are used to test whether the model stays physically sound.
arxiv-2511-12234:
Soham Sarkar and Arnab Hazra review statistical and machine learning methods used to assess coral bleaching, a major threat to reefs worldwide. More than half of the world's reefs have bleached or died in recent decades, in their account. The main cause is rising sea surface heat. Other factors in the sea and air also play a role, and they vary in space and time.

The review surveys regression, generalized linear and additive models, Bayesian and spatiotemporal models, and resilience indicators. It also covers machine learning tools such as random forests and decision-based methods. The authors stress that work on stochastic modeling for bleaching is still scarce, and that data-driven assessment is central to reef management.
arxiv-2511-12334:
Marios Kalomenopoulos and four co-authors test how galaxy clustering affects estimates of the Hubble constant from gravitational wave events with no light counterpart, known as dark sirens. Without a host galaxy identified, the distance to each event must be matched, in a statistical way, against galaxy lists. Clustering could help or bias that matching.

Using detailed computer simulations of the cosmos with realistic clustering and a near-future detector network, they find clustering speeds the convergence of the Hubble constant estimates. The input value is recovered clearly with a modest number of events, while uniform catalogues stay poorly constrained even with more. Partial catalogues still compete well, which underlines how much the clustering signal contributes.
arxiv-2511-12834:
Rohit Kundu and five co-authors build SAGA, a system that does not just flag a video as fake but names the generator that made it. Hyper-realistic synthetic video has outgrown simple real-versus-fake detectors, and forensic work needs provenance. SAGA attributes a video at five levels of detail, from authenticity and generation task down to model version, the team behind it, and the exact generator. Its video transformer reads spatio-temporal artifacts through cues from a strong vision foundation model.

A pretrain-and-attribute strategy makes the system data-efficient: it matched fully supervised results while using only half a percent of the labeled data per class. A companion method, Temporal Attention Signatures, visualizes the temporal quirks that distinguish one generator from another, giving the first explanations of generator differences. The authors aim the tool at forensic users who must defend an attribution.
arxiv-2511-12934:
Zhi Kou and seven co-authors restructure how recommendation systems score candidates before ranking. In industrial systems, a pre-ranking model fetches features and scores items only after an upstream stage delivers candidates. The same users and items are recomputed again and again, and everything waits in line. Their Asynchronous Inference Framework splits the model: parts that depend only on the user run in parallel with retrieval, parts that depend only on the item run nearline, ahead of time. Only the truly interactive part happens in real time.

That reorganization cuts latency and frees budget to enrich the precomputed parts with better features and bigger models. Approximate methods handle the interaction terms online. The framework is deployed in Taobao's display advertising system, where the authors report notable gains without meaningfully higher cost. It is a systems lesson: when computation happens can matter as much as what is computed.
arxiv-2511-13034:
Rahul Misra, Manuela L. Bujorianu, and Rafał Wisniewski train a controller that pursues several goals at once, in the long run. Their reinforcement learning framework targets Markov decision processes where the reward is a vector, and success means the time-averaged reward vector settles into a predefined target set. Scalar algorithms cannot eat a vector, so the authors scalarize dynamically, guided by Blackwell's approachability theorem, which tells them how to adjust the weighting so the average is steered toward the target.

The algorithm nests two loops: an inner policy gradient runs between successive returns to a chosen recurrent state, which ergodicity guarantees, and an outer loop updates the scalarization after each return. They prove the long-run average reward converges to the target set and validate the scheme on a numerical example. Multi-objective control is the norm in real systems; this gives it a convergence guarantee.
arxiv-2511-13134:
Ali Asadi, Krishnendu Chatterjee, David Lurie, and Raimundo Saona determine how hard it is to analyze decision problems where the agent cannot see the full state. Partially observable Markov decision processes model such uncertainty, and parity objectives, which can express every omega-regular specification, are the general goals one might impose. For ordinary POMDPs, most analyses for parity objectives are undecidable. The authors work with a restricted class called revealing POMDPs, where observations eventually disclose enough, and for which almost-sure analysis was recently shown to be EXPTIME-complete.

They extend the frontier: for revealing POMDPs, the limit-sure analysis for parity objectives, asking whether success probability can be pushed close to one, is also EXPTIME-complete. Even the quantitative analysis, approximating the optimal success probability, can be done in EXPTIME. This tells algorithm designers which questions are answerable, and at what cost.
arxiv-2511-13734:
Saif Ur Rehman and Wajid Yousuf solve a hard two-phase flow equation with an extended physics-informed neural network. The Buckley-Leverett equation governs oil and water pushing through porous rock, and its nonconvex flux creates sharp fronts that break standard neural solvers. Splitting the domain is their answer to the stiffness.

The extended network divides space and time into pre-shock and post-shock zones that evolve with the front, each with its own subnetwork. A jump condition drawn from Rankine-Hugoniot physics couples the zones so fluxes stay consistent. Against standard and patched neural variants, the extended method resolved fronts most accurately while using only a simple optimizer where rivals needed heavier schemes.
arxiv-2511-14134:
Sogen Ikegami, Kiyu Fukui, and Shun Okumura study how selective random defects reshape the topology of electrons on a honeycomb lattice. Their lattice interpolates between the full honeycomb and a version with one sixth of its sites removed, with defects placed selectively rather than purely at random. They track how the spectrum and topological character change along the way.

In some parameter ranges the two endpoint lattices connect smoothly, keeping their topology. In others the defects trigger a genuine topological transition. An effective model explains the defects as a modulation of hopping amplitudes between sites. The authors highlight defect placement as a design tool for tuning electronic properties across many material platforms.
arxiv-2511-14234:
Michael Cranston and Mariia Khodiakova prove sharp large deviation estimates for counts of irreducible divisors. The elements under study are drawn from a distribution built on a Dirichlet series, and the question is how unlikely unusually high or low divisor counts are. Their lens is mod-Poisson convergence, a technique that tracks a counting variable against a Poisson-like limit with fine precision.

They apply a general theorem to examples from number theory, Dedekind domains, and polynomials over finite fields. The paper is probability theory aimed at arithmetic objects: precise tail estimates of this kind refine the classical picture in which such divisor counts behave roughly like Poisson variables.
arxiv-2511-14334:
Alessio Pellegrino and Jacopo Mauro test whether language models truly understand constraint programming problems or merely remember them. Turning plain-language problem descriptions into executable models is a long-standing goal, and models look strong on classic benchmarks, but those benchmarks likely sit inside their training data. The authors rephrased known CSPLib problems, preserving structure while changing context and adding misleading elements.

Three representative models were compared on original and disguised versions. Their outputs stayed syntactically valid and superficially plausible, yet quality dropped sharply under wording and context changes. The study concludes the apparent skill rests on shallow pattern matching rather than robust modeling understanding, a warning for automated optimization workflows.
arxiv-2511-14434:
Marlow Fawn and Matthias Scheutz wrap unsafe learned robot policies in a formally guaranteed safety layer. Their tool is a harmonic control Lyapunov-barrier function built from a signal temporal logic specification, which encodes both the goal and the forbidden regions. Safety certificates derived from that function filter whatever commands a given policy proposes.

The combined system preserves the policy's task-driven behavior while enforcing safety with formal guarantees, and it works online with any supplied policy. A proof of concept pairs it with an object-centric, force-based reinforcement learning policy on a stationary arm, which then avoids tabletop obstacles it would otherwise hit. The authors note the method generalizes to richer specifications and dynamic settings.
arxiv-2511-14534:
Ali Eidi and three co-authors present a Bayesian neural network method to correct turbulence models for separated flows. Standard averaged flow models lose accuracy where flow detaches from a surface. Data driven fixes often fail on new cases and give no reliable uncertainty. The team focus training on zones near separation to target the core problem.

Physics guided inputs keep the network consistent with known turbulence rules. A classifier applies corrections only where they are needed. Uncertainty from the Bayesian network flows through to the final flow solution. That lets users judge trust on unseen cases. The framework aims at more reliable engineering predictions for separated flow regimes.
arxiv-2511-14834:
Samuel Ruthven Ward, Tiago Costa, and two co-authors study what happens when winds from a feeding black hole crash into gas clouds inside its galaxy. The hot wind carries most of the energy but glows faintly, while the cool clouds shine brightly yet carry little energy. Earlier simulations by the group found the mixing of the two creates a new, strongly glowing phase.

Here they compute the X-ray light that this mixed gas should emit, from hot gas radiation and from glowing metal lines. The mixing layer turns out to shine brightly in X-rays for millions of years. That glow gives observers a new way to spot and measure black hole winds shaping their galaxies.
arxiv-2511-15634:
Benjamin Dupuis, Mert Gürbüzbalaban, and four co-authors derive privacy guarantees for learning algorithms whose noise has heavy tails, meaning extreme values occur more often than in a bell curve. Heavy-tailed gradient noise has been suggested as a realistic model for deep learning and a way to boost performance. Most differential privacy bounds, which limit what output reveals about one person data, assumed light-tailed noise and did not transfer.

Recent guarantees for heavy-tailed methods depended strongly on the number of parameters and covered only a weak privacy notion. Their framework gives the first Rényi differential privacy guarantees, a stronger standard measure, for heavy-tailed continuous processes and their discrete versions, with much weaker dimension dependence.
arxiv-2511-15834:
Rolf Haag investigates circularity and symmetries of polygons whose vertex counts are a prime or a prime squared. Polygon symmetry is measured by counting symmetry axes. Only few symmetry classes occur for these vertex counts. In the prime squared case, some polygons have no axis yet show a special circularity trait tied to the prime.

Haag studies the equivalence classes under those symmetry classes and their enumeration. Total class counts and regular case counts were known. New formulas cover the remaining symmetry classes. Complete representative sets are shown in some cases. The full account lays groundwork for extending classification to polygons with more composite vertex counts, where symmetry patterns grow far more intricate.
arxiv-2511-16134:
Marijan Soric, Cécile Gracianne, Ioana Manolescu, and Pierre Senellart benchmark tools that extract tables from scientific PDF documents. Table extraction turns printed tables into structured data for automatic processing, and many tools exist with varied techniques, making choice difficult for users. Their benchmark assesses end-to-end extraction, from PDF to final table, over tens of thousands of pages.
