They analyze extraction scoring metrics and design a rigorous process that grades each sub-task as well as the full pipeline, capturing model uncertainty. Two new heterogeneous data sets join prior collections. Tested systems range from off-the-shelf libraries to vision-language models. Results show extraction remains hard, with weak generalization to varied documents and limits in robustness and interpretability.
arxiv-2511-16334:
Kaichen Zhang and eight co-authors release OpenMMReasoner, a fully open recipe for training models that reason across images and text. Progress in multimodal reasoning has been hard to reproduce because the data curation and training choices behind strong results are usually kept private.

The recipe has two stages. A supervised stage trains on a cold-start set of about 874,000 samples, each with checked step-by-step reasoning. A reinforcement learning stage then refines the model on about 74,000 samples drawn from varied domains. The result improved on the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct baseline by 11.6 percent across nine multimodal reasoning benchmarks. All code, pipelines, and data are public, giving other groups a solid base to build on.
arxiv-2511-16634:
Mina Tarakemeh and Shenglong Xu build a symmetry-respecting way to measure operator growth in many-body quantum systems with a conserved charge. Operator size tracks how a simple operator spreads into complicated many-body terms, but charge conservation splits the story into two independent conserved quantities.

The authors construct a non-Abelian operator size basis organized by an SU(2) algebra. Operators carrying large total angular momentum stay relatively simple, while small angular momentum means complexity, so growth shows up as angular momentum loss, readable through out-of-time-ordered correlators. For the charge-conserving Brownian Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model they derive an exact classical master equation for the size distribution at any system size. The distribution follows a chi-squared form whose scale and shape are set jointly by the two charges.
arxiv-2511-16934:
Ram Kumar, Aditya H Kelkar, Neeraj Shukla, Paras Poswal, and Sheshmani Singh test how ion beams change the magnetism of highly ordered graphite. Firing ions into a material can create defects, and in graphite those defects can bring out magnetic order that pure graphite lacks. The team varies the beam energy to see how much the energy itself matters.

Samples were struck with protons and with carbon ions across a range of energies, then measured with a magnetic balance and compared with computer runs of how ions slow inside the solid. The magnetic moment changed clearly with beam energy for both kinds of ion. The results show that both the choice of ion and its energy must be set with care when this route is used to tune a material.
arxiv-2511-17034:
Identities that link symmetric functions with partition series are the subject of work by S. Ole Warnaar. He states affine forms of the dual Jacobi-Trudi identities for orthogonal and symplectic Schur functions. The functions are indexed by rectangular partitions of maximal height, and the identities write them as determinants. Affine forms would extend the reach of these formulas.

From those claims, Warnaar derives t-analogues of many known Rogers-Ramanujan identities. These include the classical pair and the Andrews-Gordon family. Such identities arise as characters of standard modules for affine Lie algebras. He also proves one affine identity outright, for Schur functions on rectangles of any height. The paper maps links between determinant formulas and partition identities.
arxiv-2511-17334:
Mary Ogborn and five co-authors build a simulation pipeline for the broad line region of active galactic nuclei, the clouds of gas whose broad emission lines surround a feeding black hole. Observations show these lines jitter in velocity over weeks to months, and their widths vary with the central source's brightness in patterns, called breathing, that remain unexplained. The team models the region as a disk that reverberates, echoing changes in the central continuum with light-travel delays.

Their pipeline drives the simulated disk with chosen continuum light curves, produces synthetic emission line profiles, and measures the same shape parameters observers use: centroid shift, velocity spread, and skewness. The simulations reproduce velocity jitter at the observed amplitude. The tools are aimed at case studies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's fifth phase, and this first paper of a series presents the model itself.
arxiv-2511-17534:
Shaoying Luo, Jinhua Wang, and Changhua Wei prove that a system of nonlinear wave equations known as the evolutionary Faddeev model has solutions that exist smoothly for all time. This holds even for a class of large initial data. The model maps spacetime into the unit sphere and arises in the study of knot-like field configurations. Its nonlinearities have a null structure and mix semilinear, quasilinear, and lower-order terms, a combination that makes global existence delicate.

The authors consider initial data of short pulse type, concentrated and large in energy norm, a regime where blow-up would not be surprising. Through energy estimates with multipliers chosen to fit the system's geometry, they rule blow-up out and obtain a globally smooth solution. The result adds the Faddeev model to the list of geometric wave equations whose large-data behavior is understood.
arxiv-2511-17834:
Jisun Park, Vinit Ranjan, and Bartolomeo Stellato analyze how well first order optimization methods perform when problems come from an unknown distribution known only through samples. Classic worst case bounds are often far too cautious compared with what users see in practice.

They combine performance estimation with robust optimization over nearby distributions, turning the analysis into a tractable conic program. Results give probabilistic guarantees for an expected score or for a risk measure focused on bad cases. Tests on quadratic problems, credit scoring data, and a sparse regression method show much tighter bounds that narrow the gap with observed behavior.
arxiv-2511-18034:
Roberto Tauraso writes a short note extending a classic formula in number theory. In the nineteen eighties, Koecher and, separately, Leshchiner found an elegant formula for the generating function of the odd zeta values. A family of numbers that sit at the heart of many deep questions. Generating functions pack a whole sequence of values into one object that can be studied at once.

Tauraso derives a q-analogue of that formula, meaning a version built around a parameter q that returns the classic result in the limit. The new version also yields a q-form of the fast series for the zeta value at three that Apéry used in his famous proof that the number is irrational. Short as it is, the note links two celebrated results.
arxiv-2511-18434:
Yongkun Du, Pinxuan Chen, Xuye Ying, and Zhineng Chen test how well large multimodal models read and translate photos of documents. Past test sets use clean scans or born digital files. Real use starts from phone shots, with bent pages, glare, and uneven light that warp the text.

DocPTBench holds over a thousand high grade photo documents from many fields, with eight translation setups. Human checked notes mark both the parse and the translation truth. Top models lose much accuracy when the input shifts from clean files to photos. The drop shows how far photo based reading lags lab tests. The set gives builders a real world bar for end to end document work.
arxiv-2511-18534:
Pengcheng Fang and seven co-authors rebuild sharp MRI scans from thinned raw data. Scanners save time by sampling less, but the rebuild must keep fine detail and true anatomy. Their model, HiFi-MambaV2, mixes a state space sequence core with a mixture of experts that routes work by content.

A split frequency pyramid feeds clean low and high bands, proof against alias flaws. A shared routed expert layer picks one expert per pixel, with shared experts and local routers for stable skill across depth. A light global context path joins an unrolled backbone tied to the raw data. On five scan test sets the model tops prior rebuilds. The design aims at clinic grade scans from fast takes.
arxiv-2511-18734:
Keyang Lu and eight co-authors build Yo'City, an agent frame that grows realistic 3D cities to any size, tuned to the user. City builds serve virtual reality and digital twins, yet most past tools train one diffusion model, which caps personal taste and city scale. Their frame leans on the reasoning and assembly skill of large off the shelf models instead.

Planning runs top down in three tiers: city, district, and grid. A global planner sets the layout and the role of each district; a local designer fills each district with grid level detail. Grid builds then run with a self critic that expands the city block by block. User custom, endless growth is the pitch. No single trained generator bounds the result.
arxiv-2511-19034:
Maria Teresa Rotolo describes the long time fate of waves under resonant, time dependent tweaks to a periodic transport equation. The base flow moves waves around a one dimensional torus. Skew adjoint perturbations that resonate with that flow can pump energy across scales, or leave all motion stable for very long spans.

For all non degenerate resonant tweaks, one of two ends holds. Some solutions grow Sobolev norms at an exponential pace, a sign of energy transfer. In the other end, all solutions stay stable on long time scales. A resonant normal form cuts the task to classic dynamics of the resonant part. The hard half is the growth case, built from an escape function with a positive commutator bound. A sharp either or closes the question.
arxiv-2511-19234:
Claudia Collarin, Matteo Fasiolo, Yannig Goude, and Simon N. Wood move data shaping steps inside the model itself. Analysts often reshape input data before fitting a model, to make results clearer or to meet the model's needs. When that shaping sits outside the fit, the extra doubt it adds is left out.

Their method builds clear reshaping steps for inputs, even complex ones with many parts, right into generalized additive models. The shaping values are learned along with the rest of the fit, and doubt is gauged with fast Bayesian tools. Smoothing choices come from the data itself, and fast math keeps the approach workable in practice.
arxiv-2511-19634:
Peize Ding, Nishchhal Verma, and Raquel Queiroz explain odd features in the Landau levels of transition metal dichalcogenides, layered semiconductors. In a magnetic field, electron energies form Landau levels, and in these materials one valence level slopes the wrong way while magnetism differs between electron and hole bands. Simple band models cannot explain either fact.

A continuum three-band model yields analytic rules for the levels in the two valleys at weak field. Their pattern follows a cyclic structure inherited from the crystal's threefold symmetry. Numerical tight-binding and kagome lattice checks agree, and the asymmetry traces to a topological obstruction in the material.
arxiv-2511-19734:
Luca A. Lanzendörfer and Florian Grötschla check whether automatic quality scores can stand in for human ears when judging neural audio codecs. Such codecs rebuild speech faithfully at low bitrates and now feed generative models, but listening tests are slow and costly. Objective metrics promise a shortcut if they track perception.

The authors run a MUSHRA listening test on high-fidelity speech and compare the human scores with widely used objective metrics. Some metrics line up well with listeners, while others miss distortions that people notice. The findings give practical guidance on which scores to trust when evaluating speech codecs.
arxiv-2511-20034:
Xingyue Lin, Shuai Peng, Xiangyu Xie, Jianhua Zhu, Yuxuan Zhou, and Liangcai Gao present COVec, a method for turning real photos into editable vector graphics. Vectorization should keep visual fidelity while staying semantically clean, but existing methods fragment complex real-world images into messy shapes. The authors borrow the clair-obscur idea of light and shade contrast from painting.

COVec is the first method to split an image into albedo, shade, and light layers inside the vector domain itself, in one unified representation. A semantic-guided start and a two-stage optimization then refine the layers through differentiable rendering. On varied datasets, COVec reaches higher visual fidelity and much better editability than existing methods, and the code is slated for release.
arxiv-2511-20134:
Das and Green review why conservation laws discipline theories of tiny electrical currents. Their 2025 paper covers high-field quantum transport. At small scales, strong fields push devices far from equilibrium. Simple linear response rules then break down. Charge continuity and Poisson's equation still must hold exactly.

Two exact laws govern three coupled unknown functions. Extra physical relations are needed to close the system. Phenomenological conductivity rules like inverse Ohm's law help. The review recalls what any microscopic description requires. A quantum point contact serves as the worked example. Driven hard, it shows prominent interband coupling effects. Minimal assumptions yield a workable transport solution there. Conservation is built in rather than checked afterward. Electrical neutrality of the whole circuit anchors everything. The authors stress bookkeeping errors masquerade as new physics. Mesoscopic and nanoscopic devices are the intended audience. Careful accounting keeps high-field models honest.
arxiv-2511-20234:
Moulin, Francois-Lavet, Elbers, and Hoogendoorn read an agent's weights to predict how well it will generalize. Their 2025 paper tackles overfitting in reinforcement learning. Agents ace their training worlds, then flop in new ones. Fixes usually act on data or world design. The team instead inspects the trained networks themselves.

A predictor learns patterns inside agent weight matrices. Those patterns forecast scores on unseen environments. Training data came from Minigrid and Coinrun worlds. Many trained agents supplied weights and true scores. The predictor proved accurate enough to act on. The team then rewired PPO's loss function. The new term rewards weight patterns tied to generalization. Agents trained with the improved loss generalized better. Gains showed against the stock PPO algorithm. Weight signals thus serve twice in the pipeline. They diagnose generalization before deployment testing. They also steer training toward broader competence. Overfitting research gains an internal, measurable handle.
arxiv-2511-20434:
Zeng and colleagues catch a galaxy's jet swinging to a new direction. Their 2025 paper studies the radio galaxy 0954+556. Its jets point northwest on large scales, stretching about 24 kiloparsecs. On small scales the structure runs north-south instead. That mismatch suggests the jet changed direction between outbursts. Deep images at many frequencies test the idea.

The team combined Very Large Array and Very Long Baseline Array data. Frequencies spanned from 1.4 to 43 gigahertz across instruments. They located the core and found faint counter-jets for the first time. A diffuse bridge connects the small and large scale jets. The forward jet bends about 120 degrees between scales. Spectral aging points to at least two episodes of activity. Polarization maps show a spine-sheath pattern near the core. The direction change likely took about one million years. Accretion disk instabilities may have flipped the jet.
arxiv-2511-20534:
Bian, Lin, and Cheng blend voices in latent space to help speech recognition play fair. Their 2025 paper tackles the data gap between languages. Speech systems shine for English thanks to abundant recordings. The world's other seven thousand languages get far worse service. Collecting more data for each is slow and costly.

Their augmentation mixes hidden representations inside voice conversion models. Blending latent voice traits creates new synthetic speakers. That diversifies training data without any new recording sessions. Classic tricks like noise and speed changes do not add speaker variety. SpecAugment masks spectrograms but keeps the same voices. Experiments showed solid gains for low-resource languages. The method outperformed existing augmentation strategies overall. Smoother decision boundaries follow from latent interpolation. Speaker characteristics diversify while words stay intact. The approach offers practical help for underrepresented language communities. Equity in speech technology is the paper's stated goal.
arxiv-2511-20934:
Biagio La Rosa and Leilani H. Gilpin ask in 2025 whether the standard explanations of what a neuron detects are actually the best possible ones. Compositional explanations phrase a neuron's behaviour as a logical rule over concepts, scored by spatial alignment. Searching every concept combination is infeasible, so the field uses beam search, which keeps only promising partial rules and offers no optimality guarantee. The authors build the first framework that can certify the optimum.

Their method decomposes the alignment score into factors, derives a heuristic estimating alignment mid-search, and prunes safely. In the standard vision setting with convolutional networks, they find that 10 to 40 percent of beam-search explanations are suboptimal when concepts overlap. A beam variant guided by their decomposition and heuristic recovers quality while matching or beating prior runtimes. The work gives explanation research a yardstick: heuristics can now be measured against the true best rule.
arxiv-2511-21234:
Cedric Baijot, Maria Groyne, and Michaël De Becker use methanol as a detective tool in a 2025 astrochemistry study of shocked gas near a forming star. Young stars drive outflows that slam into surrounding clouds, and the resulting shocks come in two types, continuous C-type and jumpy J-type, which leave different chemical fingerprints. The team wanted a reliable way to tell the types apart for the outflow region called L1157 B2.

Baijot and his coauthors ran grids of Paris-Durham shock models at speeds from 5 to 19 kilometers per second and compared how much methanol escapes from icy dust grains in each type. The methanol desorption share separated the types cleanly, especially above 15 kilometers per second, and it correctly matched four already known shocks used as a benchmark. Applied to L1157 B2, the test diagnoses a non-irradiated C-type shock.
arxiv-2511-21534:
Matvey Ortyashov and AmirEmad Ghassami ask how wrong a causal study can be when treatments spill over between people, in 2025. Interference, where one person's treatment affects another's outcome, is routine in vaccine and social-policy studies, yet analysts often lack the data to adjust for it. Their framework quantifies the systematic bias that ignoring spillovers creates.

The weighting-based approach handles three bias sources at once: omitted interference, unmeasured confounding, and lack of transportability, meaning results that fail to travel to a new population. Earlier tools tackled these one at a time, and the combination of interference with hidden confounding is especially treacherous. Ortyashov and Ghassami express the total bias through a few interpretable sensitivity parameters that practitioners can set from domain knowledge, without strict parametric assumptions. Special cases where the bias formula simplifies are worked out, giving applied researchers a structured way to stress-test naive estimates.
arxiv-2511-21634:
Ernest Ma, Partha Kumar Paul, and Narendra Sahu build a dark matter candidate out of a leftover symmetry of neutrino physics, in 2025. The type-I seesaw, the standard account of tiny neutrino masses, preserves a symmetry, lepton parity. A Majorana fermion even under it can never decay, making it stable dark matter. An extra singlet scalar lets it couple to right-handed neutrinos.

Production is freeze-in, a slow leak rather than a thermal freeze-out. Two regimes depend on the universe's reheating temperature: decays of heavy neutrinos when reheating is hot, or Higgs decays when it is cool. The candidate's mass can span mega-electronvolts to tera-electronvolts. Observable imprints follow either way. Strong coupling triggers a first-order electroweak phase transition, heard as gravitational waves. Weak coupling leaves extra radiation, seen as a shift in the effective neutrino count. Future experiments can test both channels.
arxiv-2511-21734:
Shiguang Wu and Quanming Yao show that asking a language model to check an answer before solving can sharpen its reasoning almost for free, in 2025. Their strategy, Verification-First, hands the model a candidate answer, even a trivial or random one, and asks it to verify the candidate first. Checking turns out to be cognitively easier than generating, and it primes critical thinking.

This reverse reasoning complements standard chain-of-thought. The authors extend the idea into Iter-VF, which cycles verification and generation repeatedly, each round refining the model's own previous answer. Experiments spanned mathematics, coding, and agentic benchmarks, and models from open 1-billion-parameter systems to leading commercial ones. Verification-First with even a random candidate consistently beat plain chain-of-thought at minimal added cost. Iter-VF in turn outperformed rival test-time scaling strategies, a cheap upgrade for reasoning pipelines.
arxiv-2511-22134:
Fang, Liu, Liu, Chen, and colleagues fix a side effect they name action degeneration in robot foundation models. A specialist vision-language-action model manipulates objects well but reasons poorly; fine-tuning it on mixed reasoning data restores general reasoning yet quietly degrades its manipulation skill, even though the training set grew. Their DualVLA post-training attacks two causes: repetitive, low-information reasoning annotations that bias learning, and undifferentiated supervision for two very different skills sharing one network.

A dual-layer pruning step strips redundant embodied reasoning from the data, and a dual-teacher distillation strategy gives robot data an action specialist's supervision and multimodal data a reasoning teacher's, adaptively. DualVLA reaches a 61.0 percent average success rate in the SimplerEnv simulator and 65.4 average across eight multimodal benchmarks. The team also introduces VLA Score, an evaluation splitting capability into reasoning, intention, action, and alignment.
arxiv-2511-22234:
Du, Fang, de Miguel-Arribas, and colleagues study how reputation sustains cooperation when interactions happen in groups, not just pairs. Most cooperation theory uses pairwise networks, but real social life runs through higher-order structures, triangles and larger groups captured by simplicial complexes. The team introduces an edge-based reputation mechanism tracking both direct reputation, earned from one's own partners, and indirect reputation, gathered through common neighbors. The mechanism lets reputation guide whom agents imitate in evolutionary games on such complexes.

Coupling reputation with higher-order structure strongly promotes cooperation, direct reputation most; indirect reputation helps in stable settings but spreads slowly, and a hybrid lands between. The interplay is nonlinear: when temptation to defect is low, higher-order interactions amplify cooperative signals and cluster cooperators. At high temptation the same coupling spreads bad reputations and erodes cooperation, a caution for designing reputation systems.
arxiv-2511-22634:
Weston and colleagues prepare astronomers to find host galaxies in Rubin's deepest fields. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time will flood brokers with an estimated ten million alerts nightly, and matching each transient to its host supplies context and often distance. In the Deep Drilling Fields, many hosts are too faint for all-sky catalogues. So the team assembled 70 overlapping deep catalogues, homogenised them, and ranked them by content such as spectroscopic redshifts and morphology.

Testing association methods on a Dark Energy Survey sample with known hosts, the Directional Light Radius method matched the A-Value method but was more robust against contaminants such as diffraction spikes. A gradient-boosting confidence model missed fewer good matches. The top-ranked catalogues, 784,000 sources across three fields, entered the Sherlock tool of the Lasair broker, where matching adds about 0.8 percent of runtime, some 18 microseconds a transient.
arxiv-2511-23434:
Goldstein-Gelb and colleagues design COMPAS, an architecture for running the multi-party SWAP test, a key basic quantum subroutine. Across a network of smaller interconnected quantum processors instead of one big chip. The target task is multivariate trace estimation, useful for measuring Rényi entropies, virtual cooling and distillation. And some quantum signal processing, and the design spends pre-shared entangled Bell pairs as its communication resource in the work.

COMPAS adds only a constant depth overhead and consumes Bell pairs at a rate linear in the circuit width. And unlike rival schemes it achieves asymptotic optimality in both circuit depth and GHZ width at the same time. The authors analyze circuit-level and network-level noise to map the trade-off between node count and error. Arguing the architecture is realistic for near-term modular hardware and enables several distributed quantum applications in practice.
arxiv-2512-00134:
Translating assembly code back into readable source code is vital for reverse engineering, security work, and software maintenance. Parisa Hamedi and co-authors present Asm2SrcEval in 2025, a benchmark for testing language models on that task. Systematic benchmarks for this problem have been scarce.

The authors evaluate five leading large language models on assembly-to-source translation. Their study is described as the first comprehensive evaluation of its kind. Clear benchmarks help security analysts judge whether AI tools can be trusted to reconstruct code from compiled programs. That task arises whenever source code is lost or suspect. The benchmark gives model builders a shared yardstick for a task that security work depends on.
arxiv-2512-00234:
Translating speech directly is harder than translating text, because the words must first be heard. Sai Koneru, Matthias Huck, and Jan Niehues present OmniFusion in 2025, a system for simultaneous multilingual multimodal translation. It uses modular fusion to combine the relevant inputs.

Open-source text translation models have improved in coverage and quality, but speech translation still usually chains speech recognition before translation. That cascaded pipeline compounds errors and adds delay. A fused system could serve live interpretation and accessible media, where many languages and fast turnaround matter at once. Modular fusion keeps each input stream's strengths instead of blending them into mush. Simultaneous output matters most when listeners cannot wait for a finished sentence.
arxiv-2512-00434:
Synthetic health records could let researchers train models without exposing real patients. Benjamin Ballyk and co-authors study privacy-preserving generative modeling of longitudinal health records in 2025, with clinical validation for chronic disease. Privacy rules rightly restrict access to electronic records, which limits model training.

Machine learning has shown promise for diagnostic accuracy and personalized care, but only if data can be used safely. The authors generate records over time for the same patients and check them clinically, not just statistically. Valid synthetic cohorts could open chronic disease research to more teams without putting patient confidentiality at risk. Longitudinal records, visits over years, are what chronic disease research actually needs.
arxiv-2512-00634:
Breaking a chemical bond with hot carriers drives radiation damage, catalyst action, and semiconductor aging alike. Woncheol Lee and co-authors study resonant states and nuclear dynamics in bond dissociation in 2025, focusing on the silicon-hydrogen bond. Describing such processes from first principles has remained an elusive goal.

Hot-carrier degradation and activation of dopant-hydrogen complexes in semiconductors both hinge on how nuclei move once a bond is excited. Resonant states capture the temporary configurations that decide whether the bond breaks. First-principles insight here could help engineers design chips that resist degradation and catalysts that exploit it. Silicon-hydrogen bonds are central to solar cells and chip passivation alike. For chip firms, the gain is parts that last. If a bond's weak spots are known in depth, the next run of chips can be built to guard them well.
arxiv-2512-00734:
Aaradhya Pandey, Arian Maleki, and Sanjeev Kulkarni work on the math of privacy in a 2025 paper. Differential privacy limits what data analysis can reveal about any one person. A modern way to state those limits uses hypothesis testing, where a trade-off curve shows how hard two datasets are to tell apart.

The paper studies infinitely divisible privacy, a setting where guarantees can be split and recombined in clean ways. It also reports a resolution of a named conjecture about a key parameter case. Stronger math here helps designers prove privacy claims for systems that run many analyses in a row.
arxiv-2512-01034:
Mansi Maheshwari, John Raisbeck, and Bruno Castro Da Silva address a learning failure in reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. In supervised learning, a network trains on one fixed dataset and does well. In reinforcement learning, the data keeps changing as the agent acts, and the network's ability to keep learning fades over time.

That fade is called plasticity loss: the network grows rigid and stops adapting to new experience. The authors frame the tension as the plasticity-stability dilemma. A learner must stay stable enough to keep old skills yet plastic enough to gain new ones. Their work seeks methods that protect continued learning.
arxiv-2512-01334:
Yexin Liu and co-authors fix a flaw in text-guided video made from a still image. New tools can start from one image and a text prompt. They keep the subject steady and the motion smooth. But they often miss fine points in the prompt.

When a prompt asks to add, drop, or change an object, the tool may keep the old scene. The team calls that miss semantic negligence. Their fix, AlignVid, scales attention with no new training. It steers the tool to heed the prompt more. That helps the video match what the user asked for.
arxiv-2512-01534:
Alexander Frotscher and co-authors run a large fair test of anomaly finding in brain scans. Deep methods can flag odd spots in MR scans with no lesion labels. That path could help clinics a lot. But past tests were split, with mixed data and mixed scores.

Their benchmark spans many centers with one protocol. It also checks for bias across groups. A shared test shows which methods truly work and which just fit one site. That clarity is key before such tools can aid real diagnosis at scale. Bias checks span age and sex groups, since a detector that works for one group and fails for another is not clinic-ready.
arxiv-2512-01734:
Yi Huang and co-authors analyze resonances of one-dimensional acoustic media with propagation matrices. Resonances are tones at which a medium rings strongly. Their placement shapes how sound passes or blocks. General media make that placement hard to compute directly.

The team shows resonant frequencies are zeros of an explicit trigonometric polynomial. Nevanlinna value theory then gives their distribution traits. A closed form for resonances helps design acoustic filters and barriers. It also serves non-destructive testing, where ring tones reveal flaws in parts. One-dimensional media model layered pipes and strings, so the polynomial route serves both lab acoustics and musical instrument design.
arxiv-2512-02434:
Theory says our galaxy should hold on the order of a hundred thousand binaries pairing a black hole with a neutron star, yet decades of intensive radio searching have found none. Man Ho Chan's 2025 paper examines these exotic black hole-neutron star binaries and the puzzle of their absence.

Such pairs are prized because their mergers would broadcast gravitational waves and light together, a rich double signal. Their invisibility so far may reflect beaming, lifetimes, or formation rates rather than true absence. Working through the discrepancy sharpens both the searches and the population models behind them.
arxiv-2512-03134:
More massive galaxies tend to hold more heavy elements. Zach Lewis and a large team study that link, the mass-metallicity relation, in this 2025 work. They focus on galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago, at high redshift.

Hidden biases in how galaxies are picked and measured can skew the link. The authors test how those effects change the relation that surveys recover. Clean results matter because the link reveals how galaxies form stars and lose or gain gas. The work helps teams read early galaxy data with more care. Correcting those biases is vital before drawing lessons about galaxies in the young universe.
arxiv-2512-03234:
Diffusion models can be steered toward outputs people prefer. Jean Pachebat, Giovanni Conforti, Alain Durmus, and Yazid Janati offer a method for that steering in this 2025 work. They call it iterative tilting, and it needs no gradients.

A big reward tilt is split into many small tilts in sequence. Each small tilt allows a simple update to the model's score. Stepwise steering is easier to control than one large jump. The method could help tune image and data generators toward safer or more useful outputs. Small tilts keep each update stable, which guards the model's original skills.
arxiv-2512-03334:
Speakers often switch languages mid-sentence. This 2025 study models topics and social variation in such code-switched speech. It covers two settings: Spanish with English, and Spanish with Guaraní.

The authors built a pipeline that uses large language models to label the text. They labeled topic, genre, and discourse function across thousands of code-switched sentences. Data come in part from the Miami Bilingual Corpus, with new topic labels for the Guaraní set. The work helps linguists study how bilingual speech carries identity and meaning. Topic and genre labels help compare how the two bilingual settings switch for different aims.
arxiv-2512-03934:
A basic comfort of convex mathematics is that strongly convex functions are always continuous. Nguyen Thi Van Hang, Felipe Lara, and Nguyen Dong Yen ask whether the same comfort holds for strongly quasiconvex functions, a wider class used in optimisation. Their 2025 preprint answers a long-standing open question on the topic, and the answer is no.

The authors show that real-valued strongly quasiconvex functions on multi-dimensional space can be discontinuous, in sharp contrast with their convex counterparts. Such a function can have infinitely many points where continuity fails. Some also lack lower and upper semicontinuity at infinitely many points. The examples are built in detail rather than merely asserted. For optimisers, the message is practical: algorithms and theorems that quietly assume continuity for this function class rest on ground this paper shows is not there.
arxiv-2512-04034:
Out-of-distribution detectors should flag inputs unlike anything a model was trained on, yet they fail badly when training used images from a single domain. Hong Yang and colleagues explain that failure with information theory in a 2025 preprint. Supervised training on one domain, they claim, inevitably throws away exactly the information a detector needs.

The phenomenon, named domain feature collapse, means the learned representation carries no information about domain-specific traits, only class traits. They prove this follows from information bottleneck optimisation, and use Fano's inequality to measure partial collapse in realistic settings. To test the theory they build Domain Bench, a suite of single-domain datasets. A simple remedy, filtering features through pretrained representations so domain information survives, repaired the failure. The authors draw wider lessons for transfer learning and for when to fine-tune versus freeze a pretrained model.
arxiv-2512-04234:
Bifurcations in smooth dynamical systems are well charted; their nonsmooth cousins, where the rule changes abruptly across a boundary, are stranger, and can produce strange nonchaotic attractors. Rafael Martinez-Vergara and Joan Carles Tatjer study such bifurcations in a 2025 dynamical systems preprint. Their systems are one-dimensional maps forced quasiperiodically, with the map itself piecewise linear.

They consider four families of these forced maps, two with a symmetry and two modelled on saddle-node and period-doubling bifurcations. Under stated assumptions on one parameter, they prove a curve exists in the two-parameter plane along which a nonsmooth bifurcation occurs. On that curve, the system has a strange nonchaotic attractor. These are piecewise-linear counterparts of smooth families that appear to show the same phenomenon. The authors note their period-doubling family is, as far as they know, the first example of its kind.
arxiv-2512-04434:
Ali Rabeh, Suresh Murugaiyan, and Adarsh Krishnamurthy build a fast stand-in for wind and water flow simulations that works across many shapes. Full flow solvers are accurate but slow, which blocks design loops that test hundreds of forms. A geometry-aware operator network offers a shortcut. Their 2025 arXiv paper trains one on hundreds of high-fidelity runs and tests it on shapes it never saw.

The network reads shape through a signed distance field, which marks how far each point sits from the surface. A vision branch reads the recent flow history. Together they predict the next velocity field for flows of moderate strength. Single-step error stayed near five percent on held-out shapes. Speed beat the classic solver by up to a thousandfold. Long rollouts drift in fine wake detail, worst near sharp corners. The authors chart those failure modes and suggest practical fixes.
arxiv-2512-04534:
Youze Huang, Penghui Ruan, Bojia Zi, and co-authors introduce object retexture, the task of dressing an object in the surface pattern of another. Diffusion editors can swap styles, but fine local texture transfer stays shaky. A plain ControlNet setup takes the reference photo as is, so stray structure leaks in with the texture. It also fails to split the source object's own texture from its shape. Their 2025 arXiv paper answers with Refaçade.

The first design is a texture remover trained to strip structure away, leaving pure surface pattern. The second design keeps the target's shape fixed while the clean pattern is applied. Tests cover both still images and video clips. Transfers kept the target object's form while wearing the reference surface faithfully. Such control could serve product design, film props, and online shopping previews, where a buyer wants this shape in that finish.
arxiv-2512-04634:
Raul Borsche, Tobias Damm, and Axel Klar work out how to join flow equations at the junctions of a network, starting from the kinetic level. Networks of pipes, channels, or vessels carry flows that simpler models describe with wave equations. The catch sits at the nodes, where branches meet and coupling rules decide what passes through. Their 2025 arXiv paper derives those rules from a linear kinetic BGK model as the Knudsen number shrinks.

Near each node, the team solves coupled half-space problems for the kinetic layer. A discrete velocity version yields exact analytic results for the layer. An efficient spectral method then solves the coupled problems numerically. From those solutions come the fitting coefficients of the macroscopic coupling rules, the so-called extrapolation lengths. Sound junction rules matter for gas grids, blood flow, and traffic models built on networks.
arxiv-2512-04734:
Abdul Haseeb Nizamani, Dandi Zhou, Xinhai Sun, and co-authors present MT-Depth, a depth completion system that uses object outlines to fill sparse depth maps. Cars, robots, and headsets sense depth at scattered points and must densify it before acting. Many tools lean on semantic segmentation for guidance yet ignore object-level structure. Their 2025 arXiv paper adds instance awareness: per-object masks act as spatial priors for where depth should stay smooth or break.

The design joins four parts. A frozen YOLO branch draws instance masks. A U-Net backbone predicts depth. Cross-attention fuses the two streams, and a guided head writes the final map. Masks steer the network to respect object borders, where depth errors hurt most. Tests target driving and robotics scenes. Cleaner depth at object edges can sharpen obstacle checks and grasp planning in mixed indoor and street settings.
arxiv-2512-04834:
Vignesh Kumar Kembu, Pierandrea Morandini, Marta Ranzini, and co-authors test whether open multilingual language models can pull structured facts from Italian hospital records in a zero-shot setting. Clinical free text is messy, varied, and dense with meaning, and older extraction tools often miss its subtleties. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks the title's question directly: are today's models truly multilingual when the stakes are medical?

The team probes open models on electronic health records written in Italian, with no task-specific training. The models must find and structure key clinical information from raw notes. Results gauge how far English-centric training carries into a specialist, non-English domain. Findings of this kind guide hospitals that cannot train their own systems, and they expose where multilingual claims outrun reality. Honest measures help vendors and clinicians set safe expectations.
arxiv-2512-04934:
Dong-Hui Yu, Mian Zhu, and Yong Cai test whether a quantum-motivated energy bound allows Genesis cosmology, a scenario where the universe begins calm instead of in a Big Bang singularity. Genesis models start from an almost flat, empty state and grow into the hot universe, which requires breaking the null energy condition. Unbounded breaking worries theorists, since negative energy could pile up without limit. Their 2025 arXiv paper applies the smeared null energy condition, a semi-local cap on such violations, to these models.

The cap bites. Within the generalized Galileon theories where Genesis models are usually built, the smeared condition rules out stretches of parameter space that once looked viable. Surviving models must thread tighter limits on how long and how strongly the energy condition can fail. The result promotes the smeared condition into a sharp screening tool for any cosmology that tries to skip the initial singularity.
arxiv-2512-05234:
Felix Mulitze, Herbert Woisetschläger, and Hans Arno Jacobsen present MAR-FL, a peer-to-peer federated learning system designed to communicate sparingly. Federated learning trains models across many devices without centralizing data. Dropping the central coordinator is attractive for wireless networks where clients come and go. But it usually means peers must exchange far more messages, and the cost explodes as the group grows.

MAR-FL aggregates in iterative groups instead of all-to-all exchanges. That cuts the communication cost from quadratic growth in the number of peers to a far gentler rate. It also stays resilient when unreliable clients drop out mid-round. The system can also fold in private computing techniques. The authors position the design for next-generation wireless settings, where churn is constant and bandwidth is precious: a federated system that stays efficient exactly when the network is least cooperative.
arxiv-2512-05334:
Samaneh Mohtadi, Kevin Roitero, Stefano Mizzaro, and Gianluca Demartini test a tempting shortcut in evaluating search engines: letting language models judge relevance from summaries instead of full documents. Human relevance judgments are the gold standard for information retrieval evaluation but are slow and expensive to collect, so model judges are taking over. Almost all prior work fed those judges whole documents; whether shrinking the input changes the verdicts was unknown.

Across several standard test collections and leading models, the authors compare judgments from full texts with judgments from model-written summaries of varying lengths. System rankings stay about as stable as with full-document judging, which makes the shortcut attractive for large-scale evaluation. But the label distributions shift systematically, with biases that depend on the model and dataset. Summarization, they conclude, is both an efficiency opportunity and a methodological choice whose distortions evaluators must reckon with.
arxiv-2512-05434:
Y. Wang and a large team from the TCV tokamak's collaboration confront plasma simulations with experiment, filament by filament. In the scrape-off layer at a fusion plasma's edge, turbulence forms filaments that carry heat and particles outward, and predicting them tests basic simulation. The team checks the GBS turbulence code against measurements from the TCV tokamak in a shared test case, with two-dimensional imaging of the turbulence added.

To compare fairly, they run a fake gas-puff imaging diagnostic inside the simulation, modelling the helium physics and line-of-sight effects the real camera sees. Filament speeds agree well between simulation and experiment, while simulated filaments come out too large and their relative fluctuation levels too small. The simulations also confirm that the filaments are mainly density structures, not temperature ones. Their motion mostly follows the average electric drift, with telling exceptions in the divertor leg.
arxiv-2512-05534:
Yiming Tang and eight co-authors give the first theory of sparse dictionary learning, the family of methods mechanistic interpretability uses to unpack what neural networks represent. Networks encode concepts as directions, many of them superposed in the same space; sparse autoencoders and their cousins try to disentangle them into single-meaning features. In practice the results are plagued by features that stay polysemantic, features that get absorbed, and neurons that die. Almost no theory explains why.

The authors cast every major variant as one piecewise biconvex optimization problem. They pin down its global solutions, its non-identifiability, and its spurious optima. The analysis explains feature absorption and dead neurons as consequences, not accidents. A new benchmark with full ground-truth access exposes the pathologies. A technique called feature anchoring, guided by the theory, restores identifiability. It markedly improves feature recovery on synthetic and real representations alike.
arxiv-2512-05634:
K. Abe and the many hundreds of members of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory collaboration report a search for very high energy light from a magnetar. Magnetars are neutron stars with immense magnetic fields. The one studied, SGR 1935+2154, sits in our galaxy and has lately fired many bright bursts. The team used the prototype Large-Sized Telescope, LST-1, to watch it during active spells in 2021 and 2022.

No steady glow and no burst linked flash was found at tera-electronvolt energies. For nine short X-ray bursts, the team set tight upper limits on any matching flash at those energies. For the brightest burst, the high energy flux was under a thousandth of the X-ray flux. It suggests any such component appears only under conditions not covered here. It also marks magnetars and fast radio bursts as promising targets for the coming full array.
arxiv-2512-05734:
Jinfeng Zhong, Emmanuel Bacry, Agathe Guilloux, and Jean-François Muzy built KANFormer, a model that predicts whether a limit order will be filled, and how long it will take. Such orders wait in a queue at a set price. Knowing the odds and timing of a fill shapes strategy. Most models read only snapshots of the order book. KANFormer also uses what traders themselves do, and where the order sits in its queue.

The design joins a dilated causal convolution network with a transformer encoder, sharpened by Kolmogorov-Arnold layers that bend curves flexibly. Fill prediction is cast as survival analysis, the statistics of waiting times. On labeled orders from CAC 40 index futures, the model beat earlier work on both calibration and discrimination measures. A SHAP based study shows which signals matter over time. Rich signals plus an expressive network give forecasts traders can trust and interpret.
arxiv-2512-05834:
José Campos-Martínez and Marta Hernández report a counterintuitive result for membranes made of graphdiyne, a carbon sheet pierced by uniform nanoscale pores. Such sheets are proposed as sieves for separating atoms, molecules, and isotopes. Their three dimensional quantum wave packet calculations compare a single layer against two stacked layers, tracking how quantum particles cross.

The bilayer wins: transport through the pair is enhanced over the monolayer, not reduced. On top of the familiar single layer profile, the bilayer shows resonances, sharp peaks in transmission probability. Those peaks are not a quirk of graphdiyne: they appear in stacked nanoporous sheets generally, and move strongly with layer spacing. Spacing thus becomes a tuning knob for quantum sieving. For isotope separation, where differences between species are minuscule and energy costs dominate, a second layer that helps rather than hinders could change the design of quantum filters.
arxiv-2512-05934:
Qianxu Wang and six co-authors listen to crowds of atomic scale defects inside quantum hardware, and learn to conduct them. Two-level system defects, tiny flaws in amorphous materials, are a leading source of decoherence in superconducting quantum devices. This team uses a broadband method, spectroscopy through a three dimensional waveguide, sweeping three to five gigahertz at once, with no full device fabrication required.

The ensemble answers coherently. Spectra show sharp V-shaped features at the defects' natural frequencies. From them the authors extract the defect density in a silicon sample, about eighty four defects per gigahertz across the measured span. Shaped pulse pairs map interference fringes proving the dynamics are coherent and controllable. A minimal spin model with dipole interactions reproduces the behavior. The platform diagnoses a whole defect bath at once.
arxiv-2512-06134:
Georgi Hrusanov and eight co-authors, working with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, build a machine to forecast a mind's decline. Predicting decline is central to managing Alzheimer's, but models must stay interpretable. Their machine lifts nonlinear trajectories into a space where they evolve linearly.

Domain knowledge guides the architecture. Grouped features feed layered attention. It beat traditional and deep models at predicting several scores at once. It reports which biomarkers and brain regions drive each score. That layer is the prize. An interrogable model can shape care; a black box cannot. Personalized prognosis in dementia needs both the number and the story.
arxiv-2512-06634:
Jaime Munoz Rivera, Elena Ochoa Ochoa, and Ramon Quintanilla ask how smooth the solutions of heated elastic systems can be. Their models are of phase lag, parabolic type, where heat conduction carries a delay that changes the character of the equations. Smoothness here is not a nicety: the strongest forms, where the solution flow can be differentiated endlessly, tie regularity and stability together through dissipation.

For a fully thermoelastic plate that bends across its width, they prove the flow is analytic, the gold standard of smoothness in time. For a second plate built of two parts, one coupled to heat and one purely elastic, they prove the flow sits in a Gevrey class. That class is a notch below analytic, and the result holds for round, symmetric solutions. Both results are stated as optimal. The work maps exactly how much smoothing heat can lend to elastic motion in each design.
arxiv-2512-07134:
Lauren Levine and Amir Zeldes build a resource for one of reading's quiet miracles: bridging, where a new phrase is understood through an earlier, different one. Mention a house, then say the door is red, and every reader knows whose door. Computers struggle with that leap. Existing English resources for bridging are small, cover few of its varieties, and span few kinds of writing.

GUMBridge annotates bridging across sixteen diverse genres of English, with fine-grained labels for the subtypes of the phenomenon. The authors check the annotation quality and then test modern language models, both open and closed, on the tasks the data supports: finding bridges, resolving them, and naming their type. Even strong models find those tasks hard. The corpus gives the field a broader, more careful yardstick for a skill humans exercise on nearly every page.
arxiv-2512-07234:
Biao Chen and co-authors borrow an old neural network trick, dropout, and apply it to the prompts that steer vision-language models. Ordinary dropout silences random neurons to stop memorization. Here the dropping happens to tokens, the chunks of image and text the model reads. Crucially, the odds of dropping each token are not uniform. They are scored by how much the token matters within its own stream, and how well it lines up with the other stream.

A regularizer based on residual entropy keeps the two goals in balance, preserving the semantic alignment that lets knowledge transfer while still harvesting the diversity dropout creates. Across fifteen benchmarks the method proved itself in the hard corners of the field: learning from very few examples. It also classified rare categories in long-tailed data, and generalized to distributions unlike the training set.
arxiv-2512-07334: Samantha Sbarra and co-authors stretch a beam of laser light into a rainbow spanning three octaves, from visible green to the mid-infrared. The trick is supercontinuum generation inside waveguides carved from crystalline aluminum nitride on sapphire. By regrowing the nitride layers in a tailored way and refining fabrication, the team sharpened how sensitively the waveguide's dispersion reacts to its cross-section. That control pushed both ends of the spectrum outward under tuned pumping conditions.
arxiv-2512-07434:
Bram Pellen and María Belén Rodríguez wrote this 2025 computer science paper with Frits Vaandrager and Petra van den Bos. It tests a method called black-box checking, first proposed by Peled, Vardi, and Yannakakis. The method hunts for bugs in software that must follow a formal safety rule.

Black-box checking mixes active learning, model-based testing, and model checking. Most users run the model check only at the very end, on the final learned model. The original idea checks every interim model as well, and this study tests that full version. The team ran many benchmarks drawn from real network protocols and controllers. Checking early found rule breaks with only a small share of the usual test effort. Even when the full model stayed out of reach, the method caught most safety violations. It also beat standard model-based testing tools at finding deep bugs.
arxiv-2512-07634:
Filip Bočinec and Stanislav Nagy wrote this 2025 statistics paper on robust ways to find a center. Data can be poisoned by outliers, so a median must resist contamination. Halfspace depth gives one respected route to a multivariate median.

A landmark earlier result set the best possible error rate for such medians. That result covered location and scatter under elliptical symmetry. Bočinec and Nagy widen the stage to alpha-symmetric distributions. The family includes heavy-tailed data, where extreme values are common. For location, they bound the error of the halfspace median under contamination. Scatter is trickier, since its classic depth leans hard on elliptical shape. They therefore design a modified scatter depth that fits the wider family. Its matching median matrix earns its own error bound. Further properties of scatter depth under this symmetry round out the work. Robust statistics gains firmer ground beyond the elliptical world.
arxiv-2512-07834:
Yi-Chuan Huang, Jiewen Chan, Hao-Jen Chien, and Yu-Lun Liu wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper. Voxel art, the chunky block style of games and digital media, has a strict charm. Turning a smooth three-dimensional mesh into that style automatically is surprisingly hard.

A good conversion must simplify geometry without losing the character's identity. Colors must also snap to a small, coherent palette, pixel by pixel. Their framework, Voxify3D, works in two differentiable stages. Orthographic pixel art supervision aligns voxels and pixels without perspective distortion. A patch-based alignment step keeps meaning intact as detail is stripped away. Palette-constrained quantization, made differentiable, picks the discrete colors end to end. Users can dial the palette size and resolution to taste. Tests across diverse characters show top performance for the method. Human judges strongly prefer its output over rival conversions.
arxiv-2512-08234:
Liping Zou, Pengming Zhang, and Y M Cho, theoretical physicists, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about magnetic monopoles in non Abelian gauge theories. Monopoles, isolated magnetic charges, play deep roles in theories of fundamental forces. The authors argue that several standard theories contain more kinds of monopoles than textbooks usually list.

In the standard model, they describe two very different families: Cho Maison monopoles dressed by weak bosons, and neutral magnetic monopoles, bare or dressed, carrying a neutral magnetic charge. The Georgi Glashow model gains a new Wu Yang monopole with weak boson dressing, beside the famous t Hooft Polyakov one. Quantum chromodynamics likewise gains a Wu Yang monopole dressed by chromons. The paper shows how to construct each new monopole and explains where its topology comes from. The authors suggest the new objects could matter for both high energy and low energy physics.
arxiv-2512-08534:
Zhangli Hu, Ye Chen, Jiajun Yao, and Bingbing Ni, computer vision researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, PaintFlow, generates and edits oil paintings interactively. Oil paint is a hard medium to imitate digitally, and earlier tools mostly restyled photographs rather than truly painting.

Users can steer PaintFlow three ways at once: reference images for meaning, hand drawn sketches for layout, and text prompts for high level guidance, while one unified style holds across the result. Training adds conditioning that maps sketches and masks into spatial constraints and references into feature constraints. To beat data scarcity, a stroke based rendering pipeline converts real images into paired oil painting training data that keeps brushstroke texture. A blending operator at inference keeps the style consistent. In tests, the system allowed fine grained editing while preserving the artistic feel of real oil painting.
arxiv-2512-08634:
A Naeimi, F Herz, and S A Biehs study how heat moves by radiation along a chain of tiny particles. The chain follows the Su Schrieffer Heeger pattern and is made of indium antimonide particles placed near a matching substrate. Coupling to surface waves on the substrate changes the bands of modes that run along the chain.

By tracking a phase quantity, the authors show a topological change still occurs when the substrate is present. Finite chains gain protected edge modes in the non trivial phase, and heat travels much farther along the chain. Heat flow is also stronger in that phase, thanks in part to the edge modes. The results point to ways to guide heat at very small scales using surface effects.
arxiv-2512-08734:
L Bandiera and a large team study radiation emitted when low energy electrons pass through scintillator crystals that are carefully oriented. When the beam lines up with a crystal axis, coherent interactions can greatly boost electromagnetic radiation. Experiments at the Mainz Mikrotron used three crystal types, each aligned along a chosen axis.

Enhanced emission was seen when the beam matched the crystal axes, with first time results for two of the crystal types. The effect is stronger along specific crystal directions, which can be exploited in detector design. Possible uses include very compact and sensitive calorimeters for particle and astroparticle physics. High performance gamma detectors for nuclear physics and medical imaging could also benefit. The work gives experimental grounding for a new class of oriented crystal detectors.
arxiv-2512-08834:
Gia Dvali and coauthors argue that the strong CP problem points toward a gauge axion solution, and in turn toward fundamental strings. The puzzle concerns a boundary term in the theory of the strong force that should cause effects, yet appears to be absent. Viewing the vacuum through topological susceptibility reframes the issue clearly.

In that view, the relevant vacua are those of a Chern Simons gauge theory, which makes the physical role of the boundary term immediate. The gauge axion then emerges as part of the gauge redundancy itself, with exact quality and no reference to a global symmetry. Unlike the standard axion, it avoids the quality problem that plagues a scalar field completion. Its completion leads directly to a fundamental theory of gravity. Domain walls and strings tied to the axion must belong to that theory, giving a new argument linking axions, gravity, and strings.
arxiv-2512-09034:
Gerard Angles Munne and coauthors study how rich Bell the effect becomes in systems of many quantum particles. Bell the effect is a central form of nonclassical correlation,. For two party rules, the effect is strictly monogamous: violating one rule blocks violations of others on shared systems.

In the many party setting, the picture reverses and the effect becomes polygamous. Past work showed that for parts formed by removing one particle. The authors generalize the result to parts formed by removing any number of particles. A single multi qubit state can violate all relevant Bell rules at once. They also build a joint rule, by combining the smaller ones, that is fully violated by such states. Violations exceed those of a standard linked state family, showing an advantage for testing tasks. The behavior can also occur across several subsystem sizes at once, a pattern the authors call hyper polygamy.
arxiv-2512-09234:
Callie A. García and seven co-authors follow a solar prominence, a cool dense cloud held above the Sun, as it erupts and travels to Earth. Prominences often leave the Sun inside coronal mass ejections, but by the time those clouds pass spacecraft they are usually heated and changed. A rare event let the team track one that kept its cool, weakly ionized state.

Using ultraviolet views from several spacecraft, they estimated the cloud's density, temperature, and speed. Part of it stayed dark in absorption long after liftoff, a sign of little heating. When it passed near Earth, its ion charges showed a mix: cool, weakly ionized gas alongside much hotter plasma carrying highly ionized iron. Simulations matched that mix with a cloud made of mostly cool plasma plus a hotter share. The authors say such mixed heating calls for better wide views of the corona.
arxiv-2512-09434:
Sebastian Nagl and colleagues introduce CourtPressGER, a dataset for turning German court rulings into press releases. Germany's highest courts issue official releases that explain decisions to citizens as well as experts. Earlier language technology work focused on technical headnotes, the summaries written for lawyers, and ignored this citizen-facing communication.

The dataset holds several thousand triples: a ruling, the human-written press release, and a synthetic prompt designed to make a language model produce a comparable release. It serves both to train and to evaluate models at writing accurate, readable summaries of long judicial texts. The team benchmarks small and large models with reference-based scores, factual consistency checks, model-as-judge ratings, and expert rankings. Large models produced high-quality drafts with little loss, while smaller models needed hierarchical setups to handle long judgments. Human-written releases still ranked highest overall.
arxiv-2512-09634:
Karl Gustav Gailit, Kadri Muischnek, and Kairit Sirts present a dataset measuring subjectivity in Estonian texts. Subjectivity, how much a text reflects opinion rather than fact, matters for media analysis and language technology, but resources for smaller languages are scarce. Their dataset is the first of its kind for Estonian at the document level.

It contains one thousand documents: three hundred journalistic articles and seven hundred selected web texts. Four annotators rated each document on a scale from fully objective to fully subjective. Agreement between annotators was moderate, with some texts scored at opposite ends of the scale; a subset of the divergent texts was re-annotated, which improved agreement. The dataset also includes scores from GPT-5, testing automated annotation. The model's scores resembled the humans' overall, but with differences, leading the authors to conclude that language model scoring is feasible yet not an interchangeable replacement for human annotation.
arxiv-2512-09834:
Michele Banfi, Paolo Zentilini, Sebastiano Corli, and Enrico Prati train a transformer to translate quantum circuits between gate sets. A quantum circuit is a sequence of operations on qubits, much like a low level program. Different hardware runs different native gates, so circuits written in a standard language must be transpiled for a specific machine. The authors treat that translation as a language task, the setting where transformers excel. Their model converts circuits in the qasm standard into the native gate set of IonQ trapped ion computers.

The team demonstrates faithful translation for circuits of up to five qubits, with nearly all target circuits coming out correct. They also prove a scaling result: in the worst case, the model's complexity grows only polynomially as circuits get deeper and longer. Learned tools may join the standard quantum software stack.
arxiv-2512-09934:
Joner Assolin, Diego Kreutz, and Leandro Bertholdo present IoTEdu, a platform for Internet of Things security on campus networks. University networks host growing fleets of smart devices, often with no unified rules for registering, monitoring, or responding when one misbehaves. IoTEdu combines three functions in one system: access control, incident detection, and automatic blocking of offending devices. The aim is to replace ad hoc manual handling with one standard process from registration through response.

The team evaluated the platform in a controlled environment with mock attacks. Once an incident was detected, blocking followed in under half a minute on average. The authors report less manual intervention, more consistent responses, and a single unified workflow where previously there were separate fragments. The work is short and hands-on, aimed at schools that lack their own security staff for their device fleets. It was accepted at a regional computing conference in 2025.
arxiv-2512-10034:
A team led by Salomé Guilbert presents DynaMate, an agent system that runs molecular dynamics simulations of proteins and their drug like partners by itself. Such simulations reveal how biomolecules move and bind, but setting them up is fiddly work. Parameter choices, input files, and software configuration form a real barrier. Language model agents have automated other scientific workflows, but not this one. DynaMate is a modular multi agent system that plans the study, runs the simulation, and analyzes results, with tools, web search, and literature answers built in.

It can also estimate binding free energies with a standard endpoint method. The team tested it on twelve benchmark systems of varying complexity. DynaMate completed full simulations reliably, caught and fixed runtime errors through iterative reasoning, and produced useful analyses of protein ligand interactions. The payoff is standard, scalable simulation pipelines.
arxiv-2512-10334:
Yi Liu and Yichi Zhang make synthetic training images to teach networks how to trace the cell's thinnest structures. Microtubules and actin filaments, the scaffolding of cells, must be segmented in microscopy images before anyone can measure them. Deep learning segments them well, but only with many pixel level labels, and labeling dense, hair thin filaments by hand is extremely slow. The authors' conditional generative system, built on the Pix2Pix image translation architecture, manufactures realistic microscopy images from simple binary masks, for which perfect labels are free. A new filament aware structural loss pushes the generator to respect the thin geometry.

Trained with this synthetic augmentation, segmentation models beat models trained without it in the authors' tests. The pipeline attacks the real bottleneck of biological image analysis, which is rarely the network architecture and almost always the labeled data.
arxiv-2512-10834:
Tiago Simões and co-authors explain why big brains run cool. Allometric laws, like Kleiber's law for metabolic rate, show living systems gaining efficiency with size, and brains follow a sublinear pattern: larger brains fire at disproportionately lower rates. The authors trace that economy to avalanches, cascades of neural activity that, at criticality, follow scale-free statistics, a regime many experiments place the cortex near.

From avalanche statistics alone they derive analytical scaling laws showing that any system ruled by critical avalanches must show sublinear activity-size relations. The prediction checks out in integrate-and-fire neuron networks tuned to criticality and in classic self-organised criticality models. So the effect is generic rather than a quirk of one model. The predicted exponents also match measurements across mammal species, connecting the dynamics of single cascades to the metabolism of whole brains.
arxiv-2512-11034:
Harry Shum and colleagues derive a new set of equations for simulating spacetime in gravity theories that add a scalar field to Einstein's theory. Numerical relativity codes evolve black holes and merging objects, but many popular formulations were built only for general relativity. Recent gauge ideas open a path to stable simulations beyond it.

The team adapts those ideas into a BSSN type formulation, a workhorse scheme used by many codes, for scalar tensor theories whose equations stay second order. Along the way they also produce modified versions of two related formulations, completing the links between them beyond Einstein's theory. They test the scheme on black hole systems and benchmark it against an existing modified formulation. The result lets established codes explore alternative gravity theories more easily.
arxiv-2512-11234:
Wentang Chen and fellow authors introduce RoomPilot, a system that generates indoor scenes a designer can in fact control. Such scenes feed games, architectural visualisation, and robot training, but current generators accept few input types or hide their process, blocking precise control over layout and meaning. RoomPilot accepts both written descriptions and CAD floor plans.

All inputs are translated into a purpose built indoor domain language, a structured and readable picture of the scene. Making then proceeds in stages from building to room to individual objects, keeping multi room layouts coherent and functional. A curated asset library with rich meaning based labels supports lifelike, steady results. Tests showed strong understanding of mixed inputs, fine grained control over generation, and better physical consistency and visual fidelity. The authors present the setup as a significant step toward controllable 3D interior synthesis.
arxiv-2512-11334:
Cong Yao, Chunye Gong, and Jin Zhang build a hybrid model for predicting energy losses in magnetic cores, a key inefficiency in power electronics. Accurate core loss estimates are essential for efficient converters, and a recent international challenge gathered data driven attempts on shared material data sets. Purely learned models fit well but generalise poorly and explain little.

Their SEPI TFPNet model pairs standard empirical formulas with deep learning. A spectral entropy mechanism first picks the empirical formula that best suits each excitation waveform. A data driven branch then extracts flux density patterns using convolutional layers, attention, and bidirectional memory networks. An adaptive fusion module merges the two views. Tested on the challenge data set spanning many magnetic materials, the hybrid beat twenty one challenge entries and three recent advanced methods, improving both hit rate and robustness.
arxiv-2512-11534:
Yiqing Yang and colleagues select the best frames from a long video for a given question, treating the choice as a set problem rather than a frame by frame vote. A subset's value depends on how its frames interact: individually top scoring frames may repeat each other and miss key moments. Earlier methods either scored frames independently, used fixed set criteria, or trained without a proper set quality objective.

Their framework trains end to end. A chain of thought prompt guides a small language model to extract task specific query vectors, which combine with visual features for dynamic scoring. A continuous objective rewards relevance, coverage, and low redundancy, and a differentiable sampling trick picks the final combination. A student teacher scheme aligns the small selector with a large multimodal reasoner. Across four major video benchmarks the method significantly outperformed existing approaches.
arxiv-2512-12234:
Hironori Yamaguchi and six co-authors report a lab test of the line between quantum and classical behavior in a 2025 paper. They built a three leg spin ladder in a radical manganese polymer, with spin values of 1/2 and 5/2. Spin ladders are chain like magnets used to study quantum effects.

The material showed an antiferromagnetic shift, and its magnetization curves matched classical mean field theory well. Yet computer simulations of its spin model predict strong quantum fluctuations. The real system instead showed near total suppression of quantum behavior. The authors say lattice shape may tune the balance, making the result a useful benchmark.
arxiv-2512-12534:
Qi Sun and five co-authors present Animus3D, a system that animates still 3D objects from text, in a 2025 paper. Given a static 3D asset and a prompt, it must invent a motion field that moves the object in line with the words. Older methods distill motion from text to video models with a standard score distillation loss, yielding tiny movements or jitter.

Their Motion Score Distillation uses a video model tuned with LoRA to define a still source, plus an inversion trick to keep looks intact. Added time and space regularizers cut shape distortions. A refinement module raises temporal resolution for fine detail. Tests showed much larger, cleaner motion than top baselines, with visual quality kept.
arxiv-2512-12734:
Zhan Wang, Yuxin Wang, Kun Jiang, Jiangping Hu, and Fu-Chun Zhang compute testable signatures of pairing symmetry in a nickelate superconductor in a 2025 paper. La3Ni2O7 is a high temperature superconductor in the Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate family, and its discovery opened new paths in the search for unconventional superconductivity. Which pairing symmetry its order takes, s plus minus or d wave, remains unresolved.

Using the known Fermi surface with phenomenological pairing functions from both classes, they compute observables that experiments can measure. Tunneling density of states, point contact spectroscopy, superfluid density, and Raman spectroscopy each behaves in a distinct way for the two cases. Those contrasts give labs a concrete route to pin down the pairing.
arxiv-2512-13534:
Marianne Rakic and co-authors introduce Pancakes, a framework for splitting medical images into labeled regions in more than one way. One brain scan can be split by tissue type, blood zones, broad anatomy, fine anatomy, or disease. Most models support only the one scheme they were trained on, or need hand prompts.

Given an image from a new domain, Pancakes builds multi-label maps for several plausible schemes on its own. It keeps the labels consistent in meaning across related images. In tests on seven held-out data sets, it beat current foundation models by a clear margin. The authors frame this as a new task those models cannot yet do.
arxiv-2512-13834:
Naman Balbir Singh Makkar presents VajraV1, a family of real-time object detectors built on the YOLO line. Real-time detection has advanced fast with YOLOv10 through YOLOv13 releases in 2024 and 2025. VajraV1 mixes design choices from those prior models with new architectural changes.

On the COCO validation set, VajraV1-Nano reached 44 point 3 percent mean average precision, beating YOLOv12-N by 3 point 7 points at competitive latency. VajraV1-Small reached 50 point 4 percent, VajraV1-Medium 52 point 7 percent, and VajraV1-Large 53 point 7 percent. VajraV1-Xlarge reached 56 point 2 percent, which the report says beats all existing real-time detectors. The technical report runs 20 pages with 7 figures and focuses on accuracy at real-time speed.
arxiv-2512-13934:
Aleksei Bykov and Ekaterina Sysoeva study the coupling matrix of a family of supersymmetric gauge theories. The theories are N=2 SU(N) gauge theories with 2N fundamental hypermultiplets, taken in a special vacuum. There, a residual Z_N symmetry restores a rich modular structure to the couplings.

Using symmetry and dimensional arguments, they build the general form of the coupling matrix. They identify a set of coupling constants equal in number to the floor of N over 2, in their most natural basis. In the massless theory, these transform independently under S-duality, and the bare coupling is a modular function of any of them. One constant stands out, ruling the asymptotic regime and instanton recursion, and keeps that role in the massive case.
arxiv-2512-14134:
Sungwoo Kang studies stock returns in Korea from 2020 to 2024 in a 2025 paper on the high volume return premium. Earlier work had found a puzzling low volume premium in Korea, which clashed with evidence from other markets that high trading volume predicts higher returns.

Kang shows the high volume effect was hidden by pooling unlike investor types and by scaling trading intensity the wrong way. When buying intensity is scaled by market value, the strongest institutional buying earns the highest later returns, while retail trades show a flat pattern. During the Donghak Ant Movement of 2020 and 2021, coordinated retail buyers briefly acted like liquidity providers instead.
arxiv-2512-14534:
Xavier Tolsa works on rectifiability, the question of whether a measure in space secretly concentrates along smooth, well-behaved surfaces. His tool is the Riesz transform, a singular integral whose good behavior often signals hidden geometric order.
