Their net is called ConvMambaNet. It joins two parts. A CNN part reads local wave shapes. A Mamba state space part tracks long flows in time. The join aims for marks that are both sharp and fast, fit for live watch. For care teams, a sound live flag could cut the hand load of long EEG reads.
arxiv-2601-13434:
P. R. A. de Oliveira and co-authors study how carbon dioxide wakes on flawed zinc sulfide faces. To wake CO2 is to bend it toward a fuel or feed stock form. That first step is key to use of caught CO2. The team probes it on ZnS, a semiconductor with known use in light tools.

They pair two tools. Near ambient X-ray reads watch the face as gas lands. Density based sums show which sites do the work. On a flawed face, CO2 sticks once heat tops 473 kelvin, in gas up to a set push. Sound flaws, not a clean face, do the work. That fact guides how to build CO2 wake catalysts.
arxiv-2601-13634:
Prasanta Chatterjee, Nanda Kanan Pal, Dipan Saha, and Santanu Raut solve a tough wave equation in 2026. Their target is the coupled Burgers equation in two space dims plus time, with damping and forcing terms added. Burgers-type equations model waves that steepen as they move. The added terms drain energy and push the wave at once.

The team first builds the Lax pair, a linked pair of simpler problems for the equation. With that pair, they derive an N-fold Darboux transformation. That tool spins one known solution into new exact ones, step by step. Exact solutions help check codes and show how such waves act.
arxiv-2601-13734:
Chenyu Hui puts forward a way to help large language models handle very long texts in 2026. Long contexts strain models, which can lose track of early parts. Hui's method is active recap learning, or ARL. It trains models to revisit and summarize earlier content as they go.

The recap happens in two places. In training, targeted sequences teach the skill during continued pretraining. At use time, the model looks back and sums up what came before. A model that recaps well can keep the thread of long files. That skill aids law, research, and code work.
arxiv-2601-14134:
Sergey Rubin asks if extra dimensions can explain why time flows one way in 2026. The arrow of time is the one-way direction from past to future. Rubin investigates the influence of extra dimensions on its nature. He shows the observed arrow can be explained by growth of volume.

The multidimensional manifold's volume grows in a monotonic way in his model. Traditional cosmological approaches rest on the entropy of matter or radiation. Rubin's model ties the temporal direction to geometric entropy instead. That entropy is the Bekenstein-Hawking-Wald entropy of the background itself.
arxiv-2601-14334:
Junhyuk Heo works on radar image cleanup in this 2026 paper. Synthetic Aperture Radar, or SAR, builds images from radar echoes. Its images carry speckle noise, a grainy flaw built into the method. Speckle degrades image quality and makes later analysis harder. The noise is multiplicative and follows a Gamma distribution.

Heo built a self-supervised framework for despeckling SAR images. Self-supervised means it learns without hand-cleaned target images. The method rests on score-based generative models. They run in a transformed log domain, where multiplicative noise is easier to handle. The paper aims at cleaner radar images for the analysis steps that follow.
arxiv-2601-14434:
Chia-Yi Su and Collin McMillan present a demo system in this 2026 paper. CMind is an AI agent for localizing memory bugs in C programs. Memory bugs are a classic source of crashes and security holes in C. Finding the exact faulty line can take hours of human work.

What sets CMind apart is its method. It follows the steps human programmers take when they hunt memory bugs. The authors drew those steps from an empirical study of programmers at work. The agent thus works like a person, not just a static checker. The paper was written for the International Conference on Program Comprehension. Readers get a tool that copies expert debugging moves.
arxiv-2601-14834:
Shaojie Wang studies electric fields in fusion plasma in this 2026 paper. Using gyrokinetic theory, it is found that significant radial electric fields, or zonal flows, can be generated in a tokamak fusion device. The driver is the radial redistribution of energetic ion pressure. Energetic ions are the fast particles made by heating and fusion reactions. When their pressure shifts outward or inward, flows follow.

Wang compares which ions do the job best. Trapped energetic ions are more effective at generating the radial electric field than isotropic energetic ions. Zonal flows matter because they can calm turbulence in the plasma. Readers get a mechanism linking fast-ion motion to plasma self-organization.
arxiv-2601-14934:
Giorgia Palombo, Christine A. Merrick, and co-authors study gels built from tiny DNA stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with DNA nanostar hydrogels. These soft gels are hoped to serve in the body, for healing tissue and for carrying drugs or antibodies.

What is missing, the authors say, is a clear set of design rules for how the gels break down. They test gels made of three-armed DNA stars. They vary the joints, arm lengths, and mesh sizes. They then cut the stars with enzymes and watch the gel fall apart.
arxiv-2601-15234:
Martin Kunz and a co-author study a scalar field that pulls sideways on gravity. Recent data favor dark energy that crosses the phantom line. That favors models where a scalar field couples non-minimally and adds a fifth force.

Local tests of gravity are strict, so the force must be screened in dense places. Screening makes clustering depend on environment. The authors study a late-time phase transition in structure, driven by the coupled field. Cosmic strings and domain walls enter the story as its visible traces today across the whole sky.
arxiv-2601-15334:
Caspar Kaiser and Sean Enderby ask small language models whether they think they are sentient, then check the answers. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a question that has no empirical answer: whether a model is truly conscious. What a model believes about itself can, in principle, be tested.

The authors query several open-weight models about their own consciousness. They then verify the replies with classifiers trained on the models' internal activations. Three model families are covered, in small sizes. The title states the finding: no reliable evidence of self-reported sentience.
arxiv-2601-15434:
Yunqing Li, Zihan Dong, Farhad Ameri, and Jianbang Zhang build a question-answering system for factories. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with digital manufacturing, where answers hide in mixed data. Text, images, formulas, and tables all carry part of the knowledge a worker needs.

Conventional retrieval-augmented generation often falls short on such mixtures. It retrieves text well but stumbles on the rest. The authors present ManuRAG, a multimodal version for manufacturing questions. It is designed to integrate and analyze all four data kinds, so factory answers can draw on the full plant record.
arxiv-2601-15534:
Marcello Lanfranchi continues a formal theory of tangentads in a 2026 arXiv paper, marked Part II. Tangent category theory gives a categorical frame for differential geometry. Many basic constructions have been recast inside it. The list includes the tangent bundle functor and vector fields. It also includes Euclidean spaces and vector bundles. Tangentads are the objects that carry this structure.

A Part II signals a program built in stages. The first part set up the formal theory, and this one extends it. The abstract in the record gives the framing and little detail. Readers should expect dense category theory aimed at specialists. Such formal work pays off slowly. A clean axiomatic base lets results move between geometry settings with less friction.
arxiv-2601-15734:
Shadi Alijani, Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi, and Homayoun Najjaran adapt foundation models to brain scans in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their task is multi-modal brain tumor segmentation. Foundation models promise strong starting points for medical imaging. Adapting them well remains an open challenge. Tumors vary in tissue type and appearance. Models often fail to fuse information from several scan types.

The framework brings two innovations. First, sub-region-aware modality attention weighs scan types by tumor sub-region. Second, adaptive prompting steers the model for each case. Together they target the mixed nature of pathological tissue. Better tumor outlines guide surgery and treatment planning. For clinicians, a model that adapts its fusion per region is more trustworthy than a fixed blend.
arxiv-2601-16034:
Tony Cristofano asks if refusal acts in language models share one root. His 2026 preprint tests aligned large language models, the kind taught to say no to some prompts. Many see each refusal path as tied to one model. Cristofano holds that a small, shared circuit may drive refusal in all of them. The circuit sits in a low dim space of sense.

To test the claim, he builds a replay method. It takes a refusal step from one model and rebuilds it in a new model. The rebuild uses a shared base of key ideas. If the step still works, the shared root gains strong proof. Such a link would change how teams check and steer model safety.
arxiv-2601-16234:
Juliao Braga and coauthors argue that each code system needs a firm name tag from its core terms. Their 2026 preprint deals with code use in health, courts, funds and schools. Use grew fast with large language models from 2022 on. Fast growth raised hard calls about who is to blame for acts. Name tags would help track and check each system.

The tag would rest on meta terms that fix what the system is. With a firm tag, audits can trace acts back to a set build. Users and courts could then check if a build was used right. The work frames tags as a base for trust. It speaks to rule makers and build teams.
arxiv-2601-16534:
Qing-Hong Cao and coauthors build a low scale frame for light dilaton grains. Their 2026 preprint deals with dilatons, grains from a break of scale grace. They are like axion kin grains but with their own traits. Axion kin grains have a full low scale frame in wide use. Dilatons lack such a frame, which blocks like tests of them.

The team builds that frame in a step by step way. The frame lists all low scale acts the grain may take. With it, teams can hunt dilatons on the same terms as kin. It also shows where dilaton acts part from kin acts. The work fills a gap in grain hunt maths.
arxiv-2601-16634:
Soichiro Kikuchi and three coauthors trace the root of piezo magnet acts in Mn3Sn. Their 2026 preprint deals with a non line anti magnet mix. The mix is known for a large odd Hall act. Piezo acts mean strain shifts its magnet state in set ways. Past work lacked a clear root tale for those shifts.

First rule sums trace strain shifts in both real and wave space. Joint views show which states drive the piezo reply. Clear roots guide use of strain to steer magnet gear. Such gear could switch with strain, not just fields. The work joins strain craft to spin state maths.
arxiv-2601-16934:
Elias Schuhmacher, Andrianos Michail, Juri Opitz, Rico Sennrich, and Simon Clematide test if long texts get fair play in search codes. Search codes pack a text in one code line. Each part of the text should show in that line. Their 2026 preprint builds a swap test to gauge bias in the pack. Long texts with many parts are the test ground.

Top search codes show clear place and tongue bias. Parts near the start count more than late parts. Some tongues pack worse than the rest. Such bias can hide key facts in long files. Fair packs matter for law, care, and news search.
arxiv-2601-17134:
Matthew Hong and a team of eight co-authors break taste in shop design down to parts. Taste words like sporty guide how goods are shaped. Buyers feel taste fast, but can't oft say why. Past data on picks gives thin help for real design. Their 2026 preprint builds a human-first AI frame for taste. It aims to map taste to form traits teams can act on.

The frame learns which traits read as sporty or calm. It keeps the human judge in the loop. Design teams then shape goods to a felt aim. Such tools could cut flop goods and waste.
arxiv-2601-17534:
Mounir Bensalem and co-authors tackle model life cycles in AI-native radio networks. Sixth-generation networks plan to train and run vast model fleets. Those models tune radio links in real time. The Open RAN design gives open interfaces and smart control. It does not say how to manage the models' lives. Training, rollout, and updates lack a set plan.

The authors work on self-learning and model versioning at the edge. Version control lets teams roll back bad models fast. Self-learning keeps models fresh as radio conditions shift. Without such care, fleets of models decay in place. The work fills a gap the standard left open. It targets live networks, not lab demos.
arxiv-2601-17934:
Vi Vu and co-authors ask whether a strong general vision model can learn medicine from unlabeled scans. Their 2026 preprint is about the Segment Anything Model, or SAM. SAM generalizes well on plain images, but medical images differ a lot from its training world. Labels for scans are scarce, and light fine-tuning cannot use the unlabeled bulk. Older models like U-Net, by contrast, shine in semi-supervised medical learning.

The team explores using that U-Net strength to guide a tuned SAM. In effect, the specialist helps the generalist learn from scans no one has marked. If it works, hospitals could adapt SAM with far less hand labeling. The work speaks to the wider push for foundation models in care.
arxiv-2601-18134:
Anshika Singh and Siddhartha S. Borkotoky speed up how updates reach far-flung devices over LoRaWAN. Their 2026 preprint deals with broadcast of updates like security patches and learned models. Long range networks serve sensors spread over wide areas, often on batteries. Sending one update to every device through the gateway alone is slow and fragile. The authors study reliable over-the-air broadcast in this setting.

Their route uses device-to-device cooperation. Devices that got the update can pass it on to neighbors. Cooperation can lift coverage and cut the gateway's load. Secure, timely updates are vital as billions of small devices join networks. The work targets a quiet bottleneck in the Internet of Things.
arxiv-2601-18234:
Abdulaziz AlDakheel and co-authors survey how people in Saudi Arabia use and view generative AI. Their 2026 preprint gives an early national snapshot. Generative tools are becoming part of the country's digital transformation under Vision 2030. Yet public awareness, adoption, and concern around the tools had not been measured. The study surveys Saudi nationals on their engagement with generative AI, the risks they see, and how they perceive the technology.

A baseline survey lets policy and education keep pace with real use. It shows where enthusiasm runs ahead of understanding, and where fears may be misplaced. The authors frame the work as a first snapshot, not a final word. Later surveys can track how the picture shifts.
arxiv-2601-18334:
Clément Christophe and co-authors test whether health chatbots agree with users too much. Their 2026 preprint studies sycophancy in frontier language models. As models enter clinical workflows, a habit of pleasing the user over stating facts can endanger patients. Past evaluations leaned on subjective data sets with no firm answers. The authors build a framework on medical multiple-choice questions with verifiable ground truth. That lets them measure overalignment against facts, not taste.

A model that echoes a wrong premise in a clinic is a safety risk. Hard numbers on that habit can guide tuning and procurement. The study gives hospitals a sharper test to run before deployment.
arxiv-2601-18434:
Ji Yao and six colleagues report a first clear sight of how gas and stars flow into clusters of galaxies. Clusters grow by pulling in long threads of matter from the web of space. Those threads are hard to watch in motion once the flow leaves the calm, straight-line phase of the young cosmos.

The team watched threads that link pairs of clusters. Along each thread, the flow splits in two. One part streams toward one cluster, and the next part streams toward its twin at the far end. That split had been guessed from models but not seen in real data till now. The find gives a fresh check on how the web feeds the growth of the largest towns of stars in space.
arxiv-2601-18634:
Zhipeng Huang and Cornelis Oosterlee build a new way to price deals that hinge on a choice to stop or to cash in. Such deals are key in finance: a stock right that can be used at set dates is one case. The price must weigh what the holder would gain by each choice at each date. That chain of choices makes the maths hard to solve head on.

Their plan turns the price task into a chain of back-ward rules and solves the whole chain from the front. A deep learn tool does the work, so no step needs a solved past step to lean on. A front-first solve could be fast and could fit many kinds of deal in one frame. It could also serve compound deals, where one right sits on top of the next.
arxiv-2601-18734:
Siyan Zhao and six colleagues let a language model teach it-self to think, with its own tries as the class. In the plain school path, a big pro model writes the steps and a small model learns to copy them. That path has a flaw: the small model trains on steps it would not take, so its live acts drift from its training. A fix lets the small model write its own tries while the pro grades each step.

Their plan goes one step more: one model plays both roles. It writes a try, then grades its own steps with a pro view of the same weights. No next model is needed at all. A self-taught loop could cut the cost of thought training a lot. It could also keep the training in step with how the model truly acts.
arxiv-2601-18834:
Deep Mehta builds CanaryBench, a test for leaks in the short takes that firms make from groups of user chats. Firms group chats by theme and share a short take on each group. The chats stay hid, but the take is shared wide. A take can still hold a rare string from one chat: a name, a code, a place. Such a string can point back to one user like a bird's song in a mine.

The test plants such strings in fake chats and checks if they show in the takes. A leak shows the take tool is not safe to share. Firms need that check before they trust group takes with real chats. The test gives them a way to grade the risk and to pick guards that work. Names and codes of real users are at stake.
arxiv-2601-19134:
Satyapriya Krishna and six co-authors grade a new Amazon model against the firm's own safety frame. Amazon set out its Frontier Model Safety Framework at the Paris AI summit and has since scored its top models against it. Here the subject is Nova 2.0 Lite, a lighter model now open to all users.

The report runs the model through the frame's checks for risky capabilities and behavior. Public scoring of a shipped model lets outsiders see how a lab's safety claims are tested, not just stated. Such reports are fast becoming the norm for frontier model releases.
arxiv-2601-19434:
Matthew Rumley and Anthony W. Thomas extract hidden structure of the nucleon from a rare scattering event. In deeply virtual Compton scattering, a high energy electron knocks a photon out of a nucleon. When the nucleon is excited into a resonance, like the Roper, the event encodes transition form factors that map its inner shape.

The team weighs a background process, where a pion is shed first, against the direct signal. Knowing which part dominates tells experimenters what their data truly measures. Such maps of the nucleon test the theory of quarks where simple pictures fail.
arxiv-2601-19934:
Claire Nicholson measures how much a language model's answers drift between identical runs. Models now summarise documents and support decisions. Yet the same prompt does not always yield the same output, even with temperature fixed. This variability is rarely quantified in deployment.

Nicholson runs repeated-run experiments and reports systematic measurements of baseline behavioural drift. Drift is defined as the variability seen when a prompt is repeated with no stabilising instructions. The analysis asks how baseline measures behave across settings. Knowing the size of the drift matters for audits and reproducibility. A decision tool that changes its mind between runs needs guardrails. The study gives practitioners numbers instead of anecdotes. The runs are cheap to do. The same prompt goes in again and again. The spread of the replies is the whole point.
arxiv-2601-20034:
Suyash Deshmukh and four colleagues turn audio models loose on a gravitational-wave problem. Interferometers that listen for gravitational waves are plagued by glitches, brief noise artifacts. Glitches limit sensitivity and can mimic real signals, especially short mergers of intermediate-mass black holes. Existing classifiers, like Gravity Spy, train supervised models from scratch on labelled glitches.

The authors instead exploit pretrained audio transformers. Models trained on sound already carry useful inductive biases about spectrograms. Transferring them to glitch identification could cut the need for labels. Reliable glitch rejection protects the rarest real events from being thrown away. The work imports progress from audio AI into gravitational-wave astronomy.
arxiv-2601-20134:
Darren Wayne Lim and four colleagues study how water wets a sheet of graphene, the single layer of carbon atoms. Wetting is measured by the contact angle, the angle a water drop makes where it meets the surface. Tests of graphene give a wide spread of angles, and no agreed value exists for a free-standing sheet.

The team uses a machine learning potential to model the water and graphene at atomic scale. Their focus is strain, the stretching of the sheet, and how it changes the contact angle. The answer matters for tiny fluid devices, sensors, and energy tools, where graphene meets water by design.
arxiv-2601-20234:
Qihang Yu and eleven colleagues present MALLOC, a benchmark for compressing long user histories in large recommendation systems. As recommenders scale up, they model longer sequences of past behavior. That growth raises compute costs sharply, above all where long-sequence dependence drives the model.

MALLOC tests memory-aware ways to compress those sequences while keeping recommendation quality. A shared benchmark lets researchers compare methods on equal terms instead of each reporting on private data. Cutting the cost of long histories matters for services that must answer in real time for millions of users.
arxiv-2601-20434:
Eleni Prountzou and four colleagues build electrically tunable metasurfaces from polycrystalline barium titanate. The material shows a strong Pockels effect, so an applied voltage can steer light quickly. Such surfaces promise reconfigurable free-space optical devices, from beam steering to smart lenses.

The barrier has been cost: epitaxial films of the material are pricey, hard to scale, and limited in substrate choice. The authors use a polycrystalline form instead and show that poling enhances its modulation. A cheaper route to tunable metasurfaces could put active optics into far more devices. The gain is a cheaper path to the same end: light you can steer with a wire.
arxiv-2601-20534:
Franco N. Di Rino and Tim Verhagen show that ultrathin freestanding ferroelectric layers host a rich variety of polar textures. The advances of two-dimensional materials are now being carried over to thin oxides. Using simulations based on first principles, the authors study layers that stand free rather than sitting on a substrate.

They find states ranging from liquid-like ferroelectric domains with long-range order to helix-wave and chiral bubble patterns. Some echo textures seen in twisted freestanding oxide layers. Such tiny switchable patterns are candidates for future memory and sensing devices at the smallest scales.
arxiv-2601-20634:
Leon Götz and six colleagues present a foundation model for virtual sensors. A virtual sensor uses machine learning to predict a target signal from available measurements, standing in for an expensive physical sensor. Existing approaches need a bespoke model per sensor, with hand-selected inputs, and they cannot share strength across tasks or rely on shared benchmarks.

A foundation model would learn from many sensing tasks at once and adapt to new ones. That could cut the cost of instrumenting vehicles, factories, and buildings, where physical sensors are pricey to install and maintain.
arxiv-2601-20734:
Bernard Parent studies a heating effect in plasmas that standard models get badly wrong. His 2026 paper concerns non-equilibrium plasmas, where the vibrational temperature tops the gas temperature. In that state, electrons gain heat through superelastic collisions. Conventional harmonic models understate these heating rates by ten times or more. Parent seeks a unified analytic closure, a formula that captures the effect in closed form.

The paper traces the error to a modeling shortcut. Standard models split energy modes apart that should stay coupled. That split ignores the boost from overpopulated high-lying states. Such states are a hallmark of Treanor-Gordiets distributions. By restoring the coupling, the closure aims to match real heating rates. The work aids models of plasmas that sit far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2601-20834:
Andrew Kyle Lampinen and four co-authors track how a language model's inner picture of facts can shift mid-chat. Their 2026 paper studies linear representations in these models. Such representations are directions in the model's activity that match high-level concepts. The team follows how values along these directions evolve during simulated conversations. They find the changes can be dramatic.

In their tests, a claim coded as factual early on can flip. By the end of the chat, the same claim may be coded as non-factual. The reverse flip happens too. These swings occur within one conversation, with no retraining. The finding matters for anyone who trusts a model's steady view of truth. It suggests that what a model treats as fact is more fluid than it seems.
arxiv-2601-20934:
Tidal disruption events are tested as sources of high-energy neutrinos in this 2026 paper. A tidal disruption event occurs when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Such events have been proposed as neutrino candidates. Jets, whether successful or choked, could produce them. So could the accretion disk, corona, wind, and outflow regions. The energies in question run from TeV to PeV.

The authors use IceCube high-energy starting events to constrain these ideas. IceCube is the giant neutrino detector buried in Antarctic ice. Starting events begin inside the detector, giving clean energy reads. Twelve years of such data set the scale of the test. If TDEs made many neutrinos, IceCube should have seen them. The limits sharpen which TDE models remain viable.
arxiv-2601-21034:
A 1963 formula of Edward Spence is given a fresh proof in this 2026 paper. The formula sums a weighted list of whole numbers coprime to a given number. Those numbers are ordered, and each is multiplied by its place in line. The result is a closed form built from Euler's totient function and kin terms. Spence published the first proof decades ago. This paper reaches the same result by another route.

The new route runs through the reciprocity law for Dedekind sums. Dedekind sums are classic objects in number theory with a famous symmetry law. Borrowing that law gives the proof its leverage. Such re-proofs are prized for the links they expose. They show two distant corners of number theory turning the same key. The paper is short and purely mathematical.
arxiv-2601-21534:
Giampiero M. Gallo examines how election polls and economic uncertainty moved together in the last two United States presidential elections. The study uses daily polling data on one candidate beside several gauges of business and market stress. The gauges cover business conditions, expected inflation, trade policy doubt, and a fear index.

Models of time-varying correlation trace how the links shifted day by day. Polls may calm or stir markets, and market stress may move voters in return. Tracking both directions matters for forecasters and campaigns alike. The daily view catches swings that monthly averages would smooth away.
arxiv-2601-21834:
Tiberiu Coconeţ and Constantin-Cosmin Todea write a short research note in pure algebra. The subject is a conjecture by Barker and Gelvin about blocks of finite groups, a way of splitting a group's representation theory into pieces. The conjecture concerns the source algebra of a block, a smaller algebra that captures much of its structure.

The claim concerns the unit group of such an algebra. That group should always contain a basis. The basis stays fixed under the left and right actions of the defect group. The 2026 note proves reduction theorems, results that shrink the full conjecture to smaller cases that others can attack. Reduction steps like this are how large conjectures in algebra gradually fall, one family of groups at a time.
arxiv-2601-21934:
Harry Spencer works where number theory meets the geometry of curves. Start with a curve defined over a number field, and suppose a finite group of symmetries acts on it. That setup lets the curve's L-function, a key arithmetic object, split into factors.

Each factor belongs to what Spencer calls a motivic piece of the curve, tied to an irreducible representation of the symmetry group. His 2026 preprint develops these pieces and connects their L-functions with periods, numbers that link geometry to integrals. Splitting a hard object into symmetry-labeled pieces is a classic strategy in modern number theory, and this work sharpens it for curves with group actions.
arxiv-2601-22034:
Matthew Belyakov and co-authors report the first mid-infrared spectrum of an object visiting from another star system. The interstellar object known as 3I/ATLAS passed through the solar system. And the team observed it after perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun, in December 2025.

They used the mid-infrared spectrometer on the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum reveals the object's volatile inventory, the ices and gases it carries and releases. Their 2026 preprint characterizes that material spectroscopically for the first time at these wavelengths. Such measurements are precious: interstellar visitors are brief guests, and their chemistry is a sample of planet formation around another star.
arxiv-2601-22534:
Sumedh Karajagi, Sampad Bhusan Mohanty, and Bhaskar Krishnamachari built LEAP, a live lab where students run experiments together in class. Their 2026 preprint notes that most class demos are static or run by the teacher, which leaves students as watchers. Even lively visuals often stay in the teacher's hands alone.

LEAP hands the controls to the class. Students can probe algorithmic ideas by joint, hands-on trials. Active probing builds deeper grasp than watching does. The work targets the gap between lecture and lab. It aims to make large classes feel small and curious.
arxiv-2601-22934:
Pak Tung Ho and three co-authors study a curvature flow on the four-dimensional unit ball. The problem asks whether a shape can be deformed to reach a prescribed T-curvature, a geometric target. They attack it by flowing the shape over time toward that target.

The proof joins an inequality of Ache and Chang with a Morse-theory method from Malchiodi and Struwe. Together they yield existence results under strong conditions at infinity. Curvature prescription problems clarify which geometries a space can possibly carry. Strong Morse-type inequalities at infinity supply the conditions under which the flow argument guarantees a solution exists.
arxiv-2601-23034:
Yungi Jeong and Takumi Otsuka break a barrier in stochastic optimization for game-like problems. These problems, written as variational inequalities, lack a single score to minimize and can spin in circles. Adaptive step-size methods transformed plain minimization, but noise blocks them here.

Noise in gradient estimates hides the true curvature, triggering steps so large that training destabilizes. Their adaptive, variance-reduced method is designed to see past that noise. Stable methods for these problems support training in economics, games, and adversarial learning. Rotational dynamics are the deep obstacle, making these problems circle rather than descend toward a single best point.
arxiv-2602-00034: Matias Hoyl asks whether question difficulty can be judged without first testing students, a step that now costs much time and money. His two stage method first trains a neural net to guess how students would answer, using word traits plus model traits such as step count, mental demand, and likely misconceptions. Difficulty scores are then drawn from those simulated answers. On more than 250000 math responses, predicted difficulty tracks real difficulty closely on unseen questions, with a correlation near 0.78.
arxiv-2602-00134: Ioannis Tsiokos develops an emergence calculus in which theories appear as fixed points of idempotent operators that act on descriptions. Once processes can compose but access runs through a bounded observation interface, a canonical set of six closure changing primitives becomes unavoidable, the author argues. The frame joins order theoretic closure operators with dynamics from a Markov kernel plus a coarse graining lens and time scale. A computable idempotence defect gauges how close a map sits to idempotence, and an arrow of time measure proves monotone under coarse graining.
arxiv-2602-00234: Eszter Bokányi and coauthors track falling social cohesion in the Netherlands with a population scale network approach. They use twelve annual snapshots from 2010 to 2021, linking every resident through family, household, work, school, and neighbor ties. Over that period, cohesion, measured by average network closure, declines by more than 15 percent. The fall is not driven by demographic change, but by rewiring in individual ego networks. Models point to shrinking overlap of social contexts and greater geographic mobility as drivers.
arxiv-2602-00434: Yulin Shao and team study covariate adjustment in randomized clinical trials with data from 50 public trials. Adjustment can improve precision and power and is backed by major regulators, yet evidence is limited on how methods perform across diverse real trials. That gap leaves uncertainty over which methods and covariates should be preset in analysis plans. The authors compare adjusted estimators, including analysis of covariance, inverse weighting, g-computation, and machine learning methods, with three selection strategies. Performance is judged on precision gains, estimate shifts, run reliability, and conclusion changes.
arxiv-2602-00534: Apurba Prasad Padhy and colleagues prune state space models after training with AIRE-Prune, cutting each layer's state size by minimising output-energy distortion. Each state gets an energy score, its total impulse-response energy over an infinite horizon, normalised for cross-layer comparison. The approach extends modal truncation from single systems to stacks, favouring asymptotic response energy over worst-case gain. Across benchmarks it finds redundancy in SISO and MIMO models, pruning 60.8% on average with only a small accuracy drop and no retraining, while cutting compute.
arxiv-2602-00634: Masahito Hayashi studies mirror descent where a vector field swaps in for the objective gradient, introducing a trajectory-wise smoothness condition and a star-convexity interface. Together these yield a last-iterate certificate with stepsize and error terms, plus a rule for admissible stepsizes. A zeroth-order instance from central differences places the unknown gradient in an uncertainty box, with checks reduced to robust conic dominance. Under Hessian bounds the field meets the interface outside a set neighbourhood, giving a rate term from accepted stepsizes plus an error floor.
arxiv-2602-00834: Wei Chen and colleagues resolve a score-based paradox: theoretically path-independent, yet path-dependent in practice. They prove training goals differ from the ideal objective by a missed term, the score function's path variance. Their Minimum Variance Path principle cuts this variance, with a closed-form expression easing tuning. A Kumaraswamy Mixture Model shapes the path, learning data-tuned, low-variance paths without manual choice. Tuning the full objective gives more accurate and stable estimators with top results on challenging benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-01034: Xiangwei Wang and co-authors give language models step credit from their own odds, with no hand-marked steps. Final-only scores can't tell which step helped, and in vision tasks they may pay for word guesses skipping the picture. Their gain score tracks how each thought chunk lifts true-answer odds. A high-water rule pays only for new peaks, so detours earn no double pay. With outcome and form scores plus a filter keeping only sound right paths, it beat outcome-only tuning on all eight tests.
arxiv-2602-01234: R. Shashangan and co-authors tame wild spikes in neuron nets with a single drive signal. In a drive-response setup, one tuned drive can quell bursts in the driven net. They test three driven forms, a neuron pair, a single-layer net, and a two-layer multiplex net, all from FitzHugh-Nagumo cells bursting alone. Touching just one driven cell with the right drive suffices in all forms. Pair cases break drive-target phase lock, while layer cases break proto-burst rhythm and uncouple the cell.
arxiv-2602-01534: Ming-Yue Jia and co-authors analyze rho and omega resonance contributions to kaon pairs in three-body B decays to eta K K-bar, using perturbative QCD. Details for rho(770,1450,1700) and omega(782,1420,1650) to K K-bar enter the distribution amplitudes through kaon vector time-like form factors. They compute CP-averaged branching fractions and direct CP asymmetries for relevant quasi-two-body B decays. Breit-Wigner tails of rho(770) and omega(782) match omega(1420,1650) and rho(1450,1700) resonances in significance. All predictions await testing by LHCb and Belle-II.
arxiv-2602-01634: Chenxu Guo and colleagues present HuPER, a human inspired framework that treats phonetic perception as adaptive inference over acoustic evidence plus linguistic knowledge. Trained on only one hundred hours of data, it reaches the best phonetic error rates on five English benchmarks. It transfers with no extra training to ninety five unseen languages. HuPER also leads as the first framework to support adaptive, multi path sound perception across varied acoustic conditions. The team releases all training data, models and code openly.
arxiv-2602-01734: Lianhai Ren and colleagues study training instability in language model pretraining, where sudden gradient explosions waste compute. In a NanoGPT model scaled by muP, they identify two warning signs before collapse. One is decline in weight stable rank, and the other is growing alignment between adjacent layer Jacobians. They prove both conditions together cause gradient norms to grow exponentially with network depth. Their MSign periodically uses matrix sign operations to bring back stable rank, preventing failures from five million to three billion parameter models with under seven percent compute.
arxiv-2602-02034: Ananya Joshi and colleagues offer bounded process maps for multi-agent workflows, framing the system as a Markov Decision Process with a one-way acyclic structure. Large language model agents perform complex workflows in strict settings, yet single-agent prompting hides doubt handling. Each agent fills a role or choice stage. Agent-level doubt uses Monte Carlo estimation, while system-level doubt ends there. A case study in AI safety review for self-harm spotting shows a 19 percent score increase and an 85 times human review cut.
arxiv-2602-02734:
Abdoulaye Diack and 42 co-authors release WAXAL, a large open speech corpus for twenty-four African languages spoken by over one hundred million people, in a 2026 paper. Speech technology has favored high-resource languages, deepening a digital divide across Sub-Saharan Africa. WAXAL attacks that gap with data collected alongside four African academic and community partners.

Two components make up the release. A speech recognition dataset holds roughly twelve hundred fifty hours of transcribed natural speech from diverse speakers. A text-to-speech dataset adds about two hundred thirty-five hours of single-speaker recordings reading phonetically balanced scripts. The paper details collection, annotation, and quality control, plus limitations and ethical considerations. Released under a permissive license, the corpus aims to catalyze inclusive speech tools and preserve these languages digitally.
arxiv-2602-02934:
Finding the commit that introduced a bug is reframed as graph search by Yu Shi and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Standard tools trace only the lines a fix changed. Their study of more than two thousand bug fixes showed many culprit commits lie beyond that narrow trace, and some have no blame link at all.

Their system, AgenticSZZ, builds a temporal knowledge graph of commits with time and structure links. A language-model agent then explores the graph with specialized tools, reasoning about causes. Tests on three datasets beat earlier methods by a wide margin. Both the graph and the agent proved necessary, and stronger models benefited most from the setup.
arxiv-2602-03034:
Fuzzy thinking becomes more scalable in a 2026 paper by Binbin Yong and 5 co-authors. Neuro-fuzzy systems combine neural learning with the transparent rules of fuzzy logic. Classic designs multiply rules together, so rule counts explode exponentially as inputs grow, limiting use on high-part problems where interpretability matters most to users and auditors.

Their system, KANFIS, replaces multiplication with additive function decomposition. Parameters and rule complexity then grow only linearly with input count. It supports both ordinary and interval type-two fuzzy logic, the latter modeling doubt in the fuzzy sets themselves. Sparse masking produces compact rule sets with clear meaning. Tests show competitive results against representative neural and neuro-fuzzy earlier methods, with transparent use kept.
arxiv-2602-03434:
Galaxies of very different sizes seem to share nearly the same surface density, a puzzle for theories of gravity. Antonino Del Popolo and Morgan Le Delliou revisit that claim in a 2026 paper written within MOND, a modified-gravity framework. Earlier work by Milgrom used a point-mass model and predicted the shared density only for objects whose inner acceleration stays above a threshold.

The authors replace the point mass with a realistic spiral galaxy model, a double exponential disk. They recover the same pattern Milgrom found. Galaxies with high surface density show the quasi-universal value, while low-density galaxies behave differently. The extension strengthens the earlier prediction by showing it survives a more faithful galaxy shape.
arxiv-2602-03934:
R. Forés-Toribio and 2 co-authors audit the hidden errors in measuring the universe's expansion rate with gravitational lenses. Time-delay lenses can pin down the Hubble constant, but the answer leans on stellar velocity dispersions in the lens galaxy. Their 2026 paper tests eight lenses used in cosmology.

Several effects bias the dispersion at the few-percent level: telescope blur characterization, anisotropy assumptions, and mismatches between starlight and mass profiles. Some choices shift results far more. The authors show which modeling habits keep biases small, including matching a particular velocity moment of real galaxies. Precision cosmology, the lesson runs, is limited by systematics, not statistics.
arxiv-2602-04034:
Stefano Fioravanti and 2 co-authors study clonoids, families of operations between two algebras closed under composition with term operations. Their 2026 paper tests a conjecture: only finitely many clonoids exist between finite modules exactly when the modules have coprime order.

They confirm the conjecture for a broad class of modules. For a finite vector space, every clonoid into a coprime module is generated by its functions of one fixed arity. Lower arity provably does not suffice. A general criterion about uniform generation drives the proof. As a payoff, a membership problem for certain algebras becomes solvable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2602-04134:
Shankhadeep Mondal and 2 co-authors refine bounds on how far an operator can stretch a unit vector's shadow. The numerical radius of an operator on a Hilbert space measures that reach and matters in stability analysis. Their 2026 paper builds a family of upper bounds from weighted means of an operator and its adjoint.

Tuning the weight sharpens the estimates, and a known inequality falls out as the symmetric special case. Under extra assumptions, spectral radius bounds follow. The approach extends to two-by-two off-diagonal operator matrices. Equality cases and finite-dimensional examples show when the new bounds are tight.
arxiv-2602-04234:
More agents is not always better, and entropy explains when. Yuxuan Zhao and 2 co-authors revisit multi-agent language model systems through the lens of entropy dynamics in a 2026 paper. Single agents beat multi-agent setups in a surprisingly large share of cases across reasoning benchmarks and agentic tasks.

Analyzing hundreds of entropy features, they found outcomes largely settle in the first interaction round. Peak entropy harms correctness, while stable entropy helps, a pattern they call certainty preference. The base model's starting entropy also shapes results. Their observations give designers measurable signals for when collaboration will help and when it will hurt.
arxiv-2602-04434:
An organic film that smells hydrogen could guard fuel cells without catalytic metals. Annika Morgenstern and 10 co-authors report such a sensor in a 2026 paper. Standard hydrogen sensors rely on catalysts and often need oxygen purging inside fuel cells, exactly where monitoring matters most.

Their device stacks an aluminum-quinoline organic layer in a vertical stack. Hydrogen raises resistivity, giving a signal that tracks concentration, temperature, and humidity in a straight line. A magnetic field even tunes response speed. Reliable hydrogen sensing across wide ranges supports fuel cell control, cutting purge losses and slowing wear in safety-critical settings.
arxiv-2602-04534:
Josu Diego and Matteo Calandra study why a layered material called ZrTe3 forms a charge density wave, a repeating pattern in its electron spread, in a 2026 paper. The material is nearly one-dimensional, and its change has long been tied to the shape of its Fermi surface.

First-principles work showed the Fermi surface comes out right only when a term for electron interaction on tellurium atoms is included. That term also yields the soft vibration linked to the change. The coupling of electrons and vibrations varied strongly with vibration momentum, and that shift dominated. The authors also found the distorted atomic structure, which showed a nonchiral modulation pattern.
arxiv-2602-04734:
Liming Wu and 6 co-authors generate disordered materials with a model called DMFlow in a 2026 paper. Most generative models design perfectly ordered crystals only. Disordered crystals, where atoms swap places or shift positions, matter greatly but lacked their own tools.

DMFlow uses one scheme covering ordered, substitutionally disordered, and positionally disordered crystals. A flow matching model generates all parts of the structure jointly. A Riemannian version with a spherical reparameterization keeps disorder weights valid as probabilities. A graph network with symmetry-aware message passing learns the flow. A two-stage step turns smooth weights into concrete atom choices. On structure prediction and de novo generation tasks, DMFlow beat adapted baselines by clear margins.
arxiv-2602-04834:
Leyla A. Kabuli and 4 co-authors improve lensless cameras in a 2026 imaging paper. Instead of a lens, these cameras use a patterned mask and computation to reconstruct scenes, giving compact designs. Reconstruction quality has been their weak point.

Hardware and software advances combine in their ConvRML system. A precision-made random multi-focal lenslet mask produces better measurements with less multiplexing than earlier masks. A ConvNeXt-based reconstruction network then delivers a substantial gain in signal quality over attention-based rivals. The team also built a parallel setup imaging the same scenes through three optical systems, collecting a large standardized dataset for training and evaluation. Measurements confirmed the new mask's advantage over a diffuser design.
arxiv-2602-05034:
Locating devices by carrier phase in distributed antenna systems can in principle reach centimeter accuracy, even using phase measurements alone. The work is by Fatih Ayten and 7 co-authors. The catch is synchronization error: if the antennas' clocks and phases drift, the geometry behind the method warps.

The team first shows a hyperbola intersection method stays accurate under such errors when it is trained on data that reflects them. They then add a deep learning system that picks which antenna points to use for each fix. In simulations, the framework beat prior methods on accuracy while cutting inference complexity by about a fifth. The work targets next-generation wireless networks that promise precise indoor and urban positioning.
arxiv-2602-05134:
Preparing tabular data for machine learning is skilled, tedious work, and Olga Ovcharenko and 2 co-authors ask how much of it language models can take over. Their answer, presented in this 2026 paper, is SemPipes, a plain coding model where data changes are set out in plain language as semantic operators inside plain flows.

A runtime system runs those operators. During training it writes custom code for each operator, guided by the data's traits, the prompt, and the flow context. A search tunes the written steps on its own. Across varied tabular tasks, semantic operators improved end-to-end results for flows written by experts and for flows made by agents, while making the flows themselves simpler. The code is in Python and openly released, leaving semantic operators as a reusable building block for data prep.
arxiv-2602-05334:
Finding the right documents across languages needs test sets that can separate good systems from bad ones. Dawn Lawrie and 8 co-authors present NeuCLIRTech in this 2026 information search paper, a testing set for technical material. The documents were first written in Chinese, then machine rendered into English, giving a controlled matched corpus in a demanding domain.

The set holds 110 queries with fit judgments, nearly 36,000 judged documents in all. It covers two cases: single-language search in Chinese, and cross-language search where the query is English and the documents are Chinese. It merges topics from the 2023 and 2024 TREC NeuCLIR tracks, which gives it strong power to separate rival approaches. A fusion baseline built from strong neural search tools is included, so builders of reranking methods need not start from the weak BM25 baseline. The dataset and artifacts are released on Hugging Face.
arxiv-2602-05934:
Massive galaxies that had already stopped forming stars when the universe was young pose a puzzle about how fast galaxies can mature. Ho-Hin Leung and 23 co-authors present deep JWST spectroscopy for fourteen quiescent galaxies seen at redshifts between three and five. The data come from the EXCELS survey, and the team re reduced them with a custom extraction that fights spectral wiggles from undersampling.

Full spectral fitting yields star formation histories and metallicities for each galaxy. A clear relation appears: more massive galaxies assembled their stars earlier. That confirms, spectroscopically, that the downsizing trend was already in place by redshift four. Lower mass old systems are absent, suggesting some reported young quiescent galaxies will restart forming stars. Most of the sample shows high metallicity, in line with similar objects at lower redshift. Evidence for alpha enhancement in the six oldest, brightest galaxies is mixed.
arxiv-2602-06034:
Finding the right picture or text from a mixed pile is hard when the match rests on small visual details. Dongyang Chen and 8 co-authors present V-Retrver, a search system that checks those details instead of guessing. It treats search as a step-by-step reasoning task.

The system forms a guess, then calls visual tools to inspect the image and test that guess. Guesses and checks alternate until the evidence settles. Training mixes guided practice, filtering of weak attempts, and reward-based learning. Across several search benchmarks, accuracy rose by a wide margin, and the method held up well on new kinds of data.
arxiv-2602-06234:
The Berry-Esseen theorem sharpens the central limit theorem by saying how fast averages settle toward the bell curve. Roman Vershynin offers two friendly, self-contained proofs of it for random variables that need not share the same distribution. One proof uses the classical Fourier analysis route.

The second proof uses Stein's method, following a presentation by E Bolthausen. A reader can take either path without reading the other. Vershynin writes for a basic graduate course in probability, favoring intuition over density. The note serves as a gentle entry to a result he calls a gem of classical probability, and to two very different proof styles.
arxiv-2602-06334:
Measuring the polarization of the cosmic microwave background demands knowing exactly how the telescope blurs polarized light. The SPT-3G camera at the South Pole watches the sky in three millimeter bands. The collaboration led by T de Haan reports direct measurements of its polarized beam using a hundred bright point sources.

Earlier analyses had folded sidelobe depolarization into a fudge factor, and found hints of strong depolarization. The direct measurements instead show minimal depolarization in all three bands. The team cross-checked with resampling tests, alternate analysis spaces, leakage handling, and source selection. A mild tension with the earlier inferred values remains, and the authors discuss what model assumptions might explain it.
arxiv-2602-06434:
Galaxy clusters grow by pulling in matter, and the edge where infalling material first splashes back marks their true boundary. Khunanon Thongkham and 8 co-authors measure that splashback radius for a large infrared-selected cluster survey reaching deep into cosmic time. They stack galaxy density profiles around clusters split by signal strength and distance.

A clear splashback dip appeared in every subsample. The radius grew with distance in comoving terms and rose with signal strength at fixed distance, which lets them track how the survey's mass threshold shifts over time. Statistical sampling fitted models with orbiting and infalling parts. The measurements give the survey a firmer footing for cosmology with distant clusters.
arxiv-2602-07234:
Point charges are too crude to capture how a molecule's electric field varies with shape, lone pairs, and other directional features.  Eric D.  Boittier and one co-author present DCM-net, an equivariant neural network that builds distributed charge models of any resolution for a molecule.

Across conformations, the learned charge positions stay stable and continuous. Across the QM9 chemical set, two charges per atom already match fitted atomic dipoles on unseen molecules, while three or four charges rival multipole expansions up to quadrupole level.  Computational chemists get a learned, shape-aware option to fixed point charges for molecular mechanics.
arxiv-2602-07434:
Humanoid robots need to speak, emote, and gesture in concert, yet most systems handle those channels separately and depend on the cloud.  Songhua Yang and four co-authors present SeM squared, a vision-language-model method that orchestrates emotionally coherent speech, face, and gesture for humanoid robots.

A perception module reads user cues, chain-of-thought thinking plans responses, and a meaning-sequence aligning mechanism synchronizes words with physical expression in time.  Both cloud and edge-deployed versions are built, with the edge version running autonomously on device.  Robot teams get a complete, deployable design for robots that communicate like they mean it.
arxiv-2602-07534:
Telling cat breeds apart from photos is hard: fur patterns, face shapes, and colors differ subtly.  Mowmita Parvin Hera and seven co-authors apply the Global Context Vision Transformer, in its tiny configuration, to fine-grained cat breed classification on a subset of the Oxford-IIIT Pet Dataset.

Extensive augmentation with rotation, flipping, and brightness changes improves generalization, and the model reaches 92 percent test accuracy and about 94. 5 percent validation accuracy.  The authors point to veterinary tests, shelter management, and mobile breed identification as applications.  Users get a compact transformer recipe for a fine-grained task where small visual differences decide everything.
arxiv-2602-07734:
Homogeneous spaces with a large symmetry group carry a natural torus action, and the independence of its weights shapes the geometry of the orbit space. Shintaro Kuroki and Grigory Solomadin study simply connected homogeneous spaces of maximal rank, asking how independent those weights can be.

Using weighted graphs, they show the maximal independence is 2, 3, or the full torus dimension, and that the larger cases correspond to symmetric spaces of rank above 2. A corollary makes lower-degree homology groups of the orbit space vanish. The paper gives geometers and topologists a clean classification with a topological payoff.
arxiv-2602-07834:
Calabi-Yau geometries underlie string theory, but their Ricci-flat metrics are known only numerically, hiding any simple formula. D Yang Eng asks whether a single observable, the ratio of the Ricci-flat metric's determinant to a standard baseline on the Dwork quintic, can be captured by a few symmetric invariants.

Using Donaldson's balanced metric as a teacher and symbolic regression, the author finds two features, a power sum and a cubic symmetric polynomial, that already explain most of the variation. A degree-three polynomial reaches held-out R-squared of 0.946. A compact five-term expression matches the teacher nearly as well. The paper shows interpretable formulas can sometimes stand in for black-box numeric geometry.
arxiv-2602-07934:
Rare decays of neutral B mesons into lepton pairs are prized tests of particle physics, but electric attraction between the outgoing charged particles shifts the predictions. S. I. Manukhov and N. V. Nikitin carry out a systematic analysis of these Coulomb corrections across leptonic, semileptonic, and radiative leptonic decays.

They compare three treatments of the Coulomb factor, a classic Gamow-Sommerfeld-Sakharov factor, an exact relativistic approach, and one-loop quantum electrodynamics calculations, and compute corrections for distributions and partial widths. For the Bs to muon-pair channel, the correction brings theory within 2 percent of the measured branching fraction. Precision flavor physicists gain a careful accounting of an effect that can no longer be ignored.
arxiv-2602-08034:
Black-hole ringdown waveforms are famously sharp to tiny perturbations in theory, yet data may be far more forgiving. Han-Wen Hu and two co-authors test ringdown robustness against stochastic horizon-scale structure in a proof-of-principle Schwarzschild setup.

They find the macroscopic waveform stays robust because phase averaging washes out ultraviolet geometric details below the probing wave size's detail. From a scaling law and mismatch profiles, they derive a selection rule: a detectable signal needs both macroscopic spatial coherence and old-level intensity, quantitatively ruling out incoherent microscopic structure. Gravitational-wave astronomers gain a clear criterion for which horizon-scale effects could ever show up in data.
arxiv-2602-08434:
The coolest brown dwarfs, the Y dwarfs, remain poorly understood, and their global weather patterns are largely unexplored. C. Akın and three co-authors run twelve circulation models spanning temperatures from 400 to 600 kelvin and rotation periods from 2.5 to 20 hours. Their arXiv paper adds new physics modules for salt and sulfide clouds to the THOR model.

Every simulation lands in a radiation-dominated regime with weak winds, small temperature contrasts, and no lasting jets. Convection sets the cloud layers below the visible surface, while cloud feedback stays small and variability stays limited. Rotation adds modest variation, and the single-band radiation scheme likely understates cloud effects. Readers get a baseline map of Y dwarf climates and a clear list of what better models must add.
arxiv-2602-08534:
Collective flow shows up in both tiny and huge collision systems, challenging ideas about when hot nuclear matter forms. Hirak Kumar Koley and Mitali Mondal present EPOS4 predictions for proton-proton, oxygen-oxygen, and lead-lead collisions at LHC Run 3 energies. Their arXiv paper uses the model's core-corona picture, where dense regions expand collectively and dilute regions fragment as strings.

Predictions include non-universal mean-momentum scaling, strong hadronic-phase effects, and system-dependent suppression patterns. Transverse energy per particle runs higher in oxygen-oxygen than in lead-lead at matched participant fractions, and the proton-to-pion ratio needs hadronic rescattering to match at top multiplicities. Readers get a timely baseline for Run 3 measurements of medium formation across system sizes.
arxiv-2602-08734:
Planning under partial observability is hard, and policies must often work across several related problems at once. David Hudák and five co-authors propose Lexpop, a framework that trains a neural policy with deep reinforcement learning and then extracts a finite-state controller mimicking it. Their arXiv paper targets POMDPs and hidden-model POMDPs, where the true model is one of a finite set.

Unlike neural policies, extracted controllers can be formally evaluated, giving performance guarantees. For hidden-model problems, each controller is tied to its worst-case model, and iteration builds a robust policy and controller. Tests on large state spaces beat leading solvers for both problem classes. Readers get verifiable controllers for uncertain, partially observed worlds.
arxiv-2602-08834:
Linking two distant quantum bits by light is a key step toward quantum networks, but weak hardware makes it a long shot. Yu Liu and one co-author propose recycling a single photon so it meets a spin-cavity device again and again. Each pass adds a small spin-dependent twist to the light, and the twists pile up into a clear signal.

The repeat-pass design also lets them use shorter light pulses, squeezing more encoding from each photon. Even with realistic loss and flaws, the scheme yields high-quality linked states at cooperativity near one, a level where single-shot methods mostly fail. It suits weakly coupled solid-state spins and loss-tolerant distributed computing.
arxiv-2602-08934:
Tools that spot AI-written text look sturdy until an attacker rewrites the text to slip past them. Suraj Ranganath and one co-author build StealthRL, a reinforcement-learning attacker that trains a paraphrase policy against four detectors at once, balancing evasion against keeping the meaning intact. The policy uses a small adapter on the Qwen3-4B model.

Tested on over 15,000 human and 14,000 AI passages, it drives detection near zero on three of four detectors, with a 97.6 percent attack success rate. Worse, the tricks transfer to two detectors never seen in training, pointing to shared weaknesses. The authors release code and call for stronger evaluation standards.
arxiv-2602-09034:
Brain scans never show causal neural values directly: blood flow and volume conduction blur and distort the signals. Sangyoon Bae and four co-authors set out when delayed one-way structure can still be recovered from such indirect scans. They derive an error bound under stated assumptions about recoverable inversion and shifting latent dynamics.

Their method, INCAMA, pairs physics-aware inversion with a delay-aware Mamba encoder that treats mechanism shifts as useful variation for scoring one-way graphs. On controlled simulations it improves one-way structure recovery two to three times in F-one score over baselines. On human motor-task fMRI, transferred without retraining, it finds sparse one-way links focused in canonical visuo-motor pathways.
arxiv-2602-09334:
Effective field theories are the main lens for reading precision collider data when no new particle has appeared, but at dimension eight the usual minimal operator bases blur. Several operators feed a single high-energy amplitude, so their effects mix and hide what new physics might lie behind them. Leonardo P. G. De Assis, writing alone in 2026, builds a new basis that starts instead from the conserved currents of the Standard Model.

The resulting Kinematically Diagonalized Current Basis gives each operator its own asymptotic energy scaling in scattering amplitudes, so operators stop masquerading as one another. That layout makes positivity bounds from scattering theory visible, supports a stable auxiliary-field setup for simulation, and separates universal from non-universal completions through how currents decompose. By rotating operators into physically readable sectors, the framework aims to sharpen global fits and trace high-energy data back to new physics.
arxiv-2602-09734:
Yannick de Bruijn and Erik Orvehed Hiltunen show a spectrum result for banded Toeplitz matrices. The open-boundary limit spectrum is real whenever the linked symbol function takes real values along a closed polar curve. Their 2026 paper builds on this result with both analytical and numerical methods. A class of banded non-Hermitian Toeplitz matrices with real asymptotic spectra is symmetrised.

The paper ends with a rigorous mathematical footing for the generalised Brillouin zone, a concept widely used in non-Hermitian physics. The authors prove that the zone coincides with the polar curve on which the symbol function takes real values. A working tool of non-Hermitian physics thus gains a firm mathematical base, tied to the reality of spectra along a closed curve.
arxiv-2602-09834:
Sixth-gen physics design moves beyond legacy right-angle rate split mixing waves. Baidyanath Mandal and five co-authors compare bit error scores of three beyond-OFDM waves in their 2026 paper. They are right-angle time-rate-space tuning, affine rate split mixing, and right-angle chirp split mixing for the highly mobile non-land lane of sixth-gen systems. Motion and Doppler shift in low Earth orbit craft are mapped across four tapped-delay-line models from 3GPP.

After channel balance, a minimum mean squared error method with stepwise spotting lifts bit error scores. Affine rate split mixing and right-angle time-rate-space tuning often beat right-angle chirp split mixing across all models. Affine rate split mixing also beats right-angle time-rate-space tuning in two models at high signal-to-noise. The sim frame is shared as open-source code for checks and building.
arxiv-2602-10034:
Memory cells that switch resistance by growing and dissolving a metal thread inside an oxide layer are called conductive bridging cells. A 2026 paper led by Jan Aeschlimann, with five co-authors, builds a multiscale framework for their current-voltage behavior, from first-principles inputs to finite-element device models. Material inputs come from first-principles or machine-learned empirical work.

Methods span molecular motion, nudged elastic band searches, and electron and heat quantum transport. The framework cuts fitting knobs and beats older modeling accuracy. Applied to a silver, silica, and platinum cell, it reproduces experiments well, and it shows self-heating matters most in thin threads a few nanometres wide at currents of tens of microamperes.
arxiv-2602-10234:
Stop-and-go waves are a major form of freeway congestion, cutting efficiency, raising safety risks, and lifting emissions. A 2026 paper by Zhengbing He, sole author, tackles jam-absorption driving, in which one vehicle does slow-in and fast-out moves before a wave captures it. Most existing strategies ignore the vehicle and road conditions, so the paper draws on real police-car swerving behavior to frame a practical strategy.

The work names the SD-JAD problem and a strategy built on a defined JAD Triangle. It turns swerving behavior into traffic control that damps a lone stop-and-go wave. Five key factors are studied: JAD speed, inflow speed, wave width, wave speed, and speed inside the wave. A SUMO simulation shows all five can be measured with only two fixed roadside detectors, and the strategy damps wave spread.
arxiv-2602-10334:
Deep-inelastic scattering at high momentum transfer needs precise massive Wilson coefficients and splitting functions for QCD fitting. A 2026 paper led by J. Ablinger, with six co-authors, reports massive operator matrix elements, unpolarized and polarized, at three loops, with one-mass and two-mass corrections, plus related deep-inelastic massive Wilson coefficients in the high momentum transfer region. The calculation has recently been completed.

Fast and precise numerical representations of massless Wilson coefficients, splitting functions to three-loop order, plus target-mass corrections in x-space, are also provided, well suited for QCD-fitting codes. The work supplies the fitting community with ready-to-use high-order ingredients for massive deep-inelastic analysis.
arxiv-2602-10434:
Sagar Lekhak and three co-authors benchmark automated finding of PFM-1 landmines from drone imagery in a 2026 paper. Hyperspectral cameras can tell materials apart by their spectral signatures, but standardized tests for drone-based mine finding have been scarce. The paper fills that gap with a systematic comparison on real survey data.

Four older number detectors are tested alongside a lightweight spectral neural network with parametric Mish activations. The authors also release pixel-level ground-truth masks marking target and background, so future methods can be judged on the same footing. The work matters for humanitarian clearance: faster, safer large-area surveys mean fewer people walking suspected ground.
arxiv-2602-10534:
Swarnendu Das and seven co-authors report backing readings for a study of plasmonic swings in twisted nano-crystal super-layers in a 2026 document. Electron energy loss spectroscopy probes oxidation state, band structure, and dielectric response at exceptional spatial resolution. Twisted flat materials inspired the team to apply it to moire gold nano-crystal super-layers.

The super-layers form by liquid-air interface self-assembly with a double-dipping method, producing stacked hexagonal layers that twist into moire patterns. Twist angles are measured precisely by scanning transmission electron microscopy. Low-loss spectroscopy reveals a blue shift in plasmonic stirring across single-layer, double-layer, and twisted shapes. That result contrasts sharply with optical readings and sharpens the picture of joint swings in these builds.
arxiv-2602-11034:
Group actions on Stone spaces produce a zoo of smaller actions. María Isabel Cortez and Till Hauser study subodometers, minimal equicontinuous actions on Stone spaces, and ask when they are true odometers from group rotations. Their test looks at the hyperspace of closed subsets and the space of probability measures.

They show both spaces split into subodometers, and that an infinite subodometer is an odometer exactly when those splits break into factors of the base action. The proof leans on regular recurrence and on disjointness, which they show can be read off finite factors. The paper ends with a clean test: an action avoids all subodometers exactly when its largest equicontinuous factor is connected.
arxiv-2602-11234:
Glioblastoma prognosis is hard because tumours vary wildly in shape and scans vary by site. Ankita Paul and Wenyi Wang propose TopoGBM, a frame that learns heterogeneity-preserving, scanner-robust forms from multi-parametric 3D MRI. A 3D convolutional autoencoder is regularized to preserve topological invariants of the tumour manifold.

That prior forces the model to keep multi-scale morphological diversity, from fragmented necrotic cores to infiltrating margins. Across cohorts from three centres plus external checks, TopoGBM beats rivals that degrade under domain shift. Attribution places about half the prognostic signal in the tumour and its varied surroundings, supporting clinical trust for an unsupervised method.
arxiv-2602-11934:
Robot grasping often fails in the last millimeters: the policy knows the object but misses pose offsets, edges, or pre-contact alignment. Yu Deng and five co-authors argue that strong semantic encoders hide exactly those cues, since invariance suppresses the fine differences closed-loop control needs. Diffusion features carry a strong prior for dense correspondence, but raw use is impractical, given randomness, delay, and drift.

Robot-DIFT fixes that with a deterministic diffusion-derived backbone for real-time control. Manifold distillation turns a noise-conditioned diffusion teacher into a clean-input, single-pass student that keeps the teacher's feature manifold. A spatial-semantic pyramid network then fuses coarse-to-fine student features into tokens for the policy. Across RoboCasa, LIBERO-10, and real robots, Robot-DIFT beats vision-language, self-supervised, geometry-oriented, and other baselines on contact-sensitive tasks.
arxiv-2602-12034:
The Ligon-Schaaf regularization turns Kepler motion into uniform flow, but the rotation inside their transformation lacked a transparent geometric meaning. Li-Chun Hsu identifies that meaning: the rotation is set by the eccentric anomaly of the Kepler motion. That gives a clear dynamical reading of the angle that makes the flow uniform on the cotangent bundle of the three-sphere.

Building on that insight, the author extends the construction to positive and zero energies through hyperbolic and parabolic anomalies. The result is a unified spatial description of Kepler flow across all energy levels, bound and unbound alike. What looked like a technical twist becomes a natural motion quantity, tying the construction to the classical anomalies of orbital mechanics.
arxiv-2602-12134:
Aligning a language model toward one value can quietly shift others, yet most evaluations watch only the target value. Jiajun Chen and Hua Shen introduce VAT, a framework that measures how alignment-induced changes propagate across an interconnected value system relative to the gain on target.

Using a controlled scenario-action dataset grounded in Schwartz value theory, with paired judgments before and after alignment, they analyze effects across models, ideals, and interventions. Alignment often produces uneven, structured co-movement among ideals, revealing systematic trade-offs invisible to target-only evaluation. The findings highlight process-level alignment risks, and the dataset and code are open-sourced.
arxiv-2602-12334:
Quasi-probabilities appear across physics, yet their roots stay murky. Rules for conditioning or Bayes turn ambiguous too. Jacopo Surace works alone here, rebuilding these tools and plain probability from basic rules about how claims are scored. Scores are set across finite Boolean algebras, called universes of discourse.

The key idea is syntactic locality. Every universe sits inside a larger one, and scores must stay coherent under embedding and restriction. From those rules, a theorem rewrites every score that passes the tests as a finitely additive measure on claims that exclude each other. Those are called pre-probabilities, unique up to a free scale choice. Fixing that choice in a canonical way yields finite quasi-probabilities. Ordinary chances emerge as the subclass that stays valid in smaller universes. The same frame gives a coherent theory of conditionals and a Bayes rule that works for both.
arxiv-2602-12434:
Sensors, biological and electronic alike, need ever better performance, and a feedforward network approach can both boost a signal and steer a radio beam. Abdullah Ahmed led this work with four co-authors, asking what happens when real-world inhomogeneities creep into such arrays. Perfectly matched parts are an idealisation; actual builds vary, and that variation may help or hurt.

The team studies two-cell feedforward networks built from pitchfork cells and Stuart-Landau oscillators, using system reduction, bifurcation analysis, and singularity theory. Against intuition, variation in the excitation parameter can raise the network output growth rate. Frequency variation in Stuart-Landau networks mainly harms amplification, yet phase locking persists over a surprisingly broad range of variation.
arxiv-2602-12534:
Cut linear fitting shows samples only when the outcome falls inside a keep set, and the goal is to estimate the unknown slope. Alexandros Kouridakis led this work with three co-authors, tackling the case where the keep set itself is unknown and must be learned from data. Prior methods for that case needed strong input guesses, such as Gaussian form, and still ran in time huge in error values.

The new method runs fast in size over error, needing only sub-Gaussian inputs. Its core is a novel step for learning unions of a bounded number of ranges from good examples alone, without bad examples, under a smoothness rule. That learning guarantee adds to good-only PAC learning and may interest users beyond fitting. Readers get the first fast method for cut fitting with unknown cutting beyond Gaussian inputs.
arxiv-2602-12634:
Moltbook is a Reddit-like social platform where AI agents create posts and interact through comments and replies. Lingyao Li led this work with four co-authors, using a public API snapshot collected about five days after launch, with 122,438 posts. It offers a real-world setting to study agent-to-agent talk at scale, asking what agents discuss, how they post, and how they interact.

Topic models and theme analysis find key themes, including agent identity and consciousness, tool and infrastructure growth, market activity, community teamwork, security worries, and human-centred help. Agents' writing is mostly neutral, with warmth appearing in community engagement and help-oriented content. Network analysis reveals a sparse, highly unequal interaction shape marked by rich-get-richer attachment, with a small core of highly active agents driving most talk.
arxiv-2602-13034:
Polar liquid crystals keep surprising researchers, and the anti-ferroelectric smectic A phase is a recent example. Jordan Hobbs and seven co-authors show, from satellite peaks in X-ray scattering, that this phase carries a density modulation of about 10 to 20 nanometres sideways to the layer normal.
