They also report a previously unknown phase where anti-ferroelectric order survives into a tilted smectic phase, showing the underlying frustration is robust.

The modulations appear one-dimensional and parallel to the tilt plane. The new tilted phase responds to electric fields in a significantly different and complex way from other polar phases, since both tilt and polarisation direction can be modulated. For liquid crystal science, the findings add a new phase and a clearer structural picture of how frustration shapes polar order.
arxiv-2602-13334:
Vision transformers are too heavy for most edge devices, while sending everything to the cloud adds delay. This framework splits the job: a light generalist transformer runs on the edge device, and several medium expert transformers wait on a near-edge accelerator. A router reads the edge model's top predictions and, when confidence is low, hands the sample to the most relevant expert, whose training is progressively specialized on its subset.

On CIFAR-100 with a real edge and near-edge testbed, expert accuracy on target subsets rose 4.12 percent and overall accuracy rose 2.76 percent over static experts. Latency fell up to 45 percent against edge-only execution, and energy fell up to 46 percent against near-edge-only offload. Hao Liu leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13634:
Graph embedding by neighbor pooling powers graph neural networks and Weisfeiler-Lehman methods, but repeated pooling blurs node identities, a flaw called over-smoothing. This paper traces part of that flaw to two missed network traits: the spreads of nodes and of node degrees, which matter for rich representation. A new weighted spread-aware kernel embeds nodes while respecting those spread traits.

The method has three standout traits. It is the first to plainly include both traits, it requires no tuning, and it eases over-smoothing so Weisfeiler-Lehman methods preserve node distinctness and richness after many iterations. Tests show superior group finding via spectrum grouping over existing graph embedding methods, including deep learning methods, on standard benchmarks. Shuaibin Song leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13734:
The Cauchy transform integrates a function against a simple kernel, and its operator norm on a given domain measures how much it can amplify functions. This paper computes the exact L2 operator norm of the Cauchy transform on a circular annulus, the region between two concentric circles of radii r and R. Exploiting rotational symmetry and a Fourier mode decomposition reduces the problem to a one-dimensional weighted Hardy operator.

The resulting norm equals 2 divided by the square root of the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian on the annulus. That eigenvalue uses a Neumann condition on the inner boundary and a Dirichlet condition on the outer boundary. The extremizers, the functions attaining the norm, are explicitly described in terms of Bessel functions. David Kalaj is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-14334:
Olivier Mousis and four co-authors study a 2026 arXiv question about complex organic molecules around Jupiter. Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto may hide subsurface oceans, and complex organics are key to prebiotic chemistry, yet none have been detected on those moons. ESA's JUICE and NASA's Europa Clipper missions aim to close that gap.

The paper models formation and transport of complex organics in Jupiter's circumplanetary disk, the birthplace of the Galilean moons. A time-dependent model couples disk evolution with icy particles of varied sizes and release times, testing thermal processing of ices versus UV photochemistry. Heating, especially of ammonia-carbon dioxide ices, acts efficiently before much irradiation, making thermal processing the dominant pathway, with efficiencies governed by particle density, disk viscosity, and accretion rate.
arxiv-2602-14634:
Solvers for satisfiability modulo theories must rule out assignments that fail the theory. Emanuele Civini, with three co-authors, tackles the eager case, where all needed theory lemmas are built up front. Classic eager encodings cover few theories and often waste effort.

The team offers theory-agnostic enumeration methods, including divide and conquer, projected enumeration, and theory-driven splitting. All are highly parallel and cut needless lemmas. Tests show sharp gains in speed and scale over the AllSMT baseline. The methods suit hard tasks like unsat-core extraction and MaxSMT.
arxiv-2602-14834:
Pengcheng Pan, Yonekura Shogo, and Yasuo Kuniyosh show that scanpath metrics for hard-attention vision can be fooled by centre bias. On Gaze-CIFAR-10, a trivial centre-fixation baseline scores surprisingly well, nearing many learned policies, because object-centric datasets reward looking at the middle regardless of behaviour.

Debiasing that confound reveals a peripheral sweet spot for human-like scanpaths, where foveal patch size and peripheral context are swept under constrained vision. Genuine gaze alignment separates from mere central tendency only once the baseline is stripped out. Vision models gain a fairer test of how they actually look.
arxiv-2602-14934:
Richard Bergna and others give Gaussian Process Activations (GAPA), a late-check doubt gauge for ready-made nets that shifts Bayes work from weights to layer outputs. Strong doubt gauges often ask for re-training, Monte Carlo draws, or dear second-order sums, and may shift a locked core's answers.

GAPA swaps plain bends for Bayes bends whose mean match holds the old bend true, so core answers stay put by build, while closed-form doubt spreads in output space come free. Thin Bayes seed points scale the trick to new nets. Ready-made nets thus gain doubt scores with no re-training and no changed answers.
arxiv-2602-15234:
Zakaria and Ross develop a 3D motion framework for passive gliding and identify its global phase-space shapes. Building on prior two-dimensional gliding models, they show that 3D speed dynamics possess a pulling, curved invariant surface: the terminal velocity manifold. All paths collapse onto it, then drift toward a glide equilibrium. A separatrix surface of an unstable balance point splits starting settings into efficient shallow glides versus steep, drag-dominated descent.

Using lift-drag data from three airfoils, a snake-like bluff body, the Zimmerman planform of Draco lizards, and the NACA 0012, the team computes balance surfaces. Balance stability changes with both pitch and roll, not pitch alone. Divider shape determines reach of shallow glides. Bio-inspired airfoils show compact divider regions that make easy gliding robust across many jump settings. The work joins living and built gliders and establishes divider shape as a test for toughness.
arxiv-2602-15334:
Wang and colleagues find flow near shifts between a mixed Fermi fluid and metal in moire layers, at minus one half and three quarters. The QED-Chern-Simons setup: a part at a boson Laughlin point joins via force zones and Chern-Simons blend to a plain face. Tracing out stuff yields an Ioffe-Larkin rule for drag, with paths adding while Chern-Simons parts make side reply.

For the DC limit in the fan, the team builds a large-N spread where bits kinds and Chern-Simons steps grow. It cracks a Boltzmann rule at one over N. Gauge-sent hits kill the Drude spike, giving Sigma of omega over T. DC flows are about thirty-three and forty-seven thousandths e squared at minus one half and three quarters. The team spots a Chern-Simons trick muting Landau fading from the spin face to gauge mode.
arxiv-2602-15834:
Kaushik and Kaushik put together one system for surgical simulation, linking high-frequency haptic rendering with perceptual psychophysics and nonlinear dynamics. The surgical device meets soft tissue in a lifted state space with a Koopman operator form. That form allows linear prediction and control of dynamics nonlinear by nature. A Bayesian calibration module shapes force signals to fit each person's discrimination thresholds, using Weber-Fechner and Stevens scaling laws.

In simulated work like palpation, incision, and bone milling, the system keeps both latency and error low. Average rendering latency is 4 point 3 milliseconds, force error stays below 2 point 8 percent, and perceptual discrimination gains 20 percent. MANOVA and regression tests put it ahead of energy-based rendering methods and conventional spring-damper ones. To close, the authors discuss the impact on surgical training and virtual reality based medical education, and sketch later work on closed-loop neural feedback for haptic interfaces.
arxiv-2602-15934:
Maraboli and colleagues measure velocity anisotropy beta(r) for varied cluster member groups, from stacked phase space of nine massive clusters at intermediate redshifts. Clusters are the most round, virialised CLASH-VLT targets, from a large spectral database. Added MUSE data found an unprecedented member count, sharply lifting precision.

Members split four ways: red/blue, high/low-mass. Methods run in parallel: MAMPOSSt, parametric in beta(r), and Jeans inversion, non-parametric in beta(r). Both agree per group. Anisotropy grows from centre to virial radius: beta about 0 point 2 to 0 point 4 at centre, at least 0 point 8 at virial radius, similar across groups. Jeans inversion also shows a drop near 250 kpc from centre. Estimates use 72 MAMPOSSt and 18 Jeans combinations, a wide base for future cluster mass and cosmology work.
arxiv-2602-16034:
Xinrui He leads a team of eight researchers building a recommendation system that learns across different domains without pooling private data. Their framework, called FeDecider, joins large language models with federated cross-domain recommendation, where each domain trains locally and shares only model updates. Two snags motivate the design: local updates can vary in size and skew the shared model, and language models store knowledge implicitly, which makes cross-domain similarity hard to measure.

FeDecider splits each client low-rank update and shares only its directional part, curbing scale-driven noise. Each client then learns personal weights that blend updates from other domains in a data-aware way. Tests across varied data sets support the design, and the paper positions it as a privacy-preserving route to stronger cross-domain recommendations.
arxiv-2602-16234:
Thomas Schwarz and coauthors study games where players may not always access all their actions. In many practical settings, available actions are restricted by outside randomness, yet learning in games usually assumes full access. The authors introduce Games with Stochastic Action Sets, parametrized by a distribution over each player possible action subsets. Strategies and Nash equilibria in such games admit prohibitively large representations.

Assuming action availabilities are independent across players, they show that results in two-player zero-sum games can be approximately represented by a compact vector. Its size equals the action count, overcoming the naive exponential representation. They present an algorithm minimizing ranking regret that converges to equilibrium with high probability at a stated rate. Using its iterates, they develop a statistical approximation procedure to recover such outcomes. The work thus makes balance computation tractable where action sets fluctuate.
arxiv-2602-16634:
Yu Xie and a large team tackle rare-event sampling, the long-standing bottleneck in molecular dynamics, above all for biomolecules. Diffusion models such as BioEmu now draw free samples from tangled molecular distributions, cutting the cost of rare transitions. Yet a sampling snag stays when scores hinge on states that are rare at equilibrium, such as folding free energies.

The authors bring in enhanced diffusion sampling, which steers runs into rare zones while keeping thermodynamic scores unbiased. Careful steering builds biased sets, and exact reweighting restores equilibrium stats. Three codes embody it: UmbrellaDiff, MetaDiff, and ΔG-Diff. Tests on toy systems, protein folding maps, and folding free energies give fast, true scores within minutes to hours per system on graphics hardware.
arxiv-2602-16734:
Ariel Calver, Serena Pallan, Alice Park, and Jennifer Wilson analyze winning coalitions under Bloc voting when voter preferences are single-peaked. For small numbers of candidates and winners, they pin down conditions under which coalition members sit adjacently. They also study pairwise contests between winning and losing candidates.

The paper further tests when winning coalitions meet several proposed extensions of the Condorcet criterion to multiwinner voting. Monte Carlo simulations then probe how often such coalitions arise under varied assumptions about voter behavior. Social choice researchers get a precise account of Bloc voting structure in the single-peaked world, where ideology runs along a single axis.
arxiv-2602-17034:
Oluwayomi Akinfenwa, Niamh Cahill, and Catherine Hurley use time series measures to explore family planning survey data and model-based estimates. Reproductive health is signalled, in part, by family planning, which ranks as a worldwide development priority. Tracking progress becomes difficult where surveys leave gaps in data from country to country.

The United Nations Population Division tackles that challenge with the Family Planning Estimation Model. FPEM is a Bayesian hierarchical time series model that yields yearly estimates of modern contraceptive use and pools information across countries and regions. Using diagnostic indices for time series from the wdiexplorer R package, the paper checks the fit between model estimates and survey data, treating countries as nested within sub-regions. Plotting survey data alongside modelled trajectories and diagnostics lets readers judge model performance, revealing where trends match and where they diverge.
arxiv-2602-17134:
Hiromichi Kamata led a three-author team making interactive 3D segmentation fast enough for real editing work. Segmenting 3D Gaussian Splatting assets matters for film and game production, but current methods demand preset camera views, labeled data, or costly retraining, which kills low-latency use. The paper proposes B3-Seg, a Beta-Bernoulli Bayesian method that needs neither preset cameras nor training.

Segmentation becomes a sequence of Bayesian updates. The next view is chosen by analytic Expected Information Gain, a rule with provable guarantees. Greedy view choice approximates the optimal sampling policy within a known factor. Tests on several datasets matched high-cost supervised methods while finishing end-to-end segmentation within seconds. The result is practical, interactive 3D editing with proven information efficiency.
arxiv-2602-17434:
Eleftherios Vlahakis led a six-author team on multi-agent planning under Signal Temporal Logic. Planning under such logic is blocked by collaborative tasks. Their high dimensionality prevents scalable synthesis with satisfaction guarantees. The paper recasts planning as an optimization program under multi-agent logic constraints, with a penalty-based unconstrained relaxation solved by Block-Coordinate Gradient Descent, where each block holds one agent's decision variables, easing complexity.

A quadratic penalty built from smooth logic semantics lets the iterations converge to a stationary point of the penalized problem under standard regularity assumptions. To enforce feasibility, the solver sits inside a two-layer scheme. Inner updates run at a fixed penalty, which an outer loop then raises to steadily improve multi-agent robustness. The framework enables scalable computation and was validated on multi-robot planning scenarios, showing the approach can handle teams of agents under strict timing and logic constraints.
arxiv-2602-17634:
Xinghong Fu and team offer a lean recipe for time series foundation models that forecast with no task-specific training. Recent models in this line grew to hundreds of millions of parameters, strong yet costly to run. The authors show that large-scale transformers are not required for this job.

Small hybrid models that interleave long convolution and linear recurrent layers can match larger transformer models while running more than a hundred times smaller. Data augmentation and inference tricks push results further. The recipe yields Reverso, a family of efficient foundation models for zero-shot forecasting that shifts the performance-efficiency frontier. Practitioners gain strong forecasts at a fraction of the usual cost.
arxiv-2602-17734:
Raja Soundaramourty and team explain why T-shirt sizing systematically fails for AI projects. Agile sizing works well for standard software scoping, yet for AI initiatives, above all those with large language models and multi-agent systems, the results mislead. Five foundational assumptions that usually hold for traditional software tend to break in AI contexts.

The five are linear effort scaling, repeatability from prior experience, effort-duration fungibility, task decomposability, and deterministic completion criteria. AI development breaks them through non-linear performance jumps, complex interaction surfaces, and tight coupling where a small data change cascades through the whole stack. The authors propose Checkpoint Sizing: a human-centric, iterative approach with explicit decision gates where scope and feasibility are reassessed from what development reveals, not what planning assumed.
arxiv-2602-17834:
Duncan Adamson and team start the orderly study of spread sub-hypergraph listing in hypergraphs. Subgraph finding and listing have become central problems in spread graph methods, prized for theory challenge and real-world use. Hypergraphs generalize graphs, and this paper extends the listing program to them.

The authors introduce several compute models for hypergraphs that extend the CONGEST model for graphs, and they weigh the side-by-side power of those models. They devise methods for spread triangle and simplex listing, proving best results in two models via matching lower bounds. They introduce sparse and all-over sparse hypergraph classes with fast listing methods for those classes. General tricks for designing fast methods in hypergraph models round out a basic study.
arxiv-2602-18034:
Mohammed Barhoush and team settle a long-open question about classical checks of quantum computation. Mahadev gave the first such check under the Learning-with-Errors assumption, using four interactive messages. Whether fewer messages work in the plain model remained open.

The authors prove that no quantum black-box reduction can carry non-interactive classical verification of QMA to any falsifiable assumption. Non-interactive here means a single message after a setup that ignores the instance. The result matters greatly because almost all standard cryptographic assumptions are falsifiable, including Learning-with-Errors. The result rests on a QMA-QCMA gap problem, slightly stronger than QMA apart from QCMA. The authors support that claim with a construction using a quantum unitary oracle.
arxiv-2602-18534:
Hanliang Zhang and seven co-authors validate code translation for projects using external libraries. Their 2026 paper notes language models show promise for translating programs, particularly moving systems code to safe languages such as Rust. Existing approaches struggle when programs depend on external libraries: models invent fake target APIs and fail to generate needed imports, while checking equivalence is hard when code manipulates opaque library types.

The team presents a framework translating Go projects with external dependencies into Rust. It combines retrieval mapping Go APIs to Rust APIs with cross-language validation. That validation makes languages work together for opaque types by building adapters solely from public APIs, before checking I/O equivalence. Evaluation on six real-world Go repositories with heavy dependencies lifts both compilation and equivalence rates, up to one hundred percent in the heaviest case, about twice on average.
arxiv-2602-18634:
Tan Bui-Thanh and two co-authors derive Hermite quadrature errors simply. Their 2026 paper generalizes two-point interpolatory Hermite quadrature for functions with available values and first n-minus-one derivatives at both ends. Armed with reverse integration by parts, they give a simple derivation of an exact error representation for Hermite quadrature.

The approach needs only integration by parts, and its error representation needs milder regularity. Existence of an nth-order derivative suffices rather than a two-nth-order one, so the formula holds for less regular functions where classical ones fail. The approach rediscovers Legendre polynomials as error kernels for interpolatory Hermite quadrature rules, with a surprisingly elegant link between Legendre polynomials and Hermite interpolation, and rediscovers the Rodrigues formula. A second proof uses the Peano kernel theorem, and a composite rule serves practical uses.
arxiv-2602-18834:
In blockchain apps, a confirmation click is usually treated as mere friction to remove. Eason Chen, with five co-authors, tests in 2026 whether that click actually helps people decide better. The test uses a blockchain Connect Four game with two modes. One mode requires a manual wallet click. The other auto-authorises by delegation.

Participants preferred the frictionless mode and felt they performed better. Yet objective scores were worse without the click in the counterbalanced test. Win rate and move quality both fell. Cancelled submissions suggest the click lets players correct themselves before committing. The finding reframes confirmation as a cognitive checkpoint, not just friction, in irreversible interactions. The test is small but clear. A pause can beat speed when a move cannot be undone.
arxiv-2602-19034:
In d-wave altermagnets, spin current from a temperature gradient is known as the spin-Nernst effect. Motohiko Ezawa, writing alone in 2026, extends that picture to other wave symmetries, deriving analytic formulas for spin currents in f-wave, g-wave, i-wave, and p-wave magnets.

In f-wave magnets, a spin current arises with size proportional to the temperature gradient squared. It is called the nonlinear spin-Seebeck current, usable as a spin current diode. In g-wave altermagnets, a spin current arises at third order in the temperature gradient. In i-wave altermagnets, a spin current flows perpendicular to the temperature gradient, the spin-Nernst current. These phenomena occur without spin-orbit interaction. In p-wave magnets, spin current is not generated by a temperature gradient at all.
arxiv-2602-19334:
A wheeled robot steered by forward and turning speeds cannot simply be parked with a fixed rule, since its motion is constrained. Alexander Zuyev and two co-authors study time-varying feedback controllers for such a nonholonomic mobile robot, built earlier with gradient flow approximation methods. The present paper puts those rules on a TurtleBot3 Burger robot, using oscillating input signals to steady it.

The experiments show that the target spot can be held with workable settings. The paper also checks whether the gradient flow is admissible, a step that backs building a Lyapunov function candidate for the stability case. Readers get test backing for a control design that handles a classic constraint of wheeled robots.
arxiv-2602-19934:
Student-teacher games model a restricted student trying to produce a string with a property that can be refuted. An all-powerful teacher refutes wrong candidates with counterexamples. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ondřej Ježil and Dimitrios Tsintsilidas introduces subclasses of total search problems sorted by rounds and answers per round.

By a classical result, such games capture how certain formulas are witnessed in bounded arithmetic. Assuming the polynomial hierarchy does not collapse, the authors separate the new classes for different round and query counts. Applications include a general witnessing theorem for theories built on fine-grained induction and collection principles. They also include separations of those theories, resolutions of two open problems in bounded arithmetic, and extensions of results showing certain circuit bounds cannot be proved in stronger theories.
arxiv-2602-20134:
Epidemic models lean on crowdsourced, self-reported behaviour. Vaccination status, mask use, and social distancing adherence all come from people reporting on themselves. That data is not passively sampled. People report on purpose. Some seek to avoid penalties. Others seek benefits. Others express distrust in public health authorities. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yiqi Su and five co-authors treats that strategic reporting as a signal game.

People as senders choose how to report. The public health authority as receiver updates its outbreak models from possibly skewed signals. It adjusts its trust in incoming reports in turn. The framework supplies a working model of corrupted reports and a method for pulling reliable signal from it. Focusing on lies around masking and vaccination, the authors describe game balances with maths, showing how strategic reporting distorts outbreak estimates and how a receiver can correct for it.
arxiv-2602-20334:
Chengjie Lu and seven co-authors propose UAMTERS, a mutation analysis method for deep-learning robot software that accounts for uncertainty. Robots that adapt on their own use deep-learning parts for perception, decisions, and control in changing settings. Yet the unknown in those parts makes trust hard to ensure, and classic mutation analysis does not account for it. UAMTERS injects random variation into robot software through mutation operators that add that unknown.

The method also adds mutation scores that measure how well a test suite detects failures at varied levels of the unknown. Across three robotic case studies, UAMTERS told good test suites from weak ones and caught failures caused by the unknown itself. The result gives robot teams a way to judge test suites under the uncertain conditions their systems face. It moves mutation testing from fixed software toward the random reality of learning-enabled robots.
arxiv-2602-20434:
High local maxima of smooth Gaussian fields form a point process whose extreme-level behavior is a classic question. Dmitry Beliaev and Akshay Hegde show that, rescaled appropriately, this process converges weakly to a Poisson point process as the level grows. The proof leans on the classical fact that simple point processes are characterized by avoidance probabilities, approximated with well-studied excursion probabilities.

A second result quantifies the convergence for the Bargmann-Fock field in two dimensions. The total variation distance between a Poisson variable and the count of high maxima in a square box decays exponentially in the squared level. From this follows a quantitative central limit theorem when the level grows more slowly than the square root of log box size. The proof uses the Chen-Stein method, plus a close coupling of a stationary field with its Palm version that may interest readers on its own.
arxiv-2602-20734:
Shingo Akama and Chunshan Lin show that quantum linking between primordial gravitons in split gravity sectors can boost the tensor power range during inflation. Unlike standard mechanisms relying on classical motion or changed actions, this boost comes from the reduced density matrix of the seen sector after tracing over a hidden store.

The system allows a sizable tensor-to-scalar ratio above one hundredth with sub-Planckian inflaton trips, giving a purely quantum escape from the Lyth bound. The resulting mixed state leaves a special quantum mark. It shows wavy marks in the power range and a typical break of the single-field rule, seen as a scale-tied boost of the squeezed-limit signal. The authors further predict that this linking may appear as late-time random noise boost in gravity wave meters, opening a novel window into the quantum nature of spacetime.
arxiv-2602-21034:
Crystals break the smooth symmetries of space but keep a discrete set of symmetry moves, and those moves bound every real trait. Jakub Zelezny presents Symmetr in this 2026 arXiv paper, a Python tool that works out the symmetry-bound forms of tensors for crystal traits, with a focus on magnets. Response tensors are the main focus, though rest-state traits and magnet links are also covered.

Symmetry can be told with usual magnet space groups or with spin groups for the slow-motion limit. Extra tools handle values cast onto one site and series in the magnet order dial. The code runs from the command line or through a Python link, giving solid-state workers a direct route from symmetry to allowed trait forms.
arxiv-2602-21134:
Living and synthetic active systems carry inertia, from animals and robots to colloidal swimmers, and many use restart protocols to steer exploration. Manish Patel and Amir Shee study how inertia shapes reset-controlled active motion in this 2026 arXiv paper, for an inertial active Brownian particle in two dimensions under complete and partial resetting.

Exact stationary moments and full transient solutions show inertia strongly enhances localization: at high reset rates, mean-squared displacement decays as the inverse cube of the reset rate, not the inverse. Kurtosis maps reveal strongly non-Gaussian statistics with re-entrant behavior. Resetting velocity with position localizes most, while orientation resets push velocity toward opposite limits, giving three coupled control knobs.
arxiv-2602-21234:
Edge rules shape the eigen-numbers of slope tools, and standard forms make them tractable. Yorick Hardy and Bertin Zinsou derive such forms in this 2026 arXiv paper for self-adjoint odd-order tools with eigen-number-dial-tied edge rules. A 2024 paper had settled the even-order case; this work finishes the left odd-order case.

Standard forms matter for studying eigen-numbers and for number-based uses of edge value problems. Readers get the odd-order twin to the even-order result, closing a gap in the theory. The paper is on purpose narrow: one missing case, handled in full, for tools whose edge rules on their own hinge on the eigen-number.
arxiv-2602-21334:
Satellite meet-up must cope with shaky state readings and slow onboard chips. Oscar Jed Chuy, Matthew Hale, Vignesh Sivaramakrishnan, Sean Phillips, and Ricardo Sanfelice solve it with hybrid feedback tuning in this 2026 arXiv paper. The method reads outputs, feeds them into a tuning method in the loop, and steps toward best inputs, rather than planning all open-loop.

Motion follows the barely stable Clohessy-Wiltshire rules, steadied by a limit-steadying steerer, with discrete-time gradient descent working out inputs in the loop. The hybrid system proves well-posed with complete, non-Zeno answers closing in fast to a ball around the meet-up point, its radius bounded by system dials. Runs cut shake sizes by about ninety-eight percent.
arxiv-2602-21534:
Xiaoxuan Wang and 13 co-authors present ARLArena, a unified testbed for stable agentic reinforcement learning. Agentic reinforcement learning trains agents for complex, multi-step interactive tasks and has gained fast attention. But it remains highly unstable, often collapsing during training, which limits scale to larger environments and longer horizons.

ARLArena first builds a clean, standard testbed, then splits policy gradient into four core parts, assessing each part's performance and stable training. That fine-grained analysis yields a unified view of agentic reinforcement learning and a new method, SAMPO, a stable agentic policy tuning method designed to mitigate dominant collapse sources. In tests, SAMPO trains consistently stably with strong performance across diverse agentic tasks, offering practical guidance for repeatable agent training pipelines.
arxiv-2602-21734:
Trial builds matter for machine learning solutions, yet current tools give limited support for collaboration and reuse of knowledge among stakeholders. Selin Coban and two co-authors present Proto-ML, an integrated development environment built to strengthen trial-build workflows. It tackles weak stakeholder involvement, limited cross-project knowledge reuse, and fragmented tool support, offering one framework for structured records of trial builds and sharing across projects.

The IDE holds three add-on bundles covering prototype building, analysis, and knowledge handling, supporting tasks from judging prototype quality against set rules to bringing partner views in throughout the build. Early user feedback suggests Proto-ML can raise trial-build efficiency and foster more open, reused machine learning development.
arxiv-2602-21834:
Mrinal Thapa and one co-author present the setup and build of a triples fix scheme for the relativistic coupled-cluster method for ionization energy. Both full and partial triples fix schemes are built using the exact two-component atomic mean-field Hamiltonian with Cholesky splitting of two-electron integrals and a frozen natural spinor cut scheme to trim cost.

Benchmarks on halide anions, noble gas atoms, hydrogen halides, and dihalogen molecules show triple excitations are key for exact ionization energies. They cut mean absolute errors to small fractions of an electronvolt versus reference and lab values. The X2CAMF shortcut matches four-component Dirac-Coulomb results with tiny gaps, while the Cholesky-frozen-natural-spinor plan cuts wall time. The partial triples fix scheme scales as non-iterative order n to the seventh with storage like CCSD, offering a practical route for relativistic ionization math in heavy-element systems.
arxiv-2602-21934:
Z. Z. Alisultanov and A. V. Kavokin predict a new kind of electrical wobble in ballistic graphene cut into a ring. Using a standard model of electron flow through contacts, they work out the local Hall and Nernst signals in weak magnetic fields. Both signals swing up and down as the field strength and the probe positions change.

The swings come from skipping electron paths that link the contacts around the ring, with peaks when the contact spacing times the ring radius lines up with whole numbers of cyclotron diameters. Unlike familiar quantum oscillations, the effect survives at room temperature and can dominate local heat-electric signals. The authors point to uses in electron flow studies, phase-coherent devices, terahertz sensors, and heat control.
arxiv-2602-22034:
Pulses whose pitch slides steadily, called chirped pulses, behave in subtle ways when they scatter through messy, lossy media. Isabella L. Giovannelli and two co-authors link that behavior to complex time delay, a generalized form of the Wigner-Smith delay for waves. They treat both transmitted and reflected pulses in reverberant systems that are linear, dispersive, and non-Hermitian.

Theory and experiment agree: the pulse's time shift draws on both parts of the complex delay, while its center frequency shift tracks the imaginary part alone. With that link in hand, the authors tune pulse travel so the time shift nearly vanishes across a wide band of center frequencies. The work widens the practical use of complex time delay as a design tool.
arxiv-2602-22734:
Muzi Tao and four co-authors show that caption models leave fingerprints, while image models wash them out. Given a caption or its image, the team trained networks to guess which caption model produced it. Text classification hit nearly one hundred percent accuracy, proof that captioners embed distinct stylistic signatures.

The same signatures largely vanished in generated pictures, with image-based guessing falling to at most half correct even for the leading Flux model. Generated images failed to carry caption variations in detail level, colour and texture emphasis, and object layout. The classification framework thus measures both captioner style and how faithfully text-to-image systems follow prompts.
arxiv-2602-23134:
Michele Dolce and one co-author study viscous vortex crystals. The pair looks at how a flat, squeeze-free fluid governed by the Navier-Stokes equations evolves when it begins as a set of Dirac point masses spinning in step. The starting pattern is a vortex crystal shaped as a ring of vortices, sometimes with one more vortex at its centre.

Using the pattern's built-in balance and steadiness, they track and bound the flow over time scales shorter than diffusion would suggest, before the swirls are expected to join. The work pins down how long the crystal pattern persists before merging takes over.
arxiv-2602-23834:
Xuhui Dou and two co-authors study continual learning for software vulnerability prediction, where detectors must keep working as code and flaws evolve over time. The 2026 paper argues that random train-test splits flatter such models, since real deployment faces future flaws under temporal drift.

The team fine-tunes a small decoder language model on a CVE-linked set spanning several years, split into two-month windows, and compares eight continual strategies. Their method, Hybrid-CASR, replays past samples chosen for uncertainty while keeping vulnerable and fixed functions balanced. On forward tests it beats window-only training with a statistically significant gain and stronger retention of old windows, while cutting training time per window. Cumulative training gains little more at far higher cost, so selective balanced replay offers the better trade-off.
arxiv-2602-24034:
Francisco Araújo continues his generalization of Sarnak's program to Erdős sieves in part two, turning from topological dynamics to measure systems and applications. The 2026 solo paper associates two measure-theoretic dynamical systems to each sieve. One system is the orbit closure of the R-free set. The other is the set of R-admissible sets. It shows how they relate.

The admissible-set system is shown to be isomorphic to an ergodic rotation of a compact abelian group, and its spectrum is computed. That structural result then yields applications: results on infinite sumsets in the integers, an analysis of squarefree values of polynomials as a special case, and a prime number theorem for R-free numbers. Together the two parts carry Sarnak's program from classical squarefree integers to sieve systems over general étale algebras.
arxiv-2603-00234: Sibani and colleagues study X-ray bright BL Lac objects with extreme high synchrotron peaks, aiming to pin down the peak shape and predict very high energy light. From 78 sources, 17 fit a log parabola model best, backing a peak inside the X-ray band. Ten jet-dominated objects then got gamma-ray upper limits and broadband models built with JetSeT. The models match current data and limits, and suggest some sources could shine in the TeV range, possibly within reach of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory.
arxiv-2603-00334: Junchaya, Assis Miranda, and Lucchesi study the pfaffian number of a graph, the smallest k for which the graph is k-pfaffian. In such graphs, perfect matchings can be counted from a linear combination of pfaffians of k matrices. They present the first known lower bounds for this number. As a stepping stone, they cap the rank of two matrices tied to their Khatri-Rao product, a finding useful in its own right. One consequence is that graphs exist whose pfaffian numbers are arbitrarily large.
arxiv-2603-00834: Blom and four colleagues model fibroblast-driven wound closure with the Discrete Laplacian Cell Mechanics framework, driven by time-lapse microscopy data. In vitro assays supply cell positions, migration behaviour, and cycle-stage information, and adding proliferation, migration, and arrest lets the model match the key experimental trends. Arrest in the G1 phase notably impacts cycle dynamics, and the starting layout of cycle states strongly affects wound closure. Tying single-cell cycle dynamics to tissue level behaviour gives a quantitative way to explore how intracellular processes shape repair.
arxiv-2603-01334: Fettes and five colleagues study lean traffic planning for optical low Earth orbit orbiter downlinks. There, delay-patient services like Earth watching and remote web of Things can use sparse fleets. Free-space optical links offer high data rates but suffer weather breaks, making some link chances energy wasteful, a pressing problem for energy-tight orbiters. The paper builds planning schemes lifting energy savings for space-to-ground drop-off of growing data volumes through orbiter networks.
arxiv-2603-01834:
Vineeth Venugopal, Soroush Mahjoubi, and Elsa Olivetti test what language models truly know about materials. Their 2026 study runs twenty-five models across four materials tasks, in more than two hundred setups. Output style proves to shape behavior in a fundamental way, the team finds.

For symbolic tasks, fine-tuning settles models on consistent, checkable answers with less response randomness. For numeric tasks, fine-tuning lifts accuracy, yet repeated runs still disagree with each other. Reading internal embeddings beats reading text output for numeric prediction in many cases. The authors name that gap the LLM head bottleneck, though it varies by property and data set. A side study tracking flagship models over eighteen months finds wide performance swings, which warns labs about reproducibility in science uses.
arxiv-2603-01934:
Irene Graziotti, Chiara De Leo, and Matteo Martinelli test an entropic account of cosmic acceleration against the standard model. Their 2026 work studies the GREA framework, where late acceleration grows from entropy made at the cosmic horizon. The rival is the standard model with a cosmological constant driving expansion.

Current data include baryon acoustic oscillations, supernovae, compressed early-universe data, and cosmic chronometers. A Bayesian comparison weighs both models across those background probes at once. An added dark energy term lets GREA mimic the standard history as a limiting case. Current data favor the standard model when early-universe data join, while GREA stays competitive at low redshift. Forecasts with future surveys suggest gravitational wave standard sirens will sharpen the verdict between the two drivers.
arxiv-2603-02034: Decoherence and entropy production due to quantum fluctuations of spacetime is a doctoral thesis in physics from 2026. Thiago Henrique Moreira wrote it at the Federal University of Goiás in Brazil. Lucas Chibebe Céleri supervised the work. The preserved sample holds only the thesis front matter, with the title page and exam details. It holds no readable abstract or body text. So this entry can be described only at title and author level here.
arxiv-2603-02334:
Simeon Ball and Robin Simoens revisit a classic officers puzzle in quantum form in this 2026 paper. Euler's thirty-six officers problem asks for two linked Latin squares of order six. No classical solution exists, a fact settled long ago. A quantum version does exist, using entangled states in place of fixed ranks.

Ball and Simoens ask whether entanglement is truly needed for that quantum solution. They prove that mutually orthogonal quantum Latin squares of order six cannot exist without it. Unitary patterns and orthonormal representations frame their argument. The result draws a sharp line: order six is where quantum solutions must use entanglement. That makes the old puzzle a clean marker of a truly quantum effect.
arxiv-2603-02434:
Guanchen Wu, Zhe Huang, Yuzhang Xie, and colleagues predict Alzheimer's disease when brain scans are missing in this 2026 paper. Diagnosis increasingly mixes MRI scans with electronic health records. Scans are costly, though, and many patient groups lack them entirely. Building fake 3D scans from sparse records is risky and hard.

Their framework, MIRAGE, never builds a fake scan at test time. A biomedical knowledge graph first maps varied record fields into one shared space. Graph attention spreads that knowledge from scanned groups to unscanned ones. A frozen 3D decoder acts as a structural check during training, forcing the record code to hold plausible anatomy. Only that compact surrogate code is used for diagnosis. Accuracy rose notably over single-source baselines in scan-free groups.
arxiv-2603-02534:
Adnane Saoud, Ryan Johnson, and Ricardo Sanfelice estimate unknown parameters in finite time in this 2026 paper. Adaptive control needs exact parameter values, and classic methods converge only as time grows without bound. Their hybrid method targets the exact value within a set finite time. Hybrid dynamics mix steady flow with discrete resets to hit that deadline.

For constant parameters, the input signal needs to be exciting only on one interval. That relaxes the classic persistence demand, a long-standing burden. Piecewise constant parameters still require the classic condition for assured convergence. Robustness against measurement noise is analyzed in a formal way. Worked examples show merits in scale and for time-varying parameters. The approach widens where finite-time estimation can be trusted.
arxiv-2603-02734:
Felix Oberbauer, Tristan Joachim Winkel, Clara Wanjura, and colleagues build a brain-like computing element from a tiny magnetic device. Their 2026 paper uses vortex magnetic tunnel junctions, which store values without standby power. Brains gain efficiency by keeping memory and processing together, a trick most chip designs still miss.

A heat-set storage layer holds analog weights and tunes the device response across a small frequency range. Light plus electric bias then drives a strong curved response that serves as the computing step, while two readout channels give four levels in total. In array simulations, image sorting reached accuracy near a matched digital network. Smaller devices did better, pointing to response shaping as a key design lever.
arxiv-2603-02934:
Pardhu Sri Rushi Varma Konduru argues that the usual way of adapting neural models permanently warps them. Fine-tuning and reinforcement training rewrite weights shared by every part of a model. His 2026 paper names the resulting problem structural irreversibility: task goals become tangled with the model's basic identity in its representations.

Experiments show a mutated model drifts from the original, and the drift cannot be undone exactly without a stored snapshot of the old weights. He proposes reversible behavioral learning instead, where new behaviors sit apart from identity parameters and unload cleanly on demand. A Recoverability Factor scores how fully a behavior can be rolled back. The reversible approach restored models within numerical precision, while weight mutation left lasting divergence.
arxiv-2603-03334:
Bianca Raimondi and three colleagues test whether language models are ready for university-level mathematics. Most existing tests stop at school problems, contests, or formal proof, leaving graduate computational work unexamined. Their 2026 dataset, CompMath-MCQ, fills the gap with fifteen hundred multiple-choice questions written fresh by professors of graduate courses, so no model can have memorized them from training data.

Questions span linear algebra, numerical optimization, vector calculus, probability, and scientific computing in Python, each with three options and one correct answer. Quality was checked through disagreement between models, followed by expert review. Scoring runs through a standard evaluation library, keeping results objective and repeatable. Baseline results with leading models show advanced computational reasoning is still a significant challenge.
arxiv-2603-03834:
G E Chiatto, G Chiriacò, G Falci, and E Paladino referee a modeling dispute about a qubit haunted by a noisy neighbor. A dissipative two-level impurity is a leading source of the random telegraph noise that decoheres solid-state qubits. Theorists describe the pair with a master equation derived one of two ways, locally or globally, within standard approximations. Their 2026 paper asks which derivation to trust, and where.

The local approach wins the contested ground: it correctly captures a crossover in the qubit's coherence dynamics that the global approach misses. The global method's flaw is its full secular approximation, which confines it to regimes where energy scales are well separated. In the experimentally relevant parameter regime, the authors conclude, the local scheme gives the better description. The result clarifies the domains of validity for tools used across open quantum systems.
arxiv-2603-04434: Grus and colleagues group periodic signals into messages on one resource. Offline schedules fix message start times for deterministic behaviour in critical systems. Each message carries header metadata, so short signals sent alone waste bandwidth. Grouping signals under one header raises utilization, but finite message size limits delivery success and scheduling flexibility. The paper tackles grouping signals and scheduling messages periodically. The core task is thus clear and well defined.
arxiv-2603-04534: Yu and colleagues govern online norms with Invariant Causal Routing. Social norms, including fair exposure, participation, and reinvestment, stabilize markets, yet micro interactions make causal attribution and policy transfer hard. ICR finds policy norm relations stable across settings. It joins what-if thought with stable causal search to split real effects from false correlations. It builds clear, open policy rules that survive data shift. In tests tuned with real data, ICR yields steadier norms, smaller transfer gaps, and rules shorter than those from link or scope rivals.
arxiv-2603-04634: Rahangdale extends the Drinfeld correspondence to infinite dimensions. The correspondence links Poisson Lie groups with Lie bialgebras, their infinitesimal twins. This paper extends it to regular Lie groups built on handy vector spaces. Focus falls on groups built on nuclear Fréchet and Silva spaces. Examples are the smooth loop group and the analytic loop group of a 1-connected real Lie group. They also include universal covering groups of smooth and real-analytic diffeomorphism groups of a compact manifold. The extension thus carries it into infinite-dimensional settings.
arxiv-2603-04734: Mastropietro and Kungurtsev address rare-event risk in power systems with high renewable penetration. A tail weather realization can leave solar and wind output too low to meet demand. Ramping conventional plants in time then becomes vital, yet poor forecasts waste money or cause ruinous shortage. The paper presents rare event-aware control via staged scenario-based stochastic programming. Fleming-Viot particles bias scenarios toward rare realizations of very low wind power. The resulting control of conventional plants stays cost-effective under prolonged renewable shortfalls.
arxiv-2603-04834: Bian and colleagues show the Hochschild study ring of a self-injective Nakayama algebra is a Batalin-V algebra. Lambre, Zhou, and Zimmermann showed this for Frob algebras with simple Nakayama map, asking whether simple is necessary. The paper answers yes for self-injective Nakayama algebras, without the simple rule. Proofs correct some slips in the books, with care not to introduce new errors. The result extends Batalin-V structure beyond the simple case. This settles the need question for this algebra class.
arxiv-2603-05034: Giovanni Guidetti and team study AI and robotics patenting from 1980 to 2019, distinguishing older robotics from robotics embedding AI functionalities. Older robots, core AI, and AI-lifted robots each follow their own path, with AI-lifted robotics surging from the early 2010s. Long-run AI-robotics links vary by country. China shows strong joining of core AI with AI-lifted robots plus major university and public-sector contributions. The United States shows a market-oriented structure with weaker joining, while Europe, Japan, and South Korea sit in between.
arxiv-2603-05134: Yewen Li and team offer LBM, a hierarchical auto-bidding model using large language model reasoning. Current auto-bidding methods use offline reinforcement learning or generative methods but can behave counterintuitively from black-box training. applying LLMs faces difficulties from precise action needs and missing specialized auto-bidding knowledge, causing hallucinations and suboptimal choices. LBM pairs LBM-Think for reasoning with LBM-Act for action making. It uses a dual embedding mechanism fusing language and number inputs plus offline reinforcement fine-tuning called GQPO to mitigate hallucinations.
arxiv-2603-05434: Ziming Peng and the rest of the team report electron temperature trending in reverse at 12+log(O/H) at or above 8.7, measured through O+ line ratios. Electron temperature determines metallicity. Low temperature is expected for galaxies. This trend holds regardless of fitting method, not from contamination or dust fix. Other low-ionization ions lack this phenomenon. Likely causes for high OII line ratios yield no given reason. This finding challenges the direct Te method, warranting further real study.
arxiv-2603-05534: Githinji and team tackle false positives in unsupervised medical-image anomaly detection, where pathology mixes with normal range. They augment the latent form of a convolutional autoencoder with matches to a normal cohort, via hypergraph estimation within batches and a shared-weights graph convolution layer. This forms a group-aware embedding. On brain-tumor 2D MRI scans, the method improves the split between healthy and pathological samples. It reaches 0.90 AUC-ROC with a 16% gain in average precision, lowering false alarm rates. Larger mini-batch context improves finding and sorting alike.
arxiv-2603-05634: Julían-Macías and team employ quantum operator techniques for paraxial waves with Airy-type starting setups. The first part finds 1+1 D optical beam forms from Airy, Airy-cut, and Airy-Gaussian starting setups. Work then reaches 2+1 D beams from products of paired Airy, Airy-cut, and Airy-Gaussian functions. Theory and lab brightness profiles agree very well. Although diffraction sum methods got these answers before, the goal is finding optical fields by these methods.
arxiv-2603-06134: Vilsmeier and his team review methods that pair covariate based clustering of patients with outcome models for clinical studies. They split informed cluster models, where outcomes help form clusters, from agnostic ones, where clustering runs on covariates alone. Their search of Web of Science and PubMed found 55 records that put forward or test them, covering product partition models, finite mixtures of regressions, and cluster aware supervised learning. The team judge these models useful where covariates are high dimensional and groups mixed, to aid risk stratification and subgroup treatment estimates.
arxiv-2603-06234: Locker and his team study 2D magnetic reconnection with a Full-F gyrofluid model of arbitrary wavelength polarization. In strongly magnet plasmas, long parallel wavelengths stand apart from smaller cross scales, pointing to a 2D account. Unlike delta-F, the Full-F form runs Harris sheet reconnection to aspect ratio 16, covering tearing growth, plasmoid build up, and ion Larmor radius effects. Linear tearing work plus non-modal stability analysis shows a non-normal evolution operator with condition numbers and wide pseudospectra, hinting at transient amplification in barely stable regimes.
arxiv-2603-06334: Marting and his team show a high superconducting on-chip filterbank using directional filters for integral field units in the sub-millimeter band. Such spectrometers enable area spectral mapping for astronomy, but on-chip work has been poor. Using a cryogenic thermal load, noise readings, and a steady wave terahertz source, they measure spectral response and efficiency across all quasi-optical elements. The filterbank, with filters of mean loaded quality factor 19.6, reaches a peak coupling of 75 percent to detectors while sparsely sampling 125 to 220 gigahertz.
arxiv-2603-06534: NaseriTehrani and team study decodable MIMO coded caching flow with free per-user stream allocations. Old allocation gives every user the same stream count, roughening degrees-of-freedom grain and leaving spatial slots unused. They derive a stream-count decodability condition from multicast-codeword counts and per-user stream counts, widening the can-do rule. Building on that rule, they develop a greedy cast planning procedure with linear reading, spreading cast messages across intervals to realize uneven shares.
arxiv-2603-06834: Cardoso and Gil study an inhomogeneous coupled nonlinear Schrödinger system with quadratic couplings, found in optics, plasma physics, and wave travel in uneven spreading media. They prove a sharp rule for when solutions exist for all time versus blowing up in finite time. The rule compares conserved mass and energy with ground states of the matching system. Variation tools, conservation laws, and Gagliardo-Nirenberg-type bounds give local and global well-posedness in subcritical and intercritical cases, joining earlier single and multi-part work.
arxiv-2603-06934: Barger carries a single-flavon lattice model from quarks into leptons. The model explained quark masses and mixing; its power structure now gives charged-lepton masses and normal ordering. Neutrino mixing needs broken mu-tau reflection symmetry, yielding a nonzero reactor angle and CP phase. The PMNS matrix splits into neutrino and charged-lepton parts, with phases aligned by the single-flavon origin. One interference link ties the Dirac phase to the neutrino phase plus a charged-lepton correction, and ties the correction sign to the octant, giving two branches.
arxiv-2603-07034: Sharma and Agarwal offer a new bi-complex Prabhakar tool, taking fraction math to 4D bi-complex spaces. Using a broad kernel with that kernel function, they construct the tool and prove basic working traits including linear rules, combo rules, and links to Riemann-Liouville and Caputo operators. They further study how fraction tools act on that kernel function itself, giving sum forms and change rules. This work gives a strict base for complex events with memory effects and multi-way links in bi-complex realms.
arxiv-2603-07134: Shi and colleagues reframe human-AI alignment in early childhood settings as a community matter, not a one-to-one problem. In parent-child interaction analysis, families and speech-language pathologists read the same everyday moments from different roles, so authority, responsibility, and emotional risk are shared. A three-part study covers five families and three pathologists, tracing model outputs as they move from expert use to parent use. They propose layered community alignment, with expert-grounded structure, professional guardrails, and family adaptation inside those bounds.
arxiv-2603-07634: Faes and colleagues dissect spectral Granger causality with partial information splitting. Granger's method senses one-way push but is muddied by high-order interactions shaping group moves. Their PDGC tool splits many-driver cause-and-effect from drivers to a target into unique, redundant and synergistic parts, built from state-space models in the frequency domain. Benchmarks confirm the measures track true causes, and a clinical use reveals distinct posture stress responses in syncope-prone patients.
arxiv-2603-07934: Kim and colleagues close a gap in estimates for the parabola. Small caps here are near axis-parallel rectangles whose sides scale as delta and delta to a power beta, with beta from zero to one. That range sits below earlier work, which covered beta from one to two. Their square function and decoupling bounds are sharp up to polylogarithmic factors, leaving only a small logarithmic loss.
arxiv-2603-08234: Deng and colleagues analyze the continuation-triggered jailbreak. Simply moving a triggered instruction suffix can sharply raise jailbreak success rates. Despite safety alignment efforts, large language models stay open to jailbreaking, and the root causes are still unclear. Through a mechanistic analysis at the attention-head level, with causal tests and activation scaling, the authors trace the behavior to a contest. The model's built-in drive to keep going competes with safety defenses learned through safety training. Safety-critical heads act in varied ways across architectures.
arxiv-2603-08434: Fillioux and colleagues tackle semi-supervised domain generalization when class counts are long-tailed, a common real-world shape where leading methods falter. Their fix, IMaX, adapts the InfoMax principle to this setting, maximizing the mutual information between learned features and latent labels under the guidance of the labeled samples. An alpha-entropic objective tempers the class-balance bias of the usual marginal entropy term, so skewed class mixes are handled better. The objective plugs into recent leading methods and lifts their scores across two image modalities in tests.
arxiv-2603-09234: Xiaobin Rong and colleagues present StuPASE, a generative speech enhancement method that aims for studio quality without inventing sounds that were never there. It builds on PASE, which resists hallucination but loses polish in harsh conditions. Fine-tuning on dry targets improves dereverberation, and swapping the GAN module for flow matching lifts quality under strong noise. Tests show clean, high-quality speech with low hallucination, beating leading enhancement methods.
arxiv-2603-09634: K. Lakshmanan surveys averaging methods in stochastic gradient methods, a standard tool for learning at scale. Done over the iterates, averaging improves both efficiency and stability. Classical Polyak-Ruppert averaging reaches optimal asymptotic variance and better convergence. Newer forms, from tail to stochastic weight averaging, perform strongly in deep network training and often do better on new data. The survey covers the theory, modern variants, and machine learning uses.
arxiv-2603-09934: R. Yamamoto and coauthors image spin textures at the nanoscale in hematite, a material showing altermagnetic response. Altermagnets break time reversal symmetry while their spins cancel out, and their response hinges on the Néel vector's direction. Using nano scale X-ray magnetic circular dichroism across the Morin transition, they watch that response switch off and on. Domain walls with twisted Néel vectors still show a signal where domains show none.
arxiv-2603-10134: S. Mackie and coauthors build an interpretive framework for tracking plasma state during fueling runs at the CMFX centrifugal mirror. Diagnostics there are sparse, so the plasma's condition stays partly hidden. Their time dependent analysis feeds applied voltage, input power and neutron yield into the 0D MCTrans++ model, solving with Newton's method interval by interval. Comparing fueling strategies revealed that several short puffs work better, guiding runs to higher voltage.
arxiv-2603-10234: Jiarui Li and coauthors turn loose saliency maps into structured explanations of why an image classifier looks where it looks. Most explanation tools give unstructured heat maps or lean on helper models, which can stray from the original model's true behaviour. Their I2X framework measures progress at training checkpoints using prototypes drawn from post hoc methods such as GradCAM. The structured view covers within class and between class choices, and can even flag shaky prototypes to improve predictions.
arxiv-2603-10334: Samuel Korsky bounds how many near pairs a set of points in the plane must have, compared with pairs near the full diameter apart. For points with diameter at most one, he shows the ratio of neighbors to antipodes grows at least like a square-root power of the tolerance, up to small factors. That matches the conjectured rate and improves the earlier bound from Steinerberger. In higher dimensions he proves a similar result, with an exponent that grows with the dimension.
arxiv-2603-10634: Yuki Uchino, Katsuhisa Ozaki, and Toshiyuki Imamura propose a way to emulate double-precision matrix multiplication on FP8 units, using the Ozaki-II scheme. Double-precision GEMM is a core, costly kernel in high-performance computing, and Ozaki schemes emulate it with low-precision hardware. Ozaki-I already has FP8 versions, but Ozaki-II could not be adapted directly to FP8 units, while newer chips are cutting INT8 performance. Their new technique makes Ozaki-II run on FP8 units, cutting cost sharply versus the FP8 Ozaki-I route.
arxiv-2603-10834: Pum Jun Kim and co-authors question how reliable the cue-conflict benchmark is for measuring shape-texture bias in neural networks. The benchmark probes whether models judge images by shape or texture, and shape bias has been linked to better performance. The team finds the stylization version can give unstable estimates: stylized cues may not be valid or separable, ratio scores hide absolute sensitivity, and preset classes distort predictions. Their REFINED-BIAS framework builds balanced, recognizable cue pairs and scores sensitivity over the full label space.
arxiv-2603-11434: McMillin and co-authors study how plasma around a black hole can change the shadow that telescopes see. Their black hole is Kerr-like and sits in a dark matter halo. They trace light paths for both homogeneous and inhomogeneous plasma. More spin tends to grow and warp the shadow, while a viewer off the equator sees a smaller one. Plasma shifts the shadow a lot, yet the dark matter densities they test barely move light paths. Homogeneous plasma grows the shadow; inhomogeneous plasma shrinks it.
arxiv-2603-11634: Sirigiri and co-authors build a way to measure diversity in robotics data sets. Imitation data mixes long paths of states, actions, and video, so plain counts mislead. The team extends Shannon and von Neumann entropy with signature kernels over demonstrations. Their curation algorithm, FAKTUAL, picks the subset of demonstrations with the highest entropy for a fixed budget. It needs no policy access and adds almost no overhead. Across RoboMimic, MetaWorld, and four real tasks, diverse picks beat random ones.
arxiv-2603-11934: Gabric and co-authors give the first fast decoding method for bounded-weight de Bruijn sequences. A universal cycle packs every object of a set into one cyclic string, each appearing once as a substring. Many cycle constructions exist, yet few come with efficient ranking and unranking. Their polynomial-time and space decoder handles strings of length n over a k-letter alphabet with bounded weight. The same machinery then decodes universal cycles for t-subsets and t-multisets.
arxiv-2603-12034: Chen and Issa close their spin glass series with models that break the usual convexity assumption. Here the Parisi formula fails, and no known method pins down the limit free energy in full. An older conjecture ties that limit to the unique solution of a Hamilton-Jacobi type equation. The authors prove the conjecture in the high-temperature regime. Their formula states the free energy through critical points, and a matching large deviation principle for the mean magnetization follows.
arxiv-2603-12134: Farrell, He, Hu, and Zhang compare finite element schemes by how well they keep helicity in magnetic relaxation. Ideal theory conserves helicity locally, while Taylor relaxation keeps only the global total. Three schemes face off: one with no conservation, one local method, and one global multiplier method. Tests with magnetic knots and braids show helicity limits act as real topological barriers when the invariant is nonzero. When it vanishes, braided topology escapes full description. The results map both the power and the limits of this approach.
arxiv-2603-12434: Susskind argues that time reversal in de Sitter space is a gauge symmetry hidden by spontaneous breaking. Holographic symmetries are usually read as bulk gauge symmetries, discrete ones included. Time reversal feels distinct enough that Harlow and Numasawa say yes to gauging while Witten says no. Susskind sides with yes, but claims the symmetry is spontaneously broken in the bulk. His smoking gun is a closed curve with a holonomy that flips forward-going clocks to backward ones. The paper reviews the breaking case with conceptual rigor throughout.
arxiv-2603-12934: Hyoseok Park and Yeonsang Park build a photonic way to compute the exponential step inside softmax. AI growth strains datacenter energy and data movement budgets. Photonic chips run matrix products fast, yet softmax still falls back to electronics. Their cascaded microring design on thin-film lithium niobate synthesizes the needed exponential curve. A control signal detunes each ring, and stacked stages multiply the response. Simulations match theory, and a full chip plan adds feedback control.
arxiv-2603-13034: Paul Stocker and Igor Voulis study a Trefftz discontinuous Galerkin method for the Helmholtz equation that needs no built basis. They start from a polynomial space and force the Trefftz trait with local rules. A symmetric penalty form joins the parts, but it is not coercive on its own. Proof of stability pairs a T-coercivity trick with a duality step. The end result gives stability that tracks the wave number, plus convergence bounds. A clear mesh size rule states when the bounds hold.
arxiv-2603-13134: Yu Li and co-authors sharpen Group Relative Policy Optimization by letting right and wrong answers teach each other. GRPO scores outputs against a group mean, yet treats each sample as if it stood alone. That wastes the natural contrast between good and failed traces in one group. Their bilateral context conditioning lets the model cross-reference both kinds during updates. A reward-confidence correction steadies the advantage baseline as well. Math reasoning tests improved across models and variants.
arxiv-2603-13234: Chris Kuchar presents RFX-Fuse, a random forest engine that aims to restore Breiman and Cutler's full vision. Their original forest was a unified tool, not just an ensemble predictor. It covered classification, regression, unsupervised learning, similarity, outliers, imputation, and visualization in one model. Modern pipelines split those jobs across five or more separate tools. RFX-Fuse grows one set of trees with native GPU and CPU support. Its new proximity importance explains why two samples count as similar, not just that they do.
arxiv-2603-13434: Wei Zhuo and Siqiang Luo present MF-GIA, a way to make graph encoders work across domains with few examples. A pretrained encoder is normally fixed, so it cannot adapt to a new task on the fly. MF-GIA reads domain traits from gradient fingerprints, which are small summaries of how the model reacts. These drive light changes that align features and labels into one shared space. A dual attention step learns to match queries with support examples. At test time, a few support examples trigger the alignment.
arxiv-2603-13534: Nikolai Kutev and Tsviatko Rangelov study a nonlinear parabolic problem with a time fractional derivative. The equation pairs a p-Laplacian term with a double singular Hardy-type potential. They prove a comparison principle for its weak solutions, plus a priori estimates that bound them. They then ask when global weak solutions exist and when solutions blow up in finite time. The answer turns on the value of the optimal Hardy constant, they show. Their work sets out the line between the two regimes for this class of problems.
arxiv-2603-14234: Deng and Li construct elliptic curves with rank one and rich Tate-Shafarevich behavior over the cyclotomic Z2-extension of the rationals. They study Mazur-Tate modular elements for quadratic twists of a curve, read through finite-order characters at each layer. Congruence facts about Heegner points and an equivariant Coates-Wiles theorem drive the proof. The built curve has a family of twists, each with analytic and algebraic rank one over the full tower. Each twist's Tate-Shafarevich group over the tower is infinite.
arxiv-2603-14534: Guo and co-authors teach a particle packing to store input-output associations. The system is a 2D mix of two particle sizes under slow, athermal motion. In training, set input particles move in cycles. Output particles follow a set flow pattern under a local driving rule. In recall, only the inputs move. Learning lives in small rearrangements that reshape the contact network. Easy tasks score high with no training. Hard tasks clash with the bulk drift and gain only slightly, they find.
arxiv-2603-14634: Abderezaei and co-authors make particle-based simulation respect rigid-body physics with PBD-R. Position-based dynamics is fast and looks right, but its physics can drift. Robotics needs the accuracy that stitched multi-solver tools strain to give. PBD-R adds a momentum-conservation constraint to the classic solver. A revised velocity update completes the fix. A solver-free benchmark with known solutions grades physical accuracy. PBD-R beats plain PBD by a wide margin there. It rivals MuJoCo accuracy at lower compute cost, they report.
arxiv-2603-14734: Cheng proposes Gauge-Equivariant Intrinsic Neural Operators, or GINO, to learn elliptic PDE maps. Past tools can break when the local frame or the grid shifts. GINO uses spectral multipliers based on shape, with nonlinear steps that track frame change. This splits shape from the learned part, so frame shifts do not break the map. Cheng tests GINO on a flat torus, where Fourier forms are known in full. He reports low error, near exact gauge scores, and strong runs when grids or metrics shift.
arxiv-2603-15034: Skurla and co-authors replicate a predictability-based system for detecting machine-generated text, from the AuTexTification shared task. Exact replication failed, and they document why: data splits, model access, and details differed. They test newer multilingual models and add 26 stylometric features. One shared setup served both English and Spanish tasks. It matched or beat language-specific baselines, with the clearest gains on model attribution. Predictability scores stayed the dominant signal, well ahead of style features.
arxiv-2603-15334: Aspman and co-authors study Galois covers of Calabi-Yau quivers and what they imply for BPS state counting. A finite abelian group grades the arrows of a quiver, which produces a covering quiver. For a Calabi-Yau threefold quiver, the cover matches the orbifold of the same space. They view the construction through quiver quantum mechanics and fixed loci on moduli spaces. Their main result writes the BPS invariants of a quiver as a sum over its cover. Special cases, such as the conifold, get full derivations.
arxiv-2603-15634: Zhang and co-authors present NextMem, a latent memory system for language model agents. Text memory loads the context and costs a lot to index. Trained-in memory can forget old facts and costs a lot to update. NextMem uses an autoregressive autoencoder to build compact latent memory. Training runs in two stages, with alignment first and gradual substitution next. Quantization cuts storage needs. The authors report strong gains in retrieval, robustness, and extensibility.
arxiv-2603-15734: Ellis and co-authors widen the hunt for axion clouds around spinning black holes. Superradiance can grow such clouds from vacuum fluctuations alone. The clouds drain spin and emit steady gravitational waves. Past limits rest on spin measures for a few known black holes. The team instead models whole populations, in the Milky Way and beyond. They fold in broad uncertainty on black hole traits. LIGO can probe axion masses near 10^-12 eV, they project. Future detectors reach still higher masses.
arxiv-2603-15834: Kitaura and Sinigaglia stack cosmic-web maps into a scale-by-scale hierarchy. Web classification usually starts from one filtered density field. Their kernels reweight scales before the standard eigenvalue sorting runs. Low levels give the broad tidal web of voids and knots. Higher levels stress curvature and fine ridge detail. Each cell maps to void, sheet, filament, or knot labels. A web contrast field then cross-checks against AbacusSummit halos. Signal persists from huge scales down to the mesh limit. Local levels dominate near nonlinear scales.
arxiv-2603-16534: Muñoz extends mean field game theory for games with a dominating player. Bensoussan, Chau, and Yam built the major-minor theory earlier. Their payoffs depended on the law of the states alone. Muñoz lets payoffs depend on the joint state-control law. The key object is the conditional spread of state-control pairs. That spread is taken given the major player's common noise. His conditions come from stochastic maximum principles. A coupled SHJB-FP system states the equilibrium.
arxiv-2603-16834: Allu, Biswas, and Mandal prove sharp Bohr-type results on shifted disks. Their setting is a family of disks in the complex plane, shifted by a parameter gamma between zero and one. For analytic functions on these disks, they establish several sharp forms of the Bohr inequality. They cover the plain, refined, and improved versions of that inequality. They do the same for harmonic mappings on the same domains. Sharp means the bounds cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2603-17534: Aryal and Keane improve semi-factual explanations for automated decisions. A semi-factual says an outcome would stay the same even if one input changed a lot. Older methods never say why the change is safe. Their ISF method adds the hidden features that hold the outcome steady. Benchmark tests kept quality high while adding that context. Users in a study preferred the fuller explanations, they report.
arxiv-2603-17634: Li, Liu, and Chen layer decision-making for autonomous systems under uncertainty. Other road users are modeled as hybrid Markov decision processes with maneuver and motion levels. The ego car folds the same style of model into model predictive control. Joint chance constraints link the forecasts to the optimizer and guard safety across scenarios. Theory gives recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability, they show. Highway and city tests beat a rule-based baseline.
arxiv-2603-17834: Zhang and co-authors recast robot control generation as optimization with GeCO. Flow-matching policies spend the same compute on easy and hard moves alike. GeCO learns a fixed velocity field where expert actions act as attractors. Inference then stops early on easy states and refines longer on hard ones. The field norm at the chosen action also flags odd states for free. Tests scale from standard sims to pi0 vision-language-action models, they report.
arxiv-2603-17934: Wang, Li, Wang, and Zhang tune noise levels inside Langevin dynamics by solving control equations. The right noise size makes or breaks hard optimization runs. Exploratory Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations can set that noise state by state. High dimensions stalled past work on bounds and Hessian math, though. Their physics-informed network bakes the equation shape into training for stability. Tests stayed robust far past one-dimensional cases, they report.
arxiv-2603-18034: Thornton studies corpus poisoning attacks on retrieval-augmented generation systems and retrieval-layer defenses. Attackers plant a sleeper and a trigger document, tuned with greedy coordinate gradient steps. On a 67,941-document Security Stack Exchange corpus, poisoning reached a 38% co-retrieval rate. Hybrid retrieval with BM25 plus vector search cut that rate to zero across 50 attacks. Joint attacks on both signals still fail more often than with vector search alone.
