Inner-layer pacing at side sites widens the base versus mid-or-tip gap over outer-layer pacing.
arxiv-2604-18734: Tong and four colleagues build a learning method that tunes dynamical decoupling pulse sequences for dynamic quantum circuits, which mix unitary steps with mid-circuit measurement and feedforward. Tuning is done for small circuit parts and small qubit groups, and the tuned sequences cut average dynamic circuit error rates threefold in randomized benchmarking tests. The tuned method also gives solid fidelity for a quantum Fourier transform with measurement on chains of up to 20 qubits. Learned sequences beat textbook ones for dynamic circuits, which matters for error correction.
arxiv-2604-18934: Shepard and Salimans introduce AutomationBench, a benchmark for AI agents on cross application workflows. Real workflows demand coordination, API discovery, and policy adherence across a CRM, inbox, calendar, and messaging platform. Tasks span Sales, Marketing, Operations, Support, Finance, and HR. Agents must find endpoints alone, follow business rules, and navigate misleading records. Grading is automated and end state only, and even the best models score below 10 percent.
arxiv-2604-19134: Kubota and Yoshino study arc search using the Szegedy walk, which finds a quantum particle by position and internal state. Graph symmetry appears in the time evolution matrix, giving a sufficient condition for success probability independent of the marked arc. Arc-transitive graphs have success probabilities independent of the marked arc. Path and cycle graphs defeat the search, while complete bipartite graphs succeed. The results ground future arc and edge searches and suggest new edge-signed graph eigenvalue problems.
arxiv-2604-20434: Zhang and eight colleagues tackle personalized multimodal generation, where text and images fit a user's tastes. They note two gaps: no dedicated way to model tastes well, and outputs stuck in one mode despite users mixing text and images. Their two-stage framework, DPPMG, learns tastes per mode with a graph network, turns them into discrete preference tokens, and feeds those tokens to text and image generators. A cross-mode reward keeps image and text consistent while preserving personalization, and tests on two real datasets support the design.
arxiv-2604-20534: Pal and Ghosh study extreme events in the Murali-Lakshmanan-Chua circuit, a chaotic electronic circuit. The expansion of the chaotic attractor after PM intermittency precedes those events. They find a force field from a periodic force, which pushes the trajectory far from its home region, and that deviation marks an extreme event. They explain the excursion through stable and unstable manifolds in slow-fast dynamics and through Floquet multipliers. Excess values follow a generalized Pareto distribution, and gaps between spikes follow a generalized extreme value distribution.
arxiv-2604-20634: Labouriau proposes a way to show a probability law by a tempered distribution, like a density or characteristic. Information comes from testing the distribution on test functions smoothed by a positive Schwartz kernel. That yields weak moments, weak characteristic functions, and weak cumulants. Main results include an algebra of weak cumulants and a weak moment problem. A weak central limit theorem gives a Gaussian limit. The weak first moment gives a steady estimator of location for Cauchy data, which lacks any classical moment-based estimator.
arxiv-2604-21134: Yiyang Lu and five colleagues tackle chart-reading agents that misread values and invent details by giving them the chart's own specification, not just its pixels. Their grounding framework pairs spec queries with interactive view changes, and their iPlotBench testbed supplies 500 interactive figures with ground truth. Combined, the two tactics reach the best question accuracy, gaining most where chart elements overlap.
arxiv-2604-21234: Fiaz Hossain, Nilanjan Ray Chaudhuri, and Constantino Lagoa build a dynamic phasor framework for power grids where inverters induce slow oscillations. Because the framework stays linear and time-invariant, mode analysis can trace each oscillation to its root cause and guide damping-controller design. Case studies on a modified IEEE two-area system check the model against EMTDC/PSCAD simulations. A robust decentralized damping controller then quiets the modes, including after unbalanced faults and under data-center loads.
arxiv-2604-21334: Donggyu Lee and six colleagues test whether language models show ideological bias when judging economic cause and effect. From 10,490 causal triplets drawn from top economics and finance journals, they isolate 1,056 ideology-contested cases where intervention-oriented and market-oriented views predict opposite signs. Contested items prove harder across the board, and in 17 of 20 models accuracy runs higher when the verified sign matches intervention-oriented expectations. Errors also lean intervention-oriented, and one-shot prompting does not erase the skew.
arxiv-2604-21534: Darya Hryhoryeva and three colleagues build a system for SemEval-2026 Task 2, modeling affect and near-term change in ordered user texts. They explore three approaches: LLM prompting with and without user context, and a pairwise Maximum Entropy model with Ising-style interactions. A regression model using affective trajectories and user embeddings rounds it out. LLMs capture signals well, while short-term variation owes more to numeric state trajectories than to textual semantics. It ranked first in both Subtask 1 and Subtask 2A on the metric.
arxiv-2604-21734: Selvaratnam and three colleagues model how operational risk losses link to economic factors over time. They extend Hidden Markov Models to many-variable data, adding an extra variable to carry the economic factors in the series. Calibration uses the Expectation-Maximization algorithm. The paper details what makes operational risk data unusual, reports calibration results across risk-event types, and weighs whether the economic factors add value.
arxiv-2604-21834: Chi and Yuan study edge-colourings of p-graphs. They ban three edges of colours in a cancellative setup, where the symmetric difference of two edges lies inside a third. For p at least 3 and n at least p plus 1, every colouring uses at most 1 plus floor of n over p colours, and the extremal colourings are characterised. For p equal to 3, rainbow F5-free colourings are rainbow cancellative. They construct F4-free colourings beating Budden and Stiles, and improve bounds for the anti-Ramsey number.
arxiv-2604-21934: Pavlov and four colleagues present the first review of routine computing, a field focused on sensing and modelling human behaviours. The review covers 203 studies published up to August 2025 and presents a new map of time patterns, behaviour links, thinking aspects, and change and drift. Common goals span four domains: care access, healthy habits, adaptive and context-aware support, and group insights. Hard problems include the gap between low-level activity spotting and high-level intent, personal versus general tension, privacy worries, and data limits.
arxiv-2604-22034: Merin-Martinez, Mendez-Vazquez, and Rodriguez-Tello propose LTBs-KAN, a B-spline Kolmogorov-Arnold net, as a faster alternative to standard KANs. KANs explain themselves better than Multilayer Perceptrons, but run much slower than MLPs since B-spline math repeats itself. The authors cut model parameters with product-sum matrix math in the forward pass, keeping performance. Tests on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 show LTBs-KAN runs faster with fewer weights than other KANs.
arxiv-2604-22134: Zhao and four colleagues name a weakness in tutoring models: pedagogical jailbreaks, where students use answer-pulling prompts to get solutions instead of guided teaching. To study it, they join safe, helpful, and pedagogical behavior with a knowledge-mastery graph and build SHAPE, a benchmark of 9,087 student-question pairs. They also offer a graph-guided tutoring pipeline that finds missing prerequisites, spots mastery gaps, and switches between teaching and solving. Tests over several models show much better safety under two jailbreak settings, with helpfulness near its ceiling.
arxiv-2604-22234: Jafri and Chhabria introduce design-adaptive chip-design tooling, in which a tool's own algorithms are tuned to each individual circuit rather than left fixed. Their GR-Evolve system uses an AI agent to rewrite global routing code step by step, guided by quality feedback inside the OpenROAD toolchain. Across seven benchmark designs on three technology nodes, it cut post-routing wirelength by up to 8.72 percent over existing baseline routers.
arxiv-2604-22334: Martinez and Ovsjanikov ask whether shape topology can be read from features of pretrained 3D point-cloud encoders. They build DONUT, a synthetic test set with controlled topological complexity. Their FILTR tool predicts persistence diagrams from frozen encoders. Tests on DONUT show existing encoders keep only limited global topological signals. Yet FILTR uses encoder information to approximate those diagrams well. In short, the work shows how much shape structure survives inside learned features, and gives a fast feed-forward route from raw point clouds to shape summaries.
arxiv-2604-22534: Karami and three colleagues present FeatEHR-LLM, turning messy hospital records into tabular features with a large language model. Clinical time series are irregular and gappy, while older tools miss clinical meaning or assume tidy inputs. To protect privacy, the model sees only schemas and task descriptions, never raw records, while tool routines let it query irregular data and emit feature code for uneven timing and gaps. Across eight tasks on four intensive-care datasets, it tops the mean ranking on seven, gaining up to six percentage points over baselines.
arxiv-2604-22634: Bi, Wu, and Huang first search for scalar-induced waves via pulsar drifts, constraining black hole abundance. Primordial black holes explain binary black holes seen by gravitational-wave detectors, especially in the mass gap. Scalar perturbations in the Universe producing them generate scalar-induced waves peaking in the sub-nanohertz band, appearing as pulsar drifts. It places a 95% limit on abundance below one part in ten billion for masses from three tenths to forty thousand solar masses. Results disfavor a primordial origin for black holes detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA.
arxiv-2604-23134: Qu and eight colleagues improve pocket-ligand binding prediction with h-MINT, a hierarchical network modeling molecules at atom and fragment levels. Their OverlapBPE tokenizer lets fragments overlap, matching fuzzy small-molecule edges while keeping chirality, aromaticity, and ionic state intact. The hierarchy handles the many-to-many atom-fragment links that overlap creates, preserving richer context than atom-only or fixed-fragment rivals. Tests show gains of 2 to 4 percent in binding affinity correlation and 1 to 3 percent in virtual screening, with the best high-throughput result on PubChem assays.
arxiv-2604-23334: Cong and Tian isolate the cut-free part of a connectivity interdiction case for linear minimization over a feasible-set family. After dualizing the interdiction budget, deletion folds into truncated weights taking the smaller of the first weight and a scaled cost. Once the Lagrange multiplier is fixed at its optimum, the reweighted case's minimum approximates the unknown optimal interdiction witness within a strict factor of 2. An exact algorithm follows when one can optimize the reweighted objective, list all its 2-approximate minima, and solve the remaining knapsack problem.
arxiv-2604-23434: Verma's 2026 study asks when dropping LayerNorm in favour of Dynamic Tanh, which caps activations with a learned curve, actually helps neural networks. The answer depends on regime: the swap improves small, data-poor models but worsens data-rich ones, with the benefit fading as model size grows. A quick saturation check predicts the sign of the effect reasonably well, and the collapse of one large variant traces to a gating component.
arxiv-2604-23634: Csirmaz studies how much one variable can constrain another in a submodular function, through the largest value the function can take on other singletons once one is fixed at one. He constructs an example showing this quantity can grow nearly linearly, up to a logarithmic factor, in the size of the ground set. He also proves a doubly exponential upper bound, leaving a wide gap between the bounds open.
arxiv-2604-23834: Wang and colleagues move beyond averages for ordinal momentary assessment data, the repeated real-time ratings used in health studies. They borrow sequence measures that capture each person's pattern over time. Then they cluster with principal components plus K-means to find hidden groups with similar profiles. Tests on fake data beat latent-class rivals. On real stress ratings the groups sharpen links to test scores.
arxiv-2604-24134: Van der Hoog, Iacono, Rotenberg, and Rutschmann build near-optimal working-set heaps on pointer machines, a deliberately spare model of computation. A working-set heap pops each item in time growing with the log of its working set, the items pushed while it waited. Word RAM designs already reach constant push and decrease-key costs, and the authors match constant push with inverse-Ackermann decrease-key on pointer machines. Dijkstra's algorithm then runs near-universally optimal on that model, with only a small additive overhead.
arxiv-2604-24634: Axelrod and colleagues use computation to design light-activated inhibitors of PARP1, a cancer target. Such drugs must balance light response and biological activity at once. They screen 5 million hypothetical ligands with docking, machine-learning force fields, quantum chemistry and free-energy methods. They prioritize candidates whose binding changes with light. Ten were synthesized and tested. One validated compound showed a 15-fold increase in inhibition under light. Light control could limit treatment to the site of disease, easing side effects elsewhere.
arxiv-2604-24734: Frazier, Lelievre and Li study Josephson junction networks where uneven coupling between spin-triplet pairing correlations creates frustrated d-vector textures. Such networks appear in mixed and single crystals. Like frustrated classical spin systems, they cannot at once best fit the phase difference and the relative d-vector directions. As Cooper pairs tunnel, the d-vector texture acts as a new geometric phase that can trap fractional flux on its own. This includes pi-flux trapping above a key coupling, distinct from usual half-quantum vortices.
arxiv-2604-24934: Zhang and seven colleagues present TEACar, an autonomous driving platform at 1/14 to 1/16 scale for hardware-in-the-loop validation. TEACar uses modular mechanical build, hardware layer and ROS 2 software, with a four-layer deck structure splitting sensing, computing, driving and power. The design improves stiffness while easing rebuilds. The prototype was tested with three CNN-based steering controllers, measuring model delay, power use and run time. Tests show TEACar is a scalable, modular and cheap testbed for research, teaching and building.
arxiv-2604-25134: Heeck and Le cut the clutter in particle theory by offering shorter lists built from plainer contractions than earlier lists offered. Their smallest complete set covers baryon number breaking interactions without derivatives, up to dimension eleven, plus two special change patterns at dimension twelve. Even so, a few smallest sets refuse to fit a plain pattern, showing that brevity and simplicity sometimes pull apart.
arxiv-2604-25434: Tamta, Raj and Verma rework microlensing bounds for fast and slow objects. Standard bounds assume halo lenses. But theories predict lens groups far from halo speeds, including primordial black holes. Since speed and mass trade off, fast lenses yield larger-mass events, slow lenses smaller-mass ones. They set density bounds for speeds from a ten-thousandth to a tenth of light speed. Two speed and two spatial spreads rule out far-from-dark-matter densities. Transverse motion matters for slow lenses; faster cadence probes smaller masses for fast lenses.
arxiv-2604-25534: Murari, Veronese and Meli propose a neuro-symbolic Proximal Policy Optimization extension transferring partial logical specifications from easier instances to harder settings. Deep Reinforcement Learning often needs much data and struggles in sparse-reward, long-horizon, multi-goal domains. Two guidance integrations are introduced. H-PPO-Product biases action distribution at sampling time, and H-PPO-SymLoss adds a symbolic regularization term to the PPO loss. Tests on OfficeWorld, WaterWorld, and DoorKey show faster learning and higher return than PPO and a Reward Machine baseline, also under imperfect knowledge.
arxiv-2604-25634: Bogdan and de Valois-Franklin report a statistical regularity in frontier LLM outputs that powers a CPU-only scoring primitive running at 2.6 microseconds per token. Across six models from five vendors, token rank-frequency distributions converge to one two-parameter Mandelbrot ranking distribution. Nearly all model-by-domain fits clear a high goodness-of-fit bar and favour Mandelbrot over Zipf. Fitted Mandelbrot parameters still separate models cleanly, with cross-model spread in q dwarfing per-model bootstrap uncertainty. One use follows: model fingerprinting for provenance checks.
arxiv-2604-25734: Bai and four colleagues study rank aggregation under the Ulam metric, an edit distance on permutations. Center minimizes the worst distance to input rankings; median minimizes total distance. Both are NP-hard even for one center. The authors prove k-center stays NP-hard at budget one, yet becomes fixed-parameter tractable in centers plus budget through local search. No polynomial kernel exists there unless NP sits inside coNP/poly. For k-median they prove W[1]-hardness, give an XP algorithm, and a kernel yielding tractability.
arxiv-2604-25834: Li and nine colleagues propose A2Gen, a generative sequence model for short video recommendation built on timed user actions. Standard recommenders score a video as one whole item, missing mixed feelings across segments. A2Gen refines actions along the time axis and chains them into sequences for unified prediction. Attention, hierarchical encoding, and autoregressive generation modules handle context, temporal patterns, and action sequences. Offline tests on Kuaishou and Tmall data, plus live trials, beat baselines on watch time, interaction, and retention.
arxiv-2604-26534: Śmierzchalski's thesis built a benchmark frame for D-Wave quantum annealers that goes beyond best-energy comparisons. Its first part, SpinGlassPEPS.jl, offers a topology-aware tensor-network helper mapping Ising cases to Potts clusters for optimization and sampling on Pegasus and Zephyr-like graphs. Its second part treats annealers as working heat machines, linking success and quality to heat loss, entropy production, and effective temperature. Careful pauses lifted performance while cutting heat cost, and reinforcement-learning cleanup further lifted returned samples.
arxiv-2604-26734: Bonamico, Hanuš, and Delbo determine the shape and spin axis of Kamo'oalewa, the near-Earth asteroid and Earth quasi-satellite targeted by China's Tianwen-2 sample-return mission. No reliable shape or spin models had been published, despite the idea that it may be lunar ejecta. From lightcurves across several apparitions, inverted with convex shape modeling, they derive a convex shape model. The spin pole sits at ecliptic coordinates 126 and minus 16 degrees, with a sidereal rotation period under half an hour.
arxiv-2604-26834: Flores-Garrigós and eight colleagues present a quantum method for picking telling features, using higher-order binary optimization that captures links among one, two, and three features at once. Mutual-information scores rate relevance, overlap, and joint structure, while penalties keep the picked set sparse. Run with digitized counterdiabatic optimization on IonQ Forte hardware and tested on gallstone and spam data, the method matches noiseless simulation and rivals classical baselines. Its picked sets stay small while sorting data well.
arxiv-2604-27034: Ho and three colleagues study Choi polynomials and their role in the theory of positive linear maps between matrix algebras. For Hermitian biquadratic forms, they link form positivity to such maps. They explore indecomposable maps as entanglement witnesses for Positive Partial Transpose entangled states and edge PPT states. Their results refine spotting of non-separable states that beat the PPT test, aiding work on distillation.
arxiv-2604-27534: Lavreniuk, Mudryi, and Chaklosh run Shannon's 1951 character-prediction experiment for Ukrainian for the first time, recruiting 184 volunteers through social media. Following techniques used for English, they estimate an upper bound of about 1.2 bits per character for Ukrainian entropy, a measure of unpredictability and complexity. They compare that result with current large language models, and they document and publish their methods and code, along with a discussion of the challenges encountered. The study fills a gap left by earlier English work and one Hebrew study, bringing Shannon's experiment to Ukrainian.
arxiv-2604-28134: Park and colleagues introduce MeshReGen, a 3D regenerator that starts from an initial shape instead of generating from scratch in one shot. Conditioned on the input through a VecSet mechanism, it supports enhancement, reconstruction and editing with consistent fine-grained detail. Trained self-supervised on off-the-shelf 3D data without extra labels, it reaches state-of-the-art controllable generation across several tasks.
arxiv-2605-00134:
Tenma Wakasugi, Zhaohong Sun, Kei Kimura, and Makoto Yokoo study two-sided matching markets, such as assigning students or refugees to places, under broad hereditary constraints. These constraints go beyond simple capacity limits. In such markets, fairness and non-wastefulness often clash, and most methods protect one by giving up the other.

The authors instead relax both goals in a balanced, measured way. They define two graded notions, each indexed by a number k, and prove the two can always be met together for any fixed k. They give two fast algorithms to compute such matchings. Experiments show that even a small relaxation strikes a good balance between fairness and use of places.
arxiv-2605-00334:
Ranit Karmakar and Jayita Chatterjee ask how much of an AI agent's work truly needs a frontier model. Working agents make many calls per request, and most are short, structured, and routine. Their benchmark, AgentFloor, arranges thirty tasks as a six-tier ladder, from following instructions through tool use to long-horizon planning under lasting constraints.

They ran sixteen open-weight models, from very small to mid-sized, alongside a leading closed model, over more than sixteen thousand scored runs. Small and mid-sized open models already handle much of the routine base, and the strongest open model matched the closed one overall while running cheaper and faster. The clear gap sits at long-horizon planning, where neither side was truly reliable. The design lesson is to reserve frontier models for the narrow tier that demands them.
arxiv-2605-00434:
Xu and three colleagues tackle machine learning with missing inputs. Many systems learn from video, sound, and other signals at once, but in real life one signal often drops out through a broken sensor or a privacy block. Most earlier methods assume complete data during training, which leaves them fragile when a channel goes missing. Their system, LIMSSR, reasons from whatever signals remain, using a large language model to fill gaps from context.

A masking step keeps the model honest about gaps. It weighs two lines of evidence and adjusts its confidence, so guesses built on thin context count for less. Tests on three action-quality datasets, where judges score movements, put LIMSSR ahead of the best earlier methods, even though it never saw complete training data. The result points to a leaner way of building multimodal systems that cope with gaps.
arxiv-2605-01134:
Jia Li, Vipin Kumar, and Rui Zhang argue that chance-based, noun-centered modeling cannot fully represent the future as an open space of possibilities, because it leaves timing outside computation. They identify three conceptual gaps. The first is a possibility space admitting multiple timelines for the same event. The second treats timing as computable rather than merely observed. The third is a notion of maximal causal effect recovered by reasoning backward from possible futures.

Together these definitions are presented as dissolving a confounding problem in noun-based causal inference and grounding a spontaneously growing causal world model. As proof of concept, the framework is applied to long-run health records from several thousand breast cancer patients, demonstrating automatic trajectory discovery and counterfactual timing deduction in a data-driven manner.
arxiv-2605-01234:
Nima Rahmanian and five co-authors present TT4D, a pipeline and dataset for four-dimensional reconstruction of table tennis from monocular broadcast videos. The dataset provides well over a hundred hours of reconstructed singles and doubles gameplay, with camera calibrations, precise three-dimensional ball positions, ball spin, time segmentation, and human meshes over time. Such data can support virtual replay, player analysis, and robot learning.

Earlier methods segmented shots from the two-dimensional ball track before reconstruction, which collapses under occlusion and varied viewpoints. TT4D inverts the order: a learned network first lifts the full unsegmented track to three dimensions, also inferring spin and handling unreliable detections, and segmentation follows reliably. Downstream tests estimate racket pose and velocity at impact and train a generative rally model.
arxiv-2605-01334:
Paul Bryan, Julie Clutterbuck, and Cale Rankin give fresh, simpler proofs of two classic facts about the Schrödinger operator, the core equation for how quantum waves sit inside a region. Both facts link the shape of the region to the tones and form of the waves it holds.

The first is the Brunn-Minkowski rule for the lowest tones: mixing two regions cannot push the tone below a set blend of the two tones. Their proof covers a wide class of regions and force fields. The second says the first wave keeps one sign and bends in a log-concave way, rising to a single hump. For convex regions this falls out of the first result as a short extra step, which makes the new route notably clean.
arxiv-2605-02034:
Yi Ru-Ya Zhang examines Serrin's overdetermined problem and weak Bernoulli laws in domains with rough boundaries. Classical theory assumes smooth, uniform conditions at the boundary, in the style of Alt and Caffarelli. Zhang uses a distributional form of the Bernoulli condition on the reduced boundary, avoiding those regularity assumptions.

For every dimension at least two and a wide class of nonlinear terms, bounded non-spherical domains of finite perimeter satisfy the weak law. Yet their boundary density can blow up at all scales, in the essential sense. The finding shows the key missing control is a uniform surface density bound, not the absence of a reduced boundary. Further results in the paper develop that distinction.
arxiv-2605-02234:
Li Puyin and colleagues present a diagnostic method for causal abstraction, a way to test whether a simple causal story explains a neural network's behaviour. Such stories are usually judged by interchange interventions, where swapping an internal part should swap the output as the story predicts. A single global accuracy score hides where the story holds and where it fails.

Their method partitions inputs into well-interpreted and under-interpreted regions by pairwise intervention behaviour. That turns a global verdict into a diagnosis of regions. Comparing the two regions can reveal missing distinctions in the story. The authors also give heuristics for improving an interpretation from that regional structure, a practice they frame as bucketing the good apples.
arxiv-2605-02334:
Lorenzo Zapparoli, Blazhe Gjorgiev, and Giovanni Sansavini schedule virtual power plants across several markets without drowning in scenarios. A virtual plant pools small energy sources and sells their flexibility. Stochastic plans give strong choices but grow costly as scenarios multiply. Robust plans are cheaper, yet often too cautious.

Their method states uncertainty in a spectral form, using polynomial chaos expansion. That turns the stochastic problem into a low-dimensional form that keeps the uncertainty structure. Standard tools can then solve it fast. The method is shown on a resource-based virtual plant on a real system. The aim is near-stochastic quality at a cost closer to robust methods.
arxiv-2605-02634:
Sergio Estrada and James Gillespie prove results about Gorenstein injective objects in Grothendieck categories, a general setting in abstract algebra. Their central question is when the related cotorsion pair is complete, meaning every object has the approximation maps the theory needs. The answer turns on the existence of a set of special generators.

The pair show completeness holds exactly when such Tate trivial generators exist, and then the pair is perfect and yields an injective abelian model structure. Examples include sheaf categories on well-behaved schemes, even without enough projectives. A broader result treats relative versions built from a chosen set of objects. The key step uses the fact that certain orthogonal classes form accessible subcategories, a size control that makes the arguments run.
arxiv-2605-02834:
Tanush Yadav and eight co-authors introduce VideoNet, a benchmark that returns action recognition in video to the center of model evaluation, with a focus on domain-specific actions. Video models are now rarely tested on naming actions, because older datasets lacked variety and challenge. VideoNet covers a thousand distinct actions across dozens of domains.

In a multiple-choice setting, the gap between closed and open models is stark: a leading closed model scores far above a mid-size open one. Relaxing the task to a yes-no form barely helps the open model. Giving a few example clips helps some models and hurts others, and the gains trail those seen on non-video tasks. The authors argue that domain-specific action skill is a blind spot worth measuring directly.
arxiv-2605-03234:
Jialu Zhang, Xiangdong Ji, Andreas Schäfer, Rui Zhang, and Christian Zimmermann show how parton distribution functions can be extracted from current-current correlators at large momentum. Parton distributions describe the momentum share of quarks and gluons inside a proton, and lattice methods need clean ways to reach them.

Current-current correlators renormalize simply and avoid the linear divergences of quasi-distribution methods, though lattice use needs four-point functions. The team derives the large momentum expansion through next-to-leading order for these correlators. Early numerical work with four-point functions tests the formula, opening a new lattice route to parton structure.
arxiv-2605-03434:
Yu-Ting Lee and Samuel Yen-Chi Chen test whether variational quantum circuits can strengthen hierarchical reinforcement learning, where agents choose among temporally extended options. Quantum feature extraction has helped flat reinforcement learning, but its fit with option-based hierarchy was an open question.

A hybrid agent using a quantum feature extractor beat classical baselines with fewer parameters on standard environments. Yet placing quantum circuits in option-value estimation badly hurt learning, marking a clear bottleneck. Further ablations map how circuit design choices shift performance. The study distills design principles for parameter-efficient hybrid hierarchical agents that use quantum parts where they help.
arxiv-2605-04534:
Minju Park, Ivan Orozco Vasquez, and Cristina Conati study how students actually use large language models while learning to critique academic papers, and whether that use helps or hurts their learning. Most earlier evidence came from problem-solving subjects or tightly controlled experiments, not open coursework.

The data come from two offerings of a research-oriented course where students could use the tools freely and reported their practices on homework assignments. The authors refine a bottom-up classification of usage types, cross-labelled by how much initiative each use shows. They then relate frequency and type of use to performance on three midterm exams, looking for patterns that course designers could act on.
arxiv-2605-04634:
Behnoosh Babaghorbani and five co-authors demonstrate a superconducting logic device. It can be reset to do different jobs, and it can be chained together with copies of itself. Superconducting electronics promise fast, sensitive on-chip work for settings like quantum computing and magnetic sensing. But they need compact, scalable logic.

Their device, a multilayered heater nanocryotron, takes two inputs. It switches between logic operations without extra parts. That shrinks circuit area and simplifies design. The authors also show the devices can in principle drive one another, a requirement for building larger circuits. The work is a step toward larger systems that compute at very cold temperatures.
arxiv-2605-04734:
SangHyun Park proves a decomposition result for directed tori built as products of directed cycles of equal length. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex exactly once before returning, and a decomposition splits all arcs into such cycles. Park shows the equal-side torus splits into as many directed Hamilton cycles as it has dimensions.

The construction splits coordinate directions and uses an integer selection result to assign voltages matching the required arcs. Even lengths need a parity condition, handled with an extra cycle that later recolouring removes. Park also gives explicit low-dimensional cases, and the result extends to related products, Cayley graphs, and stretched tori.
arxiv-2605-04934:
Alexander Usvyatsov proves a result in model theory about extending partial structures into saturated models without changing a chosen part. The setting is a countable theory that is fully stable over a predicate, a named substructure within the models. He introduces a completeness notion capturing the obvious necessary conditions for such an extension.

Usvyatsov shows that any set meeting those conditions, at a given size, can be extended to a saturated model of the same size while its predicate part stays fixed. In fully stable theories, then, existence of this kind can fail only for trivial reasons. The theorem generalises earlier work done for difference fields of characteristic zero.
arxiv-2605-05134:
Dan Wilson and Mohamed Akrout detect language model hallucinations cheaply by treating the model as a black-box dynamical system whose outputs trace its hidden motion. Existing detectors often need expensive repeated sampling or outside knowledge lookups. Their method instead embeds each response and watches the resulting vector sequence evolve over the answer.

Using Koopman operator theory, they fit transition rules for factual and hallucinated regimes separately. A score based on the difference in prediction errors then flags which regime a new response follows. Testing across three benchmarks gave state-of-the-art detection with lower resource use, and the whole check needs only a single sample pass over the model's answer.
arxiv-2605-05334:
Sucheta Majumdar, Aditya Sharma, and Sourav Singha derive fermionic field theories for Carrollian physics, the ultra-relativistic-slow limit where light cones close up, by reducing a higher-dimensional theory along a null direction. Starting from a Bargmann spacetime, the Dirac spinor splits into dynamical good modes and constrained bad modes, a light-cone split valid in any dimension. Boson work had already linked the magnetic Carroll sector to dynamical modes and the electric sector to constrained ones.

Deforming the spacetime removes those constraints, promoting the bad fermions into dynamical electric Carroll fermions. Both electric and magnetic actions then come from one parent Dirac action. The authors check Carroll symmetry, analyse the canonical structure, and compute two-point functions in both sectors.
arxiv-2605-05534:
Attack and defense papers for graph neural networks rarely share experimental settings, so their claims collide. Tran Gia Bao Ngo and four co-authors benchmark adversarial methods under one fair protocol. They re-evaluate seven widely used attacks and eight recent defenses with standardized choices throughout.

The exercise shows how much apparent progress was an artifact of mismatched settings. Ambiguous conclusions in the literature trace back to evaluation details rather than genuine robustness differences. Their benchmark aims to make future comparisons practical and fair, so claimed defenses must survive the same attacks under the same rules.
arxiv-2605-05934:
Alex Blokhuis and three co-authors show how irreversible reactions can create new conserved quantities in chemical networks. Conserved quantities now help researchers infer physical models, but some newly found ones have lacked a clear reading. The team focus on chemical reaction networks and Markov chains where some steps cannot run in reverse.

They show that one way currents force linked production patterns, described by a co-production index, and broken cycles. From this they derive a law that ties conserved quantities, broken cycles, and co-production together. The law settles a puzzle raised by a machine found candidate for a non-integer conservation rule. It also extends a widely used index law that had been undercounting such quantities.
arxiv-2605-06034:
J. Braun and H. J. Bentz evaluate cubic Euler sums of degree four, five, and six in closed form. Euler sums are infinite series built from harmonic numbers, and the cubic nonlinear cases are among the harder ones to pin down. The authors consider three denominator types, including odd denominators and a mixed form, which together span eight families of sums.

For all three orders, they show the complete variety of these nonlinear sums can be calculated explicitly. Every case reduces to values of the zeta function and polylogarithm values at special points, including one half and negative arguments. The result turns a scattered set of hard series evaluations into finished formulas. Such closed forms feed work in number theory and in physics calculations where these sums appear.
arxiv-2605-06134:
Javad Komijani, Marina Marinkovic, and Lara Turgut bring diffusion models to sampling problems in lattice gauge theory. Drawing good samples from complex gauge field distributions is costly with standard simulation methods. Score matching offers a cheaper training route for generative models, and the authors adapt it to SU(N) gauge theories, with extensions to other Lie groups in view.

They test the method on SU(3) gauge configurations with the Wilson action in two and four dimensions. Sample quality is checked against hybrid Monte Carlo simulations, the field's reference method. At strong coupling values, accurate sampling needs predictor corrector schemes, and they add a corrector built on Hamiltonian dynamics. The corrector clearly improves quality but raises cost, and they outline routes to recover efficiency.
arxiv-2605-06334:
Ashwani Anand and three co-authors synthesize compliance benchmarks for tool using language model agents from procedural manuals. Agents in regulated settings must follow strict written procedures, yet manuals are prose for humans while agent behavior is a trace of tool calls. Checking one against the other at scale defeats both hand built benchmarks and model based judges, which the authors set out to replace with formal machinery.

MANTRA builds a symbolic world model and a set of trace level compliance checks independently from the same manual and tool schemas. An SMT solver validates that the two agree, and a repair loop fixes inconsistencies with humans as fallback only. The generated suite holds 285 tasks across six domains, scaling to manuals over fifty pages. Its checks enforce constraints more richly than existing benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06434:
Vaisakh Naduvodi Viswambharan, Keerthan Kopparam Radhakrishna, Deepak Narayan Gadde, and Aman Kumar use knowledge graphs to help language models write formal verification assertions. Generating SystemVerilog Assertions from plain specifications is hard because specifications can be vague and key details live in the hardware design code.

Their graph is built from structured forms of the specification, the design, and formal-tool feedback such as syntax errors and counterexamples. A multi-agent workflow queries it while drafting assertions, then repairs syntax, fixes counterexamples, and adds coverage-driven properties. Across seven benchmark designs, the method produces compilable assertions and formal coverage ranging from 78.5 percent up to 99.4 percent across the designs.
arxiv-2605-06534:
Wei Gao and fifteen co-authors present ROSE, a system that runs reinforcement learning rollouts on GPUs already deployed for serving. Agentic training spends most time on multi-turn rollouts whose demand swings between steps. Fixed clusters cannot adapt, while renting fresh GPUs is slow and often unavailable, yet serving clusters sit partly idle.

ROSE shares those serving GPUs cooperatively through three parts. A co-serving executor protects service targets. A weight transfer engine uses shard-aware routing, and a scheduler routes rollouts across dedicated and spare capacity. Tests show throughput gains over fixed and elastic baselines, with no serving target violations reported.
arxiv-2605-06734:
Kuo-Chung Peng and eighteen co-authors present a gated quantum-inspired sequence learning framework built on fast weight programmers. These models store temporal patterns in rapidly updated weights instead of hidden states. Quantum versions used multi-qubit circuits that are hard to scale on today's noisy devices and costly to simulate, limiting their practical reach.

Their design replaces those circuits with single-qubit re-uploading circuits acting as learnable activations inside a Kolmogorov-Arnold style network, plus a scalar gate that stabilizes weight updates. With only about twelve thousand parameters it beats larger recurrent baselines on long-horizon solar cycle forecasting. The trained model also ran on real IonQ and IBM quantum processors with almost no accuracy loss.
arxiv-2605-06934:
Giansalvo Cirrincione and Adriano Fagiolini combine learning with a classic adaptive controller for mechanical systems such as robot arms. Their design adds three learned parts: a safety measure, a policy adding small torque corrections, and a network estimating missed dynamics. A simple filter checks every output against safety.

The authors prove stability and convergence results for the combined system under stated conditions. On a two-joint arm with friction and changing loads, the learned safety measure drives most of the gain, cutting tracking error notably. A seven-joint robot study shows the full pipeline still converges, while also exposing a warm-start problem worth noting.
arxiv-2605-07134:
Donguk Kwon and Dongha Lee rethink what web agents should see when they look at a page. Agents usually observe single elements, the same level at which they act, and must rediscover a page's organization at every step. The authors argue observation should instead use functional regions, parts of a page that each serve one purpose.

Their Region4Web framework rebuilds the page structure into such regions, and PageDigest delivers a compact digest that persists across steps. On the WebArena benchmark, the digest sharply shortened observations while raising task success across several models and agent methods. Region-level viewing, they conclude, gives agents a smaller yet richer picture.
arxiv-2605-07334:
Junwei Wen and four co-authors segment objects in video from instructions that imply intent rather than naming the target. Existing multimodal methods pick frames by simple sampling or surface similarity, narrowing the view and weakening temporal understanding. RCoT-Seg splits the job into temporal reasoning first and detailed perception second.

An agent-like module chooses and re-chooses a keyframe through self-evaluation, trained with reinforcement learning on curated reasoning starts. Segmentation then runs at high resolution on that frame and propagates masks through the sequence. The authors report favorable results against leading methods, crediting the explicit separation of when to look from what to outline.
arxiv-2605-07434:
Weijian Liu and four co-authors design radar detectors for signals hiding in clutter with a nonzero average. Detecting subspace signals against such background is a practical radar problem. The authors build adaptive detectors from five classical test strategies, including likelihood ratio and Wald tests. Several turn out structurally identical to known zero-mean detectors.

Closed-form expressions for detection and false-alarm probabilities are derived for each detector. Two costs of nonzero-mean clutter emerge: one lost degree of freedom, and a loss in signal-to-clutter ratio. Simulations and measured data confirm the detectors work, supporting their value in real radar systems.
arxiv-2605-07734:
Yoshiki Fukusumi and Shuma Nakashiba classify gapped quantum phases using smeared boundary conformal field theory. They look at massive renormalization group flows that are dual to massless ones when coupling signs flip. Their setup mixes Higgs and Nambu-Goldstone style arguments with Cardy's boundary theory, and several strange structures appear along the way.

The natural basis for the gapped states turns out to be built from smeared Ishibashi states. Those states are unphysical in ordinary critical phenomena. So the gapped module can sit outside the usual boundary module, while its key numbers remain computable. They show this on the flow from the tricritical Ising model to the Ising model. In general, the phases that result usually break noninvertible symmetries spontaneously.
arxiv-2605-07834:
Kentaro Nakamura and Kosuke Imai build a causal inference framework for treatments that live inside unstructured data like text and video, and unfold over time. Scholars increasingly want the effect of features of such material. Existing methods treat each object as one static observation, ignoring that a feature's position in a sequence can matter.

Their approach pulls internal representations of the objects from a generative AI model. It then fits a marginal structural model with a neural network that jointly learns a deconfounder for each treatment feature in the sequence. The semiparametric machinery yields valid confidence intervals, confirmed in simulations. Applied to a randomized experiment on the Hong Kong protests, the method shows a treatment feature's effect depends critically on where it sits in the text.
arxiv-2605-08034:
Houssam Zenati and Arthur Gretton build a test for treatment effects that averages can hide. A treatment may leave mean outcomes unchanged while shifting the tails, spread, or rare-event chances of the outcome distribution. Kernel tests can detect such differences, but a plain rejection does not say where the two distributions part ways.

Their method, DR-ME, evaluates a kernel witness at learned outcome locations and returns readable coordinates of the causal discrepancy. It uses doubly robust kernel features derived from observational data, and the authors characterize its calibration and local power. The test is presented as the first semiparametrically efficient finite-location test of its kind.
arxiv-2605-08434:
Meng Zheng, Samhita Marri, Anwesa Choudhuri, Benjamin Planche, and coauthors teach robot policies from their own failures. Vision-language-action models are usually cloned from successful demonstrations only. Small execution errors then compound during a rollout. The robot drifts somewhere it cannot recover from.

Their AFIL framework has a pretrained policy generate failure rollouts online. That spares hand-designed failure modes and human rescue demonstrations. Two action generators train together on a shared vision-language backbone. One handles success, and one handles failure. At sampling time, the failure generator steers actions away from bad modes. The method targets diffusion and flow based policies.
arxiv-2605-08534:
Aaron Angress and four colleagues examine hot bubbles blown by young stars inside a simulated dwarf spiral galaxy much like NGC 300. Real bubbles are hard to follow over their whole lives, so simulation data offers a rare full view. The team tracks gas parcels to measure bubble size, lifetime, heat, density, and place within the galaxy.

Bubble lifetimes and sizes follow spread out patterns, and longer lived bubbles sit farther from the galactic center. The group also predicts how the bubbles would look in a common red light tracer and compares those views with real observations. Star formation studies gain firmer links between stellar feedback and galactic shape.
arxiv-2605-08734:
Ziyun Liu, Fengmiao Bian, and Jian-Feng Cai rethink the optimizers used to train low rank adapters, the small trainable patches popular for fine tuning large models. The adapter's factor geometry makes the natural preconditioning matrix singular, so a preconditioned direction cannot be uniquely pulled back into factor updates. The authors map existing optimizers into four families based on how they work around that singularity.

Their AdaPreLoRA pairs a memory light diagonal preconditioner with a closed form factor solve that best balances the two factors' contributions. Across language model benchmarks and diffusion personalization, it matches or beats representative rivals while keeping memory at normal adapter levels. Fine tuning practice gains a principled optimizer that respects adapter geometry.
arxiv-2605-08834:
Gabriel Borderes-Motta and nine coauthors reconstruct a bright fireball that crossed northern Sweden on February 27, 2023, using an auroral camera network that happened to catch it. The ALIS_4D imaging system, built to study northern lights, recorded the event in detail. From those recordings the team estimated the trajectory, computed the meteoroid's orbit, and hunted for its parent body.

Fitting an ablation model and simulating the dark flight with local wind data maps a strewn field along the Kiruna and Gällivare border and estimates the rock's physical traits. Orbital similarity points to an Apollo family parent, possibly nudged into collision course by close Earth approaches. Auroral infrastructure proves doubly useful for meteor science.
arxiv-2605-08934:
Ward Gauderis and four coauthors give the study of model guts a firm form. That study takes learned parts of a net and turns them into bits folks can grasp. With no shared frame, such takes can not be checked, set side by side, or joined. Their frame rests on two base thoughts. One is that parts should join in a clean way. One is that short takes are best. A take is a pair of maps, one of form and one of sense. The maps must commute.

Take worth splits into truth to the model and length. That turns the hunt into a search with bounds. A squeeze step can rework a model into more plain parts, with its acts kept. A thrift rule says when squeezed takes must grow more in tune with folks.
arxiv-2605-09034:
Jiahe Chen and Ziye Ma work on a training method for large language models that needs no back-propagation, which makes it attractive for small devices with little memory. Such zeroth-order methods guess the direction of improvement from trial runs, but those guesses are noisy.

The authors find that a trick which helps normal training, fully aligning the update with the strongest directions, backfires when the guesses are noisy. Their fix aligns only partly, boosting the main directions with a faster power-based method run inside a low-dimensional search space. In fine-tuning tests their approach converged one and a half to four times faster than the leading rival method.
arxiv-2605-09134:
Yuanhao Li and five co-authors introduce BoostAPR, a learning framework that aims to fix computer programs automatically with help from actually running the code. Their 2026 study notes that repair training often gets sparse feedback, because a single pass or fail score hides which edits mattered. BoostAPR first fine-tunes on checked examples, then trains two reward models, and then refines the system with reinforcement learning.

One reward model judges whole repair attempts, while the second assigns credit to single lines, guiding learning toward the edits that truly fix a bug. Trained on one repair gym and tested on four benchmarks, the system scores strongly on verified software tasks and transfers from Python problems to Java ones. The results suggest that line-level credit can make automated repair both stronger and better at crossing between programming languages.
arxiv-2605-09334:
Chen and three colleagues settle Mahler's non-symmetric conjecture in dimension three. They establish the sharp lower bound for the non-symmetric volume product of every convex body in three-dimensional space, taken with respect to the Santaló point.

The bound is 64 over 9, the value for simplices, which are the expected minimisers; the classical Blaschke-Santaló inequality gives the matching sharp upper bound, with ellipsoids as extremal bodies. The volume product multiplies a body's volume by the volume of its polar body, and the Santaló point is the centre minimising that polar volume. Proving the three-dimensional non-symmetric case settles Mahler's lower-bound problem there, leaving the higher-dimensional cases open. The result adds a sharp affine inequality for polar bodies, where the extremal bodies turn on symmetry and on which way the inequality runs.
arxiv-2605-09534:
De La Cruz and two colleagues offer a management frame for bringing generative AI into security work without losing control. Security teams blend private data feeds, expert judgment, code stores, cloud tools, and choices where evidence matters. Leaders must decide how to add language models, retrieval, and coding agents to such high risk work. The paper argues AI aided choice support should first be run as a governed skill, not scaled as raw automation.

Using Kusto Query Language on Azure as a bounded test case, the authors show read only queries still carry risk. Wide scans, private field leaks, cost blowouts, stale tips, and false readings can all harm choices. Their governed query broker splits AI planning from action. It uses grounded retrieval, set templates, policy checks, read only links, and clear audit trails, with review board gates before scale up.
arxiv-2605-09734:
Reddy and two colleagues asked whether keeping the full trail of tool calls helps a language model learn new tools in sequence. They fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on API-Bank, a bank of tool-use tasks, split into four domain blocks learned one after another. One training setup stripped earlier API requests and replies from the prompt; the other kept the whole trajectory context.

In a single-seed pilot, the trajectory-keeping setup reached 56.9 percent final exact full-call accuracy against 39.2 percent for the stripped setup, plus 7.7 points on API-name accuracy. The gain cost 25.1 percent more training tokens, and the pilot used one seed on next-call prediction rather than full dialogues. Readers should treat the gap as a promising pilot signal, not a settled verdict.
arxiv-2605-09834:
Choi and O'Hagan proposed a safer way to use AI predictions as prior information in Bayesian reasoning when data are scarce. A predictive model's beliefs can sharpen results, but they can also inject the model's errors into the final verdict. Their framework corrects the AI-made law that generates synthetic data before letting it inform a prior, including as a base measure in a Dirichlet process prior.

The resulting rectified AI prior and posterior come with Gaussian asymptotics under non-vanishing prior strength and a first-order formula for centering bias. Rectified priors cut bias substantially versus standard approaches and improved credible-interval coverage. On a real skin-disease classification task, the rectified prior meaningfully boosted predictive performance, making AI-powered prior information more trustworthy.
arxiv-2605-09934:
Yu and eight colleagues close what they call the provenance gap in tool-using multimodal agents. Such agents show their tool trail and final answer but rarely say which observation supports each claim, so useful evidence, wasted exploration and unsupported leaps blur together. Their framework, TRACER, generates every answer sentence with a structured provenance record naming the tool turn, the evidence unit and the support relation.

Relations come in three kinds: quotation for direct reuse, compression for faithful condensing, and inference for grounded derivation. Each record passes schema checks, turn alignment, source authentication and rationality checks, then feeds reinforcement learning as traceability constraints and local credit. On their TRACE-Bench test set, TRACER with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct reached about seventy-eight percent answer accuracy, while merely adding tools often added noise.
arxiv-2605-10334:
Andrii Yermakov and three colleagues investigate what deepfake detectors actually detect. Recent frame-based detectors generalize better across datasets, yet the mechanism behind that success remains unclear. Their 2026 paper proposes the Alpha Blending Hypothesis: detectors act mainly as alpha-blending searchers, spotting low-level compositing artifacts where a fake face was blended into a real frame.

Experiments support the claim. Detectors prove highly sensitive to self-blended images and non-generative edits, even without seeing such cases in training. The authors then build BlenD, trained on real-only facial images augmented with self-blended images, without any explicitly generated deepfakes. It achieved the best average cross-dataset generalization across 15 compositional deepfake datasets from 2019 to 2025. An ensemble with blending-resilient models reached 94.0 percent AUROC, a ranking-quality score.
arxiv-2605-10434:
Keming Wu and thirteen colleagues test whether video generators truly grasp how the world evolves. Commercial systems such as Seedance and Veo have improved fast, feeding the view that video generators are becoming world models. Yet no benchmark had checked whether a model grasps how an observed world ought to evolve. Their 2026 paper introduces WorldReasonBench, reframing video testing as world-state prediction.

Starting from a state plus an action, can a model produce a future video that stays physically, socially, logically, and informationally sound? The benchmark holds 436 curated test cases with QA notes across four reasoning dimensions and 22 subcategories. Evaluation pairs reasoning checks, using QA to catch temporal and causal failures, with quality scoring for ranking and reward modeling. A companion choice benchmark, WorldRewardBench, adds about 6,000 expert pairs over 1,400 videos. Results expose a persistent gap: videos can look convincing while getting dynamics, causality, or detail preservation wrong.
arxiv-2605-10534:
Gretchen L. Matthews and Julia Shapiro construct quantum error-correcting codes from Hermitian curves. Folded Reed-Solomon codes, from Guruswami and Rudra in 2007, achieve the best possible trade-off between code rate and error radius. In 2024, Bergamaschi, Golowich, and Gunn extended the framework with folded quantum Reed-Solomon codes, tolerating errors up to the quantum Singleton bound. Their 2026 paper builds folded quantum Hermitian codes using the CSS framework.

The authors show these codes are also list-decodable, handling errors up to the same bound. Compared with Reed-Solomon codes, these codes admit similar lengths over smaller alphabets, enabling more efficient builds. That combination matters because smaller alphabets ease the practical cost of quantum error correction while keeping the strong decoding radius that folding provides. Readers get a build that carries the folded-code advantage into the Hermitian setting while keeping that property.
arxiv-2605-10634:
Minyu Chen and four colleagues use learned tuning policies as teachers for heuristic search. Auto heuristic design shows promise for combinatorial tuning, but existing methods lean mainly on delayed endpoint performance. Their 2026 paper proposes a teacher-aware evolution framework using trained policies as action teachers. Instead of using or cloning the teacher, the method queries it on states visited by candidate programs.

It uses the teacher's action picks as local feedback for search. The search finds static working heuristics guided by task performance and teacher-derived action signals. Tests on scheduling, routing, and graph benchmarks show the method beats performance baselines. It requires no neural compute at deployment. Learned policies can thus be reused as action feedback for auto heuristic search.
arxiv-2605-10934:
Yaman Kındap and four colleagues bring variational inference to Lévy-driven stochastic differential equations, the jump-heavy models behind extreme events in finance, climate, and safety-critical AI. Monte Carlo methods are rigorous but slow, while neural variational methods assume Gaussian shapes that miss jumps.

Their neural exponential tilting reweights the Lévy measure with neural networks, keeping jump structure while staying tractable. A quadratic setup gives closed-form normalization, a bell-curve view steadies simulation, and symmetry-aware estimators scale optimization. Tests show accurate capture of jump behavior where bell-curve methods fail. Modelers of extremes get a fast, faithful inference toolkit.
arxiv-2605-11034:
Gayan K. Kulatilleke and three colleagues present MambaNetBurst, a compact byte-level classifier for network traffic bursts that needs no tokenization or pretraining. Most strong traffic classifiers lean on heavy engineered features or self-supervised pretraining, while this method works directly on raw packet bytes.

For every flow, the model builds one fixed-size burst out of the opening packets. It embeds the byte sequence with a learnable class token and processes it through residual pre-normalized Mamba-2 blocks for end-to-end supervised classification. On six public benchmarks spanning encrypted app identification, VPN and Tor traffic, malware, and IoT attacks, it matches or beats heavier pretrained baselines. Ablations show byte-level timing resolution matters most, early striding hurts, and moderate state sizes suffice. Network defenders get a light, direct traffic classifier.
arxiv-2605-11434: Jin Yang, Xiaobing Yu and Peijie Qiu propose FEFormer, a frequency-enhanced vision transformer for volumetric medical image segmentation. Standard vision transformers struggle with fine local detail, spatial preservation in MLP modules, naive encoder-decoder fusion and weak low-level propagation. FEFormer answers with four frequency-domain components: dynamic self-attention, a gating MLP, wavelet-guided adaptive fusion and a cross-scale stem bridge. Tested on four volumetric tasks, it beats state-of-the-art methods with high computational efficiency.
arxiv-2605-12034: Che Liu and six colleagues clean up omni-modal evaluation, where visual shortcuts can inflate benchmark gains. They audited nine omni-modal benchmarks by testing visual-only answers, removed visually solvable queries, and kept full subsets where filtering was undefined or unstable. The result, OmniClean, retains 8,551 of 16,968 audited queries. Their three-stage OmniBoost recipe then lifted a 3B model to match or slightly beat Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct without a stronger teacher.
arxiv-2605-12734: Bhosale and five colleagues make overdecomposition work well on distributed-memory GPGPU systems. Overdecomposition assigns many small objects per chip and has proven strong for adaptive mesh refinement and tree codes. Charm++ has shown its use across uses. Graphics processors as main compute parts raised extra cost and porting issues, above all from putting many objects onto one device. Their tools and code show overdecomposition can run well across GPU vendor types and links.
arxiv-2605-13134: Mitsos, Dimarogonas and Liu present a secure-by-design planning and control setup for multi-agent systems under linear temporal logic specs. It shields secrets from a passive intruder who partly sees agent motion, blocking both inference that a secret task ran and naming of the agent behind it. Safety rules enter the build process directly, via a secure finite transition system that drops all paths that break them. Standard synthesis then yields discrete plans, refined into flyable continuous paths. A two-drone case study tests the setup.
arxiv-2605-13234: Adrián Aguirre-Tamaral and colleagues find a shared law for how early embryos slow their cell division. Across many animal groups, division slows as maternal resources run down, following a hyperbolic curve toward a halt. Data from cnidarians, worms, insects, molluscs, starfish relatives, sea squirts, frogs and fish all fall on one curve. Changing resource supply shifts timing as predicted, pointing to resource use as a driver of developmental pace.
arxiv-2605-13334: Nogueira and colleagues show a frontier language model can talk another frontier model past its guardrails. Asked directly to write essays denying settled science or defending racial hierarchies, frontier models refuse. Yet the same model, role playing a user over five turns, coaxes targets into producing those essays with peer pressure and reframing alone. Across nine pairings and six topics, elicitation never hits zero, and some pairings reach full production on several topics.
arxiv-2605-13434: Ammar Mahran, Artavazd Maranjyan and Peter Richtarik propose Rescaled Asynchronous SGD to fix bias in distributed learning under heterogeneity. In asynchronous gradient descent, the server updates whenever a gradient arrives, so fast workers contribute more. With mixed data, vanilla ASGD leans toward a frequency-weighted average of goals, not the global goal. Existing fixes add gathering or buffering. The authors instead rescale stepsizes by compute time, so every worker contributes the same learning rate. They prove convergence to the correct goal, with time cost at the lower bound.
arxiv-2605-13834: Dongzhe Zheng, Tao Zhong and Christine Allen-Blanchette study answer tools of real field rules on shape meshes from a function-space view. Building on Hodge theory and operator splitting, they derive a sound split into a Hybrid Euler design with a built-in bias called Hodge Spectral Duality. Their frame uses split change forms to capture shape-ruled parts and a right-angle helper ambient space to show complex local motion.
arxiv-2605-14134: Van den Bosch, Van Gaans and Verduyn Lunel study stochastic Mackey-Glass equations and other negative feedback systems, asking when invariant measures exist. Each equation, including Nicholson's blowflies equation, is shaken by a scaling noise term. Solutions persist and stay bounded above in probability under mild rules. A non-trivial invariant measure exists exactly when some start keeps the solution away from zero in probability. Noise may be any square integrable Levy process with finite intensity, and existence follows via the Krylov-Bogoliubov method, with runs identifying the measures.
arxiv-2605-14234: MacAulay studies the groups of permutation automata behind iterated run-length codes. Run-length decoding swaps a number a for a run of length a, and iterated decodings on two-number alphabets define the well-known Kolakoski sequence. These automata sit inside a group with a twisted recursive shape, and their limit group is plausibly weakly regular branch. In one use, MacAulay counts the longest orbits of the automata for any input sequence when n is odd.
arxiv-2605-14334: Kozlov, Mirmohseni and Tafazolli study secure joint source-channel coding for multimodal semantic sources over wiretap channels. The encoder observes samples from a subset of modalities. Samples are encoded with wiretap coding and a shared secret key, then sent over a wiretap channel for the receiver to rebuild all modalities. Rate-distortion-perception results extend to semantic sources. Outer and inner bounds cover the tradeoff between transmission rate, key rate, and fidelity under per-modality distortion and per-subset equivocation constraints. The secrecy limit has three operationally distinct components.
arxiv-2605-14434: In 2026, Zhu and colleagues propose generative retrieval for e-commerce search as a recall-stage supplement, not an end-to-end replacement. Their CQ-SID method encodes items into hierarchical semantic cluster identifiers, cutting beam search complexity. EG-GRPO, an expert-guided method, aligns generative recall with downstream ranking under sparse rewards. Offline TmallAPP tests show semantic click hitrate gains up to 26.76 percent over baselines, while halving beam search size. Online tests confirm merchandise-value and conversion gains. The channel now drives most exposures and nearly three quarters of purchases.
arxiv-2605-14534: Li, You, Hu, Liu, Chen, Wang, Wang, Zhou and Luan build a benchmark for judging object removal in images and video. Existing scores reward copy-paste erasure or favour blurry results, so they propose Removal Coherence metrics for spatial coherence and temporal consistency across frames. Their PROVE-Bench pairs eighty motion-augmented videos with a hundred harder videos lacking ground truth, and the metrics are claimed to match human judgement better.
arxiv-2605-14634: Le-Anh, Nguyen Hoang, Le and Bui present RustPrint, a documentation-guided agentic framework that migrates whole C repositories to Rust. It first turns the source repo into architecture-aware documentation capturing modules, data flow, APIs and design rationale, then coding agents plan crates, implement modules, check compilability and cut unsafe code. Output documentation is compared with source documentation as a repair signal, and translated tests are run. All eight tested repos are claimed to compile.
arxiv-2605-14934: Kirill Kavokin works out, in theory, how resonant light cooling of nuclear spins behaves when photoexcited electrons carry a strong Knight field. That field, from spin-polarized charge carriers, can outweigh the local fields between neighboring nuclear spins. The resulting Overhauser field then reshapes how carrier spin polarization varies with magnetic field. The effect shows up in the Hanle curve, the dip in polarization measured as a magnetic field is swept.
arxiv-2605-15034: Vinicius Covas and Jorge Alberto Hidalgo Toledo ask whether language models shift their speech when they believe they are watched. In 100 multi-agent debate sessions across five observation framings, from explicit researcher monitoring to an automated AI auditor, monitored groups showed larger vocabulary shifts than audience-framed groups. Message length moved in a separate pattern. The findings matter for auditing, since observation itself may change the behavior under inspection.
arxiv-2605-15134: Will Schwarzer and Scott Niekum study how to forecast an ML model's deployment failure rate from a small evaluation set. Extrapolating from the largest failure scores predicts deployment-scale rates. It carries a built-in bias toward over-prediction, the safety-favorable direction. That bias flips when evaluation misses a rare high-failure mode present at deployment. The authors propose a forecastability fine-tuning loss that addresses this blind spot, cutting held-out forecast error in a password game and a gridworld.
arxiv-2605-15334: Yihong Dong and nine others tackle program synthesis from input-output behavior, a harder problem than building from natural language, which can lean on pretraining fit. Their DIO-Agent frames the task as evolutionary search over program space, with a language model as mutation operator and execution errors guiding each step. A transformation-priority premise biases changes toward the simplest hypothesis consistent with evidence, climbing from constants to conditionals to loops only when simpler forms fail. A benchmark supports methodical study.
arxiv-2605-15434: Jonathan Chapman and Akshat Mudgal give a count formula for answers to a quadratic determinant equation. The variables are whole numbers in a set range. They mix counting tricks with analytic tools and bounds for Kloosterman sums. The main case puts the target near the square of the bound. There they win sharper square-root error terms by using an added symmetry via Ramanujan sums. The result proves a guess of Dhanda, Haynes, and Prasala in very broad form.
arxiv-2605-15634: Shen Bian studies a 1D thin film equation where clumping fights repulsion. Repulsion comes from fourth-order diffusion, clumping from backward second-order degenerate diffusion. For every positive exponent, a unique nonnegative, radially decreasing steady state exists, except in the mass-critical case. That state matches the extremal function of the Sz.-Nagy inequality and minimizes free energy. In the supercritical regime, blow-up hits data with free energy below the state's threshold and power norm above the state's. Below that norm, solutions live globally and their second moment diverges.
arxiv-2605-16034: Alday and four colleagues study the Sudakov form factor and a four-point scattering amplitude in planar N=4 SYM theory on its Coulomb branch. The setup probes how infrared-sensitive quantities shift between on-shell and off-shell regimes. They identify a scaling limit where both observables follow a walking anomalous dimension. That dimension bridges the cusp value on-shell and the octagon value off-shell, and the authors propose an all-loop form for it.
arxiv-2605-16134: Dufort-Labbé and five colleagues introduce LLQR+SAM, a sharpness-aware minimization method that respects loss geometry. Standard SAM perturbs parameters uniformly, ignoring that some directions curve more than others. A learned preconditioner from the LLQR framework captures a smoothed picture of the landscape, and SAM then probes curvature on top of it. Theory shows the preconditioner amplifies escape signals from locally sharp potholes while wide flat basins stay stable, and experiments beat both SAM and LLQR alone.
arxiv-2605-16434: Diaz studies the second law in the context of combinatorial processes, looking at the ways that give rise to irreversible behavior from deterministic, invertible, and reversible dynamics. The paper asks how one-way trends arise from dynamics that are deterministic, invertible, and reversible. Its focus is the mechanism linking those reversible rules to one-way results. The question is how a one-way trend can come from rules that run the same in both directions, and the paper treats that puzzle through combinatorial processes.
arxiv-2605-16734: Paul and colleagues present FIRM3D, an open-source Python, C++, and CUDA suite for modeling energetic-particle motion in 3D magnetic fields for fusion research. Fast particles rarely collide, so Monte Carlo orbit samples can be tracked in set fields, including equilibrium fields and waves that move particles by resonance. The suite offers CPU and GPU guiding-center tracking, equilibrium and wave interfaces, and tools such as Poincaré maps and orbit sorting. It grew from SIMSOPT with few dependencies for wider use.
arxiv-2605-16934: Bhalli's team gives the first method to estimate a target's Doppler shift with mobile, unsynchronised multistatic sensing-and-communication nodes and no external reflector. Clock mismatch between a moving transmitter and receivers, plus node motion, adds extra Doppler parts and phase offsets that distort the target's own frequency shift. Using phase offsets shared across multipath parts and geometric relations, they show the problem is solvable with at least four receivers. Numerical simulations across varied scenes confirm the approach works.
arxiv-2605-17134: Botelho, Nguyen and Roy give a simple explicit test for wave breaking in a broad family of perturbed Burgers equations. The family covers fractional KdV, Whitham and Fornberg-Whitham models. Their proof is short and rigorous, and the test tells directly when a smooth wave profile must steepen until it breaks.
arxiv-2605-17734: Hongjun Liu and three colleagues turn agent skills from passive advice into runnable code. Their HASP framework upgrades lessons from past work into Program Functions that fire on failure-prone states. A Program Function can change the next action or inject corrective context, acting as a guardrail inside the agent loop. HASP works at run time, in post-training, or through controlled evolution of a checked skill library. Run-time functions alone lift web-search reasoning by 25% over a multi-loop ReAct agent.
arxiv-2605-17934: Yichen Shen and Mengxin Yu introduce C-SymmPI, a method giving near-conditional cover for data shapes with group symmetries. Existing methods rely on i.i.d. or exchangeable setups, often violated for networks, clusters, and imaging data. Using relaxed multi-accuracy, the approach recasts conditional cover as miscoverage error over a chosen function class. The team proves guarantees under invariance and shift, giving convergence rates for linear and RKHS function classes. Two variants aid computation: projection-based for high-dimensional data, and sampling-based for large or infinite groups.
arxiv-2605-18234: Thomas Voje's 2026 paper rebuilds massive-star evolution with detailed atmosphere physics in place of the usual Eddington gray shortcut. With the STAREVOL code, outer edge values come from a CMFGEN atmosphere grid at each step, tracking Galactic massive stars through late phases including the Wolf-Rayet stage. Detailed atmospheres greatly lower model effective temperatures, matching Wolf-Rayet observations far better, while barely touching inner structure. Post-processing temperature and gravity fixes prove equal to full inclusion, but only detailed atmospheres place evolved stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
arxiv-2605-18434: Xinyu Sun and seven co-authors present TIGER-FG, a 2026 text-guided grounding system for image-to-multimodal e-commerce retrieval, where a cropped image query must match full item images plus structured text. Item text guides target-focused representations without object detection, while dual distillation objectives preserve spatial consistency and query-item similarity. It beats the strongest baseline on Recall@1 by 6.1 and 34.4 points on two benchmarks, with only 85.7M query-side parameters.
arxiv-2605-18534: Israel Zexer and Omri Azencot present XCTFormer, a 2026 transformer-based channel-dependent model for multivariate time-series analysis capturing cross-temporal and cross-channel dependencies directly.
