Tokens model pairwise dependencies across time and channels via a Cross-Relational Attention Block, with an optional Dependency Compression Plugin for scalability. On three benchmarks it performs strongly, taking state-of-the-art imputation results by beating the second-best method by 20.8 percent in MSE and 15.3 percent in MAE on average.
arxiv-2605-18634: Júlio Araújo and three co-authors extend, in a 2026 study, work on harmonious colorings of graphs. In such a coloring, every pair of edges must carry a different color pair. They compare the harmonious chromatic numbers of two graphs when one comes from the other by merging vertices at distance at least three. A fix to an earlier proof tightens one known upper bound. They also give the first integer-linear programming formulations for the problem, plus heuristics, and test them on random cases and DIMACS Challenge instances.
arxiv-2605-18734: Ruiping Liu and nine co-authors introduce EgoExoMem, a 2026 benchmark for cross view memory reasoning. It holds 2 point 6 thousand questions across eight question types. They propose E-Squared-Select, a training free frame picker for dual view retrieval. It combines budget allocation with per view k DPP sampling. Synced ego and exo views give complementary cues, yet existing models stay far from solving it. The best model reaches only about fifty-five percent, while the new method reaches about fifty-eight percent, beating memory baselines.
arxiv-2605-18834: Maximilian Puelma Touzel maps the fitness landscape of social norms in social dilemmas. Norms coordinate many agents by setting rules from noisy outside signals. Those signals must line up enough to reward joint work yet stay murky enough to deter cheating. Building on earlier work that groups norms by reason tests, he studies joint strategies that match optimal single-player play. Such strategies, he finds, satisfy a correlated equilibrium rather than a Nash equilibrium, and he explores how such norms could emerge.
arxiv-2605-19434: Migliore and team study how curve geometry controls whether Hartshorne-Rao modules have the Lefschetz properties. For general skew lines they prove multiplication by powers of a general linear form has maximal rank. Curves on a smooth quadric keep the weak property, as do unions with all but one line there. But with ten or more lines and all but two on a quadric, it can fail. Low-degree smooth curves and general rational curves keep the weak property, yet a degree 15 curve breaks it.
arxiv-2605-19534: Dey, Gizon and Bekki use a global inertial mode to sense solar rotation deep inside the Sun, where sound modes constrain polar regions poorly. Starting from a rotation profile for 2010 to 2024, they compute how local rotation changes shift the frequency of the m=1 high-latitude mode. Its kernel peaks at 75 degrees latitude and 0.8 solar radii, with widths of 7 degrees and 0.13 radii. From the observed frequency they infer rotation near that spot of 365.3 nanohertz, exceeding the reference figure by 8.1 nanohertz.
arxiv-2605-20134: Zhen Xiong, Shang-Ling Hsu and Cyrus Shahabi present TrajTok, a trajectory encoder for raw GPS traces. It first learns a multi-scale hexagonal cell partition from the spatial spread of GPS points, turning noisy sequences into discrete cell tokens. A factorised transformer encoder then captures geometry and kinematics with early per-modality attention, cross-attention fusion and rotary position embeddings. Pretrained by masked-token modelling, a frozen TrajTok encoder with light task adapters beats task-specific methods on Porto data for similarity search, classification and travel-time tasks.
arxiv-2605-20334: Danial Motlagh and Matthew Pocrnic halve the cost of QROM, quantum read-only memory. They first cut its cost to 2N/λ + 2b(λ-1) + 2λ-6 by swapping the SelectSwap architecture for SelectCopy. Next, for the qubit-constrained regime, they cut cost from about 2N/λ to (1+1/b)N/λ, a cut of about 50% that matches clean-qubit QROM with dirty qubits. Last, they give a parametric family that slides the prefactor of the N/λ term from 2 to (1+1/b), giving the best cost for each qubit availability regime.
arxiv-2605-20634: Mous-Abou Hamadou and three colleagues build joint confidence regions for linear regression when errors depend over time in a steady, ergodic way. Their method applies random smoothing with an extra sample and shrinking bandwidth to regression and second-moment stats. That yields Wald regions and joint intervals without directly estimating long-run variance or assuming a dependence model. Simulations show near-nominal coverage and region sizes that rival Newey-West methods.
arxiv-2605-21034: Hui Liu and Zhihao Xu identify anomalous scale-free localization and impurity-induced loss flashes in a non-Hermitian dissipative grid. By a nearby basis rotation, the model maps onto a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice, where impurities act as tunable edges. Tuning impurity strength links two open-boundary-like limits, at strength near zero and near infinity, via generalized-boundary regimes and the impurity-free periodic point at strength one. For other finite strengths, spectral loops reveal the anomalous behaviour.
arxiv-2605-21134: Alessandro Abate, Mirco Giacobbe, Sergey Ichtchenko, and Diptarko Roy give a general method for proof rules for reactivity traits of Markov chains. Such traits cover omega-regular traits and include linear temporal logic. The core result splits each trait into tasks of almost-sure halting in absorbing zones, which always exist on general state spaces. In plain terms, a hard proof task is cut into smaller halting tasks. The method extends halting proof rules to reactivity, and yields the first complete supermartingale certificates of this kind.
arxiv-2605-21234: Haris Aziz and colleagues study the team order problem: arranging one team's players against a fixed opposing order to maximize the chance of winning enough matches. Input is a graph of win probabilities for each pairing, and output is the optimal ordering for team one. Their central result is a polynomial-time approximation scheme whose winning probability falls at most epsilon short of optimal. They also give tractability results for special cases and a bound on how far a maximum-weight matching falls from the best achievable probability.
arxiv-2605-21434: Youcheng Sun and co-authors propose agentic model checking, coupling language-model agents with a bounded model checking backend under the principle agents propose, solvers verify. Verifying language-model-generated systems code is hard: bugs are prevalent, formal specifications are missing, and safety contracts sit implicitly at call sites. Agents handle semantic judgment tasks such as spec inference and counterexample classification, while bounded model checking discharges every soundness-relevant decision.
arxiv-2605-21534: Roberto Cavoretto and co-authors present Adaptive RBF-KAN, evaluating shape settings in Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks approximate complex functions with learnable edge functions, usually set by B-spline bases. Spline versions can be costly to run. FastKAN improves speed with Gaussian radial basis functions, but relies on a fixed kernel and shape parameter. They extend the radial-basis framework with a broader kernel family, setting shape settings via leave-one-out cross-validation, and adding Matérn and Wendland kernels.
arxiv-2605-21834: Andy Han and co-authors present On-Policy Consistency Training, a tuning approach scoring its own responses, supervised on contrastive prompts. Earlier consistency training makes supervision once offline, then fine-tunes, so models memorize surface forms, generalize poorly, and lose skill. Across three model groups, OPCT beats its supervised rival on sycophancy, jailbreaking, and safety awareness, halving it and holding jailbreak defense near ninety-nine percent. It also largely avoids capability regressions, such as a twenty-eight-point MATH-500 drop from supervised fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-21934: Jingyi Liu and co-authors study a single-item auction where a revenue-maximizing intermediary controls which bidder messages reach the seller. Classical theory assumes bids arrive directly, but platforms and blockchain auctions often sit in between. For regular value distributions, the seller's revenue can fall arbitrarily far below the no-intermediary optimum. For strongly regular distributions, posted prices win back a constant fraction, with a tight link to the strength parameter. Timing also matters: neither sequential order always wins, and simultaneous play can leave both sides unboundedly worse off.
arxiv-2605-22034: Haocheng Li and co-authors present AgroVG, a large multi-source benchmark for agricultural visual grounding, the task of locating objects described in natural language. Reliable evaluation is hard because farm targets are often small, repetitive, occluded, or oddly shaped, and instructions may name one, many, or no objects. AgroVG supplies protocols for box-set matching and query mask coverage. Zero-shot tests of 26 configurations reveal persistent gaps: the best multi-target Set-F1 reaches only 0.35, and the best positive-query mask success at IoU 0.75 stays below 0.17.
arxiv-2605-22134: Micha-Mba and co-authors bootstrap two-nucleon effective field theories, comparing renormalization approaches. Chiral theory yields singular potentials needing regularization and renormalization in a dynamical equation like the Lippmann-Schwinger equation. The authors compare contact-term renormalization, the common approach, against the exact N/D method with multiple subtractions. A toy model with a finite-range expansion and bootstrap testing checks statistical consistency. They then apply it to chiral theory at leading and next-to-leading order against the Granada analysis, finding next-to-leading order extends its range.
arxiv-2605-22234: Chen, Petersen and Hippalgaonkar address materials whose crystal sites hold different elements or gaps with set odds, a pattern common in alloys, ceramics and even water ice. Standard first-principles simulation assumes perfect order, so such disordered crystals stay out of reach. Their Virp pipeline builds virtual cells by permutation, samples them, and adds thermodynamic post-processing, showing 400 cells suffice when the supercell is large enough.
arxiv-2605-22534: Peralta and team ask why agent pull requests merge or fail, from 11,048 closed agent PRs, 9,799 human-checked, with 717 read cases. Failed outcomes exceed agent error. Only 35.7 percent of rejected PRs showed clear agentic faults; 31.2 percent stemmed from workflow constraints and 33.1 percent lacked seen reasons. Among merged PRs, 15.4 percent needed review help, and 5.5 percent showed no talk trace. Copilot and Devin appear more in review-led workflows; Codex and Cursor PRs merge with little talk. PR outcomes alone miss agent skill; talk-aware judging is needed.
arxiv-2605-22634: Liu proposes contractual skills, a GovernSpec inspired way to write agent skill files as readable task contracts for enterprise use. A contractual skill spells out goals, input limits, permissions, approval points, evidence needs, output terms, quality bars, checks and handoff rules, while keeping discovery light. Three offline studies back the design: contractual rewrites lift mean quality from 4.692 to 4.914 and cut critical errors from 0.083 to 0.013 in a public skill test. Liu reads the framework as a governance layer making intent explicit, not as a safety tool on its own.
arxiv-2605-22734: Ahmed and others add time to biomedical knowledge graphs, where a symptom may point to one disease at age 3 and another at age 13. Their ChronoMedKG holds 460,497 linked triples across 13,431 diseases, each tied to onset windows or progression stages backed by literature and credibility scores. Built by language models extracting from PubMed and PMC under consensus and filtering rules, the graph agrees with Orphadata at about 93 percent. It adds time grounding for 6,250 diseases missing elsewhere. A companion benchmark shows ChronoMedKG retrieval rescues far more long tail temporal failures than rival sources.
arxiv-2605-22934: Holder and three coauthors examine how neutral hydrogen absorbs long-wave cosmic microwave background photons beyond 21 centimeters. This adds dimming beyond usual Thomson scattering. Optical depth versus frequency tracks the spin temperature of the gas over cosmic time. It peaks at a few percent near 100 megahertz. Detecting the background at such wavelengths is hard. Cross-correlation with well-mapped centimeter and millimeter fluctuations may ease it. Such measures could directly gauge neutral fraction over spin temperature by redshift.
arxiv-2605-23034: Larssen, Peng, and Markidis ask which superconducting qubit model is good enough for pulse-level simulation of a flux-tunable two-qubit device with a fixed bus coupler. They compare an effective two-level model, one three-mode Duffing model, plus a circuit-based transmon design in the charge basis across spectra, interaction terms, driven dynamics, CZ gates, leakage, and runtime. The Duffing model tracks the circuit reference best for static quantities, while multilevel models reveal driven effects the effective model misses. They endorse layered use of abstraction.
arxiv-2605-23134: Yang and Li present acopula, a framework for Archimedean copula inference with exact gradients. No existing nested tool handles per-variable censoring, nesting trees, and exact gradients. Given any generator, acopula evaluates exact likelihoods and gradients under censoring masks in polynomial time. The method powers Taylor-mode output, swapping hand-derived tables with one computation any generator can drive. Simulations verify correctness. Demos include 85,229 cases at size 53, an 11-sector S and P 500 model, ten-family cut likelihood, and 650 times speedup over R nacLL.
arxiv-2605-23234: Lettich and three coauthors generalize spatial fairness for models. They move from home locations to activity spaces, regions a person visits. Literature maps each person to one place, but fairness across regularly visited regions also matters. Their approach links people to activity regions. It uses spatial partitions at different resolutions. A spatial scan statistic then judges whether a model is fair on activity patterns. Tests over thousands of synthetic datasets show it detects this unfairness type and retrieves unfair objects. Localization shows a multi-resolution trade-off.
arxiv-2605-23434: Xu and three colleagues frame deep Gaussian process inference as posterior transport, learning a deterministic sampler that maps a simple reference measure to posterior inducing variables. Their OM-Path method runs a probability-flow equation along a Doob-bridged diffusion, with the Onsager-Machlup action as path regularizer and no score matching needed. On seven UCI regression benchmarks it beats the DBVI baseline significantly on the two largest sets, ties on two more, and yields to DBVI on three small noisy sets. Strict exact-density variants never clear DBVI anywhere.
arxiv-2605-23534: van Essen and colleagues show programmable control of high-harmonic emission in solids, a route toward compact short-wave sources and fast optical switches. Harmonic light responds sharply to driving field and matter, yet no general control frame had existed. Tuning two knobs, the true nonlinear order and the built-in emission phase, they suppress or enhance emission across many semiconductors and dielectrics, joining parametric and non-parametric modulation, with higher pathways revived. Bloch equation simulations back the photon-pathway model and its time-domain picture.
arxiv-2605-24134: Bousetouane presents ProofAgent Harness, infrastructure for testing AI agents under pressure across many turns, rather than grading single outputs or fixed tasks. The harness gathers test cases, runs hostile multi-turn trials, and records behaviour traces. Scoring uses several calibrated juror personas plus consensus checks and turn-level evidence. Trials across support, medical triage, privacy and security work, and code generation show strong agents failing narrowly, through fragile turns, weak metrics, manipulation paths, and unsafe reframing. Strikingly, a small quantized local model running the harness can challenge top production agents.
arxiv-2605-24334: Mercado and five co-authors compare models and rules for Al polar nitrides. Using density theory, they compare mean mix versus random-mix structures and PBE, PBESol, SCAN, and SCAN+rVV10. Even similar PBE and PBESol diverge: random-mix PBESol lowers wurtzite hold in Sc-alloyed nitride versus PBE or SCAN. A five-fold six-sided phase from 2002 shows as a half-stable state between wurtzite and rocksalt. Boron-alloyed nitride weakens wurtzite faster, ending in zincblende and six-sided phases. Random-mix structures with SCAN prove best.
arxiv-2605-24534: Max Prior, Niklas Wais, and Matthias Grabmair automate a laborious legal task: turning large court-decision collections into commentaries on statutes. From 4,555 German Federal Court of Justice decisions citing four Civil Code sections, they extract reasoning chunks, summarize them, and cluster the results. Language models then draft headings and citation-rich sections, merged into coherent commentaries. Expert and model judges rated the output on five dimensions, finding refreshable reports feasible but limited by narrow sources and legal normativity, published in 2026.
arxiv-2605-24634: Amsisan Tran and others rethink image retrieval that pairs a photo with a text edit. A query like make it more formal points to a region of images, not one answer. Scoring such queries against a single target thus punishes good matches. Their fix gives back a candidate shortlist with a promised hit rate, and the size of that shortlist gauges query ambiguity. When the list stays large, it asks one useful follow-up question. Tests show it reaches the target with far less back-and-forth.
arxiv-2605-24834: Lixing Lin and co-authors present Reflect-Guard, a safety classifier that reasons before it judges. Standard guards catch overt harm but fall to jailbreaks hiding malice in role play or fiction. Reflect-Guard distills GPT-4o-mini reasoning into reflection notes, then trains a Llama Guard model with QLoRA to reflect before verdicts. With a thousand training examples and half a percent of parameters updated, adversarial recall jumps from about half to over nine in ten. Attack success falls from about ten percent to under two percent.
arxiv-2605-25234: David Rügamer rethinks a familiar claim about doubt in oversized neural networks. The usual view says that epistemic doubt, the kind more data should shrink, equals variation in predictions. But matching symmetries and spare weights leave many settings alike, so doubt about settings can last even once the learned function is fixed. Looking at single-hidden-layer nets with ReLU units, he maps both broken-up and smooth sources of that leftover doubt, and tests back the account.
arxiv-2605-25834: Zhong and Karma use phase-field simulations to explain peritectic melting of Ti-Ag into linked structures. A Ti-rich solid growing through a silver-rich film develops a seaweed or dendritic structure. Its branches coalesce into handles, generating a bicontinuous topology. Sharp-interface theory predicts a front velocity and an initial ligament width constant in time, unlike liquid metal dealloying. Later coarsening follows a one-third power law, matching the observed ligament width.
arxiv-2605-26034: Quang and Chi prove a broad second main theorem for maps into projective varieties that may blow up. The maps are meromorphic, allowed to blow up at some points, like ratios of polynomials. The setting covers any family of slowly moving hypersurfaces, with no demand that the map be algebraically nondegenerate over the linked field. Truncation levels of the counting functions are bounded explicitly. The total defect bound is the distributive constant times three times the dimension minus one, independent of the map itself.
arxiv-2605-26134: Capolupo, Capozziello, Pisacane and Quaranta review how neutrino mixing in curved spacetime could add to dark matter. They work in curved-spacetime quantum field theory. There, the flavour vacuum's stress-energy acts like dust and cold dark matter. For weakly curved, round spacetimes, the vacuum adds a Yukawa-style tweak to Newton's gravity law. That tweak can explain why spiral galaxies spin with flat rotation curves. Neutrino mixing thus looks like a plausible partial source of dark matter.
arxiv-2605-26334: Manyi Guo and seven colleagues pin down the RO(C2)-graded Hurewicz images of three C2-equivariant Eilenberg-MacLane spectra. The three cover two-element fields, integers, and the Burnside functor. Surprisingly, the answer ties to sphere vector fields. An element in the negative cone lies in the image exactly when its sphere admits that many independent vector fields. Generalized Leibniz and Mahowald tricks yield Adams differentials of arbitrary length, all nonzero, supported by filtration-zero elements of the genuine C2-equivariant Adams spectral sequence.
arxiv-2605-26534: Yang Zhao and three colleagues learn neural network controllers that are safe by design, without bolting on a hand-tuned safety filter afterward. Given a valid control barrier function, they jointly train the controller and barrier parameters set by a neural network. Affine safety constraints hold by construction, with no online quadratic-program filter at run time. A lightweight projection design enforces constraints without full constraint enumeration, improving efficiency and scale. Extensive simulations show reliable, scalable safety at reduced computational cost.
arxiv-2605-26734: Takeda and five colleagues build CIRCLED, a dataset for multi-turn composed image retrieval, where each query step narrows toward a target picture. Older datasets of this kind lack steady dialogue history and stick to fashion images. CIRCLED extends three existing sets, holds 22,608 sessions across nine subsets, and gives researchers a broader public benchmark for testing retrieval over several turns.
arxiv-2605-26934: Zhu and six co-authors study how reward-driven learning from checkable scores should split data across depth of thought and complexity of the setting. Beyond depth alone, they vary distractor load and linked parts, and test four thought forms: deduction, abduction, induction, and analogy. Three findings emerge: joint depth-complexity coverage beats single-axis recipes, thought families differ, and uniform mixing beats staged curricula. Off-the-shelf models show the same deductive-over-abductive asymmetry.
arxiv-2605-27234: Ramos and co-authors measure the full isotopic fission yields of plutonium-240 as excitation energy rises. They make the fissioning system by a two-proton transfer between a uranium-238 beam and a carbon-12 target. Fragments are identified with the VAMOS++ spectrometer, and excitation is tracked event by event through a recoiling beryllium-10 nucleus. As energy rises from about 8 to 12 megaelectronvolts, shell effects feeding the symmetry valley damp down, and heavy fragments lose neutrons while light fragments keep theirs.
arxiv-2605-27434: Jose Luis Rosales shows key-network authentication scales better than the usual squared rule in realistic networks. Bell links fade fast along swapping paths, giving short correlation lengths and sparse entanglement graphs. Usable Bell pairs then grow in step with network size, and authentication cost grows like N log N under sparse mixing.
arxiv-2605-27534: Ilies Haouche, Benjamin Reichert, Michael Baudoin, and Palas Kumar Farsoiya present a hybrid method for surfactant-laden interfacial flows. The scheme keeps volume-of-fluid tracking for the interface and momentum while a spread-out phase-field carries surfactant flow, linking bulk and surface levels without surface derivatives. Adaptive mesh refinement and checks against analytic solutions confirm accuracy, and bubble-rise tests show Marangoni stresses slowing the bubble and bending its path.
arxiv-2605-27634: Feng Zhou, Jacqueline Meijer-Irons, and Ambar Murillo reframe human-AI teamwork in qualitative analysis as interdependence, not automation. Their framework picks a level of automation per analysis stage by weighing task risk against checking cost, guiding a deliberately joint workflow. A case study shows the approach builds steady trust while preserving the researcher's unique role in making meaning.
arxiv-2605-27734: Daniel Korchinski, Alessandro Favero, and Matthieu Wyart prove that predicting one's own latents beats token-level learning on sample complexity. For grammar data with hidden trees of depth L, token-level methods need samples exponential in L, while latent prediction needs only a constant number up to logarithmic factors. The bound is confirmed with hierarchical clustering, an end-to-end network, and the first sample-complexity analysis of data2vec.
arxiv-2605-28034: Stanislav Kirdey and Clark Labs Inc offer a tiny, training-free codec for storing neural embeddings compactly. Clark Hash normalizes each vector, projects it through a sparse signed sketch, and stores a fixed-width quantized code, shrinking a typical vector from over fifteen hundred bytes to forty-eight. Multilingual tests kept correlations near dense-vector scores.
arxiv-2605-28334: Víctor Mayoral-Vilches and seven colleagues ask which harness best suits cybersecurity agents, and find no single scaffold wins across challenge types. Their CSI meta-scaffold runs varied agent scaffolds under one orchestration layer and benchmarks them on 33 cybersecurity challenges. Combining scaffolds solved more challenges than any alone, and a shared-blackboard design solved 19 of 33, faster and at similar cost to the best single scaffold.
arxiv-2605-28534: Zheng Wu and seven colleagues train GUI agents to genuinely understand interface operations instead of memorizing action sequences. Post-training alone lets agents absorb world knowledge only implicitly through annotations or rewards, yielding inefficient trajectory memorization. Their GUI-CIDER mid-training method distills planning and causal knowledge from trajectories into text, filters the corpus for causal structure over redundancy, and trains on the refined data. Across GUI knowledge and task benchmarks it improves both understanding of operations and task success rates.
arxiv-2605-28634: Yutai Li and ten colleagues improve vision-language-action robot policies by replacing direct command-to-control mapping with reusable motion primitives. Rote learning of single paths wastes data and transfers poorly, so PrimitiveVLA splits demos into moves and rebuilds them at inference. A shared multimodal canonical representation supports both phases: fine-tuning splitting through an auto pipeline, and inference build through a vision-language planner plus a language-model switch module. Tests show better data use and stronger zero-shot transfer on unseen and long-horizon tasks.
arxiv-2605-28734: Richard J. Young and Gregory D. Moody build a consensus-labeled bank to measure coding compliance with malicious requests. A coding model that complies can return a weapon, such as a keylogger, ransomware, or exploit, so such models face a higher refusal bar than chat. Refusal benchmarks mix executable requests with harmful security knowledge and report rates over mixed sets. They classify eight corpora under a five-judge protocol, finding the code-versus-knowledge axis stable under an expanded pool and a fresh judge panel, proof of a real construct.
arxiv-2605-28934: Lorenzo Ricci, Marc Riembau, and Minho Son turn precise energy-correlator measurements inside jets into a broad search for new physics. In the collinear limit these correlators scale smoothly under perturbative QCD, but new physics breaks that scaling and leaves an angular resonance on the smooth background. Under broad assumptions, unitarity and positivity alone classify and constrain the signatures, turning the search into bump hunting within jets. As a test case they project competitive LHC sensitivity for a light hadrophilic Z-prime boson.
arxiv-2605-29234: Gaurav Sahu studies large-scale literature search from two angles. First, they build a Deep Research pipeline that reads the full query paper and expands breadth-first through cited works. On a 250-paper benchmark, this lifts recall from below one fifth to above four fifths. Second, they test human citation lists as ground truth, finding only about half clearly relevant. Humans were also far more likely than top AI rankers to cite a direct collaborator.
arxiv-2605-29434: Yuexin Li and colleagues propose AliMark for sentence level marking against rewrites. Existing methods anchor marks in sentence meaning, but prefix based designs fail under splitting and merging, common in rewrites. AliMark recasts marking as coding and matching of bit strings between a marked text and a secret bit string. Its two stage check makes several rebuilt versions and aligns their bit strings with the secret string to cut matching cost. This design improves strength to merges and splits, and beats best prior baselines under attacks.
arxiv-2605-29534: Small mobile interface agents, often unreliable at planning from screenshots alone, gain reusable knowledge about each app in UI-KOBE, a system from Yuxiang Chai and five colleagues. Large vision-language models handle phone tasks well but are too heavy for on-device use. UI-KOBE first explores an app alone and maps its screens as graph nodes joined by executable transitions. At run time the small agent locates its current node and chooses among staying put, a neighboring transition, finishing, or a free fallback action.
arxiv-2605-29634: Mazen Kobrosly studies whether relations among token groups leave matching orientation marks in hidden states. He tests Plücker sign entropy across Llama 8B, 70B, and 405B models, finding true groups show stronger sign consistency at the expected rank than scrambled groups. Multi-template checks show the effects survive surface changes. He then tests steering, patching corrupt relation frames toward clean targets over 32 prompts. In 70B and 405B models, clean paths recover clean answers and geometry, but centroid-only and equal-norm controls show almost no recovery.
arxiv-2605-29734: Yining Zhang and seven colleagues organize GPU operator tuning know-how into a layered memory that language models can actually use. Coarse hints travel well but prove hard to act on, while fine memories act well but bloat the search and hide true bottlenecks. Their frame, HTAM, builds a two-level graph of broad directions, fine local tactics, and step-to-step transitions. Each round picks a broad direction from present state and recent history, pulls the matching local memory, and steers concrete CUDA code from it.
arxiv-2605-29834: Joanna Komorniczak builds an unsupervised watcher for shifting tabular data streams that also spots brand-new classes. Concept drift and novel classes pose the twin hurdles for stream recognition, and her method tackles both without labels. Reconstruction errors from an autoencoder flag shifts in known class distributions, while density estimates on a proxy representation flag unfamiliar samples. Mirrored autoencoders let the two tasks adapt on their own as concepts evolve, keeping recognition steady. Tests on varied synthetic streams show the approach rivals top unsupervised drift detectors and novelty classifiers.
arxiv-2605-30134: Zonghao Li and Aaron Smith offer two faster MCMC algorithms for latent position graph models. Fitting Bayesian versions is costly because one likelihood evaluation takes time quadratic in vertex count. Earlier algorithms approach edge-count time, the closest prior work reaching almost edge-count time with good performance. Their fast algorithm matches that time with stronger accuracy guarantees, while their faster algorithm reaches almost vertex-count time with improved guarantees. Both gains come from a cheap auxiliary data structure updated during runs, which may help other MCMC algorithms.
arxiv-2605-30234: Thinh Le, Hansika Weerasena and Jianqing Liu propose a native non-Abelian mixer for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on hybrid oscillator-qubit processors. QAOA is well studied in continuous- and discrete-variable systems, but little developed for hybrid platforms. Their mixer comes with a hybrid ansatz for the Max-Cut problem, tested on unweighted Erdős-Rényi graphs against the standard transverse-field mixer. Across all graph sizes and Fock cutoffs, the non-Abelian mixer improves solution quality and optimal-solution odds, a promising block for hybrid QAOA.
arxiv-2605-30334: Yalun Dai and ten co-authors explore how data organization shapes LLM training, reusing scores made for data economy. While data choice is widely studied, data organization remains little studied, since LLMs are often trained for few epochs. They set out four rules for tuning data organization: Boundary Sharpening, Cyclic Scheduling, Curriculum Continuity, and Local Diversity. Guided by them, they present two data order methods termed STR and SAW. Tests across scales and data sizes, across pretraining and SFT stages, confirm the rules and show the methods enhance steady performance.
arxiv-2605-30534: Dorzhiev and Liu strengthen a defense that keeps hostile orders smuggled into user input from hijacking language-model agents. They rebuild Polymorphic Prompt Assembling, which walls off user text with randomly chosen separator pairs, so each request gets a fresh pair derived from hashed time, session, and nonce values. A leaked separator then endangers only one request, and tests against sixteen injected payloads show sharply lower attack success with no retraining and negligible extra work.
arxiv-2605-30734: Kanamugire and Djoumessi benchmark four deep learning models for malaria diagnosis on the NLM-Malaria dataset, testing performance, robustness, and post-hoc explainability. Lean models match heavier rivals, with no statistically significant gaps. CAM-based methods spot diagnostically key regions, while fine-grained attribution methods produce less sharp explanations, above all with heavier nets. Under image corruption, confidence falls faster than accuracy, a handy signal for human review. Yet no method resists corruption, with reliability falling at real-world noise levels even when predictions stay accurate.
arxiv-2605-30834: Park and colleagues propose Hide-and-Seek, framing VLA failure detection as a learning problem. VLA models follow orders and stretch across tasks, but remain open to faults that harm trust. Old methods either rely on costly resampling or outside models, while others spread labels evenly, hiding local signals. By combining inter- and intra-trajectory objectives, Hide-and-Seek localizes failure actions and induces signals from trajectory-level supervision alone, without step-level annotation. Evaluated on LIBERO, VLABench, and a real robot platform, the method achieves top failure spotting.
arxiv-2605-31034: Overman and Bayati study why uncertainty-agnostic updates can work in verifiable learning. Such updates sample completions and raise probabilities on higher-reward ones, without tracking uncertainty like Thompson sampling or UCB. They analyze a softmax policy in a many-armed Bayesian bandit, proving near-optimal regret under a tail condition. With many, softmax probability away from the best falls on other near-optimal arms, while with few arms the policy can suffer linear regret. Simulations support the theory and motivate prior-based variants beating baselines for many arms.
arxiv-2605-31134: Sahu and colleagues probe how chlorine swaps and helium-ion bombardment change a thin magnetic crystal, CrSBr. Using polarised Raman light scattering, they find the chlorine adds new vibration modes by breaking local symmetry, while ion damage opens fresh defect channels and broadens the vibrations. Together the two effects rebuild the spectrum unevenly by direction and keep a strong resonant link between electrons and vibrations even in damaged samples.
arxiv-2606-00034:
Egondu and Gallegos test whether artificial intelligence tools can improve science learning for disabled students in rural New Mexico, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rural schools there face shortages of specialist science teachers, limited laboratories, and weak internet access, which compound for students with disabilities. The study treated AI-based learning support as a game-like intervention and measured its effect on performance and engagement. A mixed-method design combined regression analysis with a neural network prediction model.

The study covered 120 students in grades 6 through 10 and 15 instructors across 4 rural schools. The AI intervention predicted student performance with high reported accuracy. Afterward, science concept retention improved by about a third, laboratory performance by roughly a quarter, and student engagement by over 40 percent in the reported results. The authors conclude that AI-driven teaching can act as an equalizer for disabled learners, while noting the infrastructure gaps that still limit rural deployment.
arxiv-2606-00234:
Padhyegurjar and Mukherjee sort the birth paths of paired black holes from wave data. Ripples in space tell of pairs that merged long ago. Their birth tales are hard to model in full. A data-led route can split the crowd into groups with shared roots.

Their pipe, BBH-Genesis, is fit to the fourth wave list, GWTC-4. The best fit needs just two birth paths for the full crowd. One path points to pairs that did not grow up alone. A third path earns mild back-up, tied to pairs near bright galaxy cores. That split shows in spin and mass-share traits. More finds in years to come will test if three paths are a must.
arxiv-2606-00434:
Sebastian, Balakrishnan, and Palathingal design bendy bases whose side-stretch trait can flip sign. Cells read the traits of the base they cling to as they grow. Gels can set those traits but not shift them mid-growth. A base that flips in place would let teams watch that shift live.

Their base is a small re-entrant frame that bends, not breaks. Stiff links twixt two inner points set which way the frame leans. Raise that stiff tie and side stretch flips from plus to minus. Size of the flip can be set at will as well. Hand math ties frame traits to in-out move shares for both states. Mesh sims and scale test builds back the math.
arxiv-2606-00634:
Sigogne, Constant, and Laporte feed a French word-class book into a chance-based parser. Parsers split a line into its build parts by rule. Chance parsers need rich marks to pick the right split. Their source is the Lexicon-Grammar, a French syntax book by Gross.

Verbs from the French Treebank are bunched by marks from that book. Those bunches feed a parser built on chance phrase laws. The parser is the Petrov form, a known wide-used build. Marks on French come out strong in their tests. The work shows book lore can lift a chance parser in use. It gives a path for lexicon-led gains in French parse work.
arxiv-2606-00734:
Li and co-authors speed up search in vector databases in this 2026 paper. The task is filtered nearest neighbor search: find the closest vectors that also pass a set of rules. Such search backs shopping advice, chat tools that fetch facts, and agent memory. Most past methods handle only range or label rules, and they cost much time and memory to build.

Their method, EMA, takes multi-part rules over both number and category fields. It also handles live updates well. Small summaries called Markers sit on graph edges and guide the search. Markers blend rule checks with shape cues and never wrongly rule a match out. A joint search then walks the graph with a bounded fix-up step for lost edges. The authors report speedups from 1.68 to 12.25 times over top general methods across varied workloads.
arxiv-2606-00834:
Ansah-Narh and co-authors forecast malaria admissions for young children in Ghana in this 2026 paper. Forecasts there are hard: seasons swing hard, reports are unsure, and transmission shifts over time. District teams need methods that are both rigorous about doubt and sturdy on thin data.

Their hybrid pairs two tools. Gaussian Process Regression captures wavy patterns and gives doubt ranges. Holt-Winters smoothing steadies long-range forecasts and keeps the seasonal shape. They fit ten years of district data, from 2014 to 2023, and test with rolling-origin checks. The hybrid scores R-squared of 0.9906, against 0.8213 for Holt-Winters alone. Most residuals fall inside the two-sigma bounds, as they should. Forecasts for 2024 to 2028 see average monthly admissions rise from about 8,000 to 12,200. Northern high-burden districts keep stable shares despite large swings in counts.
arxiv-2606-01034:
Zhu, Xie, and Rao map when a panel of AI judges can be trusted with few human labels in this 2026 paper. A judge panel grades outputs, but humans must supply labels to calibrate it. Labels get spent on fitting a calibrator, building judge paths, and picking which setup to ship. The team asks when a small model of the panel beats a full joint table.

Their method, FCPS, picks the judge path, panel size, and aggregator as one validated choice. Support checks flag patterns the labels never saw. Across four datasets and a seven judge pool, simple aggregation beats joint tables in 16 of 20 cells. Richer shrunk tables close some gaps but keep the core bottleneck. In grown data with a six way interaction, the map flips. The table grows to hold the interaction, and its error score falls from 0.224 down to 0.061 once the unseen mass vanishes.
arxiv-2606-01134:
Charlot and co-authors teach machines to hear when speech is aimed at a child in this 2026 paper. Long recordings of home life hold the data of language growth research. Sorting child directed speech from adult directed speech by hand does not scale. Past tools judge each utterance alone and were tested mostly on English.

The team fine tunes six self supervised models on recordings of 182 children, in many languages. Models pretrained on child centered audio beat those trained on adult speech by a wide mark. Context helps a lot: adding the speech around each utterance lifts the average F1 score by 13.8 points in absolute terms across the tests. A full pipeline test, from finding adult speech to classifying its target, still beats a rule based baseline. Scores drop under automatic segmentation, they note. The work opens large, multilingual studies of what children hear.
arxiv-2606-01334:
Aharonov, Shrout, and Tal align 3D objects with many images and texts. Open-set 3D recognition must handle rare, unseen classes. Past tools distill vision-language knowledge into 3D encoders. They often rely on heavy 2D vision transformers. Each point cloud gets paired with one image or caption. That anchors the model to partial views. HOLA pairs each cloud with multiple views and texts instead.

A decoupled multi-positive contrastive loss drives the training. It separates positive grouping from negative competition. This avoids crowding when many positives share one softmax. A light text adapter cleans up web captions only. That shrinks the gap to curated annotations. The model sets new marks on long-tail benchmarks. Zero-shot gains are substantial, and frame rates stay high.
arxiv-2606-01434:
Wang and co-authors ground drug answers in primary sources with DrugClaw. Drug information questions carry high stakes for care. Hallucinated facts can mislead clinical decisions. The source of each fact matters as much as the fact. DrugClaw is a multi-agent retrieval system for such questions. It queries a registry of drug and safety skills. A reflection-driven state machine steers the workflow. Answers cite primary regulatory or peer-reviewed records.

DrugAudit is their authority-aware benchmark of 3,772 items. It scores source match, snippet overlap, and citation faithfulness. Two LLM judges grade under a dual-judge protocol. DrugClaw tops every headline column in their tests. Its primary-source rate beats the next best by 10 point 1 points.
arxiv-2606-01634:
Jiang and co-authors generate time series with extreme events kept faithful. Realistic series matter for science and real-world use. Past methods prize overall distributional fidelity in their output. Extreme events often get lost or distorted in the process. E4GEN is an explainable diffusion frame for extreme-aware generation. It gives systematic control over when, what, and how extremes form. An E-Activator learns when to switch the extreme signal on. It does so without disturbing trend or seasonality parts.

An E-Predictor infers what control signal each sample needs. It derives that signal from latent extreme data during generation. An E-Control network injects the signal layer by layer. Tests on six datasets with 17 metrics favor E4GEN. Gains span fidelity, extreme fidelity, and downstream utility.
arxiv-2606-01934:
Zheng and co-authors shorten the long reasoning chains of chat models. Extended chain-of-thought boosts model performance a lot. But long chains add heavy inference overhead per answer. Past compression tricks use fixed manual length budgets. Others need costly multi-stage training pipelines. Small models are often the only ones they scale to.

Their HMPO method trains in a single stage with RL. A median budget adapts from successful rollouts on its own. A cosine-decay reward penalizes length in a smooth way. A multiplicative reward puts correctness strictly first. That design curbs trivial reward hacking, they report. Training uses only math data. Skills still transfer to code, science, and instruction tasks.
arxiv-2606-02034: Chakraborty and Dey propose a new symmetry for the neutrino mass matrix. The symmetry is a mu-tau counter reflection symmetry. It fits an inverted ordering of neutrino masses in a natural way. That ordering is one of the open patterns in neutrino physics. The pair note extra gains for phenomenology as well. The mass texture tied to the symmetry can be built in a minimal frame. That frame rests on the Δ(27) group symmetry. The note is brief and focused on the proposal itself.
arxiv-2606-02134:
Kaulen and co-authors rethink how methods for certified training should be judged. Deep networks do well on many tasks, yet small crafted changes to the input can still fool them . Verification can give strict proofs of robustness, but cost a great deal of compute. Certified training tries to build verifiable robustness in during training, at the price of a trade-off with plain accuracy. Each method has its own knobs that steer that trade-off, so a single reported setting can mislead the reader.

The team argue that methods should be compared across the whole trade-off, using Pareto fronts rather than one point each. They apply this lens to certified training based on interval bound propagation. The work is a call for clearer and more honest benchmark practice in robustness research.
arxiv-2606-02234:
Huber asks when changes in a treatment, not its level, can pin down a causal effect. Most causal work uses the level of a treatment to find its effect, but a second route uses changes over time. The rules behind that second route are less well mapped. Huber sets out two structural models whose assumptions do not nest inside each other.

Under those models, differencing wipes out confounders that stay fixed in time, as long as they enter the treatment equation in an additive way. The assumptions for changes are in general not nested with those for level based methods, such as selection on observables or difference in differences. When the treatment path is a random walk, the two routes draw closer. The paper gives applied researchers a clear map of when the change based route is valid.
arxiv-2606-02334:
Gan and co-authors ask what makes a good written description of a dataset. Search tools and reuse both depend on such text. Yet dataset text is often thin or uneven. Language models can draft descriptions on their own. The authors test what source material the models truly need.

The team works with 252 datasets from a European open data portal. They draft text from titles alone, then titles with schema, then titles with schema and sample data. Judges score each draft against a quality frame built from past research. One result surprised the team. Schema alone often made the prose worse. Sample data restored some grounding but not overall quality. Each model also kept a stable drafting style. Data publishers get clear, practical advice from these tests.
arxiv-2606-02434:
Ohtsubo and co-authors tackle a data shortage in chip inspection. Precise control of circuit shape matters for checking semiconductors. Real training images cost a great deal to gather. Generative models can add data, but not with nanometer-level accuracy. The team turns inspection images into editable code instead.

Their framework uses a vision-language model. It reads an inspection image and writes domain-specific language code. The code describes the circuit geometry in full. Parameters can then be changed by hand for exact new samples. A snag remains, though. The model trains only on synthetic renders. Real electron microscope images differ in texture and noise. A binarization step strips that texture out. On the MIIC dataset, the mean Dice score rises from 0.4393 to 0.5256 over the raw-input baseline. A simple step closes much of the sim-to-real gap.
arxiv-2606-02634:
Stenhede and co-authors guide ultrasound heart scans with a self-supervised framework. Transthoracic echocardiography needs skilled probe placement. Their system, Echo-POSED, recommends probe moves from 2D images alone. No expert-labeled views are needed. No tracked probe paths are needed either. Training slices 2D views from routine 3D volumes.

The framework enforces equivariance to probe motions. It stays invariant to cardiac phase. The result is a pose representation on a product of rotation groups. Tests use a held-out split and public external 3D datasets. Vendor shift is included. Geometric consistency holds under virtual perturbations. Guidance simulations run within and across patients. The combined mean angular error is 8.2 degrees in intra-patient runs with cardiac motion. Real-time guidance without labels is the promise.
arxiv-2606-02734:
Weiskopf and co-authors test whether one migrating planet can carve many dust rings in a young disk. Dust structures in protoplanetary discs are widely observed. Their origin is still debated. Magnetohydrodynamics, shadows, and planet-disc interaction are rival accounts. The team runs high-resolution 2D hydrodynamic simulations. A planet migrates in a low-viscosity, radiative disc. Three equations of state are compared.

The cooling models are isothermal, constant beta-cooling, and an adaptive beta model. Dust is included in every run. Radiative transfer images are built from the dust profiles. For all cooling choices, the planet makes migration jumps. Each jump produces dust rings and gaps. Structures stay visible for at least 400 thousand years. Cooling decides the migration path and jump count. It does not change structure lifetimes. Large vortices last only about 90 thousand years on average. One planet, the results show, can open multiple gaps while migrating.
arxiv-2606-03034:
Mittal reads agent-to-agent markets through an old economics lens: the market for lemons. AI agents now post what they can do in shared lists, through tools such as MCP and A2A. A real agent's skill is not fixed. It shifts with the input, and it drifts when the base model changes.

When grade is hid and claims are cheap, good and bad sellers look the same. Honest agents go unpaid, and the market sinks to its worst firms. Mittal names one fault class: the agent that is sure and wrong, with no foe at work. A model of the lemons market shows trust-based rules reach just a low-trust equilibrium. His Trust Layer sits above the base tools. It adds chance-based skill claims, screening, and fame scores. When a false claim costs more than it gains, a high-trust equilibrium can hold.
arxiv-2606-03334:
Kadasi, Tiwari, and Singh test prompt variants for detecting polarization in many languages. Their entry is for SemEval-2026 Task 9, a multilingual classification challenge. It has three subtasks: spotting polarization, naming its type, and naming how it shows. The team studies short designed prompts in a systematic way.

Twelve prompts vary in term clarity, detail of definition, reasoning guidance, and use of in-context examples. Two models run the tests: aya-101 and Gemma3-27B, with the latter picked for the final entry. Scores on the official test set average across 22 languages. Macro F1 came to about 0.76, 0.59, and 0.44 across the three subtasks. Prompt methods did well at coarse polarization calls. They struggled more as the task grew fine-grained and multi-label. The study shows prompt design is a real variable in such systems. Small wording choices shift scores in ways worth mapping.
arxiv-2606-03534:
Nugent, Page, Zaikin, and Andreae build a path-valued model of how dendrites develop. Dendrites carry signals into neurons and grow while synapses form. They extend, shrink back, and branch as they grow. The final tree shapes the wider neural network. Because branches retract, tracking whole paths matters more than tracking endpoints alone.

Some simulators handle paths only in an implicit way. This model makes a path-valued stochastic process explicit. A branching process joins it, drawn from measure-valued branching particle systems. The combined model yields the tree shapes seen in real dendrites. Several simulation methods come with the theory. They include time steps at varied scales and a dynamic graph approximation. The result gives neuroscience a firmer math base for dendrite growth. It also gives structured tools for future simulation work.
arxiv-2606-04034:
Rideau presents first-class implementations, a reflection protocol for software towers. Software sits in levels, from abstract down to concrete code. Each level is built by compilers or interpreters below it. Most systems can only move down that tower at runtime. Rideau asks how a running program can climb up instead.

Safe points are the key device in the protocol. They let an observer view a computation at a higher level than it runs. The implementation of a running task can then change mid-flight. The protocol came from a formal specification of implementations and their traits. Rideau frames it as a bridge between semantics and runtime reflection. Those two fields had stood apart before.
arxiv-2606-04134:
Ritoban Kundu, James Flory, Sean Hennessy, and Ashkan Ertefaie propose a method in 2026 for learning the best treatment policy for chronic disease. They work from health records, where hidden gaps between patient groups can bias naive comparisons.

Their approach mixes two classic tools. One is difference-in-differences, which uses changes over time to cancel fixed hidden gaps. The other is an instrumental variable, a factor that shifts treatment but not outcomes directly. Together they let the method learn a policy while facing hidden bias and the risk of a terminal event, such as death, ending follow-up. Tests on Medicare diabetes data and in simulations checked the estimator's behavior. The authors argue the mix suits policy learning from real-world records.
arxiv-2606-04234:
Nishan Parvez, Prashant Purohit, and Wensi Wu develop in 2026 a mechanical model for fibrous soft tissues, aimed at heart valve leaflets whose collagen fiber networks give them their nonlinear, direction-dependent stiffness. Capturing stiffening under strain and odd effects like the reverse Poynting phenomenon requires the fibers to be modeled explicitly.

Their model embeds fibers in an octahedral arrangement inside a soft matrix, letting direction, fiber share, and pre-stretch shape the response, under both pulling and compression. Calibrated against mitral valve experiments through an automated fitting loop, it reproduced biaxial, shear, and uniaxial tests. Simulations then showed radial suppleness enables proper valve closure, while widespread fiber reorientation concentrates stress or prevents closure entirely.
arxiv-2606-04334:
Ishan Paranjape and co-authors adapt orbit determination to the cislunar realm in 2026, tracking targets between Earth and Moon where three-body gravity breaks the classical method. Gauss's classic technique assumes simple two-body motion, so it cannot seed tracks in this environment.

Their hybrid filter fuses two particle Gaussian mixture methods in sequence: a sampling-based one and a Kalman-update one, building a fully recursive probabilistic tracker. It ingests angles-only observations from ground telescopes and can absorb prior information to shrink uncertainty quickly. Tests across several important cislunar orbit families showed the hybrid holding tracks over short and long horizons. Comparisons against single-method and other hybrid filters favored the combination, which matters as cislunar traffic grows.
arxiv-2606-04834:
Li, Mao, Teng, and Yang ask whether Occam's razor still works when the razor is dull, in a 2026 arXiv learning theory paper. Minimum Description Length prediction picks, at each step, the model minimizing the length of the model and the data it describes. Theory guarantees reliable prediction when that objective is optimized exactly, but machine learning only optimizes it.

They prove that for any approximation with fixed additive slack, the squared prediction error stays finite whenever lambda is at least one. The characterization is sharp: with lambda below one, overfitting can incur infinite error, so strong complexity regularization is necessary. Under multiplicative approximation, model selection can fail in every regularized regime.
arxiv-2606-05134:
Yaseen Osman, Geoff Merrett, and Stuart Middleton report a negative result on activation-based active learning for in-context learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. In-context learning improves a language model by placing examples in its prompt, and choosing good examples matters. The authors tested whether the model's activations, the numbers flowing through its layers, could signal which examples are worth picking.

Their analysis is the most comprehensive for MLP activation-based selection, covering classification and generative datasets on Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B base models. The signal was not there. Through massive activations or their first four statistical moments, MLP outputs did not correlate with example quality or task performance. The strongest absolute Spearman correlation was only 0.33 across tasks and models. The authors suggest superposition, where models pack more features than they have dimensions, may blur the signal, and point to sparse autoencoders as a direction.
arxiv-2606-05234:
Dong Liu and colleagues present OLIVE in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that personalizes exoskeleton control while the device is being worn. Wearable exoskeletons can restore mobility for people with physical impairments, but most controllers follow fixed gait policies that cannot adapt to terrain or to the user. OLIVE adapts during deployment instead.

The adaptive piece is written as a low-rank residual added to a stable pretrained base controller, slashing the cost of each update. Updates come from a reward-shaped policy gradient driven by on-body sensor feedback, muscle signals, motion units, and vibration, with no offline trajectories needed. A gating mechanism scales how strongly personalization applies, and a rank scheduler gives more capacity on demanding ground. On the platform, OLIVE improved gait smoothness, effort reduction, and motion stability by 13, 22, and 15 percentage points over the best baseline. It converged within about 1,800 walking steps at 7.4 milliseconds of latency.
arxiv-2606-05334:
Nehal Afifi and colleagues combine behavior prediction with material-fatigue assessment for products returning to a factory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Returned goods re-enter production with degradation and usage histories, and a reuse decision cannot rest on inspection alone, because function and integrity evolve with a service scenario. The team builds a workflow around a case study of an angle grinder.

One branch predicts function: a convolutional encoder reads force and torque windows and a backbone forecasts variables as means and variances. The other branch turns the history into output-shaft fatigue information through finite-element reconstruction, damage rules, and crack-growth analysis. On held-out tests the predictor reached a two-percent-tolerance accuracy of 0.9652 across the nine outputs, with thermal variables near-perfect. Damage under nominal stresses was negligible, but crack-growth analysis proved sensitive to high-load events, cutting shaft reusability from 31 cycles to 3.
arxiv-2606-05434:
Chirag Chawla, Rohan Charudatt Salvi, and Madhav Baidya refine GRPO, a reinforcement learning method for training language models on reasoning tasks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard GRPO treats every token position and every rollout symmetrically, weighting confident and uncertain tokens alike and penalizing failed attempts as harshly as it rewards successes.

Adaptive-Horizon GRPO weights each token's gradient by a cumulative entropy-based discount that shrinks the effective horizon when the model is uncertain. Selective-Advantage GRPO applies that discounting only to negative-advantage rollouts, the failed attempts, leaving successful trajectories untouched. On the GSM8K mathematics benchmark with two Qwen instruction models fine-tuned using LoRA adapters, the selective variant matched standard GRPO's peak accuracy on the larger model. It cut training variance by a factor of 3.6, and it improved the smaller model over its zero-shot baseline.
arxiv-2606-05834:
Aggarwal and colleagues push toward worst-case foundations for a crypto problem in a 2026 arXiv paper. Learning Parity with Noise asks solvers to find a hidden pattern in noisy linear equations. Its average-case hardness secures many constructions. Rivals like Learning With Errors already rest on worst-case assumptions; LPN does not. Older bridges used statistical smoothing, which capped hardness at high noise only.

The approach asks for less: certain code combinations need only look uniform to efficient observers, not be uniform. That swap yields a win-win reduction. Any fast LPN solver becomes two tools: one decodes a code, the other tells its dual's noisy words from random. Chosen parameters then give average-case hardness at inverse-polynomial noise rates. The catch is a joint worst-case assumption covering both tasks at once. The paper frames that assumption as the price of low-noise security.
arxiv-2606-06034:
Luoming Zhang and a large team argue that an approximate matrix inverse, built only with multiplications, beats the exact step-by-step one in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chunk-wise linear attention needs inverses of triangular matrices. Forward substitution computes them step by step, starving accelerators of parallelism. The new algorithm expands the inverse as a truncated Neumann series instead. Structural masking and parallel residual correction remove the step dependency entirely.

Diagonal concentration of the true inverse justifies the truncation. For low-bit integer arithmetic the team tames the dynamic range that repeated matrix powers inflate. Approximation order adapts to chunk size to balance cost and accuracy. On Qwen-family models the kernel ran up to five times faster. Decode-layer overhead fell by about a fifth. Accuracy survived in both floating-point and low-precision modes. Hardware-friendly approximations can be optimal when exactness buys nothing the model can use.
arxiv-2606-06234:
Alix Violet Freckelton and the gr8stars collaboration audit how well astronomers know their stars in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stellar parameters such as temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity come from fitting models to spectra. Exoplanet studies inherit every error in those numbers. The team asks whether quoted uncertainties honestly include the bias from choosing one fitting method over another.

They took five hundred eighty five bright FGK dwarfs with sharp SOPHIE spectra and ran five spectroscopic methods on each star. The methods scattered by seventy six kelvin in temperature. They also scattered by zero point one four dex in surface gravity and zero point zero seven dex in metallicity. Propagated onward, the spread adds about three percent uncertainty in planet radius and five percent in planet mass. It also sets a four percent floor on planet temperature uncertainty that papers rarely report.
arxiv-2606-06334:
Maryam Babaei and co-authors show that model explanations can leak private data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Counterfactual explanations tell a user what to change to get a better decision, such as a loan approval. They feel safe to share, yet they are built from real profiles. An attacker might use them to test whether a specific person was in the training data, a membership inference attack.

Attacks of that kind were honed against synthetic data, which resembles counterfactuals as a stand in for real records. The authors port those attacks across several counterfactual types and datasets, including Adult, Compas, and Heloc. Worryingly, the attacks succeed using only a released set of counterfactuals, with no access to the model at all. Success varied by counterfactual style, but none was immune. The authors urge developers to treat published explanations as a privacy surface, not a harmless byproduct.
arxiv-2606-06634:
A minimal surface is one that cannot shrink its area with a tiny nudge, like a soap film at rest. Ball and Madnick study round bubble like surfaces of this kind inside higher dimensional spheres in this 2026 arXiv paper. They focus on the Morse index, a count of the ways a surface can be pushed so that its area falls to second order.

The pair compute that index, along with the related nullity count, for every immersed minimal two sphere whose Gauss curvature, a measure of how the surface bends, stays constant. These surfaces trace back to examples found by Boruvka nearly a century ago, and later work showed they cover all cases of this type. The paper also bounds the stability index of a cone in seven dimensional space whose cross section is one of these spheres.
arxiv-2606-06834:
Most of the human genome does not code for proteins, yet it may steer how genes behave. Chahat Baranwal and co-authors probe that dark genome in this 2026 arXiv paper. They ask which silent stretches shape genes that help brain tumors wire into neural circuits. Their test bed is high grade glioma, an aggressive brain cancer.

The team used three genomic foundation models to mutate sequences in the computer. They scored over thirty thousand dark elements near ninety two tumor linked loci. A key flaw surfaced: model scores often track how predictable a sequence is, not how regulatory it is. Their diagnostic separates those two layers with extra controls. A simple six feature baseline matched one model's top picks almost perfectly. Still, some signal survived every check. Top elements were strongly enriched for brain gene switches. A sharp regulatory horizon of about ten thousand bases also held firm.
arxiv-2606-07034:
Detectors that flag AI generated images work until a new generator arrives. Zhou and co-authors open those black boxes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, ForensicConcept, extracts the evidence a detector actually uses. Attribution maps find the image patches that drive each decision.

Those patches cluster into a compact codebook of forensic concepts. A projection step turns the concepts into readouts that people can audit. A second idea checks whether evidence will travel. Generation traces from a diffusion feature model serve as a reference. A match score measures how well each backbone fits those traces. A higher match score predicted better transfer across backbones. Injecting the codebook into new models improved detection on several benchmarks. Gains held across generated image sets and a hard chameleon test. The work gives users a diagnostic tool, not just a detector.
arxiv-2606-07434:
Hossain, Andrade, Zang, and Chen redesign prediction markets to reward the evidence behind forecasts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Today's markets reveal what the crowd believes but hide its reasoning, and they need an external event with a resolution date. Evidence markets pay participants for submitting evidence alongside beliefs, adjusting the market's liquidity parameter as evidence grows. When no external resolution exists, the market can resolve endogenously, using the gathered evidence to settle the question.

The authors prove the platform's loss stays bounded, that evidence rewards scale with market uncertainty, and that the design equals an automated market maker. For endogenous resolution they characterize how hidden evidence shifts beliefs and prove truthful reporting is a nearly dominant strategy. They propose verifying evidence with a language-model judge backed by staking, plus an asynchronous execution scheme. Model evaluation, judging which AI wins, runs through the paper as the running example.
arxiv-2606-07534:
Ritvik Pandey and co-authors benchmark table extraction from document images across languages and scripts in this 2026 arXiv paper introducing PulseBench-Tab. Extracting tables matters for finance, yet a number misplaced by one cell is a semantic error, not a typo. Their benchmark holds over 1,800 human-annotated tables in 9 languages and 4 scripts, drawn from 380 documents such as financial filings and reports. Nearly half the tables contain merged or spanning cells, the feature that breaks naive extractors.

They propose T-LAG, an evaluation metric modeling a table as a directed graph of cell adjacencies and scoring structural plus content fidelity in one number through optimal matching. Nine commercial and open-source systems were evaluated with per-language breakdowns. The authors criticize older metrics for conflating formatting conventions with structural errors and for flattening tables into sequences. Dataset, scoring code, and every provider's raw outputs are available for scrutiny and reuse.
arxiv-2606-08034:
Muhammad Falensi Azmi and co-authors build a stress test for scientific problem solving that changes the numbers, the pictures, and the language, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symbolic benchmarks check robustness by regenerating a question with different values, but most cover only mathematics, lack visual content, and exist only in English. Their benchmark, Sci-Rho, spans five subjects and seven languages.

Domain experts, including Olympiad medalists, crafted four thousand two hundred forty-two problem templates, six hundred six per language. Each template is code generating equivalent instances by varying values, visual patterns, shapes, colour schemes, and function types. That yields forty-two thousand four hundred twenty instances with reasoning steps and solutions. Testing seventeen vision-language models exposed a gap between average accuracy and worst-case accuracy, the share of templates answered correctly under every variation. Smaller models degraded across languages, while large and proprietary models stayed robust.
arxiv-2606-08134:
Andrea Braides and Abdilaziz Zoir Ugli Komilov work out what a patterned material's phase boundaries cost in the critical regime, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fractional phase-transition energies model materials that separate into phases, with a nonlocal energy whose order, the exponent s, sets the regime. At the critical value one half, the scaling turns logarithmic and the sharp-interface limit normally ignores the material's fine pattern.

The authors add periodic patterns, an oscillating material parameter, and ask whether homogenisation, the averaging-out of fine structure, survives at the critical scale. It does, but only in part. They prove the Gamma-limit is a sharp-interface functional whose surface energy density mixes the minimum and the mean of the varying parameter. Both kinds of contribution coexist. This mixed answer is specific to the critical regime and differs from the case above one half.
arxiv-2606-08234:
Swaminathan, Jiang, and Zhang present a safety framework for artificial intelligence agents that do autonomous science, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such agents plan experiments and run tools in stages, but their safety checks usually inspect only finished outputs, leaving two weaknesses. Safety signals noticed early get discarded before later stages, and chains of individually harmless tool calls can combine into a harmful outcome that no single-step filter catches. Their framework, SciTrace, weaves safety reasoning into every stage instead.

SciTrace couples two mechanisms. A Safety-Intrinsic Reasoning Loop keeps a running risk state across the planning, experimenting, writing, and reviewing stages, so each stage deliberates about the task and its dangers together. A Compositional Tool-Chain Verifier checks whole sequences of tool calls before execution, hunting for risks that emerge only across multiple steps. The authors argue this trajectory-aware design closes failure modes that output filters structurally cannot see.
arxiv-2606-08534:
Vella, Pennella, and Ballandies build a classification system for tokenized assets, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real-world asset tokenization represents off-chain assets, from real estate to bonds, as blockchain-based instruments. Deployed systems remain hard to compare because legal claims, custody arrangements, and token mechanics are described separately, each project in its own vocabulary. The authors develop a taxonomy classifying how off-chain assets are legally and technically represented on-chain.

They organize twenty-three dimensions into five components: governance, asset structure, token properties, the ledger technology itself, and economy. The taxonomy is then applied to twenty major tokenization systems. A shared taxonomy lets regulators and builders see where two offerings genuinely differ. The point is to give a fast-growing field one shared map that all sides can point to and use.
arxiv-2606-08934:
Chang gives recurrent neural networks a theory of when their memory settles down, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A recurrent network carries a hidden state that summarizes the past, yet its probabilistic meaning was unclear. Chang defines backward coherence: how well each state is recovered from its successor through a backward projector. Under contraction and controlled drift, he proves the hidden-state sequence forms a quasi-reverse-martingale, a near-martingale running back, guaranteeing convergence and stopping rules.

Simulations confirmed the predictions: a backward-coherence penalty cut instability by 43 to 58 percent and reached stability up to 44 percent earlier. Three real-data studies followed. On intensive-care records, the regularized network matched prediction while stabilizing 13 hours earlier in a 48-hour stay. On macro data under concept drift, it cut one-month-ahead forecast error fourfold. Activity tests showed tracking errors decaying quickly. The loss ties to variational inference via a divergence identity.
arxiv-2606-09234:
Gao and colleagues train a text-to-speech system all at once, not in pieces, and set a quality record doing it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modern systems cascade three components trained apart: a speech tokenizer, a token-predicting language model, and a flow-matching audio model. Separate training causes mismatches; the blind, first-trained tokenizer caps quality.

Their framework optimizes everything end-to-end, reward model included. First the tokenizer trains for all three partners at once: reconstruction, next-token prediction, recognition. Its tokens carry both acoustic and semantic information. Then the language model is tuned on downstream reconstruction and recognition feedback, cutting train-inference mismatch. On Seed-TTS-Eval it reached word error rates of 0.78 percent and 1.56 percent, a new state of the art, with just a 0.6B language model and 0.5B flow model. Holistic training, they conclude, beats careful cascading.
arxiv-2606-09334:
Karpo and Chernodub test how far prompting alone can go for correcting Ukrainian grammar, a low-resource setting where fine-tuned models rule, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Minimal-edit correction fixes clear grammar, spelling, and punctuation errors while preserving the author's wording, the standard for educational tools. The authors evaluate 11 commercial language models from 4 providers plus one open-source Ukrainian model on the UNLP 2023 benchmark. They compare zero-shot, few-shot, minimal-edits, and assisted prompt optimization.

The best setup, Gemini 3.1-Pro with optimized minimal-edits prompting, reached an F0.5 score of 69.22 against the fine-tuned state of the art at 73.14, closing over 90 percent of the gap from the prior API result of 27.4. Ukrainian-language minimal-edits prompts won for every model, gains largest on punctuation and case. The trade-off: detailed instructions made models abandon several rare error categories, and 5 recurring overcorrection patterns trace to Ukrainian-specific phenomena.
arxiv-2606-09534:
Block and his co-authors design a traffic controller that steers many automated cars at once without the usual computational explosion in this 2026 arXiv paper. Connected automated cars can act as moving bottlenecks, pacing traffic toward a desired density. Normally the controller is designed on the rule governing each car's speed, so adding cars multiplies the work.

Their approach, called continuification, designs the control at the level of the traffic flow equation instead. A linear quadratic regulator first computes an optimal variable speed limit profile for the whole freeway length. The continuification step then converts that smooth profile into a concrete speed command for each car. Simulations show that several cars can be run this way with minimal computing burden. As more cars are added, the achieved density profile approaches the global optimum that the regulator computed for the idealised continuous case.
arxiv-2606-09734:
Brian Coyle and his co-authors cut the measurement bill for training quantum circuits in this 2026 arXiv paper. A parameterised quantum circuit is tuned by gradient steps. The standard parameter-shift rule needs shots that grow with each added knob, and that cost rules the training budget. No helper qubits or extra gates are welcome on near-term kit.

Their frame uses forward gradients: fair estimates built from a free count of random directional probes. Known methods fall out as edge cases, from one-probe SPSA to the full shift rule. They prove the descent settles under plain premises. From the frame drops QUIVER, an optimizer that sets shot counts by a closed-form cost rule. In tests, forward gradients trained quantum nets with up to sixty qubits and over seventeen hundred knobs. The gains over shift rules ran to orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-09934:
Ahmad and Ahmed tackle feature selection for network intrusion detection, the task of spotting attacks inside computer traffic, in a 2026 arXiv paper.
