Their setting is heavily imbalanced, meaning attack records are rare beside ordinary benign traffic. Older ranking methods score each feature with global statistics from all classes together. The authors argue that this hides what makes attacks stand out from normal behavior.

Their method, called nCMD, scores features by how far attack-class values stray from the benign class mean, the average of normal traffic. It adds no extra computing cost and stays easy to explain. Across four benchmark datasets, including CICIDS2017 and NSL-KDD, and three downstream classifiers, nCMD matched or beat classic filter methods on macro-averaged F1 score, a balanced accuracy measure. It won on three of the four datasets, with the clearest gains under tight feature budgets.
arxiv-2606-10234:
Arora and the Eos collaboration present first results from a four-tonne optical detector built to prove a hybrid approach for future neutrino experiments, in a 2026 arXiv paper on particle physics hardware. Eos, located at the University of California, Berkeley, aims to show scintillation-based hybrid detection, which splits Cherenkov and scintillation light to gain both direction and energy information.

Using deployed optical and radioactive calibration sources, the team performs detailed calibrations. Those calibrations enable a suite of tests for algorithms that locate and characterize particle events. Models built on the calibrated detector model are compared against the measured data to check performance. Setting the water-phase behavior first gives the team a trusted baseline. Any later change with glowing material can be judged against a response already understood from a medium whose light output is simple and known.
arxiv-2606-10334:
Dong teaches code-generating models to fix how their output looks, not just whether it runs, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. His framework, Visual-SDPO, treats rendered visual feedback as privileged context for a weight-sharing teacher and distills that feedback into a coding student through self-distillation policy optimization.

A credit weighting method traces each detected defect back to the code statements responsible for the affected elements, amplifying the training signal exactly there rather than uniformly. A sequence-level group-relative term complements the dense token objective, providing signal even for rollouts whose code fails to execute. The framework is instantiated for chart, web interface, and slide generation on a unified vision-language backbone. The approach targets the gap between code that is technically correct and artifacts that are actually presentable.
arxiv-2606-10534:
Aghashirinov and colleagues demonstrate a natural route to canalized light waves in this 2026 arXiv paper in nanophotonics. Polaritons are hybrid light-matter waves confined far below the wavelength of free light. In the canalization regime they travel as narrow beams without spreading, which normally requires twisted stacks or fabricated metasurfaces. The team shows the effect occurs naturally in MoOCl2, a layered crystal, at its transition between elliptical and hyperbolic wave patterns, at room temperature.

Near-field imaging shows canalization emerging along one crystal axis at a low-loss crossing point, staying narrow across a broad spectral window. Changing only the flake thickness tunes the canalization wavelength by more than one micrometre in both experiment and theory. The work brings canalized travel into the 4.5 to six micrometre range, past phonon-polariton limits and overlapping key vibration bands.
arxiv-2606-10834:
Bär and colleagues audit who actually sees political advertising online in this 2026 arXiv paper on computational social science. During the 2024 European Parliament elections, the authors assembled over 110,000 ads from 453 parties and 968 candidates, over 7 billion impressions, across 25 EU countries. Delivery algorithms, not advertisers alone, decide which users see an ad. Even after accounting for content, platform competition, and targeting strategies, delivery is skewed by gender and ideology.

Ads from populist parties, especially far-right ones, are shown far more to men: all else equal, a populist ad reaches an audience about six points more male. The pattern holds across the continent rather than in one country's campaign. Because such skews limit parties' access to diverse audiences and voters' exposure to the full spectrum. So the authors argue platforms and policymakers should audit delivery during elections, treating fair exposure as part of honest elections.
arxiv-2606-10934:
Rovai argues that prediction alone cannot settle counterfactual questions in this 2026 arXiv paper. Across hundreds of structural causal models, strong predictors match Bayesian answers where data identify the truth. On unidentified quantities they collapse to a single point, in 28 percent of models one no valid model allows. The truth there is an interval more data never narrows.

Rovai recasts a world model as a coupling kernel over admissible worlds: the diagonal is the usual posterior, the off-diagonal the cross-world coupling that fixes counterfactuals. Enforcing positive semidefiniteness bounds those counterfactuals in polynomial time, and ontology axioms tighten the bounds by up to a third. Full access, though, is counting, tractable only below a known threshold.
arxiv-2606-11034:
Steffen and co-authors describe a 2026 arXiv paper on controlling a humanoid robot with a spiking neural network, whose neurons fire in brief pulses like brain cells. Earlier spiking controllers handled walking or arm movement alone, never both together. Their architecture joins force-based arm control with bipedal locomotion, meaning two-legged walking, in one system built on the Neural Engineering Framework.

A spiking model of the basal ganglia, the brain circuit that selects actions, switches the robot between tasks. In joint Nengo and Isaac Sim simulation, the humanoid reached for targets, drew a figure eight with its arm, and followed walking paths. Splitting the arm's motion problem into three smaller networks cut the input space and improved decoding accuracy. The authors call it the first integrated spiking controller of its kind on a full-scale humanoid, suited to low-power neuromorphic hardware, chips modeled on the brain.
arxiv-2606-11134:
Ricci rebuilds the analytic foundations of indicial umbral calculus in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is an operational method that treats indices like exponents to handle special functions, powerful but long short on solid grounding. Ricci turns its operators into continuous linear functionals, objects with rigorous definitions, grounded in Mellin-Barnes integrals, Borel-Laplace summation, and resurgent analysis.

Formal swaps become well-defined pairings between geometric kernels and allowed ground states, in a duality like Gelfand-Shilov theory. Divergent evaluations gain precise meaning as sectorial asymptotic expansions of functions rebuilt exactly by such integrals, with Stokes effects encoded by jump functions. A central spectral transmutation law relates entire and rational kernels through Gamma functions. It shows classical umbral identities are only local views of a global correspondence. Examples include Hankel contours, Barnes-type forms, and Lerch functions, resolving formal algebraic obstructions exactly.
arxiv-2606-11234:
Pathania, Singh, and Yadav study gamma-ray emission from pulsars in a 2026 arXiv paper. Pulsars are spinning, magnetic neutron stars, and Fermi's Large Area Telescope has detected over three hundred at high energies. Population studies find gamma-ray brightness scales with spin-down power raised to an exponent near 0.68. That emission, arising near the light cylinder, is usually modeled as purely curvature or purely synchrotron radiation.

The authors instead adopt a synchro-curvature framework, blending both mechanisms. Comparing observed cutoff energies with the framework's predictions, under the radiation reaction approximation, they find the equilibrium Lorentz factor and pitch angle of the emitting particles. That measures how much energy loss each mechanism contributes per pulsar. The result gives a grounded reading of the overall brightness trend, linking single-pulsar spectra to the whole group.
arxiv-2606-11334:
Ferrer, Müller, Penneys, and Stehouwer organize the many notions of higher Hilbert space in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. Finite-dimensional operator algebras can be viewed as C-star, W-star, or H-star algebras, leading to different module and correspondence categories. Such work matters for quantum information theory and unitary quantum field theory, but there is no unique generalization to higher categories.

The authors show how the differences can be understood through G-dagger categories, for different subgroups of the orthogonal group O(2). They introduce G-Hermitian 2-vector spaces using fixed points of an O(2) action on 2-vector spaces. They then propose criteria for when such pairings are positive, generalizing the passage from Hermitian vector spaces to Hilbert spaces. Finally, they outline an inductive approach to defining higher Hilbert spaces in arbitrary dimension, suggesting an extension beyond the 2-categorical setting.
arxiv-2606-11434:
Gassner, Chaudhary, and Claassen recast the photon drag effect in a 2026 arXiv paper. The bulk photovoltaic effect probes the quantum geometry of Bloch bands, but in the dipole picture it requires broken inversion symmetry. The finite momentum of light produces the effect even in centrosymmetric crystals, an effect called photon drag. The authors recast photon drag at leading order in the optical wavevector.

They highlight a previously neglected term from the electric quadrupole correction to light-matter coupling. In band-geometry language, they identify this interband quadrupole as a multiband metric tensor quantifying how two resonantly driven states vary outside the subspace they span. They predict systems where three or more bands strongly admix in momentum space show distinctive signatures. The work names this extrinsic quantum geometry, geometry arising from states outside the driven pair, as a measurable ingredient of the quadrupolar response.
arxiv-2606-11534:
Starfeldt, Molina, Kerr, Yang, Holmes, and Hain present an AI-ready dataset for urban heat research in a 2026 arXiv paper. Urban heat is amplified by sealed surfaces and varied built environments, yet street-level variability is hard to quantify because multi-sensor observations rarely come in consistent, analysis-ready form at the needed scales. Their Urban Heat MiniCubes dataset is public and FAIR-oriented.

It provides harmonized 90-by-90 kilometer gridded data cubes for 48 cities in the Western Hemisphere, spanning 2022 to 2023, with variables reprojected and collocated to a common grid. Two modalities complement each other: sharper, less frequent Landsat and Sentinel-1 radar data, and more frequent, coarser GOES-R infrared and microwave temperature data. The team documents variables and metadata, and assesses quality with inter-variable analyses and autoencoder rebuild-error summaries across pixel classes like water and cloud. Use cases and limitations are discussed for machine learning applications.
arxiv-2606-11634:
Kai Liu and seven colleagues test a cheaper attention design for mathematical reasoning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Full self-attention grows with the square of context length, which is costly. Sliding-window attention only looks at nearby tokens, growing linearly instead, but usually reasons worse. Their recipe, SWARR, first converts a pretrained full-attention model using supervised fine-tuning, avoiding pretraining from scratch.

Conversion alone leaves a clear gap, blamed partly on training data written for full-attention models and full of long-range links. The second stage fixes this with reinforcement learning, where the model learns from its own generated solutions under the window limit. On maths benchmarks the gap mostly closes. The strongest window model finishes within half a percentage point of the full-attention model trained the same way, while keeping the linear cost. The authors caution that results cover models up to four billion parameters.
arxiv-2606-11834:
Tobias Hey and Julian Frattini test how sloppy requirements writing affects automated tooling in this 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering. Traceability links connect written requirements to the source code implementing them, easing maintenance. Recovering those links automatically is a studied task, but the input texts themselves often carry quality defects, and their impact was barely measured.

The authors labelled twenty-eight types of quality defect in 189 use case descriptions from two datasets, from sentences not starting with noun phrases to included coding details. They then ran five distinct link recovery approaches and tested with statistics how each defect changed performance. Some defects genuinely harm recovery, while others, surprisingly, help: coding details in a use case give the algorithms more textual hooks. Different approach families react differently to the same defects. The best recovery tool depends on the quality profile of the dataset.
arxiv-2606-11934:
Sai Geetha Mada and three colleagues make Wi-Fi 6 share its airwaves dynamically in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wi-Fi 6 divides channels into resource units, blocks of spectrum assigned to devices. The default static assignment wastes capacity and inflates delays when traffic fluctuates, a problem for factories needing deterministic communication. Time-Sensitive Networking, a set of Ethernet standards, guarantees bounded latency for critical traffic.

The authors propose a dynamic allocation algorithm that maps those traffic classes onto Wi-Fi quality-of-service mechanisms. Using the ns-3 simulator, they compare dynamic against static allocation. Dynamic sharing adapts as load changes: each flow gets an exclusive unit when resources are plentiful, and units are shared only as demand grows. Throughput stays stable even near saturation, while latency, jitter and packet loss all fall relative to static schemes. The authors present this as early evidence for hybrid industrial networks.
arxiv-2606-12234:
Macocco and co-authors measure what it costs to steer a language model's output, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conditioning means pushing a model to include or remove a concept, like a topic or a toxic style. Methods range from prompting to activation steering, nudging inner signals, to full fine-tuning. Studies usually score only whether the concept landed, ignoring damage to fluency, how natural the text reads. This study scores both, in injection and removal tasks.

Efficient steering methods buy success at a steep fluency cost. A surprise: activation steering works far worse on instruction-tuned models than on their base counterparts. Prompting and fine-tuning inject concepts well but remove them poorly, as the toxicity tests show. No method wins everywhere. Cheap text metrics track expensive judge scores closely, a practical shortcut for evaluations. The authors urge that steering be judged on quality kept, not only concepts moved.
arxiv-2606-12334:
Gyenes and co-authors fix a frequency blindness that keeps robot hands clumsy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Imitation learning trains robots from human demonstrations. Point clouds give policies true 3D geometry, better than flat images for precise tasks like insertion. Yet results vary oddly by task. The authors blame spectral bias: neural networks learn low-frequency functions first and struggle with fine detail. Slow-moving Cartesian coordinates, raw x-y-z positions, hide exactly the high-frequency cues precision needs.

Their fix borrows from neural rendering: map point clouds into Fourier features, wave-like encodings exposing fine spatial detail directly. The encoder then sees high frequencies instead of inferring them. Across RoboCasa and ManiSkill3 benchmarks, and on a real robot, the change brings significant gains. Benefits hold across encoder architectures and survive hyperparameter variation. A simple input mapping, not a new architecture, unlocks geometric detail the policies needed.
arxiv-2606-12434:
Mushkani proposes governing city AI as a public utility, with a right for the public it depicts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. City agencies use machine learning to inventory sidewalks, score streetscapes, and generate images of planned spaces. Those scores and pictures steer budgets and designs. Yet judgments about inclusion, safety, and belonging are contested; no evaluation target is neutral. Pluralistic-Alignment Urbanism organizes governance around entitlements, duties, documentation, and recourse.

Two Montréal case studies test the idea. Street Review elicits residents' criteria for streets and trains a subgroup-aware model scaling their judgments, reaching an R-squared of 0.89 on held-out data. A second project builds pluralistic preference data for text-to-image models, treating neutral choices as indeterminacy rather than noise. After preference tuning, neutral selections made up 52.4 percent of 2,100 comparisons. Disagreement, Mushkani argues, is structured information about plural values. Rules should preserve it, not average it away.
arxiv-2606-12834:
Shin and colleagues propose AgentBuild, a method for constructing scientific LLM agents from a contract written by the scientist, in this 2026 arXiv paper. AgentBuild treats agent construction as a workflow stage driven by a contract: a rubric, a difficulty-graded curriculum, and a curated knowledge base.

A rubric-driven judge gates a meta-optimiser coding agent that edits the agent only within a boundary, so the build compiles the agent rather than the scientist's judgement. The authors instantiate the approach for Rietveld refinement of X-ray diffraction data, driving the GSAS-II program behind agent protocols. A blank-harness build progresses through a lithium lanthanum zirconium oxide signal-to-noise ladder and reaches the 4-hour scan as a frontier case. Because the rubric scores trajectory scope as well as fit quality, that frontier failure registers as a contract failure, not a pattern-fitting failure.
arxiv-2606-13034:
Kataria and colleagues present a quantum algorithm for random number generation with a provable quadratic speedup over classical Markov chain mixing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The construction builds on the Diaconis-Shahshahani Fourier analysis of the top-to-random card shuffle, a classical Markov chain whose mixing behaviour is understood.

The quantum Fourier transform diagonalises the Markov transition operator. Controlled phase rotations encode the shuffle's eigenvalue spectrum. The Grover diffusion operator acts as a quantum analogue of a uniform stopping time, reflecting amplitudes about their mean at each iteration. For an n-qubit register, the mixing time falls to on the order of the square root of n log n iterations, against the classical n log n bound. Extending the construction to qudits reduces the iteration count and cuts the Fourier transform circuit depth. Both variants are tested on IBM superconducting hardware.
arxiv-2606-13234:
Sharma develops a sampling method for mixture distributions in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sampling means drawing random points from a distribution, often to estimate averages that cannot be computed directly. Finite mixtures blend several Boltzmann-Gibbs distributions, and they arise in physics and statistics. Sharma's switching Hamiltonian Monte Carlo simulates a particle whose motion follows Hamiltonian dynamics, the energy-based equations of classical mechanics, while randomly switching between mixture components. The switches are generated with standard techniques for jump processes.

The paper proves geometric ergodicity, meaning the sampling chain forgets its starting point at a fast rate of that kind and settles to the target distribution. An error analysis based on a discrete Poisson equation shows the integrators carry only second-order bias in their long-run averages. The same proof approach extends to related methods such as kinetic Langevin sampling. An experiment confirms the predicted convergence behaviour.
arxiv-2606-13534:
Haniš and colleagues dissect the superconductivity of a vanadium gallium compound in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiband ones carry several distinct energy gaps, and structural anisotropy, properties that differ by direction, makes their pairing hard to untangle. The compound studied becomes superconducting at about three and a half kelvin. The team combines first-principles structure work with heat capacity readings and directional scanning tunnelling spectroscopy, which probes the gap structure atom by atom from several crystal faces.

They build a self-consistent multiband model with singlet pairing in the symmetric channel. The model reconciles puzzles in the specific heat and the upper critical field, the magnetic field that destroys the state. The tunnelling data reveal a reversal of the bulk gap order: the gap that looks larger depends on how it probes. Explaining that reversal through band-selective probing resolves a puzzle in multiband work.
arxiv-2606-13634:
Bottman and Richardson give question decomposition a rigorous foundation using operads in this 2026 arXiv paper. Splitting a complex query into simpler sub-questions, then composing the sub-answers, is a common strategy for improving model reasoning. It has lacked rigorous structure. Operads, algebraic objects modelling many-input, one-output operations and how they compose, fit the practice naturally. The authors define the questions operad, whose operations are question templates and whose composition swaps sub-answers into a parent question. Question-answering models then become algebras over this operad.

Beyond reframing, the view yields a notion: operadic consistency, whether a model's answers agree across the collapses of a tree. A companion paper finds this agreement strongly related to answer quality. Inconsistent decomposition, where answering sub-questions separately contradicts answering them jointly, is a failure mode that can be diagnosed. The framework turns a prompting folk practice into an object of mathematics.
arxiv-2606-13734:
Valdes reanalyses a surprising claim about artificial intelligence literacy and usage in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recent evidence suggested that lower AI literacy predicts greater openness toward AI, a surprising link with policy implications. Valdes revisits the claim using the original study's public data, which measured usage of five AI tool types on a scale. He reproduces the negative association between literacy and total usage under several models, from ordinary regression to ordered and multinomial ones. The overall relationship, however, masks variation by tool type.

In the adjusted primary model, it does not predict text AI usage at all. It still predicts non-text AI uptake, covering tools such as image and audio generators, and that effect is robust under the original study's controls. The distinction between openness and adoption breadth is the paper's point: an aggregate index blended two different behaviours. Tool-specific analysis should become the norm.
arxiv-2606-13834:
Arasu and Gupta present one general solver for a broad family of hard graph problems. Many tasks, from network design to facility location, amount to extracting the best subgraph under rules such as staying connected. Each field usually builds its own custom heuristic, a fast but imperfect search method. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces Delta Search, built on reward-penalty optimization, which needs only the rules and the scoring criteria from the user.

The method rests on a difference-of-monotone formulation that unifies several problem classes. Tests covered maximum planar subgraph, minimum Steiner tree, and uncapacitated facility location, among others. Delta Search matches or beats the best known heuristics on three problems at similar runtime. On the rest it reaches about eighty-nine percent of the best solution quality, with no problem-specific tuning. Added to exact solvers, its pruning speeds one test up two point six times.
arxiv-2606-13934:
Lu and co-authors show how to predict which concept combinations a language model will fail to combine, before testing it. Compositional tasks require recombining known ideas in new ways, as in multihop reasoning or multilingual recall. Developers usually hunt failures with ever larger test sets. Their 2026 arXiv paper, Adversarial Concept Search, instead reads the geometry of the model's internal representations.

The key signal is interference. When two concepts are encoded in nearly perpendicular directions, the model composes them reliably. When their encodings sit close together, they interfere and composition fails. This pattern held across toy programmatic tasks, multihop reasoning, and factual recall in many languages. Because the prediction uses internal geometry alone, no specific inputs need evaluating. The method can flag risky examples in advance. It could also guide stress tests and active learning, focusing effort where models are likeliest to break.
arxiv-2606-14134:
Kumar, Srivastava, and Talpeanu retune the one free knob of a standard solar model across three solar cycles: the best setting follows the Sun's mood. The potential field source surface model extrapolates the Sun's magnetic field; its source surface height, conventionally fixed at two point five solar radii, feeds the Wang-Sheeley-Arge wind speed model. Their 2026 arXiv paper optimizes that height using GONG and SDO/HMI magnetic maps spanning cycles twenty-three to twenty-five.

Optimizing the height significantly improved wind speed predictions over the fixed convention. The optimal direction flipped with solar activity. During solar minimum, higher source surfaces, at or above the conventional value, predicted better. During active phases, lower heights won. Absolute optima varied between cycles, but the pattern stayed similar, suggesting a durable relation between height and cycle phase. Optimized heights scattered more at maxima than minima, partly because the model strains during high activity.
arxiv-2606-14534:
Bicchi and co-authors build an imaging pipeline for breast surgery in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hyperspectral imaging records a spectrum at every point. It can flag suspicious tissue during a lumpectomy, the removal of a breast tumor. Surgeons need that flat spectral data mapped onto the specimen's 3D shape. Then they can locate regions needing follow-up.

The pipeline is automated and needs no calibration. It rebuilds the shape from ordinary camera photos. A deep-learning method infers 3D form from the views. Four printed markers anchor the result. The spectral cube is then registered through marker corners seen in both views. On two specimens, the median 3D registration error stayed below one millimeter. The reprojection error was far smaller still. Each specimen took under four minutes to process on accelerated hardware. That speed supports use inside the operating room.
arxiv-2606-14834:
Muhammad Fitrah Alfian Rangga Sakti and Piyabut Burikham study a charged, spinning black hole in a 2026 arXiv paper. The object is the dyonic Kerr-Sen black hole, from string-inspired gravity. Dyonic means it carries both electric and magnetic charge. The authors work out the heat-like laws at its inner and outer horizons. A horizon is the surface past which nothing escapes.

One neat result concerns entropy, the measure of a black hole's disorder. The product of the horizon entropies is universal. It depends only on the hole's spin, not its charge or mass. The matching dual field theory gives central charges with the same spin-only pattern. The static, non-spinning case still yields nonzero charges, unlike some rivals. The team also derives a closed formula for the hole's ring-down tones. Those quasi-normal modes are set by the hole's own parameters.
arxiv-2606-14934:
Batley and coauthors introduce the Separable Neural Architecture in a 2026 study of physics-based machine learning. The architecture splits a function into localized coordinate pieces, called atoms, plus a sparse low-rank object governing global interactions. Used as a trial space in a variational solver, it aims to beat the exponential cost growth of grid methods. The target is a single model that engineers can solve once and query anywhere.

The variational version carries standard guarantees of well-posedness, stability, and convergence under the Lax-Milgram theorem. Tests span the Poisson, Burgers, and a six-dimensional advection-diffusion equation, matching predicted scaling rates. In a seven-dimensional laser powder bed fusion model, a million-query optimization sweep ran in about one hundred seconds on a laptop. A second case mapped thermal histories to tensile properties of a nickel alloy with far fewer parameters than earlier models.
arxiv-2606-15134:
Bhatnagar and coauthors train image encoders with attribute-level feedback from a frozen multimodal model in a 2026 study. Metric learning usually supervises pairs with one label: same class or different. That scalar pushes every attribute apart or together at once, even when images differ in only a few traits. Two blue birds may differ solely in their wing bars.

Their framework, SAGA, asks a multimodal language model to judge pairs shown through the encoder's tokens. A group-relative policy optimizer rewards correct verdicts, so tokens must expose the deciding attributes. An attention-distillation loss anchors embeddings to the tokens the supervisor used. A standard metric loss still shapes the space for nearest-neighbor search. The supervisor stays frozen and is discarded at deployment, keeping inference cost unchanged. On four fine-grained retrieval benchmarks, Recall@1 rises by three to six points over strong baselines.
arxiv-2606-15234:
Ecik and coauthors present a framework for signal-integrity-compliant circuit board design in a 2026 engineering paper. Signal integrity rules limit how bent a waveform may become along a board interconnect. Standard AI optimizers search the design space as a black box, hiding their reasoning. The proposed pipeline instead evaluates designs in a fixed order. Neural surrogates first predict waveform features from design settings. A decision tree then gates out designs that violate the integrity rules.

Surviving designs are ranked by the Earth Mover's Distance to an ideal reference signal. That distance measures how much work it takes to reshape one waveform into another. Ranking by it favors superior designs without inverse modeling. The team demonstrates the pipeline on a set of modeled DDR3 fly-by waveforms. The framework maps admissible regions by rule rather than by random search. It offers an open, efficient option for AI-assisted board development.
arxiv-2606-15734:
Su and colleagues introduce ReGrad in 2026, a method that stores knowledge as gradients rather than text or permanent weight changes. Continual post-training lets deployed models absorb new knowledge, but repeated updates accumulate weight drift and cause catastrophic forgetting. Retrieval-augmented generation avoids drift but stays shallow, since the model only reads retrieved text.

ReGrad pre-computes a gradient for each document offline and stores the gradients in an indexed Gradient Bank. At inference it retrieves only the gradients relevant to the query and applies them as a temporary weight change, leaving base weights untouched. A bi-level meta-learning objective reshapes raw language-modelling gradients, which are tuned for rebuilding documents, into signals useful for answering questions. Across general and domain-specific settings, ReGrad beats continual post-training and retrieval baselines, and complements in-context retrieval. Updates become selective, scalable, and reversible, with no drift piling up.
arxiv-2606-15834:
Zhou and colleagues build AIChilles in 2026, a tool hunting hidden weaknesses in programs from AI evolution loops. Such frameworks rewrite systems code in loops and report score improvements of twelve to sixty percent over human designs. The catch: evolved programs may regress on unseen workloads or scale badly, beyond what manual review can catch.

AIChilles takes a human baseline and its AI-evolved counterpart, then searches for valid workloads where the evolved version regresses in runtime, memory, or output quality. It combines extraction of workload parameters, differential oracles, and code-frequency coverage to find distinct failures, not duplicates. Across five system applications and thirty evolved programs, it uncovers forty-nine distinct hidden weaknesses. Feeding the tool into the development lifecycle lets teams mitigate several of them. Average-case benchmark wins, the work argues, are not evidence of safety: worst-case workload search has to accompany AI code evolution.
arxiv-2606-15934:
Pelletier and colleagues measure titanium in the dayside atmosphere of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-189b in 2026, testing whether cold trapping hides the element from view. Titanium oxide, a potent optical absorber, was long cast as the driver of thermal inversions. Yet some inverted planets look strongly titanium-depleted, likely because the element condenses on the cooler nightside and is trapped there. The team asks whether the full titanium budget appears in gas phase on the dayside.

From HARPS and NIRPS thermal emission spectra, they detect iron and titanium emission and recover a strong temperature inversion. The atmosphere is slightly metal-poor, and its titanium-to-iron ratio falls marginally below the stellar value in both retrievals. Partial nightside cold trapping explains it, titanium being the more refractory element. Across the population, titanium's gradual onset tracks the nightside temperature at which it should vaporise: measured underabundances are atmospheric, not inherent.
arxiv-2606-16034:
Chagas and colleagues argue in 2026 that many temporal classification errors are decision errors, not representation failures. Temporal classification labels data that unfolds over time, such as price moves or heart signals. A trained model turns evidence into scores, and a decision rule turns scores into labels. The authors ask how much error comes from missing evidence versus poorly used evidence.

Their framework keeps the trained classifier frozen and splits two inference-time fixes. A conservative residual branch adds multi-scale evidence as extra scores, while a branch-aware calibrator recombines the scores at decision time. Across five datasets, gains prove strongly regime-dependent in the tests. Residual evidence helps most in noisy, short-horizon settings and with weaker recurrent backbones. Calibration helps when the two score sets hold complementary evidence the raw rule underuses. Near-saturated settings gain little from either fix, a useful warning against universal add-ons.
arxiv-2606-16134:
Ericson revisits a 1995 Courant Institute technical report in 2026 by rebuilding its results inside the Lean 4 proof assistant. The report studied the average-case complexity of multilevel syllogistic, a set-based logic once used to reason about program specifications. Average-case analysis asks how hard problems are on typical inputs, not worst cases.

The development encodes the Reischuk-Schindelhauer average-case classes and an axiomatic semantics layer for the logic and its extended form. It includes a partial decision procedure, after Ferro, Omodeo, and Schwartz, with proved soundness and partial completeness on a membership-free fragment. Serialization and step budgets are included as well. Conditional corollaries recover NP-average completeness and non-membership in the average-polynomial class, modulo stated structural axioms. The project shows how legacy complexity results can be made permanently verifiable.
arxiv-2606-16334:
Goswami and co-authors benchmark in 2026 whether vision-language models can reason about time in pictures, and find them nearly blind to it. People easily tell ripening from rotting, or building from demolition, and can guess elapsed time between two photos. Their benchmark, ChronoSight, tests five such skills: ordering image sequences, locating a stage from one image, estimating elapsed time, spotting reversed sequences, and finding the temporal outlier.

The set holds 1,000 items balanced across eight process families, from food change and weathering to human ageing and urban growth, spanning minutes to millennia. Eight open models score at most 0.40 overall, against human performance of 0.89, per the report. The authors split the gap into format failure, vocabulary failure, and perceptual failure. Light LoRA fine-tuning on just 151 examples lifts time-gap estimation from near zero to 0.43, with partial transfer to sibling tasks.
arxiv-2606-16434:
Wen and co-authors package battery health prediction in 2026 as an autonomous service that learns its own features from raw charging data. State of health estimation tells operators how much capacity a lithium-ion battery has left, but classic pipelines rely on hand-crafted features and opaque models. Their system, TC-SOH, is modular and plug-and-play. A temporal-contrastive mechanism with a cross-window prediction task extracts degradation-relevant representations directly from live data.

Checks keep the service honest: sensitivity and redundancy analyses, and probing tests show the learned features overlap expert descriptors while carrying extra health-relevant signal. Ordered time context proves important for later health prediction. Across 386 batteries from four public datasets, TC-SOH beats the physics-informed and data-driven baselines considered, cutting mean absolute percentage error by a factor of 1.91 and root mean square error by 2.13, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16534:
Bantel and co-authors test in 2026 whether AI coding agents can write parallel Julia code that scales on supercomputers. Julia promises one language for high-performance computing, but scalable parallelism still demands expertise. The agents, built on an OpenCode framework with a Julia documentation server attached, must plan, generate, and refine code. Three models are compared: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, and the open-weight Qwen3-Coder-Next.

The tasks span three parallel structures: pi approximation, tiled matrix multiplication, and tiled Cholesky decomposition. Agents write task-based Dagger.jl versions plus Base.Threads and MPI.jl baselines, on up to 192 cores and two nodes. Agents produce executable implementations and auto-correct many typical errors through iterative testing. Yet correctness often fails to survive scale: deadlocks, oversubscription, and memory blowups appear at larger sizes and thread counts. Agents handle the established Threads and MPI models more reliably than task-based Dagger.
arxiv-2606-16934:
Patomporn Payoungkhamdee and colleagues dissect what makes code-interpreter reasoning work in a 2026 paper on language models. Letting a model write and run code improves its reasoning, but nobody had mapped which behaviors inside the traces drive the gains.

The study separates two property families. Extrinsic properties are crucial tokens, the few tokens that steer a solution. Intrinsic properties are code-specific habits of mind, such as verifying results, backtracking after errors and chaining backward from a goal. Across several models, stronger code reasoners show more crucial tokens and more of these habits, with verification and backtracking standing out. At test time, appending crucial code tokens helps on math, ordering and optimization tasks but little elsewhere. At training time, adding the habits to a leading framework improves fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in two of three models. The habits also curb overthinking in wrong answers and save tokens.
arxiv-2606-17034:
Li and colleagues teach language models to forget a span of context cheaply in a 2026 paper on efficient inference. Long-context systems cache key-value states for everything read. When a retrieved fact turns out stale, wrong or harmful, deleting it exactly means recomputing every later token, a cost set by the suffix, not the span.

KVEraser instead replaces only the erased span's cached states with learned steering states, leaving the rest of the cache untouched. Training has two stages: generic span-neighbor pretraining teaches the eraser to suppress a span's influence, then task-specific fine-tuning adapts it. Across context lengths up to tens of thousands of tokens, post-erasure quality nearly matches full recomputation on in-domain tasks, while latency grows only slightly where recomputation balloons. On unseen long-document question answering with planted false facts, it beats other approximate methods and runs several times faster than recomputing.
arxiv-2606-17234:
Marashian, Palmer, and von der Wense present a 2026 arXiv paper on whether language models know when their own translations are wrong. Translation quality can be judged at token, word, or span level, so confidence should work at those levels too. Internal signals such as token probabilities are a poor guide, since they measure certainty among rival wordings rather than correctness of the chosen one.

The authors devise five ways to extract a model's stated, or verbalized, confidence for each token, with no access to internal signals. They then compare those methods against internal signals on two tasks: spotting errors at fine grain and matching stated confidence to real accuracy. Both families performed much the same, though results varied by model. Notably, the internal and verbalized scores showed little to no correlation with each other.
arxiv-2606-17334:
Bhuian and Kang present a 2026 arXiv paper on object detection with event cameras, sensors that report brightness changes one by one instead of taking frames. Event streams are sparse and asynchronous, which clashes with standard deep learning models built for dense images. Common fixes chop the time window into fixed sub-bins, but that throws away fine timing detail and caps detection at low rates set by the training labels.

Their framework, FATE, encodes events into spatial pillars and describes each pillar's evolution with a continuous-time polynomial basis, avoiding internal sub-binning entirely. A frequency-aware training scheme uses a mean-teacher setup to make dense pseudo-labels, bridging low-rate supervision and high-rate inference. Tests show FATE transfers across model designs and beats strong baselines. It supports robust detection at temporal resolutions up to two hundred hertz with little overhead.
arxiv-2606-17434:
Hong, Xu, and Hu present a 2026 arXiv paper characterising Lipschitz spaces that are adapted to a Schrödinger operator, a Laplacian plus a nonnegative potential. Such spaces measure smoothness with a built-in length scale set by the potential itself, through its critical radius function. The potential is assumed to sit in a reverse Hölder class, a mild regularity condition used throughout this branch of harmonic analysis to keep the adapted theory close to the classical one.

Two new characterisations are proved for smoothness indices in a stated range below two. One describes the space through Littlewood-Paley decompositions, which split a function into pieces at separate frequency scales. The other uses Carleson measures, which test how mass piles up near the boundary of the upper half-space. Together they give analysts two workable tests for membership in these operator-adapted spaces.
arxiv-2606-17734:
Xenos and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on SOCCA, a model that reads an asteroid's shape, spin, and colours from sparse survey photometry alone. Sky surveys record millions of small bodies in scattered snapshots across filters, a rich data type. Standard phase models ignore that a rotating, elongated body brightens and dims as it turns, biasing what they retrieve. Shape-and-spin methods exist but cost too much to run at survey scale, leaving most objects with rough parameters or none.

SOCCA extends a classic phase formalism with the projected face of a rotating triaxial ellipsoid, fitting all bands. On a decade-long survey simulation and on real data for one asteroid, residuals halved against earlier models. Absolute magnitude came out with a third of the usual scatter, and spin period, axis direction, and axis ratios were recovered too. The method is built to scale to coming surveys.
arxiv-2606-17834:
Erös and colleagues define a way to measure how much a timelike curve bends inside a rough spacetime, in a 2026 geometry paper. Their setting is a Lorentzian length space, a synthetic stand-in for spacetime that needs no smooth structure, with curvature bounded above. The team introduces a synthetic notion of total curvature for timelike curves, the paths that observers and clocks can follow.

They prove this notion matches the classical one wherever the space is smooth, and that curves of finite total curvature can be measured for length in the usual way. The main payoff is a sharp lower bound: the length of such a curve is controlled from below by just the time gap between its endpoints and its total curvature. The estimate gives relativists a tool for spaces far rougher than textbook spacetimes.
arxiv-2606-17934:
Dabetić designs a faster solver for the stiff linear systems that structure-preserving finite element methods produce, in a 2026 numerical analysis paper. For equations posed on the de Rham complex, mixed discretizations keep the physics honest but yield indefinite systems that standard smoothers cannot handle. Multigrid methods, the workhorse for such problems, need a new angle here.

The framework pairs mass-lumped versions of the finite element exterior calculus mass matrices, whose inverses are explicit, with transforming smoothers. Those smoothers recast the operator into block form with positive definite diagonal blocks, where Gauss-Seidel style relaxation works. Dabetić proves stability of the lumped systems under mild assumptions, giving spectral equivalence with the original ones. Tests on Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems and a magnetostatics system, in two and three dimensions, show the preconditioner stays robust.
arxiv-2606-18134:
Polok and colleagues teach spoken language models to follow one voice in a crowded room, in a 2026 paper. Far-field recordings with several talkers defeat models trained on clean single-speaker audio. Retraining the decoder to serialize speakers risks catastrophic forgetting of its language skill. Their strategy instead conditions the acoustic encoder on diarization masks, the who-spoke-when map, so it can pull out the target speaker while the decoder stays frozen.

The resulting system, Dixtral, pairs a diarization-conditioned Whisper encoder with the Voxtral spoken model. Across four meeting and mixture datasets it beat Gemini, VibeVoice, and Voxtral's own transcription variant on speaker-attributed transcription by wide margins. On a new long-form multi-speaker question answering benchmark, the zero-shot system matched Gemini on far-field understanding, and fine-tuning pushed it past both rivals even against close-talk microphone input.
arxiv-2606-18334:
Rusakov and colleagues study early galaxies that carry far more nitrogen than standard chemical evolution models predict, in a 2026 paper built from public JWST survey data. They assemble seventy-six nitrogen-enhanced galaxies seen when the universe was young, the largest such high-redshift sample yet, and track how common these systems become at earlier times.

The enhanced fraction climbs from a few percent to nearly a fifth across the redshift range they probe, far above the local rate. Stacked spectra point to very young, metal-poor Wolf-Rayet stars as one nitrogen source soon after a starburst, while ionized outflows appear in many systems and help reset the gas. Older bursts instead suggest asymptotic giant branch stars taking over after several tens of millions of years. Together the evidence portrays brief, bursty episodes catching galaxies at different moments after renewed star formation.
arxiv-2606-18634:
Yin and Ma present EffiNav, a training-free framework that helps a robot find a named object in an unfamiliar indoor space without wandering wastefully, in a 2026 robotics paper. Object-goal navigation is judged not only by whether the agent arrives but by how direct its path is. The crux is deciding where to explore next when nothing about the scene is known in advance.

EffiNav fuses depth sensing with the reasoning of an off-the-shelf vision-language model to guide exploration, using everyday context to prioritize promising regions. On two standard simulation benchmarks it matched or beat recent baselines on both success rate and path-efficiency measures, and the team validated it on physical robots in real rooms. With minimal changes it also handled a memory-augmented navigation variant, which the authors offer as evidence the design generalizes as vision-language models improve.
arxiv-2606-18734:
Xue and the team predict wireless channel behavior at city locations where no signal measurements exist, in a 2026 wireless communications paper. They fuse radio data with a map of the environment. Optimizing networks needs site-specific channel models. The leading statistical approach infers the angular power spectrum from received-power measurements, but only where measurements were taken.

Their framework PC-TGS represents environmental scatterers as anisotropic 3D Gaussians, derived from a LiDAR point cloud. It projects each onto a local tangent plane in the angular domain. It splats their electromagnetic contributions with depth awareness, including a closed-form formula for integrating over angular bins. On a city-scale dataset of five million points and over six thousand power samples, the method beat state-of-the-art baselines on both spectrum and power prediction. That points toward geometry-aware digital twins for network planning.
arxiv-2606-18834:
Nanavati, Vreeken, and Kaltenpoth show how to detect whether causal data are spoiled by hidden confounding or by selection bias, using only the way causal mechanisms shift across settings. The work is a 2026 machine learning paper. Causal discovery assumes every variable is known, and samples are independent and identically distributed. When those assumptions fail, models can be wrong. People rarely know which failure they face.

The insight is that mechanism changes are independent, whereas structural biases force the mechanism shifts of variables to become dependent. The authors turn this into a testable criterion, based on mutual information. They state when it spots each bias type, and build it as the StruBI algorithm. On synthetic and real data, including a cell-signalling case study, StruBI found which variables were hit, and by which bias. It beat the state of the art by a margin, even where the theory held only roughly.
arxiv-2606-19034:
Pai and colleagues carry out a broad test of learned spatial indexes in 2026. Learned indexes adapt their search build to the data and query mix, which can speed range queries on maps and other spatial data. Their trade-offs are still poorly known, since speed depends on model accuracy plus skew, block size, selectivity, and storage behavior. The study sets out to sort those factors in a controlled way.

The team poses seven core questions on block size, skew, scan versus refinement costs, disk versus memory settings, build cost, best choice per workload, and transfer from synthetic to real data. All indexes run on a shared storage backend with the same query pipeline, so contrasts stay fair. Tests vary data and query skew in a planned way to isolate each effect. Builders can use the findings to pick an index and tune block size per workload.
arxiv-2606-19334:
Peskoff and colleagues introduce LOCUS in 2026, a corpus of local ordinance codes for the United States. Legal AI needs authoritative legal text at scale. Local ordinances govern zoning, housing, licensing, health, noise, and animal control, yet they are fragmented across vendor platforms built for browsing, not bulk research. That layer of everyday law has been largely absent from machine-readable corpora available to researchers.

The raw corpus holds codes from thousands of cities and counties, nearly all publicly available municipal and county codes. A county-harmonized access layer covers the largest counties, accounting for a majority of the population. Optical character recognition handles the many document formats that kept this law from being a public resource. The team also trains text classifiers and scorers to aid analysis of the codes. Released with coverage metadata, the corpus supports reproducible legal AI research and wider machine-readable access to local law.
arxiv-2606-19934:
Marta Fernández, Margarita Guerrero, Rosalia Rementeria, Pablo Mesejo, and Raúl Moreno measure how unsupervised pre-labelling speeds pixel-level annotation in 2026. Labelling every pixel of a high-resolution image is slow, error-prone work, and materials science needs large labelled sets of steel microstructure images. Earlier studies timed labelling or tried unsupervised aids, but none had quantified the actual time saved.

Unsupervised vision algorithms draft the labels first, and humans correct them, cutting the job from 170 hours to 37 hours. That is a saving of roughly four fifths on images up to 1280 by 959 pixels. The team also releases the largest public steel microstructure segmentation dataset so far, under an MIT licence with a permanent identifier, plus an expert-checked model. Industrial annotation pipelines gain a measured, reusable shortcut.
arxiv-2606-20134:
Giovanna Kobus Conrado and Andreas Pavlogiannis test whether monadic second-order logic can serve as a uniform language for weak memory models. These models are the formal rules describing how concurrent programs behave on modern hardware. Their 2026 paper addresses a growing tangle: compilers and processors reorder memory operations, each platform defines its own model, and verifying programs model by model does not scale.

The results draw sharp boundaries. Executions under sequential consistency have bounded treewidth, while those under total store order already do not. A broad family of models, including release-acquire and the full RC20 model, can be axiomatized in the logic. Strong release-acquire and total store order cannot, unless a famous hard problem becomes easy. The authors also define reads-from robustness, a new correctness criterion, and show the bounds yield algorithms that verify a program under any axiomatizable model.
arxiv-2606-21034:
M Winter and many colleagues track spin textures in 2026 in the chiral magnet Mn1.4PtSn, from a soliton lattice to a fan state. In most helimagnets, a magnetic field turns the spin helix toward the field, giving a conical state. That hides the unwinding process. In this material, crystal symmetry pins the propagation direction along a chiral axis. A field applied across that direction opens a different regime.

Resonant elastic X-ray scattering in a vector magnet follows the textures. Simulations support the measurements. The zero-field chiral soliton lattice transforms into a fan-like state. Spins oscillate about the field direction, while propagation stays transverse. Modulation length shrinks steadily as the field rises. Magnetostatic effects in finite samples play a key role in simulations. A new unwinding path matters for spintronics, where controlled spin textures are candidate carriers for memory and logic devices.
arxiv-2606-21234:
JungHoon Sung, Boeun Kim, and five colleagues present GARD in 2026, a system that generates sign language one gloss at a time. A gloss is the basic meaning unit of a signed sentence. Most producers render a whole sentence at once, which drifts and blurs hand motion as sentences lengthen. GARD instead builds each gloss with a diffusion model that reads both linguistic context and the motion just produced, capturing coarticulation, the blending between signs.

Two added steps smooth the joins: transition guidance aligns poses at gloss boundaries, and a global harmonizer refines the full sequence around those joins. On the Phoenix-T and CSL-Daily datasets, GARD beats prior systems on both language accuracy and motion similarity. The gloss-wise control also lets each sign be checked and adjusted on its own.
arxiv-2606-21334:
Gabriel Hoerning and fifteen colleagues present a new all-sky model in 2026 of diffuse Galactic emission at radio and microwave frequencies, where synchrotron, free-free, and spinning dust emission dominate. Such foreground maps are essential for cleaning cosmic background data. The model extends the Planck 2015 component separation with newer surveys, fitting thirty-five full and partial sky maps at one-degree detail.

Using the Bayesian Commander code, they derive maps of strength and spectral shape for each foreground part. The recovered synchrotron signal at 4.76 gigahertz comes out about twice as strong as Planck 2015 predicted, thanks to better low-frequency anchoring. Residual errors stay below ten microkelvin over ninety-five percent of the sky up to 353 gigahertz. The products give a fresh reference for foreground modeling and sky simulation.
arxiv-2606-21434:
Jakub Peleska and Gustav Sir tackle a portability problem in 2026 for relational deep learning, which learns from multi-table databases by viewing them as graphs. Existing models are welded to one database schema, so each new database means training from scratch, or they fuse row encoding with graph processing in one monolith. The authors set out four pillars for a foundation model in this space, covering meaning, structure, time, and unified training.

Their Universal Row Encoder is a transformer module. It reads raw cell values together with schema metadata, column meanings, table names, and global statistics, and emits row embeddings of fixed width for any table. Pretrained once, it plugs into any downstream graph architecture as a backend. On RelBench benchmarks it improves cross-database transfer, convergence speed, and memory use.
arxiv-2606-21634:
Iliya Milman and Michael Karp study how free-stream disturbances pass a bow shock and evolve along a blunt body's stagnation streamline in 2026, in supersonic flow. Receptivity, how outside noise seeds downstream unsteadiness, matters for hypersonic vehicles. They solve the linearized shock-fitting problem with a spectral method, on a base flow from a nonlinear shock-fitting solver.

Revisiting Morkovin's 1960 analysis, they find and fix an error in a key coefficient. The old conclusion of body-induced damping flips: the flow amplifies disturbances instead. Post-shock entropy disturbances behave singularly near the stagnation point and are handled analytically. Acoustic waves dominate pressure and velocity responses, density answers to acoustic and entropy modes together, and the true stagnation-line flow amplifies everything more than simpler models, across a range of Mach numbers.
arxiv-2606-21734:
Awais Rauf, Ahmed Hasssan, and Greg Slabaugh split long-video understanding into two jobs in 2026 and let a program do the exploring. Vision-language models currently cram perception and multi-step reasoning into one forward pass, and the reasoning half starves. Their Hierarchical Programmatic Probing instead has a coding-capable language model plan and run a multi-step strategy in an interactive coding environment, calling a vision model only for localized perception on demand.

Three components keep probing tractable over hours of video: information-density-aware hierarchical segmentation, late-interaction semantic retrieval, and structured probing functions for coarse-to-fine localization. On LongVideoBench the decoupling yields substantial gains. Results on EgoSchema, VideoMME, and MLVU confirm the approach travels across benchmarks, arguing that for long video, agents should look around deliberately rather than swallow the whole film at once.
arxiv-2606-21934:
Deakin and colleagues warn, in 2026, that a small component limits the value of power converters that utilities hope to use for balancing their networks. Four-wire converters can actively control flows and release spare capacity on distribution assets, helping avoid costly upgrades. Unbalanced operation, however, drives neutral current and power ripple at twice the line frequency into the converter's direct-current link, heating its capacitor.

Thermal limits on that capacitor therefore constrain how much neutral current the converter may carry, shrinking the benefit it can deliver. The authors compared nine voltage source converter topologies with different ripple-handling abilities, using analytic bounds on ripple. For mitigating phase current unbalance, the upper bound on extra network headroom rose by more than eighty percent when ripple capability was allowed, versus the no-ripple case. The gap shows how strongly capacitor ripple governs what these converters can actually achieve.
arxiv-2606-22034:
Alpay and Sarıoglu ask, in 2026, how anyone can audit a public randomness source, such as a lottery or a randomness beacon, from a finite public transcript of its draws. An auditor must keep false alarms low while staying alert to tampering or implementation faults. For draws without replacement, the transcript space is combinatorially huge, and fully general uniformity testing runs into a hard sample-size barrier.

They recast that barrier as an auditability frontier and build generator-agnostic geometric audits aimed at structured failure modes instead. Draws are mapped onto a hypersimplex and scored with exactly calibrated statistics covering marginals, pairs, serial overlap, and small-scale geometry. On 1,956 real EuroMillions draws, no statistic survived false-discovery adjustment. In Monte Carlo experiments, though, joint-structure failures invisible to one-dimensional tests were caught by pair and geometric statistics with substantial power.
arxiv-2606-22134:
Bernicot gives, in 2026, first results on the boundedness of a bilinear square function built from disjoint strips in the frequency plane. Bounded here means the output stays controlled by the input size in Lebesgue spaces. The object merges two classical ones.

One parent is the Rubio de Francia square function, which sums frequency projections over disjoint ranges. The other is the bilinear Hilbert transform, whose singularity structure brings modulation invariance. Bernicot proves the bound for the merged object, an initial step toward a bilinear theory over any strip collections. Such estimates feed the analysis of multilinear operators.
arxiv-2606-22234:
Tran and colleagues show, in 2026, that fine-tuned machine-learned interatomic potentials can match density-functional theory for the structure and vibrations of twisted two-dimensional materials. Twisted bilayers form moiré superlattices whose properties hinge on local stacking and atomic reconstruction. Direct quantum calculations are far too expensive at small twist angles, so a faithful learned potential is valuable.

The test cases are twisted bilayer graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and molybdenum disulfide, with varied stiffness and rebuilding. Broadly trained foundation models prove too crude for the subtle interlayer energetics involved. Fine-tuning is essential. Their fine-tuned MACE model reveals a shared strain landscape in all three: extended low-energy stacking domains separated by narrow soliton lines where strain concentrates. Rebuilt structures and moiré phonon spectra agree well with reported experiments.
arxiv-2606-22334:
Jen-Yu Chang, with En-Jui Kuo, Chih-Yu Chen, and Tsung-Wei Huang, published this 2026 study on numerical integration with quantum walks. A quantum walk is a quantum version of a random walk, and it spreads much faster than a classical one. The team asks whether that fast spreading can estimate integrals and pi better than Monte Carlo sampling.

Their method replaces the sample average with a ratio built from lattice points, grid points with whole-number coordinates, counted inside a region. The count is divided by the square of a radial quantile from the walk's positions. Tests show the remaining error is a fixed number-theoretic offset set by walk depth. The authors give a formula for that bias floor and verify it at every depth tried. Benchmarks use a classical walk with the same estimator, isolating the quantum part.
arxiv-2606-22534:
Jun Wu, Wenchao Liu, Weijie Yuan, and Nanchi Su combine wireless power with drone control in this 2026 paper. Their setting is a low-altitude wireless network where a multi-antenna base station guides a fleet of uncrewed aircraft. Through simultaneous wireless information and power transfer, the station sends both control commands and harvestable energy, splitting its signal between the two.

The aircraft must track reference paths to their destinations while avoiding several moving no-fly zones. Smooth, safe reference trajectories are first built with stream function theory. A real-time optimization then balances control cost against energy sustainability, choosing control inputs, beamforming vectors, and power splitting ratios. Model predictive control generates the control inputs, and an iterative algorithm using semidefinite relaxation and successive convex approximation handles the rest. The relaxation is proven tight for this formulation. Numerical results show gains over benchmark schemes in tracking accuracy and harvested energy.
arxiv-2606-22734:
Philip Zucker tackles variable binding inside e-graphs in this 2026 programming-languages paper. E-graphs are data structures that store many equivalent expressions at once, powering compilers and automated provers. Variables are subtle there: keeping bound variables canonical, so that expressions differing only in bound names are recognized as equal, is easy to get wrong.

Zucker describes a lifting e-graph with a built-in lifting combinator, supporting rigid alpha-canonical variables. The implementation fattens integer identifiers with thinning bitvectors, which track which variables a term uses. Smart constructors pull lifts through the structure automatically. A thinning-aware union-find merges equivalence classes without breaking the discipline. The approach draws on slotted e-graphs and Co-de Bruijn syntax, two lines known for disciplined variable handling. The paper presents the design as a practical route to correct binding support in e-graph libraries.
arxiv-2606-22834:
Dominik Kroupa, Marek Vaško, Muh Yuzril Ihza Baharuddin, and Adam Herout present a camera guidance method in this 2026 paper. Their goal is precise capture of flat targets, such as documents or artifacts. Instead of treating the homography, the geometric map between two views of a plane, as an output, they make it the organizing variable for learning and evaluation.

From one annotated reference image, homographic augmentation generates unlimited synthetic training data. A single-shot model then predicts sparse keypoints to recognize and locate several artifacts at once, and also reports confidence for each keypoint. A two-pass scheme first detects globally, then refines locally, which helps precision when model input resolution is limited. Their Stable Warp training strategy improved accuracy further, especially in the high-precision regime. The results show accurate planar alignment is possible from minimal supervision, laying groundwork for geometry-driven camera guidance.
arxiv-2606-23234:
Juan Morales and Mikhail Kiselev present lecture notes on Wess-Zumino terms in superspin systems in a 2026 paper. These terms are geometric additions to a system's action that shape its quantum dynamics. The notes are self-contained and start from the SU(2) spin coherent-state path integral. There the Berry phase appears as a Wess-Zumino term encoding the geometry of the Bloch sphere. From that example, the authors explain the geometric origin of such terms, their link to cohomology classes, and the Berry curvature as a first Chern class.

Morales and Kiselev then turn to physical cases, including geometric quantum noise in magnetic quantum dots and adiabatic Berry phases. Much of the notes covers why higher SU(N) symmetry matters in condensed matter, through Heisenberg models, spin-orbital systems, and multipolar orders. They finish with the SU(N) superspin construction and explicit local terms for SU(3) and SU(4).
arxiv-2606-23534:
Paukstys tests whether contactless sensors can tell how a person lies in bed, in a 2026 study motivated by safety during sleep. Lying face down, called the prone position, has been linked in past studies to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The setup pairs a bedside radar unit, which senses movement with radio waves, with a small thermal array that senses heat patterns, and it records twenty volunteers in supervised posture holds.

Judging each person with a model trained on everyone else, combined radar and heat data separate in-bed from out-of-bed cases with a median balanced accuracy near eighty-seven percent. Four-way posture classification peaks lower, near sixty-seven percent, and prone detection is weak, with recall of one half and precision below one half. Heat data fix left-versus-right confusion, so Paukstys argues the limit lies in the sensor output format, not the classifier.
arxiv-2606-23734:
Bouzari Nezhad works out when gravity theories with several scalar fields and higher derivative interactions stay free of a notorious instability, in a 2026 paper on theoretical physics. Adding scalar fields to gravity underlies models of cosmic inflation and of today's accelerating expansion. If the equations climb to higher derivative order, an unwanted extra mode, the Ostrogradsky mode, usually appears and destabilizes the theory. Degenerate theories dodge this: their kinetic structure forces constraints that delete the extra mode.

Working in the ADM split of spacetime, Bouzari Nezhad performs a Hamiltonian analysis for theories with any number of fields. A primary degeneracy condition is not enough alone. Keeping it consistent generates extra conditions with no single field analogue. Together with a final rank condition, these keep exactly the healthy modes.
arxiv-2606-23934:
Benavides-Riveros, Sharma, and Šimkovic speed up a standard algorithm for finding quantum ground states by letting it read the local shape of the energy landscape, in a 2026 paper on quantum algorithms. Imaginary time evolution cools a quantum state toward the lowest energy state, but it creeps, completing only in infinite time. The augmented version replaces the plain downhill flow with a geometrically informed descent. At each step it chooses locally optimal directions, identified from higher order statistics of the energy distribution, including its skewness.

The augmented flow beats standard evolution at every point of the journey. It shows two regimes: a superlinear convergence phase, then an extinction phase where the energy error hits exactly zero at a finite imaginary time. Standard evolution reappears when the skewness vanishes, so the acceleration extends across the whole imaginary time family.
arxiv-2606-24234:
Chen and colleagues teach inspection robots to recognise where they are aboard a ship, from open deck to cramped cabin. Visual place recognition matches a camera view against a database of known locations. Maritime settings break urban-trained methods, though. Decks offer sparse texture under harsh changing light. Cabins repeat the same structures until every corridor looks alike. Their 2026 framework, ProteusVPR, retrieves first and refines second.

A standard model proposes candidate matches. A geometric-visual estimation network then fuses the retrieved image with two preceding frames. It uses geometric descriptors, a local affine frame, and camera azimuth to pin the location. Supporting the task, the team releases the XHZ dataset. It holds panoramic imagery at 8K resolution from an operational vessel. It spans multi-floor cabins and deck transition zones, with strict separation between queries and database. Chen targets robots crossing scene boundaries without losing themselves.
arxiv-2606-24334:
Steuernagel and colleagues describe beam splitters through the flow of a quantum phase-space fluid. A beam splitter superposes two light modes. The Wigner distribution shows their quantum state over position and momentum. That map evolves under a continuity equation, the same bookkeeping that governs a flowing fluid. It has a current, which the team sets out to derive, for variable beam splitters whose mixing strength changes.

The current's form allows a classical-trajectory analysis of how the two modes influence each other. For variable splitters the dynamics reduce to something beautifully simple. A rotation inside the plane spanned by the two modes' positions. Together with the identical rotation inside the momentum plane. Rotated Wigner maps and currents then follow in full from classical trajectories. Steuernagel's 2026 expressions turn mode mixing at a beam splitter into geometry that can be drawn. That builds intuition for such devices.
arxiv-2606-24434:
Utley and Hackl check whether theme park planners' folk typology of guests survives GPS evidence. Planners informally sort visitors into waders, who drift and sightsee, swimmers, who plan moderately, and divers, who maximise attractions. Their 2026 pilot study grounds the scheme in observed movement. GPS tracks and an exit survey come from recruited guests across three Southern California parks.

Each visit is summed up by eight hand-annotated movement features. They are clustered per park, and judged by a multi-criteria protocol covering quality indices, firmness under restarts and subsampling, and agreement between algorithms. Separation is modest everywhere. No cluster structure scores sharply. At Knott's Berry Farm, though, the three-group partition repeats very well. Its groups differ sharply in attractions ridden per hour. Repeating without sharp separation suggests a conduct continuum, rather than discrete species of guest. The typology gestures at something real but graded, not three kinds of visitor.
arxiv-2606-24934:
Faruk Alpay and Taylan Alpay give cloud GPU tenants a way to check the hardware they are renting, without any privileges. Tenants must trust claims that the accelerator stays the same machine, matches the billed class, and sits at the advertised site. Vendor attestation answers such questions only on some confidential computing parts. The authors' primitive is software only. A CUDA probe measures a latency matrix between streaming multiprocessors and memory regions.

A streaming reducer commits the statistics, configuration, code hashes, and network evidence into a compact SHA-256 certificate. Three claims are supported. The latency map fingerprints the physical die stably over a six hour full load run, and separates distinct dies perfectly in tests. Memory sweeps recover hardware class topology across three GPU generations. Network landmarks then tie the certificate to a coarse location, placing one chip within 44 kilometres of its claimed data centre and rejecting eleven decoy sites.
arxiv-2606-25034:
The Yuvion Team at Alibaba's Security AGI Lab presents Yuvion VL, a family of multimodal models built for content and AI safety. General purpose models struggle to spot multimodal risks, because harmful content is designed to slip past checks by mixing image and text. The team treats safety as an adversarial, multimodal problem throughout. A data pipeline synthesises adversarial examples, with multi stage quality control, domain knowledge, and reasoning annotations. Training then runs in three stages, from risk concept alignment to instruction tuning to reasoning training.

A new fine tuning method, Confuse then Contrast, mines the model's confusions. It builds multi image contrast groups that force the model to separate visually similar cases whose safety implications differ. Fine grained visual and semantic details become decisive, exactly where adversarial content hides its tricks. For evaluation, the team introduces Yuvion VL RiskEval, a suite of 58 benchmarks spanning open and internal tests.
arxiv-2606-25234:
Interpretability tools usually explain a vision network one direction at a time, as if each concept were a single arrow in activation space. Thomas Fel and a large group of colleagues challenge that picture in 2026, arguing that concepts live on small curved surfaces called manifolds. Their block sparse featurizers group directions into blocks, so a concept can occupy a low dimensional region instead of a point. A description length analysis checks which view compresses the network's activity better.

All three versions of the new featurizer described activations more compactly than direction based tools, with recovered concepts typically two to four dimensional. Known curve detectors in an older vision model turned out to read from one continuous curve surface. The method also exposed shadow and lighting structures in a modern model and steered image generation in a diffusion system.
arxiv-2606-25634:
Some camera models answer questions about people seen from several angles, but standard tests cannot tell true multi view reasoning from lucky single view guessing. Tianchen Guo, Chen Liu, Ling Chen, and Xin Yu build a diagnostic benchmark in 2026 with three thousand three hundred curated question pairs about people and the objects they handle. Every task is labelled by whether one view suffices or several views are genuinely necessary. Seventeen leading multimodal models then face systematic changes in which views they are shown.

Two failure modes stood out. Given redundant extra views, models degraded badly, distracted by material they should ignore. Given views that each held only fragments of the answer, they failed to fuse the pieces geometrically. Scores suggested the models average single image impressions and favour preferred views instead of synthesising across cameras.
arxiv-2606-25834:
Spin waves carry information through magnetic films, and their quanta, magnons, are candidates for linking quantum devices. Reading them optically inside a dilution refrigerator, colder than deep space, had never been done. David Schmoll and colleagues achieve it in 2026 with Brillouin light scattering on a yttrium iron garnet film. The experiment drives spin waves coherently. It records the optical scattering and the electrical transmission of the same mode at once. All this happens deep in the sub kelvin regime, where thermal magnons are frozen out.

Across a range of magnetic fields, the optical spectra tracked the electrical ones faithfully. Laser heating was audited carefully: at the lowest usable light power, the sample sat near five hundred millikelvin overall, with the focal spot modelled below nine hundred. Free space optical access to magnons in the quantum regime is a milestone toward magnon based quantum transduction.
arxiv-2606-26334:
Kyle McGregor and the CHIME/FRB team correct the census of fast radio bursts for the telescope's own blind spots. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space, and CHIME catalogues them by the hundreds. What the survey misses skews what astronomers infer.
