That balance has made the pathway a drug target. Several treatments built on steering apoptosis are already in trials or in medical use. The review sums up where those efforts stand.
europmc-pmc3395634:
Murrell and co-workers introduced a statistical method in 2012 for spotting single sites in genes that natural selection has favored, but only now and then. Selection often flares briefly in a few lineages, and older tools built for constant pressure miss those sites. Their mixed effects model, called MEME, was designed to catch both patterns.

On real and simulated data, the new method beat older ones across a wide range of situations. Applying it broadly, the team found episodic selection to be widespread in protein-coding genes. That implies the true count of positively selected sites has been badly underestimated. The tool gives evolution researchers a finer net for one of their main questions.
europmc-pmc3454434:
Marcilla and a large team reported in 2012 that parasitic flatworms release tiny vesicles packed with their secreted proteins, and that host gut cells swallow those vesicles. Parasite molecules released into the host are prime targets for drugs and diagnostics, but how proteins without export signals escape was puzzling. The team worked with two trematode worms, Echinostoma caproni and the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica.

Protein analysis, gold-tagged microscopy, and electron imaging agreed: the vesicles carry most of the proteins long known from worm secretions, plus some host proteins picked up along the way. Living worms release them actively. Their uptake by intestinal cells suggests a delivery channel between parasite and host. The finding reframes how these worms talk to the bodies they inhabit.
europmc-pmc3458434:
Schimel and Schaeffer asked in 2012 when the makeup of soil's microbial community actually steers carbon cycling, and when it does not. Microbes run decomposition and the turnover of soil organic matter, processes that decide whether carbon stays buried or returns to the air. Narrow jobs, like making trace gases, clearly track which microbes are present; the broad jobs were less certain.

The authors argue that species-level variety mostly reflects backup copies of the same functions, sorted into guilds by deep life-history splits. In loose surface litter and around roots, community makeup can move the breakdown rate. In mineral soil the bottleneck is physical access to protected food, so who is present matters less than how microbes spend the carbon they capture. That spending decides long-term storage.

Kim and co-authors build a smart contact lens that checks eye health without wires. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Earlier lens sensors tracked only one measure at a time. Many also blocked the wearer's view. This team put their sensor on a real soft lens. The parts are clear and stretchy. They use graphene mixed with metal nanowires. Light passes through, so vision stays open.

The lens measures two things at once. It reads glucose in tear fluid through a resistance change. It reads pressure inside the eye through a capacitance change. The two signals stay separate. A radio-frequency circuit sends the data with no battery on the lens. Tests on a live rabbit eye tracked glucose in real time. Tests on a cow eyeball tracked pressure. Such lenses could aid diabetes care and early glaucoma checks.
europmc-pmc5430734:
Smith proposes a third phase of pluripotency between the naïve and primed states. His hypothesis article appeared in Development. Pluripotency is the power to form all embryonic lineages. The field long sorted it into two forms. Naïve cells match the pre-implantation embryo. Primed cells match the post-implantation stage. The two were often treated as directly interconvertible. Smith argues that picture skips a step.

He calls the missing phase formative pluripotency. It sits between naïve and primed in one continuum. During it, cells remodel core networks. Gene expression, epigenetics, signaling, and metabolism all shift. The payoff is competence for lineage choice. Formative cells can answer specification cues. Naïve cells, by contrast, cannot execute decisions yet. Primed cells have already begun to respond. They are thus partly specified and fate-biased. Defining the formative phase should clarify multi-lineage decisions.
europmc-pmc5483234:
Pauthner and co-authors report a vaccine study in Immunity on HIV envelope trimers. These lab-made proteins mimic the spike on the HIV surface. Antibodies that block real-world HIV strains have been very hard to raise. Past primate results with trimers were weak and uneven. The team compared many designs and dosing plans head-to-head.

Shots under the skin on both sides gave reliable responses, they report. Two shots eight weeks apart already raised strong neutralizing antibodies. A third shot raised them further. Slow, continuous delivery also beat single bolus shots. Germinal center activity in lymph nodes tracked the antibody response closely. The authors offer the work as a framework for future trials.
europmc-pmc5490534:
Plaza-Díaz and co-authors present a review in Nutrients on probiotics and gut inflammation. Probiotics are live microbes taken for health benefit. Synbiotics pair them with fibers that feed them. Both are used against chronic intestinal diseases. The authors weigh lab, animal, and human trial evidence.

Selected strains lowered inflammatory signals in cell studies, they report. Animal trials mostly showed better symptoms and gut lining. Human results look promising for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. One strain, Bifidobacterium longum 536, eased mild to moderate colitis. Caution is urged during relapse phases, though. Mechanisms still need pinning down before firm guidance.
europmc-pmc5495834:
Franchi, Reeves, and Narici present a review in Frontiers in Physiology on muscle remodeling. Muscles contract by shortening or by lengthening under load. Lengthening, or eccentric, work yields more force at lower energy cost. Many assumed it must build more muscle mass than shortening work. Study results on that claim conflict, though.

When load or total work is matched, both modes build similar size, they conclude. The routes to that size differ, however. Each mode reshapes muscle architecture in its own way. Protein synthesis responses look much alike between modes. The molecular signals behind the split remain partly unclear. Coaches can use either mode with confidence.
europmc-pmc5508034:
Spires-Jones, Attems, and Thal present a review in Acta Neuropathologica on clumped proteins in brain diseases. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and related disorders each carry a signature protein lump. Amyloid beta, tau, alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43 recur most often. Yet these lumps often share one brain, even in healthy people. The review asks how they interact.

One lump can seed another's growth, lab studies suggest. Mixed lumps may also add up to worse damage. The authors sketch a cascade from a first lesion to full disease. Extra pathologies then bend how the illness shows itself. Trials aimed at a single protein may need to heed this mix, they imply.
europmc-pmc551534:
Dufresne, Garczarek, and Partensky report a genomics study in Genome Biology. Prochlorococcus are ocean bacteria and likely Earth's most plentiful photosynthetic organisms. Some strains carry strikingly small genomes. Genome shrinking was known mainly in bacteria that live inside hosts. These bacteria live freely, so their path must differ.

The team compared four genomes of marine picocyanobacteria. Two strains kept gene order highly stable despite size gaps, they report. The smallest genome also drifted in its base makeup. Gene loss prevailed over gene gain in these lineages. The pattern fits streamlining for life in nutrient-poor surface waters. Change sped up as genomes shrank, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc5605934:
Belzer and co-authors trace food webs at the gut mucus layer in mBio. One gut microbe, Akkermansia muciniphila, lives on host mucus alone. It frees sugars and acetate as it feeds. Neighbors near the gut wall can use those scraps.

The team grew Akkermansia with three butyrate makers. None of the three can break down mucus itself. Together, each pairing grew and produced butyrate. The trade ran both ways. Eubacterium hallii made a form of vitamin B12. That supply let Akkermansia produce propionate in return. The result is a diet-free supply line. Butyrate and B12 arise from host mucus, not food. Butyrate feeds gut wall cells and calms inflammation. Readers see cross-feeding turn one specialist into support for the whole niche.
europmc-pmc5618634:
Rosa and co-authors review lactoferrin in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lactoferrin is an iron-binding protein in milk, tears, and other secretions. Neutrophils release it as well. It stands guard at the body's surfaces.

The review ties the protein to two linked balances. Iron control and inflammation control rise and fall together. Lactoferrin starves bacteria of iron and blocks their docking. It also curbs interleukin-6 inside inflamed cells. That shift raises ferroportin, the iron exporter. Iron then moves out of overloaded cells into blood. The effect can ease anemia of inflammation. Trial results in pregnant women showed lower IL-6 and better blood counts. Bovine lactoferrin even helped guard against preterm delivery. Readers get one protein cast as a traffic cop for iron.
europmc-pmc5645934:
Dubinkina and co-authors report a metagenome survey in Microbiome. It links gut microbes with alcohol use and liver disease. The study covered 99 patients with alcohol dependence. One group had liver cirrhosis, and the other did not. A control group aided comparison. Gene sequencing profiled species and functions in stool.

Both groups showed deep shifts in gut communities. Helpful gut species were depleted in each group. Dependence tracked with loss of butyrate makers in one order. Cirrhosis instead depleted many species of another order. Oral microbes turned up more often in cirrhosis guts. Two probiotic genera rose under each factor, but in distinct species. Patient microbes also showed more capacity to make toxic acetaldehyde.
europmc-pmc5695134:
Gloor and co-authors argue that microbiome data must be treated as compositional. Their review covers data from high-throughput sequencing of microbes. Such data come from gene surveys, metagenomes, and related methods. A sequencer can only read a fixed total of DNA pieces. That limit makes each dataset a set of shares, not true counts.

Treating shares as counts can distort results, the authors warn. They show the errors that follow from that misuse. The review gives a short primer on compositional data. It then offers guidance for each stage of analysis. Pointers to tools and worked examples help readers apply the approach.
europmc-pmc5698434:
Lopatkin and co-authors ask why plasmid-borne resistance persists without antibiotics. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Costly resistance genes should fade when drugs vanish. Yet many persist for long periods. Gene transfer between bacteria may explain it. Critics said transfer rates seemed too low.

The team tested common conjugal plasmids in E. coli. Even costly plasmids transferred fast enough. They persisted without any antibiotic pressure. The result held for nine plasmids. Those plasmids spanned six major groups. Mixed plasmid populations behaved the same way. The authors warn that cutting drug use alone will not reverse resistance. They suggest blocking conjugation instead. Promoting plasmid loss could help too.
europmc-pmc5708534:
Rogge and co-authors review porous frameworks as single-site catalysts. Their review appeared in Chemical Society Reviews. Two framework families are covered. Metal-organic frameworks are one family. Covalent organic frameworks are the other. Both can host well-defined active sites. That makes them platforms for solid catalysts.

Single sites are easy to define in molecules. They are murkier on solid surfaces. Nanoparticles hold many site types at once. Frameworks offer a cleaner structure. Their pores and nodes can be designed. The review weighs the evidence thoroughly. It covers how sites are made and proven. The authors assess promise for real reactions.
europmc-pmc5723634:
Bach and co-authors map how mammary gland cells change across adult life. Their study uses single-cell RNA sequencing in mice. They profiled cells at four stages: before pregnancy, mid gestation, lactation, and after involution. Knowing this cell hierarchy helps explain how breast cancer arises.

The team analyzed 23,184 cells and found 15 clusters. Few clusters could be defined by a single marker gene. Cells in the luminal layer instead formed a smooth spectrum of states. The data support one shared luminal progenitor cell. It gives rise to more restricted cell types, including hormone-sensing ones. That progenitor group shifts its gene activity across pregnancy and lactation.
europmc-pmc5850834:
Huerta-Cepas and co-authors present eggNOG-mapper, a fast annotator for whole genomes. Their paper appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution. Function follows orthology, genes split by speciation rather than duplication. Computing orthologs at genome scale used to be painfully slow.

The mapper borrows precomputed clusters and trees from the eggNOG database. Benchmarks show cleaner Gene Ontology calls than BLAST searches. Against InterProScan it matched coverage while naming far more terms per protein. It runs about fifteen times faster than BLAST. Metagenome data, the messiest test, also annotated well.
europmc-pmc5904434:
Janssen and co-authors show that placing exact amplicon sequences on a tree sharpens clinical links. Their article appeared in mSystems. Microbiome studies now resolve exact sequence pieces, called sOTUs. Short pieces carry too little signal to build good trees alone. A common fix, building trees from scratch, can mislead. The team tested placement with the SEPP method instead.

Placement placed fragments into a large reference tree, they report. It beat de novo trees in human gut studies. It also kept the fine resolution sOTUs offer. Sample groups split along clinical traits more clearly. The team improved SEPP memory use for huge trees. Researchers get a safer path to tree-aware analysis.
europmc-pmc5976434:
Hemani and co-authors present MR-Base, a platform for causal inference across the human phenome. Their paper appeared in eLife. Genome-wide association results can hint at cause between traits. Two-sample Mendelian randomization does this without individual-level data. But the methods change fast and GWAS data are poorly curated. MR-Base joins a curated database with tools that automate the method.

The database holds 11 billion variant-trait links from 1,673 studies, they report. It is updated on a regular basis. Web, API, and R package access are all provided. Sensitivity checks probe pleiotropy and broken assumptions. Millions of possible causal links can be screened this way.
europmc-pmc5992634:
May and co-authors review how Normalization Process Theory is used in feasibility studies and process evaluations of complex health interventions. Their systematic review appeared in Implementation Science. The theory names mechanisms that help or hinder new practices taking root. A large literature now applies it to health care change. The team searched three databases for peer-reviewed work. They kept only studies that used the theory as their main approach.

After screening, 130 papers from 108 studies were included. The theory gives a shared language for implementation work, they report. It helps explain why projects succeed or fail. About ten percent of papers critiqued some part of it.
europmc-pmc6065434:
Vidaurre and co-authors chart how resting brain activity organizes into brief network states. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The team recorded magnetoencephalography from 55 healthy adults. A new hidden Markov method tracked fast state changes. Each state carried its own pattern of power and phase coupling.

States matched sensory, motor, and higher cognitive networks. Each network favored a specific frequency band. A rear alpha network and a front delta-theta network stood out. Both mapped onto parts of the default mode network. The states lasted only briefly before shifting. Readers get evidence that rest is not idle. The brain cycles through tuned communication modes instead.
europmc-pmc6075434:
Horvath and co-authors build a sharper epigenetic clock for skin and blood. Their study appeared in Aging. DNA methylation clocks estimate age from chemical marks on DNA. Older clocks read fibroblasts and cultured cells poorly. The new clock uses 391 CpG sites.

It tracks age well across many sample types. Skin, blood, saliva, and brain all fit. Cells from progeria patients showed mild age acceleration. Earlier clocks had missed that signal. Cultured cells aged steadily as they divided. The clock also predicts lifespan and age-linked conditions. Readers get a tool for lab aging studies. Forensic age checks may benefit as well.
europmc-pmc6079034:
Kiu and Hall update knowledge of Clostridium perfringens, a toxin-heavy gut pathogen. Their review appeared in Emerging Microbes and Infections. The bacterium grows fast and makes over 20 toxins. It sickens both humans and farm animals. New genome tools made a fresh survey timely.

The review covers the bacterium's genes and virulence factors. It traces diseases from food poisoning to gas gangrene. Bowel disease in pre-term infants gets close attention. Typing and detection methods are summed up. Open questions close the survey. Readers get a current portrait of an old pathogen, pairing lab detail with clinical stakes.
europmc-pmc6086934:
Zeisel and co-authors census cell types across the mouse nervous system. Their study appeared in Cell. The team sequenced about half a million single cells. The result maps types in space. It builds a hierarchy from the data itself.

Neurons proved the most diverse group. They sorted by birth region and signal chemistry. Seven regional astrocyte types emerged. Oligodendrocytes instead lost regional identity before diversifying again. Genes for wiring and signaling drove the variety. The resource supports targeted genetic work on cell types. Readers get a foundation map of mammalian brain diversity.
europmc-pmc6093334:
Smith and co-authors review metabolic flexibility in health and disease. Their review appeared in Endocrine Reviews. Flexibility means switching fuels as supply and demand change. Bodies store fuel in plenty and burn it in need. Liver, fat, and muscle run that system together.

Hormone signals coordinate the organs. Mitochondria sit at the center of the switch. Enzymes and transcription factors tune the pathways. When flexibility fails, metabolic syndrome and diabetes follow. Cancer also exploits broken switching. Diet pattern, meal timing, and exercise all shift flexibility. Some drugs do too. Readers get a full tour of a core survival skill and its breakdown.
europmc-pmc6122734:
Mami-Chouaib and co-authors wrote a review in Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer on resident memory T cells in tumors. CD8 T cells are the main killers of cancer cells. One memory subset stays put in tissues and does not recirculate. These resident cells are found inside solid tumors.

The review describes what marks these cells and keeps them in place. They carry tools for killing, such as granzyme B. Their presence in human cancers tracks with better outcomes. That link holds in lung cancer and other types. The cells also carry brake proteins like PD-1. Blocking those brakes can restore their killing power.
europmc-pmc6164434:
Hoter and co-authors wrote a review in International Journal of Molecular Sciences on the HSP90 family of proteins. These are chaperone proteins, helpers that fold and stabilize other proteins. They are highly conserved and found in many cell compartments. Their spread underlines how central they are to cell balance.

Together with co-chaperones, HSP90 proteins steer cell survival, the cell cycle, hormone signaling, and cell death. They also help drive cancer and brain diseases when things go wrong. Blocking them is an attractive strategy against tumors and other disorders. The review covers their structure, regulation, and functions. It closes with their roles in health and disease.
europmc-pmc6206834:
Singh and co-authors review green ways to make metal and metal oxide nanoparticles. Their review appeared in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology. Green synthesis uses natural extracts instead of harsh chemical methods. The extracts come from plants and other living sources. Plant chemicals such as flavonoids and alkaloids do much of the chemical work.

Early sections explain how the particles form and stay stable. Later sections cover safety, toxicity, and surface treatments that make particles safer for living tissue. The final part turns to cleanup uses. The authors describe germ killing, chemical breakdown of pollutants, dye removal, and sensing of heavy metal ions. Readers get a clear map of a cleaner route to useful nanomaterials.
europmc-pmc6225734:
Haijen and co-authors studied how to predict responses to psychedelics. Reactions to these drugs are hard to predict. Interest in their therapy use is growing fast. The team ran a prospective online survey. The study appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology.

People who planned to take a psychedelic joined the survey. They answered questions before and after the event. The survey tracked traits, setting, and the acute experience. Well-being rose two weeks after the experience. It stayed at that level after four weeks. Mystical-type experiences predicted the rise in well-being. Challenging experiences and visual effects did not. Clear intentions made mystical experiences more likely.
europmc-pmc6237934:
Saeidi and co-authors review T-cell exhaustion in chronic infections. Exhausted T cells lose their protective power. The state appears in HIV and hepatitis B and C. It also appears in cancer. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

Exhaustion mostly affects CD8 T cells. CD4 cells can also be exhausted in some infections. The authors cover the gene control of this state. They discuss metabolic faults in exhausted cells. Antioxidants aimed at mitochondria may restore function. Mitochondrial growth may also shape exhaustion. The review weighs strategies to reverse the state. Reinvigorated cells could protect better against viruses. The authors stress that key mechanisms still need study.
europmc-pmc6244934:
Blauvelt and Chiricozzi review a signal protein in psoriasis. Psoriasis is a chronic immune skin disease. Its joint form is called psoriatic arthritis. A cytokine called IL-17 drives much of the disease. The review appeared in Clinical Reviews in Allergy and Immunology.

IL-17A comes from several cell sources in patients. Mast cells and T cells are among them. The protein acts on skin cells, vessel cells, and bone cells. It triggers antimicrobial peptides and more cytokines. Those effects fuel tissue inflammation and bone change. The IL-23 and IL-17 axis is now a prime drug target. New biologic drugs block these cytokines. They greatly improve skin and joint symptoms.
europmc-pmc6266234:
Lee and Han review how vitamin E shapes immune function. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Vitamin E is a fat soluble antioxidant. It guards cell membranes from oxidative damage. It also affects how immune signals are made and sent. Effects have been seen in both animal and human studies.

Recent work sorts those effects cell by cell. Dendritic cells, macrophages, natural killer cells, T cells, and B cells are each covered. Changes in each cell type help explain wider immune shifts. The authors also track what added vitamin E does in health and in disease. Only one form, alpha-tocopherol, meets the human need for the vitamin. Food oils and nuts are the main sources. The review links cell level findings to whole body outcomes.
europmc-pmc6294734:
Fellmeth and co-authors review how parental migration affects children left behind. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in The Lancet. It covers low-income and middle-income countries. The team searched many databases for studies of children aged 0 to 19. Outcomes included nutrition, mental health, injuries, and abuse.

The review kept 111 studies with 264,967 children in total. Most studies came from China and internal labour migration. Left-behind children faced higher risks of depression and anxiety. They also showed more suicidal thoughts and conduct problems. Wasting and stunting were slightly more common too. The authors found no health benefit from being left behind. They urge policy action to protect these young people.
europmc-pmc6315734:
Busatto and co-authors test a filtration method for gathering extracellular vesicles. Their study appeared in Cells. Vesicles are shed by cells into body fluids. Labs often use ultracentrifugation to collect them. That method is slow and gives uneven yields. The team instead used tangential flow filtration.

Filtration matched the spin method on vesicle traits. It gave higher yields in half the time. Batches came out more consistent as well. Fewer stray proteins and aggregates appeared. The team then applied it to patient fat tissue fluid. Such vesicles may mirror the healing power of their parent cells. The method suits large sample volumes for clinical work.
europmc-pmc6327034:
Singh and co-authors show how a gut microbe product strengthens the gut barrier. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The compound is urolithin A, made from berry and pomegranate parts. Gut microbes produce it during digestion. It was already known for anti-inflammatory effects. The team tested a lab-made stronger version too.

Both compounds tightened the gut lining in their tests. They switched on two protective pathways, AhR and Nrf2. That raised the proteins that seal gaps between gut cells. A leakier barrier lets irritants drive gut inflammation. In mouse models of colitis, treatment eased disease. It repaired barrier faults and calmed inflammation at once. The authors say microbe products can guard the gut two ways at once.
europmc-pmc6342934:
Strecker and co-authors engineer a new CRISPR enzyme for human genome editing. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The enzyme family, Cas12b, comes from bacteria. Known members need high heat to work well. That blocked use in human cells at body temperature. The team searched the family for a better candidate.

They chose a version from Bacillus hisashii. At body temperature it only nicked one DNA strand. Single nicks edit far too weakly to use. The team found mutations that fixed the flaw. The engineered enzyme cut both strands cleanly. It edited human cell lines with strong results. It also worked in primary human T cells. Tests showed it more precise than the standard Cas9.
europmc-pmc6356834:
de la Cuesta-Zuluaga and co-authors link fecal fatty acids to metabolic risk in adults. Their study appeared in Nutrients. Gut bacteria make short-chain fatty acids from fiber. Some are absorbed, the rest leave in feces. Studies conflict on whether they help or harm metabolic health. The team studied 441 community-dwelling adults.

Stool fatty acids and gut microbes were both measured. Gut leakiness and metabolic outcomes were assessed too. Higher fecal levels tied to lower microbe diversity. Seventy microbe types linked to at least one fatty acid. Higher levels also tracked with obesity and hypertension. Cardiometabolic risk factors clustered with them as well. The authors suggest fecal levels may signal imbalance. Absorbed amounts, not stool amounts, may be the healthy share.
europmc-pmc6398034:
Qiu and co-authors report a cell study in the Journal of Diabetes Research. Diabetes makes heart damage worse when blood flow returns after a block. Their work asks how a bacterial product, LPS, adds to that harm in heart cells under high sugar.

Heart cells raised in high sugar were starved of oxygen, then fed again. LPS made the injury worse, tests showed. It raised reactive oxygen and switched on the NLRP3 inflammasome. That drove pyroptosis, a fiery cell death. The chain may explain part of the extra heart risk when diabetes meets infection.
europmc-pmc6420634:
Verheijen and co-authors report a solvent study in Scientific Reports. DMSO is used widely in labs, for freezing cells and dissolving drugs. Regulators once classed it among the safest solvents, and its own effects were often ignored.

The team exposed heart and liver microtissues to 0.1 percent DMSO. Gene activity, proteins, and DNA methylation all shifted in both tissue types. More than two thousand genes changed in each tissue, early results show. Such shifts could skew lab results that use DMSO as a neutral carrier. The authors urge labs to treat DMSO as an active ingredient.
europmc-pmc6422534:
Bujang and co-authors offer sample size guidelines in the Malaysian Journal of Medical Sciences. Logistic regression is a workhorse for medical studies on yes-or-no outcomes. Choosing too small a sample makes its estimates stray from the truth.

Using real clinical data, the team tested how estimates settle as samples grow. At a sample of five hundred, sample values sat close to population values. Their audit of a mid-size population backed that rule. The guidelines target observational studies with large populations. They give researchers a simple floor for planning such studies.
europmc-pmc6458534:
Gentry and co-authors systematically review serious games and gamification for training health professionals, a sector facing a worldwide worker shortage. Seven databases were searched from 1990 to August 2017 for randomized trials. Thirty trials with 3,634 participants qualified, only two of them gamification rather than full games, and differences between studies ruled out a pooled analysis.

Individually delivered games beat traditional teaching for knowledge with moderate-to-large effects in five studies, and ten studies showed small-to-large skill gains. One primary care study even found faster blood pressure control among a subgroup of patients. Evidence for attitudes, satisfaction, and cost outcomes stayed thin, and patient-level benefits remain barely tested.
europmc-pmc6500134:
An and co-authors synthesize research on the severe winter haze that often covers northern China, writing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. One event in January 2013 lasted nearly a month, spread over 1.3 million square kilometers, and touched some 800 million people. The authors argue the haze comes from a synergy: heavy human-made emissions plus the air processes that trap and transform them.

Fine particles come from direct emissions and from gases that convert into new particles in the air. Stagnant weather, high humidity and a low boundary layer let them build up fast. The particles also cool the surface, warm the air above, and seed clouds, which in turn feeds more haze. The review calls for a better grasp of sources, chemistry and weather links, since sharper forecasts, sound rules and public awareness all depend on it.
europmc-pmc6502834:
Lin and co-authors report a cancer study in Nature Communications that has since been retracted. The paper claimed that m6A, a chemical mark on RNA, rises as cancer cells undergo the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a key step toward spread. It named the enzyme METTL3 as a writer of that mark.

Deleting METTL3 lowered m6A and, the authors reported, curbed migration, invasion and the transition in cells and in animals. The mark on the coding region of the Snail gene was said to boost Snail protein output through the reader protein YTHDF1. High METTL3 and YTHDF1 levels were also linked to worse survival in liver cancer patients. Because the article is retracted, these claims should not be relied on.
europmc-pmc6532434:
Hanna, Hossain and Kocerha survey the promise of microRNAs as medicines, in a mini-review in Frontiers in Genetics. These tiny RNAs, about 22 letters long, tune whole gene networks at once. The first small-RNA drugs have now reached patients, and microRNA candidates are moving through labs and trials.

One microRNA can touch hundreds of genes, which suits complex diseases that single-protein drugs often fail to reverse. The same breadth raises fears of off-target effects. The authors cover how candidates are picked and tested before trials, their use as biomarkers, their role in drug resistance, and where trials now stand. They expect these RNAs to reshape both diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc6587234:
Pijuan and co-authors lay out four bench protocols for measuring how cells move, invade and stick, writing in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Migration drives development, immunity and wound repair — and, when deregulated, cancer spread. Each protocol here pairs a wet-lab assay with its image analysis pipeline, step by step.

Two assays watch sheets of cells close a gap: the classic pipette-tip scratch and a cleaner culture-insert version. A third tracks single cells by live imaging. A fourth moves into three dimensions with spreading and transwell setups that test true invasion. Together they give orthogonal views of motility and adhesion, suited to screening drugs that block migration or probing the molecules behind metastasis.
europmc-pmc6602434:
Blin and co-authors announce version 5 of the antiSMASH software. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. antiSMASH scans bacterial and fungal genomes for gene clusters. Those clusters build secondary metabolites, a rich source of antibiotics. The tool has served genome mining since 2011.

Version 5 is a full redesign written in Python 3. Detection rules now cover 52 cluster types, up from 44. New rules flag clusters for acyl-amino acids, β-lactones, and fungal RiPPs. Type II polyketide predictions are now more detailed. The HTML output was rebuilt for clearer browsing. A new JSON output file feeds downstream tools. Full bacterial genomes now annotate within a few minutes.
europmc-pmc6614034:
Masson and co-authors set out shared rules for a fast-growing protein method. Their recommendations appear in Nature Methods. Hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS, probes protein shape and motion. It tracks how backbone hydrogens swap with solvent over time. Use of the method has spread fast in recent years.

The guidance grew from talks at the first HDX conference, held in 2017. The authors cover how to run exchange experiments with proper controls. They advise on data analysis, presentation, and interpretation. Small shifts in pH or temperature can bias results, they warn. Careful repeats are needed to judge precision. Shared practice, they argue, will help nonspecialists trust and use the data. The paper states a consensus view for the field to refine.
europmc-pmc6616534:
Mao and co-authors review the chemistry and health effects of ginger. Their article appears in the journal Foods. Ginger is a kitchen spice with a long record in herbal medicine. Its sharp taste comes from phenolic compounds such as gingerols. Those compounds drive most of its reported benefits.

The review catalogs ginger's phenolics, terpenes, polysaccharides, and fibers. Heat and storage turn gingerols into shogaols and paradols. Studies credit ginger with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action. Reports also cover antimicrobial, anticancer, and heart-protective effects. Ginger eases nausea and may help in diabetes and obesity. The authors explain the mechanisms behind each claim. They hope the survey spurs functional foods and nutraceutical products.
europmc-pmc6688334:
Liu and co-authors review the emerging role of the piRNA and PIWI complex in cancer. Their review appears in Molecular Cancer. Piwi-interacting RNAs are small non-coding molecules. They run about 24 to 31 nucleotides long. They bind PIWI proteins to regulate genes. The system was first known from the germline. It silences transposons and guards genome integrity. Expression also occurs across somatic tissues. Signalling pathways feel its influence there.

Cancer studies find abnormal piRNA expression widely. Specific piRNAs track tumour development and prognosis. Breast and lung cancers provide early examples. The review covers biogenesis in detail. Cluster transcription and ping-pong amplification feature. Biomarker and therapeutic uses close the discussion. Mechanisms remain only partly understood.
europmc-pmc6939334:
Lu and co-authors review how antibody drugs are made and sold. Their review appeared in the Journal of Biomedical Science. More than three decades have passed since the first such drug won approval, in 1986. Since then, lab methods have grown far better. These drugs hit their targets with high precision, so they tend to cause fewer side effects. That is why they now lead new drug work.

By December 2019, the United States FDA had approved 79 of these drugs. They treat cancers and diseases of the immune system, metabolism, and infection. The authors set out the main ways such drugs are built. Teams can adapt mouse antibodies for human use, or grow them from human cells. They can also screen vast libraries of antibody parts, or breed mice that make human antibodies. Sales keep rising, and more growth is still expected.
europmc-pmc6974434:
Schmaal and co-authors review two decades of brain imaging studies on suicidal thoughts and behaviour. Their review appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Finding brain changes behind suicide risk could guide better prevention. Study numbers have grown fast in the last decade.

Evidence converges on brain systems that govern emotion and impulse control. Regions at the front of the brain, in ventral and dorsal prefrontal areas, recur across disorders. So do the insula and its partners in deep brain and memory areas. The authors suggest weakened ventral regions feed crushing negative states that spark suicidal thinking. A faltering dorsal system may then fail to brake attempts. A switch zone, the dorsal anterior cingulate and insula, may tip thoughts into action. Bigger, longer studies including development and sex differences are needed.
europmc-pmc6985034:
Pal and Kundu review two viral proteins that drive cervical cancer, and how to attack them. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Human papillomavirus causes this cancer, a major killer of women in poorer regions. Late diagnosis and poor outlook drive its toll.

Two viral genes, E6 and E7, run constantly in the cancer cells and are required for the tumour to grow. The authors describe their structure and how they switch on the classic hallmarks of cancer. Therapies that shut E6 and E7 down remove the engine of the disease. Options surveyed include vaccines, gene editing, T-cell therapy, and plant-derived compounds. Each has cut infected cancer cell numbers in studies. Targeting these two proteins, the authors argue, is the sharpest route to treatment.
europmc-pmc7013734:
Hong and Choi review sarcopenic obesity, the pairing of muscle loss with excess fat, and its link to insulin resistance. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The condition grows commoner worldwide, above all in aging populations. People over 65 already make up 13 percent of the world's population.

Fat stored inside muscle sparks inflammation and oxidative stress. Mitochondria falter, insulin signalling dulls, and muscle wastes further. Less muscle then deepens insulin resistance, a vicious loop. Signals exchanged between muscle and fat, myokines and adipokines, feed the decline. The authors trace the molecular routes connecting the condition to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and fatty liver disease. Those cardiometabolic diseases are leading killers worldwide. Understanding the loop's mechanics, they argue, is the route to breaking it.
europmc-pmc7036934:
Janusz and co-authors review laccase in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Laccase is a copper-holding enzyme, first described in 1883. It turns up across all kingdoms of life. It can oxidise a wide range of substances while reducing oxygen to water, with no harmful by-products.

The review describes the enzyme's structure and its family, the multicopper oxidases. It then traces how laccase likely evolved in different groups of organisms. Roles in fungi, bacteria, plants, and animals are compared in depth. The authors conclude that the enzyme evolved for a shared protective task. Its famous lignin-breaking role in fungi came later, they argue, as a specialisation of an older protein.
europmc-pmc7052834:
Huestis and co-authors catalogue the adverse effects and toxicity of cannabidiol in Current Neuropharmacology. Cannabidiol, or CBD, is a non-intoxicating cannabis compound attracting intense medical interest. A purified CBD medicine, Epidiolex, won United States approval in 2018 for hard-to-treat childhood epilepsy. Elsewhere, CBD use is expanding into conditions where proof of benefit is thin, and its risks are less widely discussed.

The team gathered studies from three databases through January 2019 that reported harms, balancing them with benefit studies to judge risk against gain. In animals, high doses caused developmental toxicity, liver cell injury, reduced sperm production, and low blood pressure. Human epilepsy studies reported infections among the common unwanted effects, and the review details dose-related harms in children treated for Dravet syndrome. The verdict is plain: CBD is not risk-free, and dose matters.
europmc-pmc7058534:
Cortés-Ciriano and co-authors map chromothripsis across human cancers in Nature Genetics. Chromothripsis is a catastrophic event in which a chromosome shatters and is stitched back in scrambled order, creating massive clustered rearrangements. Earlier work in selected cancers hinted it was more common than low-resolution data suggested. The team tested that idea across the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes collection.

They analysed 2,658 tumours from 38 cancer types. Chromothripsis proved pervasive, reaching a frequency above 50 percent in several cancer types. Classic events oscillate between two copy-number states, but many involved multiple chromosomes and extra structural changes. Repair signatures pointed to non-homologous end joining plus replication-based processes and templated insertions. The shattering can amplify oncogenes and disable genes, including mismatch-repair genes. The authors conclude chromothripsis is a major engine of genome evolution in cancer.
europmc-pmc7061634:
Ashammakhi and co-authors review bioinks and bioprinting in Materials Today Bio. Living tissue is a layered mix of cell types, matrix materials, and signalling molecules. Traditional tissue engineering, seeding cells onto a prebuilt scaffold, has struggled to reproduce that complexity. Three-dimensional bioprinting can place materials and cells with spatial precision, promising constructs that better mimic real tissue.

The key ingredient is the bioink. Multicomponent inks blend natural, synthetic, or hybrid materials with different cells and soluble factors. Advanced printers lay these inks down in multiple materials at microscale resolution, quickly and continuously. The review highlights progress in such heterogeneous inks and printing methods, and discusses hurdles such as growing blood vessels into printed constructs so cells survive after implantation. The authors close with the opportunities and challenges that will decide how fast printed tissues reach the clinic.
europmc-pmc7073134:
Sarasamma and co-authors expose zebrafish to nanoplastics in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Plastic pollution is a growing global emergency, and the smallest particles worry toxicologists most. Nanoplastics slip through biological membranes more easily than microplastics, and their huge surface area lets them carry extra toxic cargo. Data on their effects in vertebrates were scarce, so the team chose a standard test animal.

Adult zebrafish swam in water dosed with polystyrene nanoplastics about 70 nanometres across. The particles built up in the gonads, intestine, liver, and brain, in patterns set by particle size and shape. Exposed fish showed disturbed lipid and energy metabolism, oxidative damage, and clear changes across several behaviour tests, plus altered biomarker responses. Reproductive tissues were among the build-up sites. The authors frame the results as an alarm: if tiny plastics do this to fish, the wide exposure of wildlife and people deserves urgent attention.
europmc-pmc7098034:
Zhong and co-authors surveyed Chinese residents on their knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward COVID-19. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. The quick online survey ran during the rapid rise of the outbreak. It drew 6,910 completed responses, mostly from Hubei.

Respondents scored 90 percent correct on a 12-question knowledge test. Almost all, 97.1 percent, felt China could win the fight against the disease. Nearly all said they wore masks when going out. Better knowledge linked to calmer attitudes and safer habits. The authors warn that their sample skewed toward higher status, so results may not hold for poorer groups. Readers get a snapshot of public understanding at the crisis peak.
europmc-pmc7109134:
Zhu and co-authors run a metagenome-wide study of the gut microbiome in schizophrenia, in Nature Communications. They sequenced gut microbes from stool samples of 90 patients who had never taken medication, plus 81 healthy controls. The team then tested its findings in a second group of 45 patients and 45 controls.

A set of microbial species sorted patients from controls with fair accuracy in both groups. The patient microbiome differed in making short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan, and in building neurotransmitters. One enriched bacterium, Streptococcus vestibularis, was then given to mice. Those mice showed weaker social behavior and changed neurotransmitter levels. Readers get fresh leads on how gut microbes may shape a severe mental illness, ready for cohort and animal follow-up.
europmc-pmc7174434:
Bravata and co-authors review the research on impostor syndrome. Their article appeared in the Journal of General Internal Medicine. People with this pattern doubt their own success despite clear evidence of skill. The media often links it to poor performance and burnout. Yet no published review had summed up the evidence on it.

The team searched medical and psychology databases for studies on the topic. They covered how common the feelings are and who gets them most. They also reviewed related conditions and the treatments tried so far. Studies used varied methods and groups, from students to professionals. The authors show where the evidence is thin. Clinicians and researchers get a map of what is known and what still needs testing.
europmc-pmc7186534:
Li and co-authors map where the ACE2 gene is active across human tissues. Their study appeared in Infectious Diseases of Poverty. SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 protein as its doorway into cells. Knowing where that doorway sits helps explain how the virus attacks the body. The team compared expression in 31 normal tissues.

They split the data by sex and by age, younger versus older than 49 years. ACE2 levels also tracked with immune cell patterns in several tissues. Some links appeared only in males, others only in females. The lung, thyroid, liver, and kidney all showed notable patterns. The authors offer the map as a guide to infection mechanisms. It may also hint at which organs need closest watching.
europmc-pmc7211934:
Dowd and co-authors argue that demography is essential to understanding COVID-19. Their article appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Deaths concentrated heavily at older ages. A country's age structure can therefore explain much of its fatality rate. The authors compare early outcomes in Italy and South Korea.

Italy, with an older population, faced a far heavier death burden. The team shows how two countries of similar size can diverge sharply. Older populations must act more aggressively, they argue. Protecting care homes and older people becomes the priority. Age also shapes how distancing protects hospitals from overload. The article gives governments a simple lens for planning. Ignoring age structure leads to badly wrong forecasts.
europmc-pmc7226834:
Lin and co-authors update the science of rheumatoid arthritis, a long-term joint disease in which the body attacks its own tissues. Their review appeared in Cells. The disease inflames joints on both sides of the body at once. Over time, the swelling eats into cartilage and bone, and the joint slowly loses its shape. Until the 1990s this often ended in disability and early death.

Newer drugs have changed that outlook a great deal. The main drug family slows the disease itself instead of only easing pain, and it comes in three broad kinds. Some are older pills that calm the immune system, some are newer pills aimed at one cell signal, and some are injected proteins that block a single immune messenger. The review weighs gains against harms, which can include eye damage from one older drug. It also covers how doctors spot the disease earlier.
europmc-pmc7231234:
Nguyen and co-authors study depression and quality of life in people with suspected COVID-19 symptoms in Vietnam. Their article appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. The survey ran from February 14 to March 2, 2020. It recruited 3,947 people at nine hospitals and health centers. Printed questionnaires covered health literacy, mood, and health-related quality of life.

People with suspected symptoms were more likely to be depressed. They also rated their quality of life lower. Health literacy changed that picture, the analysis suggests. More literate participants coped better on both measures. The authors argue that clear health information is itself a protective tool. Hospitals could ease distress by teaching patients how to judge health claims. The study links a mental health burden to an information gap.
europmc-pmc7248934:
Yetisgin and co-authors survey therapeutic nanoparticles, tiny particles built to carry medicines to chosen targets in the body. Their review appeared in Molecules. Particles can vary in size and shape, carry a large load, and bind both water-loving and fat-loving substances. Stable links to guiding molecules let them aim at diseased tissue.

The authors describe the kinds of nanoparticles already used in clinics and how each behaves inside living tissue. Delivery plans are covered for cancer, infections, autoimmune, heart, brain, eye, and lung diseases. Benefits over plain therapy are weighed against side effects and toxicity, which remain open concerns. Knowing how particles interact with the body, they argue, is the route to safer, more targeted treatments.
europmc-pmc7257134:
Chen and co-authors tested a brain-protective approach after bleeding inside the brain. Their mouse study appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Bleeding in the brain often triggers harmful swelling and inflammation. The team focused on TREM2, a receptor found on immune cells in the brain. They asked if turning TREM2 on could limit damage.

They used 216 male mice with induced brain bleeding. One hour later, mice got a nasal dose of COG1410, a peptide that activates TREM2. Treated mice moved better, had less brain swelling and showed less cell death. Blocking TREM2 or its PI3K/Akt pathway erased those gains. The authors report TREM2 activation may be a future treatment lead.
europmc-pmc7272234:
Wu writes about social isolation and loneliness among older adults during COVID-19. The article appeared in Global Health Research and Policy. Wu is the sole named author. Lockdowns and bans on care home visits cut many older people off from family and friends. Older adults also faced the highest risk of death from the virus itself.

Wu links isolation and loneliness to poor heart, brain and mental health. In the United States, about one quarter of older adults living at home were already classed as isolated. Wu urges public messages that stress staying connected. Family help, community networks, new technology and screening in health care are all proposed.
europmc-pmc7402634:
Kuri-Cervantes and co-authors map immune changes in severe COVID-19 in Science Immunology. Critical illness had been tied to runaway swelling and damage, but the immune details were unclear. The team took a deep look at blood from 42 infected and recovered people.

Severe cases stood apart from healthy donors, recovered patients, and moderate cases across many cell types at once. T cells were highly active, antibody-making cells grew in focused clones, and innate cells changed the markers on their surface. A simple ratio of two white cell types predicted how severe the case was and whether organs failed. Severe disease, the picture shows, is not one path gone wrong but a broad upheaval across white blood cells. Each branch of it deserves study as a drug target.
europmc-pmc7418434:
Tang and co-authors review three forms of cell death and their links to cancer immunity. The three are ferroptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis. Each kills cells in a way that can wake up the immune system.

Immune checkpoint drugs help some patients, but most tumors resist them or resist cell death by apoptosis. The authors show how the three death paths can work with checkpoint drugs and boost attack by CD8+ T cells. Most proof so far comes from animal and cell studies. Human tissue data from public sources partly backs the link. The review maps a route to stronger combined cancer treatment.
europmc-pmc7452134:
Fuhrmann and co-authors study how low oxygen changes iron handling in human macrophages. Iron is vital for cell work, but free iron in excess can harm cells. Under low oxygen, the control system was poorly understood.

Macrophages grown with little oxygen lowered their free iron. They raised ferritin, the iron store protein, including its mitochondrial form. A regulator named NCOA4 fell, which slowed ferritin breakdown. A small RNA and the JNK pathway drove that fall. Ferritin stores then shielded the cells from ferroptosis, an iron-linked cell death. Tumor cells of another type did not show this control loop. The study links iron storage, oxygen levels, and cell death risk in immune cells.
europmc-pmc7477834:
Jiang and co-authors present cuteSV, a tool that finds structural changes in the human genome from long reads. Long-read sequencing promises full discovery of such variants. Noisy reads and complex signatures make the task hard.

cuteSV gathers signatures for each type of structural variant with tailored methods. A clustering and refinement step then calls the variants with care. Tests on simulated and real data show higher yields than leading tools. The tool also scales well to large data sets. Speed and sensitivity come together in its design. The software is free online for other teams. The authors frame it as a step toward routine, complete variant maps from long-read data. Such maps can sharpen disease gene hunts.
europmc-pmc7482434:
Jewell and co-authors model what COVID-19 disruption could do to HIV programs in sub-Saharan Africa. The region held more than two-thirds of the roughly 38 million people living with HIV in 2018. Five established models ran the scenarios.

The teams tested breaks in prevention, testing, and treatment over 6 months. A half-year stop in antiretroviral drug supply for 50% of treated people drew the worst toll. Models gave a median excess of 296,000 HIV deaths over one year in that case. Mother-to-child transmission would also climb sharply. Poor clinic care, other drug breaks, and paused testing each added deaths. Condom breaks could raise new infections. The authors urge guarding HIV services during pandemic strain.
europmc-pmc7615134:
NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) pools measurement studies on adult body-mass index in 200 countries from 1975 to 2014. Both low weight and severe obesity carry high risks for health over a life. Long trends show if a global goal to halt obesity rise can be met.

The pooled work used 1698 studies with measured height and weight. More than nineteen point two million adults took part. Estimates covered 186 of the 200 countries. Mean index for men rose from twenty-one point seven to twenty-four point two units. For women it rose from twenty-two point one to twenty-four point four units. Low weight shares fell for both sexes across four decades. Obesity rose from three point two percent to ten point eight percent in men. It rose from six point four percent to fourteen point nine percent in women.
europmc-pmc7616034:
Passaro and co-authors review cancer biomarkers and their role in personalized treatment of solid tumors. Biomarkers have reshaped how cancer care is planned. They let doctors match treatment to each tumor profile.

A biomarker signals a normal or abnormal process in the body. In cancer it can flag type and likely course. Some markers predict response to a given treatment. Others give outlook apart from any treatment choice. The review traces key milestones in biomarker science. Gains came from tumor biology and better test methods. Knowledge of the immune setting also moved the field. Profiling tumor material in blood adds new options. The authors look ahead to better patient outcomes from these tools.
europmc-pmc7694534:
Alakunle and co-authors review monkeypox virus, with a focus on Nigeria. The virus causes a zoonotic disease akin to smallpox. It returned in Nigeria in 2017 after 39 years with no reported case. Travelers then carried it abroad in 2018 and 2019, which raised world concern.

The review covers how the virus infects, spreads, and evolves. Gene gain, gene loss, and mixing all shape its genome. Tree analysis showed the 2017 outbreak strains formed one group, distinct from 1970s strains. The animal reservoir is still unknown. The authors list current treatments and mark the gaps that future work must close.
europmc-pmc7825134:
Ropejko and Twarużek review zearalenone, a toxin made by Fusarium fungi. Fungal toxins are among the most common food contaminants. Over 400 such toxins are known. Zearalenone mainly acts like estrogen in the body. It can enter food at growing, harvest, storage, or processing stages.

Contaminated grain and feed cause large money losses. Animal and human health face real risk. The authors gather the basic facts on this toxin. They cover how it forms and where it shows up. Its breakdown products, called metabolites, get full treatment. Toxic effects across species are summed up. The review aims to give a single, clear account of the topic.
europmc-pmc7829634:
Xu and co-authors present tools that merge and label single-cell gene data with deep generative models. Single-cell datasets keep piling up. A shared map of cell types is the natural next step. Comparing gene levels across datasets is not simple, though. Labels from one study rarely transfer cleanly.

Their earlier method, scVI, models cell data with probability. It separates real biology from measurement noise. A new variant, scANVI, learns from existing labels. It then labels new cells in a semi-supervised way. Both tools beat rivals on accuracy in tests. They also scale well and adapt to hard cases. One model handles many datasets and feeds later analyses directly.
europmc-pmc7925634:
Husain and co-authors present a review of the APOE gene and Alzheimer's disease. The disease is marked by amyloid plaques outside brain cells and tau tangles inside them. APOE codes for a protein that carries lipids in blood and brain fluid. People inherit one of three forms of the gene. Form ε4 raises the risk of the disease. Form ε2 lowers it.

The protein helps build, maintain, and repair the central nervous system. It also steers several key signalling pathways. The review follows its role from normal lipid transport to the disease process itself. It explains how the risky form may tilt the brain toward damage. Therapies built around this protein are then surveyed. The authors weigh which of them may reach patients. The review gives a full account of the strongest genetic risk factor for the disease.
europmc-pmc7947934:
Ioannidis presents a study estimating the infection fatality rate of COVID-19 from antibody surveys. The rate is the share of infected people who die. It drives forecasts of total deaths and the case for strict controls. Early guesses varied wildly. Antibody surveys show how many people were truly infected, which lets the rate be worked out after the fact.

He gathered 61 studies and eight early national estimates. Inferred rates varied widely across places. The median across 51 locations was 0.27% of infections ending in death. The corrected median came out slightly lower. Places with heavier death tolls showed higher rates. Age structure and the mix of patients explain much of the spread, he argues. The rates came out far below the guesses made early in the pandemic.
europmc-pmc7980034:
Towler and co-authors report a structural study of ACE2, the enzyme that serves as the doorway for the SARS coronavirus. ACE2 helps govern heart function. It is a membrane protein of 805 amino acids with one zinc-binding site. The team solved the first crystal structures of its outer part, both free and bound to a potent inhibitor. The forms were read to fine detail.

Comparing the two forms showed a large hinge-bending motion. One part of the enzyme swings by about 16° when the inhibitor binds. That swing brings key residues into place for cutting. The inhibitor's contacts in the active site explain its strength. Small residue changes versus the related enzyme ACE explain why ACE2 cuts differently. The work gives drug designers a moving picture of a key virus receptor.
europmc-pmc8115834:
Islam and co-authors catalogue the rumors and conspiracy theories that swirled around COVID-19 vaccines online. A cross-disciplinary team hunted them across search, social, and news platforms. The sweep covered the first eleven months of the pandemic era. It netted 637 vaccine-related items from 52 countries. Rumors made up 91% of the catch. Conspiracy theories formed the other 9% of items.

Fact-check ratings were grim reading for the truth. A full 83% of the items, 528 of 637, rated flatly false in agency checks. Misleading items added 10% and exaggerated ones 2% of the total. Only 5% of the items checked out as true. Among rumors, development and access claims led at 36% of the set. Death and illness claims came next in the pile. The authors urge live tracking of such claims. Fast, plain correction on the same platforms could blunt the harm.
europmc-pmc8155034:
Gligorijević and co-authors present DeepFRI, a graph method that predicts protein function from structure. Protein databases grow fast, and known functions lag far behind. Their method pairs sequence features from a protein language model with structure graphs.

The authors report that DeepFRI beats leading methods and sequence-only networks. Adding homology models to the training set widened the functions it can predict. Performance held up well when models replaced measured structures. Site-level maps let users see which residues drive a prediction. The tool scales to the size of current sequence collections.
europmc-pmc8257534:
Martí and Reith survey arginine-dependent immune responses. Evolution seems to have made arginine a control node for immunity. A good supply of it has long been tied to stronger immune responses.

Beyond building proteins, arginine feeds pathways that shape immune cells. Macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells feel its level keenly. How much is made, used, or broken down steers outcomes. The balance can tip responses toward attack or calm. The review follows these paths across the body. Fine-tuning arginine may offer a lever on inflammation. The fine-tuning of supply is the theme throughout.
europmc-pmc8262734:
Sehnal and co-authors present Mol* Viewer, a web app for viewing large biomolecular structures. Labs resolve big structures daily by crystallography and electron microscopy. Hybrid methods now model machines with hundreds of millions of atoms.

Older viewers strain under that load. Mol* was built jointly by PDBe and RCSB PDB teams. It runs natively in the browser, with no installs. It renders and analyses huge assemblies at speed. The design builds on lessons from LiteMol and NGL Viewer. Structural biologists gain a shared, open window on their largest models. Huge assemblies are the design case, not an edge case.
europmc-pmc8494634:
BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network reports a full cell census and atlas of the mammalian primary motor cortex. Knowing brain cell types, and how they are organized, is basic to brain science. This project joined many labs in one coordinated push.

The team merged single-cell gene data with chromatin, methylation, and spatial maps. Cell shape, electrical traits, and wiring data joined the mix too. The result is one shared landscape of cortical cell types. A shared taxonomy held from mouse to marmoset to human. Spatial maps placed each type in the cortex. Genetic tools for targeting key neuron types were released. The atlas is the network's first product.
europmc-pmc8584034:
Chen and co-authors report prime editing systems that make more exact DNA changes. Prime editing can swap, add, or remove small pieces of DNA. Yet cell factors that shape the result were not well known. The team asked which cell systems help or block the edit.

Pooled CRISPR screens showed that DNA mismatch repair blocks prime editing. It also raised unwanted small errors near the edit site. The new PE4 and PE5 systems use a protein that slows that repair for a short time. The authors report gains of 7.7-fold and 2.0-fold over older systems. Silent changes near the target also helped edits escape repair. A tuned editor form, PEmax, raised results further across seven cell types.
europmc-pmc8791834:
Sammut and co-authors build a multi-omic machine learning predictor of breast cancer therapy response. Tumors are ecosystems of cancer cells and their surroundings. That mix shapes how well chemotherapy works. The team profiled pre-treatment biopsies from 168 patients with clinical, genomic, and image data.

Response at surgery was matched to the biopsy profiles. Remaining disease tracked with mutation patterns, tumor growth, and immune traits. T cell dysfunction and exclusion also played a part. A combined model predicted full response in a separate group of 75 patients. Its accuracy score reached 0.87. The work argues the whole tumor ecosystem sets therapy response.
europmc-pmc9076534:
Kamath and co-authors profiled human dopamine neurons one cell at a time to find which ones Parkinson's disease kills first. They sampled 387,483 nuclei from patient and control brains, including 22,048 dopamine neuron profiles. Ten dopamine populations emerged, each mapped to its zone of the substantia nigra. One subtype, marked by the gene AGTR1 and seated in the ventral tier, was nearly wiped out in patients.

That same group carried the strongest signs of stress pathways and the inherited risk for the disease. The authors argue that cell-intrinsic traits decide which neurons fall. The map may guide models and cell-specific therapies.
europmc-pmc9252834:
Ianevski and co-authors introduce SynergyFinder 3.0 for analysis of multi-drug combination data. Drug combinations can raise efficacy and slow resistance. High-throughput screens test thousands of pairs at many doses. Judging which pairs truly synergize is tricky, since scoring models rest on unlike assumptions.

Version 3.0 adds interactive multi-sample analysis across many data sets at once. A new consensus score combines several synergy models into one call. Better outlier detection cuts false positives from noisy single-drug data. Users can weight synergy by drug dose and split potency from efficacy effects. New visuals and export options round out the release. The free web tool aims at robust, repeatable combination discovery.
europmc-pmc9388534:
Hosomi and co-authors test a gut bacterium, Blautia wexlerae, against obesity and type 2 diabetes. A survey of Japanese adults first flagged the genus as scarce in people with those conditions. The team then fed the bacterium to mice on a high-fat diet. Metabolic and immune readouts were tracked in both settings.

Treated mice gained less weight and showed better diabetes markers. The bacterium makes unusual products, including S-adenosylmethionine, acetylcholine, and l-ornithine. Its sugar handling stores amylopectin and yields succinate, lactate, and acetate. Gut community makeup shifted along with the host changes. Inflammation eased in treated animals. The authors suggest this microbe, common in Japanese gut profiles, as a preventive or treatment candidate. Human trials would be the next test.
europmc-pmc9453634:
Wang and co-authors test whether distress before infection raises the risk of post-COVID-19 conditions. Long COVID can bring fatigue, brain fog, and breathlessness for months. Known risk factors cover age, weight, and illness severity. Mental state before infection had barely been studied.

The cohort study drew self-reported data from 3 large ongoing studies. Distress was scored before infection, in the early pandemic months. Types covered depression, anxiety, worry, perceived stress, and loneliness. Among 3,193 participants later infected, higher distress was linked to higher long COVID risk. The link grew in a dose-dependent way for probable depression. People with distress also reported more symptoms. Their symptoms more often blocked daily activity. The authors frame distress care as part of prevention work.
europmc-pmc9470534:
Zhou and co-authors join de novo and inherited variants to widen the genetic map of autism. Past work leaned on new mutations found in family trios. Inherited rare variants were harder to pin to single genes. The team built a two-stage study to catch both kinds.

The study covered 42,607 autism cases in total. Of these, 35,130 were new cases recruited online by SPARK. Analysis found 60 genes at exome-wide significance. Five were new risk genes, among them NAV3 and ITSN1. NAV3 risk came mainly from inherited loss-of-function variants. Its relative risk was estimated at 4, a moderate effect. People with faults in the moderate-risk genes showed less cognitive impairment. The authors warn that far larger case counts are needed for more such genes.
europmc-pmc9617234:
Damschroder and co-authors present an updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, built from user feedback. The framework helps teams judge context factors that block new practices. It is among the most used tools of its kind. More than ten years had passed since its first release.

Feedback came from two sources for this update. A systematic search found 376 articles that used the framework by name. Of those, 59 held direct comment on its design. A survey of past users drew replies from 40% of those asked. Users rated the tool well on sense and ease of use. They also asked for clear changes in places. The update revises domains and constructs across the board. Some constructs were added, dropped, or moved. New weight falls on innovation recipients and on equity factors. Old and new versions still map onto each other.
europmc-pmc9774434:
Ngo and Duennwald survey Nrf2 and oxidative stress, covering mechanisms and roles in human disease. Cells face reactive oxygen species from inside and outside sources. At low levels these molecules serve useful signal roles. At high levels they damage cells and drive disease.

Oxidative stress is tied to nearly all major human diseases. Brain, heart, metabolic, and cancer conditions all make the list. Cells evolved antioxidant defenses against this threat. The switch protein Nrf2 runs that defense system. It turns on a wide panel of cleanup enzymes. The review explains how Nrf2 is held, freed, and tuned. It then walks disease by disease through Nrf2's roles. Faults in the pathway can protect tumors in some settings. The authors weigh Nrf2 as a drug target with care. Both boosting and blocking it carry risks and gains.
europmc-pmc9825434:
Szklarczyk and co-authors report the STRING database in 2023, a network resource for protein associations. Cell complexity grows from proteins acting in concert. Interaction knowledge lies scattered across many sources. STRING gathers physical contacts and functional links together.

Evidence flows in from experiments, texts, and predictions. Co-expression, genome context, and curated pathways all feed it. Each link is scored and checked before display. Scores transfer to less studied species through family trees. The newest build lets users submit a whole new genome. Its full protein network can then be browsed and mined. Co-expression now leans on a new learning method. Single-cell and proteomics data joined that channel. Confidence scores now reflect how each contact was found. Enrichment tools work on user genomes as well.
europmc-pmc9971534:
Kropp and co-authors frame diabetic retinopathy as a leading cause of blindness and an early warning sign. Proliferative disease is the advanced sequel of this diabetes complication. It blinds many people of working age. Current screening often misses disease until damage cannot be reversed.

Small vessel disease and nerve changes in the retina feed each other. The cycle brings mitochondrial harm, chronic inflammation, and new vessel growth. Vision field shrinks as damage grows. The authors call this a domino effect across diabetes complications. Retinopathy can predict later events such as ischemic stroke. They argue for mitochondrial health checks in care. Multi-omic tear fluid analysis may aid early detection and risk control.
frus-1861-d134:
William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 June 1861. It is document 134 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As June ended, Paris settled into its neutral watch on the war. Dayton's reports grew steady, focused on ships, trade, and court talk. His letter closes the first full month of the French file in the record of 1861. The French file's first month set habits that lasted the whole war. Habits set in a first month can bind a post for years, for good or ill. First month habits bound the post for years.
frus-1861-d234:
In a report dated 30 April 1861, Mr. Murphy wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 234 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the month the Civil War began, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d34:
On 12 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford. The letter is document 34 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford's energy made him useful and, at times, hard to hold. Seward's steady stream of letters kept the Brussels post tied to a single plan. This mid August note shows the center guiding the edge, one dated page at a time. The Brussels file swells in August, as Sanford took up fresh tasks for the cause. Fresh tasks that August ran from arms contracts to the watch on French ports.
frus-1862-d134:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 25 August 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 134 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d234:
Dated 6 September 1862, Document 234 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William Stuart of the British legation in Washington. It is one of two Seward letters to Stuart under that date in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Early September was the season's diplomatic high tide: invasion in Maryland, mediation talk in Europe, and a British cabinet watching for a reason to act. Seward wrote into that moment with his usual frequency. The pair of letters for 6 September shows the Department pressing its case while the military question hung open. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d334:
Two Dayton reports are dated 14 October 1862, and the first stands as Document 334 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote in the week when the French truce plan was complete and only London's answer was missing. His reports tracked the court's confidence and its fallback plans. For Washington, Paris reporting in mid-October was intelligence of the first order, since France's next step depended on signals Dayton was placed to catch. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d34:
Seward wrote again on 17 March 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 34 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d434:
Two days after the Spanish minister's note, on 9 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Gabriel García Tassara. The reply is Document 434 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the annual printed record.

Quick replies kept small disputes from growing, and Seward made a habit of prompt, courteous answers to resident ministers. The Spanish file in Washington covered neutral duties, maritime questions, and the aftershocks of the allied landing in Mexico. In August 1862, with a fresh draft of troops at home, the Union needed its foreign ties steady. The note shows Seward tending one of those ties in person, at the pace the wartime post allowed.
frus-1862-d534:
A second note dated 9 June 1862 passed from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 534 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

The doubling of notes on a single day, repeated across this exchange, reflects how enclosures and separate subjects were handled. Nothing was mixed. Everything was numbered and answered in kind.
