For the Netherlands, the stakes in Washington were commercial and legal, not military. Van Limburg's steady formal pressure was how a small power defended them. The document completes the densest cluster in the Dutch file, five days of letters that show the State Department's wartime desk work at full stretch.
frus-1862-d634:
The year's closing instruction to Constantinople went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Edward Joy Morris on 18 November 1862. It is Document 634 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November's orders everywhere repeated the Union's refusal of foreign mediation. The instruction to the Ottoman post carried that settled policy to the edge of the system. Morris needed it less as guidance than as record: Washington's position, stated to all its ministers alike, could be quoted anywhere. The letter ends the Turkish file for 1862 on the year's dominant diplomatic note. It was sounded as firmly at Constantinople as at London. Yet the audience there could hardly have mattered less to the outcome.
frus-1863p1-d134:
Charles Francis Adams closed the month with this third dispatch of 27 March 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 134 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of a three-letter day wound up the post's March work. Adams's spring file is dense because the stakes were: warships for the South in British yards, and a British cabinet that trod a fine line. This letter ends the day's set. It is a working piece of the great London run, the part of the volume most read by students of the war.
frus-1863p1-d234:
On 13 July 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 234 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d334:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 10 December 1862. It stands as document 334 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d34:
Charles Francis Adams closed his heavy mail day with this third dispatch of 16 January 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 34 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The run of Adams letters in this volume is the spine of the British file. His reports let Washington know, steamer by steamer, whether Britain leaned toward or away from the South. This letter ends a three-sheet day in mid-January, when the freedom edict's echo was still fresh in London. It is a working piece of a watch that helped keep Britain out of the war.
frus-1863p1-d434:
31 March 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d534:
Writing on 26 May 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in an official letter. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d634:
A 8 October 1863 dispatch from the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d134: General Joseph McNarney, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army, wrote to the Secretary of State on November 16, 1943. The letter is Document 134 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Army-to-State letters in summit season usually meant men, planes, or bases crossing department lines, though this record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the week the parties converged on Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d234:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a wide-ranging secret telegram from Washington on 19 November 1943. Sent through the White House Map Room to Roosevelt at Oran, it bundles short reports from several capitals, led by news from Lebanon.

The British deadline for French release of the Lebanese prisoners has slipped from Sunday to Monday morning at ten. On Italy, no move will be made against Marshal Badoglio or the king until Rome falls, though staff changes in Badoglio's government are listed. Giraud still awaits written pledges from the French Committee. The note ends with Romania's quiet feelers for peace terms, passed to Madrid: Washington's answer was unconditional surrender, and nothing else.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d334:
Madame Chiang Kai-shek wrote a personal letter to President Roosevelt at Cairo on 26 November 1943, the day the Chiangs said goodbye and left for China. She apologizes for her handwriting at the start, saying she is still, in her word, Cyclops, and the letters run together unneatly.

The letter carries her husband's message. The Generalissimo, she writes, could not find words at parting to thank Roosevelt enough for all he has done and is doing for China, or to say how much his friendship means. He felt the wistfulness of farewell, trusts Roosevelt as a friend, and hopes the bonds between them will strengthen with time. Madame Chiang closes in her own name, with a heart overflowing with affection and gratitude.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d34: Ronald Campbell, the British chargé in Washington, wrote directly to President Roosevelt on September 17, 1943. His letter is Document 34 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A chargé carries an embassy in the ambassador's absence, and a letter from him to a head of state was a formal step. The catalog record supplies the parties and the date and no subject. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series for its text to explain.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d434:
Sent from Tehran on December 4, 1943, this short secret telegram went from W. Averell Harriman, the American ambassador to the Soviet Union, to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant. It was sent on to Cairo through Army channels while the Allied leaders were meeting in Tehran and Cairo. The text survives in the Hopkins Papers.

Harriman passes on a message from Soviet foreign minister Molotov, relayed through the Russian Embassy in Tehran, saying Vyshinsky would represent the Soviet Union at Cairo. He adds that he will leave Tehran for Moscow on the morning of December 5. An editor's note corrects the record: Vinogradov, not Vyshinsky, actually represented the Soviets at Cairo, and he attended none of the formal meetings.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d534:
Officials in the Department of State prepared this memorandum on December 27, 1943, and the Department later printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume. A prepared departmental paper, unlike a cable, gathers facts and views into one place for decision-makers.

Such memoranda were the department's way of thinking on paper after the conferences: setting out a question, the background, and the choices as Washington saw them. Readers who want to know how the permanent government absorbed the summits will value this kind of record. It lacks a famous signature, but it shows the institution at work in the last days of 1943.
frus-1944-quebec-d134:
Under the heading "The Italian Situation," State Department planners briefed Roosevelt for Quebec in September 1944. Italy was both a defeated enemy and a co-belligerent fighting beside the Allies, an awkward double status. Premier Bonomi's government had survived its first two months, but the paper calls its position precarious without proof of Allied sympathy.

Relief and rebuilding dominate the paper. It weighs financing supplies from lire paid to American troops, a limited UNRRA relief program costed at 35 to 50 million dollars, and trucks and coal to move food. It also questions the outdated armistice terms, the future of the Allied Control Commission, and the stigma on Italian prisoners. Churchill, it notes, had dropped his idea of a preliminary peace treaty.
frus-1944-quebec-d234:
Marshall answered Deane from Quebec on September 14, 1944, in telegram Octagon 26. The question was whether the Warsaw relief arrangements required representatives to fly from London to Moscow. Deane had argued they did not, since planning belonged in London and only Soviet approval was needed in Moscow. Marshall accepted his judgment in full.

If arrangements satisfactory to General Spaatz could be completed between the Russians, Deane, and Spaatz without the London journey, that was satisfactory at Quebec. Deane and Spaatz were to complete the arrangements and carry out the project as the two of them saw fit. The message is a model of delegation: the theater men closest to the problem were given the decision.
frus-1944-quebec-d34:
Edward R. Stettinius, the Under Secretary of State, recorded this memorandum on August 28, 1944. Stettinius, a former steel executive, was then running much of the department while planning the future world organization. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Stettinius had just come from the Dumbarton Oaks talks, where the United Nations was being drafted, and Quebec would take up questions touching that design. A memorandum from his desk in the pre-conference file shows the department preparing its positions. For readers, it marks the State Department's place in a conference remembered chiefly for soldiers and finance.
frus-1945-50-intel-d134:
Quinn, director of the Strategic Services Unit, wrote to Petersen, assistant secretary of war, on 11 April 1947. The SSU still existed on paper in the spring of 1947, a shadow of the wartime OSS. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Late papers from a dying unit concern the last things: records, men still on the rolls, and duties not yet handed over. Quinn's letter to the War Department's civilian side belongs to that winding-down. Readers should not skip it as an echo. The care with which a government buries a secret service, its files above all, decides what later ages can know. This volume exists because such papers were kept.
frus-1945-50-intel-d234:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 7 May 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 234 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d334:
The Executive Secretary (Souers) addressed a memorandum to the National Security Council on 10 December 1947. Readers meet it as document 334 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d34:
General Magruder sent a formal report to Lovett, the assistant secretary of war for air, on 24 October 1945. Magruder reported as director of the Strategic Services Unit, the OSS remnant in the War Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A report differs from a letter: it accounts, in order, for a unit's state and work. Magruder had to prove, again and again, that his leftover service still earned its keep. His report to Lovett reached one of the War Department's most influential civilians, a man whose judgment the secretary trusted. Readers can use the report to see the SSU as its chief wished it seen. It looks lean and useful, ready to form the core of whatever central agency might come.
frus-1945-50-intel-d434:
Dated 3 March 1950, National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 14 is document 434 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Fourteen numbered orders in just over two years show a rule book built by use. Each new one answered a gap found in daily work across the agencies. For the reader, the directive is a dated marker of how the postwar intelligence system kept changing its own design. Within months of this order, wartime need would force yet more change on the system it governed. Change, in this series, was not a flaw but the normal state of things.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d134:
“The Treatment of Germany” is the fullest briefing book paper in this group, dated 12 January 1945. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary lists what the United States should seek in the first period after organized resistance ends.

Accept the European Advisory Commission's draft on control machinery without reserve, it begins, and make the Control Council's authority supreme. Disband all German armed and para-military forces, seize and destroy their weapons, and wreck plants that cannot turn to peaceful uses. Destroy the Nazi system itself: dissolve the party, strike down its laws, and clear active Nazis from public office and from leading posts in private firms.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d234:
President Roosevelt answered the Iran memorandum in his own hand on 8 December 1944. His short note from Warm Springs, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sends the matter to the top. Harriman, he directs, should take the Soviet-Iranian question up with Stalin in person.

The Tehran agreement, Roosevelt writes, was pretty definite. He then revives an idea of his own from that meeting. He had proposed that three or four trustees build a new port in Iran at the head of the Persian Gulf, a free port. The trustees would take over the whole railroad from there into Russia, and run it for the good of all. Stalin's only comment, he recalls, was that the idea was interesting; he offered no objection.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d334:
Lunch with the three foreign ministers on February 5, 1945, mixed toasts with hard business, and Edward Page's minutes record both. Molotov opened by toasting the three leaders. When Harriman announced that Manila had been captured, Molotov at once proposed a toast to that Allied victory. Eden then honored Molotov as host foreign minister.

Stettinius added his own toast and passed along greetings from former Secretary Hull, then in a hospital but on the mend. The listed subjects move from toasts to the conference's name, then to Germany and its economy. The page shows ceremony and policy sharing one table at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d34: On 30 December 1944 Roosevelt sent Churchill a message, one of the last exchanges of a crowded year. Filed as document 34 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta, it keeps the two leaders in step entering 1945. Within weeks both men would travel to Malta, then on to the Crimea for the summit itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d434:
Britain's full formula for Poland, dated February 8, 1945, settles borders first. The Curzon Line would be Poland's eastern frontier, with adjustments of five to eight kilometers in Poland's favor in some regions. In the west, Poland would take the free city of Danzig. It would also take East Prussia west and south of Königsberg, the Oppeln district of Silesia, and lands east of the Oder.

Germans in those regions would be repatriated to Germany. Poles in Germany could return at their wish. With western Poland freed by Soviet armies, the paper turns to forming a fully representative provisional government. The text is the high-water mark of British drafting on Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d134:
Captain Pinney, aide to Admiral Leahy, passed on a shipping question on July 9, 1945. The short telegram is document 134 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Admiral Emory Land, who ran American merchant shipping, had learned that Britain's Lord Leathers would probably attend Terminal.

Land believes he should be there too, Pinney reports, and he is standing by under Leahy's orders, ready to go if wanted. The point at issue is practical. The Joint Chiefs thought it urgent to use certain large captured ships to move troops home. Land and Leathers had been negotiating the matter for some time. A note adds that Land did leave Washington for Babelsberg on July 17.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d234:
Assistant Secretary Dunn reported British agreement on the foreign ministers council in an extract dated July 14, 1945. The extract is document 234 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, drawn from his two-hour talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam.

Cadogan expressed general agreement with the American proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers to handle the peace settlement. He felt it should not come first on the agenda; German questions should open the conference instead. The council's deputies and staff would need a fixed home, probably London, while the ministers might meet in various capitals. Dunn also raised ending the European Advisory Commission, and explained why Washington had settled on five members, following the Security Council, rather than four. Cadogan agreed that including China made sense on that basis.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d334:
Money in occupied Germany is the subject of a Joint Civil Affairs Committee memorandum. British and American troops, it explains, were spending Allied Military Marks. The printing plates for that currency had been shared with the Soviet authorities, who issued the same marks in their zone. German and emergency currencies also still circulated.

The committee calls a single currency system basic to trade, contracts, and any sound level of business in Germany. It also asks that the purpose of the currency in each zone be defined, so that occupying forces and others use it alike. The memo shows how even banknotes became a four-power problem in 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d34:
Davies repeated his Chequers performance at the Foreign Office in this second supplemental report of June 12, 1945. On Monday, May 28, Ambassador Winant presented him to Foreign Minister Eden. Following Churchill's suggestion, Davies covered the ground practically as in his talks at Chequers, set out in his earlier report.

In view of Eden's connection with the San Francisco Conference, Davies spoke very frankly, in a friendly and not critical spirit. His theme was the unfortunate manner in which issues had arisen between the Soviet delegation and those of Britain and the United States. The report shows the envoy carrying one brief — Soviet feelings — to both British leaders.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d434:
Blaisdell answered Clayton from London on July 13, 1945, about the German coal policy he had been sent. Clayton's cable of July 4 had repeated a letter laying out policy on stimulating German coal production for export and distributing the surpluses. Blaisdell apologizes: the cable reached him only on July 8.

That day he discussed it with Ambassador Winant. They agreed he should go to Frankfurt and get General Clay's slant on the policy points he was asked to act upon. On July 11, with Wayne Jackson of the Department and R. S. McCaffery of his mission, he had his talk with Clay. The letter shows policy being carried, in person, to the commander who must execute it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d534:
Moscow cools the air route in Vyshinsky's reply to Harriman, dated July 11, 1945 and printed in translation. Acknowledging the ambassador's letter of July 7 on a civil air lines connection at Berlin, served by American and Soviet airplanes, Vyshinsky reminds him of their earlier conversation. Practically speaking, he had pointed out, air communications over the route had already much improved.

He recognizes the matter's importance, he writes. But he does not believe that at the present time this question is sufficiently prepared for discussion in substance. As to the future, he can inform the ambassador only upon receipt of instructions from the Soviet government. The polite letter leaves the Berlin connection stalled where it stood.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d634:
Ambassador Murray sent a short secret wire from Tehran on July 5, 1945, about Iran's hopes for Potsdam. It is document 634 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The wire was repeated to London and Moscow as well.

Murray says Iran's foreign minister spoke on cabinet instructions this time. Iran strongly hopes the U.S. will work at the Big Three meeting to stop foreign meddling in its inner affairs. He named the parliamentary elections due that fall or winter as a special concern. The minister also raised again Iran's wish for an early exit of British and Soviet troops. The message repeats a plea the prime minister made on June 19, but now with the full weight of the cabinet behind it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1034: Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Winant in London on July 29, 1945. The President has approved the agreement signed three days earlier by the European Advisory Commission. It amends the September 1944 protocol on occupation zones in Germany and on Berlin rule. The covering report and letters go with it. Winant must tell the other members at once. The editors note the other approvals followed in August: Britain on the 2nd, France on the 7th, and the Soviet Union on the 13th.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1134:
Shipping chief Emory Land and his aide Morse wrote down the chain on 23 July 1945. Their note went to regional chief Monroe and to Carnwath of the maritime board's London branch. The message ran from Washington's shipping heads to the men who ran the joint fleet in European waters.

With Germany beaten, Allied shipping was swinging toward new work. The Pacific war still had to be fed, and freed Europe had to be kept from hunger. Orders from the top of the agency set that shift in motion. This cable shows wartime supply lines bending to a changed war, handled by the men who ran them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1234:
Sato reported to Togo on 25 July 1945, the day before the Allies issued their terms to Japan. His Moscow soundings had run for weeks and gained nothing firm. The Soviet side still smiled, still stalled, and still kept its own plans dark.

An envoy's report at such a moment carries the weight of a mission ending. Sato could offer Tokyo only his judgment: that Moscow would act for itself when it chose. This cable is that judgment, sent hours before the Potsdam Declaration spoke. It closes the first phase of the exchange, though neither writer yet knew how the story would end.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1334:
Wallace Murray, the American ambassador in Iran, cabled the acting secretary of state in Washington on 27 July 1945. Murray reported from Tehran while President Truman and Secretary Byrnes were at the Potsdam Conference. Truman, Churchill. Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Embassy cables like this one carried news from posts that the summit leaders could not watch themselves. Iran mattered in 1945 as a supply route to the Soviet Union and as a land watched closely by both London and Moscow. The cable lets readers see a distant post speak to Washington at the very moment the big powers were drawing the postwar map.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-134: Among the pieces printed without numbers after document 710 sits this brief editorial note. It was written by the editors of the Potsdam volume, not by a wartime hand. Foreign Relations notes like this one supply context, cite files, and warn of gaps. Readers passing through the conference papers find it a short, useful pause.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-34:
Gromyko talked trusteeship with Secretary Byrnes on the morning of July 20, 1945, and no minutes were kept. The gap is marked by an editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers. It is the thirty-fourth unnumbered item following document 710.

The editors know of the meeting only from a later letter. In a letter to Byrnes dated July 20, printed as document 734, Gromyko referred to our conversation this morning. The question of trusteeship was discussed at that talk, the note adds. No minutes of the conversation have been found. The entry thus preserves the fact and subject of a meeting, and nothing more. It is one of many such notes in this volume, where the editors flag gaps in the archive rather than fill them with guesses.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d734:
Andrei Gromyko, the Soviet ambassador in Washington, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 20, 1945, in document 734. Gromyko was Moscow's polished voice in America. Though the leaders met in Germany, the Washington channel stayed busy. His letter joined the papers printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An ambassador's formal letter fixes his government's words. Gromyko chose them with care; he was famous for precision. Readers see Soviet diplomacy working its second front: the embassy. The document shows that Potsdam's arguments echoed in capitals far away. It also marks the respect each side paid to exact written form, even mid-crisis.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d834:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Kennan in Moscow on July 16, 1945, in document 834. Grew sent guidance to the chargé holding the Moscow embassy. The letter predates the Potsdam opening by a day. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside Kennan's replies.

Instructions to Moscow carried special care in 1945. Every word to the Soviet capital was weighed twice. Readers see Washington briefing its watcher before the summit began. The document opens the Grew-Kennan channel in this volume. Their exchange forms a quiet subplot: the home office and the Moscow desk, thinking together about the ally they least understood.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d934: American staff prepared this undated memorandum on the worth of East Prussia, filed with the July 24, 1945 papers. Another copy heads it Statistics by Lubin. Factory, farm, and timber resources in the province were valued near four billion Reichsmarks in 1941. Real estate added about 1.28 billion more. The area north of the Goldap-Braunsberg line holds 40 percent of the people and two-thirds of those resources. Converted at set rates, the resources of the part going to the Soviet Union come to roughly one billion dollars.
frus-1981-88v04-d34: A 1981-1988 FRUS editorial note on the Soviet Union. The context. This note provides that background. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-295434: Total Industrial & Packaging contested a February 2005 award, and GAO's ruling closes the case. The packaging firm's claims were weighed and judged on the merits. The box was sealed on the dispute for good. The dispute was over. The case was closed.
gao-gaoreports-b-296334: Trajen and Maytag Aircraft tangled four dockets in July 2005 — a multi-firm protest pile — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firms challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Mega-filings get one careful answer. Four dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-296534: National Beef Packing took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298734: Leader Communications doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one comms fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-309734: Florida and Vermont's Medicaid experiments drew GAO's legal eye in 2007 — were the waiver approvals properly done under the law? The ruling tests the demonstration projects against the statute's fine print. Health-policy labs, the call reminds, still need a solid legal foundation to stand on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-134: Two years of health fraud fight reports got graded in 2005, and GAO's review covers the 2002 and 2003 annual results. The scorecard shows what the anti-fraud program delivered. The cheats who billed the system were the target. The results were counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-234: The post-9/11 arms export system got a GAO review in 2005, and the report covers the control regime. The review checks the gates closely. The weapons trade deserved the watch. The gates were checked. The regime was reviewed. The gates were watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-334: The Kennedy Center needed a firmer hand in 2005, and GAO's report calls for stronger watch over fire safety, construction, and finances. The review covers all three fronts. The nation's stage deserved the oversight. The oversight had to be stronger. The nation's stage deserved the oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-434: The homeland shop's hacker defense lagged in 2005, and GAO's report says the cyber duties went unmet. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the digital homeland deserved protection. The digital homeland deserved protection. The duties had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-534: Military training ranges needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says planning and funding priority were required to improve conditions. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the troops' ranges deserved good ground. The planning had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-634: Pornography on peer-to-peer networks got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the file-sharing problem. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the kids deserved protection. The use had to be understood. The kids deserved protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-134: Enlisted recruitment needed an action plan in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed a plan to address the challenges. The findings demand the strategy. The report warns that the ranks deserved filling. The plan had to be made. The ranks deserved filling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-434: Credit card minimum-payment disclosures needed customizing in 2006, and GAO's report says tailored disclosures would inform consumers more. The findings prescribe the fix. The report warns that the plastic's fine print needed clarity. The disclosures had to be customized. The fine print needed clarity.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-634: The Webb telescope needed a smarter buying approach in 2006, and GAO's report says a knowledge-based acquisition method was key to the program's challenges. The findings prescribe the discipline. The report warns that the billion-dollar eye needed building right. The approach had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-834: Disaster relief billions needed tracking in 2006, and GAO's report says a governmentwide framework was required to collect and report the spending. The findings demand the system. The report warns that the relief dollars should not vanish into fog. The framework had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-934: New Orleans' levees needed more than patches in 2006, and GAO's report says strategic planning was required beyond the interim repairs. The findings demand the long view. The report warns that the city's walls needed a real future. The planning had to be strategic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1034: The world's anti-slavery projects were flying half-blind in 2007 — GAO's report says U.S.-backed trafficking programs lacked solid tracking, though experts saw fixes. The findings pair a measurement gap with a reform sketch. Good intentions, the report argues, need good yardsticks to free anyone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-134: The SEC's books got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the commission's financial statements for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the market cop's own ledger got checked. The regulator's books had to balance. The market cop's ledger got its audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-234: The Pentagon's supply chain was slowly improving in 2007, and GAO's report says progress had been made on the high-risk fixes, though the full gains were unclear. The findings balance credit and doubt. The report warns that the war machine's shelves had to stay stocked. The chain had to hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-634: Airport screening rules were finally getting risk-based in 2007 — GAO's report says threat levels, hard experience, and passenger gripes drove the changes. The findings grade the new approach. The report's balance: safer skies without treating every grandma like a suspect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-734: Ultrasound billing needed a second opinion in 2007 — GAO's report weighs payment reforms and tech-qualification rules for the scans. The findings probe whether Medicare paid right for the pictures. The report's question is dollars and sense: fair price, qualified hands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-134: The Government Accountability Office dug into chemical Demilitarization: Additional Management Actions Needed to Meet Key Performance Goals of DOD's Chemical Demilitarization Program in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-34: GAO's 2007 report looks at a bold fix for clumsy agencies: put a top boss in charge of just running the shop. The chief operating officer idea splits policy from plumbing, giving one leader the job of making the agency work. The report tracks how agencies tried the role — and whether the new bosses truly changed how business got done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-634: The Government Accountability Office dug into prison Construction: Clear Communication on the Accuracy of Cost Estimates and Project Changes is Needed in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
hercules-piochymicus-1634: Hercules piochymicus, 1634. The pious chemical Hercules. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
hippolytus-apostolic-tradition-easton-19:
Hippolytus of Rome wrote the Apostolic Tradition around A.D. 215, and Burton Scott Easton translated it into English in 1934 with an introduction and notes. The work is the earliest surviving church order, a rule book for how a Christian community should run its shared life.

Inside, Hippolytus spells out how bishops, priests, and deacons were chosen and prayed over. He describes baptism step by step, along with fasting, daily prayer, and the shared meal of the Eucharist. Because so little else survives from that early, the text is a key witness to how worship took shape in the third century.
howe-mormonism-unvailed-1834:
Eber Dudley Howe was an Ohio newspaper editor who published Mormonism Unvailed in 1834, the first book-length attack on the new faith. Joseph Smith had published the Book of Mormon only four years earlier, and converts were gathering fast. Howe set out to stop the movement with print.

The book gathers sworn statements from Smith's neighbors calling him a fraud and a money-digger. Its famous claim, the Spalding theory, holds that the Book of Mormon was copied from a lost novel by Solomon Spalding. Howe's attack set the terms of anti-Mormon writing for the rest of the century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-benjamin-wo:
Benjamin Wolf Löw, a Polish-Hungarian rabbi, receives a biographical entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Wodzislaw, Poland, in 1775, he learned Talmud from his father, Eleazar Löw. He became a rabbi at a young age in a Polish congregation. In 1812 he followed his father to Austria and took the rabbinate of Kolin in Bohemia.

The article follows his later posts at Gross-Tapolcsany and Verbo, where he spent the rest of his life until 1851. His one book, Sha'are Torah, sets out the principles of Talmudic law in a methodical way. Three parts were printed, while the fourth stayed in manuscript. The entry also traces his family, including his son Jeremiah, a leader of Hungary's Orthodox party. It shows how the encyclopedia mapped rabbinic dynasties as well as single lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccaban-the-10:
The Maccabaean, a monthly magazine of Jewish life and literature, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Published in New York, it was founded in October 1901. It grew out of a resolution passed by the Federation of American Zionists at Philadelphia. The entry names Richard Gottheil and Isidore Singer among its contributors.

The article records the magazine's early changes. Until June 1902 it appeared partly in English and partly in Yiddish, under editor Louis Lipsky. The Boston convention then dropped the Yiddish section, and J. de Haas took the editorial chair. In 1903 the magazine was incorporated as a stock company, with the Federation holding most shares. Gottheil served as its first president. The short entry fixes the birth of a Zionist periodical while it was still new, giving names and dates a later historian would need.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malki-ezra-ben-:
Ezra ben Raphael Malki, a rabbi of Rhodes, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the seventeenth century and was brother-in-law to Hezekiah de Silva, author of Peri Hadash. His own books were printed long after his death. They appeared at Salonica and Constantinople between 1749 and 1811.

The article surveys his writings by subject. Malki ba-Kodesh treats the laws of Passover in the Shulhan Aruk and comments on the Haggadah itself. It also covers the Passover lamb, the New Year, the Day of Atonement, and the lulab. Shemen la-Ma'or defends Zerahiah ha-Levi against Nahmanides on a chapter of Baba Mezia. Other volumes hold his responsa and his sermons. The entry maps a Rhodes scholar whose work reached print a century late, through editors in two Ottoman cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marriage-ceremo:
Jewish marriage ceremonies, from the first matchmaking talks to the wedding day itself, are described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Cyrus Adler and M. Grunwald. Because contact between the sexes was closely restricted, betrothals were usually arranged by a third person, often a professional matchmaker, the shadkan, who was paid a fee fixed by law.

The article explains why marriages often came early, including the Russian rule that excused married men from military service. It covers the betrothal terms, the penalty set for breaking the contract, and the glass broken underfoot. It then walks through the week before the wedding, with its feasts, gifts, and the rules that kept the betrothed pair from going out alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-manuele:
Menahem Manuele ben Baruch ha-Levi was a Polish rabbi and author. He died at Lemberg in 1742. Herman Rosenthal and N. T. London enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came of distinguished stock, descended from Joseph Cohen of Cracow, Isaac Shrenzel, and Saul Wahl. He served as dayyan, or judge, at Lemberg. Hayyim Rapoport presided there. His signature as judge appears in deeds preserved in the Lemberg memor-book.

His "Zera Baruk" was printed at Wandsbeck in 1730. It offers novellae on several tractates of the Talmud. A second work followed from Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1745. Its title is "'Emek Halakah we-Ta'am Man." It mixes discourses on law with explanations of the Haggadah and carries contributions from two other Lemberg rabbis. In its preface he mentions a third book. That book treats the order Kodashim. The entry can report it only on his word.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messing-10734:
Messing was a Prussian family whose members settled in the United States during the nineteenth century, profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Cyrus Adler and Isidore Singer. The entry centers on Joseph Messing, a Talmudist and rabbi born at Argenau in 1812, and on the sons and grandson who followed him into the rabbinate.

Joseph held pulpits at Gostyn and Witkowo and wrote commentaries on Megillah, the tractate Abot, and the Haggadah before his death in London in 1880. Three of his sons became American rabbis, serving in New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Indianapolis, and St. Louis. The youngest figure, Abraham Joseph Messing, graduated from Hebrew Union College in 1897 and took a pulpit in Montgomery, Alabama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milhaud-latin-a:
Milhaud is a village in the French department of Gard whose medieval Jewish community left almost no documents behind. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The writers warn against confusing it with Millau in Aveyron, where Jews probably never lived at all. What is known can be told quickly.

The Jews of Milhaud were expelled in 1306 and found refuge in the Comtat-Venaissin, above all at Carpentras, where their descendants still lived four centuries later. The surname Milhaud, in its several spellings, stayed common among southern French Jews. The entry closes with a roll of the village's scholars, several of them physicians and translators of medical works, who carried its name abroad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moll-albert-109:
Albert Moll was a German physician born at Lissa on May 4, 1862. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They present him as a pioneer of two young sciences: hypnotism and the study of sexuality. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1885, after study at four universities. Then he toured the clinics of Vienna, Budapest, London, Paris, and Nancy.

From 1887 he settled as a neuropathologist in Berlin and wrote steadily. Der Hypnotismus came in 1889. A study of contrary sexual feeling followed in 1891. Investigations of the libido came in 1897, and a medical ethics in 1900. The entry also notes his inspection tours. He visited eastern European institutions in 1894 and North American ones in 1898. It is the bibliography of a doctor mapping new fields.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morton-martha-1:
Martha Morton was an American playwright whose name fills a long list of stage titles in her Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote the entry. Born in New York City on October 10, 1865, she was educated in the public schools and at the Normal College.

The article names her plays in order, from Helene, played by Clara Morris, to The Merchant, a prize play produced in 1888. Her A Bachelor's Romance ran for eight years in the United States and reached England as well. Later titles include Her Lord and Master, The Diplomat, and A Four-Leaf Clover. The entry also notes three plays written for William H. Crane and her marriage to Hermann Conheim in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nasi-reyna-1133:
Reyna Nasi was the Duchess of Naxos and a patron of Jewish books. Her entry was written by Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Portugal, she was the only daughter of Francisco Mendes-Nasi. Her mother was Gracia Mendesia, also called Beatrice de Luna. Reyna lived in Antwerp and Venice before Constantinople.

About 1552 she reached Constantinople with her mother. There she married her cousin Joseph Nasi, Duke of Naxos. After his death in 1579 she had no children of her own. She gave her fortune of 90,000 ducats to Jewish learning. In 1593 she opened a printing office at Belvedere near Constantinople. The press later moved and issued rare Hebrew works and Bible studies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neisser-albert-:
Albert Neisser was a German doctor of the skin. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Schweidnitz on Jan. 22, 1855. His father was a doctor at Charlottenbrunn. Neisser studied medicine at Erlangen and Breslau.

He took his degree in 1877 at Breslau. There he rose to lead the dermatological clinic. In 1879 he found the gonococcus, gonorrhea's germ. Local treatment based on that find is now universal. He traveled to Norway and Spain to study leprosy. He showed the lepra bacilli to the medical world. He also proved that lupus has a tubercular origin. Journals and handbooks carried much of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nierop-frederik:
Frederik Salomon van Nierop was a Dutch banker and statesman. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Amsterdam on March 6, 1844. He took his law doctorate at Leyden in 1866. He then practiced law in Amsterdam itself.

In 1871 he became director of the Amsterdamsche Bank. Amsterdam's council has held him since 1879 as member. Voters often chose him alderman of finance there. Each time he refused to accept that office. North Holland's States held him from 1883 to 1899. Then the First Chamber of Parliament took him in. Since 1898 he heads the Centrale and Permanente commissions. The Netherland Lion decoration came to him in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nussbaum-myer-1:
Myer Nussbaum was an American lawyer from Albany, New York. Cyrus Adler and G. Herbert Cone wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His parents came from Neustadt-on-the-Saale, in Bavaria. He went to the public schools of Albany. He then read law in a local law office.

In 1884 Nussbaum was named a police judge of Albany. Voters sent him to the state assembly in 1893. Two years later they sent him to the state senate. He held seats in bar groups at state and county level. He also joined the Republican Club of New York. For fifteen years he served as a trustee. That post was with the Jewish Home in Albany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-lewis:
Lewis Oppenheim was an English doctor born in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in December of the year 1832. He died in London on January 7, 1895. He entered the London Hospital as a pupil in 1850.

In 1853 Lewis went to the Crimea, a land at war. He joined the medical staff at Scutari there. He did hospital work under Florence Nightingale's lead. He came home in 1854 when peace was made. A great charge of sick troops was placed in his care. He then served as surgeon on the ship Kent. He sailed twice to Australia and back in her. Then he settled into a private practice in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ozar-ha-sifrut-: Ozar ha-Sifrut was a Hebrew book that came out each year. Herman Rosenthal and Schulim Ochser wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaac Shaltiel Gräber founded it at Yaroslav, in Galicia. It was given to books, science, verse, and fine tales. The first book came out in the year 1887. Three books came out on time, year by year. A fourth came in 1892 and a fifth in 1896. Known scholars of the age wrote for its pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-alois-1213:
Alois Pick was an Austrian army doctor and medical writer. He was born near Prague on October 15, 1859. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his medical degree at Prague in 1883.

Pick joined the army hospital corps the same year. He rose to regimental surgeon and chief physician in Vienna. He also taught at the university there from 1890. His papers treat lungs, heart, and stomach disease. His lectures on stomach and bowel illness appeared in 1895. He even wrote two small stage farces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polak-herman-jo:
Herman Josef Polak was a Dutch scholar of Greek born at Leyden in 1844. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his doctorate at Leyden in 1869. He taught classics and history at schools in Leyden and Rotterdam.

In 1894 Polak became professor of Greek at Gröningen University. He belonged to the Royal Academy of Sciences at Amsterdam. His first book dealt with notes on Homer's Odyssey. He later made a selection of Greek poets for students. The selection came out again in a second edition. He wrote many essays for Dutch and German journals of classics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahab-12534:
Rahab, in this article, is an old name for the sea and chaos. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The name first points to a sea monster or dragon. Later writers used it for Egypt.

The article cites Job and Psalms for the sea sense. It notes a Talmud line that calls Rahab ruler of the sea. Isaiah uses the name when it recalls the Exodus from Egypt. Jewish commentators often read the word more plainly. They took it to mean pride, noise, or tumult. The entry traces how one word moved from myth to place name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reform-judaism-:
Reform Judaism is a phase of Jewish religious thought in modern times. Kaufmann Kohler, Emil G. Hirsch, and David Philipson wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It grew after the age of Mendelssohn. Efforts for civil rights in the 1840s helped shape it.

The article says Reform first appeared in German synagogues. It then moved to the United States and developed there. The writers warn that the name can mislead. Reform did not aim to rebuild primitive Mosaism. Early changes mainly made worship shorter and more orderly. Old prayers tied to vanished Babylonian schools were dropped. Hard medieval poems were also cut from services. The entry defines a movement through its own eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riblah-12734:
Riblah was a town in the country of Hamath. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It is now a small hamlet in a broad valley. It stands between the Lebanon and Hermon ranges.

The article explains why armies kept stopping there. A mountain stream and a fertile plain served them well. The road from Egypt to Babylon passed close by. Pharaoh Necho chained King Jehoahaz at Riblah. Nebuchadnezzar later made it his siege headquarters. King Zedekiah was brought there for judgment in 586 B.C. Most modern scholars read Riblah in Ezekiel too. A second Riblah on Israel's border remains hard to place. The entry joins geography to two royal downfalls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenau-milton-:
Milton Joseph Rosenau was an American physician born in Philadelphia on January 1, 1869. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He earned his medical degree from the University of Pennsylvania in 1889.

Rosenau joined the Marine Hospital Service and worked on quarantine and disease control. He served in Hamburg, Antwerp, and San Francisco during cholera and plague scares. In 1899 he set up new quarantine rules for Cuba on original lines. From 1900 he directed the service's hygienic laboratory in Washington and wrote on disinfectants. He also taught bacteriology at the Washington Postgraduate Medical School from 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-gotthol:
Gotthold Salomon was a German rabbi born at Sondersleben on November 1, 1784. Isidore Singer and David Leimdörfer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He first taught at Dessau's Jewish Free School, editing the journal Sulamith.

In 1818 Salomon was called as preacher to Hamburg's new congregation. He studied famous Christian preachers to shape his own homiletic method. Copenhagen sought him in 1822, but he declined that call. In 1835 he answered Hartmann of Rostock, who opposed Jewish emancipation publicly. His German Bible for the people and schools appeared in 1837. Six volumes of his journal Sulamith appeared in his Dessau years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-nakda:
Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Naḳdan. He was a Masorite and grammarian of the twelfth century. Masorites guarded the exact text and reading of the Hebrew Bible. Samuel's one known work is called Deyaḳut. A copy survives in the Royal Library at Berlin.

The Deyaḳut treats points of Hebrew grammar. It also deals with the accents used in chanting Scripture. Steinschneider prized the book for a special reason. It shows grammar study just starting among the Jews of France. That was before the Spanish school and Ḳimḥi shaped the field. Samuel may also be the Samuel le Pointur named in a Bristol tax roll of 1194.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saulcy-louis-fe:
Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Louis Félicien Joseph Caignart de Saulcy. He was a Christian archaeologist and coin expert. Saulcy was born at Lille on March 19, 1807. He died in Paris on November 5, 1880. He first chose a military career. In 1842 he became keeper of the Museum of Artillery in Paris.

Saulcy then traveled through Palestine, studying the land around the Dead Sea. He claimed to have found the ruins of Sodom and Gomorrah. He also gave the Louvre a tomb he insisted was King David's. His books of Jewish interest are many. They include a voyage around the Dead Sea and studies of Jewish coinage. His Numismatique de la Terre Sainte, from 1873, was the standard work on its subject. He also wrote a history of Herod.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwab-low-call:
Isidore Singer and Immanuel Löw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Löw Schwab. He was a Moravian rabbi. Schwab was born at Krumau on March 11, 1794. He died on April 3, 1857. He studied under Mordecai Benet and Moses Sofer. He held pulpits at Gewitsch, Prossnitz, and, from 1836, Budapest.

Schwab taught himself French and German unaided. He also gained a strong grasp of mathematics and philosophy. A conservative, he allowed only the reforms that taste truly required. He was the first Moravian rabbi to preach in German. In 1832 he first held a wedding inside the synagogue. In 1852 he dissolved Budapest's Reform association. After the 1849 revolution a court martial jailed him for twelve weeks. He still advised the government on Jewish affairs. His efforts gave Budapest its great synagogue and first hospital.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sequira-isaac-h:
Isaac Henrique Sequira was a Lisbon-born doctor who built his career in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born in 1738, he came from a family of physicians. He studied at Bordeaux and then at Leyden, taking his degree in 1758.

In London he joined the Royal College of Physicians as a licentiate in 1771. His uncle helped launch his practice, then left for Bath. Sequira won a strong name among fellow countrymen in England. He served as physician to the Portuguese embassy and to Portugal's prince regent. The entry follows a doctor who carried Portuguese learning into London life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shekalim-13534:
Shekalim is a Mishnah treatise on the half-shekel tax that funded the Temple service. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Exodus and Nehemiah both ground the tax in scripture. The treatise also covers other Temple institutions at Jerusalem.

It usually stands fourth in the order Mo'ed, with eight chapters. Those chapters hold fifty-one sections in all. The call for payment went out on the first of Adar. Money changers set up tables in Jerusalem on the fifteenth. By the twenty-fifth they worked inside the Temple itself. Then pledges were taken from those who had not paid. The entry maps how a sacred tax was gathered, step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sick-visiting-t:
Visiting the sick, in Hebrew bikkur holim, is a duty rabbis lay on every Jew. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the practice. A visitor should show sympathy and cheer the sufferer. Help and relief for the sick person matter too.

The duty holds even when the sick person is a Gentile. No written law commands the act in so many words. Rabbis found hints for it across the Pentateuch. Walk after the Lord, Deuteronomy says, and rabbis read imitation there. As God visited Abraham in his illness, so should we. Other verses about showing the way carry the same hint. The entry grounds a kind custom in careful biblical reading and daily practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhah-b-samuel:
Simhah ben Samuel of Vitry was a French Talmudist who died in 1105. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a pupil of Rashi. He is best known as the compiler of the Vitry Mahzor. That prayer book held rulings and rules for religious practice.

The Mahzor also held responsa by Rashi and other authorities. Later hands added much material, marked as tosafot. Isaac ben Dorbolo added a large share of those notes. Three manuscripts of the work still survive. The entry traces those copies and a flawed printed edition from 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-louis-wil:
Louis William Stern was a German psychologist born in Berlin on April 29, 1871. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at the Kölnische Gymnasium in Berlin. He earned his doctorate at the university there in 1893. In 1897 he became a lecturer at the University of Breslau.

At Breslau, Stern founded a branch of a German psychology society. His books treat analogy in everyday folk thinking. One 1900 work studies how people differ from each other. Another surveys psychological work in the nineteenth century. In 1902 he wrote on the psychology of testimony. He also placed many articles in psychology journals. The entry catches a young scholar at the start of a notable career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terni-daniel-be:
Daniel ben Moses David Terni was an Italian rabbi, poet, and Bible commentator. M. Seligsohn wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Terni was born at Ancona. He taught at Lugo, then served as rabbi of Florence.

His books cover sermons, charity, and Jewish law. One volume marked the opening of a new Florence synagogue. It took the form of a dramatic poem in two parts. Another work summed up laws from the Shulhan Aruk. He ordered them by older and newer responsa. Two of his works were never printed. His Pentateuch commentary survived only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toledano-or-de-:
Toledano, or de Toledo, was a widespread family named for Toledo, Spain. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its members became printers, scholars, rabbis, and diplomats. They lived in Turkey, Africa, Holland, and England. Branches remained at Salonica, Jerusalem, and Tiberias.

Aaron de Toledo published religious lectures at Salonica in 1795. Abraham Toledano served as rabbi there around 1640. Daniel Toledano advised Sultan Muley Ismail in Morocco. He knew both Talmud and statecraft well. Eliezer Toledano ran a Lisbon printing house from 1489. His press issued the Pentateuch with Nahmanides' commentary. The long entry traces dozens of family members by city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vallentine-isaa:
Isaac Vallentine was an English journalist and community worker. He was born in Belgium in 1793 and died in London in 1868. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vallentine founded the earliest Anglo Jewish periodical. That paper later gave rise to the Jewish Chronicle.

Vallentine also helped found the Jews' Orphan Asylum in London. He supported other charities and literary groups in the city. In 1848 he published a Hebrew almanac and calendar. It listed holy days and fasts for the next twenty five years. The almanac continued year after year and became a popular pocket calendar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vorarlberg-1473:
Vorarlberg is the westernmost district of the Austrian empire. Gotthard Deutsch and Aaron Tänzer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the Middle Ages it was called Vor dem Arlberg. Jews lived there as early as the fourteenth century. Most were exiles from Swiss and German lands.

The entry corrects two old errors about Feldkirch. Tales blamed its Jews for Black Death deaths in 1348. Another tale charged ritual murder in 1443. Both events in fact belong to another town. The plague never broke out in Vorarlberg then. When Feldkirch turned Austrian, its Jews left entirely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-emanuel-1:
Emanuel Weill was a French rabbi. He was born at Ensisheim, Alsace, on October 21, 1841. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He trained at Colmar and at Paris's rabbinical seminary. He received his rabbinate in 1861. In 1865 he became rabbi at Versailles.

In 1876 Paris called Weill as assistant chief rabbi. Since 1882 he has served the Portuguese synagogue on Rue Buffault. His books treat Jewish women in Bible and Talmud. That work reached a second edition in 1881. Another book tells of Judah Maccabee and Rabbi Akiba. The entry records a quiet, learned career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilna-14934:
Wilna is an old Lithuanian city on the Vilia River. Herman Rosenthal, Baer Ratner, and Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish settlement may date to the thirteen hundreds. One historian claims Jews filled a fifth of the city then. Reliable records, though, begin much later.

Historian Bershadski found no official trace before the fifteen hundreds. Records do prove a community by the later fifteen hundreds. Some writers put its size at ten thousand then. The entry weighs legend against the archives. It then follows Wilna's Jews through charters and crises. The city became a famed center of Jewish learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wurttemberg-150:
Wurttemberg is a kingdom in southwest Germany with a long Jewish past. Isidore Singer and Theodor Kroner wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first traces of Jews there date to the 1200s. Town names and dates mark where they first lived and worked.

In 1298 wild bands led by Rindfleisch fell on the Jews. The entry lists town after town that felt the blow. At Heilbronn alone two hundred Jews died as martyrs. Their rabbi and their chief died with the rest. A large group at Ulm had its own grave yard then. Town law of 1274 had given that group clear rights. The long entry tracks the Jews of the land through the next ages. It joins town lists with tales of faith and loss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yuly-yulee-samu:
Samuel Yuly was a Moorish envoy sent to the court of England. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Mogador in Morocco late in the 1700s, he died in 1872. He died at Portsea in England at the end.

He was kin to the Guedella firm of that port town. That firm served the Sultan of Morocco as his agents. It ranked as one of the rich trade houses of Mogador. In 1820 Yuly came to England with royal writs in hand. He came as the true voice of the Sultan there. He then chose to live in England for good. He kept his trade links with Mogador all the same. The short entry sends the reader to the piece on Morocco.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zelophehad-1523:
Zelophehad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh in the Bible. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In one verse he is the son of Hepher of that tribe. In one more verse he is the second son of Manasseh.

The root of his name is in doubt to men now. Some read it as a Syriac word for first break. That sense would mark him as a first-born son in line. He died in the wilds and left five girls and no sons. Those girls came to Moses with a plea for their rights. They sought the land share of their dead sire in full. They said their sire died for his own sin, not in revolt. Moses took their plea to God and won their claim in full. So the girls got their sire's lot in the land split.
laennec-auscultation-forbes-1834:
Rene Laennec invented the stethoscope and described its use in his French treatise of 1819. John Forbes translated that work into English, and the edition here dates to 1834. Laennec called his method mediate auscultation, meaning listening through an instrument. The stethoscope let doctors hear the chest with new precision.

Laennec links each sound in the chest to a state of the lungs or heart. Breathing, voice, and cough all become signs a doctor can read. His system founded modern diagnosis of chest disease. English speaking medicine learned the method largely from Forbes's version. The book changed what a doctor does at a bedside. Its plates and terms shaped practice.
landor-citation-shakspeare-1834:
Landor invented a legal scene for young William Shakspeare in this playful work of 1834. In his telling, the future playwright stands before Sir Thomas Lucy in September 1582, charged with stealing deer from the knight's park. Witnesses named Euseby Treen, Joseph Carnaby, and Silas Gough support the case, by the title page.

Shakspeare defends himself in dialogue with wit, while the magistrate blusters at him. The piece gives the old Stratford deer-stealing legend a full hearing it never had in real life. Added at the end is a talk between Edmund Spenser and the Earl of Essex on the state of Ireland in 1595.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-3:
Planetary motions and lunar theory fill books six and seven of Laplace's Mecanique Celeste. Nathaniel Bowditch published his translation of that third volume in 1834. The Moon's path posed some of the hardest problems in all astronomy. Sailors and navies needed exact lunar tables for finding position at sea.

Laplace attacks the Moon's many small wobbles with powerful analysis. Bowditch adds commentary and tables that make the work usable. The volume stands third in his four volume English set. It shows theory serving a plain practical need. Few books join deep math to sea travel so directly. Its tables guided real ships.
lectures-on-phrenology-delivered-before-: Amos Dean delivered these lectures on phrenology to a young men's association in 1834. The hosted sample shows only the scanner's public domain notices. Title, author, and date still identify the work clearly. Phrenology then drew large lecture audiences across America. Dean presented its claims about character and the skull to young listeners. The book belongs to that early wave of popular phrenology print.
lettres-a-camille-sur-la-physiologie-de-: Isidore Bourdon addressed his Letters to Camille on human physiology in 1834. H. Dumont published them at Brussels. The subtitle promises a precise account of the phenomena of life. Bourdon belonged to Paris's Royal Academy of Medicine. Plates drawn after Gall's system accompany his text. His letters bring body science to a general reader.
marcus-aurelius-meditations-casaubon-163:
Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations in Greek, and Meric Casaubon made the first English version in 1634. Casaubon gave England the Roman emperor's notebook, not meant for any eyes but his own. He wrote on campaign along the Danube, in Greek, amid war and plague years there.

The notes urge calm, duty, and scorn for fame, wealth, and the fear of death. All is flux, he reminds himself, and the mind can stay free in any fort. He thanks gods and kin, and checks his temper toward fools and flatterers at court. Stoic counsel here is plain, brief, and meant for daily use in hard times. Casaubon's version made the book a fixture of English moral reading for centuries.
milton-comus-1634:
John Milton's masque Comus was first performed in 1634 at Ludlow Castle. This volume joins it with L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas. Together they form the classic set of Milton's essential early poems in English and Latin.

Comus, a tempter with a magic cup, traps a lost Lady in his wood. Her brothers and a guardian spirit free her through chastity's strength. L'Allegro praises mirth, and Il Penseroso praises sober thought and study. Lycidas mourns a drowned friend in some of the finest pastoral verse in English. The set shows a young poet of rare range and control.
openalex-w2159284134:
Jeffrey Cummings, Jacobo Mintzer, and Henry Brodaty led this 2014 consensus paper in International Psychogeriatrics. A work group of the world psychogeriatric body set out to define agitation in people with thinking disorders. Agitation is common and hard on patients and carers, yet the field had no shared meaning for the syndrome.

The group built accord through open online talks, face-to-face meetings, and surveys. More than nine hundred people took part across the phases. The working definition they agreed on should serve many study types, from large surveys to drug trials. A shared meaning should help experts talk, let studies be compared, and aid drug approval work.
openalex-w2768742734:
Raquel Fernandes Mendonça, Roger A. Müller, and David W. Clow, with colleagues, compiled lake carbon burial data in Nature Communications in 2017. Buried organic carbon leaves the short-term carbon cycle and escapes becoming greenhouse gas. Lakes and reservoirs bury carbon surprisingly efficiently for their size. Yet global numbers rested on scattered local studies.

The team assembled direct burial measurements from water bodies worldwide. Rates varied enormously, from near zero to extremely high values per square meter each year. Reservoirs showed much higher typical rates than natural lakes. The dataset is heavily skewed: most measurements come from North America and Europe. For most of the world's major catchments, no direct measurement exists at all. The authors provide a global estimate while warning how thin the evidence remains in lake-rich regions like Russia and South America.
openalex-w2891785734:
Peter Dillon, Pieter J. Stuyfzand, and Thomas Grischek lead this history of managed aquifer recharge, published online in 2018 in the Hydrogeology Journal. Managed recharge deliberately refills aquifers with treated water for later use. Sixty years of it have passed amid soaring groundwater extraction. The paper is the first attempt to total its volume worldwide.

New water treatment technologies helped drive recharge's advance, the authors write. Research on facility design, clogging, and water quality changes underpinned practical gains. Recharge wells greatly sped replenishment, especially in cities and mine water management. Recent work adds governance, economics, and reliability to the engineering. With climate extremes intensifying, recharge grows as a core water strategy beside demand management. The review relates each technical advance to the rules and research that enabled it.
openalex-w2966305634:
Antonio Zanatta published this study in Scientific Reports in 2019. Working alone, he revisits how scientists measure the optical bandgap of semiconductors. The bandgap is the energy threshold that decides how a material absorbs light and where it can serve in electronic devices.

Zanatta studied three classic semiconductors, silicon, germanium, and gallium-arsenide, in crystal, powder, and thin film forms. He shows that fitting a smooth S-shaped curve, called a Boltzmann sigmoid, to their light absorption spectra gives accurate bandgap values. The method is straightforward compared with traditional approaches. He proposes it as a unified way to determine bandgaps across materials and forms.
openalex-w2966591034:
Felipe Bastida, Carlos García, Noah Fierer, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It seeks the global drivers of the soil priming effect. Priming happens when fresh carbon entering soil speeds up microbe activity and releases extra carbon dioxide from older soil carbon.

The team surveyed soils at eighty-six sites spread across the world, covering wide ranges of climate, life communities, and soil types. They fed the soils labeled glucose and measured the burst of carbon dioxide that followed. The size of this positive priming effect varied with ecological conditions they could identify. Knowing those predictors helps scientists model how soils store or release carbon.
openalex-w3003604034:
Dolores Aguilar-Cázares, Rodolfo Chavez-Dominguez, Ángeles Carlos-Reyes, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Oncology. It examines how angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, feeds both inflammation and cancer. The two processes are deeply linked inside tumors.

Growing new vessels and stirring inflammation both count among the classic hallmarks of cancer. A tumor is a shifting mix of abnormal and normal cells, including immune and support cells. Inflammatory cells release signals that switch on vessel growth, and new vessels in turn sustain the inflamed tumor. The review traces this two-way traffic and explains how it helps cancers grow, invade nearby tissue, and spread.
openalex-w3040709534:
Robert Lücking, M. Catherine Aime, Barbara Robbertse, and colleagues published this paper in IMA Fungus in 2020. It asks where the field stands on naming fungi without ambiguity, and how accurate DNA barcoding really is. Fungi may hold around three million species, the second largest tally of any organism group.

Fungi have simple body plans and obscure structures, so looks alone often cannot pin a species down. The authors offer a framework that joins family trees, visible traits and habits, and breeding biology into one integrative approach. They stress that checking identifications, a step often skipped, is crucial. No single tool serves every fungal group, so barcoding must be judged group by group.
openalex-w3170240134:
Sarah Davies, Hollie Putnam, Tracy Ainsworth, and colleagues argue that science rewards the wrong things. Their essay appeared in PLOS Biology in 2021. Success in science is often judged by citation counts and journal impact factors. The authors say these measures are flawed and biased against groups already pushed to the margins.

They call for wider measures that credit mentoring, collaboration, and community work alongside papers. Good mentoring, they argue, should support the well-being of younger researchers. Changing the reward system will take shared effort, led by senior scientists and administrators. The goal is a fairer system that keeps more talented people in science.
openalex-w4283803434:
The CMS collaboration presents a portrait of the Higgs boson in Nature in 2022, ten years after its discovery. In July 2012, CMS and its sister experiment ATLAS announced a new particle near one hundred twenty-five gigaelectronvolts. It matched the Higgs boson predicted by the standard model. The Higgs is the visible trace of a field that fills the whole universe and gives particles their mass.

That field, proposed in 1964, breaks a symmetry of the early theory. It grants mass to the W and Z bosons and to matter particles. This paper reviews a decade of CMS measurements of the boson's properties. It checks how the particle is produced, how it decays, and how strongly it couples to others.
openalex-w4380871934:
Giacomo Grasselli, Carolyn Calfee, Luigi Camporota, and colleagues present European guidelines on acute respiratory distress syndrome, in Intensive Care Medicine in 2023. The syndrome, shortened to ARDS, is a severe lung failure seen in intensive care. These guidelines update the 2017 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidance. They cover adults only, and focus on breathing support that does not rely on drugs, including cases caused by COVID-19.

An international expert panel, with a methodologist and patient representatives, reviewed the evidence formally. They used the PRISMA reporting approach and the GRADE system to rate certainty. The panel answered twenty-one questions and issued twenty-one recommendations. Topics run from how ARDS is defined and subtyped to high-flow oxygen and other support strategies.
openalex-w4412648834:
Yuanzhao Yao, Afshan Begum, Naoki Ikeda, and colleagues build mid-infrared topological edge modes for light. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. Topological edge modes travel along boundaries in one direction only. They shrug off defects.

The team designs and builds photonic crystal structures for the mid-infrared range. At the boundary between two crystals, one-way light channels appear. The challenge is proving their polarisation states directly. The authors use reflection spectroscopy at finely varied angles. Their measurements confirm the designed polarisation behaviour.
