pmc-13232634:
Mochun Zhang and colleagues fix in 2026 a hidden flaw of solid plastic battery layers, where leftover solvent attacks the lithium metal anode. Their filler is a cage-like material carrying both positive and negative charged parts. Mixed into the plastic, it competes for lithium ions and holds back the negative ions that usually drag along.

Freed lithium moved faster through the layer, and a tough mineral-rich skin formed where the layer meets the metal. Test cells ran more than a thousand hours in steady cycling without shorting. Full cells kept most of their capacity after a thousand cycles, even at high voltage and fast charge rates. Solvent leftovers stop being a trade-off when coordination is managed this carefully.
pmc-13232834:
Tolera Gudissa Damme and colleagues gather in 2026 what mothers and maternity staff see as the blocks and boosts to emergency birth care in western Ethiopia. Emergency obstetric and newborn care saves lives when labor or delivery turns dangerous. Sixty-five women and providers across four public hospitals joined group talks and interviews during mid-2024.

Barriers clustered around missing supplies and cramped facilities, too few skilled staff, and training that lagged behind need. Weak referral links and thin community awareness of danger signs added to the strain, alongside disrespectful care. On the other side stood free maternity services, teamwork across professions, newborn intensive units, blood banks, and ambulance access. Fixing the supply and staffing side would let goodwill already present do more.
pmc-13233034:
Hubert and colleagues hunt for factors tied to death in patients treated with damage control surgery for abdominal trauma. Damage control means doing the least surgery needed at first, because a badly hurt patient's body cannot bear a long operation. The team set out to learn which features, on arrival and in intensive care, mark the highest risk.

Their list spans sex, age, cause and mechanism of injury, and a trauma severity score. It also covers body cooling, acid build-up in the blood, lab values at intensive care admission, and choices in anaesthesia and surgery. Knowing which factors truly predict death could sharpen triage for the next patient wheeled in.
pmc-13233934:
Hauke O. Wernecke, Andrew B. Lehr, and Arvind Kumar published a 2026 computational neuroscience study on steering sequences of brain activity by tweaking just a few connections. Behavior unfolds as ordered patterns of neural firing, and flexible behavior needs those patterns to start, stop, and reroute quickly. The team simulated recurrent networks whose wiring density varies smoothly across space, a pattern that asymmetric neuron shapes can create.

Changing synaptic strength at a handful of well-chosen spots could launch, halt, extend, gate, or redirect a traveling sequence. Those high-impact spots sat in neighborhoods with middling connection counts. The result suggests brains could reconfigure activity routes fast through tiny local changes, while the underlying pathways stay stable and reliable. The authors offer the scheme as a framework for flexible computation on behavioral timescales.
pmc-13234034:
Raphael Trefzer and colleagues published a 2026 long-term follow-up of partial shoulder replacements, comparing implants with and without a stem anchored in the arm bone. Rebuilding the joint's natural offset matters, since an overstuffed joint wears the socket. Forty-eight patients operated between 2001 and 2011 were examined after an average of nearly seventeen years, with X-ray measurements of three offset values.

Function scores did not differ between stemmed and stemless groups. Reconstruction landed close to the patient's original anatomy for one offset, slightly under for another, and slightly inward for the center of rotation. One offset error stood out statistically: widening the lateral humeral offset was tied to worse function scores. The authors use the data to argue for precise, patient-matching reconstruction targets.
pmc-13234234:
Kian D. Samadian and co-workers issued a 2026 scoping review of set care pathways in emergency department observation units. These units give time-limited care to patients who may not need full admission, but the pathway literature lay spread thin. Searching PubMed for work from 2000 to mid-2025, the team screened thousands of papers and kept 239 describing set pathways for adults.

Most studies were watch-based and based at teaching hospitals, and pathway papers grew year by year. Heart care, above all chest pain pathways, led the field, with infection care next, while pathways for older patients and viral illness grew fastest of all. Most pathways were diagnostic or mixed, with purely treatment-based ones rising lately. Studies mostly counted where patients ended up, deaths, and return visits, while how patients and doctors felt went largely uncounted.
pmc-13235234:
Dae Ho Kim and co-authors reported in 2026 a new tiny cup fungus species from Korea, plus a first Korean record of a relative. The genus Erioscyphella forms minute fruiting bodies on decaying plant material in East Asia. Korean collections were examined under the microscope and sequenced at three gene regions. Combined shape evidence and family trees guided the species decisions.

The new species, named Erioscyphella koreana, formed its own distinct branch near three named relatives. Its spore size, spore-producing cell shape, and fruiting body colour set it apart from each relative. Specimens matching a species known from Hainan were also found, extending its known range to Korea. Three Korean members of the genus share similar cups yet differ in spore divisions, hair-like cell shape, and preferred substrate. The work shows how pairing microscopy with DNA clarifies subtle fungal boundaries.
pmc-13236534:
Jing Xian Lim and co-authors tested in 2026 an extract fraction from an oriental conifer on retinal support cells stressed by high sugar. Diabetic eye disease damages both vessels and nerve cells in the retina, often early in its course. Chemical profiling found terpenes, phenolic compounds, and fatty acids in the tested fraction. Rat retinal Müller cells were cultured under different glucose levels for the experiments.

The fraction showed low toxicity to the cells at the doses examined under high sugar. Treatment lowered several growth and signalling proteins that drive harmful vessel growth and cell stress. A survival pathway protein became more strongly activated under treatment in the results. Adding a drug that switches on an energy sensor deepened the protective effect measurably. Blocking that same sensor made sugar damage worse, supporting the proposed mechanism in cells.
pmc-13236734:
Değirmençay and colleagues test blood markers of heart damage in cattle sick with anaplasmosis. The tick-borne infection destroys red blood cells, causing severe anaemia. Starved of oxygen, the heart muscle itself can be injured, yet that damage had never been mapped carefully with modern blood tests in naturally infected animals.

The team measured several candidate cardiac markers in infected cattle and judged which ones flagged heart injury most reliably. A dependable marker would let vets spot hidden heart damage from a blood sample, rather than after an animal fails. The study links a blood parasite to the heart, a connection easy to miss in routine farm practice.
pmc-13236834:
Dóra Lili Brassó and team raised 75 ostrich chicks for four weeks in a 2026 study. They tested how starter feed, hatching time, and hatching help shape early growth and survival. Chicks got feeds made for ostriches, turkeys, or chickens, mixed with alfalfa hay, and some chicks hatched unaided on day 40 while others needed help on day 41 or 42.

The richest feed, high in protein and energy and low in fiber, gave the fastest growth and the best survival, at 85 percent. A very high-fiber, low-energy feed did far worse, with most chicks dying. Chicks that hatched unaided on day 40 also faced the lowest risk of being culled. The results show how strongly the first weeks of an ostrich chick's life depend on feed quality.
pmc-13237334:
Adnan and colleagues use an AI training method to solve a heat-flow problem in nanofluids. Their fluid carries tiny particles and flows over a flat horizontal plate, while heat radiation and a magnetic field act on it at the same time. Such mixed flows appear in cooling systems and energy devices, but their equations resist tidy solutions.

The team applies a Levenberg-Marquardt back-propagation algorithm, a fast learner borrowed from neural networks, to compute the flow and temperature fields. Checking AI answers against known results tests whether the method can replace slower solvers. If it holds, engineers could explore many design settings quickly instead of re-solving hard equations each time.
pmc-13238234:
Edathadathil and colleagues sort sepsis patients in an Indian hospital into distinct clinical types. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, looks different from patient to patient. Its patterns also vary by region, so types found in Western hospitals may not fit Indian practice, where infections and resources differ sharply.

The cohort covered every adult admitted through the emergency department with presumed sepsis under standard guideline criteria. Grouping their signs, lab values, and courses revealed phenotypes, recurring patterns that may predict who worsens and who recovers. Matching treatment to type, rather than to the sepsis label alone, is the long-term prize such sorting aims at.
pmc-13239034:
Yiming Feng and colleagues collected Klebsiella bacteria from mastitis milk on eight dairy farms in China's Henan Province in 2026, sequencing sixty-five isolates to trace drug resistance. Most were Klebsiella pneumoniae, falling into twenty-four sequence types with two dominant. Nearly half produced enzymes that defeat front-line penicillin-type antibiotics, and one isolate carried the carbapenem-breaking gene NDM-1.

The cow strains were genetically distinct from human hypervirulent strains and lacked their key attack genes. Resistance genes rode mainly on one plasmid family, and identical types clustered in ways that suggest spread between animals. The authors warn that dairy cattle form a reservoir of multidrug-resistant Klebsiella. Both clonal spread and plasmid hopping drive the problem, with possible spillover to people.
pmc-13239534:
Rebecca L J Strong and colleagues survey British parents about baby slings and carriers in a 2026 study prompted by infant deaths linked to unsafe use. Wearing babies in fabric carriers is rising in the United Kingdom, yet how families actually use them and what safety guidance they know had not been mapped.

Nearly fifteen hundred parents, mostly mothers of babies under one year, answered an online questionnaire. Almost all had used a carrier for mobility, bonding, soothing, or keeping hands free. Manufacturers gave little safety information, and many parents relied on social media or blogs. A quarter did not know the existing national guidance, supporting antenatal safety teaching.
pmc-13239634:
Juan C Cubillos-M and co-authors built a water-based DNA test for one of the world's most endangered fish in a 2026 conservation study. The largetooth sawfish once ranged across tropical coasts worldwide, yet nets and habitat loss have shrunk it drastically, and survivors are hard to find.

Their droplet digital test can detect a single DNA copy shed into water and was checked to work across the species' old range. Sampling at ninety-nine sites in Panama and Colombia during 2022 found no sawfish DNA, even where habitat models rated conditions highly suitable. The team recommends wider repeat surveys to locate any remaining pockets.
pmc-13239834: A 2026 correction notice in the journal MedComm fixes the equal-contribution statement for a study by Du and co-authors on a lycorine derivative against SARS-CoV-2. The notice is a correction only, with no new data or altered findings. It clarifies that four authors, Tingfu Du, Ruixue Liu, Xintian Zhang, and Longying Shen, contributed equally to the work, where the printed version had named only three and formatted the statement incorrectly. The authors apologise for the error.
pmc-13240634:
Chu and co-authors at Brown call on dermatology to prepare for agentic artificial intelligence. Unlike passive tools, these systems act on their own across many steps. Skin care looks well placed to benefit, with heavy patient volumes and office load. The authors propose sorting uses by risk and how easily each task undoes.

Their plan aims to guide safe, staged uptake of self-running tools. Barriers remain steep: shaky model trust, poor record sharing, and open questions of blame and privacy. Early users in other fields show it can work, but field-specific guardrails are thin. The authors urge skin doctors to engage through their societies and industry ties now.
pmc-13241734:
Yiying Zhu offers a 2026 primer on hunting for unknown protein modifications with mass spectrometry. Standard searches assume the modification type is already known, which biases what analysts can find. Drug-linked attachments, chemical changes, and rare natural modifications can slip past such lists.

The framework walks readers through key decision points instead of one fixed recipe. Chemically informed guesses generate candidate modifications, then searches narrow step by step. Controls help separate real signals from artifacts. The guide also covers pinning a modification to an exact amino acid position. Zhu argues this decision-driven approach suits modifications from drugs, lab chemistry, or the body itself.
pmc-13241934:
Madelyn J Blake and a large team present a 2026 study of amino acid handling in pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease of high pressure in lung arteries. The three branched-chain amino acids are building blocks whose breakdown is disturbed in several heart and vessel diseases. Their role in this condition, and in related liver damage, was unsettled.

The authors set out the case that faulty breakdown products can switch on stress programs inside lung vessel cells. Breakdown failure also connects to ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death already implicated in this disease. Prior work in brain and kidney models shows that boosting amino acid burning can limit that cell death. The study frames lung amino acid metabolism as a lever worth testing for treatment.
pmc-13243234:
Anita Muglia and a large Italian team search for early blood signs of severe COVID-19 in a 2026 study. They used stored samples from the first pandemic wave, when doctors had few ways to spot who would crash. The team measured seven immune signals taken when patients reached the hospital.

Their group held 103 confirmed patients treated in Rome between January and May 2020. One signal, CXCL10, stood out as the strongest marker of death or intensive care need. Each step up in its level raised the odds of a poor outcome in adjusted models. Breathing rate and a kidney marker also carried weight, while IL-6 did not. Early CXCL10 testing could help teams triage scarce intensive care beds.
pmc-13244134:
Liya Zhang and co-authors identified a protein switch that tips stem cells toward making bone, with implications for osteoporosis. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Endocrinology in 2026. In bone marrow stem cells learning to become bone, levels of the protein TRIM27 more than doubled. Mice stripped of ovarian hormones, a standard model of postmenopausal bone loss, showed the opposite: TRIM27 fell as bones thinned.

Boosting TRIM27 in cells raised the hallmarks of bone building, from mineral deposits to bone marker genes, while silencing it stalled the process. The mechanism is targeted destruction: TRIM27 binds the fat-promoting regulator PPARγ and tags it for disposal, clearing a brake on bone formation. Knocking down that regulator rescued cells harmed by TRIM27 loss. In the mouse model, extra TRIM27 reduced bone loss. The authors nominate the pathway as a drug target for bone metabolism disorders.
pmc-13246934:
Elsabaawy, Eissa, Atef, and co-authors tested whether everyday movement predicts survival in liver cirrhosis, in this 2026 Scientific Reports study. They followed one hundred sixteen patients for a year, scoring physical activity with a short standard questionnaire and building an index from the answers. That simple index tracked with liver severity scores, blood clotting, albumin levels, and muscle wasting.

Low activity independently doubled the risk of death within twelve months, alongside advanced liver class, older age, low albumin, and muscle loss. Combining the activity index with standard factors separated patients into four risk tiers, from about eighty-nine percent one-year survival down to eighteen percent. The authors propose adding activity questions to routine cirrhosis assessments.
pmc-13247834:
Zhang, King, Boehnke, and co-authors priced two school mental-health programs in this 2026 BJPsych Open cost-effectiveness analysis. The AWARE trial randomized English schools for year 9 pupils to one of two programs, the Youth Aware of Mental Health course or a curriculum guide, or to usual practice. The economists combined delivery and service-use costs with pupils' quality-of-life scores over two follow-ups.

Differences were small on both sides of the ledger: tiny quality-of-life gains and tiny cost changes. At the first follow-up, neither program looked cost-effective. By the second, the Youth Aware program's gains had grown enough that its cost per quality-adjusted life-year sat within the range England's health technology assessor usually accepts. The authors present the timing lesson: school well-being programs may need a year before their value shows.
pmc-13248234:
Onywera and many colleagues report the proceedings of a regional laboratory workshop held in Mombasa, Kenya, in August 2025. Africa CDC, the continental public health agency, convened the meeting under its pathogen genomics program. Twenty-four laboratory heads and senior experts from fifteen member states took part over three days.

Speakers described weak supply chains, scarce equipment servicing, patchy sample transport, and heavy reliance on outside funding. Countries with stronger home financing and settled leadership kept services running more steadily. The group set shared priorities, including quality management, digital links across health sectors, and leadership networks that help labs withstand outbreaks.
pmc-13248334:
Aigner and colleagues compared machines against language models for screening research papers, in a 2026 Systematic Reviews study. Review teams must judge thousands of titles and abstracts, and automation could speed that first pass. The authors tested four classic supervised learning methods beside one open language model, Llama, on the same labeled sets.

Across six finished systematic reviews, both approaches matched or beat single human reviewers at catching eligible papers. The classic models balanced catches and false alarms better overall. The language model judged each paper alone and explained itself, which suits working alongside a person. The authors match each tool to a different screening job.
pmc-13248434:
Xie and colleagues tested patterned light stimulation on developing myopia in guinea pigs, reported in 2026. The retina reads brightness through ON and OFF pathways, and the team wondered whether favoring one pathway changes eye growth. Sixty-three animals wore a minus lens on one eye while receiving twelve hours of stimulation daily for a week.

ON stimulation slowed the myopic shift compared with both natural light and OFF stimulation. It also raised a dopamine breakdown product in the retina, hinting at stronger dopamine activity. OFF stimulation instead preserved the choroid layer and its blood flow. The authors suggest good myopia control may need both pathways working together.
pmc-13249934: Scientific Reports retracted this 2021 article in 2026, and this note is the formal record. Xue and Liu had reported DNA sequences and community diversity of soil fungi in Xinjiang grape fields over several years. After publication, editors found that many of the paper's references could not be confirmed to exist, and two appeared to be duplicates. The authors did not answer the concerns or supply their raw data, so the editors lost confidence in the article's integrity and withdrew it. Its findings should not be relied on.
pmc-13250234:
Kneifati-Hayek and co-authors build an automatic way to catch imaging orders placed for the wrong side of the body. Their 2026 BMJ Open Quality study works within a six-facility health system, screening imaging orders written during 2021. Such errors delay diagnosis and can harm patients, yet routine reporting systems miss most of them.

The method adapts a medication safety trick: flag orders that are withdrawn and re-entered for the opposite side within a day. Checking the flagged charts confirmed most were real near-miss errors, giving an estimate of about four confirmed errors per thousand orders. Risk ran higher for outpatient orders, orders entered by administrative staff, and CT scans compared with X-rays. The authors offer the tool for ongoing safety monitoring across hospitals.
pmc-13250434:
Asiedu and co-authors gather what women around the world know and feel about diabetes that appears in pregnancy. Their 2026 SAGE Open Medicine systematic review covers fifty studies with nearly thirty thousand women, published between 2000 and 2025. Gestational diabetes is common and can harm both mother and baby when it is missed.

Most studies found limited knowledge of risk factors, screening steps, and the long-term effects of the condition. Culture, emotions, and past care experiences shaped how women took up screening and care. Planned teaching, earlier contact with the disease, supportive staff, and family involvement all raised knowledge and follow-through. The authors call for teaching that fits local culture and clearer talk with staff, plus more treatment studies using shared measures.
pmc-13250834:
Aymen Ahmed and a large team track a deadly pairing in United States death records in this 2026 study. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat rhythm, kills more often in people with obesity, and the team charted how that toll changed from 1999 to 2024.

Using the national CDC WONDER database, they counted 63,853 deaths where both conditions were listed. The adjusted death rate rose roughly eleven-fold over the period. Rates ran higher in men than women and in White Americans than Black Americans, and rural areas beat cities. The Midwest had the highest rate while the South rose fastest. The authors call for targeted prevention.
pmc-13251034:
Schröter and co-authors chart fungal infections after kidney transplantation across five German centers. Their 2026 BMC Infectious Diseases study follows more than twelve hundred adult recipients treated between 2011 and 2022. Fungal disease is a serious but poorly mapped threat for transplant patients taking immune-suppressing drugs.

About one in fifteen recipients developed a fungal infection, led by Candida albicans and other Candida species, then Aspergillus and Pneumocystis. Fever was missing in most episodes, and bacterial infections often came first. Each fungus had its own risk profile, from intensive care stays to earlier antibiotic exposure, and one pneumonia type clustered in colder months. Invasive aspergillosis killed the largest share of patients, supporting risk-tailored monitoring.
pmc-13251434:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued this 2026 safety opinion on bacillolysin, a protein-cutting enzyme from a soil bacterium. It is made by a non-modified Bacillus strain and is planned for use in eight food manufacturing processes.

Because the production strain qualifies for a safety shortcut used for well-known microbes, the panel required no animal toxicity studies beyond allergy checks. Estimated intake in European diets was modest. One match with a known breathing allergen was found, so an allergic reaction through food cannot be fully excluded. Even so, the panel concluded the enzyme raises no safety concern under its intended uses.
pmc-13251834:
Yan Li and colleagues profile single brain cells in early Rett syndrome in this 2026 study. The disorder stems from faults in a gene on the X chromosome, so girls carry a mix of working and faulty cells while boys carry only faulty ones.

Reading gene activity cell by cell in young mice, the team found a core set of mis-set genes present only in faulty cells, in both sexes. In females, even the healthy nerve cells behaved oddly, showing the mix itself strains circuits early. One small class of calming nerve cells was the most disturbed of all. The work separates effects of the faulty gene from effects of the mosaic mix.
pmc-13252834:
Zhao and co-authors identify a light-regulated protein that helps plants stretch away from shade. Their 2026 PLOS Genetics study works on shade avoidance, the growth response triggered when neighbors change light quality. A known light sensor, phytochrome B, and its partner PIF4 sit at the center of that response.

The team found that phytochrome B stabilizes the protein BBX5 in the light, while a destruction enzyme breaks it down in shade. BBX5 switches on the PIF4 gene early in shade exposure and directly activates two auxin growth-hormone genes as well. That combined action pushes the plant to grow and escape crowding by neighbors. The authors frame BBX5 as a transcriptional accelerator wired into the classic shade pathway.
pmc-13253134:
Gul Nawaz and co-authors show that sprouting peanuts before roasting improves the resulting oil in a 2026 food science study. Roasted peanut oil owes its appeal to a rich, nutty aroma, and processors work hard to deepen that flavor and slow spoilage. The team germinated peanuts for up to forty-eight hours before microwave roasting and pressing.

Germination woke up the seeds' own enzymes, raising free amino acids and soluble sugars that feed flavor-forming reactions during roasting. Longer sprouting lifted vitamin E type compounds in the oil and stretched the time the oil resisted oxidation from 9.81 hours to 14.89 hours in shelf-life testing. Flavor analysis found more of the pyrazine compounds behind nutty, roasted notes and fewer stale aldehydes. At the full forty-eight hours, though, burnt and smoky off-notes appeared. The authors recommend brief germination as a gentle pretreatment that tunes both taste and keeping quality.
pmc-13253234:
Zun Wang and co-authors review how the mouth's immune barrier is built, remodeled, and repaired in a 2026 article. The oral mucosa is the body's first defense line for everything swallowed or breathed through the mouth. Its protection is layered: a physical sheet of epithelial cells, chemical weapons in saliva, a resident microbial community, and immune cells that mediate fast defense, fine regulation, and memory.

That network stays in balance through constant cross-talk among epithelium, immune cells, and microbes. Local threats such as infection, autoimmune mouth disease, and oral cancer can break it, as can body-wide conditions like diabetes and cancer chemoradiotherapy. A failing barrier then worsens mouth lesions and can feed body-wide inflammation through the oral-systemic axis. The authors survey repair strategies from microbe tuning and immune pathway drugs to biological scaffolds and nanoparticle drug carriers.
pmc-13254234:
Maryam Yuhas and colleagues study sugar intake in low-income preschool children in a 2026 paper. Caregivers of 170 children aged three to five in Head Start programs filled out surveys on food and drink intake, home setting, and feeding practices. The team tested which home factors tied to children's free sugar intake.

Children averaged 4.05 sugary foods or drinks a day, and caregivers averaged 3.78, with intakes strongly linked. In adjusted models, caregiver intake, allowing sugary foods on a bad day, and home availability stayed as predictors. Both groups passed advised limits, so the authors urge action on several home levels.
pmc-13255634:
Qiwei Yang authored a 2026 review of epigenetic control in uterine smooth muscle tumors, a family spanning common harmless fibroids and rare aggressive leiomyosarcoma cancers. Both tumor types start in the same muscle layer, yet behave very differently. Genes matter, but the review focuses on histone modifications, chemical marks on the proteins that package DNA.

In fibroids, altered marks connect to hormone responsiveness and the excess tissue buildup that causes bleeding and pressure symptoms. In leiomyosarcoma, disturbed marks accompany rapid growth and unstable genetic material. The marks also interact with other regulatory systems inside the cell. Because these changes are reversible in principle, Yang argues they offer drug targets beyond standard therapy. Better mapping of the marks could eventually sharpen diagnosis and personalize treatment.
pmc-13255934:
Springer and colleagues built simple prediction equations for the soluble protein fraction of horse feeds, a value needed by updated equine requirement models. They mined a large commercial feed library, grouping thousands of analyses into forages, grains, grain byproducts, and oilseeds or meals. Candidate equations used crude protein and fiber measures, ranked by information criteria.

An equation using only crude protein and neutral detergent fiber won for both outcomes, explaining nearly ninety-nine percent of variation in soluble protein and in estimated pre-cecal digestible protein. The authors argue that adding fiber fractionation to routine protein figures sharply improves estimates of protein actually available to the horse.
pmc-13256434:
Ping Zhou and a large team report a 2026 study of chlorogenic acid, a coffee and plant polyphenol, against experimental asthma in mice. Asthmatic airways suffer chronic inflammation, and the team suspected a link through fat metabolism and ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell damage process. Mice were made asthmatic with ovalbumin, then treated with the compound at several doses.

Treatment calmed airway inflammation in step with dose, lowering allergy-linked cytokines and IgE while improving lung tissue appearance. Lipid profiling showed asthma had distorted DHA fat metabolism toward inflammatory breakdown products, and the compound reversed that profile. It switched on the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway, raising two ferroptosis defense genes, and suppressed iron and reactive oxygen buildup in airway cells. The authors propose ferroptosis control as a fresh strategy for asthma therapy.
pmc-13257034:
Bojana Voučko and co-authors publish a 2026 correction to their study of gluten-free flatbread made with carob flour and sourdough. The notice fixes calculation errors in two tables of the original article. Readers who cite the nutrition values need the corrected figures.

A wrong dilution factor and fiber calculations had distorted several values in one table, and two fiber rows were swapped. A second table carried wrong significance letters for zinc, though the zinc means themselves were right. Corrected fiber values change the abstract claim from nearly doubling to a rise of over sixty percent. Discussion figures were updated to match, including fresh bread fiber values. The correction keeps the record usable for bakers and nutrition researchers who rely on exact composition data.
pmc-13257234:
ChingHao Chen and colleagues evaluate workflow in a busy London emergency urology clinic in a 2026 service study. Urgent specialty clinics must move patients quickly, yet bottlenecks are rarely measured. Two weeks of timed observations covered eighty patient journeys, alongside staff surveys.

An average visit lasted two hours and forty-two minutes, with nearly two-thirds spent after assessment. Ordering investigations caused the main delay, more than doubling doctor-to-discharge time for tested patients. Senior escalation, often blamed, did not slow flow significantly. Nurses cited unsuitable attendances, short staffing, and cramped space as pressures. Staff showed moderate trust in future artificial intelligence support, though no system was tested. Managers get a clear first target: fix investigation timing before buying new technology.
pmc-13257734:
Meng Gu and co-authors review silver-doped phosphate glass for radiation measurement in a 2026 article. The glass stores radiation exposure as light-emitting centers that can be read later, erased, and reused. Older detector materials often trade dose range, precision, or stability against each other, and this glass promises a better balance.

Glass structure and the sites silver ions occupy are analyzed in depth, since both govern the glow response. Dose response mechanisms and how emitting centers evolve with exposure are traced. Uses covered include personal dose monitoring, high-resolution X-ray imaging, and tiny-scale detection for nuclear work. Radiation physicists gain a single reference joining materials science to device practice. Remaining hurdles include manufacturing consistency and readout speed at scale.
pmc-13258434:
Jianghuai Zhan and colleagues test how carbon dioxide slowly eats into low-carbon concrete blends. Their mixes swap in two industrial by-products, fly ash and silica fume, for part of the cement. The 2026 study tracks strength, carbonation depth, and the microscopic reasons behind both.

A quarter fly ash weakened the concrete and let carbonation run much deeper. A small silica fume dose did the opposite, raising strength and tightening the zone where paste meets aggregate. Microscopy and hardness probing traced the split to how eagerly each powder reacts and fills pores. Cement chemistry, high or low in calcium, widened the gap further.
pmc-13258834:
Chaoqi Li and colleagues harden a tracking filter against lying measurements. Bearings-only tracking follows a target using direction readings alone, common in passive sonar and radar watching. A few wild readings can wreck the estimate entirely. Their 2026 filter borrows a robust-statistics trick to tame those outliers.

Suspicious readings are smoothly down-weighted, and extreme ones are thrown out by thresholds set from confidence levels. The design avoids slow repeat loops, keeping the filter nearly as fast as the standard version. In simulations where outliers flooded in, its position error barely grew. Rival filters, including the standard one, degraded catastrophically under the same attack.
pmc-13260334:
Minghui Yin and co-authors mined in 2026 a United States safety database for mental and nervous system side effects linked to three diabetes drugs. The drugs, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin, lower blood sugar by making the kidneys release glucose. Their search covered reports filed from late 2015 to late 2025.

From about 141,000 eligible reports, roughly one in thirteen involved neuropsychiatric events. Men and people aged 45 to 65 stood out as higher-risk groups in the data. Diabetic neuropathy appeared as a signal shared by all three drugs, while each drug also carried its own distinct signals. The authors stress that such database signals flag patterns to watch, not proof that a drug caused the events. They advise closer monitoring, especially for older patients and people using the drugs off-label.
pmc-13260534:
Marc Leon and colleagues staged in 2026 a blinded test of five large language models on hard cardiac surgery decisions. Senior surgeons wrote fifteen realistic scenarios with reference answers and a ten-part scoring frame. In round one, a separate surgeon panel graded model answers without knowing their source.

The reasoning-focused model O1 earned the highest median score, followed by O3-mini-high and DeepSeek-R1. Across models, grasp of the scenario scored best, while patient safety, avoiding invented facts, and efficiency scored worst. In round two, judges saw the reference answers and could revise their grades. Most revisions moved downward, showing that first impressions had been too kind. The authors call this overacceptance the main teamwork risk, and they judge the models not yet safe for complex surgical use.
pmc-13261334:
Kunkun Han and colleagues examined in 2026 a fat-processing enzyme called acylglycerol kinase in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer kills most patients within a short time, largely because it is found late and resists treatment. Their laboratory work compared cancer tissue and cell lines with normal counterparts using gene and protein tests.

The enzyme was markedly more abundant in cancer samples, and higher levels tracked with poorer patient outlook. Turning the gene down slowed cancer cell growth, while forcing it up sped growth through known proliferation genes. The enzyme switched on the NF-kB signaling pathway by moving its p65 part into the cell nucleus. High enzyme levels also blunted the effect of drugs and radiation on the cells. The authors name the enzyme a possible drug target and diagnostic marker.
pmc-13261434:
María Eugenia Taverna and colleagues explored in 2026 bacterial nanocellulose, grown from a kombucha tea byproduct, as a greener additive for drilling fluids. Drilling fluids need steady thickness to lift rock cuttings, and producers usually rely on xanthan gum. Their cellulose came out highly pure, strongly crystalline, and mechanically robust.

Fluids thickened with the cellulose ran thicker than gum-based ones while keeping the same thinning flow under motion. After heat aging at ninety degrees, they kept about four fifths of their starting thickness, beating the gum on endurance. Filtrate loss ran slightly higher, a noted trade-off. An enzyme treatment can later thin the cellulose on demand, easing removal of the filter cake left on well walls. The authors frame this double behavior as a circular-materials win for drilling operations.
pmc-13261534:
Taira Shiratori and co-authors report a 2026 case of hypoglycemic encephalopathy caused by an insulinoma. An insulinoma is a rare pancreatic tumor that secretes too much insulin, driving blood sugar dangerously low. The resulting brain dysfunction can mimic epilepsy and leave bright signals on special MRI scans.

Their patient was a 66-year-old man with recurrent involuntary movements, impaired consciousness, and psychiatric symptoms, without any diabetes treatment history. His blood glucose was critically low at 29 mg/dL. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed reversible bright signals in white matter, including the internal capsule, corona radiata, and corpus callosum. A fasting test and contrast CT confirmed the insulinoma. Intravenous glucose brought rapid improvement, and symptoms resolved fully within one day. Surgeons removed part of the pancreas. Follow-up imaging at two months showed complete resolution of the brain changes.
pmc-13262134:
Steffen Lückerath and André Euler reported in 2026 a case where photon-counting CT with iodine maps exposed large-vessel vasculitis that other scans had missed. Their patient, a sixty-nine-year-old woman, arrived with severe headache and sharply raised inflammation markers. Brain scans and ultrasound first showed nothing significant.

When she returned, a photon-counting scan hunted for infection and instead found the aorta and its upper branches thickened in rings. Iodine maps rebuilt afterward from the same data showed the vessel walls soaking up far more iodine than normal, a sign of active inflammation. Later MRI, PET imaging, and a repeat artery ultrasound agreed on giant cell arteritis. Steroid treatment brought rapid relief in symptoms and blood markers. The authors commend the technique as an on-demand problem solver when early pictures stay silent.
pmc-13262534:
Sinknesh Wolde Behaksra and a large team reported in 2026 Djibouti's first therapeutic efficacy study of its frontline malaria treatment. Artemether-lumefantrine has served since 2014 without any in-country check of how well it still works. Their twenty-eight-day study at one Djibouti City clinic enrolled eighty-eight patients with uncomplicated falciparum malaria.

Seventy patients finished follow-up, and the corrected cure rate reached close to ninety-nine percent, with a single late failure. The drug therefore still works in Djibouti. Warning signs gathered elsewhere in the results: the common rapid test built on one parasite protein caught barely a third of infections, because nearly all parasites had deleted that protein's genes. Resistance-linked gene patterns were widespread, and sexual-stage parasites lingered for weeks. The authors urge combined molecular surveillance and transmission-blocking steps such as single-dose primaquine.
pmc-13263334:
Noemi M. Fricke and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a blood test that watches for the return of throat cancer driven by HPV, the human papillomavirus. The test measures HPV cell-free DNA, small virus DNA fragments floating in blood plasma. Samples came from 59 patients at diagnosis and during follow-up.

At diagnosis the test found the virus DNA with about ninety-five percent sensitivity and specificity. Among 24 patients followed over time, four saw their cancer return or persist. In two of them, the blood test turned positive three and eight months before doctors found the recurrence. A positive result after treatment carried a seventy-five percent chance of recurrence within a year.
pmc-13263734:
Médéa Locquet and colleagues followed in 2026 a heart stress marker in breast cancer survivors for two years after radiotherapy, in the BACCARAT cohort. Radiation can injure the heart silently years later, so a blood signal of strain could give early warning. Their study charted NT-proBNP, a peptide released when heart walls stretch, from before treatment to twenty-four months.

The marker rose late, with the clearest increase at the two-year mark rather than right after treatment. Women starting with higher levels followed distinct trajectories from those starting low. High cholesterol, a moderately split radiation schedule, and aromatase inhibitor hormone therapy each accompanied steeper rises. Higher marker levels also traveled with silent heart dysfunction found on testing. The authors argue the delayed pattern justifies long cardiac follow-up for survivors.
pmc-13264334:
Costanza Di Chiara and colleagues track child flu hospitalizations in Canada across the pandemic in a 2026 tracking study. Twelve large children hospitals reported lab-confirmed cases for children under seventeen from 2012 to 2023 through a national tracking network. Seasons were grouped as pre-pandemic, the quiet 2021 to 2022 season and the rebound 2022 to 2023 season. Severe disease meant intensive care, breathing support or heart-lung bypass. Death during the admission also counted as severe.

More than ten thousand hospitalizations were counted. Case counts collapsed during pandemic limits, then surged with slightly older children in the rebound season. Intensive care shares dipped then rose partway but stayed below pre-pandemic levels. The record helps planners plan for child capacity when breathing viruses return after the break.
pmc-13264634:
Tamara T Mueller led a large team on a 2026 study of whether medical scans can measure how fast a body is ageing. Ageing differs by organ, and scans might reveal who ages faster than their years suggest. The team trained AI models to guess age from scans of single body parts and the whole body.

They used 70,000 MRI scans from the UK Biobank and a German national cohort. Comparing guessed age with true age gave an age gap for each person. Wider gaps linked to diseases such as multiple sclerosis and chronic lung disease, and to habits like smoking and low activity. Swapping one body region between people in a virtual test shifted the whole-body age result. The authors say imaging can flag abnormal ageing for personal risk checks.
pmc-13264934:
Daniel D Kim and Maxwell J Smith review how coercion is defined in public health, in a 2026 scoping review. Public measures are often called coercive, a label that can stir opposition. Definitions vary widely, and that vagueness can weaken trust and policy design. The review asks what writers mean and when they say coercion can be justified.

Five databases were searched, yielding 56 publications. Infectious disease and ethics were the most common settings. Five recurring elements emerged: fewer options, reduced voluntariness, fear of consequences, state enforcement, and being left worse off for not complying. The authors urge clearer shared definitions for fairer evaluation.
pmc-13265234:
Qingqing Wang, Xiaojian Zhang, and Jie Zhang study a protein called TRIM37 in liver cancer cells, in a 2026 laboratory investigation. TRIM37 tags other proteins for disposal and is implicated in many cancers. Its precise role in liver cancer was insufficiently understood. Two liver cancer cell lines were engineered to raise or lower it.

TRIM37 was overexpressed in tumour tissues and cell lines. Raising it boosted cell growth and invasion. Mechanistic tests showed it tagged a protective protein, PTEN, for destruction. Losing PTEN switched on a growth pathway involving AKT and beta-catenin. The authors propose blocking this chain as a treatment approach.
pmc-13266134:
Stephanie N Co-Chang, Nicole Bernadette S Terre, and Cybele Lara R Abad report interim tracking of hospital infections and expert input effects (2026). Adults in hospital at least two days in one big hospital were tracked for a year. Bloodstream infections and ventilator pneumonia were tracked. Timing of expert input was the key factor.

Among 115 patients, bloodstream infection density exceeded pneumonia density. Death was common, especially with combined infection. Most cases got expert input. Late input showed worse raw counts without statistical weight. Expert input itself showed no link to results in this small interim sample, and rates still carried high death tolls.
pmc-13267534:
Christian KuonYeng-Escalante and colleagues present a 2026 case report about a reopened vein seen during liver cancer care. Their patient was a 62-year-old woman with fatty liver disease, scarring, and two liver tumors. She was receiving a treatment that blocks tumor blood flow, on the path toward a transplant. High pressure in the liver's portal vein had reopened her umbilical vein, a vessel that normally closes soon after birth.

Contrast ultrasound was used to check tumor blood flow before and after treatment. After treatment, the tumor showed no inner brightening, as hoped. The scan also clearly showed the reopened vein, matching earlier cross-sectional images. The authors say this real-time method can confirm vessel changes tied to portal pressure.
pmc-13267834:
Lina Liu, Dan Yang, and Jin Fu present a 2026 rat study of hair follicle stem cells for Alzheimer's disease. Current Alzheimer's drugs ease symptoms but do not rebuild the brain. Stem cells from hair roots are easy to gather and raise no ethical concerns. The team tested plain, unmodified cells in rats given a toxic protein fragment to mimic the disease.

Two weeks after the disease model was set, cells were placed into the hippocampus, a memory center. Treated rats later showed higher levels of two proteins that mark healthy synapses, the links between brain cells. The grafts also spurred new neuron growth in the region. Immune cells in the brain, which overreact in Alzheimer's, calmed down. Inflammation signals shifted toward a quieter profile. The authors call the cells promising for future therapy.
pmc-13268634:
Cordula Charlotte Josefine Kreuzenbeck and Silvia Angerer present a 2026 audit study of online booking and insurance inequality in Berlin. Germany has two insurance systems, and privately insured patients usually wait less for specialists. The team used two fake patient profiles, one per insurance type, to query 1,867 listings on a large booking platform, keeping 492 practices bookable for both.

Publicly insured patients waited about 50 days on average for the earliest slot; privately insured patients waited about 23, a gap of roughly 28 days. Practices favoring private patients made public patients wait far longer still. Platform ranking correlated with earlier private availability, suggesting visibility rewards the gap. The authors call for transparency in ranking rules so platforms do not deepen access inequality.
pmc-13269034:
Lingyun Ren and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on heart ultrasound after a heart attack. They asked whether color Doppler ultrasound, which shows blood flow and heart size, can predict later heart failure. All patients had a blocked artery, and some had it opened by a stent procedure.

The study tracked 81 patients for six months, 49 who had the stent procedure and 32 who did not. Heart size grew less in the treated group over time. Among treated patients who later developed heart failure, heart chambers grew and pumping strength fell. The number of blocked arteries, blood pressure history, and early ultrasound results each helped predict heart failure.
pmc-13269234:
Marcus T A Jackson and co-authors argue in 2026 that protecting fetal hemoglobin could prevent the eye disease that blinds many premature babies. Retinopathy of prematurity grows from oxygen swings that first stall, then overdrive, vessel growth in the immature retina. Babies whose fetal hemoglobin falls fastest, especially around weeks thirty-one to thirty-four, develop more and worse disease in recent data.

Adult blood transfusions speed that fall by swapping fetal for adult hemoglobin, which releases oxygen more freely and may raise oxidative stress. Fetal hemoglobin grips oxygen tighter and handles oxidation better, possibly shielding the retina. A cord blood transfusion trial missed its main goal, yet babies who followed the protocol needed less treatment. The authors propose HbF stewardship: routine monitoring, smarter transfusions, and oxygen tuned to hemoglobin type.
pmc-13269734:
Jennie M Scarvell and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on cutting wait times for knee arthritis patients in public hospitals. Senior physiotherapists ran expert clinics that could spot patients who do not need surgery. The service expanded those clinics and improved referral routes to community programs.

Three six-month groups totaling 563 patients were compared across 2022, 2023, and 2024. The share seen by physiotherapists rose from 20 percent to 81 percent, then 76 percent. Median wait fell from 114 days to 45 days in 2023 and 46 days in 2024. The share listed for surgery dropped from 48 percent to about 35 percent. Patients sent on to surgeons were then twice as likely to need knee replacement.
pmc-13270634:
Marina Velado and co-authors report in 2026 a copper-catalyzed method for selectively modifying small ring molecules that carry two boron groups side by side. Such bis(boronates) on three- and four-membered rings are prized building blocks, because each boron handle can be swapped in turn to build complex, precisely shaped products. Earlier copper methods worked mainly on chain ends, leaving ring versions largely untouched.

With a simple alkoxide base, the diboryl cyclopropanes coupled cleanly with allyl, propargyl, and alkynyl halides and with electrophilic amines. On spirocyclic cyclobutanes, the reaction chose the less crowded boron, leaving the second handle free for later steps. The sequence gives stereodefined cyclopropanes and spirocyclobutanes with heavy functional decoration, widening the toolbox for assembling strained ring systems.
pmc-13271334:
Ulrich Eckhard is lead author of a 2026 review titled around the protease code of gut bacteria. Proteases are enzymes that cut proteins, and gut microbes use them not just for digestion but as precise signals that shape the microbial community and its contact with the human host.

The review first covers how proteases remodel the protein scaffolding of microbial biofilms and jam chemical signals bacteria use to coordinate. It then details attacks on host barriers, from enzymes that thin the protective mucus layer to named toxins that cut the joints between gut lining cells. Finally, it shows proteases hijacking host signalling, splitting antibody defences and switching on inflammation receptors.
pmc-13271934:
Jacinta Yap and coauthors review in 2026 how wider energy acceptance in proton therapy beamlines could make cancer treatment far faster. Proton beams can target tumors precisely, yet switching beam energy between layers slows each session. Slow delivery raises cost and lets patient movement blur the dose.

A beamline that carries many energies without repeated magnet adjustments could cut that switching delay sharply. The authors survey designs that widen the accepted energy range and weigh what ultra-fast delivery would change. Faster sessions could improve dose accuracy, patient comfort, and clinic throughput, opening proton therapy to more patients.
pmc-13272434:
Yang Liu and Ziyang Li present in 2026 a three-stage method to find and cut gender bias in Japanese language models used to judge sentiment. Most bias work has focused on English texts, so Japanese models have gone unchecked. Their method tests for bias first, then retrains the model, then tests again with the same tools.

The test sets set stereotype-matching lines against stereotype-breaking and neutral lines in the same sentiment task. Two new scores measure how far the model leans toward stereotypes and how its sentiment differs for male, female, and neutral wording. Retraining on gender-swapped text then aims to repair the lean, giving builders an audit they can rerun.
pmc-13273134:
Leyi Zhang leads a 2026 study engineering baker's yeast to make three prized cosmetic ingredients at once. The compounds are ergothioneine, salidroside, and gadusol, valued for moisture, skin brightening, and sun protection. Yeast is already widely used in cosmetics and is regarded as safe.

The team fixed a rate-limiting step and improved a poorly soluble enzyme, raising one product from 34 to 132 milligrams per liter in flasks. Adding many copies of the pathway lifted it to 690 milligrams per liter in a 5-liter reactor. The final strain in fed-batch culture made all three at once, reaching 1,329, 224, and 556 milligrams per liter respectively.
pmc-13273434:
Fauve Poncelet leads a 2026 illustrative case of a rare neurenteric cyst in Meckel's cave, a small pocket at the skull base. Such cysts are benign congenital lesions, usually in the spinal canal, and intracranial ones are exceedingly rare. The patient was a 52-year-old woman with sudden left-sided headache, nausea, and later double vision.

MRI showed a cyst 14 by 9 millimeters with bright signal and wall calcifications, suggesting protein-rich content. Because a nerve palsy had developed, surgeons removed the cyst fully through a pterional opening. Tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis. After surgery she had temporary facial numbness, and double vision persisted but was managed with prism glasses.
pmc-13274134:
Deblina Nath and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on a dangerous Klebsiella pneumoniae germ taken from a newborn with sepsis, a life-threatening blood infection. The strain, called Sil80, belonged to a previously unrecognized type, K39. It carried both drug resistance and hypervirulence genes, a combination doctors fear.

Lab and genome work showed one plasmid, a small DNA ring, carried the gene that defeats carbapenem antibiotics, while another carried the virulence toolkit. Yet small mutations had dialed those virulence genes down, leaving a thin capsule and weak harm in adult mice. The strain still caused sepsis in a vulnerable newborn. Its virulence plasmid could hitchhike into other bacteria with a helper plasmid's aid.
pmc-13275534:
Megan Glassford, Caroline Jennings, and Anne Slavotinek present a 2026 case report of the first inherited case of a rare developmental disorder tied to the gene GNB2. All previously reported patients carried brand-new variants, causing delays, low muscle tone, and seizures. Gene sequencing in this family found the same change in two brothers with developmental delays and their mother.

The mother was only mildly affected, with a large head and subtle facial features matching the disorder, and this particular variant was already known for milder effects. The family also raises a possible widening of the condition's reach, to overgrowth features and a slow-growing brain tumor called pilocytic astrocytoma seen in the family. The report stresses how widely severity can vary, even within one household.
pmc-13275634:
Shakir Ali leads a large team behind a 2026 review article on fluoride in groundwater around the world. Fluoride is a natural mineral that seeps from rocks into underground water. In small amounts it protects teeth, but too much can damage teeth and bones, a harm called fluorosis.

Following a standard review framework, the authors gathered studies published from 1953 to 2025. They found high fluoride on almost every continent, worst in parts of Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Americas. Hotspots include the East African Rift Valley, the Indo-Gangetic plains, and northern China. Dry climates, long contact between water and rock, and certain water chemistry raise levels. The review maps cheap ways to remove fluoride and notes that rural areas still lack good monitoring.
pmc-13275734:
Saswati Debnath and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on using artificial intelligence to judge diabetic foot ulcers. These are open sores on the feet of people with diabetes. Left unchecked, they can become infected and lead to amputation, so fast and fair assessment matters.

Their system sorts photos of skin into ulcer or healthy, then outlines the sore so its area and width can be measured. It also builds a rough depth map from a single photo and marks which image areas drove its choices. A final module turns all of this into a short report a clinician can read. The authors report strong test results, but say trials with doctors in real clinics must come before routine use.
pmc-13276034:
Hussein Karam Abd El-Sattar and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on predicting where fish can survive in polluted rivers. Fish farms need clean, oxygen-rich water, but real river data are often scarce. The team blended physics-based modeling with artificial intelligence to fill that gap.

First they solved equations for how pollution and oxygen move through a river, creating fifty thousand simulated readings. Then they trained a hybrid program that pairs a random forest with a neural network. It learned to map survival zones and to find the slowest water flow and lowest starting oxygen that stay safe. Against nine rival programs, the hybrid scored near-perfect accuracy and trained far faster than the slowest rival. The authors offer it as a planning tool for farm siting.
pmc-13276334:
Khalid Youssef and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on predicting bleeding inside the heart muscle before emergency treatment. After a major heart attack, reopening the artery can cause hemorrhage within the heart wall, which worsens outcomes. About four in ten treated patients are affected, and no tool flagged risk beforehand.

The team enrolled two hundred eighty-eight heart attack patients, using most to build the model and the rest to check it. Heart scans two to three days after treatment confirmed who had bleeding. An explainable artificial intelligence method, designed so its reasoning shows, picked just three predictors. These were collateral vessels, how blocked the artery was, and a sum score from the heart tracing. Turned into a bedside point score, the model reached about eighty-five percent accuracy and held up in validation.
pmc-13276534:
María Antonia Ocampo, Katherine Arias, and Margarita Maria Chancy report a 2026 surgical case in a seven-year-old boy. After circumcision, an abnormal channel formed between his urethra and the skin, a rare complication. Passing urine grew harder until he could not empty his bladder at all.

Examination showed heat injury to the penile urethra and a complete break in the channel. Long defects like this are usually repaired in two operations. The surgeons instead removed the damaged section and rebuilt the urethra with a foreskin flap in one operation. Recovery brought no complications, and the authors argue single-stage repair can suit selected children.
pmc-13277734:
The EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed issued a 2026 scientific opinion on a chicken feed additive called monensin sodium, sold as Elancoban G200. The European Commission asked the panel to check the identity of the microbe strain that makes the additive and its safety for the target birds. The additive prevents a parasitic gut disease in poultry.

New data show the production strain is a new, not yet described Streptomyces species. The panel could not confirm safety at the currently allowed top dose for fattening chickens. It judged the additive safe at a lower maximum level in feed, and extended that finding to chickens reared for laying.
pmc-13278234:
Andrea H Johnson leads a 2026 study of how metabolic syndrome affects recovery after hip or knee replacement surgery. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of high blood pressure, obesity, diabetes, and abnormal blood fats. The team reviewed 2,181 patients at one institution from 2020 to 2023, all of whom rated their physical function before surgery and one year after.

Metabolic syndrome was present in about seventeen percent of hip patients and about twenty-five percent of knee patients. After adjustment, those patients were less likely to reach a meaningful gain in physical function at one year. Among obese hip patients the gap was clear as well. Added risk from the syndrome, beyond weight alone, is the study's warning.
pmc-13278434:
Zirije Hasani leads a 2026 comparison of four deep learning models, computer vision programs, for classifying plant diseases from leaf images. The team used the PlantVillage dataset with fifteen disease classes and repeated each test five times for sound statistics. They also weighed speed, since farm devices often have weak hardware.

One model reached the highest accuracy, at about ninety-nine point six percent, with low response time, giving the best trade-off. A densely connected model was nearly as accurate but slower. A binarized model was fastest but dropped to about eighty-eight percent accuracy. The authors caution that the dataset's controlled photos limit how far results generalize to real fields.
pmc-13278934:
Meijuan He and colleagues report an aggressive intestinal lymphoma that burst the bowel twice, in a 2026 case study. A 72-year-old man arrived with an acute abdomen needing emergency surgery. Tissue tests named monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, a rare cancer with a grim record.

He first refused treatment, then returned nine months later with a second perforation from relapse. Tumour staining showed strong BCL-2, a protein that helps cancer cells avoid death. Four cycles of CHOP chemotherapy plus the BCL-2 blocker venetoclax followed. Scans then showed complete metabolic remission without major blood count suppression. The authors call the approach biologically sensible but unproven beyond this single case.
pmc-13279034:
Reidar Naevdal and colleagues report a 2026 study of therapist views on online therapy in Norway. The care is internet delivered cognitive behavioural therapy, or iCBT, a talk therapy given on the web. The study tracks views as the whole country moved to a new web platform over eighteen months.

Forty six therapists, most of the national group, filled forms at five time points. Overall approval was high at the start and stayed high through the switch. Views of how easy the tool felt for patients rose over time. Approval was high even before hands on use, which hints that clear hopes set before launch can ease big tech change.
pmc-13279434:
Tengfang Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 case of a chest tumour first read as lung cancer. The tumour was a calcified solitary fibrous tumour of the pleura, the thin lining round the lungs. Such tumours are rare and can mimic lung cancer on scans. Their patient was a fifty two year old man with four months of repeat cough.

A CT scan showed a small lump near the left lung tip with patchy hard deposits, read as lung cancer. In surgery, the lung looked normal, and a white, cauliflower like lump sat on the chest wall by a rib. It split from lung tissue with ease. Key scan clues were broad base on the pleura and coarse hard deposits. Spotting them can spare needless lung removal and keep lung function intact.
pmc-13280034:
Mitchell Mologna and colleagues published a 2026 matched case-control study testing whether particular knee shapes predict osteochondritis dissecans. In this lesion, bone and cartilage loosen inside the joint. The study focused on lesions of the thigh-bone knuckle, the medial femoral condyle. Eighty-six patients under 21 diagnosed between 2016 and 2024 were matched by age and sex to 86 controls imaged for unrelated reasons. Two observers measured the scans.

Three features separated the groups. The condyle index, condyle width against shin-bone width, was significantly larger in patients, while the notch width index was significantly smaller. A steeper inner tibial slope also emerged as a predictor, though raw slope values alone did not differ significantly. Crossing thresholds multiplied the odds sharply, up to roughly nineteen-fold for the condyle index. The authors argue these markers could flag at-risk knees.
pmc-13280134:
Leonor Jane Paulino Pereira and colleagues report a 2026 study that adds urinary symptoms to prostate MRI triage. Men with suspected prostate cancer in primary care often face hospital referral and MRI scans. Many scans prove needless. The team built a model that adds lower urinary tract symptom severity, scored by the IPSS questionnaire, to standard risk facts. IPSS asks how often urinary signs occur. The group was biopsy naive men, who had no prior prostate biopsy.

The model cut unneeded hospital referrals and MRI scans by twenty three percent. At the same time, it kept high detection rates for clinically significant prostate cancer, the type that needs care. The authors call it the first model of its kind for primary care triage. Fewer scans free slots for high risk men and spare low risk men travel and worry. Cost gains could follow if it holds.
pmc-13280334:
Ying Fan and colleagues published a 2026 paper presenting PIT-Net, a physics-informed learning system for quantitative photoacoustic tomography, an imaging method that listens to sound waves generated when tissue absorbs light pulses. Turning those signals into absorption maps is ill-posed because light fades as it travels, entangling brightness with depth. Their design pairs a transformer backbone reading features across wavelengths with a differentiable physics module that solves the light-diffusion equation inside the network. An acoustic feedback loop enforces agreement with the measured sound.

Trained on synthetic data, the system transferred directly to tissue without retraining. In tests it scored high and rebuilt absorption images in phantoms and animal tissue. Repeated mouse tumor imaging showed stable monitoring. The authors position the framework as an interpretable route to such imaging in deep tissue. Data-driven models often fail to carry over from training examples to real bodies.
pmc-13280434:
An editorial in The Lancet Regional Health Americas argues a 2026 call for more primary prevention of stroke. Neurological conditions are the top cause of disability adjusted life years, years of healthy life lost. Stroke alone makes forty two percent of that burden, ahead of migraine and dementia. In the world, an estimated twelve million new strokes strike each year, and ninety four million people live post stroke. Stroke is the third top cause of death.

Most stroke risk factors are preventable, the editorial stresses. Its June 2026 series on stroke prevention in the Americas gives regional counts: about one point two million new cases and about fifteen point seven million prevalent cases in 2023 data. Those counts rose about nine and twenty two percent from 2021 estimates. The piece urges health systems to shift funds and focus to primary prevention, before the first stroke strikes.
pmc-13280534:
Rebekka Schröder and colleagues published a 2026 representative survey study of teachers' wellbeing and health in Germany, a workforce whose heavy responsibilities can erode both. Randomly drawn from a large population panel, 1,005 teachers completed the 2022 web survey. Results were weighted to match the population by gender, age, school type, and state. Wellbeing was scored with the PERMA profiler, which rates positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment. Health literacy questionnaires were also used.

Teachers reported intermediate to high wellbeing. Two forms of knowledge stood out as predictors. Teachers with stronger general and mental health literacy reported better wellbeing in the model. Age and experience pulled the other way. Teachers in their forties and fifties, and those holding ten to nineteen years of experience, scored lower than reference groups. The authors argue that building health literacy may be a lever for protecting teacher wellbeing, rather than only reducing workload.
pmc-13280734:
Chun-Gu Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 nationwide cohort study asking whether people with Fabry disease suffer injuries more often than the general population. Fabry disease is an inherited enzyme deficiency that damages nerves, balance organs, and the brain, all plausible routes to accidents. Using Taiwan's national insurance database, the team followed adults diagnosed between 2001 and 2015. They compared them with four matched controls per patient, tracking injury diagnoses over time.

Injuries occurred at 33 per thousand person-years in the Fabry group against 22.5 in controls, and adjusted analysis put their risk 64 percent higher. Traffic accidents ran 86 percent higher and falls 56 percent higher. Risk also climbed with winter season, heavier comorbidity, and greater urbanization. The authors describe this as the first demonstration of the injury burden in this disease. They recommend injury-risk assessment and tailored prevention, from balance support to driving advice, as part of standard Fabry care.
pmc-13280834:
Hari Om Singh and colleagues published a 2026 review of plant- and waste-derived carbons for stripping the antibiotic tetracycline out of water. Tetracycline passes through many treatment plants intact, accumulates in waterways, and promotes antimicrobial resistance. Cheap adsorbents made from farm and industrial biomass waste are a countermeasure. The review covers activated carbon and its less processed cousin biochar.

Choice of feedstock, the heating route, chemical or physical activation, and surface changes all shape the pores and chemistry that decide performance. The authors evaluate each lever. They explain the binding mechanisms in play, including aromatic stacking, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, surface binding, and pore filling. They also explain how acidity, salt content, and the drug's chemical form tilt the balance among them. Models infer how the drug travels and binds. The review ends with practical obstacles to wastewater deployment and design guidance for next carbons.
pmc-13280934:
Viper Sharma and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a rare artery layout found during major belly surgery. The patient needed removal of the head of the pancreas for a cyst-like growth in its ducts. That surgery is long and risky, and blood vessel maps guide each step. One artery to the liver came from an odd source. Such a layout is so rare that standard charts do not list it.

Scans before surgery missed the odd artery. Surgeons found it only by careful work during the operation itself. The team also searched past reports and found just four papers on five such patients. Their case adds one more. They warn surgeons to expect surprise vessels in this surgery, since harming that artery could starve part of the liver of blood.
pmc-13281234: Kun-Ling Tsai and colleagues published a short correction in 2026 to their 2021 study of a diabetes drug in heart cells. The drug work claimed the drug guards the heart when blood flow returns after a block. In the correction, the authors say one figure showed the wrong lab blot image. They print the right image in its place. They state the error does not change what the study found.
pmc-13281734:
Yixia Wang and colleagues tested how look-alike characters affect reading in Chinese in a 2026 study. A character's neighbors are other characters that share most of its strokes. Old ways of counting neighbors split each character into just two parts, a rough guide. A newer code spells out stroke patterns and their layout in fine detail. The team ran three studies with the fine code, holding character frequency and stroke count steady. They timed how fast readers named single characters.

The classic counts showed no neighbor effect at all. One fine count showed a weak slowing from many neighbors. Another fine count showed a small speeding, and it held after scaling. The effects flipped sign by method and stayed small throughout. The authors say if neighbor effects exist in Chinese reading, they are faint and unstable. Better measures alone, they conclude, did not rescue a clean theory.
pmc-13282134:
Tran Kien Vu and co-authors present a 2026 case of bowel blockage caused by a rare internal hernia in an elderly man. A hernia here means bowel slipped through a natural opening, the foramen of Winslow, into a pocket behind the stomach. The patient was eighty-eight years old, with two days of upper belly pain, nausea, and vomiting, and no past belly surgery. His belly was mildly swollen.

Scans showed widened small bowel loops sitting in that pocket. Emergency open surgery confirmed that parts of the small bowel and the start of the large bowel had slipped through. The bowel was congested but still alive, so surgeons eased it back without removing any of it. Because the right colon moved too freely, they fixed it to the belly wall. He recovered well and left hospital stable.
pmc-13283134:
Alexander von Eye and Wolfgang Wiedermann present a 2026 methods paper on testing effect direction in frequency data. The method is Configural Frequency Analysis, which checks count patterns in data tables. The authors use formal logic to sharpen which patterns truly support a claim.

A key point is that some patterns match a claim only by chance logic. When a starting claim is false, any result can follow, so such patterns prove nothing. Those cells should not count as support in a fair test. The paper covers joined claims and if-then claims in detail. Worked examples use data on partner violence effects. Clearer cell choice should make tests more honest and strict.
pmc-13283434:
Pregnancy complicated a repeat collapsed lung that ended in keyhole surgery, Zymantas Jagelavicius's team recounts in 2026. Collapsed lung in pregnancy is very rare, with few cases in English reports. Care must protect both mother and unborn child at each step.

The patient was a 31-year-old woman at 17 weeks of pregnancy. She arrived with breathlessness and chest pain and got a chest drain first. Three days after discharge the lung collapsed again with a lasting air leak. Keyhole chest surgery was done to fix the problem directly. Tissue tests showed enlarged air spaces without specific lung disease. Recovery was smooth, and she later delivered a healthy newborn.
pmc-13284734:
Edmond Tchiakpe and co-authors report a 2026 case of HIV-1 resistance to dolutegravir in Benin. Benin follows World Health Organization advice and uses dolutegravir in first and second line care, with staff trained on dosing and side effects. The patient in this report had poor adherence, so the regimen had to be changed.
