The virus strain was named as CRF02_AG. The authors argue genotyping helps track resistance in non-adherent patients and that stronger patient teaching is needed to reach the UNAIDS third 95 target.
pmc-13285034:
Roland Ngwese Akwelle and co-authors report a 2026 computer design study for new mpox test antigens. Field-friendly blood surveillance tools are needed, since PCR tests are hard to deploy widely. The team built two multi-part antigens from short pieces of known mpox proteins and tested their shapes and binding by computer methods alone.

Both designs scored well on predicted antigen strength and showed stable, water-friendly traits in the models used here. Shape checks passed standard quality tests, and docking work tested binding to parts of three antibody types. Motion analysis added support for stability. The authors stress these are in silico results, so lab and field tests must follow before any real test kit.
pmc-13285734:
Neggie Chinyanga Mkundika Mndolo and colleagues explored how midwives in Malawi view a modified early warning system for mothers, in a 2026 qualitative study. The scoring tool helps staff spot women who are becoming gravely ill during or after pregnancy. Before wider use, the team asked whether the midwives who must use it find it workable.

Interviews held in mid-2025 covered 30 midwives at two large hospitals in Lilongwe, from frontline staff to policy roles. Judged against a standard acceptability framework, the system scored well on all seven parts. Midwives said it could guide judgement and ease their workload during busy shifts. Shortages of paper forms and basic equipment stood out as the main threat to lasting use, a fixable barrier the authors flag for planners.
pmc-13285834:
Alexander I Papolos, Christopher F Barnett, and Jacob C Jentzer answer a critic in a 2026 reply letter about staffing in cardiac intensive care units. Their earlier survey described how units led by doctors trained in both heart care and intensive care are now organized. The letter takes up worries about who answered the survey and how its terms were set.

The authors grant that replies came mostly from academic centers and that the response rate was modest. They note that no tested survey tool existed, so they built one with broad terms to fit varied real-world units. A one-time survey cannot prove cause, they agree, yet its links between job design and career contentment may still guide leaders. They close by urging longer studies with shared terms and ties to patient outcomes.
pmc-13285934:
Ruijuan Yan and colleagues review early liver lesions that can turn into cancer in a 2026 survey of pathology and risk tools. Liver cancer usually grows through a slow chain from chronic disease to cirrhosis, then to nodules that edge toward tumors. Catching that middle stage offers the best window for early action, and the review maps how doctors spot and grade it.

Lesions range from cell changes and small foci to low- and high-grade nodules, each with rising odds of turning malignant. Scans, contrast imaging, blood markers, and newer liquid biopsy tests each add clues, though none settles the call alone. Risk scores that blend age, sex, and marker levels help sort who needs the closest watch. The authors see imaging math, smart software, and combined gene data as the next aids, once proof in daily care catches up.
pmc-13286834:
Kresimir Cosic, Anđela Kuljanac, and Sara Palermo argue in 2026 that brain science and AI should be joined to make armed forces stronger. Wars now play out in the mind as much as on the ground. The authors sketch a layered aid that backs human choice rather than taking its place. AI can sort vast data and flag what may come next. Brain-based training can help staff stay sharp under load. Joined with hard power, they claim, such tools could raise deterrence and help states last through long crises. The plan is a concept, not a tested system.
pmc-13286934:
Fredrick O. Olewe and colleagues test lung function in children and teenagers with sickle cell disease attending a referral hospital in Kisumu, Kenya. The 2026 study enrolled 138 patients aged six to seventeen from the Lake Victoria basin. Lung damage is a major source of illness and death in this inherited blood disease, and early testing can catch decline in time to act.

Breathing tests came back abnormal in more than a quarter of participants. Two thirds of the abnormal results showed a restrictive pattern, where lungs cannot expand fully, and the rest an obstructive pattern. City living, low weight, charcoal use, hydroxyurea treatment, and past admissions showed no firm links with abnormal results. Routine lung checks for this population are the authors' recommendation.
pmc-13287034:
Fengyi Gao and Siew-Pang Chan present a reusable data science workflow for analyzing medical costs, aimed at closing the gap between research findings and real policy use. Their 2026 paper demonstrates the pipeline on a large public United States health expenditure survey, while designing it for adaptation to Singapore's claims data. Rising costs in aging populations motivate the work.

Implementation frameworks enter only as lenses for reflection, not as tested strategies. The contribution is methodological: transparency and repeatability that other health systems can copy with local adjustments.
pmc-13287134:
Isabell Noichl and Clarissa Schönecker report laboratory work from 2026 on small spheres settling through fluid close to a solid wall. They tracked soft and rigid particles starting from rest inside a narrow channel, at very low particle Reynolds numbers.

Early in each fall the particles drifted toward the wall, a pull the authors link to fluid inertia. At somewhat higher flow speeds rigid spheres later moved away, matching older lift models, while slower runs stayed unsteady. Computer flow simulations backed the readings. Their regime map may help interpret how deformable microplastics move near boundaries in water treatment settings.
pmc-13287234:
Robert Hincapie and co-authors wrote a 2026 mini-review on soft gel implants that gather immune cells into organised local groups after placement in the body. Such gels can be adjusted chemically and physically, so the authors treat them both as treatments in development and as test beds for learning how these cell groups form.

Signals carried in the gel, such as antigens and messenger proteins, shape which cells arrive and how they switch on. Firmness, stretch, pore size, and breakdown rate shape movement and behaviour. New mapping tools are starting to chart group layout and cell talk. The authors call for closer joint work across materials, immune, and computing fields.
pmc-13287434:
Lisa Tan and colleagues compared in 2026 how adults with epilepsy in city, fringe, and rural parts of the United States rated their confidence, daily function, and quality of life. Data came from baseline measures in a self-management trial, grouped by official rural codes and adjusted for income and schooling.

Rural participants scored lower on confidence in handling their epilepsy. Their overall quality of life scores averaged about eleven points lower than city participants. Thinking and memory sub-scores were also lower. The authors link the gaps to poorer access to specialist epilepsy care outside cities. They argue that support programmes should be designed for rural delivery from the start.
pmc-13287734:
Yoshikazu Ganchiku and co-authors tested in 2026 a redesigned version of interleukin-2, a growth signal for immune cells, in mouse organ transplants. pmc-13288534:

pmc-13288834:

pmc-13289234:

pmc-13289634:

pmc-13289934:
Ali Ibrahim, Shaikha Alshehhi, Nikolaos Tsingilis, and Yaser Mohammed Al-Worafi study a 2026 survey link between shared leadership and teacher commitment in United Arab Emirates schools. pmc-13290434:
Liming Zhu and colleagues review how gut microbes may raise immunotherapy power in lung cancer, in a 2026 article. pmc-13290934:
Adding scalp and tongue acupuncture to standard rehab helped autistic children gain skills faster, Qinliang Zhang and colleagues report in a randomized trial from 2026. pmc-13291034:
Kenneth Färnqvist and colleagues survey survivors of esophageal and gastric cancer in Sweden in a 2026 cross-sectional study of self-care. pmc-13291334:
Daily light habits may steer sleep more than we think. Ann-Sophie Loock leads a 2026 study of people in many countries. Light tells the body clock when to rest. Habits decide how much light each person gets.

pmc-13291434:
Voluntary study groups help Japanese emergency doctors keep growing. Takeshi Kawaguchi leads a 2026 study of these non-formal groups. Formal courses clash with shifts and distance. Self-run special interest groups offer a flexible swap.

Shared aims to change emergency care added fuel. A safe, mixed network kept them engaged. Gains flowed through tools, shared roles, and group norms. Leadership itself shifted as members took turns.
pmc-13291634:

pmc-13291734:

pmc-13291934:

pmc-13292334:

pmc-13292434:

pmc-13292934:

pmc-13293434:
Collins Mukubesa and colleagues study, in a 2026 cohort paper, who dies during tuberculosis treatment at a rural hospital in Zambia. Tuberculosis stays a top infectious killer, yet local data on death risk during care are scarce.

pmc-13293734:

pmc-13294134:

pmc-13294234:

pmc-13295434:

pmc-13295634:

pmc-13295834:

pmc-13296134:

pmc-13296434:

pmc-13296534:

pmc-13296634:

pmc-13297134:

pmc-13297234:

pmc-13297934:

pmc-13299234:

pmc-13299634:

pmc-13299734:

pmc-13300234:

pmc-13300534:

pmc-13301134:

pmc-13301334:

pmc-13302834:

pmc-13303334:

pmc-13304234:

pmc-13304434:

pmc-13305134:

pmc-13305734:

pmc-13306034:

pmc-13306334:
Naphatsawan Vongmanee built an electrode sensor for a hard to treat hospital germ in a 2026 study. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, fights off many drugs and forms films, so fast and sharp tests aid early control of lung, urine and wound illness.

A plastic coat on the electrode holds moulded holes that match the germ shape and skin traits, made from three base parts. The test found as few as 1 CFU/mL of germ, across a range to 104 CFU/mL in reported runs, with no need for antibodies. Repeat runs stayed close, with spread of just 5 to 12 percent in the reported checks.
pmc-13307734:
Yiyang Zhang and a large team characterise in 2026 a highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu strain taken from migratory birds at Beidaihe wetland in northern China during 2022 to 2024. Gene family trees place the surface gene in the globally spreading clade, while other genes cluster with strains from several continents. That mix signals a reassortment event across continents.

The virus shares high sequence similarity with human H5N1 isolates and carries mutations tied to virulence, stronger human receptor binding, and possible drug resistance. Mouse infections confirmed body-wide replication and high killing power at low doses. Antigen tests showed good cross-reaction with a widely used poultry vaccine strain, which is reassuring for control. The authors frame stopover wetlands as priority surveillance sites for early warning.
pmc-13308934:
Tsuyoshi Ueda and co-authors recount a 2026 stomach held splint tube trick that saved a bile duct scope run in a woman aged 76 years with a severe chest hernia. Gallbladder cancer blocked her bile flow, and most of her stomach sat in her chest, which bent the scope path.

The first scope run failed as loops kept forming and blocked the way past the stomach exit each time. On the retry, a soft tube sat in the lower stomach and held the gut axis straight for the scope. The scope then slid in with ease, and a metal stent opened the duct. Gut wall harm risk may fall when the tube skips the bulb.
pmc-13309134:
Keshinisuthan Kirubalingam, Peng You, and Demir Bajin sum up in 2026 five key points on otitis externa, a canal infection that strikes as many as 10 percent of people in a lifetime. Most cases follow damp or a small scratch, with bacteria the usual cause and fungi in about a tenth of cases.

Pain on tug of the ear, itch, fullness, and discharge mark the usual case, with a red, swollen canal on scope view. Drops that kill germs, with or without steroids, clear 65 to 90 percent of cases in 7 to 10 days in past data. Deep pain, lumps in the canal, or nerve signs warn of a bone eating form that needs urgent expert care.
pmc-13309434:
Leonardo García-Heveling presents a 2026 mathematics article on a volume-based way to mark time in models of the universe. General relativity lacks one shared clock, so researchers build time measures from the shape of space-time itself. An earlier volume measure offered an option beside the better known time measure.

Building on prior work by other mathematicians, the article shows the volume measure changes smoothly in many cases that matter for research. Smooth change lets the space-time split cleanly into space and time parts and yields a paired distance measure. Further results and examples cover both volume and time measures. The work serves readers in mathematical relativity.
pmc-13309534:
Serdar Koltuk examines how grid fineness in computer models changes shaking results for wet sand in a 2026 study. Earthquake engineers model soil with small elements, but coarse grids miss detail while fine grids cost time and money. Finding the right balance is a practical design question.

Three sands of loose, medium, and dense packing were modeled with a standard sand behavior law. Ninety-six runs used four recorded shaking motions and varied grid choices. Outcomes showed how grid size and shape shift surface motion and soil response. The author turns those patterns into guidance for picking grids that stay accurate without wasted computing cost in quake engineering work.
pmc-13309634:
Lía Nattero-Chávez replies to a letter about a diabetes device study in a 2026 journal response. The original study tracked adults with type 1 diabetes who switched glucose sensors while using an automated insulin pump system. A commenter, Dr. Zhang, raised method points, including whether pump setting changes explained the gains.

The response agrees that setting changes likely played a part, since 27 participants, or 29 percent of the group in the study, adjusted settings during follow-up. Fresh repeated-measures analysis added setting changes as a factor across all visits. The authors note that sensor gains, setting tuning, and growing user skill blend in daily care. They thank the commenter and stand by careful reading of the results.
pmc-13309834:
Kamran Sattar, Mohamad-Hani Temsah, and Shaukat Ali Jawaid weigh in 2026 how generative artificial intelligence should enter undergraduate medical assessment, writing, and peer review. Local studies give the essay its footing: one found a chatbot could spot some flawed exam questions but missed others and gained no efficiency from training. Assessment decisions steer student progression and public trust, so the stakes are high.

Speed is the obvious promise, from drafting feedback to flagging ambiguous questions and grading short answers. The authors warn against confusing efficiency with validity, since marking is a professional judgement about future doctors. Accepted quality criteria for good assessment still apply when software assists. Formative uses, such as rapid practice feedback on clinical reasoning, look safer than high-stakes scoring. Their call is for educational governance: clear rules, oversight, and validation before tools touch decisions that shape careers.
pmc-13310434:
Nok Chhun and co-authors gather health worker views on adding HIV prevention drugs into drug-use services in Kampala, Uganda, in a 2026 study. People who use drugs face high HIV risk, yet prevention pills reach them poorly. Clinics for opioid treatment and needle exchange already meet this group regularly, making them natural hosts.

Workers from five program sites, spanning nurses to social workers, were interviewed between March 2021 and September 2022 under a shared implementation framework. Thirty workers gave views on barriers and priority fixes for joining the services. Workers likened full joining to a full course meal, a gain worth the effort in their accounts. The authors sort the fixes health teams judged most urgent.
pmc-13310734:
Fay Manning and co-authors report a 2026 survey study on imaging care as felt by larger bodied patients in the United Kingdom. Staff views have been studied before, but patient views are less known. The team asked adults to share their most striking visit for scans or radiation treatment and what could improve.

Ninety two people replied through social media links. Most wrote about scans, and some wrote about radiation care. Themes covered life before, during, and after visits, plus broad social views and ideas for change. Poor fit of gear, blunt staff remarks, and blame left some people avoiding care. Good practice gave others hope for future visits.
pmc-13310934:
Qianyi Ren and colleagues build an anti aging eye drop for dry eye disease in a 2026 study. Dry eye grows common with age, as aged cells release factors that fuel stress and swelling in a loop. Standard drops do not break that loop, so a nano carrier that clears aged cells was designed.

Drops pack quercetin with an antioxidant enzyme in a smart protein shell that escapes cell traps and crosses the cornea well. In aged dry eye models, drops cut stress and cell death, restored tear gland work, and eased disease signs. Quieting aged cell signals drove much of the gain.
pmc-13311134:
Yu Wang and colleagues build a learning model to foretell breathing failure in acute pancreatitis in a 2026 study. Lung failure is the most common organ failure in this pancreas illness and carries high death risk. Early warning would speed intensive care, so records from a large United States database and Chinese hospitals were mined.

Nine top traits, including temperature, oxygen level, and seven blood measures, fed five learning methods. A logistic model scored highest across home, outside, and cross specialty tests, with strong sensitivity marks. A free web tool hosts the model for clinic use. Tests in pregnant patients marked a boundary of safe use.
pmc-13311234:
Christy Ilia and colleagues audit in 2026 a dosing change that cut drug costs at their transplant centre without obvious clinical harm. Rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin, a potent immune suppressant given at kidney transplant, had been dosed by actual body weight. The centre switched to ideal body weight, and this retrospective review compared kidney recipients from the two eras.

The primary measure was drug purchasing cost per recipient at standard wholesale pricing. Ideal-weight dosing saved a median of about 3,838 dollars per transplant and reached statistical significance. Rejection rates, infection readmissions, and blood-count suppression looked broadly similar between eras. One virus, Epstein-Barr, appeared more often under one strategy without raising infection admissions. With roughly 250 kidney transplants yearly, the authors estimate annual savings near nine hundred thousand dollars. Cost discipline in induction therapy frees budget without trading away early graft outcomes, they conclude.
pmc-13311334:
Hong-Liang Lu and colleagues present a 2026 study joining brain scans and gene activity maps to attention problems in schizophrenia. Faulty attention is a core feature of the illness and drags on daily life.

The study enrolled 137 people, 65 with schizophrenia and 72 healthy controls, for MRI scans and thinking tests. Patients took longer on key attention responses. Their scans showed larger pallidum on both sides, a smaller right hippocampus, and thinner cortex in some areas. Alertness scores tracked with pallidum size in patients, and that link matched a distinct gene activity pattern. The work ties behavior, brain shape, and genes together.
pmc-13312134:
Laura McKain and colleagues quantify, in a 2026 claims-based study, the burden of anemia among women with fibroids and heavy bleeding. Using a large United States commercial claims database, the researchers followed newly diagnosed women aged 18 to 55 for a year before and after diagnosis. They sorted patients by whether heavy bleeding appeared before or after the fibroid diagnosis and matched them against women with neither condition.

Each fibroid cohort held 22,057 women, with 110,285 controls. Anemia after diagnosis was far more common when heavy bleeding was in the picture, at 32.0 and 35.3 percent in the two bleeding cohorts, against 14.3 percent for fibroids alone and 4.4 percent among controls. Women with anemia also underwent more hysterectomies and transfusions and cost more to treat in every cohort. The authors press for earlier detection and active management of both fibroids and anemia.
pmc-13312534:
Fushuang Zheng and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, new work on engineered nanozymes for lung cancer therapy. Lung tumors resist treatment by adapting, and standard care struggles to reshape the tumor microenvironment, the neighborhood that shields cancer from drugs and immunity alike.

The authors frame nanozymes, catalytic nanomaterials that mimic enzymes, as active agents rather than passive carriers. By generating reactive species, adjusting oxygen, and running cascade reactions, these particles disturb the tumor's redox balance and metabolic dependencies. They sensitize it to chemotherapy, radiation, and light-based treatments, and provoke immunogenic cell death that recruits the immune system. The review lays out design logic around setting when and where the catalysts switch on, then maps the barriers still blocking use in patients and a route toward next-generation enzyme-like medicine.
pmc-13312834:
Erandis Dheni Torres Sánchez and co-authors present a 2026 narrative review of Helicobacter pylori at the crossroads of mouth and stomach disease. The bacterium drives ulcers, chronic gastritis, and gastric cancer. Evidence increasingly suggests it also shelters in dental plaque and periodontal tissue, forming a reservoir outside the stomach that standard treatment never reaches.

The review describes how the organism might survive the oral environment and what that presence means clinically. The authors propose traffic in both directions: periodontitis fuels body-wide inflammation that may encourage stomach infection, while an oral reservoir can reseed the stomach after eradication therapy and cause relapse. They suggest that clearing the bacterium from the mouth could become part of preventing gastric reinfection, and point to metagenomics and proteomics as tools to test the idea properly.
pmc-13315434:
Shuichi Hayashi and co-authors study in 2026 how a release protein helps a special hippocampus connection grow up. The mossy fiber to CA3 link, key for learning and memory, has giant boutons that grip spiny growths on target cells, and how that shape forms was unclear.

When SNAP25, a protein needed for controlled vesicle release, was missing, boutons were more numerous but smaller, and a scaffold protein on the receiving side was misplaced. Combined light and electron imaging showed axons still found targets and made synapses, yet the spiny growths failed to form, shrinking contact area. Odd large vesicles also built up inside boutons.
pmc-13315634:
Amit Saraf and colleagues report, in a 2026 phase I trial, a safety readout for an eye-grade bevacizumab supplied to inject. The drug is used off-label for neovascular age-related macular degeneration but reaches the syringe through compounding, with particulate quality. Their formulation, GBL1204 at 1.25 milligrams in a prefilled syringe, met particle standards for eye injections. Sixteen patients aged fifty or older at five Indian centers received one injection into the eye and were watched for a month.

No ocular or systemic adverse events occurred. Nine participants reported fourteen events, thirteen ocular and one systemic, just over half mild, and all resolved without sequelae. Vision improved, gaining a mean of three letters on charts by day twenty-eight, while central macular thickness fell by sixty-five micrometers over the same span. Blood levels of the target protein fell. The authors recommend advancing the product to a phase III trial.
pmc-13315734:
Karim Al-Ghazzawi and a large team profiled gene activity in 2026 in uveal melanoma, an eye cancer that often spreads to the liver, comparing first tumors with their matched metastases. The cancer is genetically well defined yet varies a lot in behavior, so the team asked how cell character changes during spread.

Two main molecular subtypes appeared in both settings, but matched pairs matched poorly, showing wide reprogramming during metastasis. About half of first tumors showed a fast-growing, MAPK and PI3K driven pattern. Immune settings also split, with first tumors led by adaptive responses and metastases by innate signals and suppressive macrophages.
pmc-13316234:
Dokyung Jung and a large team built a discovery platform in 2026 that screens plant-derived nanoparticles for immune effects in a systematic way, moving past the one-plant-at-a-time habit. They assembled a library of 110 nanoparticles from diverse plant groups, with full physical profiling and high-throughput function tests.

Particles from Allium tuberosum stood out, pushing macrophages toward an inflammatory state. Their power came mostly from inner RNA cargo, above all a microRNA that acts on the Bcl6 signaling axis to reprogram the cells. The particles also made cold tumors more sensitive to immune checkpoint therapy in tests.
pmc-13316634:
Donlaporn Saetae authored a 2026 study building a digital twin for a plant-based Greek-style yogurt made from okara, the soy pulp left from tofu making, blended with coconut milk. Plant yogurts often set weakly and leak liquid, and raw material swings make factory control hard.

Tests showed the mix forms a compact, space-filling gel network. Tuning landed on 14 percent okara with 18 percent coconut milk for the best balance of firmness, low leakage, and taste scores. A hybrid model joining a classic growth curve with learning tools predicted fermentation with very high accuracy, and live data updates cut forecast error sharply. The setup offers makers a smart control template for variable plant inputs.
pmc-13318734:
Siyan Liu and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of drinks and diabetic eye disease. They cover alcohol, wine, spirits, sugary and artificially sweetened drinks, coffee, tea, juice, and yogurt. Searches ran across four databases through February 15, 2026.

Twenty-five studies with 94,119 participants were included, most of high quality. Alcohol showed no overall link, but it pointed opposite ways by disease stage. Tea linked to lower risk, with a hazard ratio of 0.72 at 295 g per week in their modelling. Coffee helped only at very high intake. Heavy artificially sweetened drink intake raised the risk of the proliferative stage. Sugary drinks, juice, and yogurt showed no clear links.
pmc-13320034:
Karla E Lopez and colleagues explore, in 2026, how two cell proteins cover for each other when colon cancer cells face DNA damage. Caspase-2 can help or hinder tumour growth depending on context, and its partnership with the guard protein p53 was unclear. High caspase-2 levels tracked with worse survival in colon cancer patients.

In a colon cancer cell line, losing either protein alone barely changed cell cycle arrest. Losing both slowed growth, lengthened one cell cycle phase and weakened a DNA repair route. Each loss triggered more of the other protein, showing direct compensation. A second cell line copied the pattern only when a growth pathway was switched on. The authors suggest blocking both proteins together could seriously hamper colon cancer growth.
pmc-13320334:
Tomáš Radovnický and co-authors compare scope washing with standard drain care for blood pooled inside the brain in a 2026 matched study. Bleeding into the brain inner spaces kills often and heals poorly, and drains alone clog, infect, and keep people in intensive care for long spans. A scope wash that rinses clots out under direct view was set against drain care alone in matched pairs.

Forty six adults split evenly, matched by age, coma score, and clot load at entry. The wash cut clot load by about two thirds in the counts reported and more than halved drain days and intensive care days next to drains alone. Fewer wash patients needed a lasting shunt, and function scores at ninety days ran clearly better. A random trial should test the gain next.
pmc-13320434:
Xiaolin Tan and co-authors build a cloaked mineral particle for sepsis care in a 2026 mouse study. Sepsis is a body wide overreaction to infection that floods tissues with harmful oxygen forms, skews immunity, and fails organs. Their particle uses a cerium mineral that soaks up those forms as a core, loads a broad germ killer inside, and wears immune cell skin as a coat.

The coat helps the particle dodge immune patrols, home to kin cells, and soak up bacterial toxin on contact. Dish tests showed strong germ kill, toxin capture, and swelling calm. In mice with gut puncture sepsis, the particle cut swelling signals in blood and organs, eased liver, kidney, and gut harm, and lifted survival while guarding cell power houses.
pmc-13320534:
Jianing Fan and co-authors report a 2026 hospital study on closing a small heart opening in people with migraine. The opening, a patent foramen ovale, sits between the upper heart chambers. Standard tubes can struggle to pass a tiny shunt, so the team tested a Swartz sheath support method to steady the route.

Among 285 patients treated from 2020 to 2022, 82 had the support method and none had surgery linked harm. Headache relief and full stop rates were much alike with or without the method, though total migraine burden fell more in the support group before weighting. After fair weighting, outcomes matched, marking the method as a safe option for hard cases.
pmc-13321034:
Kazumi Kubota and colleagues link social network size to mental health in older Japanese adults in a 2026 survey study. Social ties support healthy ageing, but nationwide proof on network size was thin. Data came from the 2024 Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey, with 6786 respondents aged 65 to 84 years.

Overall, 11.8 percent reported a poor mental health day in the past month, and 1.9 percent had severe distress on the K6 scale in the survey. Smaller networks went with worse outcomes in a step by step pattern. The lowest network group had far higher odds of moderate and severe distress than the highest group, even after wide checks. Keeping older adults connected looks protective.
pmc-13322934:
Kai Lin and co-authors link a combined inflammation and nutrition index to diabetic foot ulcer severity, in a 2026 hospital study. They analysed 1,221 patients with type 2 diabetes and foot lesions admitted to a Wenzhou hospital centre between January 2020 and January 2025, grading ulcers with the Wagner system.

The index, called NPAR, joins neutrophil share with albumin level. Higher values tracked higher ulcer grades, longer stays, higher costs and more surgery. Risk rose in a dose-like pattern across quarters of the index, and climbed sharply once values passed a threshold near 21.4 in their modelling. The link held after wide adjustment, leading the authors to propose NPAR as a cheap severity signal.
pmc-13323234:
Scott James Ramsay and colleagues analyse mental health service use by Canadian children during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 study of the CHILD cohort. Survey data covered 1,554 parent-child pairs between January 2021 and March 2022, with service use reported for a 15-month span.

About 17 percent of the analysis group reported using mental health services or supports in that period. Missed school, recent worry and a chronic health condition each raised the odds of use after adjustment, while strong pre-pandemic mental health ratings lowered them. Receiving pandemic income support linked to lower use. The authors note similar worry effects among children with chronic conditions.
pmc-13325034:
Mia Hollekim, Lucy Smith, and Priscilla Erickson compare cold hardening in the invasive African fig fly with six other fruit fly species in a 2026 study. Zaprionus indianus has spread across eastern North America, but winter cold may cap its range.

Flies were held at 10, 15, or 25 °C for four days, then exposed to minus 5 °C for set times. The invader matched other widespread species in basic cold tolerance and gained protection after time at 15 °C. Its hardening beat that of tropical species yet lagged the strongest widespread ones. Survival curves fed estimates of the exposure time that kills half the flies. Cold winters may indeed fence in this invader.
pmc-13325734:
Sadaf Ataei-Alamdari and colleagues review pairing probiotics with bacteria-killing viruses against drug-resistant infections in a 2026 article. Resistant germs were tied to 4.71 million deaths in 2021 and could reach 10 million a year by 2050 on current trends.

Probiotics shore up the host microbe community while phages strike target pathogens directly, so the pair attacks on two fronts. The review weighs how the two interact at the molecular level, their safety records, and their fit for clinic use. Hurdles include product formulation, delivery to the infection site, and regulation. The authors frame the pairing as a tailored, microbiome-friendly route for the post-antibiotic era.
pmc-13327934:
Guo Li and co-authors test a CT sign for blocked central veins in dialysis patients in a 2026 study. Backup vessel routes hint at stenosis, and the team checked one route, the lateral thoracic pathway, on low-dose scans. Records covered 355 patients with kidney failure, split by catheter, fistula, or graft access.

The pathway sign appeared in 54.4 percent of scans against 12.1 percent for visible chest varices on exam, and both signs ran far higher in patients with stenosis. The CT sign caught over nine in ten stenosis cases in each access group, with sensitivity near 0.939 to 0.956 across them, far above the exam sign. A plain low-dose scan may thus flag vein blockage early.
pmc-13328034:
Jinxia Hao and co-authors test whether a B-cell drug in transplant conditioning prevents Epstein-Barr virus after stem cell transplant in a 2026 study. With modern CMV prevention in place, EBV infection has grown more common after half-matched transplants. Records covered 100 patients with acute leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome, 25 of whom received rituximab before transplant.

Within one year, EBV in the blood appeared in 4.00 percent of the rituximab group against 22.67 percent of controls, and acute graft-versus-host disease also ran lower, at 28 percent against 50.67 percent in that comparison. The rituximab group had received the drug for donor antibodies, so groups were not randomized, yet the signal supports testing the shield in planned trials.
pmc-13328434:
Yingru Wu and co-authors probe a fatigue model in rats for brain chemistry clues in a 2026 study. Chronic fatigue syndrome brings exhaustion that rest does not lift plus foggy thinking, and the calming cytokine TGF-β1 may play a part. Rats underwent ten days of repeated sleep deprivation with short rests, then behavior and tissue tests.

Fatigued rats moved about as much as controls in daytime but showed more anxiety-like behavior and far weaker spontaneous alternation in a Y-maze, a sign of dulled working memory. Their prefrontal cortex held more TGF-β1, while blood and striatum levels stayed level between groups. A brain-local rise, not a body-wide one, may track mental fatigue, the authors propose.
pmc-13329234:
Mantu Jain and colleagues reply in 2026 to comments on their trial of bowel preparation before lower spine surgery. The trial tested cleaning the bowel with antibiotics and probiotics to speed gut recovery after surgery from the back. The reply agrees that no clear benefit was shown.

Key recovery marks, such as first wind, bowel sounds, and first stool, were alike with and without preparation. All cases of stalled bowel action arose in the prepared group, and low blood pressure after surgery was also more common there. The authors note that fluid shifts and salt imbalance may explain slower recovery. They support choosing bowel preparation case by case for short one or two level surgery, not as routine.
pmc-13330234:
Yixiao Zhang and co-authors review the balance of immune messenger proteins in health and disease in a 2026 article. Cytokines that drive swelling and those that calm it must stay in dynamic balance for immune replies to stay apt. Feedback loops tune the strength and length of each reply.

When balance breaks, swelling signals can cascade, calm signals can fall short, and gene control can warp. The review links such breaks to sepsis, psoriasis, joint and bowel disease, and cancer, shaped by infection, autoimmunity, and tumour settings. Care options covered include antibody drugs, Janus kinase blockers, dual-target antibodies, and cell therapy. Gains, risks, and next steps are weighed for precision immune care.
pmc-13330734:
Ahmad Abdulhadi and a large team review new tuberculosis tests in a 2026 article. Tuberculosis infected 10.8 million people in the cited global counts, with millions of cases missed each year. Searches across three databases covered studies from 2019 to 2024, with quality checks by standard tools.

In total, 25 studies entered the pool, with group sizes from 100 to 6,520 people in the reported range. Approaches spanned molecular tests, biomarker methods, and artificial intelligence tools, with cartridge molecular tests most common. Pooled sensitivity came to 0.79 and specificity to 0.93 in the values given, though spread between studies was very high. New tests hold promise, the authors conclude, with field hurdles still to solve.
pmc-13330834:
Bhumi Patel and team present a sparfloxacin and 4-aminosalicylic acid salt. Their 2026 crystal structure paper covers sparfloxacinium 4-aminosalicylate, where two sparfloxacin and two 4-aminosalicylic acid units link through N-H···O bonds, forming an R44(12) ring. Fluoroquinolones are broad-spectrum antibiotics with good oral uptake and wide body spread, killing Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and salt-making changes drug traits.

In the crystal, dense strong intra- and inter-unit bonding appears. The cation-anion pair links through an N-H···O bonded ring motif with mirror partners. It forms between the piperazine NH2 group of the cation and the carboxylate group of the anion, with rings further joined through C-H···O bonding. Inner ring motifs from the hydroxy group and nearby oxygen in 4-aminosalicylic acid stay, matching other known sparfloxacin salts. The analysis adds a characterized salt to drug crystal engineering.
pmc-13331034:
Erick R. Guerra Bocanegra and team reported laparoscopic and open repair of an intercostal abdominal hernia. Their 2026 case paper presents a 53-year-old man with growing bulging of the left lateral abdominal wall. Intercostal hernias are rare thoracoabdominal wall defects, and CT scan with the Valsalva maneuver showed disruption of the left outer oblique muscle with uneven muscles matching a hernia defect.

Surgery went well using a combined laparoscopic and open approach. The case highlights dynamic imaging for spotting it, since how the defect looks under strain shows the disruption, and a tailored surgical plan for complex lateral abdominal wall defects. By mixing keyhole and open methods, the team fixed a rare defect that neither approach alone would suit as well. The report adds a combined-approach repair to the sparse reports on intercostal hernias, guiding surgeons facing similar thoracoabdominal wall defects.
pmc-13331134:
Gabriela Nieva and colleagues study early immune cell activation in mouse models of TDP-43 disease in a 2026 report. TDP-43 clumping marks diseases such as motor neuron disease and frontotemporal dementia. Two gene-switch mouse lines were compared after one month of altered protein expression: one with normal human protein, one with protein stuck outside the nucleus.

Microglia patterns differed by brain area and by model in the staining results. The normal-protein line showed swelling microglia in cortex and dentate areas with simpler branching. The stuck-protein line showed denser microglia in hippocampus zones. Astrocyte water channel placement also slipped near vessels in that line. Early glial shifts may shape area weakness, the authors argue.
pmc-13333334:
Zishi Liu and colleagues characterize a 2026 East Asian cohort with CNGA1-associated retinitis pigmentosa, seeking endpoints for gene therapy trials. The multicenter, retrospective cohort study reviewed medical records for age at onset, symptoms, best-corrected visual acuity, ultra-widefield retinal imaging, spectral-domain OCT, full-field electroretinography, full-field stimulus threshold, multiluminance mobility testing, and static perimetry. Main outcomes included molecular findings, acuity decline rate, stimulus threshold, mobility score, retinal sensitivity, and image findings.

The cohort included 57 patients with mean age about forty-two years. Eighteen disease-causing CNGA1 variants were found, eleven of them novel, with the c.253delC variant predominant in both Chinese and Korean cohorts at about sixty-nine percent allele frequency. Fundus autofluorescence patterns are detailed in the full paper. The study gives trial designers a natural history baseline and candidate endpoints for gene therapy in this inherited retinal disease.
pmc-13333434:
Mahmoud Obaid and co-authors built a two-step deep learning pipeline for spotting breast cancer on mammograms in a 2026 study aimed at low-resource regions such as Palestine. There, breast cancer makes up over 34 percent of women's cancers, while scanners, specialists, and budgets run short.

First, a U-Net model with a VGG16 backbone, trained on 2,206 mammograms from the CBIS-DDSM collection, outlines suspicious lesions, reaching an overlap score of 0.70 and a Dice score of 0.74 on 576 held-out images. Second, a VGG16 classifier pre-trained on everyday images judges the cut-out regions as harmless or malignant. Tested only on outside data, 34 Palestinian hospital patients never used in training, it reached 91 percent accuracy with an AUC of 0.97, beating ResNet50 at 85 percent and MobileNet at 82 percent. The authors call it a promising proof of concept needing validation on a larger local set before deployment.
pmc-13333734:
Fanantenana Raholiarimanana and co-authors ran a 2026 mediation analysis of public works participation, home water and hygiene, and child diet in southern Madagascar. Child undernutrition there is made worse by weak water and hygiene systems.

The team combined the 2018 Madagascar Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey with 2021 survey data mapped by place. Instrumental variable methods within a potential-outcomes model handled the fact that families choosing the HIMO public works program may differ from others. Participation was linked to better home access to improved hygiene and water, and the analysis estimated how much of the diet link runs through those home gains. The results help officials judge whether workfare programs can support child growth indirectly through healthier homes.
pmc-13336434:
Chih-Ying Huang and co-authors slipped chiral molecules between catalyst layers to make oxygen evolution spin-selective in a 2026 electrochemistry study. Splitting water efficiently matters for green hydrogen, and electron spin turns out to steer the reaction's energy path.

Phenylalanine, a chiral amino acid, was intercalated into cobalt-iron layered double hydroxide, widening the layer gap and imprinting chirality. Through the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect, the hybrid polarized electron spins and favored forming triplet oxygen along a lower-energy route. It reached the benchmark current at an overpotential of 245 millivolts, beating its achiral twin with faster charge transfer. In situ spectroscopy and nanoscale electrochemical mapping traced the behavior to the chiral interface, suggesting a general design trick for spin-aware catalysts.
pmc-13336534:
Niloofar Eshaghian and colleagues study 2026 the link between a food-based swelling index (FDII) and breast cancer odds in Iranian women. No study has yet looked at the link between FDII and breast cancer odds. This study tested that link in Iranian women.

This population case-control study enrolled 350 new breast cancer cases confirmed by lab tests. The 700 controls matched cases by age and social and money status. FDII scores came from what people ate. A positive link tied FDII to breast cancer odds, with an odds ratio of 1.38 and a 95 percent range of 1.01 to 1.88 in this sample. Women in the top third of FDII scores were 1.52 times likelier to have breast cancer than those in the lowest third. The odds ratio was 1.52, with a 95 percent range of 1.05 to 2.18, after taking other factors into account. The same positive link was seen among postmenopausal women.
pmc-13336734:
Mengxin Mu and co-authors build a heat-based cancer vaccine platform in a 2026 study using a stabilized radical anion. Light-heated tumor killing can train body-wide immunity, but tumors often defend themselves against that training. Their nanoparticles pack a dye called terrylene diimide inside a carrier, locking its active charged form in place.

Set into an injectable gel, the particles stay in the tumor, soak up tumor markers freed by heated cell death, and add immune-stimulating effect. In mice, laser switching at the main tumor destroyed it and sparked responses that slowed distant tumors too. pmc-13336834:
Toru Taharabaru and co-authors exploit sliding rings to target the liver in a 2026 drug delivery study. The standard liver homing tag uses a costly three-armed sugar design. Their carrier instead threads sugar-tagged rings onto a polymer axle, where the rings can rotate and slide freely.

pmc-13337034:
Jun Shen and colleagues found a three-protein control module that helps rice and Arabidopsis survive drought, in a 2026 genetics study. A CRISPR screen of rice mutants turned up osdt2, a weak-drought line lacking the zinc-finger protein OsDT2, while extra OsDT2 made plants far more drought-hardy. A third partner, OsNF-YC4, joins both proteins and helps guide them to the OsLEA3 promoter. pmc-13337434:
Arpita Chowdhury and co-authors mine a paddy-field bacterium for antioxidant and anticancer compounds in a 2026 study. Actinobacteria are rich sources of useful metabolites, and rice fields favor pigment makers. Their yellow Streptomyces strain, taken from Meghalaya soil, was profiled by microscopy and chemical analysis.

pmc-13337634:
Rakesh Kumar Sahoo and colleagues pool studies of AI listening for tuberculosis in cough sounds in a 2026 meta-analysis of the systematic review literature. TB remains the deadliest infectious disease, and diagnosis is hardest where resources are thinnest. The team searched five databases for studies from January 1, 2009, to December 31, 2024, and checked bias with a dedicated tool.

pmc-13339134:
Pengxi Chen and colleagues build complex sugar chains on proteins by a chemoenzymatic route in a 2026 study. Natural glycoproteins mix many sugar forms, so pure samples for study are scarce. Branched N-glycans with several arms are especially hard to assemble evenly.

Sulfate on one sugar also guided enzyme action on a neighbor as reported. The method yields varied, defined glycans for probing how exact sugar patterns affect protein behavior.
pmc-13339734:
Christian Rosendal and colleagues scan bone and joints in controlled acromegaly in a 2026 study. Excess growth hormone deforms joints and weakens bone even after hormone levels normalize. Seventeen patients with long-controlled disease were matched to seventeen controls.

High-resolution scans of hand joints, shin, and wrist plus bone hardness and spine checks were used. Patients averaged 61.8 years old with 13.1 years of disease as reported. Joint spaces were wider, spine deformities far more common at 88 percent versus 47 percent in the reported counts, and spongy bone density lower. pmc-13339834:
Jingsheng Xie and colleagues automated secretome profiling in 2026 to read proteins cells release, a dynamic window on cell state that can be sampled without harming cells. Old methods needed over 2 millilitres, covered limited protein depth, and processed fewer than 30 samples a day. Their workflow pairs optimised sample prep with magnetic bead proteomics.

pmc-13341434:
B cells take center stage in a 2026 review by Yaru Liu's team on immune recovery after lung transplant. Long-term success stays limited by chronic rejection and infection, and B cells matter by making antibodies, showing antigens, and releasing cytokines.

Injury at surgery, infections, and drugs such as tacrolimus each reshape B cell conduct across recovery phases. Single-cell sequencing and receptor profiling now track these shifts closely. The authors see these tools enabling immune checks fitted to each patient rather than blanket drug pressure.
pmc-13341934:
Half of palliative cancer patients screen depressed, in a 2026 meta-analysis by Han-Yu Deng and colleagues. Twenty-nine studies covering 6,054 patients with advanced cancer in palliative care were pooled from seven databases searched to April 2026, using self-report instruments.

The pooled prevalence landed at 50.9%, with a wide confidence interval from 41.2 to 60.5%. Estimates swung by study design and by which questionnaire was used, and overall heterogeneity stayed extremely high even after subgroup work. The authors urge services to adopt suitable screening tools and act on results, since emotional distress in this group is the rule, not the exception.
pmc-13342434:
Thomas J. Altree and Robert J. Adams reviewed multi night sleep apnoea testing in 2026, arguing a single night can mislead. Sleep varies night to night even in sound sleepers, and obstructive sleep apnoea severity, measured by the apnoea hypopnoea index counting airflow drops per hour, also varies. Multi night testing improves diagnostic accuracy, and emerging multi night devices offer practical advantages but need further validation. The review weighs benefits and limits of repeated testing for a common disorder where one night may understate or overstate severity. Clinicians gain guidance on when extra nights change management.
pmc-13343134:
Muhammad Waheed Iqbal and co-authors study greener extraction of polyphenols from the king oyster mushroom Pleurotus eryngii in 2026. Mushroom processing throws away bases, stalks, and damaged fruiting bodies that still hold useful phenolic compounds, yet tough fungal cell walls make those compounds hard to pull out with standard methods.

The team pairs ultrasound with deep eutectic solvents, a lower-impact solvent class, and tunes the process for the best yield. Extracts then face tests of antioxidant and antifungal activity to judge practical value. Turning processing waste into a source of health-linked compounds could serve food and nutraceutical makers while cutting the footprint of mushroom production.
pmc-13343234:
Yi Ren and colleagues tested cone implants by computer in 2026 for large bone gaps from weak bone shin fractures. A model of a fake medium shin bone was used, with six gap patterns and 50 millimetre cemented stems under walking and stair loads. Cone support gaps of 0, 16, and 32 percent and four bone strength levels were varied.

Gap healing limits from 0 to 50 micrometres judged bone to implant contact, with extra 100 millimetre long stems for very weak bone. At a 50 micrometre limit, worst gaps at 32 percent unsupported reached best contact in set patterns. The models guide cone choice for fragile bone gaps.
pmc-13343834:
Janelle Maskell and co-authors report, in a 2026 letter, two Australian cases where a gonorrhea test fired falsely on a harmless throat bacterium. Both men were symptom-free screening patients in Tasmania whose throat swabs tested positive on the Abbott Alinity m assay, yet a second platform said negative.

Culture grew Neisseria meningitidis from both swabs, and retesting pure colonies reproduced the false positive on Alinity while other assays mostly stayed negative. The cases warn labs that single-gene tests can misread throat samples, where the harmless cousin commonly lives, and confirm with a second target.
pmc-13343934:
Minghan Guan and co-authors probe how a common gut germ may feed pancreatic cancer growth in 2026. Enterococcus faecalis turns up enriched in pancreatic tumor tissue, yet its active role was undefined, so the team grew the bacterium alongside pancreatic cancer cells and watched the signaling that followed.

The bacterium also raised reactive oxygen species inside cancer cells, which Toll-like receptors may sense on the path to EGFR firing; scavenging those molecules or blocking the receptors calmed the effect. The chain offers fresh diagnostic and treatment targets against microbe-driven tumor growth.
pmc-13344134:
Monika Gautam and colleagues studied placenta changes in 2026 in anaemic mothers in India. Anaemia is a major global health problem there, driven by low dietary iron, blood disorders, nutrient gaps, and infections such as malaria, HIV, and hookworm. Low oxygen from anaemia triggers blood vessel and structural changes in the placenta, potentially harming mother and fetus.

Placentae from anaemic mothers often show growth, with increased placenta weight relative to fetal weight, plus infarcts and calcium deposits from inadequate blood flow leading to tissue death. The study links placenta changes with maternal anaemia severity and fetal outcomes. The findings link maternal nutrition to placenta health and birth outcomes.
pmc-13347634:
Miguel F. Altamirano-Muratalla and co-authors run a pilot biodiesel plant on power from its own blended fuel, in an engineering study from 2026. A 30 kW diesel generator burning diesel-biodiesel mixes fed heat and motors for a 1,000-litre batch plant that makes 100 batches a year. Savings were scored by a national cogeneration method.

Blends with 20, 25, and 30 percent biodiesel each passed the efficient mark, saving 10.8, 16.4, and 21.9 percent of primary energy in the reported order. Smoke haze fell steeply as biodiesel share rose, reaching a 53.3 percent cut at the richest blend, while carbon monoxide also dropped and nitrogen oxides held near steady. Cleaner self-power looks workable at pilot scale.
pmc-13348034:
Jun-Oh Min and colleagues trace human black carbon in Antarctic fjords, in a field study published in 2026. Water and mud from Marian Cove and Maxwell Bay held low levels of dissolved black carbon. Chemical marks pointed to local fossil burning as the main source. They did not point to aged plant smoke blown in from far away.

Mixing models put the fossil share rising 2.7-fold across the study years, from 6 percent in 2019 to 16 percent in 2023, as tourism and station work came back after COVID limits. Mud traps caught steady soot rain each day. That soot buried better than bulk carbon and dated back thousands of years. Fjords thus lock away human soot for the long term.
pmc-13350034:
Ceyhun Açarı and a Turkish team compared mouth health and gum bacteria in children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis against healthy children in a 2026 study. Sixty patients and 26 controls had their teeth scored for decay and fillings and their gums graded for cleanliness, swelling, and bleeding.

Sequencing plaque from under the gumline found similar overall diversity, though Porphyromonas and Peptostreptococcus appeared more often in patients. Painful or stiff joints can make brushing hard, so these findings argue for closer dental care in this group.
pmc-13350434:
Alicia G. Dugan and co-authors ran a participatory design study in 2026 where employed breast cancer survivors built their own peer support intervention. Among millions of working-age survivors, jobs bring income and normality, yet many feel cut off socially, which threatens staying at work.

Six survivors met researchers for seven hour-long sessions, naming three roots of disconnection: changed self-image, symptoms driving withdrawal, and unhelpful reactions from others. They drafted and scored three intervention models on reach, effect, cost, and barriers. A package of written materials, a website, a peer-led group, and an online forum won out, designed by the people who would use it.
pmc-13350534:
Rongqin Zhang and colleagues compared two scans for finding leftover thyroid tissue after surgery in a 2026 study of 505 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer receiving radioiodine therapy. Judging the remnant accurately decides how ablation treatment is planned.

One scan used technetium tracer, the other a small diagnostic dose of iodine-131, each paired with three-dimensional imaging across eight neck regions. Sensitivity, accuracy measures, and links to blood hormone and antibody levels were compared against the full treatment scan. Patients had no spread to nodes or beyond, keeping the comparison clean. A cheaper or clearer pre-check could spare patients mistimed or needless treatment.
pmc-13350634:
Omar Abdalla and co-authors weighed in 2026 yttrium-90 radiation segmentectomy using resin microspheres against microwave ablation. The focus was early primary liver cancer. Glass microsphere radiation and ablation show like tumour response and survival in early disease. Radiation may give a progression-free gain. Yet resin microspheres had not been directly weighed against ablation.

Sixty patients with stage one solitary tumours were studied in look-back. Tumours were no larger than four centimetres. Treatment ran from 2016 to 2024. Efficacy, progression, and survival were weighed between the two paths. The weigh-up fills a specific gap for interventional radiologists. It guides picks between internal radiation and thermal ablation for small, early liver tumours.
pmc-13352434:
S E Barnes and M R Maxwell present a 2026 perspective on the Biology through Art teaching project. Drawing has long supported science work, from forming ideas to sharing results, yet art tasks stay rare in undergraduate biology. Barriers include student worry about drawing skill, teacher unfamiliarity with art methods, time pressure, and scaling to large classes.

Course tasks built for organismal and integrative biology classes use artistic work to drive active learning and idea synthesis. The authors share ways around each barrier, including flexible models that fit different class sizes. Working with art faculty is part of the approach. Their aim is graduates who are scientifically sharp, creative, and engaged.
pmc-13353534:
Annie Wang and colleagues review hydroponic teaching platforms at mainly undergraduate colleges in 2026. Many such colleges teach plant biology and environmental science without greenhouses or growth chambers. At their college, commercial and home-built hydroponic units were fitted into existing teaching labs.

Faculty, lab staff, and undergraduate work-study students maintained the systems together. Steady indoor conditions allowed year-round growth, repeated student experiments, and hands-on training in plant care and biotechnology. Course-based research experiences grew around the units. pmc-13354434:
Abdihakim Ali Nour and Sakarie Mustafe Hidig argue that hospitals miss delirium far too often, in a 2026 letter to the editor. Delirium is a sudden break in attention, awareness, and thinking that strikes many inpatients, above all older adults and the critically ill. Rates run 10 to 30 percent on general wards and up to 50 to 70 percent in intensive care, passing 80 percent among ventilated patients.

pmc-13356734:

pmc-13357334:

pmc-13358534:

pmc-13358734:

The authors ask whether both lungs can be kept open, at least in part, during such surgery. They weigh how collapse, the breathing machine, and a dip in immune defenses combine to harm patients. pmc-13358834:

pmc-13359934:

pmc-13362634:

pmc-13362734:

pmc-13363434:

pmc-13364434:

pmc-13369034:

pmc-13369234:

pmc-13370134:

pmc-13371734:

pmc-13373234:

pmc-13373834:

pmc-13374734:

pmc-13375834:

pmc-13376134:

pmc-13378134:

pmc-13378534:

pmc-13378734:

pmc-13380934:

pmc-13382834:

pmc-13383934:

pmc-13386734:

pmc-13387834:
Moin and colleagues reported a new drug candidate in 2026 that switches on AdipoR1, a receptor for the hormone adiponectin, to fight muscle wasting. Muscle loss rides along with many long-term diseases, yet no approved drug treats it. Earlier attempts stalled for lack of compounds that hit this receptor alone with a clean safety profile.

A screening test in engineered cells picked out the salt CDRI-1709S as a strong, selective switch for AdipoR1, active at very low doses. In mouse muscle cells it turned on energy and sugar-handling pathways, pushed young muscle cells to mature into fibers. Shielded fibers from wasting caused by steroids, inflammatory signals, and starvation, in part by silencing two wasting genes. In rats, it eased muscle loss after steroid treatment and after nerve cutting. The authors present it as a first-in-class lead for a condition with no drug options.
pmc-13389134:
Lexy Farrington and co-authors systematically review, in 2026, how foot and ankle factors may raise the risk of knee ligament tears that occur without contact. These anterior cruciate ligament injuries are common in sport and often lead to long-term knee problems for athletes.

Working to standard review guidelines, the team searched three databases for English studies from 2010 to 2025 and kept 48 of more than 1700 reports screened. About two-thirds of the kept studies linked some foot or ankle trait, landing pattern, or past ankle injury to higher risk. Sports medicine readers gain a sorted evidence base for designing prevention training that starts from the ground up, plus a clear view of where proof remains weak.
pmc-13390034:
Pelin Kurt leads a 2026 laboratory study asking whether artemisinin can lessen acute liver damage from paracetamol overdose. Paracetamol is a widely used pain and fever drug, but overdose is a leading cause of liver failure, and the standard antidote has clear limits.

In a paracetamol injury model, the team measured liver enzymes, markers of oxidative stress, and inflammatory gene signals, and examined liver tissue under the microscope. Paracetamol sharply raised the injury enzymes, setting the baseline against which artemisinin, a plant compound that fights cell stress and swelling, was judged. Drug researchers gain a well-ordered early test of a would-be protector. The proof spans blood tests, gene signals, and tissue checks. The work is a lab test, not a trial in sick people.
pmc-13390334:
Sungmin Kim's team shows that the kinase VprBP drives prostate cancer by switching off growth-regulating genes through phosphorylation of histone H2A at threonine 120. VprBP is overexpressed in prostate cancer cells, but how it picks substrates in each cancer type was unknown.

Blocking its kinase activity reactivated the silenced genes and slowed cancer cell growth. Screening derivatives of an earlier inhibitor, B32B3, yielded B0045, a second-generation compound far more potent at blocking the histone mark and gene switching off. B0045 also curbed tumour growth in mouse xenografts, marking it as a promising prostate cancer lead.
pmc-13391134:
Pablo A Slullitel leads a 2026 investigation of the gut-joint axis in hip osteoarthritis, asking whether microbes and their products inside the joint help drive its inflammation. Gut imbalance and leakage of microbial material into the body have been proposed as contributors to chronic joint disease.

In a prospective group of 48 patients having hip replacement, the team collected joint fluid, cartilage, and socket tissue from twenty patients with primary hip osteoarthritis and from non-arthritic controls. They characterised microbial signatures and inflammatory metabolic pathways in the joint itself. Orthopaedic researchers gain direct tissue evidence for or against a gut-joint link in the hip, rather than inference from blood or stool alone.
pmc-13391434:
Chetan Modgi and colleagues compare, in 2026, denture status, unmet dental need, nutrition risk, and quality of life among older adults in rural and urban Pune district, India. Tooth loss and poor prosthetic care can impair chewing, nutrition, and social wellbeing, especially where services are scarce.

The cross-sectional study assessed older residents in both settings for dentures in place, care still needed, food intake state, and life quality as oral health shapes it. Dental planners gain a rural-urban contrast for a fast-ageing population. It shows where denture provision would most improve eating and daily life. Appearance alone is not the point.
pmc-13392234:
Jingyu Zhan's team caught five inward-facing shapes of fish Abcb4, a multi-drug pump twin of human P-glyco-protein, to explain how one pump spots many drugs. The human pump's broad-taste workings was unresolved, and the fish protein, which defends against water-borne poisons, showed comparable ATP enzyme activity.

Cryo-electron scope work showed a global open-and-close motion past published P-glyco-protein shapes, coupled to helix movements that loosen the target pocket. Structures bound to blockers tariquidar and elacridar and target vincristine support odd protein-ligand links behind broad drug recognition.
pmc-13392634:
Sri Hastuti and colleagues compared three treatments drawn from umbilical cord tissue in rats with epilepsy triggered by the drug pilocarpine. One arm received the stem cells themselves. The other arms received the broth of substances the cells release, or tiny parcels called exosomes shed by the cells. Thirty male rats were split into five groups, including healthy and untreated epilepsy controls. Doses went into a vein on three occasions after seizures were induced.

Animals given whole stem cells showed the least hippocampal damage, close to healthy levels, and relearned a water maze fastest. Two marker genes tied to synapse health and support-cell function also returned to near-normal values only in that group. The released broth helped moderately, while exosomes helped least. The ranking suggests the cells themselves do more than any single product they shed, at least in this model.
pmc-13393734:
Minhua Hu and eight colleagues compared two ways of harvesting bone from the iliac crest, the pelvis rim that supplies most graft bone, measuring harm at the donor site. Their newer approach preserves the crest's outer wall while taking the graft beneath it. One hundred one patients split almost evenly between the preserving technique and the conventional harvest, with blood loss, complications, pain scores over the first week, and daily function all recorded.

The preserving group bled less during surgery. Its complications ran at under half the usual rate, ten percent against about a quarter. Fluid collections, infection, and lingering pain made up their list. Pain scores and satisfaction with walking, stairs, and hip function matched between groups. The authors present crest preservation as a way to cut donor-site harm without costing patients function.
pmc-13393934:
Nadia Gulnaz and others pull together studies of mock drills for surgery leadership in a 2026 careful review. Lead skill and team skill are vital for safe surgery, yet mock drills are mostly used for hand skill, and their lead-skill gains were told in mixed ways.

With PRISMA rules, the review took in twelve studies with 430 people, mostly mixed teams of two to six, scored with two bias tools. It sums drill types, scoring frames, lead gains, and patient safety signs. Training chiefs gain one joined case for using mock drills to grow leaders, not just hands, in the surgery suite.
pmc-13394334:
Shariva S. Kariman and others test home scans done by mothers-to-be with live expert help in a 2026 forward study. Home scans with remote help could shore up hospital-at-home birth care, but ease of use and trust in the scans needed proof.

Mothers-to-be with plain single-baby pregnancies from week 24 to week 37 used a pocket scan tool at home for expert-led live scans twice a week, eight scans over 28 days. Ease was judged by scan capture, scan read, reader match, and tech snags, plus ease scores and a group talk. Birth teams gain proof that home scans can be safe and welcome.
pmc-13395834:
Haoran Huang and co-authors profile, in 2026, blood fats across the stages of ischemic stroke. Stroke care lacks early flags for diagnosis and outcome. The team read plasma fats in 223 stroke patients and 57 healthy controls with broad targeted tools. Fats were tracked across acute, healing, and chronic stages, and machine learning picked marker panels.

From 607 fats found, 54 differed between patients and controls in four clusters. A six-fat panel named stroke with near-perfect test scores. A second six-fat panel forecast outcome with strong scores too. Panels share one fat member. The authors offer the panels as candidate aids for stroke wards, pending wider proof.
pmc-13395934:
Isabeau Vermeulen and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on tiny particles called extracellular vesicles that brain cells shed into cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that bathes the brain and spine. Because these vesicles carry proteins, nucleic acids, and fats from the cells that made them, they may reveal brain disease without a tissue biopsy.

Vesicles from spinal fluid sit closer to the brain than those in blood, so their signals are less diluted by the rest of the body. The review weighs that promise against low yields, purity problems, and the lack of shared isolation methods. It argues that standard steps plus combined molecular profiling could turn these vesicles into useful tests for disorders of the central nervous system.
pmc-13396034:
Stijn Verschueren and co-authors tracked mammals in a burned savanna landscape in eastern Namibia, in a 2026 study of how wildlife reacts in the first months after fire. Camera traps and temperature loggers covered 650 square kilometers, spanning burned ground, nearby zones, and unburned controls.

Six months of records, one before the fire and five after, fed a model of where 31 medium and large species were present. Burned areas ran hotter and drier at ground level. The authors traced how the wider community, and groups sorted by diet and size, shifted across ground at different stages of regrowth, giving park managers an early picture of post-fire change.
pmc-13396234:
Linshan Wu and others offer UniBiomed, a base AI for body-scan reads tied to scan spots, in a 2026 paper. Clinic AI must be right and checkable, yet old models rarely gave a read while also pointing at the spot that proves it.

UniBiomed joins a word-and-image AI with a spot-cutting AI, trained on 27 million scan-spot-word triples to span many body tasks. It gives reads tied to cut-out spots, so doctors can check AI claims with their own eyes. The paper moves scan AI from black-box guess to proof-backed help.
pmc-13396534:
Dank and colleagues ran a randomized split-mouth trial in 2026 comparing two dental implant surfaces in patients with a history of gum disease. Each of 39 patients at three centers received both a hybrid implant, smooth near the gum and rougher below, and a moderately rough implant in the lower jaw. Standard X-rays tracked bone levels around each implant over the first year.

Thirty-six patients finished the study, and both implant types survived at the same rate, with the few losses failing to bond with bone at all. Bone level changes over the year did not differ between the two surfaces at any measured site around the implants. Because disease around implants often appears later, the team plans a three-year follow-up before drawing firm conclusions. For now, surface choice alone showed no early advantage in these higher-risk patients.
pmc-13396734:
Min Wei and others pin a thalamus-to-insula wire for pain-plus-worry in sugar nerve harm in a 2026 mouse study. Painful sugar nerve harm oft brings worry, but the wire that ties sore nerves to low mood was dim.

Brain-wide glow maps, virus tracers, fiber light reads, cell taps, and wire-specific spark and chem switches in a sugar-harm mouse model found stir-prone insula cells lit in worried sugar mice. Two-way switch of those cells flipped worry and touch soreness in step. The wire gives a sharp aim for pain-plus-worry care.
pmc-13396934:
Arnulf Soleng and co-authors tested 3,437 castor bean ticks from southern and southwestern Norway for the microbes they carry, in a 2026 survey. This tick species spreads the most serious tick-borne infections in Europe, and warming climates are pushing it into new ground.

The panel covered two viruses, tick-borne encephalitis virus and louping-ill virus, plus the Lyme disease bacterium. It also covered a blood parasite relative that attacks white cells, and two harmless tenants that live inside tick cells. Prevalence figures for each microbe, named by place, tell health services which infections to expect locally and give a baseline against which future spread can be measured.
pmc-13397734:
Li Wang and others test structured early rehabilitation for severe acute pancreatitis in a 2026 randomized controlled trial. Long bed rest causes deep deconditioning in these intensive care patients, yet structured rehab plans were little studied.

From 2019 to 2024, 400 intensive care patients were randomized evenly to a protocol-led multidisciplinary early rehab program or usual care. Hospital length of stay was the primary outcome, with intensive care stay, inflammatory marks, muscle strength, and longer-term function, quality of life, and survival as secondary outcomes. The trial gives intensive care teams proof for mobilizing even the sickest pancreatitis patients early.
pmc-13398134:
Haoran Liu and co-authors propose a plant-to-plant loop for breaking down plastic, using alfalfa and nanomaterials made from plants themselves. Their 2026 study tackles polyethylene, whose toughness forces a choice between harsh synthetic catalysts and slow plant cleanup. The plant-made particles serve as catalysts that sunlight and living plants can both drive.

Under ultraviolet light the particles degraded about 16.09 percent of polyethylene film in 28 days, and in soil beside growing alfalfa they cleared about 11.35 percent in 90 days, beating two commercial carbon rivals. Moving film placement changed rates, showing position and timing matter. Microbe and gene checks suggest the particles work with, not against, the soil community.
pmc-13399234:
Turon and colleagues replied in 2026 to critics of their earlier study on ventriculitis, an infection linked to a brain drain, after bleeding around the brain. Two letters had questioned the study's design, its handling of risk factors, and the possible effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. The reply walks through each concern.

The authors stress that their aim was the rate of drain-linked infection and its effect on outcomes, not the risk factors for placing a drain. Most patients had severe bleeding and fluid buildup that justified the drain under standard criteria, and none received clot-dissolving treatment through it. On the pandemic point, all patients were tested before intensive care entry and only negative cases were included. The reply also explains how delayed brain ischemia was told apart from other decline causes.
pmc-13399634:
Chen-Jian Peng and co-authors describe a modified way to reattach a torn lateral meniscus root inside the knee, in a 2026 surgical technique paper. The meniscus root anchors the cartilage ring that spreads load across the joint. Sound repair must restore the root to its anatomical footprint on the tibia.

Their method blends two established approaches. A transtibial tunnel is drilled at the footprint, but at only 2 millimeters wide instead of the usual 4.5, sparing bone and avoiding clashes with any cruciate ligament graft. An all-suture anchor's limbs are passed through the root at two points, forming a suture ball that sits on the meniscus surface and grips it. Those sutures are then drawn down the small tunnel and fixed with an Endobutton below the tibia. They present the construct as stable and minimally invasive.
pmc-13399934:
Stephane Lima Calixto and colleagues reviewed what happens to gut bacteria in rats and mice whose bile duct is tied off, the standard laboratory model of cholestasis, in this 2026 review. Following PRISMA methods, the team searched PubMed, Scopus, and Embase for bile duct ligation studies from 2020 to early 2025 that profiled the intestinal microbiome without testing treatments.

Twenty-two studies qualified, most using 16S rRNA sequencing. A consistent pattern emerged: ligation lowered microbial diversity in most studies, reshuffled community structure, and shifted the major phyla. Two organisms increased often enough that the authors read them as possible responses. The synthesis links this dysbiosis to a weaker gut barrier, more bacteria crossing into the body, and fiercer liver inflammation. Because nearly all the evidence is from animals, the authors caution that microbiome-based therapies for cholestasis still need proper human trials.
pmc-13400234:
Kirk Terada-Herzer and colleagues graded the fifty most-watched YouTube videos about clavicle fractures, in a 2026 study of online patient education. The team searched four fracture-related terms, took the fifty most-viewed English videos, and scored each with two independent reviewers. Scores used the JAMA benchmark for reliability, a four-point comprehensibility scale, and an eighteen-point checklist of what a complete clavicle fracture education should cover.

The verdict is that popularity and quality barely meet. The median completeness score was just 3 of 18 points, and the mean reliability score was 1.4, even though comprehensibility averaged a friendly 3.46 of 4. Physician-made videos scored significantly higher on reliability, while patient-made videos were significantly easier to understand, an awkward trade-off. The authors conclude that the YouTube content patients actually find is insufficient for the decisions clavicle fractures force.
pmc-13400534:
Maryam Zolnoori and a team present, in 2026, SpeechDETECT, a speech analysis pipeline meant to spot early cognitive decline from voice recordings. Brain scans and spinal fluid tests work well but are costly and hard to reach, especially in underserved areas. Speech offers a cheap, noninvasive signal.

The pipeline cleans recordings, extracts fine sound and timing features in short slices, selects the most useful ones and trains classifiers that can explain their calls. Tested on two English datasets, one built on a picture description task, its best model beat six rival toolkits on standard accuracy measures. The authors frame it as a step toward large-scale, explainable screening that clinics could run from short voice samples.
pmc-13400734:
Jasmin Walter and co-authors present, in 2026, FRED, a toolkit for creating and managing standardized metadata for omics research. Sharing raw data is now routine, but the descriptive metadata that make data reusable often lack standards. The toolkit follows the FAIR principles, which ask that data be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.
