Built around a flexible machine-readable file format, FRED guides users through dialog-based metadata creation, checks entries semantically and supports searching across files. It can connect to external systems and run as a self-hosted website. The team demonstrates the full workflow on a published single-nucleus RNA dataset, ending with export in a major repository submission format. No dedicated IT staff is required.
pmc-13401434:
Mohamed Boualane and colleagues present a 2026 report of two cases where a sinonasal mucocele, a mucus-filled cyst from a blocked sinus, expanded into the eye socket and pushed the eyeball outward. Mucoceles are benign, but steady growth can erode bone and threaten vision.

The first patient, a 34-year-old man, arrived with sudden eyeball protrusion, double vision, and reduced sight, and imaging showed a frontoethmoidal lesion extending into the orbit. The second, a 43-year-old woman, had slowly progressive protrusion with her vision intact, from a similar frontoethmoidal mucocele. Care differed: the first cyst regressed on its own, while the second needed surgery, and both patients did well. The authors stress imaging for diagnosis and early treatment to protect sight.
pmc-13401534:
Francesco Pera and co-authors carried out a 2026 cadaver study of guided dental implant placement in sockets right after tooth extraction, asking whether operator experience changes accuracy. Static computer-assisted surgery promises precision, but fresh extraction sockets are an awkward test bed.

Twenty teeth, incisors, premolars, and molars, were removed from two cadaver heads, and implants were planned digitally from cone beam CT and intraoral scans. Custom tooth-supported guides were printed. Two operators, one with over five years of experience and one with fewer, neither previously trained in guided surgery, placed twenty implants in total. Postoperative scans were overlaid on the plans to measure head, tip, and angle deviations. Accuracy at the implant head was similar between operators, near 1.3 versus 1.5 millimetres of deviation on average, with no significant difference.
pmc-13402234:
Jana Slovackova and colleagues compared two ways of growing glioblastoma organoids, small tumor models grown from patient tissue in the lab. One route keeps tissue fragments intact and cultures them; the other breaks tissue apart into single cells first. Using mass spectrometry, they compared the protein makeup of both model types, grown with or without growth factors, against the tumors they came from.

Fragment-grown organoids kept a wider set of matrix proteins tied to collagen building, vessel support, and cell-to-matrix signaling, and they matched the source tumors more closely overall. Broken-apart cultures leaned toward added basement membrane material and fast-growing, growth factor driven states. Both routes were technically steady in their own media. The message for cancer labs is blunt: how tissue is handled at the start reshapes the model, so protocol choice decides what a drug test really measures.
pmc-13402634:
Feyerabend and co-authors compare, in 2026, the electrical personality of neurons in two stations of the visual system, primary visual cortex and lateral prefrontal cortex, in the marmoset. Using patch-clamp records and structural reconstruction in slices from 51 marmosets of median age 5.08 years, they profiled excitatory, fast-spiking inhibitory, and non-fast-spiking inhibitory neurons in the upper layers of each area.

Of the recorded cells, 483 passed quality control, 269 from prefrontal cortex and 214 from visual cortex in the dataset. Excitatory and fast-spiking neurons fired broader action potentials in prefrontal cortex; prefrontal excitatory cells were less excitable while its fast-spiking cells were more excitable and burst more than visual counterparts. Those neurons also grew longer dendritic arbors, and its fast-spiking neurons showed more complex axons. A classifier distinguishing cell types reached 88.6 percent accuracy in marmoset tests. The authors frame neuronal diversity as a substrate of area specialization.
pmc-13402734:
Chen and co-authors explain, in 2026, why the world's great rare earth deposits cluster at the margins of ancient continent cores. They run high-pressure, high-temperature experiments on how light rare earth elements behave when carbonate-rich sediments are recycled into the Earth. Rare earths power magnets and devices, and carbonatite magmas host most primary deposits, yet their origin was unclear.

In the experiments, calcic carbonates concentrated the rare earths step by step during subduction, becoming their main carriers, and melting at higher pressure released rare-earth-rich melts. As those melts rose through the thick mantle beneath craton edges, precipitation of magnesite, itself very poor in rare earths, enriched the remaining melt. The enrichment reached up to 156 times the concentration of the starting sedimentary carbonates, matching natural ore-forming carbonatites. Their compilation showed carbonatite rare earth content rising with deposit tonnage, linking magma chemistry to reserve size.
pmc-13402834:
Fadi G Haddad and Hagop Kantarjian review how recent advances should reshape chronic myeloid leukemia treatment algorithms. Their 2026 review covers chronic-phase disease treated with BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitors and newer STAMP inhibitors, which block the cancer protein differently. Frontline choice depends on treatment goals, cost, disease risk, and other illnesses, yet guidance had lagged new options.

Reaching a complete cytogenetic response within a year tracks with normalized survival, while deeper molecular response may allow stopping therapy with possible treatment-free remission. Post-approval studies show lower, optimal biologic doses can match approved doses more safely, and dose reduction beats switching for most toxicities. For frontline failure, second- and third-line options now include ponatinib, asciminib, and investigational agents. The review challenges several established practices.
pmc-13402934:
Riffat Mehboob and colleagues run the first blood study of substance P and its receptor NK-1R in dengue fever, hunting for markers that explain the illness leaky vessels and inflammation. Both molecules regulate inflammation and vascular permeability in other viral infections, yet dengue work had never measured them. Forty diagnosed patients and 12 healthy controls gave serum for ELISA testing, alongside full blood counts.

Receptor levels came out far lower in patients, a mean of 0.57 against 2.681 in controls in the reported units, with a p value below 0.0001 for the gap. Substance P levels, by contrast, showed no significant difference between male and female patients. The authors link the receptor dip to the permeability, immune activation, and cytokine patterns of dengue, and propose NK-1R as a thread worth pulling in larger cohorts.
pmc-13403034:
Somayeh Mohamadi and a large team systematically review molecular diagnosis of Trichomonas vaginalis, a protozoan sexually transmitted infection that mostly hides without symptoms. Between 70 and 85 percent of infected men and women show few or no signs, yet the parasite links to pelvic inflammatory disease, cervical changes, and preterm delivery. The World Health Organization counts about 156 million new cases a year in people aged 15 to 49, more than chlamydia, gonorrhea, or syphilis.

Because most infections stay silent, laboratory detection decides control, and older wet-mount and culture methods miss many cases. The review weighs molecular tests, which amplify parasite DNA, for accuracy in both women and men. The authors aim their synthesis at laboratories in the resource-limited regions carrying most of the 154 million yearly cases there.
pmc-13403634:
Erlon Gabriel Rego de Andrade led a 2026 study of how nursing students view hidden tuberculosis infection after testing positive themselves. Thirty-seven students at a public university in Belém, Brazil, took part in one-on-one interviews. All had a positive skin test yet no signs of active disease.

Word-pattern software sorted their accounts into themes. Students drew on their own lives as they tried to work out where exposure may have happened. Many reflected on risk in clinics and classrooms alike. The authors call for joint work by health and school sectors, plus stronger basic care, to keep students safe.
pmc-13403734:
Hao Guo and co-authors reviewed aerogel gas sensors in 2026, sorting how their spongy build shapes sensing skill. Aerogels are feather-light solids full of pores, with huge inner surface area. Sensors built from them serve air checks, factory safety, and even breath-based disease clues.

The review covers metal oxide, sulfide, and carbon types, plus how each one detects gases. It benchmarks results for targets such as nitrogen oxides, ammonia, and aldehydes. Pore size and surface area link closely to speed and sharpness of response. Open work includes firmer design rules, tougher builds for damp air, and ways to make sensors at scale.
pmc-13404534:
Jacob Dairaghi and colleagues introduce Sof-T, a 2026 low-cost method for making hollow, branched gel structures shaped like body parts. Printing hollow tubes and branching shapes matters for models of blood vessels and airways. Existing bioprinting routes need pricey machines and many steps, which shuts out smaller labs.

Sof-T starts with a water-soluble printed template coated in hydrogel, meaning a soft water-rich gel. Ions spreading from the template set the gel skin, and the template then dissolves away. The team produced forked aorta models, some with bulges like aneurysms, plus branched windpipes and small hearts and bladders. They present the method as fast, cheap and workable with basic equipment.
pmc-13404634:
Eleanor Ferris and colleagues describe the UK FLAME study, a 2026 protocol to improve access to flat closure after mastectomy. Up to 40 percent of women with breast cancer need a mastectomy, and rebuilding the breast is routinely offered. Some women instead want the other breast removed so both sides sit flat and even, an option with patchy access in the United Kingdom.

Patients, clinicians and other stakeholders will build an agreed care pathway together. Development follows the Medical Research Council framework for complex interventions, with behaviour-change tools layered in. Women seeking flat symmetry often report feeling unsupported, while clinicians worry about later regret. The pathway aims to settle fair access and better outcomes for this group.
pmc-13404934:
Amey Salvi and colleagues study why overdose review teams in Indiana struggle to use population data, reporting in 2026. Fatality review teams normally examine single deaths in depth to shape local prevention. Case review alone cannot show wider risk patterns across a county.

A live dashboard was built to display trends at five touchpoints where services met people before an overdose. Researchers watched 26 team meetings in 11 counties over ten months and interviewed participants. They tracked when the dashboard appeared in discussion, whether its figures shaped recommendations and what blocked wider use. Tension between case storytelling and population statistics sits at the centre of their findings.
pmc-13405334:
Kate N Thomas and co-authors tell of a leg vessel injury that hid for 27 years, in a 2026 case report. A climbing accident in 1997 drove an ice axe into a man's thigh, silently joining an artery to a vein. Such a fistula lets high-pressure blood shortcut into the vein, straining the heart over time.

Now aged 74, the man reported two years of leg swelling, with varicose veins and a small old scar. Heart scans showed stretched chambers and high-output failure. Ultrasound revealed the fistula between the superficial femoral artery and the femoral vein. Tests also compared vessel widening in both legs to show long-term effects of the extra flow.
pmc-13405934:
Ákos Suhajda and colleagues pair a fungal toxin with a last-resort antibiotic against drug-resistant Pseudomonas, in 2026 lab work. The bacterium sits on the World Health Organization critical list for its resistance and hospital infections. Beauvericin, a toxin from fungi, had shown hints of boosting antibiotics.

Seven multidrug-resistant isolates faced colistin alone and with beauvericin at doses that alone did nothing measurable. In six of the seven strains, the toxin sharply strengthened colistin at the tested doses, cutting surviving growth. The effect varied by strain, the authors note. They frame beauvericin as a helper compound worth study, while flagging that its own toxicity needs care.
pmc-13406634:
Angeliki Margoni and co-authors review markers for a rare bone inflammation disease in a 2026 article. Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis causes sterile bone lesions, mostly in children, with no infection to blame and no validated blood marker to guide care. New evidence reframes it as a shared endpoint of several immune disturbances.

An inflammasome and interleukin-1 beta axis sits at the centre of the proposed mechanism, driving bone-eating cell activity. Standard markers like C-reactive protein perform poorly, the authors note. Whole-body MRI remains the main assessment tool, but pairing scans with molecular markers could sort patients better. Genetic and cytokine findings are gathered toward that goal.
pmc-13407434:
Carolin Schröder and co-authors, in 2026, compared two keyhole operations for repairing a caesarean scar defect, a pouch in the womb wall that can cause bleeding, pelvic pain, and infertility. At one German hospital, 28 women underwent either robot-assisted or standard keyhole repair between late 2019 and March 2026, and the team tracked symptoms, imaging, and later pregnancies.

No surgical complications occurred in either group. Among eight women trying to conceive, six achieved a live birth, split evenly between approaches. Robot-assisted cases showed clear shrinkage of the scar pouch and thicker remaining muscle after surgery, with similar but weaker trends in the smaller keyhole group. Most women reported symptom relief, especially for bleeding and pain. One later pregnancy involved scar separation, another a placenta attachment disorder.
pmc-13408134:
Maximilian H. Ganser and co-authors identify, in 2026, the self-assembling proteins behind the near-indestructible shells of tintinnid ciliates. These planktonic single-celled organisms have ornate housings that shrug off high heat and the strongest chemicals in sea and fresh water alike. Combining single-cell gene readouts with protein analysis of the shells themselves pinned down the building material.

The shell proteins form a brand-new family, named Tintinnidorin, found only in these ciliates. Their design, aromatic-rich chains with flexible unfolded segments strung around a folded sheet core, supports a string of talents. The talents include storage inside the cell, self-assembly outside it, wet adhesion, heat stability, and salt tolerance. A living, accessible system for learning how sequence becomes super-material, with biomaterial design as the intended beneficiary.
pmc-13408834:
Nico Sollmann and a Munich team ask in 2026 whether the neck muscles of headache patients carry a measurable signature of their disorder. Migraine and tension-type headache often come with neck pain, plausibly through shared wiring between neck and head pain circuits, yet no objective marker of muscle involvement exists. Seventy-one young adults, split between healthy controls and three headache groups, had their upper trapezius muscles scanned.

Magnetic resonance T2 maps, which brighten where tissue holds extra water, were mined for texture patterns beyond simple averages. Significant differences separated the headache groups from controls on several image-derived features, and statistical models linked those features to headache and neck pain characteristics alongside sleep and sport habits. The authors position muscle texture analysis as a candidate objective biomarker for the myofascial side of primary headaches, pending confirmation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13408934:
Chenshuo Wang and a food science team ask in 2026 whether the age of the brine in a pickle crock leaves a fingerprint on the chillies fermented in it. Brines in traditional production can be kept going for decades, and makers swear old brine makes better pickles. Chillies were fermented in brines aged from fresh to fifty years, then profiled for flavour chemistry and resident bacteria.

Gas analysis found well over a hundred volatile compounds. Statistical screening picked ten candidate marker volatiles tied to brine age. It also picked six non-volatile markers whose drift tracked bacterial breakdown of proteins and sugars. Bacterial diversity shifted with brine age too, dominated by one phylum and led by a lactic genus whose abundance tracked several flavour compounds closely. The panels separated the age groups consistently, giving producers measurable targets instead of folklore.
pmc-13411134:
Luisa Voßbeck and colleagues show in 2026 that a growth marker in brain lining tumors predicts recurrence mainly in the first years after surgery. Grade 2 meningiomas vary wildly in behavior, and the standard Ki67 growth count suffers from inconsistent hand scoring. The team paired an automatic counter with molecular risk profiling.

Ninety-eight tumors were scored by software that also discards image artifacts. Automatic values ran far lower than routine hand estimates, which warns against mixing the two. Above a set cutoff, the score strongly predicted local recurrence within about 38 months, then faded. Molecular risk added separate information, so the cheap automatic count may work as a stand-alone watch tool where profiling is unavailable.
pmc-13411234:
Christina Amory and Walther Parson compare in 2026 machine-based and hand-based DNA extraction from degraded bone. Forensic and ancient DNA work stands or falls on squeezing usable DNA from poor material. An automated concentrator system was pitted against a respected manual protocol on bones from twelve people.

Both routes gave similar yields and sequence results for moderately degraded bone. In the worst-preserved samples, the manual method usually won more DNA and cleaner sequences. Doubling the machine's input helped only with better-preserved material and stayed inconsistent on the hard cases. Matching method to preservation state is the practical takeaway: automation for routine bones, handwork for the most fragile remains.
pmc-13411434:
Lena Petersson, Luís Irgang, Ingela Mauritzon, and Magnus Holmén report in 2026 on Swedish doctors quietly using unauthorized AI tools at work. Formal adoption lags behind the technology, so clinicians reach for general chatbots that never passed medical device checks. Risks to privacy, safety, and legal compliance ride along.

A survey of 357 physicians, with a response rate near two thirds, collected free-text answers on actual use. Four purpose groups emerged: clinical decisions, paperwork, research and learning, plus plain curiosity. Doctors described the tools as a colleague offering a second opinion on diagnoses. The authors read this shadow use through lenses of professional pride and practical pressure.
pmc-13412334:
Teva Amir and colleagues describe in 2026 how Israel's National Trauma Registry kept working through the Swords of Iron War. Registries normally feed surveillance and quality work, and wartime raises the need for fast, population-level injury data. Their analysis covered every hospitalized civilian and military casualty with war injuries logged between October 2023 and July 2025.

The registry recorded 4,317 casualties, 71.1 percent of them military personnel, with admissions peaking in the first three days. Soldiers more often suffered penetrating wounds and critical injury grades, while civilians carried more leg trauma. Over half of all casualties had surgery, and in-hospital mortality stayed near two percent. The authors credit registry adaptations for steady data under extreme strain.
pmc-13412834:
Vincenzo Bettoli and co-authors survey in 2026 the treatment journeys of Italians living with hidradenitis suppurativa, a chronic inflammatory skin disease that scars the armpits and groin. Despite better understanding of its biology, diagnosis and care still lag badly. A patient association shared a 45-question online survey in a dedicated Facebook group in January 2023, and 320 people completed it.

Respondents had seen roughly five clinicians before anyone named their disease, a delay averaging ten years. Dissatisfaction with primary care ran high at 73 percent, while dermatologists anchored later management. Only 24 percent received biologic drugs, the treatment class users rated most satisfying. Psychological wellbeing suffered for 58 percent, and patients asked for better mental support and wider drug access.
pmc-13413634:
Alessandra Francica and co-authors compare in 2026 two generations of cow-tissue heart valves over up to six years after aortic valve replacement. The newer INSPIRIS Resilia valve was engineered to resist the stiffening that ages tissue valves. At one institution, 2,053 patients received either it or its predecessor, the Perimount Magna Ease, between 2017 and 2023, and statistical matching produced 224 well-balanced pairs for comparison.

Freedom from cardiovascular death at six years was statistically similar, 98.2 percent for the new valve and 96.6 percent for the older one in the matched groups. Stroke, infection of the valve, and reoperation rates also matched closely. Only one severe structural failure appeared in each arm, while valve infection drove most reoperations. Longer watching is needed, the authors say.
pmc-13413934:
Emmanuel Ortega-Robles and co-authors argue in 2026 that walking deserves promotion to a vital sign of brain health. Gait weaves cortex, deep brain, cerebellum, cord, and nerves into one act, so its pattern betrays disease across Parkinson's, stroke, multiple sclerosis, ataxias, and nerve disorders. Bedside watching misses subtle or early changes, and the review surveys wearable sensors, instrumented walkways, and AI analysis that quantify stride far more finely.

Digital measures can already separate Parkinson's from its mimics, track recovery after pressure-relief surgery, and forecast falls or decline in several diseases. Stride variability and double-support time may flag trouble before clinics notice deterioration. Translation stalls on inconsistent methods, thin disease-specific validation, and privacy ethics, the authors caution.
pmc-13414034:
Piao Ma and colleagues compare in 2026 the gut microbes and blood chemistry of plateau zokors living at two heights on the Tibetan plateau. These burrowing rodents thrive in thin, cold air, and their insides may hold part of the trick. Droppings and serum from six animals at 3,700 metres and six at 2,700 metres underwent gene sequencing and metabolite profiling, then the datasets were woven together.

High-altitude zokors carried fewer Firmicutes and more Bacteroidota, with seven species differing clearly between the groups. Pathways for energy production and antioxidant defence ran hotter at altitude, while two sulfur amino-acid routes quieted in the integrated analysis. Two bile acids rose in high-altitude blood and a third fell. The authors frame gut and host chemistry as a joint adaptation system.
pmc-13415134:
Federica Campana and colleagues survey the new class of RAS inhibitors in a 2026 review. RAS genes are among the most often mutated drivers in solid tumors, yet for decades every attempt to drug them failed. Two drugs against the KRAS G12C mutation, sotorasib and adagrasib, recently broke that deadlock.

The review explains how each compound works, how the body handles it, and what side effects appear in trials. RAS proteins act as switches, flipping between off and on states as they bind energy molecules. New agents exploit pockets that show only in one state. Efficacy results across tumor types are summarized for clinicians choosing among fast multiplying options.
pmc-13415534:
Qihua Zou and colleagues combine a liposomal chemotherapy with an immune drug for a hard to treat lymphoma, in a 2026 phase 1b/2 trial. Patients had relapsed or stubborn extranodal natural killer and T cell lymphoma. Forty patients joined between mid 2022 and late 2024, six in dose testing and thirty-four in expansion.

No dose limiting toxicities appeared, so the higher mitoxantrone dose, twenty milligrams per square meter, moved forward. Complete responses reached 53 percent, meeting the preset goal. Median time without progression was about eight months at a median follow-up near fifteen months. Low white cell counts were the commonest severe side effects.
pmc-13416034:
Dapeng Zhang and colleagues tighten near term forecasts of Afro-Asian summer monsoon rain by anchoring them to a giant high pressure system, in 2026. The South Asian High, an upper air feature stretching from West Africa to the western Pacific, explains up to ninety percent of monsoon rain variance across six decades. Billions depend on this rain for farming and water.

Weighting climate models by how well they capture that high gave a stronger projected high than raw model averages under all three emission paths. Constrained forecasts trim monsoon rain by ten to fifty millimeters. Abnormally wet conditions over Africa fall most sharply, while dry conditions grow over Africa and North China.
pmc-13416134:
Aliza Geller and colleagues compared two ways to measure unequal pupils in 2026, testing near-infrared eye scans against smartphone photos. Unequal pupils are hard to judge in young children and dark-eyed patients. The team photographed 30 people aged eight months to 68 years after dilating drops, then had three eye specialists measure the images blind.

Near-infrared scans gave excellent agreement within and between raters, while phone photos fared worse, especially for dark irises where agreement dropped sharply. Clinics gain evidence that infrared imaging beats phone snapshots for this subtle but telling eye sign.
pmc-13416734:
Mayar Al Mohajer and co-authors study antibiotic choices for older adults seen in emergency departments, in a 2026 cohort report. They ask how neighbourhood deprivation relates to whether treatment matched the diagnosis, and to outcomes over the next 30 days. Records cover more than 1.3 million visits at 119 facilities in 15 states.

Care that matched guidelines linked to shorter stays and lower risks of return visits, death, and severe gut infection. Extra antibiotics given without need linked to worse results throughout. Deprivation itself showed only small links to outcomes, and matched care explained little of that gap. The findings support stewardship efforts in busy emergency care.
pmc-13418334:
Xintong Zhang and co-authors review how microplastics alter carbon and nitrogen cycling in water and soil, in a 2026 article. Plastics in nature are a mixed soup of polymer types, sizes, shapes, and weathered states, not a single pollutant. That variety decides how strongly they disturb the microbes that run element cycles.

Biodegradable plastics changed transformations more than conventional ones, partly as direct carbon input. Tiny biodegradable particles especially blocked plant nitrogen uptake, and weathered surfaces released carbon that can raise greenhouse gas output. Most evidence is from short lab studies, so the authors call for long field work with standard methods.
pmc-13418434:
Valentina Foglia Manzillo and colleagues tested combined vaccination and a repellent collar against canine leishmaniosis on Favignana Island, Italy, in a 2026 field study. The sandfly-borne disease threatens dogs and people in endemic areas, yet field proof for using both protections together was thin.

Of 154 screened dogs, about 12 percent already carried the parasite. Among 62 enrolled negative dogs followed for two years, only two fell ill while nine more showed low antibody levels without symptoms. Island vets gain field evidence that the combined shield holds up well across two transmission seasons.
pmc-13418534:
Yang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a smart coating for vascular stents, the mesh tubes that prop open blood vessels.  The team built a coating, layer by layer, from a human-like collagen and a modified sugar polymer, and tuned its stiffness so it softens in response to local chemical signals.

Early on, the coating curbed clot formation and guided cell attachment. Later, it supported a complete, working lining layer, pushed muscle cells toward their calm contractile state, and steered immune cells toward an anti-inflammatory mode. In animals, coated stents showed far less of the tissue overgrowth that re-narrows vessels. At twelve months the healed surface looked and behaved much like a natural vessel lining.
pmc-13419234:
Pavitra Jindahra and colleagues sort the Thai population into patterns of living with several long-term illnesses at once. Having two or more chronic conditions is rising worldwide and strains care built around one disease at a time. Their study drew on a national health survey covering 142,753 participants across the country.

Nine chronic diseases fed a grouping method that sorts people by which illnesses travel together. The team then mapped which traits, habits, and city-versus-country living lined up with each pattern. Patterns of illness varied with local culture, setting, and the health system around people. Thai health planners can use the named patterns to build combined clinics rather than forcing patients through separate single-disease lines.
pmc-13420334:
Nelson L S Tang and colleagues test a simple blood ratio test to tell Kawasaki disease from viral infection in children. The two conditions look alike but need different treatment, and large gene panels do not suit routine laboratories. Their 2026 study uses an assay that measures gene activity in monocytes, a single white blood cell type, directly in whole blood.

Three ratio markers based on interferon-stimulated genes were calculated from two public datasets and compared between the diseases. Viral infection patients showed much higher values on all three ratios. The best performer, built on the gene IFI27, separated the groups slightly better than a conventional eight-gene interferon score. The authors suggest that little or no interferon activation argues against viral infection and supports Kawasaki disease, making the ratio a useful exclusion test.
pmc-13420534:
John Shen and colleagues use a large United States claims database to find which patients with stomach flu end up hospitalized after seeking care. Norovirus leads the causes of acute gut illness nationally and drives heavy health care use each winter. Their cohort study spans cases from 2022 to 2024 in a deidentified commercial claims set.

Patients could enter more than once if separate illness episodes met the rules, each with a year of prior coverage. Earlier claims work links heart disease, kidney disease, and weak immunity to higher admission rates in this illness. A veterans study cited found lab-confirmed norovirus carried 13 percent higher admission risk within three days than test-negative illness in its cohort. Naming who crashes early could let clinics watch the right patients closely from the first visit.
pmc-13421334:
Gavin M. Traber and eight colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about an experimental drug, PMD-026, for acute myeloid leukaemia carrying FLT3 activation. This leukaemia grows fast, relapses often, and leaves adults with five-year survival near 30 percent, while intensive chemotherapy harms many patients who cannot tolerate it.

PMD-026 blocks RSK, a signalling protein downstream of FLT3. The letter reports that selective RSK blockade suppressed the FLT3-driven leukaemia while sparing normal blood formation, the balance that conventional chemotherapy fails to strike. The authors frame the selectivity as the point: a mechanism-based drug that hits the cancer's wiring without the broad damage of cytotoxic treatment.
pmc-13421534:
Akiteru Takahashi and five colleagues observe, in a 2026 paper, heat radiation with a sharp spectral peak from membranes made of sorted carbon nanotubes. Heated nanotubes can glow through excitons, bound electron-hole pairs. Their glow is narrow, not the broad glow of plain hot objects. That narrowness promises selective thermal emitters for energy devices.

Earlier demonstrations used single tubes under laser heating. The team worked instead with membranes of a single nanotube type, heated through contact. At 850 kelvin the exciton peak ruled the measured emissivity. The membranes stayed clear below their optical gap even when hot. Stacking nanotube and dielectric layers boosted emission at the resonance. The authors point to selective emitters for high heat as the use case.
pmc-13422634:
Salvato and colleagues ask in 2026 whether strength of religious faith changes the sense of agency, the feeling that you caused your own movement, when the senses disagree. They tested healthy women with a mirror box illusion.

Sixty-two participants judged ownership and agency while their hand movements and visual feedback matched or clashed, and they also reported faith strength and body sensation awareness. Matching feedback strengthened the illusion for everyone. Women with stronger faith reported agency even when feedback clashed with movement, suggesting they trusted the visual signal over their motor sense. Stronger faith also came with lower awareness of internal body signals, though that trait did not explain the agency effect.
pmc-13422934:
Sjöblom and colleagues published a protocol in 2026 for a randomised trial of online emotion regulation therapy for adolescents. Mental health problems are common in teens, but early evidence-based care is hard to reach. The Swedish trial will enrol 388 adolescents aged twelve to seventeen, plus their parents, through primary care and self-referral. Half will get the emotion regulation treatment and half an active control of supportive therapy, each for six weeks with therapist guidance.

The main outcome is overall symptom severity rated by assessors who do not know each teen's group. Outcomes are checked right after treatment and again three months later, by both blinded ratings and self-reports. The authors note that teens and therapists cannot be blinded, which may bias results.
pmc-13424634:
Kashiwa and co-authors discuss in 2026 the practical problems of running ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work, for children. Two dangers dominate: clots forming in the circuit and hemolysis, the tearing apart of red blood cells.

The authors explain a Japan-specific problem. Pumps built for the low flow rates children need are not approved there, so teams must use adult centrifugal pumps run slowly. Slow running raises shear stress on blood, making hemolysis much more likely than in adults, and the widened tubing around the pump invites clots. Careful blood-thinner dosing and circuit design can reduce the risks. The authors conclude that children need purpose-built low-flow systems, and until those are approved, teams must manage knowing hemolysis is the likelier outcome.
pmc-13424834:
Shane T. Ahyong and three colleagues restore a name to the books: Bathynomus propinquus, a supergiant deep-sea isopod from the Philippines, described in 1910 from a single juvenile and long shelved as unidentifiable. Settling its identity matters because the old name takes precedence over younger ones in its group, and its home waters overlap a species named in 2017.

Re-examining the original specimen alongside fresh material and DNA showed the supposed single species splits in two along geography. The northern form keeps the 2017 name, ranging from Vietnam toward Hainan; the southeastern form, from the Verde Island Passage and southern Luzon, is the 1910 species revived. New distinguishing characters and size-related variation are laid out.
pmc-13425534:
Zhai and colleagues survey in 2026 nearly forty thousand health-care workers in Xi'an, China, on workplace violence and mental health, asking whether perceived work stress carries part of the harm. Violence at work is a pervasive hazard in health care.

Of the 39,773 workers analyzed, just over 46 percent reported experiencing workplace violence. Those workers had roughly four times the odds of depression and of anxiety compared with colleagues who reported none. That held after the team's statistical adjustments in this very large survey sample from one Chinese city. Perceived stress explained part of the link. About a fifth of the depression association and about a sixth of the anxiety association ran through stress in the mediation analysis they performed. The authors call for prevention of violence itself plus stronger mental health support for affected staff.
pmc-13425934:
Miguel Angel Fernández-Vaquero and coauthors built a machine learning airway tool in a 2026 prospective observational study at one center. Videolaryngoscopy is now first-line for placing breathing tubes, yet older airway exams were designed for direct laryngoscopy and say little about blade choice or extra aids. Their cohort of 250 adults having elective surgery received clinical airway assessment plus point-of-care airway ultrasound before operation.

Combining bedside measures with ultrasound anatomy, the model aims to predict the videolaryngoscopy strategy each patient will need. Anesthetists could plan equipment earlier, reducing surprises during intubation for patients rated ASA physical status I to III.
pmc-13426234:
Albayrak and colleagues asked in 2026 whether age changes how well shock wave therapy works for mild-to-moderate erectile dysfunction. Their prospective study treated fifty-two men with the same protocol. It compared patients under fifty with those fifty and over, scoring erection function and hardness before treatment and at one, three, and six months after.

Both groups started alike. The younger group's function scores rose to about twenty-two and stayed there at every check. The older group improved more slowly, reaching about nineteen at six months. It scored significantly lower than the younger group at each point. Hardness gains were similar in size for both groups. The authors conclude shock wave therapy alone may be sufficient for younger patients, while older patients improve less.
pmc-13427234:
Yiru Wang and colleagues trace how oesophageal cancer cells ship a circular RNA, a ring-shaped genetic message, to immune cells to help the tumour grow. The cancer type studied is squamous cell carcinoma, the flat-cell form of food-pipe cancer.

The ring message, named circAP2B1, ran high in tumour tissue and patient blood, and high levels tracked with poor outlook. Cancer cells packed it into tiny parcels called exosomes, which delivered it to macrophages, the immune cells that patrol tumours. Inside them, the ring acted as a scaffold that moved a gene switch into the cell core and boosted energy output. Blocking this chain flipped macrophages back against the tumour and slowed its growth in lab and animal tests.
pmc-13427434:
Maxime Antoni and coauthors assessed mixed reality navigation for reverse shoulder replacement in a 2026 retrospective series of 45 shoulders. Correct socket angle, meaning version and inclination, limits notching, instability, and loosening, yet surgeons traditionally copied plans from a nearby screen freehand. Their approach projected a scapular hologram onto the patient's anatomy through a head-mounted display with real-time navigation guiding the planned trajectories.

Postoperative CT-based planning data in dedicated software let the team measure deviation between planned and achieved component angles. Low deviations support holographic guidance as a precision aid for a technically fussy step in shoulder arthroplasty. Each joint was planned on scans first, so the worn bone could be matched to its twin in the air with care at each step of the case.
pmc-13427534: Giri, Glassock, and Fervenza reply to critics of obinutuzumab trials in primary membranous nephropathy, a kidney disease. They concede the MAJESTY trial ideally would have tested obinutuzumab against rituximab, the current standard. But a trial to prove it better would need 1,005 to 3,684 randomized patients. The range hinged on the remission rates assumed, making such a trial too big to run. Beating tacrolimus could still win United States approval. It could also help patients who cannot get rituximab paid for.
pmc-13427634:
Catalá-Lahoz and colleagues built a field-programmable photonic gate array, a reconfigurable light-based circuit, on a hybrid silicon and barium titanate platform that holds its settings without power. Conventional photonic phase shifters burn constant power and leak heat into neighbors, blocking scale-up, so the team used ferroelectric domain switching as non-volatile memory instead.

Their hexagonal waveguide mesh integrates 58 programmable unit cells and 116 actuators on a single chip for the demonstration. Switching took 80 nanoseconds, while static power fell to a negligible 560 nanowatts per pi phase shift, effectively zero holding power. The team configured the same mesh as a tunable filter, a 4 by 4 unitary transformation block, and an optical router. They present ferroelectric silicon photonics as a heat-free route to large, energy-efficient photonic computing hardware.
pmc-13428034:
Herron and colleagues build virtual clinical trials to set dosing targets for antivirals against respiratory syncytial virus, a common cause of severe lung illness in infants and older adults. Candidate drugs have cleared virus in volunteer challenge studies, then failed in real patients, a costly translation gap. Their 2026 study uses a quantitative systems pharmacology model, a mathematical copy of infection and drug action, tuned to two drugs that block different viral proteins.

Virtual populations reproduced the viral load curves of the challenge studies. A virtual child population matched a pediatric phase two trial of one drug. The simulations say efficacy needs drug levels that stay above a threshold potency value at their daily low point. On that coverage, starting treatment five to seven days after symptoms begin could still show virus clearing in children. The authors offer those targets as design rules for a phase three trial.
pmc-13429134:
XiaoMei Li and co-authors gather, in a 2026 evidence summary, the best guidance for bladder self-care after spinal cord injury. A neurogenic bladder, one whose nerve control is lost, needs daily management to protect the kidneys and skin. The team searched Chinese and international databases and guideline libraries through October 2025. Eighteen sources made the cut, including eight clinical guidelines, and each was quality-checked with standard tools.

The synthesis produced 26 evidence statements grouped under nine themes, from full assessment and structured teaching to fluid planning and catheter care. Each statement carries a strength grade based on feasibility, fit, meaningfulness, and effect. Clean intermittent catheterization training stands out as a practical centerpiece. The authors caution that evidence must bend to local resources and to each patient's hand function and thinking ability before it becomes a care plan.
pmc-13430834:
Wei Wang and colleagues use near-infrared light sensors to probe resting brain networks in teens with idiopathic scoliosis, a spine curve that appears in adolescence, a key window for brain growth. Most scoliosis work studies the spine or behaviour, leaving brain function unclear.

Twenty-five patients and 25 age-matched healthy controls lay at rest while functional near-infrared spectroscopy recorded brain activity. Connectivity and network shape were compared, with links to age and disease traits examined. The study opens a brain-side view of scoliosis, where altered networks might explain features that spine measures alone cannot.
pmc-13431734:
Chenjie Qiu wrote a 2026 letter that probes a trial of a new pain drug plan. The plan served older patients after bowel cancer surgery and aimed to speed gut recovery. Gut slowness from strong pain drugs ranks as a chief block to smooth recovery after such surgery. The trial set the new drug against a standard strong drug, both self-dosed through a vein pump.

The letter grants the trial's worth, then presses on what its main score truly proves. The gap on a gut recovery scale was small, with no set bar for a gap that counts in real life. A four-hour edge in first gas passage may mark softer symptoms more than faster gut motion. The letter also notes that some scale parts double as side-effect counts. A further worry flags the choice to drop fourteen patients from the main count.
pmc-13432734:
O Krug and colleagues investigate how two modafinil analogues, flmodafinil and fladrafinil, are broken down and cleared from the body for sports drug testing. Both drugs stimulate the central nervous system and have grown popular outside medicine for claimed cognitive gains.

As class S6 stimulants on the World Anti-Doping Agency list, both are banned in competition. Six volunteers took 20 milligrams of one drug or the other, and urine and blood samples were tracked for parent drugs and metabolites. Anti-doping labs get elimination profiles for catching these analogues in athletes' samples.
pmc-13432834:
Mikaela Whitty and co-authors fished out in 2026 the first virus known to burst a famed health-linked gut germ, a germ that thins in people with heart, mind, and body-fuel faults. Viruses of gut germs shape crowd balance in the gut, yet only dormant forms had been found for this host. The team named the find and read its full gene set.

Gene kin work places the virus as a fresh kind inside a known virus clan. Near kin turned up in reads from human gut virus banks, which hints that such viruses roam gut settings in the wild. The germ fills a large share of a healthy gut and serves as a mark of gut health. The authors frame the find as a base for work on how viruses steer gut crowds.
pmc-13433434:
Zhenrun Zhan and co-authors weighed rival fatness rules in 2026 against bone breaks and heart disease in a vast clinic set of diabetic patients. World burden data from 1990 to 2021 frame the work: China's high-weight rate more than doubled, at a pace near twice the world climb. The clinic set held near eighteen thousand patients from one Chinese center.

Three fatness rule sets split the crowd, with waist-to-height share read as a twin gauge. One rule set tied firmly to heart disease. The waist share tied to heart disease and hip breaks at each step of tuned math. The top third for waist share carried clear extra risk on both, and curve fits showed risk climb in dose steps. Fat at the waist earns the sharper eye, the authors close.
pmc-13434234:
Wei Guo and colleagues introduce a 2026 microscope method that tracks single glowing molecules and also reads which way each one points. Older tracking shows place alone and misses tilt and shape. The team used a sheet of boron nitride at a liquid surface as a hard test case.

More than 100,000 glow events were caught at room heat. The tilt of the molecules matched the three fold pattern of the crystal below. An electric signal could shift how the molecules moved in the liquid. Side drift at the wet surface proved far livelier than in dry solids, a fact that matters for sensors.
pmc-13434534:
Tomasz Skóra and colleagues report long-term results for proton beam therapy in 76 patients with rare skull base tumours. The tumours, chordomas and chondrosarcomas, grow beside the brainstem and eye nerves, so surgery alone rarely clears them.

Patients received finely aimed proton beams, at higher doses for chordomas than for chondrosarcomas, between 2016 and 2020. At five years, about 84 percent of patients were alive and about 87 percent had no local regrowth. Control was stronger for chondrosarcoma, at about 96 percent, than for chordoma, at about 82 percent. Serious late side effects hit about 9 percent, mainly hearing loss and brain tissue damage, the team reports.
pmc-13434634:
Naito Ishimoto and coauthors image a bacterial mating spike at fine detail in 2026. Bacteria pass DNA to each other through such spikes, a route that spreads drug resistance. The spike from plasmid RP4 turns out to break a rule thought to hold for all such spikes.

Its building unit carries no fat tag, a tag long seen as a must for spike growth. Cells stripped of a key fat could still send RP4, while three rival plasmids failed without it. Sharp images at 2.74 angstrom scale back the claim. A fat free build path widens models of how bacteria swap genes.
pmc-13437234:
Jiaojiao Cheng and colleagues asked whether freezing ovarian tissue can still help girls and young women who have already had a stem cell transplant. Their 2026 study covered 142 patients whose tissue was frozen before or after transplant, with only sixteen in the after-transplant group. That group averaged about twelve years old at freezing, and half had not reached puberty.

Compared with patients who had no chemotherapy before freezing, the after-transplant group showed clear ovarian damage. A hormone that signals low egg supply ran higher, a second hormone tied to egg reserve ran lower, and each ovary was smaller. Counts of early eggs per ovary were also lower, most plainly in children up to twelve. Freezing before transplant stays the best plan, the authors conclude. Yet they judge later freezing a real fallback for carefully chosen survivors, and they call for long follow-up to spot who can still benefit.
pmc-13438134:
Huaiyan Chen and a large team uncovered a placental switch that helps time the start of labor. Birth timing depends on mother and fetus talking to each other, and the placenta's part was murky. Studying mice lacking two helper proteins for hormone signaling, their 2026 paper traces a chain in the placenta. Enzyme AOC1 falls, spermidine rises, and a tagged protein switches on a self-cleaning program in placenta cells.

That cleaning program lowers the placenta's output of estrogen and prostaglandins, two labor drivers. Estrogen in turn raises AOC1, closing a feedback loop that keeps the system in balance. Deleting the enzyme in the placenta delayed labor sharply by letting the cleaning program run hot. Most striking, giving spermidine rescued mice from inflammation-driven early labor. The authors offer the chain as a new account of how birth is timed, and spermidine as a candidate guard against preterm birth.
pmc-13438534:
Yongliang Sha and colleagues fused microscope images with gene activity data to predict whether breast cancer has reached the lymph nodes. Their 2026 study drew slides, gene readings, and records from a public cancer atlas, then checked the model on hospital slides from Xuzhou. Four deep learning designs were tried on the images alone before the team merged the best signals with hub genes into a single scoring chart.

The combined chart sorted patients almost perfectly in the atlas data, well above any single model. The team chased one gene, B3GALT4, through lab stains and a mouse model: it eased the cancer's move to nodes and wore the killer T cells down. The authors propose the chart and the gene as working tools, the first for sorting patients, the second as a target and warning marker. They note atlas-perfect scores usually soften in real-world sets.
pmc-13439534:
Jing Zhang's team tracked adiponectin and cytokines in 2026 among eighty ALS patients over eighteen months to predict progression and survival. ALS kills through respiratory failure within a few years, yet markers that flag fast progressors are scarce. Blood adiponectin, IL-10, progression rate, and function scores were tested in survival models with hazard ratios.

Fast progressors showed lower adiponectin and IL-10, and all four markers, adiponectin, IL-10, progression rate, and function score, predicted survival risk in the models. Clinicians get candidate blood and clinical markers for stratifying ALS care and trials. The small, single-cohort design means the markers need independent validation before bedside use.
pmc-13439734:
Beichen Cai and colleagues review what drives baby birthmark tumours called infantile hemangiomas to grow, then shrink away, writing in 2026. These soft red growths swell fast after birth and later turn to fatty scar tissue, yet the switch behind each phase was fuzzy. Some lesions endanger function or resist the standard drug, propranolol. The review favours human lesion tissue and patient-linked phase data over dish and animal models where possible.

Growth, on their account, is a team effort among stem cells, vessel-lining cells, support cells, and macrophages, the immune cells that also feed vessel growth. Fuel use shifts toward sugar burning, and macrophage signals shield partners from an iron-driven cell death. Shrinkage follows when that support web fails and fat-forming programs take over. The authors call for phase-by-phase human cohorts and spatial maps to guide sharper treatment.
pmc-13439934:
Overton and colleagues measured in 2026 whether a CRISPR gene drive element quietly raises the mutation load of its host, a safety worry for plans to edit wild populations. Gene drives spread a chosen trait through mating, but the Cas9 cutting tool can snip off-target DNA, possibly causing mutations and loss of heterozygosity, where paired gene copies become identical. The team ran a mutation accumulation experiment in baker's yeast carrying a drive element or Cas9 alone.

Genome-wide rates of new mutations and loss events showed no detectable rise in either strain. Power calculations bound any true effect below about thirty percent, far under natural variation between yeast lines. Drive and Cas9 strains hinted at altered lengths and locations of loss events, but the evidence was weak. The authors conclude well-designed drives add at most a slight mutational burden in yeast, while urging checks in other organisms.
pmc-13440134:
Hanna Rinne's team studied sickness allowance in 2026 among over 1.7 million Finnish residents aged twenty-five to sixty-two, comparing employed and unemployed people in 2022 and 2023. Unemployed people report poorer health yet do not claim sickness allowance more often, and when they do, spells run longer, hinting at under-claiming. Random and fixed-effects models tracked allowance onset, prevalence, and total days.

Among women, unemployment linked to slightly lower onset but higher prevalence in cross-sectional views, while within-person moves into unemployment cut onset more clearly and raised total days. Men showed similar but weaker patterns. Policy makers get evidence of a take-up gap: unemployed people may forgo short-term sickness benefits they need. Outreach and simpler claiming could close it.
pmc-13440434:
Zachary T Sanger and colleagues hunt for a live brain signal that shows whether thalamic stimulation is working in drug-resistant epilepsy, reporting in 2026. Deep brain stimulation of the anterior thalamic nucleus helps some patients, yet benefit takes months to judge and settings are chosen blind. Eleven trial participants had brain rhythms recorded from the target during clinic visits and across follow-up with an implanted sensing device.

Seven participants showed slow gamma oscillations, rhythmic activity in the 20 to 50 hertz band, and six of those seven proved responders with seizures at least halved. Steady fading of that gamma signal under ongoing stimulation tracked long-term seizure relief in most responders. Brief in-clinic stimulation also suppressed the signal under many settings, not only the standard one. The authors propose gamma suppression as a guide for spotting responders and tuning settings.
pmc-13442434:
Renjie Pan and colleagues sum up how waste goods from tumors can block immune attack in a 2026 mini review. Drugs that free immune brakes have changed cancer care, yet many tumors resist from the start or learn to resist. The review argues that tumor waste acts like a set of extra brakes, apart from the known PD-1 and CTLA-4 paths.

Four waste streams get the closest look. Lactate from sugar burning draws in calm-down cells and dulls killer T cells. Adenosine, made through the CD73 step, quiets killer cells while it feeds calm-down groups. Breakdown goods from tryptophan work through wider nets than the classic IDO1 route, and UDP signals push macrophages toward help for the tumor. The authors suggest pairing waste blocks with brake-freeing drugs, matched to where each waste pools.
pmc-13443934:
Yaru Xia and colleagues identify a 2026 mechanism linking tumor metabolism to muscle wasting in lung cancer cachexia, a syndrome that saps strength and treatment tolerance in most advanced cancers. The team found the protein PEBP4 sharply reduced in cachectic lung models and inversely tied to tumor lactate levels.

PEBP4 steadied the antioxidant regulator NRF2 by competing for its keeper KEAP1, boosting antioxidant defense, quieting inflammatory signaling, and dialing down the atrophy genes MuRF1 and Atrogin-1. Restoring PEBP4 in cells and tumor-bearing mice preserved muscle mass, strength, and endurance, with benefits fading when NRF2 was blocked. The axis offers a fresh therapeutic target, pending human validation.
pmc-13446034:
Murat Erten and colleagues report a sixty-five-year-old woman who developed a bone infection at the tailbone after a steroid shot given through the tailbone route for back pain, published in 2026. Such shots are widely used and count as safe, yet deep infection is a rare and grave risk. She also carried diabetes, heart disease, and past spine surgery with metal hardware.

The shot first eased her pain, yet by day three she felt unwell with burning at the site, and blood tests showed strong inflammation. MRI scans fit infection of the tailbone bones with spread into nearby soft tissue. Vein antibiotics, started after expert consult, brought marked gains in how she felt and in her lab values. The case flags new pain after a shot as a warning.
pmc-13446134:
Xinyi Zhou and colleagues review how molecular dynamics simulation, a method that tracks atoms in motion, is reshaping study of traditional Chinese medicine, in a 2026 paper. Herbal formulas hold many compounds hitting many targets, a tangle that still pictures cannot untie. Motion at atomic detail can show how a compound grips its target and how the grip shifts over time.

The review maps the method's growth, software, databases, and work steps, then walks through cases for five compound families, from flavonoids to sugars. Joined with network mapping, multi-omics, and lab checks, simulation turns flat compound-target links into claims that can be tested. Costs, sparse sampling, force-field doubts, and thin lab proof stand as the chief limits the authors name.
pmc-13446334:
Alexis O'Neil and colleagues ask whether the fine vessels at the back of the eye can flag future stroke risk, in a 2026 cohort study from Canada. The eye offers a clear window on small vessels that mirror the brain's state. Past work leaned on vessel width alone, so this team also weighed vessel area and twist.

Data came from a national aging study with some thirty thousand adults, tracked over six years. Wider small arteries at the start went with lower stroke odds later. Larger vein area raised the odds, while larger artery area cut them. Sex bent the twist links in both vessel kinds. The authors say area measures earn a place in future stroke forecast tools.
pmc-13447934:
Ali Paşaoğlu and colleagues introduce a 2026 low-part-count high step-up DC-DC converter for renewable energy, where solar panels and fuel cells deliver low voltage that must be boosted for use. Their non-isolated design uses a coupled inductor with two windings to reach very high gain at modest duty cycles.

Gain adjusts through duty cycle and winding turns ratio, giving two independent design freedoms, while low duty cuts switch losses and stress. A 400 watt prototype at 50 kilohertz stepped 29 volts up to a regulated 400 volts, validating analysis and feasibility. The converter suits solar, medical, harvesting, and microgrid applications.
pmc-13448034:
Elmekaty and colleagues compared two ways to treat adjacent-segment pathology in 2026, the breakdown of spinal levels next to an earlier fusion that causes new symptoms. Using the Swedish spine registry, they studied 2,521 patients treated between 1997 and 2019, some with decompression alone and others with decompression plus extending the fusion.

At five years, the estimated chance of needing another operation was eighteen percent after decompression alone, against twenty-five percent after extended fusion. Adjusted analysis put the extended fusion group's risk about twenty-six percent higher. Mean follow-up was just over six years, and most patients were women around sixty-one years old. The authors warn the comparison is not proof of cause, because registry data could not confirm instability or deformity that might have justified the bigger operation.
pmc-13448134:
Woo Hyeon Lim reviews practical imaging of air and blood collections in the chest after trauma in a 2026 article for radiologists. Collapsed lung from leaked air and bleeding into the chest cavity can deteriorate fast, so early sorting matters. Lying-flat chest X-rays remain the first screen yet miss much in trauma patients, pushing clinicians toward ultrasound and CT.

Bedside ultrasound now detects both problems quickly, while CT gives the definitive whole-chest picture and can reveal active bleeding points. Distinctive signs on flat films differ from upright films, and the review catalogues those patterns plus common traps that cause missed or false calls. Structured report formats are proposed to standardise communication. Artificial intelligence tools entering trauma workflows are also surveyed for their error-reducing potential.
pmc-13448334:
Majeed and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract DSAI-13, a machine learning model that predicts which patients with solid tumors will develop brain metastases. Clinicians cannot forecast this complication well; the model uses the large MSK-MET cancer dataset.

The team trained a regularized logistic regression on primary tumor samples from over fourteen thousand patients. It mixed clinical features with mutations and copy number changes, then trimmed the model to its fifty most informative features. On held-out primary tumors the model scored in the low seventies on the standard discrimination measure. It caught about sixty-five percent of future brain metastases at about seventy-two percent specificity. It held up on an independent set of over ten thousand metastatic samples with similar performance. Cancer type and recurring genomic changes drove the predictions, several mapping to brain-relevant biological pathways.
pmc-13449234:
Anastasia Keller and co-authors publish in 2026 the protocol for STEP-RAISE, an early-phase trial of electrical stimulation for acute spinal cord injury. No proven therapy yet protects the cord in the first hours after trauma, when lasting paralysis is often sealed. Stimulation through skin electrodes over the lower back helps some patients with chronic injury, so the team will test starting within 72 hours of injury in moderate-to-severe cases, using the ARC-Ex device.

Phase 1 enrolls five participants for safety work, checking blood pressure stability, cord perfusion, and skin reactions. Phase 2 then randomizes ten participants in a triple-blinded, placebo-controlled design. Recovery is tracked with the standard neurological examination, muscle recordings, patient reports, and blood and spinal fluid markers of nerve and support-cell injury, through six months. The trial, registered as NCT07090473, is sized to estimate effects and shape a larger study.
pmc-13450234:
Abdulkadir Calavul reports in 2026 the repair of a scarred, outward-turning eyelid left behind by shingles of the eye's nerve branch. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus can inflame the tissues around the eye, and in rare cases the healing skin contracts until the lid cannot close, exposing it to dryness and damage. His patient, a 65-year-old woman, developed lid retraction, lash loss, and incomplete closure two months after her diagnosis, despite antiviral treatment and lubricants, her vision and cornea stayed intact.

Once inflammation had burned out and the scar remained, he released the contracted tissue under anesthesia. The defect, 1.8 by 0.8 centimeters, was covered with a full-thickness skin graft from in front of the ear, chosen for its match in color, thickness, and flexibility. At eight months her lid closed fully, symptoms had resolved, and the graft blended acceptably. The author positions grafting as a practical option when timing is right.
pmc-13450634:
Carolina Barroso, Antonio Fonseca, and Ana Cabrita review in 2026 whether fat supplements from fish and other sources can lift the immune health of dogs. The fats in view are the omega families found in fish oil, and they shape how the body makes swelling signals. Pet food with health claims is a fast-growing shelf.

Fish-oil-rich diets cut some swelling signals in past work, and two fish fats lowered such signals in dogs with heart disease. New sources such as algae and krill stay little used, and no one has pinned down the best mix of the two fat families. The authors call for work on how the fats act so diets can rest on proof.
pmc-13451934:
Afshari and colleagues test whether extra exercise around colon and rectal cancer surgery eases the deep tiredness many patients feel afterward. Their 2026 report draws on the PHYSSURG-C trial. That trial assigned 518 patients to usual care or to moderate exercise done on their own. The program started two weeks before surgery and lasted four weeks after. Patients rated their fatigue, pain, quality of life, and mental recovery at four weeks and at twelve months.

The exercise group reported a hint of less fatigue at four weeks, and the gap held among patients who stuck to the plan, reaching a clearer edge at twelve months. Yet the groups did not differ on quality of life, pain, or mental recovery at either check. The authors call the fatigue signal a suggestion, not proof, and ask for larger trials to pin down what dose of exercise, if any, truly helps.
pmc-13452234:
Lotfalizadeh and Nazifi reviewed in 2026 how anti-seizure drugs change routine lab tests in dogs and cats. These drugs are given for years and can shift blood values in ways that mimic real disease. The authors searched three large databases for studies on each drug type. 

Rises in liver enzymes were the most common change across the studies reviewed. In dogs these rises were often adaptive, meaning the liver adjusted without true damage. In cats the same changes were rarer but more likely to signal a real problem. Blood cell changes, such as anaemia or low cell counts, were less common in both species. Most changes were mild and could be managed without stopping treatment. The review offers patterns to help vets tell drug effects from true disease and calls for clearer monitoring rules.
pmc-13452334:
Pi-Hong Zhang, Xiao-Bing Fu, and Yue-Sheng Huang present in 2026 a Chinese expert consensus on repairing leg ulcers from faulty veins, in its 2025 edition. Such ulcers spring from many tangled causes and resist simple care. Past guides covered vein disease broadly yet left surgical wound repair thin.

A wound repair body of the Chinese Medical Doctor Association drew a cross-field panel to settle the gaps. Advice covers cleaning methods, when to repair, and which repair route to pick, drawn from world proof and Chinese practice. The panel aims to steady surgical choices, lift healing rates, and ease daily life for patients whose leg wounds stall for months.
pmc-13453034:
Vu M N Phan and Omar Alberto Quintero-Carmona probe how chemical tagging switches off a motor protein that helps build the ear's sound sensing hairs. The protein, myosin IIIA, carries its own tagging enzyme and shapes thin cell fingers called filopodia. Their 2026 study used COS7 cells and tweaked copies of the protein that mimic the tagged state.

Cells with the mimic versions grew fewer filopodia than cells with the plain protein. Adding just the tagging part of the protein had the same damping effect when paired with the motor. Shape predictions suggest the tags block the motor from gripping actin, the rail protein it walks on. The work ties the tagging of this motor to control of hair like cell parts, a link that matters for hearing research.
pmc-13453334:
Marcos‐Perez and colleagues test whether supervised exercise can reverse molecular signs of frailty in this 2026 multi-center study. Frailty in older age has been linked to biomarker panels from two earlier projects. Those projects are FRAILOMIC and BIOFRAIL. But whether exercise changes the panels was unknown. The study assigned 44 older adults, median age about 79, to a 16-week multicomponent exercise program, with 24 controls for comparison.

The exercise group improved on a physical performance battery, grip strength, and walking speed, and their frailty and sarcopenia scores eased significantly. Four of six FRAILOMIC markers and six of seven BIOFRAIL markers reversed their expression after training, moving back toward non-frail patterns. A statistical split found 36 responders, most from the exercise group, and four markers best predicted who responded.
pmc-13454434:
Chen and a large team finger the epigenetic enzyme JMJD3 as a driver of benign prostatic hyperplasia, the non-cancerous prostate enlargement that obstructs urination in aging men. Single-cell and bulk sequencing showed JMJD3 switched on more strongly in hyperplastic tissue, a finding they confirmed in patient prostate samples collected for the study.

Forcing JMJD3 up in prostate cell lines accelerated proliferation and cell cycle progression. Blocking it with the inhibitor GSK-J4 or gene silencing triggered cell death and halted growth in the hyperplasia cell model. In mice, GSK-J4 eased prostate enlargement induced by testosterone or by bacterial inflammatory challenge in the in-vivo experiments reported. Mechanistically, JMJD3 strips a repressive chemical mark from the TGF-beta1 gene's promoter, raising its expression and fueling the disease process. The authors propose JMJD3 blockade as a candidate therapy for this condition.
pmc-13454534:
Léa Wagner and eight colleagues report, in 2026, a self-driving search for better recipes for cell-free gene expression systems. Such systems run genetic programs in a tube, free of living cells, yet they make too little RNA for full sequencing. The team paired a smart search algorithm with automated lab gear to explore the recipe space.

The search space held over 1.6 million possible buffer mixes, of which 653 were actually tested. One winning buffer raised RNA output twentyfold. A second mix raised it thirteenfold while keeping protein output strong. With these buffers, the team sequenced the full gene activity of the T7 virus in a tube. Comparisons with infected bacteria showed the tube system mirrors real expression well, including RNA cutting sites that simpler systems miss.
pmc-13455234:
Akash Kumar Srivastava and others wrote up indigenous food feasts and festive rites of central India in 2026, from deep fieldwork in Maikal Hills villages. Central India holds several indigenous groups in forest lands whose lives turn on nature, with deep respect for Mother Earth and linked natural beings. Food-led feasts mark ancestor rites, farm cycles, and devotion to nature.

The study reads feasts that oft fall on key farm dates, which shows how feast days form the region's foodways through green thought and indigenous identity. Food shapes cultural settings in a big way, with feasts built on a whole-life view where food, land, and kin intertwine. Anthropologists gain first-hand feast records and their symbolic meanings from village fieldwork.
pmc-13455334:
Tang and colleagues looked at gut microbes from American Gut Project volunteers with autoimmune disease, with and without depression. They hunted microbe signatures of the common comorbidity. The main cohort held 344 people: 115 with both, 120 with the disease alone, and 109 healthy controls, plus a bowel-disease subgroup of 75.

Between-community variety was lower in the depressed autoimmune group, while within-sample diversity did not split across the cohort comparisons. Forty microbe taxa split between autoimmune patients with and without depression, and 12 taxa split inside the inflammatory bowel subgroup analyzed separately. Predicted microbe functions pointed to disrupted carbohydrate handling, energy metabolism, and glycan building in the joint group relative to autoimmune patients without depression. Co-occurrence networks also rewired distinctly in joint patients, and the authors present the patterns as exploratory leads.
pmc-13457134:
Dominik Hofmann argues, in a 2026 theory article, that talk of blurring borders between science and medicine misreads how the two systems actually touch. Writing in the tradition of Niklas Luhmann, Hofmann treats each as a closed system with its own code: science trades in truth, medicine in health and illness. Contact between them is structural coupling, a stable pattern of irritation, not a merger.

The comparison case is law and politics, whose coupling theory already describes well. Both pairs, the article shows, push justification outward: each system lets the other carry the burden of legitimating hard choices. Medicine handed that burden to science as the two grew up together over centuries. Today's frictions, from gene editing to AI diagnosis, then read as strain on an old coupling under faster innovation. The blurring metaphor, Hofmann concludes, mistakes heavier traffic for a vanished border.
pmc-13457634:
Xiaofang Zhang, Qiongying Wang, and Jing Yu review the case of a woman whose adrenal tumor returned years after surgeons removed it. Pheochromocytomas grow from chromaffin cells and flood the body with adrenaline-like chemicals, causing attacks of headache, pounding heart, and blood pressure spikes. The patient fell ill in 2013 with episodes reaching 180 over 101, and imaging found a left adrenal mass about five by six centimeters, removed by keyhole surgery.

Pathology at the time already hinted at malignant potential. She stayed well without blood pressure medicine until 2018, when the attacks returned stronger, with breathlessness and chest discomfort. Pressures reached 190 over 110, even though a contrast CT showed no recurrence. The case report walks through her 2021 readmission workup, diagnosis, and treatment. The authors offer the timeline as a reference for clinicians, underlining that these tumors can relapse or spread long after apparently complete removal, deserving prolonged follow-up.
pmc-13458234:
Gemma Webb and co-authors compared bloodstream infections caused by two related staphylococcal bacteria in Melbourne hospitals between 2012 and 2024. One bacterium, Staphylococcus lugdunensis, is usually classed with milder skin staphylococci but can act aggressively. The other, Staphylococcus aureus, is a well-known dangerous pathogen. Their 2026 study matched 57 patients with the first infection against 66 patients with the second. They compared symptoms, treatments, complications, and survival.

The two infections looked similar in patient backgrounds. They also matched in how often they caused endocarditis, infection of the heart lining, which struck nine of 57 patients in one group and fifteen of 66 in the other. Death rates in hospital and at ninety days were also comparable. Differences did appear: lugdunensis infections more often grew alongside other bacteria and were wrongly dismissed as contamination in twelve cases. Aureus infections lasted longer and more often seeded bone and spinal infections.
pmc-13458334:
Altuğ Güner and Sümeyye Tuna Güner examine two windows onto the smoldering inflammation of familial Mediterranean fever, an inherited condition of recurring attacks. Between attacks the fire never fully dies, and cumulative damage matters more than any flare. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured tissue deposits of advanced glycation end products, sugar-damaged proteins building up under chronic inflammation, using a skin autofluorescence reader in 87 patients and 52 healthy controls.

The readings correlated with inflammatory and metabolic markers and moved opposite to the CALLY index, a composite of C-reactive protein, albumin, and lymphocyte counts blending inflammation with nutrition. The authors suggest the two measures capture complementary sides of burden: what has accumulated in tissue versus the body's current state. Paired, they may help clinicians judge who needs tighter control even when a patient feels well between attacks.
pmc-13459334:
Yuqun Zhang and co-authors built and validated a questionnaire meant to measure the whole ecosystem of humanistic care teaching in medical schools. Existing tools, they argue, assess fragments.
