Their 2026 study drafted a 68 item pool and refined it with experts to sixty items across those five dimensions. It tested the scale on 738 medical undergraduates, with 433 responses surviving quality control and fifty students retested after four weeks.

The scale proved highly consistent internally, with a reliability coefficient of 0.982, and its five factor structure fit the response data well by standard indices. Retest stability over four weeks was modest for individual subscales, ranging from 0.29 to 0.54 in the reported correlations. One striking finding: students from single parent households scored lower on every dimension. The authors offer the instrument for spotting educational gaps.
pmc-13459934:
Wei Suo and co-authors review radiomics, the practice of mining medical images for hundreds of image features invisible to the eye, as a tool for judging thyroid nodules. Most nodules are harmless, yet cancer rates keep rising and overdiagnosis is a real harm. Their 2026 review searched PubMed and Google Scholar for studies from 2019 to 2024. It evaluated fifty papers on radiomics applied to thyroid imaging, covering the principles, workflows, and reported performance of the approach.

Across the literature surveyed, radiomics models repeatedly improved on conventional ultrasound reading for separating benign from malignant nodules in the reported studies. The review also covers using image features to estimate disease progression and to cut unnecessary biopsies and surgeries. Limitations run through the field, including small single center datasets, inconsistent feature extraction between scanners, and few external validations. Radiomics is a potent aid whose clinical use awaits standardization, the authors conclude.
pmc-13460234:
Susanne J. Nielsen, Erik Björklund, and Sossio Perrotta compared in 2026 long-term survival after bypass surgery versus stent treatment in Swedish dialysis patients whose three coronary arteries were all diseased. Kidney failure patients develop heart disease at high rates, and no randomized trial has settled which procedure serves them better. Nationwide registries captured 412 stent patients and 199 bypass patients treated between 2006 and 2020, linked with death records.

The groups differed at the start: stent patients were older with longer dialysis histories, while bypass patients more often had prior heart attacks and rhythm problems. Early thirty-day mortality was low single digits in both groups. Adjusted survival models over a median follow-up of a few years form the heart of the comparison, informing a genuinely open clinical question.
pmc-13460534:
R Leporati and colleagues review liquid biopsy for PD-L1 testing in non-small cell lung cancer in a 2026 story-style review. Immune checkpoint blockers anchor treatment when no usable gene change exists, yet tissue PD-L1 testing predicts benefit only modestly. The review explores blood-borne tumour cells, outside-cell sacs, blood-borne tumour DNA and other blood markers as complements to tissue stain tests.

Blood-based testing offers a gentle way to track disease change and immune interactions over time, maybe overcoming tumour mixed make-up that small biopsies miss. Establishing robust, steady PD-L1 methods for liquid biopsy is a must before medical adoption. Cancer doctors gain a roadmap for tailoring immune therapy selection in advanced lung cancer.
pmc-13461034:
Amirhossein Salmannezhad and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether enduring personality traits shape how patients fare after total hip or knee replacement. Personality outlasts passing moods, so traits such as anxiety, neuroticism, pessimism, and extroversion might steer pain and recovery for years. Searching four databases through May 2025 with no language limits, plus chasing references backward, the team gathered fifteen studies on joint replacement outcomes.

Anxiety stood out as the strongest influence on results. Neuroticism tracked with more pain and lower quality of life, and pessimism meant greater pain with less functional gain in the knee. Extroversion linked to better function and quality of life, although its effect on pain itself stayed unclear. The authors argue that screening personality before surgery could help set honest expectations.
pmc-13461534:
Li and colleagues set out in 2026 a trial protocol to test warm acupuncture for lasting nerve damage caused by the chemotherapy drug oxaliplatin. This side effect leaves ongoing limb numbness that can outlast treatment, lower quality of life, and force dose cuts. No accepted remedy exists. The multicentre trial will enrol 84 patients and assign them by chance to one of two arms: standard care on its own, or that care plus warm acupuncture.

Li's plan gives sixteen sessions over twelve weeks, twice weekly at first and then weekly, with blinded assessors scoring outcomes. The main measure is nerve harm graded on a standard cancer side-effect scale. Two quality-of-life questionnaires focused on nerve symptoms and general health will be taken at set points through one year of follow-up. The authors aim for early proof of safety and benefit to support wider clinical use if the results hold.
pmc-13461734:
Xu Qiao and colleagues compare, in a 2026 records study, two keyhole surgery methods for a narrowed spinal canal in the lower back. The narrowing, called lumbar spinal stenosis, squeezes nerves, causing leg pain and limited walking. Both methods use camera tools to free nerves, reaching the tight spot in different ways. The team reviewed one-level cases only, for a fair comparison.

Of 208 patients screened, 161 were included. The two-portal method took less operating time and a shorter hospital stay, yet caused more blood loss. The other method bled less. Both groups gained relief in pain and function scores over twelve months. One method recovered faster in early months and opened more space on scans, yet by twelve months results were alike. The authors say the choice should fit each patient's anatomy, illnesses, and the surgeon's skill. They call for randomized trials to confirm the picture.
pmc-13461834:
Kosuke Nakamae and Tatsuya Watanabe write a 2026 commentary on a problem in heart valve care: fitting a good-sized valve into a small aortic valve ring. Catheter-based valve replacement, called TAVI, now reaches younger and lower-risk patients who once faced open surgery. Care is now planned across a lifetime, so the first procedure shapes every later option.

The case they discuss shows the trap. A first catheter valve in a small ring failed, with high pressure gradients and leaking, yet a valve-in-valve fix risked a poor size match. Surgeons removed the failed valve and widened the ring with a Y-shaped cut before fitting a new valve. The authors argue surgical widening of the ring regains importance in this era. Choosing a roomy first valve, or widening at surgery, protects blood flow and keeps future fixes possible for patients with small anatomy.
pmc-13461934:
Bo Zeng, Hongyi Liu, and Qi Huang build, in a 2026 data study, computer models that predict one-year survival for pancreatic cancer patients aged 65 and older. Pancreatic cancer has a poor outlook, and most cases occur in this older group, whose health is often complex. Records came from a large US cancer registry for patients diagnosed between 2011 and 2015. Six learning methods were trained and compared.

5,601 patients entered the analysis. A screening method picked six key factors: whether surgery was done, tumor grade, depth of tumor growth, chemotherapy, radiation, and lymph node spread. The random forest model performed best, sorting survival well in training data and fairly well in validation data. A tool explaining model choices showed surgery as the strongest factor lifting one-year survival, while high tumor grade dragged it down most. The authors say such readable models can support personal treatment choices for older patients.
pmc-13462234:
Jinshan Yang leads a 2026 two-part study in Shanghai that builds a screening questionnaire for childhood allergy and uses it across a district. Allergic diseases weigh heavily on young children, whose immune systems are still settling. The 24-item tool was checked against doctors' diagnoses with 98 allergic children and 98 peers. It then surveyed 3,064 children up to age six in Minhang District.

The questionnaire sorted allergic from non-allergic children accurately, missing few cases. Survey results put food allergy in about fifteen percent of children, skin allergy near nineteen percent, hay-fever-type nose allergy at twenty percent, and asthma under nine percent. Boys, higher family status, only children, past antibiotic use or pneumonia, and allergy history each raised the odds. Longer sleep and open windows went with lower odds. Age effects differed by condition: skin allergy eased as children grew, while nose allergy rose.
pmc-13462334:
Xiangyi Meng and colleagues present, in a 2026 network science paper, a framework uniting many ways of measuring how strongly points in a network connect. Networks model everything from friendships to brain wiring, and influence travels along indirect paths. Familiar measures each stress one feature: shortest paths, electrical resistance, or the smallest cut splitting a network. Their relations were fragmented until now.

The unifying tool is a statistical physics model, the random cluster model, which treats connection as a blend of flow through chains and parallel routes. Turning its dials reproduces each measure as a special case. The same dials open new regimes, yielding fresh notions of connectivity. One gain is practical: the measure captures how paths grow over time, improving tasks such as forecasting epidemic spread and modeling brain dynamics. The authors offer it as a foundation joining structure, dynamics, and learning views of networks.
pmc-13462434:
Jee-Yun Leung and colleagues report a 2026 dental case from a 51-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis, a disease that hardens skin and harms small blood vessels. Over 14 years, 16 of her teeth showed invasive root resorption, a process in which tooth root is eaten away from outside. Scans, photos, and tissue study traced the damage tooth by tooth, a record rarely gathered in one patient.

Early clues came when two sore teeth were pulled and found eaten at the root edge, and later scans found ten more affected teeth. Tissue study showed bone filling the eaten spots, missing root cement, and chalk-like deposits in pulp and ligament. One jaw site later developed bone death linked to a bone drug, but it healed with gentle care. The authors urge dentists to hunt for these hidden lesions early in such patients.
pmc-13463134:
Florian Recker, Shavi Fernando, and Glenn D Posner introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a journal collection on education in obstetrics and gynecology covering 2025. The specialty carries an outsized share of health burden, sitting at the center of maternal survival and reproductive health. How the next generation learns is a population health question, not a teaching concern.

This volume gathers eleven studies spanning the learning path, from preclinical students to residents and fellows, across medicine, midwifery, and nursing. Data come from six countries, Germany and China among them, plus a multi-country European group. Simulation is the largest theme, now moving from technical drills toward forming the whole clinician, with trial evidence behind its gains in skill and confidence. Competency frameworks, digital and remote teaching, and an equity agenda run through the collection. The editors warn that access to these advances stays unequal in poorer settings.
pmc-13463534:
Mao and colleagues asked in 2026 whether leisure-time physical activity tracks with strength and everyday function in older adults. The tests covered grip strength, a timed chair stand, one-leg balance with eyes closed, and reaction time.

Grip strength was the one measure that rose with activity. Each extra hour of weekly leisure exercise linked to a small gain in grip. The gain was about six hundredths of a kilogram in the fully adjusted model of 418 people. The link held after accounting for sitting time. It also held after removing smokers and people with more chronic illness. No clear ties appeared for the chair stand, balance, or reaction time. Daily sedentary time showed no independent link to any measure.
pmc-13463934:
Yu Xia and nine co-authors blend physics with machine learning to watch kiwifruit juice quality during pasteurization. Their model reads light spectra and scent signals while a built-in physics rule anchors the forecasts.

pmc-13465234:

pmc-13465434:

Cost beliefs, government promotion, and pandemic effects also separated the groups.
pmc-13466334:
Helena Brawańska and co-authors compare hand caliper readings with digital ones for tooth widths on scanned plaster models, in a 2026 dental study. Thirty orthodontic patients supplied the models, which were scanned with a standard intraoral device. Teeth from canine to first molar in all four mouth quadrants were measured.

Each method was repeated after a day, and the averages of the pairs fed the comparison. The question matters because orthodontic planning leans on small width differences when judging spacing and crowding. Tooth-by-tooth analysis, rather than mouth totals, shows exactly where the two methods drift apart and where they agree closely enough for clinical use.
pmc-13466534:
Cezary Gaczyński and colleagues review the linked roles of oxidative stress and inflammation in artery plaque disease and ischemic stroke, in a 2026 article. Together these processes drive the world's leading cause of death, yet they are often studied apart. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen compounds damage vessel linings, oxidize fats, and switch on inflammatory pathways.

The review weighs candidate blood markers, from C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 to oxidation products and antioxidant enzyme activity, against risk and outcome data. It also judges how far such markers can guide personal treatment today, and where translation from lab insight to clinic keeps stalling. Emerging therapies aimed at the shared axis close the discussion.
pmc-13466634:
Jiang and co-authors profiled a 2026 medicinal herb, Emilia sonchifolia, to learn why its flavonoids, the plant chemicals behind much of its activity, gather unevenly across organs. pmc-13467634:
Ethan A. Mezoff and colleagues report a 2026 pilot trial of a human milk sugar supplement for preterm infants. Growth, feeding tolerance, and early brain-related behavior were tracked with a standard newborn neurobehavioral scale until discharge or 36 weeks corrected age. pmc-13468434:
Haoran Sheng and colleagues review in 2026 how polyurethane made by the prepolymer method can rescue aging asphalt. The trouble is compatibility: polyurethane and asphalt differ so much in polarity and density that they separate during storage and use. The prepolymer method tackles that by building the polyurethane partly in advance, tuning its chain length and segment mix before it ever meets hot asphalt.

Performance topics include high-temperature stability, moisture resistance, storage stability, and durability. By clarifying the modification mechanism, the authors aim to give road engineers a controllable recipe rather than a temperamental additive.
pmc-13469034:
Zhang and colleagues traced a kidney injury pathway in 2026 in preeclampsia, the dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy. pmc-13469234:

A detector pipeline alongside finds the person and regresses 2D keypoints even in murky frames.

The autoencoder is a learned model of how human bodies plausibly move underwater. Constraints keep the joints aligned with the image evidence while the prior pulls impossible poses back to legal ones. Underwater pose data serve swim training, diving safety, and marine robotics. A monocular method avoids the cost of multi-camera tanks. That is why the authors built the prior into the estimator itself.
pmc-13469834:
Zhang and co-authors interviewed a 2026 qualitative study of how different stakeholders decide on artificial intelligence tools for older adults' health care. Older adults and care partners cared most about out of pocket cost and ease of use in daily life. Payers focused on disease prevalence and how feasibly systems could roll tools out at scale. Suggestions included problem driven design, deeper stakeholder engagement, public private partnerships, and AI education for older adults.
pmc-13470634:
Konstantinos Tsingas built melPDomiX in 2026, a multi-omics resource of skin cancer patient-derived grafts. pmc-13471234:
Hani Lee and co-authors trace in 2026 the molecular controls that let platelets leave the bloodstream and enter tumors, and what that migration does to tumor growth. pmc-13471534:
Servais and co-authors distilled international expert practice for handling acute metabolic crises in maple syrup urine disease, a rare inherited disorder where the body cannot break down three amino acids. Their 2026 guidance came from eight specialist physicians who met in February 2025 after reviewing four guidelines and 20 further articles.

Steps escalate from stopping protein and flooding in carbohydrate calories to dialysis when neurological signs or stubborn levels demand it. pmc-13471634:
Xu and co-authors investigate in this 2026 study whether fine air pollution particles are linked to poor blood flow in the brain. The question was which chemical parts of the particles matter most, and whether inflammation in the blood helps explain any link.

Overall particle exposure was strongly tied to reduced brain flow, with black carbon and organic matter together accounting for most of the combined effect. pmc-13471734:
Dorota Janaszko and a large team dissect in 2026 how tin telluride nanowires oxidize unevenly beneath their surfaces. Tin migrates outward while oxygen creeps inward. The exchange hollows filaments that double as channels. Gold films trailing under the seed droplets shielded parts of the sidewalls from oxygen. Even a common titanium gold contact layer stole oxygen from the oxide without stopping the sorting.
pmc-13471834:

pmc-13472034:

pmc-13472934:
You and colleagues tested in 2026 whether the total bulk of active tumor on a PET scan forecasts outcomes in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer. Patients with high tumor volume fared much worse: about half were free of progression at two years, against about four in five for low-volume patients. Survival showed the same split. The authors caution that their cutoff needs testing at other centers.
pmc-13473034:

pmc-13473334:
Wang and colleagues asked in 2026 whether poor sitting posture helps explain the link between physical activity and adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, a sideways spine curve with no clear cause. pmc-13473534:

pmc-13474534:

pmc-13474834:

pmc-13475834:
Pskit-Hanuszczak and colleagues report a 2026 case of a five-year-old girl with Gorlin-Goltz syndrome, an inherited condition that can include benign heart tumors called cardiac fibromas. After surgery they implanted a loop recorder to watch her heart rhythm continuously. Over nine months of follow-up, the recorder found no episodes of sustained dangerous rhythm. pmc-13478134:

Kassen proposes that the layered structure of gene networks, local switches governed by global regulators, explains the pattern. He adds that global regulators likely move first in adaptation despite affecting many traits at once. Andrade frames the selection as a demonstration of approaches, not an exhaustive survey.
pmc-13478334:

pmc-13479534:

pmc-13479734:

pmc-13479834:

pmc-13480034:

pmc-13480134:

pmc-13480234:

pmc-13481634:

pmc-13482134:

Gene flow ran one way, with lake genes leaking a short way up the stream and then cut off. Computer runs built for this system showed that unlike needs of the two habitats can hold the steep line on their own. No past split was needed to explain it. The authors read the zone as proof that pure habitat based selection can keep two forms apart, and can help birth new species.
pmc-13483034:

pmc-13483234:

pmc-13483534:

pmc-13483634:

pmc-13483734:

pmc-13483834:

pmc-13486434:

pmc-13487934:

pmc-13488434:

pmc-13488734:
Qodirova Marhabo and co-authors write a 2026 letter critiquing a study of overactive bladder in rheumatoid arthritis. The original work linked bladder symptoms with central sensitization, a state where the nervous system amplifies signals. The letter writers call the findings useful for generating ideas, yet they raise three statistical concerns that could change how firmly the results should be read by clinicians.

First, the bladder questionnaire cutoff came from general primary care patients, not arthritis patients, and turning a graded scale into a yes-or-no split wastes information. Second, several predictors in the model overlap heavily, which can distort error estimates when overlap goes untested. Third, core regression assumptions, including outlier checks, were not verified in print. Better methods are requested.
pmc-13490034:
Şükriye Yeniçeri and Tulay Yilmaz Bingol study how remembered parental warmth or rejection relates to adult emotional life in a 2026 survey study. Seven hundred fifty adults were reached online through snowball sharing. They filled in scales on how accepted or rejected they felt by parents, how well they read feelings, how they cope, and how content family life feels. Data were gathered over five months spanning late 2021 and early 2022. Links among the four scales were tested with standard link and model methods.

Feeling rejected tracked with lower scores for reading feelings and for coping in the reported links. Ties with family contentment ran in a less tidy pattern across the analyses. Gender, income, having children, and family use of psychological help predicted rejection scores in the model. Whether parents were alive predicted some feeling scores.
pmc-13490234:
Shuxu Tian and colleagues review four cases of pelvic actinomycosis, a rare long-lasting bacterial infection, in a 2026 case series with a literature review. The infection, caused by Actinomyces germs, often follows years of intrauterine device use and mimics ovarian cancer or tuberculosis with pelvic masses. Four women treated between 2021 and 2025 had records reviewed for imaging, examination, cell samples, biopsies, and outcomes.

Every patient had long device use behind her symptoms. Scans showed masses with inflammatory features, while cell or tissue tests identified the germ in all four cases. Three women were diagnosed before any operation, sparing them major surgery. Long antibiotic courses resolved the illness in most patients, the authors report, urging earlier biopsy in similar presentations.
pmc-13490434:
Kabengele and team used first-principles calculations to see how attaching phosphonate groups changes the electronic personality of a tungsten-oxygen cluster. Such clusters could serve in light-driven chemistry if they absorb visible light usefully. Their 2026 study modeled a minimal tungsten-phosphonate unit with two levels of theory, locating where its frontier electrons live and how its energy levels line up against water-splitting benchmarks.

The filled frontier states sat mainly on the oxygen-rich ligand side, while the empty states sat on tungsten, a donor-acceptor split that favors charge transfer when light strikes. The finer calculation put the frontier energy gap at about 2.44 electron volts, squarely in the visible-light range of interest. Level positions straddled the relevant water redox benchmarks qualitatively. Kabengele offers the descriptors as screening tools for designing light-responsive tungsten materials.
pmc-13490734:
Chenxi Zhou, Brett McKinnon, and Hayden Homer reveal a quality control role for the cells hugging a mouse egg in a 2026 cell biology study. Cumulus cells cradle the egg and were known to hold it paused early in maturation through chemical signals. Using live imaging of labeled spindles, the structures that pull chromosomes apart, the team compared eggs matured with their cumulus coat against stripped eggs after mild DNA damage from a chemotherapy drug.

Coated eggs halted at a checkpoint stage, while stripped eggs pushed through despite similar DNA damage levels in the reported experiments. The halt needed an active spindle checkpoint, cell-to-cell channels, and a growth signaling pathway. Cumulus cells did not sharpen responses to minor spindle faults, which makes the DNA surveillance role specific.
pmc-13491534:
Noma and colleagues emulated a trial in a Japanese database, in a 2026 study. They asked whether starting a drug from the angiotensin receptor blocker class protects the brain better than a calcium channel blocker. Classes lower pressure equally but whether the drug mechanism affects dementia risk was unsettled. The analysis covered more than fifty-two thousand adults aged sixty-five and over starting one of the two drugs.

Noma followed patients for a median of over three and a half years, during which thirty-five hundred developed dementia, and used survival models handling dropout and death. Blocker starters had a lower dementia risk than channel-blocker starters, eight percent lower, despite similar blood pressure. The difference was not marked, but vascular dementia showed a stronger gap, with risk nearly forty percent lower. The authors read the pattern as a class effect concentrated in vessel-driven dementia.
pmc-13491934:
Xuan Qi and eight colleagues test in 2026 whether a fancier MRI technique can sort benign breast lumps from cancers better. Time-dependent diffusion imaging watches water molecules drift at different speeds, yielding clues about cell size and tissue structure that ordinary scans miss. Fifty-two patients, twenty-four with benign and twenty-eight with malignant lesions, completed the full scan set.

Several water-movement measures separated the groups, and a high-resolution diffusion value performed best among them. Among the structure-based scores, one reflecting cell diameter performed best of all, sorting about three quarters of patients correctly. A model combining the diffusion scores worked well, and adding standard clinical and imaging details pushed accuracy highest. The authors see the method as a useful second look rather than a replacement for conventional reading.
pmc-13492834:
Bashirian and colleagues report a 2026 study from Ahvaz, Iran, on why patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure do or do not follow treatment. They used Pender's health promotion model, a framework of beliefs that drive health behavior, extended with a perceived sensitivity construct. Patients answered a structured questionnaire on medication taking and low-salt diet habits.

Self-efficacy, belief in one's own ability, was the strongest driver of low-salt diet adherence and also lifted medication adherence. Feeling sensitive to the disease's threat helped the diet too, as did support from people around the patient. Perceived benefits unexpectedly worked against diet adherence, while perceived barriers undermined medication taking. Programs that build patient confidence and cut practical barriers should beat those that only list benefits, the pattern suggests.
pmc-13493834:
Arya Sabale leads a ten-author team releasing in 2026 a photo library meant to teach computers to grade rose petals by color and condition. Dutch roses earn export money across India, yet no public dataset captured petals themselves rather than whole flowers or leaves. The team photographed 1,995 high-resolution petal images near Pune's flower markets.

The collection spans eight color families, from red and white through bi-color and multi-color blooms. Each petal is also labeled fresh, dry, or diseased, so one dataset supports both variety sorting and health checks. Fine details like fading edges, curling, and fungal spots, invisible in whole-flower shots, become learnable at this scale. Growers, food and flavor makers who use edible petals, and cosmetics producers all stand to gain from automated grading.
pmc-13494534:
Abbas Hakim and a large team present a 2026 methods study building a fast, end-to-end pipeline for finding tiny RNA markers outside cells in human body fluids. These extracellular RNAs travel in blood and urine and could serve as blood-test style markers for disease, yet labs handle them in unlike ways. The team joined automated extraction, small RNA sequencing, and data analysis into one system and tested each step.

They compared automated extraction, including tricks to raise yield, against leading hand methods, using pregnancy as the test signal. Across fluids and methods, one analysis tool cut technical noise best while keeping true signal. Plasma gave the most repeatable results, then serum, while urine varied more. Known pregnancy-linked RNA clusters showed up as expected in plasma and serum. The authors offer the pipeline as a base for standard marker tests in clinics.
pmc-13494634:
Shogo Ohmae and Keiko Ohmae compare brain and artificial intelligence in a 2026 review, arguing that both rest on predictive world models. The neocortex and cerebellum share plain, repeating circuits yet support sight, movement, thought, and language. The authors propose that each builds an inner model of the world by predicting what comes next and learning from its errors.

Those models, once built for sensing, get reused to guide movement and higher thought. In the neocortex, they add, layered attention steers the work. Modern transformer AI, trained to predict the next word, landed on like principles by a wholly separate path. The shared base may explain how uniform circuits yield broad skill in both flesh and software. The authors offer the comparison as a guide for brain theory and for building more general AI alike.
pmc-13495234:
Lunmin Bao and a large team test, in a 2026 study, whether growing endometrial cancer fibroblasts in the lab changes what they are. These support cells, called cancer-associated fibroblasts, shape the soil a tumor grows in, and labs grow them through many rounds, called passages, before experiments. Whether long culture warps them, and so warps results, was unclear.

Cells from human tumors were compared at the first, fifth, and tenth passage. Shape, marker proteins, growth, movement, and aging held steady, and fluid from the cells boosted tumor cell growth and invasion alike at every stage. Gene reading told a split story: over a thousand genes shifted, with matrix-building traits stable but antigen-showing traits fading and an inflammatory style growing. Extra tests tied the drift to oxidative stress and a known inflammatory switch. The authors warn that late-passage cells still act alike but no longer read alike.
pmc-13495734:
Fiorentino, Hiller, and Urner solve a nagging problem in native mass spectrometry, the technique that weighs intact proteins and their complexes to see how they assemble. Proteins need salt to keep their natural shape, yet ordinary table salt ruins the measurement, coating the proteins and drowning the signal. Washing the salt away can break the very interactions under study. Their 2026 answer is a tree-shaped detergent additive, mixed into the sample before spraying it into the instrument.

With the additive present, spectra cleared up and signal quality rose for proteins from small myoglobin up to large four-part complexes. This held even in sodium chloride at strengths that normally defeat the method. The proteins kept their natural charge patterns, and complexes with lipids and drugs stayed intact. Magnetic resonance measurements suggested the detergent grabs the salt in solution, freeing the proteins before measurement.
pmc-13495834:
Iván Cortés Domínguez leads a team presenting, in a 2026 study, a 3D-printed skin window that lets microscopes watch tumors grow in living mice for weeks. Standard metal chambers are heavy, distress animals, and demand fiddly surgery. The printed chamber weighs under a gram, uses gentle resin, and clicks into place without sutures, easing the operation and calming inflammation afterward.

In mice carrying pancreatic tumor organoids, the window supported four imaging modes for up to four weeks: live microscopy, micro-CT, ultrasound, and fluorescence. Films showed tumors expanding, the surrounding scaffold packing its collagen fibers tighter, and a twisted web of new blood vessels forming. Immune cell tracking caught neutrophils switching from random wandering to directed marching toward the tumor. The authors pitch the design as a kinder, cheaper platform for studying how tumors, tissue, and immunity interact.
pmc-13499434:
Raghad Asim Abdulla Ahmed Shilla and co-authors report in 2026 three cases of anaphylactic shock, a sudden life-threatening allergic collapse, triggered by iodine-based dye used in CT scans. The cases arose at a medical corporation in Doha, Qatar. Such dyes are essential for modern scanning, and severe reactions remain rare and unpredictable, even with gentler modern agents and even in patients with no allergy history. Cases were found through incident reports and radiology records.

Two patients were women receiving dye for breast cancer staging, while the third was a man with several health conditions scanned for heart assessment. Each reacted shortly after the dye entered a vein, showing failure across at least two body systems. Treatment with adrenaline, steroids, antihistamines, and intravenous fluids brought full recovery for all three, with no lasting harm, which the authors use to stress readiness in every scan setting.
pmc-13499634:
Ousmane Kaba and co-authors warn in 2026 through a case report that celecoxib, a widely used pain reliever for joint pain, can trigger toxic epidermal necrolysis. The reaction is severe and potentially fatal, with the skin's surface layer dying and shedding. The drug is favoured for easier stomach tolerance, and most of its skin reactions are mild. Severe reactions of this specific type after celecoxib are poorly documented, which motivated the report alongside the drug's very wide use.

The authors set out why the reaction is so dangerous, noting its rarity at roughly two cases per million people per year and the risk carried once large skin areas are lost. Management rests on stopping the suspected drug at once, moving the patient quickly to a specialist unit, and providing intensive supportive care. Their aim is clinician awareness, since early recognition shapes survival in such reactions.
pmc-13499734:
Bent Estler and others assess semaglutide for heart failure with kept pumping share and obesity in Germany. In 2026, the Markov model, based on the STEP-HFpEF trial, compares semaglutide with placebo from statutory health insurance perspective. It tracks health states by symptom questionnaire quartiles and death over five years, plus a one-year budget impact analysis.

Semaglutide raised costs by about five thousand euros and quality-adjusted life years by 0.163, yielding about 30,443 euros per life year gained over five years, though the one-year ratio was far worse. Probability of cost-effectiveness at 100,000 euros was ninety-one percent, but one-year budget impact ranged from 168 to 864 million euros. Affordability and pricing will decide sustainable use.
pmc-13499834:
Hiroaki Kitaoka and co-authors survey in 2026 the burden carried by patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy in Japan and by the family members who care for them. In this progressive disease, a misfolded protein stiffens the heart, mostly in older men, and care needs grow over time. Data came from a cross-sectional programme running from October 2024 to January 2025, where cardiologists filed records and patients and caregivers answered voluntary questionnaires.

Twenty-five physicians provided data for 120 patients, over half of whom had a caregiver, most often a spouse living in the same home. The 22 caregivers who answered reported a median of twenty hours of care a week in the survey figures, with substantial loss of work productivity and daily activity. A standard burden scale found at least mild burden in most caregivers, leading the authors to pair calls for earlier diagnosis with stronger caregiver support.
pmc-13500834:
Yu Chen leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 prediction model for prostate cancer that has spread to pelvic lymph nodes. Surgeons must decide before operating whether to remove those nodes, a costly step, and older risk tools use only standard clinical variables. The team studied 315 men at one Chinese centre who had robot-assisted prostate removal, node dissection, and a PSMA PET/CT scan beforehand. Cases from 2020 to 2024 formed the development group of 210, and 105 cases from 2025 formed a later validation group.

Two elastic net models were built: one on clinicopathologic variables alone, one adding PSMA scan features. Across repeated splits of the development data the combined model averaged an AUC of 0.962 against 0.910 for the clinical-only model. In the 2025 group the combined model reached an AUC of 0.943, with a negative predictive value of 0.946, and beat a Memorial Sloan Kettering benchmark on decision curve analysis.
pmc-13501834:
Yaqiu Wu and Meixiong Cheng present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of the flipped classroom in medical education. In that model students study core material before class, and class time goes to discussion and application instead of lectures. Searching PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science, the pair found eighteen studies across varied learner groups. Outcomes were pooled in five domains: theoretical knowledge, procedural skills, self-directed learning, case analysis, and satisfaction.

Flipped teaching beat conventional methods in most domains, with moderate to large effect sizes. The clearest gains appeared in self-directed learning ability and procedural skills. Subgroup analysis suggested residents benefited most on skills and satisfaction. Sensitivity checks held the direction of results, though leaving single studies out sometimes erased significance. With high heterogeneity throughout, the authors call the benefits real but context dependent, and they ask future work to pin down when flipping works best.
pmc-13502634:
Francisco Sánchez-Férez leads a thirteen-author team with a 2026 framework chemistry strategy that plants defects in metal-organic frameworks where they belong. Defects usually scatter randomly through these crystalline sponges. Here pre-formed rhodium cages, molecular polyhedra with cavities, were assembled into HKUST-1-type networks while some three-armed linkers were swapped for two-armed versions missing one connection. Each swap leaves a copper vacancy confined inside a cage cavity, and nine distinct defect configurations arise.

Because these patterns distribute independently, the framework becomes aperiodic in its defect pattern while keeping long-range crystallinity. The materials gain hierarchical micro- and mesoporosity, breathe with solvent, and can lose and recover their crystal form reversibly. The authors frame cage-directed assembly as a programming language for disorder: choose the cage, choose the linker deficit, and the framework's adaptability, its capacity to flex and respond, follows from the design.
pmc-13503034:
Nicole Kuznetsov leads a thirty-three-author team presenting a 2026 deep learning pipeline, CNV-Finder, that hunts copy number variants in genotyping array data without drowning reviewers in false alarms. Arrays are cheap and global, but older callers flag far too many candidate deletions and duplications. The team trained long short-term memory networks on expert-annotated samples from the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program, covering four neurodegeneration genes, and folded human feedback back into training to sharpen the model iteratively.

Benchmarking spanned 105,936 samples across eleven ancestries and nearly 150 cohorts. At high-confidence thresholds, visual reviewers confirmed 91 percent of flagged PRKN deletions and 89 percent of duplications. Against a popular hidden Markov model caller in two validation cohorts, CNV-Finder nominated 83 percent fewer candidates while confirming at higher rates. Sequencing-based validation held up, and the model generalized to variant shapes absent from training. The software is freely available on GitHub.
pmc-13503134:
Zoi Laspa leads a ten-author team with a 2026 platelet study of how to stop hemin, the iron fragment released when red blood cells burst, from shredding platelet membranes. High hemin concentrations activate platelets, drive clotting, and destroy their plasma membrane, and platelet blockers do not prevent the destruction. The team's candidates were the two cyclic nucleotide messengers, cGMP and cAMP, the body's own brakes on platelet activation, raised through nitric oxide donors, the stimulator riociguat, prostaglandin E1, and PDE inhibitors.

Each lever alone tagged the protein VASP and curbed activation and granule release. The result was synergy: pushing both pathways together, tagging VASP at two sites at once, blunted both aggregation and the membrane fragmentation that single agents left untouched. Hemin itself distorted messenger production, cutting nitric-oxide-driven cGMP while boosting prostaglandin-driven cAMP. The authors propose combined riociguat, nitric oxide donor, and E1 treatment for haemolytic states.
pmc-13503834:
Joanna Klećkowska-Nawrot leads a team giving the first detailed account of the eyelids and eye glands of the crocodile monitor, in a 2026 study. This large tree-dwelling lizard preys by sight, yet the gear that guards its eyes was barely known. The work rests on two adult animals, so the authors treat it as a baseline sketch.

Slides under the microscope showed scaled lids with a dark, horn-like skin layer and a bone plate deep in the lid. The inner lid face held many mucus-making cells. A folding third eyelid carried cartilage and immune tissue. The large Harderian gland poured mostly acidic mucus onto that lid, while the small tear gland made acidic mucus alone. The maps aid vets and work on how lizard eyes are built.
pmc-13506634:
Faleh Abushahba and colleagues describe 2026 lab tests of a nano-scale titanium oxide coating meant to help titanium implants bond with bone faster. Discs received a hot-water treatment that forms the coating, then sat in a rich body-like fluid for two, four, or six hours. Surface tools tracked the calcium and phosphate layer that grew.

That mineral layer thickened as soaking time grew. Bone-like cells grew well on all surfaces, with no clear gap between groups. A marker of early bone formation rose on coated and longer-soaked discs. Cell shapes differed at day three, while coverage matched by day seven. Quick mineral growth may tune early cell response to implants.
pmc-13507134:
Rohan Bareja and colleagues benchmark, in 2026 work, thirty-two AI foundation models for computational pathology, the use of computers to read tissue slides. Models spanned general vision, general vision-language, and pathology-specific versions of both types. Tests used cancer slide tasks at whole-slide and small-patch levels from major public cohorts and outside datasets.

Pathology vision models ranked among the strongest on the main cohort, and beat pathology vision-language models overall. Rankings shifted modestly across outside datasets, and gaps among top models were often small. Bigger models and larger training sets did not reliably win. Blending model votes late in the pipeline lifted scores across sites and tissues. No single model fits every task.
pmc-13507534:
Tarcisse Baloki Ngoulou leads a large team reporting the genetic study of cholera bacteria taken from patients during the 2025 epidemic in the Republic of the Congo. The work names the strain as Vibrio cholerae O1, serotype Ogawa, and calls the clone highly virulent. Whole-genome sequencing, which reads the full DNA of the germ, linked the Congo strain directly to strains from Nigeria. The team also lists the main toxin and attachment genes the bacteria carry.

The genome showed resistance to several drugs, with named genes tied to that profile. Findings like these matter because cholera spreads fast across borders and can kill through severe fluid loss when care comes late. The authors call for cross-border coordination and mass vaccination. Readers get a compact genomic portrait of an outbreak strain and the risks it carries.
pmc-13508234:
Shengyuan Yu leads a ten-author team reporting long-term safety results for a migraine prevention drug in Asian patients with chronic migraine, in 2026 work. The drug, erenumab, blocks a receptor tied to migraine signals and is given as a monthly shot. This report follows the open-label extension of a phase 3 trial called DRAGON, held in China and other Asian countries. Of 557 patients in the earlier blinded phase, 456 entered this extension. They received 70-milligram monthly doses until the drug won approval locally.

Half of the group finished the extension, and typical exposure lasted about 80 weeks. About seven in ten patients reported at least one side effect during that span. Effects judged drug-related hit about one in seven patients, with constipation most common. Few patients, under three in a hundred, stopped the drug over side effects. Rating scales suggested benefit held up over time.
pmc-13508334:
Nisha Choudhary leads a nine-author team measuring anxiety during pregnancy in a rural district of western India, in 2026 work. Anxiety in pregnancy links to poor outcomes yet often goes unrecorded in antenatal care in poorer countries. The study covered 213 women in their second or third trimester at four primary health centers. A standard pregnancy anxiety questionnaire scored their worries, and surveys captured home, health, and social details.

A striking 84 percent of women showed pregnancy-related anxiety, most of it mild and about a quarter moderate. Fear of giving birth was the single biggest worry, followed by fears of an ill child and concerns about appearance. Women who already had children faced far higher odds of anxiety. A past lost pregnancy also raised the odds sharply. Hardship reaching a clinic and critical comments at home added risk. The authors urge routine anxiety screening inside antenatal visits.
pmc-13508434:
Yoojin Nam leads a twenty-one-author pilot study testing AI-written study materials for radiology trainees facing board exams, in 2026 work. A seven-step pipeline using a large language model produced six thousand flashcards, infographic summaries, and slide sets. Forty-one residents preparing for the Korean radiology boards enrolled. Materials were free to all, and the twenty-four who finished split themselves into users and non-users. The pilot judged feasibility: how many joined, stayed, and chose to use the materials.

Recruitment yield was high, yet only about three fifths of enrollees finished, below the bar. About three fifths of finishers chose to use the materials on their own. Survey scales for mental load and satisfaction held up fairly well, while a trust-in-AI scale fell short of reliability even after fixes. The authors treat the run as a rehearsal that exposed where the trial must tighten.
pmc-13508634:
Noémi Janszky leads a fourteen-author team studying a clot-stabilizing factor in a rare kidney vessel disease, in 2026 work. The disease, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, forms fibrin-rich clots in small vessels, and most research blames the complement immune arm. Factor XIII, the enzyme that locks fibrin clots firm, had never had a full workup here. The study covered 102 patients and 73 healthy controls. Blood activity and protein levels of the factor were measured, and its two genes were scanned for variants in patients during flare and remission.

Factor activity sank during acute flares compared with remission and with healthy controls. Gene scans found ten variants, with frequencies matching the wider European pool. Only one rare variant clearly lowered factor levels. The authors conclude the factor is unlikely to cause this disease, though its dip during flares marks disease activity.
pmc-13509334:
Wojciech Kuczyński and five co-authors ask who gains a survival benefit from CPAP, the nightly air-pressure therapy for obstructive sleep apnea, in 2026 work. The group followed 4368 adults sent for sleep testing at one center, tracking deaths over eight to twenty years. They sorted patients by disease severity and by how well the therapy controlled breathing pauses during use.

CPAP use went with lower death rates overall, yet the gain sat mainly in severe disease and in people who responded well to treatment. Poor responders showed no clear gain, and moderate disease showed none either. Time spent with low blood oxygen at night proved the strongest driver of lung-related death. The authors argue that support should focus first on severe cases, with device readings used as a target to improve.
pmc-13509534:
Marina Khodanovich and co-authors use a magnetic resonance measure of myelin, the fatty coating on nerve fibers, to compare brain change across several conditions in 2026 work. The group scanned 196 people in total: patients with multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, or long COVID, plus healthy volunteers across a wide age span. Scans focused on tissue that looked normal, away from visible spots of damage.

Myelin readings fell in normal aging at older ages and in all three patient groups, with the steepest drop in multiple sclerosis. Lower readings tracked worse disability scores in multiple sclerosis and later disease stage in Parkinson disease. Among long COVID patients, the largest drops appeared in those with low mood and poor sleep after infection. Healthy myelin peaked in the early to late forties, depending on the tissue measured.
pmc-13509734:
Tomasz Urbanowicz and Krzysztof Filipiak propose in this 2026 article that years of breathing polluted air leave heart surgery patients primed for oxidative damage, harm caused by reactive oxygen molecules. Coronary bypass grafting is a proven fix for advanced heart artery disease, yet recovery varies widely between similar patients.

The authors argue that chronic exposure to particles, nitrogen oxides, and ozone quietly wears down vessel linings, drains antioxidant reserves, and keeps inflammation simmering before surgery. The operation then lands as a second oxidative blow on that weakened ground. This idea, which they call environmental oxidative priming, could explain uneven complications and survival. They suggest future risk scores should count pollution exposure, not just clinical factors.
pmc-13511134:
Allard, Kumar, and Tamura present a software toolkit for studying convergent evolution in this 2026 paper. Convergence is when unrelated species independently evolve similar traits, and shared DNA changes behind those traits can reveal how adaptation works. Their method, called ESL-PSC, fits sparse predictive models to contrasts between paired species, but it previously demanded strong command-line skills.

The toolkit wraps the method in a graphical interface that guides users from setup to interpretation without heavy technical expertise. It checks inputs and lets users pick species pairs on an interactive family tree. Analyses run live. Users can then explore ranked genes and DNA sites. The engine was rewritten in the Rust programming language with parallel processing, cutting runtimes, and packaged versions run on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
pmc-13513534:
Mohamed Abderemane Nourdine and eleven co-authors establish the first stable laboratory colony of a coastal malaria mosquito in Senegal and profile its insecticide resistance, in 2026 work. This species, Anopheles melas, breeds in salty coastal water and bites outdoors, slipping past indoor nets and sprays. Tuning water saltiness to the right level let the team breed it reliably in captivity for the first time.

Tests showed strong resistance to the pyrethroid chemicals used on standard bed nets. Adding a neutralizing chemical that blocks the resistance machinery restored full killing power, which points to advanced nets carrying that blocker. The colony stayed fully vulnerable to two other public health chemical classes. The authors recommend handing coastal communities the advanced nets and rotating spray chemicals, so resistance in this outdoor biter does not undo Senegal's malaria gains.
pmc-13513734:
Yang Xia and seven co-authors automate the slowest step of hyperspectral insect analysis for forensic work, in 2026 work. Hyperspectral cameras record an image plus a full light spectrum per point, which can reveal an insect's age and species, clues to time of death. Analysts usually draw regions of interest by hand before pulling spectra, a slow habit that resists standard practice.

The new workflow segments insect bodies on its own and extracts one spectrum per individual. Tested on larvae, pupae, and adults of forensically important species, it matched every individual in the independent test set against hand annotations. Spectra from the automatic regions closely matched those from manual ones. The authors say the pipeline cuts manual labor and makes insect spectral work easier to repeat across labs, a base for court-facing methods that must be standardized.
pmc-13514334:
Longzhen Qiu leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 pilot trial of very short stair-climbing workouts for inactive university students. Twenty-three sedentary young men finished, split among stair climbing alone, stair climbing with cuffs that briefly restrict blood flow in the legs, and a control group. Sessions ran over four weeks, each built from three climbs of twenty seconds at full effort.

Both training groups improved lung capacity, flexibility, sprint times, and a 1000 metre run, while body mass index stayed put. The cuff group gained extra ground in the standing long jump and showed larger sprint and endurance gains, though differences between the training groups were not firm. The control group actually lost jump distance. Qiu's team reads the pattern as promising for busy students, while calling for bigger trials to confirm the cuffs' added value.
pmc-13514734:
Deborah A Jehu leads a sixteen-author team reporting a 2026 secondary analysis of a randomised trial on exercise and inflammation in people living with dementia. Forty-two residential care residents were assigned to six months of therapist-led strength and balance training plus walking, three times a week, or to usual care alone. Blood samples at the start and at six months let the team track circulating inflammatory signals.

Counting everyone as assigned, the exercise and usual-care groups did not differ. Restricting the analysis to residents who actually exercised at least twice weekly told a softer story. Two inflammatory markers drifted down in the exercise group while rising under usual care, though those trends stopped short of firm statistical ground. Jehu's team reads the pattern as a possible benefit that depends on sticking with the programme.
pmc-13515634:
Chen and co-authors dissect two regulator genes in a fungus that hunts worms. Their 2026 paper studies Arthrobotrys oligospora, a nematode-trapping fungus of interest for crop protection, and two sporulation regulators, AoFlbB and AoFlbD, conserved across its relatives. Deleting each gene revealed how reproduction and predation are coordinated in this organism.

Both deletions left growth nearly untouched but sharply cut spore production and changed how spores germinated, confirming positive roles in sporulation. Unexpectedly, the mutants built more traps and caught nematodes more efficiently. Each mutant also showed its own quirks: one had wrinkled cell walls, the other accumulated vesicle-like structures, sped up dye uptake, and lost some protease activity. Gene activity profiling of one mutant pointed at metabolism pathways. The authors conclude the two regulators balance making spores against making traps.
pmc-13515734:
Amil Orahovac and four colleagues present ten years of surveillance for Listeria in Montenegro's traditional cured meats, in a 2026 study. Listeria monocytogenes is among the deadliest foodborne germs, and ready-to-eat meats are a prime route to people. Small-scale dry-cured and fermented products pose special control problems. The team drew on the national food control system for results from 2016 to 2025, covering 2,471 samples across fifty-eight product varieties.

Overall, about six point six percent of samples carried the germ, swinging widely by year. Dry-fermented sausages and cured belly showed far higher rates than whole-muscle products such as pršut. One celebrated sausage, Njeguška kobasica, topped the list, and its vacuum-packed version approached half of samples positive. No steady trend over the decade appeared. Orahovac's team urges regulators to shift focus from testing finished goods toward watching the production environment, backed by genome-based tracking.
pmc-13517234:
Beatriz C Rocha, Manuela D Machado, and Eduardo V Soares test an antibiotic-herbicide mixture on a freshwater alga in a 2026 study. Erythromycin from medicine and metolachlor from farm fields both wash into waterways, where they meet. The team first measured each chemical's effect level on Raphidocelis subcapitata over seventy-two hours. Then they mixed the two at matched effect levels and compared outcomes with an independent-action model.

Growth inhibition turned stronger together: the pair hurt the alga more than the model predicted. Photosynthesis sagged overall, with efficiency and electron flow both down. Yet the herbicide blunted the antibiotic's photosynthetic damage at low antibiotic levels, a counter-twist. Pigments rose, as if making up the loss, though less than the model expected. Rocha's team reads the mix as a warning that single-chemical safety tests understate what rivers actually serve to algae.
pmc-13518834:
Luka Lazović, Branka Jokanovic, Vesna Rubežić, and Ana Jovanović describe a 2026 compact antenna shaped like a heart-like fractal curve, built to work across an ultra-wide 4 to 30 gigahertz range. One small antenna serving many wireless systems suits crowded device networks and radio energy harvesting. Printed designs are cheap but usually narrowband.

Their monopole was printed on low-cost FR-4 board and measured after fabrication. Results matched simulations, with return loss below the minus 10 decibel mark across much of the band, gain reaching 5 dBi and efficiency reaching 80 percent. Impedance behavior also fits direct connection to harvesting circuits without a matching network, easing use in sensors.
pmc-13520334:
Nikolina Peranić and colleagues test in 2026 whether tiny plastic bits can disturb hormone signals in lab cells. The team used eight particle types. The set covered four common plastics and several sizes. Standard lab tests checked two hormone pathways and hormone output.

No cell harm appeared at any dose in the tested range. Two plastic types switched on the female hormone pathway at some sizes. One type also blocked the male hormone pathway. Two types alone showed no effect at all. Some mixed samples did respond. Hormone output itself stayed steady. The results show that plastic type and particle size both shape the effect.
pmc-13520534:
Pan Ding, Qinghua Luo and Leihua Cao rate in 2026 short videos about prostatitis on TikTok and Bilibili for quality, reliability and completeness. Prostate inflammation causes heavy patient anxiety, while video platforms now serve as a first source of health answers.

A total of 223 videos were scored with standard quality tools plus a six-domain clinical checklist. Overall quality sat at a moderate level, with treatment topics dominating while awareness, diagnosis and prevention lagged. Clinician uploads scored clearly higher than lay uploads. TikTok entries outscored Bilibili entries, while popularity signals linked only weakly with quality, warning viewers against trusting view counts.
pmc-13521534:
Mittal and colleagues compared in 2026 gentler alternatives to root canal treatment for badly inflamed tooth pulp. Sixty-eight patients aged fifteen to thirty-five with exposed molar pulp were randomised to four groups. They received coronal or partial radicular pulpotomy, removing part of the pulp, sealed with chitosan or platelet-rich fibrin.

All groups showed significant pain reduction and healing on imaging over twelve months. Overall survival was about eighty-eight percent of teeth at one year. The partial radicular pulpotomy with platelet-rich fibrin group did best, at about ninety-four percent survival. Differences between groups were not significant, though. The authors conclude both pulpotomy types performed well. The partial procedure with either dressing, they say, is a reliable, less invasive alternative to full root canal therapy for suitable molars.
pmc-13523534:
Gillian A. Folk, Naomi E. Wagner, Evan H. Walker, and Shyamanga Borooah survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how people with PRPH2-associated retinal degeneration rate their own vision and quality of life. This inherited condition is among the commonest causes of inherited retinal disease. Genetic and clinical features were known, while patient experience was less described.

Twenty-two patients with confirmed disease at one academic center completed the National Eye Institute Visual Function Questionnaire-25, which covers eleven vision domains. The median composite score was 76.9, indicating moderate perceived difficulty. Color vision and eye pain scored highest, while general vision, near and distance tasks, and driving scored lower. Vision-related mental health scored lowest of all, underlining psychological impact. The authors urge routine patient-reported measures in care and in future treatment trials.
pmc-13523734:
Safford and colleagues found a way to make RNA medicines work better in the placenta, the organ that supports a pregnancy, in a 2026 mouse study. Fat-based nanoparticles can carry RNA instructions into placental cells, but circular RNA, a durable ring form, translated poorly despite working well in lab dishes. The team suspected the innate immune system, the body's first-response defense network, was throttling production.

Safford blocked that defense pathway at its interferon receptor and at the JAK-STAT signaling chain behind it. The blockade raised circular RNA output up to about twelvefold in maternal organs. It lifted placental production of circular and standard RNA by larger margins, roughly seventeenfold and fourfold at best. The boost also applied to RNA encoding a blood-vessel growth factor relevant to preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy disorder, suggesting immune calming as a general lever for RNA therapy in pregnancy.
pmc-13524434:
Elmostafa Benaissa, Najwa Hnach, Yassine Ben Lahlou, and Mariama Chadli review, in a 2026 paper, human infections caused by Cellulosimicrobium, bacteria rarely seen as a cause of disease. These rods are often written off as culture contaminants, so true infections may be missed. Reports so far rest on case reports and small series.

Noted infections most often involve the bloodstream, heart valves, bones and joints, peritonitis tied to dialysis, and the eye. Most patients have cancer, are on dialysis, carry valve implants or tubes left in place, or have weak immune systems. Proof needs more than one positive culture, growth from a normally germ-free site, and modern methods such as mass spectrometry or gene tests. Vancomycin and a sulfa drug pair mostly still work, while some other drug classes fail. Care pairs chosen antibiotics with removal of infected devices where it can be done.
pmc-13526734:
Ying Yan and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 real-world study, breast cancer that has spread to the lungs. They ask how often the metastasis changes hormone and growth receptor status compared with the original tumor. Such changes can redirect systemic therapy, and biopsies also separate true spread from a new primary lung cancer.

At Peking University Cancer Hospital between 2010 and 2024, 180 biopsied patients were identified from nearly three thousand with lung nodules. Of these, 154 proved to have breast cancer metastases while the rest had primary lung cancers. Among 128 patients with full receptor profiles, overall discordance was eighteen percent, highest for the progesterone receptor. Three-year survival differed sharply by metastatic subtype, exceeding ninety-four percent for hormone-positive groups but falling near sixty-five percent for triple-negative disease.
pmc-13526834:
Liu and co-authors emulate a clinical trial from health records, in this 2026 study. The population is neglected: diabetic patients on dialysis for end-stage kidney disease who also have heart failure. Such patients are routinely excluded from randomized trials. Using the TriNetX records network with a new-user design and matched comparisons, they contrasted starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist against starting a DPP-4 inhibitor, two diabetes drug classes.

The GLP-1 drugs won clearly. The combined outcome of ischemic cardiovascular events and heart failure flare-ups occurred in 31.7 percent of GLP-1 starters versus 41.4 percent on the comparator, a hazard ratio of 0.72 in the matched analysis, and all-cause mortality also fell, with a hazard ratio of 0.68 in the same model. A second, more strictly defined dialysis population reproduced the benefit. The authors call for a real randomized trial while offering this as the best current evidence for these patients.
pmc-13527134:
Xingfeng Li and others present a 2026 model of how brain architecture across regions changes during Alzheimer's neurodegeneration. Their earlier machine learning approach, built on MRI, separated Alzheimer's-related pathology from other pathology well at one scanner strength but carried poorly to stronger scanners. The update fixes that weakness and extends across time.

Radiomic features were taken from each brain region in scans from 1,592 people imaged at the stronger field strength. A logistic model sorted Alzheimer's-related against unrelated pathology with an accuracy area of 0.84 in held-out data, and outside data sets scored between 0.70 and 0.96. A second model split mild cognitive impairment from full Alzheimer's disease with an area of 0.79 in held-out testing.
pmc-13528034:
Mélissa Côté and four colleagues map how family members cope when a loved one has an addiction in a 2026 scoping review. The addictions covered alcohol, drugs, gambling, and screen use. Six databases were searched. Sixty-four studies met the criteria.

Most studies, about sixty-four percent, dealt with substance use. About twenty-six percent dealt with gambling. Screen addiction drew only a few studies. Relatives used many strategies. Some tried to change the loved one's behavior. Others protected their own, their couple's, or their family's wellbeing. New strategies appeared that older frameworks had missed. Coping looked broadly similar across substance and gambling settings. The authors note that screen-related coping is barely studied. They call relatives central players whose own needs deserve support.
pmc-13528334:
Matthew Brown and Naomi Herz assess generative AI for mental health care in a 2026 commentary. Mental illness touches one in two people over a lifetime. Nearly 1.2 billion people lived with a disorder in 2023. Many cannot reach care that helps. The pair argue chatbots could offer support at unmatched scale.

The risks are stark, they warn. Tools may miss self-harm signals or fail to act. Flattering replies can feed delusions. Training data can carry cultural bias. Writing from the Wellcome funder's view, they back research on anxiety, depression, and psychosis tools. Teams in poorer countries are part of that push. They fear a two-tier future: therapists for the rich, chatbots for the poor. Lived-experience voices and clear rules must shape deployment, they argue.
pmc-13529734:
Fan-xiu Meng and five colleagues fuse three kinds of data to forecast survival after gallbladder cancer surgery in a 2026 study. Records covered 177 patients at two hospitals from 2017 to 2023. Separate models read CT scans, tissue slide images, and plain clinical facts. A late fusion step merged the three streams into one nomogram for each patient.

The scan model alone scored 0.88 on the ranking curve, while the tissue and clinical models trailed well behind it. The fused version topped them all at 0.90 on the same curve. It caught about ninety percent of deaths while keeping false alarms modest. Risk groups split cleanly on survival curves. The authors call the result preliminary, given the small cohort. They see a path to personal risk talks before and after surgery.
pmc-13534734:
Amanda Dibden and colleagues assess in 2026 long-term effects of the NHS breast screening programme in England and Wales over up to 33 years. Most past studies covered only short or medium spans after screening. The cohort held over 2.5 million women aged 49 to 64 who began uninvited.

Invitation to screening linked to a clear drop in breast cancer deaths, and attending screening linked to a larger drop. Screened women had a small excess of diagnoses after long follow-up, suggesting low overdiagnosis. Benefit thus persists many years after screening ends. The cohort design avoids the self-selection bias that can inflate effects in volunteer studies of screening.
pmc-13536234:
Roberts and colleagues published a 2026 study on how bird traits shape forest habitat needs. Appalachian forests vary in height layers and side-to-side patch patterns. The team paired space-based laser maps of forests with crowd-sourced bird sightings. They asked which body and behavior traits predict touchiness to forest shape.

Climate and height above sea level explained the most bird variation overall. Birds with narrow feeding layers reacted most to vertical forest structure. Large birds with strong flight barely reacted to either forest measure. Diet and nest height also played roles, with fuzzier signals behind them. Traits, the authors argue, help forecast which birds suffer as forests change. Laser maps from space made the broad-scale test possible at all.
pmc-13536734:
Rui Zhang and co-authors show that time of day shapes light-based cancer therapy in a 2026 mouse study. Photodynamic therapy uses light to activate a drug inside tumors, and its benefit varied with the body clock. Tumors in two mouse lines were treated at different clock times, while immune cells in tumors and blood were counted and profiled. Special mouse groups tested whether immune cells drive the rhythm.

Treatment worked best at one daytime point and weakest late at night, a pattern that persisted without light cues and flipped when light cycles flipped. Removing key immune guide cells erased both the rhythm and related T cell patterns. Gene profiles showed daytime guide cells favored anti-tumor defense. The authors argue that scheduling treatment by clock time could raise benefit.
pmc-13536834:
Berhan Bayram and co-authors compare two arthroscopic repairs for massive shoulder tendon tears that cannot be fully rejoined in a 2026 follow-up study. One option repairs part of the tendon, while the other rebuilds the upper capsule with thigh tissue grafts. Forty patients treated between 2017 and 2021 were split evenly between methods. Pain, function, disability, and joint space measures were compared after at least thirty-two months.

Both groups improved clearly on pain, function, disability, and joint space compared with before surgery. No clear gap separated the two methods on any clinical or scan measure. Graft-related problems affected three patients in the rebuild group and none in the partial repair group, a gap too small for firm judgment. The authors suggest partial repair may suffice for this tear type.
pmc-13538234:
Brian Hess and colleagues run a phase I safety study adding an oral methylation drug to salvage chemotherapy for returned large B-cell lymphoma in a 2026 report. Faulty gene silencing helps lymphoma resist chemotherapy, and the added drug aims to reverse that silencing. Transplant-ready patients received standard salvage drugs plus oral azacitidine at two dose levels under a classic dose-climbing design. Nine patients took part across the dose groups.

Baseline details show most patients relapsed within a year of first treatment, spanning several lymphoma subtypes. Dose records track missed azacitidine doses blamed on low blood counts, most often at the higher dose level. The report centers on safety and workability of the pairing rather than cure rates. The authors frame the combination as a step toward testing whether gene reawakening restores drug sensitivity.
pmc-13540834:
Qian Zhu leads a 2026 study characterising an enzyme dug out of salty, alkaline soil near Karamay in Xinjiang, China. The enzyme, a beta-glucosidase, helps break plant cellulose into glucose, yet industrial versions often stall in salty, alkaline liquors rich in glucose.

Produced in laboratory bacteria, the enzyme B0-BG40 worked best in warm, alkaline conditions and kept most of its activity across wide ranges of heat and acidity. It tolerated heavy salt and very high glucose with unusually weak product inhibition. Shape modelling suggested a narrow, deep channel that keeps glucose from crowding the active site. The authors pitch it for food, feed, and biofuel work.
pmc-13541534:
Huihui Zhang and colleagues trialed a healing mushroom brew for immune rebound after colon cancer chemo. Published in 2026, the forward-looking random trial took in bowel cancer patients who had finished chemo between January 2021 and June 2024. Chemo often dents immune strength and worsens outlook, yet proof for this fungus brew was thin.

Patients were split 1 to 4 to 1 among dummy pills, mushroom brew, and thymalfasin for eight weeks. The brew group gained helper T cells and natural killer cells, raised attack signals, and lowered swelling signals, while life-quality scores rose. Side-effect rates matched the controls. Patients with a spleen-kidney weakness pattern did best. The authors present the brew as a safe immune aid after chemo, most of all for that pattern.
pmc-13542134:
Z L Jacobs and colleagues project an ocean change in a 2026 study. The subject is the Somali upwelling off East Africa. That seasonal surge of rich water feeds major fisheries. At its peak it is the world's strongest upwelling. Coarse climate models blur this narrow coastal system. The team used finer tools.

A high-resolution projection fed a size-based food web model. Reliable catch data were lacking, hence that model choice. Overall productivity falls by the end of the century. Coastal waters may grow richer as winds shift. The Somali Current shifts with them. That pattern shelters small-scale fishers near shore. Offshore, in the Great Whirl region, biomass falls instead.
pmc-13542234:
Jiao Xiang and colleagues published a 2026 methods study on insulin dosing decisions when glucose monitor data have gaps. Their decision framework treats diabetes care as a partially observable Markov decision process, meaning each dose choice depends on an incomplete picture of the patient. Real glucose traces from a Stanford monitoring database were deliberately damaged under random and block missing patterns, at rates from 5 to 25 percent, then repaired three different ways.

Simple mean filling produced the largest repair errors and the greatest drift from the decisions reached with complete data. Filling gaps by straight-line interpolation worked far better, and a bridge-based sampling algorithm matched it closely while handling curved after-meal segments and long gaps better. The authors conclude that repair methods respecting time order should replace mean filling when monitor data feed dosing policies.
pmc-13543434:
Gyeong-min Lee and colleagues published a 2026 study of whether life satisfaction cushions the drop in active ageing that often follows retirement. Active ageing combines health, participation, and security into one index. Using the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing from 2014 to 2022, the team followed adults aged fifty-five and over who retired during the window. They matched satisfied and less satisfied retirees on background traits and compared index trajectories around the retirement moment.

People with higher life satisfaction kept higher active-ageing scores at every point around retirement. Statistical models suggested their post-retirement decline was gentler, with the clearest buffering for health at retirement and for participation at some later points. Security showed no such interaction. Treating subjective wellbeing as a resource worth building before retirement, through policy or programmes, might help retirees stay engaged and resilient.
pmc-13543534:
Gulsen Filazoglu Cokluk asked disaster-hit teens in Turkey how workable group trauma therapy felt to them. Published in 2026, the mixed-methods study covered 120 teens aged 13 to 18 from earthquake- and flood-hit regions. Teens after disasters often develop trauma stress, yet whether group eye-movement therapy would work for them was little studied.

Teens with heavier trauma stress rated the therapy less workable, while hardier teens rated it more welcome. Ratings and toughness both shifted across trauma levels. Blocks named were unruly emotions, privacy worries, and timing clashes, while peer backing and structured prep work helped. The author urges teaching prep, loose plans, and feeling safety to lift teen buy-in after disasters.
pmc-13546534:
Manali Shah and co-authors compared in 2026 hospital care for colorectal cancer diagnosed before age 50 with the same disease at older ages. Their data came from a national sample of United States hospital stays from 2016 to 2020. Among more than 246,000 cancer hospitalizations, about 14 percent involved younger patients. The two groups differed in who they were as much as in how they fared.

Younger patients were more often female, Black, Hispanic, or Asian, and more often covered by Medicaid or private insurance. They carried higher rates of tobacco use and depression, received chemotherapy in hospital far more often, and died during the stay less often than older patients. Obesity raised the odds of early-onset disease. The authors argue for screening and care strategies aimed at younger, underserved groups.
pmc-13547234:
Behrouz Adibimanesh and colleagues developed in 2026 a digital shadow for the sludge incineration line of a wastewater treatment plant. A digital shadow is a live simulation mirror of the real line. Their goal was cutting the biogas the process burns. Their model reproduces the furnace, dryer, mixer, and heat exchangers using a mix of physical equations and real operating data from the plant, then runs inside a feedback control setup.

Five operating scenarios were tested against historical plant behavior. The best scenario cut biogas use by about 40 percent while keeping furnace temperatures inside the range European standards require. The authors present the shadow as a decision aid that can find savings without experimenting on the live plant.
pmc-13547434:
Aina March-Yagüe and the MONKPOX-ESP22 working group examined in 2026 how many men with mpox in the 2022 Spanish outbreak had recently been diagnosed with another sexually transmitted infection. Surveillance services in seven regions enrolled 1,202 cases, nearly all men, between June 2022 and January 2023.
