Histories of infection in the prior one and six months were compared against behavior and health profiles.

About thirty-six percent of the men had another such diagnosis in the six months before mpox. That history clustered with chemsex practice, sex in leisure venues, living with HIV, and especially use of preventive HIV medication, which carried more than four times the odds. Illness severity and hospital stays did not differ by history. The authors argue for prevention programs that treat these infections as one connected problem.
pmc-13548534:
Dilşad Dereli and Baran Tokar review long-term kidney outcomes for boys born with posterior urethral valves, in a 2026 single-center study from Turkey. These valves block the bladder outlet and are the commonest cause of such obstruction in boys, sometimes alongside other birth anomalies. The authors followed 103 boys diagnosed and treated at one university clinic between 2014 and 2024, checking which features tracked with lasting kidney disease.

About four in ten boys showed swollen urinary tracts before birth, and a similar share had urine reflux toward the kidneys. Extra anomalies included hypospadias, blocked kidney drainage, underdeveloped kidneys, and spina bifida. Eight boys developed significant chronic kidney disease during follow-up. Poor outcomes clustered where reflux was severe, kidney tissue was already abnormal, or several anomalies combined, so the authors stress careful lifelong follow-up for that group.
pmc-13548634:
Yanian Ren and colleagues review how stem cells are being used to model and treat diseases of the intestine, in a 2026 article. Gut disorders arise partly from broken communication among microbes, immune cells, and the intestinal lining. Stem cells can renew themselves and turn into many cell types, which makes them attractive both for building disease models and for therapy.

The review covers gut organoids, miniature intestinal structures grown from human pluripotent stem cells, used to recreate disease in the dish. It then examines cell treatments for inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal infections, and colorectal cancer, explaining repair through cell replacement, secreted signals, and immune balancing. Hurdles include ethics oversight, cell variability, and quality control. New tools such as single-cell sequencing, gene editing, and three-dimensional printing are presented as the field's next accelerators.
pmc-13549134:
Angelo Corti and colleagues engineer antibody-like carriers that home in on two integrins found on many solid tumors, in a 2026 cancer study. These integrins switch on a growth factor, TGF-beta, that helps tumors hide from the immune system. A small peptide from a natural hormone blocks that switching. Fusing the peptide to antibody tail pieces created peptibodies that grip the integrins extremely tightly.

The constructs recognized only integrin-positive tumor cells, blocked growth factor activation, slipped inside cells, and rode to the lysosome, the cell's disposal unit. Hitched to drug-loaded antibodies, they ferried several potent poisons selectively into target cells. In mice, one peptibody slowed fibrosarcoma growth and, paired with a checkpoint immunotherapy drug, improved survival in a breast tumor model without obvious toxicity. The authors propose the platform for targeted delivery that also loosens immune suppression.
pmc-13550534:
Junhao Chen and colleagues build a physics model that predicts how red clay's electrical response changes with water content, sharpening ground-penetrating radar surveys, in a 2026 study. Radar estimates soil moisture from the dielectric constant, yet clay holds much of its water bound to particle surfaces, where it behaves unlike free water. Working with red clay from Guiyang, the team measured its makeup and water-holding limits, then split bound water into strongly and weakly held layers using adsorption tests.

Strongly bound water topped out near three percent and weakly bound near seventeen percent of the soil. A four-ingredient mixing model, blending air, dry soil, bound water, and free water with texture and frequency corrections, matched measured permittivity closely across the bound-water range. The authors say the model tells surveyors the moisture window where radar inversion can be trusted in red clay country.
pmc-13550634:
Gabriela Krupincová and Mercedes Pereira published a 2026 study, the third in a series, on fiber fragments shed by recycled cotton fabrics during washing. Shedding pollutes water, and recycled cotton may shed differently from new fiber. Three recycled blends were spun into weft yarns, woven with high-quality Egyptian cotton warps, dyed in two shades, and washed five times under strong agitation.

Released particles were counted and measured by image analysis, then sorted into dust, trash, single fragments, and bundles. Yarn quality and dye state changed how much material came out, with the most contaminated yarn shedding most at first. Later cycles showed less loose material but more fiber fatigue, and fragment lengths fell into ultrashort, short, and long groups.
pmc-13551534:
Heidi Espadas-Álvarez and Verónica Valverde-Garduño published a 2026 study of a gene switch in a malaria mosquito. The species, Anopheles albimanus, spreads malaria in the Americas. A switch called lola had been spotted near immune genes in a related species. The team weakened lola in live mosquitoes. They then tracked survival and gene activity after infection.

Mosquitoes with weak lola died more readily from germs. Many defense genes failed to switch on without it. The affected genes make germ-killing proteins and sensing proteins. Others make or clean up reactive oxygen, a harsh cell chemical. A signaling path called JNK was hit too. The team says lola runs much of the mosquito's defense.
pmc-13551934:
Mei Xie and nine colleagues catalogued heat shock genes in the Chinese giant salamander in a 2026 study. The animal is critically endangered and very sensitive to warm water. Heat shock proteins help cells survive stress. The team used gene data from captive animals stressed by heat and germs together. They named the family members and traced their evolution and activity.

Seventy-two heat shock genes fell into five subfamilies. Each subfamily looked conserved over time. Germ infection switched many genes on. Heat made that response stronger. Nine key genes stood out, most from the HSP70 subfamily. One gene answered heat with special speed. The team offers the catalogue as a base for breeding this species under warming conditions.
pmc-13554134:
Qi Wang and three colleagues study how rude customers wear down front-line staff in China in a 2026 survey. Rudeness from customers is common for people who serve the public. The team asked whether such treatment drains workers until they stop going the extra mile for customers. Surveys came in three waves, three weeks apart, from customer-contact staff.

Rude treatment raised emotional exhaustion, and exhaustion in turn cut proactive service. Workers with a proactive streak suffered less drain from the same rudeness. That trait also blunted the whole chain from rudeness to weaker service. The authors frame the trait as a personal resource that firms could nurture. Training and hiring that values initiative may shield service quality.
pmc-13554234:
Monja Müller, Konstanze F Winklhofer, and Fulvio Reggiori review the enzymes that tag cell parts for selective self-eating in a 2026 paper. Cells digest worn parts through autophagy, which can swallow whole power plants, clumps, and germs, unlike the proteasome that shreds single proteins. Tags made of ubiquitin mark the cargo, and reader proteins haul it into the disposal sacs. The tagging enzymes, called E3 ligases, make the final call on what goes.

While many tag readers are well mapped, the ligases themselves remain poorly studied. The review gathers what is known for four cargo classes: power plants, protein clumps, disposal sacs, and invaders. Each class has its own names, from mitophagy to xenophagy. Better maps of these enzymes could sharpen drugs that force cells to clear harmful cargo.
pmc-13555534:
Alexander Kinna leads a large team comparing two antibody shapes as the targeting head of engineered cancer-fighting T cells in a 2026 study. Standard heads, called scFv, can clump and wear out. The rival VHH shape, from heavy-chain-only antibodies, is smaller and sturdier. Ten matched pairs aimed at the same leukemia target were built and compared head to head.

VHH heads withstood heat better, clumped less, and carried a friendlier surface charge. T cells fitted with VHH heads released more immune signals in dish tests. In mice carrying human leukemia, VHH-guided cells shrank tumours more and extended survival substantially. The authors recommend VHH as the preferred targeting head for future cell therapies, backed by this side-by-side evidence.
pmc-13555634:
Roozbeh Javad Kalbasi leads a five-author team building a transistor sensor for forever chemicals in water in a 2026 study. PFAS chemicals resist breakdown and raise health worries, yet field detection stays hard. Their sensor uses carbon nanotubes wrapped in a designed polymer that processes in water. Ring-shaped parts on the polymer carry charges that grip the target chemicals' tails.

Tests confirmed the gripping interaction with two common PFAS compounds. Devices built from the enriched nanotubes showed strong, stable electrical behaviour in plain water. The sensors detected both target chemicals and told them apart from a similar harmless acid. The authors present the work as proof of concept for a model sensing platform, with real-world water testing still ahead.
pmc-13555934:
Moyuan Quan leads a six-author team reporting a rare autoimmune brain disease that surfaced years after tumour radiotherapy in a 2026 case report. The disease, driven by antibodies against the AK5 enzyme, typically erases the ability to form new memories. Their patient had surgery and radiation for a craniopharyngioma, a tumour near the brain's base. Personality change and fading recent memory followed the radiation.

Diagnosis waited years, until seizures finally appeared. By then scans showed abnormal signals and shrinkage in the hippocampus, the memory hub. Memory loss, weight loss, and fatigue are the disease's calling cards, the authors note. They raise the possibility that brain radiation can wake autoimmune inflammation, a link clinicians should watch for after such treatment.
pmc-13556034:
Qian Yang and eight colleagues reviewed in 2026 how a family of enzymes called E3 ubiquitin ligases could be targeted to make combined radiation and immune therapy work better against cancer. These enzymes tag proteins for disposal, which puts them in charge of DNA repair, immune signals, and stress responses inside tumour cells. Resistance to radiation and tricks that hide tumours from the immune system still limit how long the combined treatment helps.

Inside the cell, the review traces how these ligases set the pace of damage repair, cell-cycle pauses, and cell death after radiation. Outside it, they shape immune checkpoints, antigen display, and signals such as the cGAS-STING pathway that wake up immune attack. The authors close by surveying drugs in development, from plain blockers to degrader molecules that force the cell to destroy a chosen protein.
pmc-13558334:
Elena Candellone and three colleagues tested in 2026 whether the automatic suspicious transaction reports that investigators tend to shelve actually help Dutch anti-money laundering work. Banks file two kinds of reports: objective ones triggered by fixed rules and subjective ones based on expert judgement. The team built transaction networks from five years of the centre's records and asked what the automatic reports added.

Objective reports, though a small share of the total, widened the network with new people and companies, linked dossiers that had sat apart, and surfaced entities in cases already under investigation. Yet adding them did not sharpen network-based predictions of which entities investigators were pursuing. The authors conclude that automatic reports earn their keep as case spotters, while richer written detail would be needed to guide investigations further.
pmc-13558534:
Alireza Zangooie and ten colleagues combined in 2026 a case report with a systematic review and gene analysis to understand patients who carry two B-cell cancers at once. Multiple myeloma grows from plasma cells, while diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is a fast lymphoid cancer, and the pair rarely coexist. Their case was a 52-year-old man with abdominal pain and anaemia whose scans and biopsies confirmed both diseases together.

He received a standard lymphoma regimen first, then a stem cell transplant when the myeloma relapsed, illustrating the sequencing puzzle such patients pose. The review gathered comparable published cases for their features, treatments, and outcomes. Mining public genome databases, the authors compared driver mutations across the two cancers and mapped shared pathways. Overlapping genes and circuits, they argue, may explain the rare pairing and point to treatments that could serve both diseases.
pmc-13558734:
Pablo Ruiz-Amezcua and five colleagues released in 2026 SpineDL, an open-source deep learning system that outlines neurons and spinal cord anatomy in fluorescence microscope images. Counting neurons by hand after spinal cord injury is slow and varies between researchers. Their package holds two models: one picks out individual neuron cell bodies one by one, and one paints the cord's regions, grey matter, white matter, the central canal lining, and damaged tissue.

Both models were trained on a purpose-built set of 161 mouse spinal cord images taken by confocal microscopy. Injury researchers hand-annotated the set and refined it through rounds of error review. Performance reached researcher level on both tasks and held up across anatomical regions and injury states. The authors offer the platform as a reproducible base for quantitative histology in preclinical injury research, ready to extend to new stains and species.
pmc-13559434:
Dan Chen and colleagues pull together findings on two insulin-resistance indexes as warning signs after coronary artery bypass grafting. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis covers the triglyceride-glucose index and its body-mass variant, both computed from routine labs. Fifteen studies with 16,185 bypass patients met the criteria after a search running to May 2026.

A high triglyceride-glucose index before surgery tracked with more major cardiovascular events and more combined heart and brain events across the pooled studies. Links also appeared for death from any cause, cardiac death, heart attack, stroke, and atrial fibrillation. The ties grew stronger among patients with diabetes. For the body-mass variant, evidence was thin: one strand linked higher values to acute kidney injury in diabetic patients. The authors present the simple index as a low-cost risk marker, strongest where diabetes is present.
pmc-13560134:
Anuwar Husen, Anteneh Berhane, and Melese Sinaga Teshome check whether a simpler arm measurement can stand in for the standard mid-upper arm circumference when screening young children for acute malnutrition. Their 2026 community study measured 591 children aged six to fifty-nine months in Southwest Ethiopia during June 2023. Each child received both the random-point measurement and the standard midpoint measurement.

Standard measurement classified 61 children, 10.4 percent of the group, as wasted. Agreement between the two methods was substantial, with a kappa of 0.69 in the paired comparison. The random method caught 81.6 percent of wasted children while correctly clearing 95.2 percent of the rest in the reported performance figures. Its accuracy was strongest for severe malnutrition. The authors conclude the simpler tape placement works well enough for community screening, where finding the arm's exact midpoint slows workers and adds observer error.
pmc-13560434:
Emma C Sherman, Jack I Stomberger, and Kirsten A Porter-Stransky ask which parts of a commercial study platform actually predict medical students' board performance. Their 2026 study follows two cohorts at a public US medical school, ninety-seven students in a traditional curriculum and one hundred three in an integrated organ-system curriculum. Usage of question banks, reading bricks, flashcards, and videos was matched to exam records.

Only practice question volume mattered among the platform's tools. Question bank engagement and course grades together predicted scores on the comprehensive basic science examination in both curricula. The same two factors predicted taking and passing Step 1 on schedule before clerkships. Video, flashcard, and brick usage showed no significant association either way. The authors offer the result as evidence-based guidance for students choosing among third-party resources, at a time when first-attempt Step 1 pass rates have slipped nationally.
pmc-13560634:
Yuxuan Zhang and colleagues announce the complete genome of Gordonia sihwensis RL-BY03, a marine bacterium that eats phthalate esters, the plasticizers polluting every ocean. Their 2026 genome report describes a strain pulled from intertidal mangrove sediment in Zhanjiang Bay, China, in May 2023. It was selected on a mineral medium where a common phthalate served as the only carbon source.

Ribosomal gene comparison placed the isolate at 99.8 percent similarity to the species' type strain. PacBio long-read sequencing produced over ninety-two thousand clean reads totaling more than a billion bases, enough for a complete assembly. The authors frame the genome as a genetic window into how coastal microbes dismantle endocrine-disrupting plastic additives. Marine degraders remain scarce in genomic databases, so a finished sequence from a mangrove strain adds a reference point for bioremediation research.
pmc-13561234:
Cheema and colleagues chart where Americans dying of alcoholic liver cirrhosis spend their final day, using 25 years of national death records in 2026 health services research. Death certificates from 1999 through 2023 were analyzed for adults aged 25 and older. Place of death was sorted into hospital, home, hospice or nursing facility, and emergency or outpatient settings, then tested against demographic and geographic traits.

The records covered 302,815 deaths from alcoholic liver cirrhosis across the quarter century studied. Inpatient deaths fell from 65.2 percent in 1999 to 48.6 percent in 2023 of all deaths recorded. Home deaths climbed from 20.7 percent to 30.2 percent over the same span of years. Hospice and nursing deaths peaked at 23.7 percent in 2015 before easing back to 18.3 percent by the end. Men, minorities, and city residents remained likelier to die in institutional settings.
pmc-13561734:
Huan Zhang and colleagues pool published findings on the systemic immune-inflammation index as a prognostic marker in kidney cancer. Their 2026 pooled review searches four data banks through October 2025 for studies tying the blood index to survival outcomes. Twenty-two studies qualified, covering local and advanced kidney cancer.

Higher index values predicted worse survival on every endpoint. Overall survival carried a pooled hazard ratio of 1.89 for high versus low values in the pooling. Progression-free and cancer-specific survival pointed the same way, with ratios of 1.74 and 1.63 in their figures. Region, cutoff choices, and disease stage explained much of the mismatch between studies. Robustness checks left the findings standing. The authors call the cheap blood index a strong independent predictor, while asking future work to fix one shared cutoff.
pmc-13562634:
María Carla Navas and four colleagues listen to brain waves in the first moments of remembering one's own past, asking whether old and fresh memories sound different. Personal memory supports planning and social life, and its age might change how the brain fetches it. The 2026 study recorded scalp electrical activity from 41 volunteers during a memory task. The team measured wave power and directed information flow across the first 1500 milliseconds after a memory surfaced.

Distant memories raised theta-band power, waves around 6.5 to 8 cycles per second, over the front-central scalp near 900 milliseconds. Recent memories did not. Information still flowed from front to back for both kinds, yet the network for distant memories ran denser and more efficiently between 800 and 1100 milliseconds. The authors read theta activity as a precise clock-time marker of how memory age shapes retrieval, useful for separating the access stage from later elaboration.
pmc-13563734:
Wenting Yang and three colleagues describe a 66-year-old woman whose liver abscess burrowed into the body's largest vein, a complication they call rare and life-threatening. She had diabetes and arrived after ten days of fever and chills. Imaging showed a gas-containing abscess in the caudate lobe, the liver's rear segment, reaching into the inferior vena cava with an infected clot. Contrast ultrasound and CT pointed to Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium behind a rising share of liver abscesses in Asia.

Doctors drained the abscess through the skin under ultrasound guidance. Cultures grew a drug-resistant strain that makes extended-spectrum beta-lactamase, so antibiotics, blood thinners, and continued drainage carried the treatment. She survived an episode of septic shock. Later scans showed the abscess nearly gone and the vein clot fully resolved, without open surgery. The authors commend multimodal ultrasound for finding and treating tangled cases.
pmc-13571334:
Jaideep Menda and co-authors present this 2026 case report about a severe reaction to protamine, a drug given to reverse blood thinners after a heart valve procedure. The patient was a seventy-nine year old man receiving a replacement aortic valve through a catheter.

Right after protamine was given, his blood pressure collapsed as the right side of his heart suddenly failed under pressure overload. Standard support with inhaled nitric oxide, heart drugs, and a balloon pump did not restore him. A small implanted pump that assists the right heart then improved his pressures and breathing at once. The authors warn that patients with weak right hearts have little reserve for this rare reaction and may need such support early.
pmc-13571434:
Campana and colleagues reported a single center's experience in 2026 with screws that stray toward the aorta during spine surgery. Proposed a management algorithm based on screw position relative to the vessel wall. Such contact is rare but can end catastrophically, and no shared playbook existed. Their vascular unit reviewed all referrals from 2020 to 2025, classifying scans as near contact, contact, indentation, or penetration.

Eight patients qualified, mostly young scoliosis cases. Two had near contact, three contact, and three indentation; none had full penetration. Shallow cases had screws removed under live angiographic watch, and completion imaging showed no leaks, so no rescue stent was needed. Every indentation case received a preventive endovascular aortic repair, a stent graft placed inside the vessel, just before screw removal. All procedures succeeded, with no major aortic events or deaths, and all stayed well at a median of twenty-seven months.
pmc-13572334:
Alessandro Costa and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 retrospective study, 135 patients with myelofibrosis, a bone marrow scarring disease, asking whether living with an autoimmune disease at the same time changes outlook. Charts were searched for documented autoimmune diagnoses at the time of marrow diagnosis.

Twenty-nine patients carried thirty-one autoimmune diagnoses, split between organ-specific and body-wide types, and autoimmunity was commoner in women. After about three years of follow-up, patients with body-wide autoimmune disease survived notably worse than those without or with organ-limited disease, and body-wide autoimmunity independently predicted death in adjusted models. Infections and clots also struck autoimmune patients more often. The authors recommend closer monitoring and tailored care for that subgroup.
pmc-13572434:
Zhenlong Li, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 method for spotting bearing faults in farm machines when work conditions shift. Bearings face swings in speed and load plus dirt and noise, so a model trained in one setting often fails in the next. The team trained on source data only, with no peek at the target setting.

Two paths read each signal. One path is physics-based and hunts the ring band tied to impacts, while the other learns patterns from the raw wave shape. A gate blends the two views for each sample, and a loss term keeps the views in agreement. On three data sets, accuracy in the home setting ran from 97.53 to 99.48 percent. Cross-speed tests on a farm rig stayed near 98 percent both ways. Swapping the physics path for plain features hurt results, which backs its role.
pmc-13572534:
Xiaoxi Liu, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of two breathing machine modes for older patients in tilted keyhole surgery. In the Trendelenburg pose, the body tilts head-down, and gas in the belly pushes on the lungs. Lung problems after surgery are common in this group, so the mode of air delivery matters.

Patients were assigned at random to pressure-controlled or volume-controlled modes, both under a lung-safe plan. Lung problems in the first three days struck 13.0 percent of the pressure group against 32.1 percent of the volume group. Airway pressures ran lower with pressure control, and lung stretch, a measure of how freely lungs fill, ran higher. Carbon dioxide in the blood also sat lower. The authors say larger trials must show whether these gains change real recovery.
pmc-13573334:
Hiroyuki Fujii, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 case of a patient whose breathing worsened even as a lung procedure worked. The patient had chronic clot-based high pressure in the lung arteries, a condition treated by balloon angioplasty, which widens narrowed vessels with a small balloon. Blood flow measures improved a great deal after repeat sessions.

Yet breathlessness and low oxygen on exertion grew worse, which pointed to a second problem in the airways. The hidden culprit was severe eosinophilic asthma, a form driven by a type of white blood cell. Treatment with benralizumab, an antibody drug that targets those cells, plus sinus surgery eased the airflow block. Oxygen levels rose, and lung artery pressure fell further over time. The case warns teams to hunt for airway disease when symptoms and flow numbers part ways.
pmc-13574734:
Jize Tian reports a 2026 database study comparing bile duct cancers that start inside the liver with those that start outside it, after surgery. Both forms are rare and deadly, yet they behave differently and may not carry the same outlook. Past comparisons were clouded by uneven patient mixes.

Records came from the United States SEER database for patients treated from 2010 to 2018, with 1,586 cases in all. A matching method paired 239 patients of each type with like traits. The inside-liver group lived longer overall, with a median of 45 months against 25. Once deaths from other causes were split out, cancer-specific survival matched between the types. Age, stage, and tumour size drove risk. Taking four or more lymph nodes went with better overall survival, a possible quality mark for surgery.
pmc-13575034:
Paul Spin and nine colleagues compare broad gene testing with small gene panels in advanced cancer, in a 2026 real-world study. Broad profiling reads many genes at once and can flag patients who match targeted drugs. The question was how much more often the broad test finds changes that doctors can act on.

The study covered 406 patients with advanced solid tumours, about half with lung cancer. After weighting to balance the groups, broad testing found top-level actionable changes in 50.0 percent of patients, against 31.4 percent for small panels. Gains appeared at other action levels too. The authors argue wider coverage and payment for broad testing would open targeted care to more patients.
pmc-13575134:
Tasnim Ben Yacoub leads a 2026 study of a small peptide in the human retina and how a disease-linked variant changes its partners. The peptide, BRI23, comes from the ITM2B protein and is tied to retinal dystrophy and some inherited dementias. Its role in the eye was largely unknown.

Using peptide-coated beads, the team fished out 2,302 interacting proteins from retinal material, mostly tied to mitochondria, synapses, and light-sensing cells. The variant linked to retinal dystrophy bound a different set of partners than the normal form. Mitochondrial and synaptic proteins were more abundant with the variant. The authors read this shift as a clue to how the mutation disturbs retinal cell pathways.
pmc-13576134:
Xukai Gu leads a 2026 study training a neural network to find and outline bone defects around teeth on dental X-rays. These infraosseous defects, pockets where gum disease has eaten bone beside a root, guide prognosis and surgery planning. Overlapping structures on flat X-rays make them easy to misread.

The team trained a YOLOv8 network on 329 X-rays from Semmelweis University, each marked by hand. The model scored 0.8078 on the ranking accuracy measure, with a mid-range classification score. Its outlines overlapped expert markings well on average, strongest for one-wall, three-wall, and four-wall defects. The authors judge the model capable yet short of clinical polish. A larger, cleaner training set is their stated next step.
pmc-13576334:
Parvesh Barak, Daniel Gibney, and Chirag Jain tackle error correction for long DNA reads in organisms with several genome copies, in a 2026 paper. Correcting sequencing errors is an early step in building a genome from reads. Simple majority voting can erase the small true differences between copies that researchers most want to keep.

Their approach recasts the task in a strict mathematical form borrowed from haplotype phasing, work that sorts genome copies apart. They prove the reference-free version of the problem is NP-hard, meaning no fast exact method is expected, then add practical shortcuts so their exact solver scales. Tests on human and plant datasets sequenced with PacBio HiFi matched the accuracy of leading tools. Code is shared openly, and the authors present the method as a firmer footing for a routine step.
pmc-13578234:
An Lou and colleagues tracked fear around dental implant surgery in a 2026 study of 506 patients at a hospital in Changsha, China. Each patient rated anxiety the night before surgery, while waiting, during the numbing injection, during implant placement, and after the work ended. Pain was rated at matching points so the two could be compared.

Anxiety peaked during the injection and the placement steps, then fell sharply once surgery ended. Women, older patients, and people getting implants in the lower jaw or in both jaws showed higher odds of strong anxiety. Pain felt during and after surgery tracked closely with fear, while pain expected the night before did not. The authors urge focused support for high risk groups and firm pain control.
pmc-13578334:
Qi Shi, Yue Le, Chunjie Gu, and Yaming Geng forecast the cost of power grid upgrade projects with a tuned transformer model, in a 2026 study. Renovation bills shift as prices, labor, and scope change over long jobs, which makes early budgets hard to trust. Their model reads cost history at several time scales at once and shifts its focus as conditions change.

The test bed held more than thirteen hundred finished projects from one province in eastern China. Against nine rival methods, from classic tools to newer time series designs, the new model posted the lowest average error and the tightest fit to real costs. Extra checks traced which inputs drove each forecast. The authors warn the model was tuned on one province, so wider use needs fresh proof.
pmc-13578434:
Melanie Bommer and colleagues ask how well bedside balance tests match lab grade measures in people with multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study of thirty patients. The disease often wrecks balance and leads to falls, yet the precise lab tools are too costly for daily clinic use. Six common clinic tests were scored against force plate and motion capture readings of standing and walking.

Clinic scores tracked the plate based sway measures fairly well. One broad balance scale matched standing sway most closely. A timed walk and turn test matched the widest set of lab measures, both still and moving. One walking measure behaved oddly: wider safety margins went with worse clinic scores, likely a guarding habit rather than true skill. The authors map which cheap test stands in for which lab readout.
pmc-13582734:
Becca N. Kubick and colleagues tested a hybrid exam format in medical school, where students answer first alone and then as a group. Team-based learning is well established, but its exam ideas are rarely used outside that framework. Their 2026 study ran the format in a two-week multisystems course at the University of Cincinnati. Students took two in-house exams plus a national final taken alone. Some concepts were retested later to check retention.

Average individual scores dipped slightly after the switch, a small but real decline. Yet students did better on retested concepts, especially lower performers, suggesting group testing aided learning even as scores fell. Students overwhelmingly backed the model, saying it deepened learning and cut exam stress, though views on spreading it to other courses split by class rank.
pmc-13591234:
Lotte Verweij leads a study building yardsticks for a modern research habit: teaming up with patients and the public to plan health studies. Such teamwork can sharpen research, yet few agreed marks exist for judging whether a partnership is real or token. The team ran a three round Delphi process, a structured way to build expert agreement, co designed with patient and family advisers. A joint workshop of users and scholars drafted the first list.

Rounds of surveys trimmed and clarified the draft into 30 final indicators. They fall into three groups: set up, day to day process, and results, with 12 tied to results alone. Respondents rated the marks as relevant and mostly clear. Verweij and the team say field testing should come next.
pmc-13591534:
Hossam Ibrahim leads a 2026 nationwide comparison of two causes of cardiogenic shock, where the heart fails to pump enough blood. One cause is acute myocarditis, immune driven swelling of heart muscle. The other is takotsubo syndrome, a stress triggered weakening that usually heals. Using a national hospital database from 2020 to 2022, the team matched over 2,400 pairs of patients on age, other ills, and hospital traits.

Death rates in hospital and lengths of stay came out nearly the same for both groups, at roughly one death in four. Myocarditis patients, though, used temporary heart pumps at nearly three times the rate. Their hospital bills ran far higher as well. Ibrahim and the team say equal death rates hide a much heavier support burden for myocarditis.
pmc-13592634:
Jakia Sultana Mim and six colleagues examine who gets a skilled attendant at childbirth in Bangladesh, where mother and newborn deaths remain high. Their data come from the 2022 national health survey. Standard regression sorted the social and economic factors first. Machine learning models then classified births a second way, checking which factors mattered most and how well each method predicted attendant use.

About sixty eight percent of women delivered with a doctor, nurse, or midwife present. Schooling stood out: educated mothers had about four times the odds of skilled help compared with unschooled mothers. Wealth, four or more pregnancy checkups, and town living each raised the odds, while village living lowered them. A random forest model scored best at prediction. Mim and the team urge focused help for poor and rural mothers.
pmc-13594034:
Qi Yong Hemis Ai and co-authors put five commercial AI language models to the test of staging mouth cancer from radiologists' written MRI reports. Staging normally demands specialist judgment about tumor size and lymph node spread. Many hospitals issue only descriptive reports. The team therefore fed 104 reports to the models. Their answers were compared with a reference standard and with two expert team members.

Accuracy swung widely between models, from roughly half to about four fifths correct on overall stage, with the strongest systems matching the human experts on some measures. No model consistently beat the experts, and the humans themselves were right only about seven times in ten. The authors conclude that these models are not ready to stage cancer on their own, and that structured reports stating the stage outright would help everyone, human or machine.
pmc-13594134:
Zhenzhai Cai and colleagues showed how Coro1a lifts bubble release by building the fusion gear. Bubbles leave cells when multi-bubble bodies fuse with the cell surface via SNARE teams, but the one team and its control were unclear. Their 2026 study found Coro1a lifts build-up of the STX-12-SNAP-23-VAMP-7 SNARE team, free of neddylation, by switching on PKM2 to tag SNAP-23.

Muting PKM2 or muting SNAP-23 killed Coro1a-driven bubble output. Coro1a levels ran high in lung tumour tissue and tracked poor patient living on, hinting tumour spread gains from extra bubbles. The authors present Coro1a-run SNARE build-up as a route linking bubble birth to cancer, and a maybe target for treatment.
pmc-13594434:
Brian Olshansky surveys the top advances in clinical cardiac electrophysiology from 2025. The field moved fast, with new treatments and tests for rhythm disorders reaching patients. His 2026 review covers atrial fibrillation care, pacing, athlete heart care, ablation, and wearable monitors.

Pulsed-field ablation for atrial fibrillation stands out, backed by a registry of about 40,000 patients and sham-controlled trials showing real benefit beyond placebo. Conduction-system and leadless pacing are now mainstream, while care for athletes with fainting or prior cardiac arrest has changed. Olshansky notes some advances were surely left out for space.
pmc-13597534:
Andrea Miranda-Tena and colleagues polled unfair care in health sites among 217 young adults in Spain, setting 73 sex- and gender-minority youth beside 144 straight cisgender peers. The web poll ran from January to April 2025, with scores for unfair care, distress, trust, and care delays, plus free-text tales read for themes.

Minority youth told of more unfair care, more distress, less trust in staff, and more care delays. Unfair care tracked with distress, trust, and delay in plain tests but did not stand alone as a cause in full models. Tales told of wrong pronouns, bossy care, and moral scolds in day-to-day visits, which points to a need for kind, trained, all-welcome care even where care is free for all.
pmc-13604734:
Faiza Gaba leads a large international team presenting GO SOAR, a risk calculator built for gynecological cancer surgery. Generic surgical risk tools predict complications poorly for these women, which distorts consent talks and misses chances to prepare patients. The team fitted new models on a global training cohort of 1,811 women and validated them on a separate prospective cohort of 416. Both predicted death and any complication within thirty days of surgery.

Both a full and a condensed version were tested against established calculators such as SORT, POSSUM, and NSQIP. For mortality, the models scored area-under-curve values of 0.752 and 0.795 respectively. For complications, both sat near zero point seven. At a 90 percent specificity threshold, GO SOAR achieved the highest sensitivity among the calculators compared. The authors stress the tool needs little data entry and no laboratory values, so it can serve patients in low-resource settings as well as wealthy ones.
pmc-13612334:
Shana G Dodge leads a seven-author team asking how well the people who actually run dementia studies are holding up. Coordinators are the face of frontotemporal degeneration research for families, recruiting, consenting, and shepherding them through demanding visits. The Association for Frontotemporal Degeneration surveyed them across U.S. and Canadian research networks about training, satisfaction, and staying in the job.

Thirty-seven answered, most with more than three years of experience. Even so, 62 percent had faced situations they felt unprepared for. Genetics, symptom care, and brain donation topped the list of training gaps, topics where a wrong answer can shake a grieving family's trust. Staying hinged on competitive pay and career advancement. The authors argue for formal, disease-specific onboarding and support for this workforce. The association is now developing a modular training program for sites.
pmc-13615134:
Chiara Pittalis and colleagues reflect in 2026 on a breast health campaign in rural Malawi that ran into an unexpected problem: too many health messages at once. Between October and December 2025, the Akazi Project held participatory sessions in eight rural communities with more than 300 local leaders, including chiefs, faith leaders, youth volunteers, and women's groups. Hunger for basic breast health facts was strong.

Leaders kept asking how the new breast cancer advice fitted with guidance they already juggled on HIV, cervical cancer, and vaccines. Overlapping campaigns from different programs competed and blurred in people's minds, breeding confusion and tiredness with messages in general. The authors argue that health groups working the same villages must coordinate their words, or each new campaign can weaken all the others.
pmc-13617734:
Desai and colleagues published a 2026 study on distress after acute coronary syndrome in India. A heart attack or unstable chest pain shakes far more than the heart. The team followed 105 patients at one large hospital over five months. Their survey split distress into fear, role change, money strain, and exhaustion.

Role and relationship changes scored among the highest distress areas overall. Feeling overwhelmed and fear of another attack ranked close behind them. Women reported clearly more distress over role changes than men did. Poorer and rural patients carried heavier money and emotional strain. The authors urge routine distress screening plus support in recovery plans. Comorbid illness added to the burden in the most strained patients.
pmc-13618034:
Ying-Zhong Ma and two colleagues shine two-photon light on a special acid that releases protons only while illuminated. Metastable-state photoacids can flood a solution with acidity under light and then relax back, a trick with uses from materials to medicine, yet almost all studies excite them with single photons. The team studied a highly water-soluble indazole photoacid in water using fluorescence excited by pairs of lower-energy photons.

The glow followed the expected quadratic dependence on light intensity, confirming true two-photon absorption, and the molecule's appetite for photon pairs proved sizable. More tellingly, the timing patterns and colors of the glow differed from the one-photon case, indirect evidence that two-photon excitation activates different molecular shapes and reaction pathways. The authors say this opens uses for photoacids that single-photon excitation cannot reach, including settings where light must reach deeper.
pmc-13618934:
Metha Yaikwawong and three colleagues ask whether machine learning over routine variables can separate pre-metabolic syndrome from full metabolic syndrome in Thai adults. Metabolic dysfunction runs on a spectrum, while diagnosis uses fixed cutoffs. Their single-center retrospective study classified six hundred fifty-seven adults, three hundred fifty-nine pre-syndrome and two hundred ninety-eight with the syndrome. They raced ten algorithms on twenty-four clinical and biochemical features.

Ensemble methods won. XGBoost discriminated best, with an AUC of 0.986 on the held-out test set and the highest accuracy. A neural network and a random forest followed. Explanation analysis credited systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, fasting glucose, sex, and a triglyceride-waist index as the strongest contributors. When overlapping predictors were stripped out, discrimination fell step by step but a real signal remained. The authors read that as added value beyond the defining criteria.
pmc-13620834:
Rameesha Shauket, Inibehe Ime Okon, and Saira Maroof surveyed school-going teenagers in a peri-urban district of South Punjab, Pakistan, about hunger at home and growth. Food insecurity among adolescents is rarely measured in the country, though the teen years decide adult height and health. Their study enrolled 384 students aged fifteen to eighteen, scoring household food access with a standard scale and growth against world references.

Nearly every household, about ninety-five percent, scored as severely food insecure. About a third of the teenagers were thin for their age, more than a quarter were stunted, and a smaller share carried excess weight, the double burden in one sample. Overall insecurity categories did not map neatly onto growth, yet specific hunger experiences did track thinness, and each step up the insecurity score raised thinness odds slightly. The authors call for school-based nutrition programs tied to global hunger goals.
pmc-13621234:
Lixing Zhou and nine colleagues studied ghrelin, the hunger hormone, as an unlikely defender of the aging brain. Their work links three threads that rise together with age: fading thinking, tired immune cells in the brain called microglia, and a breakdown of autophagy, the cells' recycling system. Human data flagged ghrelin as the metabolic factor tied most strongly to cognitive impairment.

Aged mice and mice aged artificially with a sugar treatment showed the same pattern, with raised ghrelin already present. Giving ghrelin improved the animals' thinking, calmed microglial aging and inflammation, and restarted recycling markers, though high doses dulled its own receptor. Experiments in cells traced the effect through a chain involving a hormone-carrying protein, a stress enzyme, and a recycling starter protein. Blocking links in that chain erased the benefit, while boosting the last link restored it. The authors propose the pathway as a drug target.
pmc-13623134:
Hüseyin O Elmas and three co-authors test how the brain works out where a touch lands on the body. Finding a spot on the skin is not enough, since the patch moves as posture changes. Two theories compete: the brain either merges touch with body position sense into one map, or touch points to a spot whose position comes from body sense.

Nineteen volunteers located targets on their fingertips, some felt by touch and some set by body position. The team fitted the results with Bayesian models, a maths approach that treats the brain as weighing prior expectations against signals. Models letting the two senses use different prior expectations fit best, and fifteen of the nineteen people showed different expectations across the senses. The authors read this as evidence that touch and body sense use separate machinery, a result that reshapes how these skills are understood.
pmc-13623334:
Wen Tao led a 2026 genetic case study of a man whose infertility and breathing problems traced to a single gene change affecting the tiny hair-like structures that move mucus and sperm. The patient came from a consanguineous Chinese family and showed the classic pattern of primary ciliary dyskinesia, in which cilia and sperm tails share a faulty internal scaffold. Testing found two copies of a splicing change in CCDC39, a gene needed to assemble the motor arms of that scaffold.

Lab work showed sharply lower CCDC39 message and loss of the protein plus other motor proteins, while semen checks showed very poor sperm movement and a wide range of tail defects. Microscopy confirmed severe disorganization of the sperm tail core. Despite that, treatment with intracytoplasmic sperm injection, in which a single sperm is injected into an egg, achieved a pregnancy.
pmc-13623434:
Lucy Mackie and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a patient developing a sarcoidosis-like reaction while on the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab for breast cancer. Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory condition that forms immune-cell clusters in tissue, and this drug-driven copy appeared in two forms at once, a combination the authors say is unreported.

The patient, a sixty-eight-year-old woman treated for a triple-negative breast cancer, developed a plaque cluster on her nose resembling lupus pernio, a skin form of sarcoidosis, plus a forehead lump. Tender nodules up to four centimetres wide appeared on her forearms and knees, though she felt well. Scans showed swollen chest glands and inflamed lungs, and a skin biopsy confirmed the tell-tale cell clusters without infection. Blood tests backed the picture, and tuberculosis testing was negative. The team links the eruption to the immune treatment continued after her chemotherapy ended.
pmc-13626334:
Aslan Miriyev proposes a design discipline for machines that are partly alive. Robots and sensors leave mounting electronic waste, while biohybrid systems, part synthetic and part living tissue, can grow, heal, and rot away. Existing design habits treat the living part as a fixed block, wasting its dynamic gifts. So Miriyev lays out Biointegrative Design, a loop of four stages. The loop starts from a biological concept. It then designs the living and support systems together before joining them.

Growth, regeneration, and adaptation become design variables from the first sketch, not afterthoughts. The essay maps how the approach could reshape making, uses, and business models across robotics, medicine, and environmental sensing. It also drafts the institutional changes, shared labs, standards, and training, that such cross-field work would need to take root.
pmc-13626534:
Kamini Walia and eleven colleagues argue that India should retire the Widal test, a century-old blood screen for typhoid fever. Enteric fever strikes over fourteen million people a year worldwide and kills well over a hundred thousand, with India carrying a heavy share, mostly among the young. Diagnosis matters doubly in India because fevers from malaria, dengue, and other infections mimic typhoid closely.

The Widal test, the authors contend, misfires too often in both directions. False positives pour antibiotics into people who lack the disease. False negatives delay true treatment and push doctors toward broader drugs. Both errors feed drug resistance while blinding surveillance and vaccine planning. Dropping a test this unreliable, they say, is a first step toward honest diagnosis and steadier antibiotic use.
pmc-13626834:
Kai-Wen Geng and co-authors trace the brain circuit that turns a cagemate's pain into care in mice. Observer mice that match a hurting partner's stress begin grooming it and licking its injury, and the pair calm together. The team hunted the wiring and found a three-stop relay. Vasopressin, a social hormone, is released from the hypothalamus. It switches on a matching receptor in a small amygdala region. Those cells then drive the brain's reward hub.

Turning the relay's middle stop on or off moved the caregiving behavior with it, and active caregivers also felt less anxiety, as if care paid them back. Such circuits matter because failures of care mark several psychiatric conditions. A named, gated pathway gives researchers a handle for testing how comfort is built into the social brain.
pmc-13628534:
Awais W. Seyyad and three colleagues demonstrate that nitrogen dioxide, a toxic exhaust gas that feeds smog and acid rain, can be converted into the far less harmful nitric oxide without any catalyst. Their 2026 study uses simple main-group reducing agents, including boranes, silanes, and two stand-ins for hydrogen, instead of the scarce noble metals in today's converters.

Spectroscopic measurements confirmed that nitric oxide formed selectively, and computer calculations traced how the reductions proceed step by step. The finding matters because nitric oxide is comparatively benign and even serves as a signaling molecule in the body. A catalyst-free route points toward cheaper, lower-temperature ways of cleaning nitrogen oxide pollution.
pmc-13629734:
Kentaro Okamoto and five colleagues asked whether blood pressure on day one after a heart pump implant predicts early trouble. Their single-centre study looked back at 156 adults. All received ventricular assist devices between 2019 and 2025. Patients were grouped by the support plan used. Plans ranged from a durable left-sided pump alone to mixes adding right-sided or outside support.

The bad outcome was death within thirty days or dialysis by day seven. It struck about one in seven patients with full data. Each step higher in day-one average pressure came with much lower odds of that outcome. The pattern held across extra checks. It also held after accounting for support type. The authors present early pressure as a risk marker worth more study. It is not yet a treatment target.
pmc-13632134:
Yusuff Adebayo Adebisi and twelve colleagues published this 2026 review of vaping and high blood pressure. Evidence had been hard to read because studies mix people who only vape, people who both vape and smoke, and people with different smoking histories. The team searched four databases through May 2026 and kept population studies that separated those groups. Ten studies qualified, mixing one-time snapshots with follow-ups lasting several years.

For vaping alone, pooled results could not rule out no effect on either existing or new high blood pressure. Using both products together told a clearer story. Dual users had higher odds of already having hypertension and a higher risk of developing it later. Smoking alone also raised the odds in side analyses. The authors say the combined habit, not vaping by itself, carries the clearest blood pressure signal so far.
pmc-13635134:
Adding N-acetylcysteine, a glutamate-modulating antioxidant, to standard antidepressant treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder is tested by Askari and colleagues. Obsessive-compulsive disorder often responds only partly to first-line serotonin drugs. Earlier add-on studies lacked standard drug dosing or cognitive measures. The team ran a twelve-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in thirty-five adults with moderate to severe symptoms, all receiving high-dose sertraline plus either N-acetylcysteine or placebo.

The add-on group showed greater symptom reduction, driven mainly by obsessions. Compulsion scores improved similarly in both groups, and every patient in the add-on group reached the response threshold. Both groups improved on processing speed and attention, with no cognitive edge for the add-on. Askari and colleagues read the pilot as support for short-term use, while noting that larger trials must confirm the benefit.
pmc-13636134:
Rebekah Sian Cooke and five colleagues published this 2026 study mapping new ways to block a key immune protein called C5. Blocking C5 already treats several rare diseases, and two antibody drugs lead the field. The team created fresh antibodies against C5 and compared them with the marketed pair. Lab tests measured binding, competition between antibodies, and whether each one stopped the protein being split into its active pieces.

Four new antibodies blocked blood-cell destruction as well as the established drugs. Competition mapping revealed four separate blocking sites on the protein. Two sites matched the known drugs, and antibodies there stopped the split and the release of an inflammatory fragment. The two new sites worked differently: the protein still split and released its fragment, yet destruction was blocked anyway. The authors say these extra modes of inhibition widen the design space for future complement drugs.
pmc-13637834:
Nuzhat Khursheed led a 2026 study of how a cell-death receptor gene, TRAIL-R2, is switched off in breast cancer through chemical tagging of its promoter region. Breast cancer remains among the most common cancers, yet its molecular drivers are incompletely mapped. TRAIL-R2 normally helps trigger apoptosis, the programmed death that removes damaged cells, but its regulation in breast tumors was unclear. The team compared matched tumor and normal breast tissue using methylation-specific PCR, gene activity assays, and protein blotting.

Promoter methylation was significantly higher in tumors and rose as gene and protein levels fell. Heavy methylation appeared more often in invasive ductal carcinoma and in patients with a history of oral contraceptive use. Lower gene activity tracked with advanced stage and absence of progesterone receptor, while lower protein tracked with postmenopausal status.
pmc-13639434:
Yoshinori Nakata and two colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether Japan's workstyle reform for doctors raised surgical productivity over the long term. The reform capped overtime for physicians, and the team used a Malmquist index model to track output at one university hospital.

They analyzed 5,415 operations by sixty-two senior surgeons across summer periods from 2022 to 2025. Overall productivity did not change significantly between the years before and after the reform took effect. Efficiency improved while technical change declined, and the two forces cancelled out. The authors report no evidence of a lasting productivity gain.
pmc-13642334:
Tianyi Liu and a large multicenter team present a 2026 machine learning tool, POCC, for predicting kidney failure in children born with kidney and urinary tract anomalies. These anomalies are the leading cause of childhood kidney failure, yet individual risk varies widely.

The model was built from records of 2,249 children and forecasts failure risk one, three, and five years after diagnosis. It held up well in outside hospitals, and a version using inherited features performed best in children's hospitals. Deployed online, it scored about ninety-one percent accuracy in real-world checks. The authors offer it for personal follow-up planning.
pmc-13644134:
Nasteho Mohamud Mudei and five colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of why employed mothers in Mogadishu, Somalia, stop exclusive breastfeeding before six months. Workplace pressures are a suspected driver, but Somali evidence was thin.

Interviews covered 303 working mothers of children aged six to twenty-four months across four job categories in late 2024. About three quarters had stopped exclusive breastfeeding early, most often in the third month. Flexible working hours cut the odds of stopping, and family support protected strongly. Paid leave alone showed no clear protection after adjustment, possibly because leave is short. Practical flexibility and feeding spaces are urged.
pmc-13646134:
Daya Shankar Gupta proposes a hypothesis linking the firing machinery of nerve cells to faint infrared light. His focus is the sodium channels that launch nerve impulses, crowded at a trigger zone called the axon initial segment. As charged parts of these channels move during signaling, he argues, tiny back-and-forth motions could create oscillating dipoles. Those dipoles might emit very weak mid-infrared photons.

Because the channels sit packed in a space smaller than the wavelength involved, neighboring emitters could fall into step and amplify the signal cooperatively. Gupta supports the idea with rough size estimates drawn from known channel structure and chemistry. He stresses that the paper needs no long-lived quantum effects and that every signature it predicts is, in principle, measurable. The piece offers experimentalists a concrete, testable claim at the border of biophysics and photonics.
pmc-13646834:
Dongjun Kim and five colleagues compare, cell by cell, the blood immune systems of patients with two scarring lung diseases that can look alike, in a 2026 study. One disease rides on rheumatoid arthritis, the other, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, has no known cause. Their care and outlook differ, so separating their biology matters. Single-cell gene sequencing profiled more than thirty-one thousand blood immune cells from five patients in each group, matched for age and sex.

The overall mix of immune cells looked similar, yet activity programs diverged. Arthritis-linked disease showed more killer cells loaded with attack and interferon genes, plus monocytes switched on by interferon signals. The idiopathic disease instead ran a fibrotic program driven by a growth signal, with its key genes raised in a specific monocyte type. The authors say these signatures may seed blood tests and treatments that respect each disease's distinct engine.
pmc-13647134:
Jacob Widaeus and nine colleagues lay out the design of a Swedish sub-study on tiny blood vessel failure, a driver of heart and brain disease. The project sits inside a large national imaging cohort and will recruit up to nine hundred volunteers aged fifty-eight to seventy-five. Four groups are compared with controls: blocked heart arteries, chest pain without blockage, metabolic syndrome with diabetes, and a stiff-heart condition. The paper is a protocol, so it reports plans rather than results.

Every participant gets skin microvessel testing at rest and after local provocations. Most also receive stress heart scans measuring blood flow into heart muscle. Blood biomarkers join the measurements as candidate signals. The team will test whether skin vessel readings mirror heart vessel health. Approvals from Swedish ethics and medicines authorities are in place. The authors argue early detection could open a window for prevention.
pmc-13647234:
Xin Lu and nine colleagues chase a stubborn impurity that appears when making desmopressin, a lab-built copy of a body hormone used for water-balance and bleeding disorders. During a standard protection-removal step, a byproduct heavier than the target kept forming at one spot. Careful mass analysis showed a protective group had jumped from a tyrosine building block onto a sulfur atom in the first block. The two sit unusually close in this peptide's folded shape.

Extra scavenger chemicals could not stop the jump, which supports a within-molecule migration rather than the usual stray-particle pathway. The team then asked whether the tyrosine needs protection at all. Trials with the unprotected building block removed the impurity at its source. Their source-elimination strategy, backed by the mechanism, offers peptide makers a cleaner route for this drug and a warning for other sequences with the same pairing.
pmc-13647334:
Maurício Guimarães de Oliveira and four colleagues study how sewage microbes break down LAS, the world's most used detergent surfactant, inside oxygen-starved treatment reactors. The chemical washes into wastewater everywhere, yet it degrades poorly without oxygen. Two bench reactors were compared, one strictly airless and one with a trickle of air, called microaeration. Two helper foods, ethanol and sucrose, were tested in each.

Airing the reactor while feeding sucrose lifted surfactant removal by about a third. Biogas output rose too, though its methane share fell. With ethanol, air made little difference, and fermenting communities dominated either way. With sucrose, air selected a leaner team of specialists that could crack the molecule's ring and strip its sulfur group while still making methane. The authors say pairing gentle aeration with the right helper food can clean detergent wastewater without wrecking reactor stability.
pmc-13648034:
Qing Zhang and De Chang set out a frame, called Necro-Mosaic, for testing how planned cell death shapes single TB lesions. TB can grow worse even when the whole body mounts a strong immune fight. The authors say what counts is how that fight is laid out inside each lesion, not just how strong it is.

The frame sorts death-linked acts along three paths: iron-driven fat damage, joint fiery cell death, and web-like traps cast by one white cell type. It also splits three claims that are often blurred: a path exists, a path is switched on, and a path has done its work. Proof is graded by strength. The authors warn that blood tests cannot yet read lesion types or guide drug choice.
pmc-13648334:
Ryo Hagimori and sixteen colleagues trace what happens to the retina and brain-related tissues when DHA, an omega-three fat vital for neural health, stays scarce for a long time. The mechanisms linking falling DHA to aging damage were poorly understood, so the team studied deficient mice in detail.

Without DHA, neural tissues swapped in omega-six fats that oxidise more easily, raising oxidative damage and activating microglia, the immune cells of the nervous system. Restoring DHA in the diet reversed the changes, while a disposal pathway involving the protein APOE moved oxidised lipids to microglia for clearance. Overloaded microglia eventually turned harmful, and aged retinas showed the same fat shift, tying diet to age-related decline.
pmc-13649434:
Hiba Sayedali and eight colleagues hunted for tiny RNA switches that help drive allergy-type swelling in the airways of mice. They used a signal called IL-33, which spurs the growth of white blood cells named eosinophils in the bone marrow and draws them into the lungs.

After IL-33 was given through the nose, the team profiled these small RNAs in lung and marrow. The two sites showed quite distinct patterns. Known switches tied to eosinophil growth and allergy changed in both sites. One switch, miR-150-5p, fell in the marrow and proved rich in a helper cell type that makes a strong allergy signal. The authors list these switches as leads for how this swelling unfolds.
pmc-13649834:
Bao and Gabbay surveyed in 2026 religious concerns about artificial intelligence entering clinical medicine and patient care. As AI takes on roles in diagnosis, treatment, and even spiritual support, religious authorities have raised objections. The article gathers common concerns across five traditions: Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism.

Recurring worries include whether a machine can show genuine empathy, and whether humans might abandon their duty to care for the sick. Other concerns cover misuse of AI in religious rites, and treating machines as spiritual beings, which several traditions count as idolatry. Authors also flag weakened provider accountability, neglect of human intellect, hidden bias, unwanted proselytising by systems, and threats to health equity. The authors argue that hearing religious reservations early will help shape AI that serves patients without eroding core values.
pmc-13650534:
Hiba Orsud and five colleagues synthesize how the immune system behaves over time during Helicobacter pylori infection, the stomach bacterium carried by nearly half the world's people. The infection can smolder harmlessly or progress to gastritis, ulcers, and stomach cancer, and the review tries to explain why a strong immune attack still fails to clear it.

Early infection raises a chemical alarm signal in the stomach lining, followed by waves of helper T cells that release inflammatory messengers. The bacterium survives behind regulatory cells, calming cytokines, and evasion proteins that blunt the attack. Blood antibodies against it are common and long-lived, while local antibodies in the stomach vary and rarely finish the job. The resulting imbalance between inflammatory and regulatory arms, shaped by both host and bacterial genetics, decides outcomes. The authors offer the framework as a guide for research, pending prospective proof.
pmc-13651534:
Mehmet Turan Görüryilmaz and seventeen co-authors harden the platinum catalyst of hydrogen fuel cells by growing its support partly from a layered material called MXene. Platinum on carbon is the standard cathode catalyst for the oxygen reduction reaction, yet the carbon corrodes and the platinum clumps, draining performance in acidic cells.

Analysis showed the MXene had turned during preparation into titanium dioxide in its anatase form, interwoven with carbon, with platinum particles fixed through oxygen bridges to the oxide. A blend of three quarters carbon and one quarter MXene derivative beat a homemade platinum-on-carbon reference after a punishing stress test modeled on energy department protocols. Its platinum particles grew less during the ordeal. The oxide's corrosion resistance plus the anchoring chemistry explain the gain, while enough carbon stayed for electron flow and gas transport. The authors claim the first half-cell benchmarking of this kind.
pmc-1920534:
Tierney, Stewart, Ghersi, and co-authors give practical methods for adding time-to-event data into pooled analyses. Outcomes such as survival are best compared using hazard ratios, which weigh risk over time. Reviewers often lack the original patient-level records behind published trials.

The authors show how to recover hazard ratios and related figures by carefully working from published summaries and curves. That lets reviewers include trials that report results in awkward forms, instead of dropping them. Including more trials fairly makes pooled survival estimates stronger and less biased for treatment decisions.  Worked examples show how to handle curves reported in differing formats.
pmc-3142234:
Ludvigsson, Andersson, Ekbom, and co-authors carry out an external review of the Swedish National Inpatient Register. The register, or Hospital Discharge Register, serves as a principal data source for many research projects. It forms part of the wider National Patient Register.

The register began in 1964, with psychiatric diagnoses added from 1973. The team checked its coverage and accuracy against external records. Knowing how far register data can be trusted matters because hundreds of studies on disease patterns and care quality rest on it.  Hundreds of later studies on Swedish care quality rest on this validation exercise.
pmc-3197634:
Eddy presents faster methods for profile hidden Markov model searches of sequence databases. Profile models capture the pattern of a whole family of related sequences. They had contributed much to the theory of searching for distant relatives among sequences.

In practice, though, the methods were held back by how much computing existing software needed. Eddy's accelerated approach cuts that cost, making sensitive searches practical on large databases. Faster profile searches let researchers spot remote evolutionary links that simple pairwise comparison misses, guiding work on protein function.  Database centres adopted the faster search to keep annotation pipelines on schedule.
pmc-3365034:
Peterson, Weber, Kay, and co-authors present double digest RADseq, a cheap method for finding SNPs and genotyping. Finding gene types fast and well is a keystone of modern genetics. It supports clinical diagnosis, trait association studies, and reconstruction of ancestry and selection.

High-capacity methods at the time were costly or narrow. Their approach cuts DNA with two enzymes before sequencing, giving a steady subset of the genome at low cost. It works in model and non-model species alike, opening population genetics to organisms without reference genomes.  Field teams can genotype hundreds of samples without a sequenced reference genome.
pmc-3395634:
Murrell, Wertheim, Moola, and co-authors present a method for detecting single sites in proteins under episodic diversifying selection. Natural selection leaves an imprint on protein-coding genes, but that signal is often hard to identify. Selection is frequently brief, affecting only some branches of a family tree.

Older techniques were designed to find sites under constant selection across all lineages. The new method, called MEME, can catch short bursts on a subset of branches. Catching episodic change matters for viruses and immunity genes, where brief arms races shape proteins.  Immune genes in humans show exactly the episodic pattern the method targets.
pmc-4751634:
Schubert, Lindgreen, and Orlando presented AdapterRemoval version two in 2016. As sequencers produce longer reads, DNA from short inserts increasingly runs into adapter sequences at the read end. Short inserts are typical of fossil and degraded material, where DNA is broken into small pieces.

The program trims adapters rapidly, identifies them, and merges paired reads that overlap. Efficient trimming is needed so adapter pieces do not corrupt genome assembly or variant calls. Ancient DNA labs rely on such care, since their samples cannot be replaced. Version two kept pace with longer reads and higher data volumes.
pmc-5695134:
Gregory Gloor, Jean Macklaim, Vera Pawlowsky-Glahn, and coauthors wrote this methods paper in 2017. It deals with data from high-throughput sequencing of microbes in the gut and other places. Such data are now common in studies of disease and the environment.

The authors argue that sequencing counts are parts of a whole, not absolute amounts. Treating them as plain numbers can produce false results. They show how methods built for parts-of-a-whole data avoid those traps. Anyone who analyzes microbiome data needs this warning, because the choice of math shapes every claim that follows from the numbers.
pmc-5850834:
Jaime Huerta-Cepas and colleagues presented eggNOG-mapper for fast genome annotation in 2017. Genes that descend from a shared ancestor often keep the same job, so ancestry can predict function. Working out that ancestry for whole genomes is slow with older pipelines.

The mapper assigns genes to known orthology groups using precomputed data, which makes the job much faster. It then transfers careful functional notes from well-studied relatives. Accuracy stays close to slower expert methods in the authors tests. For teams facing thousands of genomes, the tool turns annotation from a bottleneck into a routine step.
pmc-5976434:
Gibran Hemani, Jie Zheng, Ben Elsworth, and many colleagues presented the MR-Base platform in 2018. Large genetic studies can be used to test causal links between traits. The method uses summary results only, so no private individual data are needed.

MR-Base gathers results from many studies into one place and runs the causal tests in a uniform way. Users can probe thousands of trait pairs in a systematic scan. Built-in checks probe for bias from pleiotropy. The platform turned a specialist method into a routine screen that many groups now run before deeper work.
pmc-6086934:
Amit Zeisel, Hannah Hochgerner, Peter Lönnerberg, and a large team mapped the mouse nervous system in 2018. The nervous system runs complex behavior through many specialized cell types. Their locations and partnerships matter as much as their names.

Sequencing RNA from about half a million single cells, the team built a census of cell types across brain regions. They charted where each type sits and how types relate. Rare types that bulk sampling had missed came into view. The atlas gives neuroscience a shared parts list for studying circuits, disease models, and drug action.
pmc-6602434:
Kai Blin, Simon Shaw, Kai Steinke, and coauthors described antiSMASH version 5.0 in 2019. Bacteria and fungi make secondary metabolites that include many antibiotics and other useful compounds. Genome mining hunts the gene clusters that build them.

antiSMASH scans a genome and flags clusters likely to produce such compounds. It compares each cluster with known ones and predicts the product family. The update speeds the pipeline and adds new cluster types. Natural product researchers use it as the first sieve when a new genome might hide a new drug lead each year.
pmc-6939334:
Ruei-Min Lu, Yu-Chen Hwang, I-Ju Liu, and coauthors reviewed therapeutic antibodies in 2020. More than three decades have passed since the first monoclonal antibody drug approval. Engineering since then has made antibodies safer and more precise.

The review follows that progress, from mouse-based antibodies to fully human designs. It surveys formats such as bispecific antibodies and antibody-drug pairs that carry a toxic payload. Approved uses now span cancer, autoimmunity, and infection. Readers see how a once fragile drug class became a mainstay of modern medicine. Safety data from approved products are reviewed to show how newer designs lowered immune reactions.
pmc-7615134:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled worldwide measurements in 2016 to chart how adult body weight changed across four decades. Their analysis combined nearly seventeen hundred population based studies, covering close to twenty million participants in two hundred countries from 1975 to 2014. From height and weight records they estimated body-mass index trends, the standard yardstick for sorting people from underweight through severe obesity.

The results show obesity rising across most of the world while underweight slowly receded, with sharp differences between regions. Both ends of the scale carry raised risks of serious illness and early death. Because the study used measured bodies rather than self reports, its trends became a benchmark for tracking one of the defining health shifts of the modern era.
pmc-9617234:
Laura Damschroder and colleagues published in 2022 an updated version of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, a widely used guide for putting health programs into practice. Many well planned efforts fail because the setting pushes back: staffing, culture, money, and workflow can overpower a good plan. The framework, known as CFIR, is among the most common tools for analyzing those contextual forces in advance.

The update was shaped by feedback from people who use the framework in real projects. The authors describe what users found unclear or missing and how the revised version answers them. Implementation scientists and health system leaders use CFIR to design rollouts and to diagnose why a program that worked in one hospital stumbles in another.
pmc-9825434:
Damian Szklarczyk and colleagues presented the 2023 edition of the STRING database, which maps associations between proteins for any sequenced genome. Much of a cell's complexity comes from proteins interacting and regulating one another. The core of that interaction web is increasingly known, yet new links still surface constantly, and the records are scattered across many databases.

STRING gathers those associations into one network resource and pairs it with enrichment analysis, which tests what a set of proteins does collectively. The update extends coverage to newly sequenced organisms and refreshes the underlying evidence. Researchers use it to move from a list of genes to a picture of the machinery those genes run.
poems-pg1034:
Wilfred Owen wrote the poems in this posthumous volume out of the trenches of the First World War, and Siegfried Sassoon, his fellow soldier-poet, supplied the introduction. Sassoon refuses to commend the work at length, saying the poems speak for themselves, backed by Owen's experience as an infantry soldier. He praises Owen's experiments in assonance and points readers to Strange Meeting and Greater Love as the finest examples of his power.
